name: EquiGraspFlow
resolvedTitle: EquiGraspFlow: SE(3)-Equivariant 6-DoF Grasp Pose Generative Flows
org: Seoul National University; Korea Institute for Advanced Study (KIAS); SAIGE
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Generative 6-DoF grasp models (6-DOF GraspNet, SE(3)-DiffusionFields) are not SE(3)-equivariant, so generated grasps do not transform correctly when the object is rotated/translated, and they rely on rotation data augmentation.
keyIdea: Model the grasp distribution as a conditional continuous normalizing flow on SE(3) trained with flow matching, and guarantee SE(3)-equivariance by construction: an SE(3)-invariant prior pushed through SE(3)-equivariant angular/linear velocity fields yields an invariant conditional grasp distribution.
architecture: Vector Neuron DGCNN point-cloud encoder (341 3D-vector features) + a novel equivariant 'lifting layer' that lifts the scalar time t to a 3D vector + VN-MLP outputting angular and linear velocity fields; trained with flow matching (rotation and translation separated) plus Guided Flows (classifier-free guidance); sampled with a 4th-order Runge-Kutta-Munthe-Kaas Lie-group ODE solver, 20 steps.
inputs: Object point cloud (1,024 points; full in main experiments, 512-point partial clouds in appendix)
outputs: Set of 6-DoF parallel-jaw (Franka Panda) grasp poses in SE(3)
actionRepr: Grasp pose generator, not a policy: SE(3) grasp poses sampled by integrating learned equivariant velocity fields (flow matching)
trainingData: ACRONYM subset: 175 laptops, 94 mugs, 38 bowls, 82 pencils (single unified model); ~1.1k-1.7k grasps per object on average

headlineResults.benchmark: Real world (Franka Panda, 2 mugs + 2 bowls incl. rotated poses)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces SE(3)-DiffusionFields' score-based diffusion (equivariance only via augmentation) with an equivariant-by-construction CNF on SE(3) trained by flow matching, needing no extra SDF data and sampling about 6x faster.
limitations: Trained on full (fused multi-view) object point clouds, so occlusion can hurt (partial-cloud results only in appendix); generates grasps without considering obstacles, so real deployment needs a separate collision checker; single isolated objects only.
notes: Code: https://github.com/bdlim99/EquiGraspFlow (paper states code available; release of trained checkpoints not verified). CoRL 2024 (PMLR v270), not on arXiv; project page https://equigraspflow.github.io/. Real-world full point clouds were built by fusing partial views from a wrist RealSense D435 with Language Segment-Anything segmentation. Evaluated on isolated objects, not clutter. Later reused as grasp generator in SE(3)-PoseFlow (arXiv 2511.01501) for uncertainty-aware grasping.

name: Implicit Grasp Diffusion
resolvedTitle: Implicit Grasp Diffusion: Bridging the Gap between Dense Prediction and Sampling-based Grasping
org: KU Leuven; HKUST (Guangzhou)
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Dense-prediction grasp detectors (VGN, GIGA) predict a fixed number of grasps per voxel and miss multi-modal orientations, while sampling-based generative methods (6DoF-GraspNet, SE(3)-DiffusionFields) use a global latent code that fails in cluttered multi-object scenes.
keyIdea: Query local features from an implicit tri-plane scene representation at a grasp center and run a diffusion model conditioned on that local feature to sample multiple grasp orientations per point, then filter with a two-stage probabilistic evaluator.
architecture: GIGA/ConvONet-style tri-plane feature encoder over a TSDF (3D conv, projection to XY/XZ/YZ planes, 2D U-Net) + Deformable Attention Module that aggregates features at learned offsets; Grasp Orientation Diffuser (MLP noise predictor, DDPM on quaternions); Two-stage Probabilistic Grasp Evaluator (Affordance Evaluator + Grasp Classifier with SE(3)-equivariant grasp-conditioned deformable attention over gripper control points, focal loss with sampled negatives); width predictor and occupancy head.
inputs: Single-view depth image converted to TSDF (40x40x40 query grid over 30 cm workspace)
outputs: 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasps (position, orientation, width) with quality scores
actionRepr: Grasp detector, not a policy: grasp orientation (quaternion) sampled by DDPM at each candidate grasp center; best-scoring grasp executed
trainingData: GIGA's open-source simulated grasp data (PyBullet), 303 training objects / 40 test objects (VGN/GIGA object sets); pile and packed scenes
whatChangedVsParent: Keeps GIGA's implicit tri-plane local features but replaces its single regressed orientation per point with a diffusion model that samples multi-modal orientations, plus deformable attention and a two-stage evaluator.
limitations: Still must query a 40x40x40 grid to find high-affordance points (inherited from GIGA); diffusion makes it slower than dense predictors; diffuses quaternions directly (not a proper rotation-manifold diffusion); failures on large/smooth objects, occluded borders, and thin objects due to low-res depth-only TSDF.
notes: Code: https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/detry-lab/public/implicit-grasp-diffusion.git (checkpoint release not verified). CoRL 2024 (PMLR v270), not on arXiv; PDF also at renaud-detry.net/assets/pdf/Song-2024-CoRL.pdf. Abbreviated IGD. Sim numbers averaged over 100 rounds x 5 seeds; real world 15 rounds per scene type with 5 objects each. Supplementary shows better robustness than GIGA under simulated depth noise.

name: DQN
resolvedTitle: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning
org: DeepMind Technologies
problem: RL from raw high-dimensional sensory input (pixels) had relied on hand-crafted features with linear value functions; deep nets were thought unstable with Q-learning because of correlated samples and non-stationary data distributions.
keyIdea: Train a convolutional Q-network end-to-end from pixels with a Q-learning variant, using experience replay (uniform sampling from a memory of past transitions) to decorrelate data and smooth the behaviour distribution.
architecture: CNN on an 84x84x4 stack of preprocessed grayscale frames: conv 16 8x8 stride 4 -> conv 32 4x4 stride 2 -> FC 256 ReLU -> linear output with one Q-value per valid action (4-18 actions). One forward pass gives Q for all actions.
inputs: Last 4 Atari frames, grayscale, downsampled to 110x84 and cropped to 84x84; clipped rewards (+1/-1/0).
outputs: Q-values for each discrete action; epsilon-greedy action selection.
actionRepr: Single discrete action (argmax over 4-18 joystick actions), repeated for k=4 frames (k=3 on Space Invaders).
trainingData: Online interaction with 7 Atari 2600 games (ALE): 10M frames per game, replay memory of 1M most recent frames.

headlineResults.metric: games beating prior RL / expert human
headlineResults.value: outperforms prior approaches on 6/7; surpasses human expert on 3 (Breakout, Enduro, Pong)

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike NFQ's batch RPROP updates on a learned low-d code, DQN does stochastic minibatch Q-learning end-to-end from raw pixels with an experience-replay memory.
limitations: Uniform replay sampling and a finite overwrite-oldest buffer do not prioritize important transitions; games needing long-horizon strategies (Q*bert, Seaquest, Space Invaders) remain far below human.
notes: Resolved to the 2013 arXiv workshop paper. The better-known Nature 2015 version ('Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning', Mnih et al.) is not on arXiv and could not be read; it adds the separate periodically-copied target network and 49-game evaluation. CONFLICT (potential): surveys often describe DQN as 'experience replay + target network'; the 2013 paper itself has NO separate target network (target uses current weights theta; loss defined with theta_{i-1}). Target network comes from the 2015 Nature paper (general knowledge, not verified here). Relevance to robotics: DQN is discrete-action, so it motivated DDPG/QT-Opt for continuous control.

keyEquations.meaning: Q-network regressed onto one-step Bellman targets computed with previous-iteration weights.
Bellman optimality equation the Q-network approximates.

algorithmSteps: Initialize replay memory D (capacity N) and Q-network with random weights.
Preprocess last 4 frames into phi(s_t).
With prob. epsilon pick random action, else argmax_a Q(phi(s_t),a).
Execute action (repeated over k frames), observe clipped reward and next frame.
Store transition (phi_t, a_t, r_t, phi_{t+1}) in D.
Sample random minibatch from D; set y_j = r_j (terminal) or r_j + gamma max_a' Q(phi_{j+1},a').
Gradient step on (y_j - Q(phi_j,a_j))^2 with RMSProp.
hyperparams: RMSProp, minibatch 32; epsilon annealed 1->0.1 over first 1M frames then fixed; 10M training frames; replay memory 1M frames; frame skip k=4 (3 for Space Invaders); rewards clipped to {-1,0,+1}; eval epsilon=0.05.

name: DDPG
resolvedTitle: Continuous control with deep reinforcement learning
org: Google DeepMind
problem: DQN only handles discrete, low-dimensional action spaces; discretizing continuous robot actions explodes combinatorially (e.g. 3^7 = 2187 actions for a coarse 7-DoF arm), and naive DPG with neural nets is unstable.
keyIdea: Deep DPG: an off-policy actor-critic where a deterministic actor mu(s) is trained by backpropagating the critic's action-gradient, stabilized with DQN's replay buffer plus 'soft' target networks and batch normalization.
architecture: Actor mu(s|theta_mu) and critic Q(s,a|theta_Q) MLPs (low-d: 400 and 300 hidden units, ~130k params, action enters critic at 2nd hidden layer; pixels: 3 conv layers of 32 filters + two FC-200 layers, ~430k params). Target copies mu', Q' updated by Polyak averaging; tanh output on actor; batch norm on state input and layers.
inputs: Low-dimensional state (joint angles, positions) or pixels: 3 action-repeated 64x64 RGB renderings stacked (9 feature maps).
outputs: Deterministic continuous action a = mu(s) (tanh-bounded) plus exploration noise at training time.
actionRepr: Single continuous action vector per step (e.g. joint torques), deterministic, tanh-bounded; Ornstein-Uhlenbeck exploration noise added.
trainingData: Online interaction in 20+ MuJoCo physics tasks (cartpole, reacher, gripper, puck-hitting, cheetah, walker, hopper, etc.) plus Torcs; at most 2.5M steps per task.

headlineResults.metric: normalized reward (random=0, iLQG=1), avg / best, low-d
raw reward, best low-d / best pixels

whatChangedVsParent: Adds DQN-style replay buffer, soft-updated target actor and critic, and batch normalization to DPG so it scales to deep nets and pixels.
limitations: As with most model-free RL, DDPG requires a large number of training episodes; Q estimates are less accurate on harder tasks and some Torcs replicas failed to learn.
notes: Summary claim in paper: most problems solved within 2.5M steps, ~20x fewer than DQN needs for Atari. Later literature (SAC paper, used in this batch) characterizes DDPG as brittle and hyperparameter-sensitive, failing on Ant/Humanoid.

keyEquations.tex: L(\theta^Q) = \mathbb{E}_{s_t\sim\rho^\beta,a_t\sim\beta,r_t\sim E}\left[\left(Q(s_t,a_t|\theta^Q) - y_t\right)^2\right],\quad y_i = r_i + \gamma Q'(s_{i+1}, \mu'(s_{i+1}|\theta^{\mu'})|\theta^{Q'})
keyEquations.meaning: Critic TD regression with targets from target actor and target critic.
Deterministic policy gradient: move actor along critic's action-gradient.
Soft target-network update, tau << 1.
Exploration policy: actor plus OU noise.

algorithmSteps: Initialize actor, critic, their target copies, and replay buffer R.
Act a_t = mu(s_t) + N_t (OU noise); store (s_t,a_t,r_t,s_t+1) in R.
Sample minibatch of N transitions from R.
Compute y_i = r_i + gamma Q'(s_{i+1}, mu'(s_{i+1})).
Update critic by minimizing mean (y_i - Q(s_i,a_i))^2.
Update actor with sampled deterministic policy gradient.
Soft-update target networks with tau.
ablations: Without target networks (original DPG) learning is 'very poor in many environments'; both target nets and batch norm were needed to do well on all tasks (Fig. 2, curves only).
Having both a target actor and target critic was required for stable critic targets.
Original DPG with replay + BN (cntrl) averages e.g. -0.008 on cheetah vs 0.903 for DDPG (Table 1).
hyperparams: Adam lr 1e-4 actor / 1e-3 critic; critic L2 weight decay 1e-2; gamma 0.99; tau 0.001; replay 1e6; minibatch 64 (low-d) / 16 (pixels); OU noise theta 0.15, sigma 0.2; action repeat 3 for pixels, 64x64 frames.

name: SAC
resolvedTitle: Soft Actor-Critic: Off-Policy Maximum Entropy Deep Reinforcement Learning with a Stochastic Actor
org: UC Berkeley (BAIR)
problem: Model-free deep RL suffers from high sample complexity (on-policy TRPO/PPO/A3C) and brittle, hyperparameter-sensitive convergence (off-policy DDPG); prior max-entropy off-policy methods (soft Q-learning) needed complex approximate inference.
keyIdea: An off-policy actor-critic in the maximum-entropy framework: maximize reward plus policy entropy, derived from provably convergent soft policy iteration, with a reparameterized stochastic Gaussian actor.
architecture: Soft state-value network V_psi with target V_psibar (EMA), two soft Q-networks Q_theta1,2 (min used for value and policy gradients), and a tanh-squashed Gaussian policy pi_phi; all MLPs with 2 hidden layers of 256 ReLU units.
inputs: Low-dimensional state observations (MuJoCo/rllab tasks).
outputs: Stochastic continuous action sampled from tanh-squashed Gaussian; mean action used for deterministic evaluation.
actionRepr: Single continuous action per step from a tanh-squashed Gaussian (reparameterized).
trainingData: Online interaction on OpenAI Gym Hopper, Walker2d, HalfCheetah, Ant, Humanoid (v1) and rllab Humanoid; replay buffer 1e6.

headlineResults.value: SAC learns; DDPG fails to make any progress
comparable on easier tasks, outperforms by a large margin on harder tasks

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces SQL's amortized sampler with a true actor-critic (soft policy iteration) and DDPG's deterministic actor with an entropy-maximizing stochastic actor, gaining stability across seeds.
limitations: Particularly sensitive to reward scale (acts as inverse temperature), which must be tuned per environment; target smoothing tau trades stability vs speed.
notes: Paper gives results as learning curves only (no numeric table of returns), so no headline numbers are quoted. The later follow-up 'Soft Actor-Critic Algorithms and Applications' (arXiv 1812.05905) adds automatic temperature tuning and drops V network; RLPD/SERL rely on that SAC variant (SERL states adaptively adjusted alpha). Humanoid rllab has 21 action dims.

keyEquations.meaning: Maximum-entropy RL objective: reward plus temperature-weighted policy entropy.
Soft Bellman residual for Q using target value network.
Soft value regression onto Q minus log-probability.
Reparameterized policy loss (KL to exp(Q)).

algorithmSteps: Initialize psi, psibar, theta_1, theta_2, phi.
For each environment step: sample a_t ~ pi_phi(.|s_t), step env, add transition to D.
For each gradient step: update V_psi on J_V.
Update both Q_theta_i on J_Q.
Update policy phi on J_pi via reparameterization (using min of two Qs).
Update target psibar <- tau psi + (1-tau) psibar.
ablations: Deterministic variant (DDPG-like, no entropy) shows very high variability across seeds on Humanoid (rllab); stochastic entropy-maximizing policy drastically stabilizes training (curves).
Reward scale on Ant-v1 swept 1/3/10/30/100: too small -> near-uniform policy fails; too large -> near-deterministic, poor local minima.
Target smoothing tau swept 0.0001-0.1: large tau unstable, small tau slow; 0.005 used across tasks. Two Q-functions significantly speed up training on harder tasks.
hyperparams: Adam lr 3e-4; gamma 0.99; replay 1e6; 2 hidden layers x 256 units; minibatch 256; tau 0.005; 1 gradient step per env step; reward scale 5 (Hopper/Walker/HalfCheetah/Ant), 20 (Humanoid-v1), 10 (Humanoid rllab).

name: PPO
resolvedTitle: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms
org: OpenAI
problem: Vanilla policy gradients are data-inefficient and taking multiple steps on the same batch causes destructively large updates; TRPO fixes this but is complex (second-order, conjugate gradient) and incompatible with dropout or policy/value parameter sharing.
keyIdea: Optimize a clipped surrogate objective that removes the incentive to move the probability ratio outside [1-eps, 1+eps], allowing several epochs of first-order minibatch SGD per batch of on-policy data.
architecture: Actor-critic: for MuJoCo, policy MLP with two 64-unit tanh hidden layers outputting Gaussian mean (state-independent learned std), separate value network; for Atari, the A3C/A2C CNN. Advantages via truncated GAE.
inputs: Environment state (MuJoCo) or pixels (Atari).
outputs: Stochastic policy (Gaussian for continuous, categorical for Atari) and state-value estimate.
actionRepr: Single action per step sampled from a Gaussian (continuous) or categorical (discrete) policy.
trainingData: On-policy rollouts: 7 MuJoCo Gym tasks for 1M timesteps; Roboschool humanoid tasks (50M-100M timesteps); 49 Atari games for 40M frames (10M timesteps).

headlineResults.comparedTo: no clipping/penalty -0.39; best adaptive KL 0.74; best fixed KL 0.72

headlineResults.metric: games won, avg reward over all training
games won, avg reward last 100 episodes

headlineResults.comparedTo: TRPO, CEM, vanilla PG adaptive, A2C, A2C+trust region

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces TRPO's KL-constrained second-order update with a clipped (or adaptive-KL-penalized) surrogate optimized by first-order SGD for multiple epochs.
limitations: On Atari final performance PPO wins fewer games than ACER (19 vs 28); the KL-penalty variant underperforms clipping; the method is on-policy and needs fresh samples each iteration.
notes: Robotics relevance: default algorithm for massively parallel sim-to-real locomotion/humanoid RL (e.g. Isaac Gym pipelines) and for RL fine-tuning of policies. OpenAI released baselines code (not weights).

keyEquations.meaning: Pessimistic clipped surrogate limiting policy change per update.
Combined objective with value loss and entropy bonus for shared networks.
Truncated generalized advantage estimation.
Alternative adaptive-KL-penalty surrogate (beta halved/doubled toward d_targ).

algorithmSteps: For each iteration, each of N parallel actors runs pi_theta_old for T timesteps.
Compute advantage estimates A_1..A_T (truncated GAE with learned V).
Build surrogate L (clipped, + value loss + entropy) on the N*T samples.
Optimize for K epochs with minibatch size M <= N*T (Adam).
Set theta_old <- theta and repeat.
ablations: Clip eps=0.2 scores 0.82 vs eps=0.1 0.76 and eps=0.3 0.70 (avg normalized, 7 MuJoCo tasks).
No clipping or penalty scores -0.39 (HalfCheetah worse than random).
Adaptive KL best 0.74 (d_targ=0.01); fixed KL best 0.72 (beta=3); both below clipping.
hyperparams: MuJoCo: T=2048, Adam 3e-4, 10 epochs, minibatch 64, gamma 0.99, GAE lambda 0.95, eps 0.2. Atari: T=128, Adam 2.5e-4*alpha, 3 epochs, minibatch 32*8, 8 actors, eps 0.1*alpha, c1=1, c2=0.01 (alpha annealed 1->0). Roboschool: T=512, 15 epochs, minibatch 4096, 32/128 actors.

name: QT-Opt
resolvedTitle: QT-Opt: Scalable Deep Reinforcement Learning for Vision-Based Robotic Manipulation
org: Google Brain; X; UC Berkeley
problem: Grasping systems typically pick a grasp open-loop and fail to generalize; continuous-action actor-critic methods are unstable at the scale needed to learn closed-loop, vision-based grasping from large real-world off-policy datasets.
keyIdea: Train only a Q-function (no actor) on large off-policy real-robot data and induce the policy by maximizing Q over continuous actions with the cross-entropy method (CEM), both for targets and for acting, in a distributed asynchronous system.
architecture: Large CNN Q-function (1.2M params): 472x472 RGB image through conv stack, with action, gripper status and height embedded by FC layers and merged mid-stack; sigmoid output Q in [0,1]. Two target nets (Polyak 0.9999 and a further ~6000-step-lagged copy) for clipped double-Q. Distributed replay buffer, 1000 Bellman-updater jobs running CEM, 10 GPU training workers.
inputs: Monocular over-the-shoulder RGB image (472x472), binary gripper open/closed status, gripper height above bin floor.
outputs: Q(s,a) in [0,1]; action chosen by CEM argmax.
actionRepr: Continuous Cartesian gripper displacement t in R^3 + azimuthal rotation as sin-cos r in R^2, plus binary gripper open/close commands and a binary terminate-episode command; one action per closed-loop step, optimized by CEM (not a learned actor).
trainingData: 580k real grasp attempts on 7 KUKA LBR IIWA robots (~800 robot hours, ~1000 training objects) off-policy, plus ~28k on-policy grasps for joint finetuning; bootstrapped by a scripted policy with 15-30% success.

headlineResults.comparedTo: Levine et al. 67% on 400k grasps of same dataset

whatChangedVsParent: Versus Levine et al.'s greedy 1-step grasp-success classifier, QT-Opt optimizes long-horizon return with Q-learning, controls gripper open/close and termination, enabling regrasping and pre-grasp manipulation.
limitations: Needs very large data (580k grasps, ~800 robot hours) and up to 15M gradient steps; failures on very small objects stuck in bin corners and soft objects (octopus toy) slipping after lift; relies on a scripted bootstrap policy because sparse reward makes random exploration too inefficient.
notes: Reward: +1 for successful lift (background-subtraction check), 0 otherwise, -0.05 per timestep penalty. Cross-entropy Bellman loss used instead of squared error because returns are bounded in [0,1]. Successor: MT-Opt (multi-task). Exploration later uses epsilon-greedy with eps=20%.

keyEquations.meaning: Bellman error with cross-entropy divergence D against target value.
Clipped double-Q target with Polyak-averaged and lagged target nets; argmax via CEM.
Implicit policy: CEM maximization of the Q-function.

algorithmSteps: Bootstrap data with scripted exploration policy (15-30% success) into replay buffer.
Bellman updaters sample transitions and run CEM (N=64, M=6, 2 iters) on target Q to get argmax a'.
Compute clipped double-Q target r + gamma*V(s') and push to training buffer.
Training workers minimize cross-entropy Bellman loss with SGD+momentum.
Update Polyak target (0.9999) and lagged second target.
At test time each step: CEM over Q(s,a) chooses action (incl. gripper and terminate).
Optionally joint-finetune with on-policy data mixed with offline data.
ablations: State: image only 53% vs +gripper status 58% vs +gripper status+height 70% (off-policy, real).
Clipped double Q-learning 81% vs double Q-learning 63% (off-policy, real).
Reward: -0.05 per-step penalty 63% vs no penalty 53% vs discount 0.7 28% (image only); 320k vs 580k grasps: 78% vs 87%.
hyperparams: CEM N=64 samples, M=6 elites, 2 iterations; Polyak 0.9999; second target lagged ~6000 grad steps; 1000 Bellman updaters, 10 training workers; up to 15M gradient steps; reward +1 success, -0.05/step; image 472x472; eps-greedy 20% for later exploration.

name: RLPD
resolvedTitle: Efficient Online Reinforcement Learning with Offline Data
org: University of Oxford; UC Berkeley
problem: Using offline data (demos or sub-optimal trajectories) to speed up online RL usually needs offline pre-training or behaviour constraints; naively adding it to an off-policy learner's buffer (SACfD) performs poorly due to Q-value over-extrapolation.
keyIdea: Minimal changes to SAC make it effective with prior data: symmetric 50/50 online/offline batch sampling, LayerNorm in the critic to bound extrapolation, and large critic ensembles enabling high update-to-data ratios, plus an environment-specific design-choice workflow.
architecture: SAC-based actor-critic with an ensemble of E (default 10) LayerNorm critics (3-layer MLPs recommended), target computed as min over a random subset Z of critics; optional entropy backup; random-shift augmentation for pixels.
inputs: State or pixel observations (V-D4RL) plus an offline dataset D of (s,a,r,s') tuples.
outputs: Stochastic continuous action from SAC actor.
actionRepr: Single continuous action per step from a SAC (tanh-Gaussian) actor.
trainingData: Online RL from scratch with offline buffers: Sparse Adroit (human demos + BC-policy data), D4RL AntMaze (6 tasks, sub-optimal), D4RL Locomotion (12 tasks), V-D4RL pixel locomotion (medium/expert). 21 state-based tasks total.

headlineResults.value: first to effectively 'solve' all AntMaze tasks, in < 1/3 of prior time-step budget

headlineResults.metric: online samples to match pre-trained prior SoTA
headlineResults.value: on the order of 10k online samples
still exceeds prior work; removing LayerNorm collapses to no progress

whatChangedVsParent: Adds symmetric sampling, critic LayerNorm, large ensembles/high UTD and drops CDQ/entropy backups where harmful, turning SAC into a strong online-with-offline-data learner without pre-training.
limitations: Several design choices (clipped double Q, entropy backups, depth) are environment-sensitive and must be ablated per domain; pure offline sampling (100% offline) fails, so it relies on online interaction; LayerNorm slightly hurts mean performance on Adroit Relocate.
notes: Code released (github.com/ikostrikov/rlpd, JAX). Core algorithm of SERL and later HIL-SERL. Paper reports mostly curves; 2.5x Door and AntMaze claims are the explicit numbers. First demonstration (per authors) of UTD=10 improving model-free pixel-based continuous control.

keyEquations.meaning: With LayerNorm, Q-values are bounded by final-layer weight norm, even for OOD actions.
Critic target: min over random subset Z of ensemble target critics (optional entropy term).

symbols.meaning: random subset of Z in {1,2} critics

keyEquations.meaning: Actor maximizes ensemble-mean Q with entropy regularization.

algorithmSteps: Choose LayerNorm, ensemble size E, gradient steps G (UTD), architecture; init E critics + targets, actor.
Load offline data into D; empty online buffer R.
Act a_t ~ pi_phi, store transition in R.
For g = 1..G: sample N/2 from R and N/2 from D.
Sample Z critic indices; compute y = r + gamma min_{i in Z} Q'_i(s', a~') (optionally + entropy).
Update all E critics on MSE to y; EMA-update targets.
Update actor to maximize ensemble-mean Q minus alpha log pi.
ablations: Removing LayerNorm on Expert Adroit Sparse (22 trajectories) collapses performance to no progress on any task.
Clipped double-Q (subset 2) hurts AntMaze Large Diverse and Humanoid Walk Expert; subsetting 1 critic recovers performance; entropy backups and 2-layer nets always worse on hard tasks.
10-member ensemble beats standard 2-critic on pixel tasks; symmetric sampling beats seeding buffer with offline data; 100% offline sampling fails.
hyperparams: Symmetric sampling 50% offline / 50% online per batch; ensemble E=10; target subset Z=2 by default (1 where CDQ hurts); 3-layer MLPs; LayerNorm in critic; entropy backup removed as starting point; UTD=10 shown for pixels; 10 seeds per experiment.

name: SERL
resolvedTitle: SERL: A Software Suite for Sample-Efficient Robotic Reinforcement Learning
org: UC Berkeley; University of Washington; Stanford; Intrinsic
problem: Real-world robotic RL is hard to adopt because implementation details (reward specification, resets, controllers, sample efficiency) matter as much as the algorithm, and no vertically integrated open-source stack existed.
keyIdea: An open-source, out-of-the-box real-robot RL stack: RLPD with demos, image-based reward classifiers (or VICE), forward-backward reset-free training, an impedance controller with reference clipping for safe contact, and relative observation/action frames.
architecture: RLPD (SAC variant: high UTD, 50/50 demo/online sampling, LayerNorm critic, adaptive entropy) with ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-10 vision encoder + 2-layer MLP; separate actor and learner processes; Gym-style robot env wrappers; 10 Hz policy over 1 kHz impedance controller with clipped reference error.
inputs: Wrist camera images (2 wrist cams; 1 wrist + 1 side for relocation) plus proprioception (end-effector pose, twist, force, torque) expressed relative to episode-initial EE frame.
outputs: 6D end-effector delta pose (twist) relative to current EE frame, tracked by impedance controller; gripper for relocation.
actionRepr: Single continuous 6D relative end-effector delta pose per 10 Hz step (SAC tanh-Gaussian), tracked by 1 kHz impedance controller with reference clipping.
trainingData: 20 SpaceMouse teleoperated demonstrations per task + online real-world RL on a Franka Panda; single RTX 4090.

headlineResults.comparedTo: BC with 100 demos: RL 10x higher success

headlineResults.value: RL at least 2x faster than BC; up to 3x faster than human demos

whatChangedVsParent: Not a new algorithm: packages RLPD with reward classifiers, reset-free forward/backward agents, a clipped-reference impedance controller and relative frames into a real-robot system.
limitations: Not a comprehensive library of RL methods and may not cover non-manipulation tasks; classifier-based rewards and forward-backward resets may not suit every setting; reward specification and reset-free learning remain open problems.
notes: Code open-sourced (serl-robot.github.io). Compared with prior insertion systems (Table 1): DDPGfD 97%/77% in 1.5-2.5 h, SHIELD 99.8% in 1.5 h, InsertionNet 78.5-100% in 40 min; SERL 100% in 20 min on PCB with no reward shaping. UTD ratio value not stated in the text read. Successor: HIL-SERL (human-in-the-loop corrections).

keyEquations.meaning: Critic TD loss with target network; batches half demos, half online.
Actor loss with adaptively weighted entropy regularization.
Reward from binary success classifier (optionally trained adversarially via VICE).

keyEquations.tex: F = k_p\cdot e + k_d\cdot\dot{e} + F_{ff} + F_{cor},\quad e = p - p_{ref},\ |e|\le\Delta
keyEquations.meaning: Impedance control law with clipped reference error bounding contact force.

algorithmSteps: Collect 20 teleoperated demos; optionally train success classifier (or use VICE / hand-specified reward).
Randomize initial EE pose; express proprioception relative to initial EE frame.
Actor node runs policy at 10 Hz, outputting 6D relative delta pose; impedance controller tracks at 1 kHz with clipped reference.
Transitions and classifier rewards streamed to learner.
Learner performs RLPD updates (50/50 demo/online batches, LayerNorm critic, high UTD) asynchronously.
For reset-free tasks, alternate forward and backward agents, each with own policy, Q and reward.
hyperparams: 20 demos per task; ResNet-10 (ImageNet pretrained) encoder + 2-layer MLP; policy 10 Hz, impedance 1 kHz (M=100 control steps per RL step); 50/50 symmetric sampling; LayerNorm critic; adaptive entropy alpha; single RTX 4090.

name: HIL-SERL
resolvedTitle: Precise and Dexterous Robotic Manipulation via Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning
org: UC Berkeley (EECS)
problem: Real-world vision-based RL has been too sample-inefficient, unstable and reward-hungry to learn precise, dynamic and dual-arm manipulation skills that beat imitation learning and hand-designed controllers in practical training time.
keyIdea: Combine a sample-efficient off-policy RL algorithm (RLPD) with a few demos plus online human corrections via SpaceMouse, a pretrained vision backbone, a learned binary success classifier as sparse reward, and careful low-level controller design, so policies reach near-perfect success in 1-2.5 hours of real training.
architecture: Distributed actor/learner system with two replay buffers (demo buffer and RL buffer). Images from wrist/side cameras (cropped, 128x128) pass through a shared ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-10; embeddings are concatenated with proprioception into an MLP actor-critic trained with RLPD; a separate grasp critic trained with DQN picks discrete gripper actions.
inputs: RGB images from wrist and/or side cameras (128x128), end-effector pose, twist, force/torque, gripper status (relative/ego-centric frame)
outputs: Continuous end-effector action (6D Cartesian twist target for impedance controller, or feedforward wrench for dynamic tasks) plus discrete gripper command
actionRepr: single-step continuous 6D Cartesian twist (per arm) relative to current EE frame for an impedance controller, or feedforward EE wrench for dynamic tasks; discrete gripper actions {open, close, stay} (3^2=9 combos for two grippers) chosen by argmax of a DQN grasp critic
trainingData: Per task: ~200 positive + ~1000 negative teleoperated frames for the reward classifier (~5 min), 20-30 human demonstrations, then online RL with human interventions; 1-2.5 h of real-world training on most tasks (6 h for timing belt).

headlineResults.benchmark: 13 real-world task settings (7 tasks incl. sub-tasks), 100 trials each
RAM insertion / Dashboard assembly / Object flipping (avg)
headlineResults.comparedTo: DP 34%, HG-DAgger 39%, BC 31%, IBRL 57%, Residual RL 32%, DAPG 33%

whatChangedVsParent: Adds online human corrections (stored in both demo and RL buffers) and a discrete DQN grasp critic to SERL, extending it to dual-arm, dynamic and flexible-object tasks.
limitations: Scaling to significantly longer-horizon tasks remains challenging (suggested fixes: pretraining or automatic task segmentation with VLMs); experiments did not involve extensive randomization or truly unstructured environments, so generalization there is untested.
notes: Code released at hil-serl.github.io (per abstract); checkpoint release not verified. Training compute: onboard single NVIDIA RTX 4090. Ablations in Table 1b: HIL-SERL without demos or interventions = 0% on all three tasks; with demos but no interventions (SERL-like, 200 demos) = 49% avg. Paper warns that persistently giving long sparse interventions that lead to success causes value overestimation and unstable training. The 1000 Hz impedance-controller rate appears in secondary summaries but was not verified in the pages read.

keyEquations.meaning: RLPD critic loss: TD regression to target network, batches half demo/intervention data, half on-policy data.
Actor loss: maximize Q plus entropy bonus with adaptive weight (SAC-style).
Double-DQN loss for the discrete gripper critic.

algorithmSteps: Choose wrist/side cameras, crop and resize images to 128x128.
Teleoperate ~200 positive / ~1000 negative frames; train binary success classifier (>95% accuracy).
Collect 20-30 demonstrations into the demo buffer.
Run policy on robot; classifier gives sparse 0/1 reward.
Human intervenes via SpaceMouse when needed; interventions go to both buffers, policy transitions only to RL buffer.
Learner samples 50/50 from demo and RL buffers, updates actor-critic with RLPD and grasp critic with DQN.
Reduce intervention frequency as success rises until fully autonomous.
ablations: RL from scratch (no demos, no interventions): 0% success on RAM insertion, dashboard assembly, object flipping.
Demos but no interventions: 48% RAM, 0% dashboard, 100% flipping (avg 49%) vs 100% with interventions.
Diffusion Policy with 200 demos: 27% RAM insertion, 18% dashboard, 56% flipping.
hyperparams: Image 128x128; ResNet-10 ImageNet-pretrained encoder; 20-30 demos; 50/50 demo/RL batch sampling (RLPD); discrete gripper action space 3 per gripper; sparse binary reward; small penalty on gripper actions.

name: Residual RL (Johannink)
resolvedTitle: Residual Reinforcement Learning for Robot Control
org: Siemens Corporation; UC Berkeley; Hamburg University of Technology
problem: Conventional feedback controllers are efficient but brittle for contact- and friction-rich manufacturing tasks, while pure RL is sample-hungry and unsafe to explore on real hardware.
keyIdea: Decompose control into a fixed hand-engineered feedback controller that handles the robot-state (geometric) objective plus a learned RL policy whose output is added as a residual to handle contacts and object dynamics.
architecture: Superposition u = pi_H(s_m) + pi_theta(s_m, s_o): pi_H is a Cartesian position controller (sim) or compliant joint-space impedance controller (real); pi_theta is a neural network policy trained with TD3 (rlkit implementation) off-policy from a replay buffer.
inputs: Sim: end-effector position, EE forces/torques, block positions, goal position. Real: camera-tracked block positions, EE position, EE force in z only.
outputs: Residual control command added to the hand-engineered controller output
actionRepr: single-step continuous residual command added to a hand-designed controller's output (Cartesian position control in sim; joint-space impedance control on real Sawyer)
trainingData: Online RL on a real Sawyer arm: corrective behaviour learned over ~8,000 samples (~3 h); simulation in MuJoCo (learning curves up to 500K timesteps).

headlineResults.benchmark: Real block insertion, misaligned standing blocks (+/-20 deg)
Real training time for corrective behaviour

headlineResults.comparedTo: RL, RL+Sim, residual RL without sim init (slower)

whatChangedVsParent: Instead of learning the full controller with TD3, learns only an additive residual on top of a conventional controller, with exploration noise applied only to the residual.
limitations: Requires a carefully crafted vision setup to infer block positions and angles in the real world, limiting application to novel scenes and bounding the quality of the learned controller if perception drops key information.
notes: Concurrent with Silver et al. 'Residual Policy Learning' (2018), which the authors describe as the most closely related work (simulated long-horizon tasks); this paper focuses on real-world contact-rich training. Used as a baseline in HIL-SERL (initialized with 200 demos there; 32% avg success).

keyEquations.meaning: Executed action is hand-designed controller plus learned residual policy.
Reward splits into robot-geometric term (handled by controller) and object term (learned).

symbols.meaning: robot-state reward, e.g. distance to goal

keyEquations.meaning: Simulation reward: reach goal while keeping standing blocks untilted.

algorithmSteps: Initialize exploration noise process N and sample initial state.
Compute residual action u_t = pi_theta(s_t) + N_t.
Execute u'_t = u_t + pi_H(s_t) on robot.
Observe s_t+1; store (s_t, u_t, s_t+1) in replay buffer.
Sample transitions and update theta with TD3.
Optionally initialize pi_H from a policy trained in simulation for sim-to-real.
ablations: Environment variation: hand-engineered succeeds 2/20 on misaligned blocks vs residual RL 15/20.
Control bias (sim, sigma=0.05, mu up to 0.2): residual RL keeps return roughly constant while hand-engineered controller degrades sharply.
Only RL (no base controller) learns slower and reaches lower final performance in both sim and real, with broader, riskier exploration.
hyperparams: TD3 (rlkit); Gaussian exploration noise on residual only; sim control-noise sweep sigma in [0.01, 0.1], bias mu in [0, 0.2] with sigma=0.05; block rotation noise U[-r,r], r up to 0.3 rad (sim), +/-20 deg (real).

name: DayDreamer
resolvedTitle: DayDreamer: World Models for Physical Robot Learning
org: UC Berkeley
problem: Deep RL needs too much trial and error to learn directly on physical robots, so most robot learning relies on simulators that are inaccurate and do not adapt to changes in the world.
keyIdea: Apply the Dreamer (DreamerV2) world-model agent online on real robots: learn a latent dynamics model from replayed real experience and train the actor-critic purely on imagined latent rollouts, with asynchronous actor/learner threads, using one hyperparameter set for all robots.
architecture: RSSM world model (encoder fusing all sensors into discrete stochastic codes, recurrent dynamics, decoder, reward head) trained by stochastic backprop; actor and critic MLPs trained on imagined rollouts in latent space; learner thread and actor thread run in parallel.
inputs: Robot-dependent: proprioception (A1 joint angles, orientation, angular velocity), third-person RGB (UR5), RGB+depth+proprio (XArm), top-down RGB only (Sphero)
outputs: Actions: continuous motor angles (A1), discrete EE increments + gripper toggle (UR5, XArm), continuous torques (Sphero)
actionRepr: single-step actions: continuous 12-D motor-angle targets for PD control (A1, 20 Hz); discrete Cartesian EE increments + gripper toggle (UR5 2 Hz, XArm ~0.5 Hz); continuous torque commands (Sphero 2 Hz)
trainingData: Online real-world experience only, no simulators or demos: A1 ~1 h, UR5 ~8 h, XArm ~10 h, Sphero ~2 h.

headlineResults.benchmark: Unitree A1: roll over, stand up, walk from scratch
headlineResults.comparedTo: SAC only learns to roll over

headlineResults.benchmark: UR5 multi-object visual pick and place
headlineResults.comparedTo: Rainbow and PPO learn only grasp-and-drop; approaches human

whatChangedVsParent: No new algorithm: DreamerV2 re-implemented with an asynchronous actor/learner split and multi-sensor fusion, and run online on four physical robots with identical hyperparameters.
limitations: Many hours of on-hardware learning cause robot wear that may need human intervention or repair; longer training is needed to probe the limits of Dreamer and baselines; harder tasks may require combining real-world learning with simulators.
notes: Software infrastructure released publicly (danijar.com/daydreamer); trained weights not stated. XArm recovered and surpassed its prior performance ~5 h after a sunrise lighting shift (Appendix A). Paper text says planning horizon H = 16 in Sec. 2 but the hyperparameter table lists imagination horizon H = 15 (internal inconsistency). A1 maximum reward is 14.

keyEquations.tex: \text{enc}_\theta(s_t \mid s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, x_t),\ \ \text{dec}_\theta(s_t) \approx x_t,\ \ \text{dyn}_\theta(s_t \mid s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}),\ \ \text{rew}_\theta(s_{t+1}) \approx r_t
keyEquations.meaning: RSSM world model: encoder, decoder, latent dynamics prior and reward predictor, trained jointly.

symbols.meaning: latent model state (h_t recurrent + z_t stochastic)

keyEquations.meaning: Lambda-return over imagined rollouts; critic regresses it, actor maximizes it.
Actor loss (Reinforce form for discrete actions) with entropy regularizer; reparameterization used for continuous.

algorithmSteps: Actor thread runs current policy on the robot and appends experience to the replay buffer.
Learner samples sequence batches (B=32, T=32) from replay.
Train RSSM world model (encoder, dynamics, decoder, reward) by stochastic backprop.
From posterior states, imagine H-step latent rollouts with the actor.
Train critic on lambda-returns (slow target critic) and actor to maximize them with entropy bonus.
Push updated policy to the actor thread; repeat without rate limiting.
ablations: No ablations of Dreamer components; comparisons only: A1 SAC fails to stand/walk within 1 h.
UR5: Rainbow and PPO converge to grasp-and-drop in same bin, Dreamer reaches 2.5 objects/min in 8 h.
Sphero: DrQv2 matches Dreamer (both ~0.15 avg distance).
hyperparams: Replay 1e6 FIFO; start learning 1e4; batch 32 x length 32; MLP 4x512 LayerNorm+ELU; RSSM 512; 32 latents x 32 classes; KL balancing 0.8; imagination horizon 15; gamma 0.95; lambda 0.95; target update 100; lr 1e-4; grad clip 100; same across all robots.

name: Domain randomization (Tobin)
resolvedTitle: Domain Randomization for Transferring Deep Neural Networks from Simulation to the Real World
org: OpenAI; UC Berkeley
problem: Models trained on low-fidelity simulated images fail on real images (the reality gap), and system identification or photo-realistic rendering is costly and incomplete.
keyIdea: Randomize rendering (textures, lighting, camera, distractors, noise) so heavily with non-realistic textures that the real world looks like just another variation, then deploy with no real data or fine-tuning.
architecture: Modified VGG-16: standard VGG conv layers (ImageNet-pretrained or random init) followed by smaller fully connected layers of 256 and 64 units, no dropout, regressing (x, y, z) of the target object; trained with Adam on L2 loss.
inputs: Single monocular RGB image from an uncalibrated webcam, downsized to 224x224
outputs: Cartesian (x, y, z) position of the target object (fed to a motion planner for grasping)
trainingData: Only simulated MuJoCo-rendered images with random textures (random RGB, gradient, checker), 0-10 distractors; performance improves up to ~50,000 training samples; no real images.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real-world localization of 8 geometric objects (480 webcam images)
YCB Spam can with unseen food-item distractors

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike CAD2RL's ~200 mostly realistic textures, uses only procedurally generated non-realistic textures (hundreds of thousands of texturizations) and targets precision localization rather than collision avoidance.
limitations: Demonstrated only for object localization of simple objects with a fixed table height (effectively 2D pose); authors list higher-resolution frames, better architectures, more randomization, multi-view/stereo/depth and combining with domain adaptation as needed for contact-rich or higher-precision tasks.
notes: Claimed first transfer of a deep net trained only on simulated RGB (no real pre-training) to the real world for robot control. Camera randomized within a 10x5x10 cm box, view angle offset up to 0.1 rad, FOV scaled up to 5%. Hyperparameter search over lr {1e-4, 2e-4} and batch {25, 50, 100}; lr ~1e-4 avoided collapse to table-center prediction.

keyEquations.meaning: L2 regression loss between predicted and true object positions (loss stated in text, formula paraphrased).

symbols.meaning: detector applied to single camera frame
true Cartesian coordinates of object i

edges: render (random textures, lights, camera, distractors, noise)

algorithmSteps: Place target object and 0-10 distractors at random positions on a simulated table.
Randomize textures of all objects, table, floor, skybox, robot (random RGB / gradient / checker).
Randomize camera pose within a box, view angle and FOV; randomize number, pose and specularity of lights; add image noise.
Render image and record object position label.
Train VGG-16 regressor with Adam on L2 loss.
Deploy on real images without fine-tuning; pass predicted position to a motion planner for grasping.
ablations: Fewer than 1,000 unique textures degrades real-world error significantly (with 10,000 training images).
No distractors in training: error with real distractors rises from 1.8 to 7.2 cm (occlusions 2.4 to 7.4 cm).
No camera randomization: object-only error 1.3 to 2.0 cm; removing noise has negligible effect; ImageNet pre-training unnecessary with enough data.
hyperparams: Input 224x224; FC 256 and 64; Adam lr ~1e-4; 0-10 distractors; camera box 10x5x10 cm, angle offset 0.1 rad, FOV +/-5%; >=1,000 textures; up to ~50,000 samples.

name: Dynamics randomization (Peng)
resolvedTitle: Sim-to-Real Transfer of Robotic Control with Dynamics Randomization
org: OpenAI; UC Berkeley
problem: Control policies trained in simulation exploit simulator idiosyncrasies and fail on real robots because of dynamics modeling and calibration errors.
keyIdea: Randomize physical dynamics parameters (95 in total) per episode and train a recurrent (LSTM) policy so it implicitly performs online system identification and adapts to the real robot's dynamics with zero real-world training.
architecture: LSTM policy with a feedforward branch (state s_t, goal g) and a recurrent branch (s_t, a_{t-1}; 128-unit embedding + 128 LSTM units), concatenated into 2 FC layers of 128; trained with Recurrent DPG + Hindsight Experience Replay; an omniscient recurrent critic also receives the true dynamics parameters mu.
inputs: 52-D state (arm joint positions/velocities, gripper position, puck position, orientation, linear and angular velocities), previous action, goal position
outputs: 7-D relative joint-angle targets for a position controller
actionRepr: single-step 7-D continuous relative joint-angle offsets for a position controller (tanh-scaled)
trainingData: MuJoCo simulation only: ~8,000 update iterations using ~100 million samples, ~8 h on a 100-core cluster.
controlRateHz: ~25 (default control timestep 0.04 s, randomized per step; sim timestep 0.002 s with 20 sim steps per control step)

headlineResults.benchmark: Real pushing with chip packet attached to puck (changed contact dynamics)

whatChangedVsParent: Moves randomization from visual appearance to physics/dynamics and replaces an explicit SysID module with an LSTM memory that infers dynamics implicitly, with an omniscient critic during training.
limitations: Demonstrated on a single state-based pushing task with mocap tracking; the authors list extension to richer tasks and more modalities such as vision as future work, and note little calibration was done (more calibration would likely help).
notes: Randomized: link mass [0.25,4]x, joint damping [0.2,20]x, puck mass [0.1,0.4] kg, puck friction [0.1,5], puck damping [0.01,0.2] Ns/m, table height [0.73,0.77] m, controller gains [0.5,2]x, action-timestep rate lambda [125,1000] s^-1, observation noise 5% of running std. Binary sparse reward (0 success, -1 otherwise); goal within 0.07 m.

keyEquations.meaning: Objective: maximize expected return averaged over a distribution of simulator dynamics.
Omniscient critic TD target: critic sees true dynamics mu, policy does not.
Randomized action timestep models controller latency; Delta t_0 = 0.04 s.

algorithmSteps: Sample goal g and dynamics parameters mu for the episode.
Roll out the LSTM policy in MuJoCo; action timestep and observation noise vary every step.
Store trajectory, rewards, goal and mu in replay buffer.
Sample an episode; with probability 0.8 relabel goal via HER and recompute rewards.
Compute LSTM memories; critic Q(s,a,y,g,mu) TD update; policy gradient through critic (RDPG).
Deploy final policy on real Fetch with no fine-tuning.
ablations: Fixed action timestep on real robot: success 0.29 +/- 0.11 (vs 0.89 all randomized).
No observation noise: 0.25 +/- 0.12; fixed link mass: 0.64 +/- 0.10; fixed puck friction: 0.48 +/- 0.10.
Architecture: memoryless FF with randomization 0.67 real; FF + 8-step history 0.70; no randomization 0.0.
hyperparams: 95 randomized parameters; episode 100 control steps (~4 s) in training, 200 on real robot; Adam lr 5e-4; batch 128 episodes x 100 steps; HER relabel prob 0.8; exploration noise std 0.01 rad; LSTM 128 units.

name: ADR / Solving Rubik's Cube
resolvedTitle: Solving Rubik's Cube with a Robot Hand
org: OpenAI
problem: Manual domain randomization needs extensive hand-tuning and a tight sim/robot iteration loop, and did not scale to a manipulation problem as complex as solving a Rubik's cube with a humanoid hand.
keyIdea: Automatic Domain Randomization (ADR): start from a single calibrated environment and automatically widen each randomization range when the model performs well at its boundary, yielding an ever-growing training distribution that produces sim-to-real transfer and emergent meta-learning in memory-augmented policies.
architecture: Control: recurrent policy (embed-and-add inputs, 2048-unit FC layer, 1024-unit LSTM) trained with PPO in an asymmetric actor-critic setup on the distributed Rapid framework. Vision: ResNet50 (weights shared across 3 cameras) state estimator predicting cube pose and face angles, trained on ORRB/Unity renders. ADR runs as distributed eval workers with Redis storage.
inputs: Policy: fingertip positions (PhaseSpace mocap), cube pose and face angles (from vision or Giiker cube), goal. Vision: 3 RGB Basler camera images.
outputs: Discretized relative joint-position targets for 20 actuated joints of the Shadow Dexterous Hand; vision outputs cube position, orientation and face angles
actionRepr: single-step discrete action: categorical with 11 bins for each of 20 action coordinates (relative joint-position changes)
trainingData: Simulation only (MuJoCo physics, ORRB rendering) with ADR; Rubik's cube policy PPO on 64 NVIDIA V100 GPUs + 29,440 CPU cores; best policies trained continuously over months.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Rubik's cube fair scramble (43 successes), best ADR (XXL) policy, Giiker face angles
Real Rubik's cube, vision-only face angles, ADR (XXL)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces hand-tuned fixed randomization ranges with an automatic curriculum that expands per-parameter ranges from a single calibrated environment based on boundary performance.
limitations: Even the best policy fully solves the fair scramble only 20% of the time and drops the cube, vision-only face-angle sensing reached 0% full solves, and results relied on a modified Giiker cube, PhaseSpace mocap and months of large-scale compute (limitations inferred from reported results, not a dedicated section).
notes: ADR entropy correlates with sim2real transfer and with how well environment parameters (e.g., cube size) can be decoded from LSTM hidden state (0.68 to 0.83 accuracy as entropy rises), evidence of emergent meta-learning. Solution sequences from a Kociemba solver; face rotations and flips issued as subgoals. PDF author list has 18 alphabetical authors (includes Lei Zhang). The '13,000 years of experience' figure appears in secondary summaries but was not verified in pages read.

keyEquations.meaning: Factorized uniform environment distribution with per-parameter bounds adjusted by ADR.
ADR entropy in nats per dimension; measures breadth of randomization.
Boundary update: widen range if average performance at boundary is high, shrink if low.

symbols.meaning: mean performance over m boundary evaluations

algorithmSteps: Initialize every range at the calibrated value (policy) or zero (vision).
With probability p_b=0.5 do ADR eval: pick parameter i, fix it at its lower or upper bound, sample others from P_phi.
Evaluate model; append performance to buffer for that boundary.
When buffer has m=240 entries, average: if >= t_H widen bound by Delta, if <= t_L narrow it; clear buffer.
Otherwise sample full lambda ~ P_phi and generate training rollouts/images.
Train policy with PPO (asymmetric actor-critic, LSTM) or vision model with focal-weighted losses (LARS).
Deploy on Shadow hand; Kociemba solver provides subgoal sequence of rotations and flips.
ablations: Curriculum matters: fixed DR at small/medium/large/XL entropy trains slower than ADR in sim2sim, and larger fixed entropy takes longer to learn from scratch.
Block reorientation real transfer rises with ADR entropy: Small 1.4, Medium 3.2, Large 13.3, XL 16.0, XXL 32.0 mean successes vs Manual DR 2.7.
Hidden-state decoding of cube size improves with ADR entropy: 0.68 (Small) to 0.83 (XL) accuracy.
hyperparams: ADR: boundary sampling prob 0.5, step Delta 0.02, t_H 20, t_L 10 successes, queue m 240, max phi 4.0; vision thresholds 70%/30%. PPO: gamma 0.998, GAE lambda 0.95, clip 0.2, lr 3e-4 to 1e-4, 11 bins x 20 actions, batch 5120 chunks x 10 transitions per GPU.

name: RMA
resolvedTitle: RMA: Rapid Motor Adaptation for Legged Robots
org: UC Berkeley; Carnegie Mellon University; Facebook AI Research
problem: Legged robots must adapt in real time to unseen terrains, payloads and wear; domain randomization gives over-conservative policies and online adaptation methods need risky real-world rollouts.
keyIdea: Train a base policy with privileged environment parameters encoded into a latent 'extrinsics' vector, then train an adaptation module to regress that latent from 0.5 s of proprioceptive state-action history, enabling sub-second online adaptation with no real-world fine-tuning.
architecture: Environment factor encoder mu (3-layer MLP, 256/128) maps e_t in R^17 to extrinsics z_t in R^8; base policy pi (3-layer MLP, 128 hidden) maps state, previous action and z_t to 12 joint targets; adaptation module phi embeds 50-step history with a 2-layer MLP then a 3-layer 1-D CNN and linear head to predict z_hat_t. Runs asynchronously on A1 (pi 100 Hz, phi 10 Hz).
inputs: 30-D proprioceptive state (12 joint positions, 12 joint velocities, roll, pitch, 4 foot-contact bits), previous 12-D action; adaptation module uses last 50 states and actions
outputs: 12 desired joint positions converted to torques by a PD controller (Kp=55, Kd=0.8)
actionRepr: single-step 12-D target joint positions for a fixed-gain PD controller at 100 Hz
trainingData: RaiSim simulation with fractal terrain generator: base policy PPO 15,000 iterations x 80,000 steps (1.2 billion simulated steps, ~24 h on a desktop with 1 GPU); adaptation module 1,000 iterations (80 million steps, ~3 h).

headlineResults.comparedTo: Robust/DR 62.4%, SysID 56.5%, AWR 41.7%, RMA w/o adapt 52.1%, Expert 76.2%

headlineResults.value: up to 12 kg (100% body weight) with high success
headlineResults.comparedTo: A1 controller degrades from 8 kg; RMA w/o adapt fails to move above 8 kg

headlineResults.benchmark: Outdoor: hiking-trail stairs / cement and pebble piles

parents: Online system identification (Yu et al. UP-OSI)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces explicit parameter estimation or real-world latent optimization with a supervised adaptation module that predicts a policy-relevant latent from recent history, needing zero real-world adaptation samples.
limitations: Blind (proprioception only): larger perturbations such as sudden falls going downstairs or multiple leg obstructions from rocks sometimes cause failures; exteroception with onboard vision is needed for truly reliable walking.
notes: Locomotion (quadruped), not manipulation, but the privileged-teacher + history-adapter recipe is widely reused in dexterous manipulation sim-to-real. CONFLICT: a secondary AI summary claimed 12 kg = 80% of body weight; the paper states A1 weighs ~12 kg and 12 kg payload is 100% of body weight. Adaptation module trained on on-policy rollouts (DAgger-like) for robustness. Reference implementation builds on RaisimGymTorch; release of weights not stated.

keyEquations.meaning: Encode privileged 17-D environment factors into 8-D extrinsics.

symbols.meaning: mass/COM, motor strength, friction, terrain height

keyEquations.meaning: Base policy conditioned on state, previous action and extrinsics.
Adaptation module estimates extrinsics from last k=50 states/actions (0.5 s).
Supervised phase-2 loss using on-policy rollouts.

algorithmSteps: Phase 1: jointly train base policy pi and encoder mu with PPO in RaiSim using privileged e_t on fractal terrain with bioenergetic rewards and penalty curriculum.
Phase 2: freeze pi; roll it out using z_hat_t from the (initially random) adaptation module phi.
Regress phi's z_hat_t onto z_t = mu(e_t) with MSE; iterate with on-policy data.
Deploy: phi updates z_hat_t at 10 Hz from last 50 states/actions.
Base policy runs at 100 Hz using latest z_hat_t, outputting joint targets to PD controller.
ablations: Removing adaptation module: sim success 73.5% to 52.1%; real step-down-15 80% to 0%.
Predicting raw system parameters (SysID) instead of latent: 56.5% sim success.
Monolithic policy taking history directly gave unnatural gaits, poor sim performance and could only run at 10 Hz on board.
hyperparams: History k=50 (0.5 s); z in R^8, e in R^17; PPO 15,000 iters, batch 80,000, lr 5e-4, gamma 0.998, GAE 0.95; penalty curriculum k_0=0.03, k_{t+1}=k_t^0.997; max forward speed 0.35 m/s; policy 100 Hz, adapter 10 Hz.

name: Teacher–student terrain (Lee 2020)
resolvedTitle: Learning Quadrupedal Locomotion over Challenging Terrain
org: ETH Zurich (Robotic Systems Lab); KAIST; Intel Intelligent Systems Lab
problem: Conventional legged controllers are elaborate state machines that break on deformable, slippery or occluded natural terrain, and exteroception (cameras/LiDAR) cannot measure friction or compliance and is blocked by vegetation, snow or water.
keyIdea: Train a teacher policy with RL in simulation using privileged terrain/contact information, then distill it into a proprioception-only student (TCN over a history of proprioceptive readings) that implicitly infers terrain from history; an adaptive particle-filter terrain curriculum keeps training at the edge of traversability.
architecture: Teacher: MLP encoder embeds privileged info x_t into latent l_t, then MLP maps (o_t, l_t) to action. Student: temporal convolutional network (3 dilated causal conv layers interleaved with strided convs) encodes proprioceptive history H; final MLP layers are copied from the teacher. Policy modulates Foot Trajectory Generators (PMTG) whose foot targets go through analytic IK to joint PD controllers; a learned actuator network models the SEA joints in simulation.
inputs: Command vector, base orientation/gravity, base linear and angular velocity (from state estimator), joint positions/velocities, FTG phases and frequencies, joint error/velocity history, previous foot targets; student uses a proprioceptive history of N steps. No cameras, no foot contact sensors.
outputs: 16-D action: 4 leg frequency offsets + 12 foot-position residuals added to FTG targets, converted to joint position targets via IK.
actionRepr: Single-step 16-D residual action (leg frequencies + foot position residuals) modulating periodic foot trajectory generators; not an action chunk.
trainingData: Procedurally generated hills, steps and stairs in the RaiSim simulator with domain randomization (friction, disturbances, observation noise); teacher trained with TRPO; student trained by supervised imitation of teacher with DAgger-style on-policy data.
controlRateHz: Policy/foot targets 50 Hz; joint PD tracking 400 Hz (per Fig. 4C). Supplement also states the network runs at 400 Hz onboard — see notes.
parents: Hwangbo et al. 2019 (actuator networks, RL for ANYmal)
whatChangedVsParent: Extends prior ANYmal RL (lab, flat ground) to zero-shot natural terrain by adding privileged teacher-to-proprioceptive-student distillation, a TCN history encoder and an adaptive terrain curriculum.
limitations: Controller is blind (proprioception only), so it reacts to terrain rather than anticipating it; the paper points to integrating exteroception as the next step (done in follow-up work).

keyEquations.tex: L := (\bar{a}_t(o_t, x_t) - a_t(o_t, H))^2 + (\bar{l}_t(o_t, x_t) - l_t(H))^2
keyEquations.meaning: Student imitates teacher action and reconstructs teacher's privileged latent from proprioceptive history.
Traversability of a terrain parameter: fraction of transitions progressing faster than 0.2 m/s.

symbols.meaning: 1 if projected velocity > 0.2 m/s, else 0 (or termination)

keyEquations.meaning: Terrain desirability: probability terrain is challenging-but-traversable; used as particle-filter weight.
Foot target = trajectory generator output plus learned residual.

symbols.meaning: foot trajectory generator at leg phase

algorithmSteps: Sample terrain parameters from particle filter; generate hills/steps/stairs.
Train teacher with TRPO using o_t plus privileged x_t.
Label transitions with traversability; reweight/resample terrain particles toward Tr in [0.5, 0.9]; random-walk particles.
Roll out student in sim; query teacher for (a, l) at visited states (DAgger).
Train student TCN on action + latent regression loss.
Deploy student zero-shot: proprioceptive history -> residuals -> FTG -> IK -> PD.
ablations: TCN history length compared at 1 step (0.02 s), 20 steps (0.4 s) and 100 steps (2.0 s): longer history approaches teacher performance on slopes, steps and disturbances (Fig. 4, qualitative from report).
Supplement compares TCN with a GRU student and ablates the latent-reconstruction loss (Sections S8, S9); numbers not extracted.
hyperparams: FTG base frequency f0 = 1.25 Hz, max foot height h = 0.2 m; 9 height-scan points per foot at 10 cm radius (teacher); traversability threshold 0.2 m/s; desirable traversability band [0.5, 0.9]; TCN filter size 5; student history N up to 100 steps (2 s).
notes: Deployed on two generations of ANYmal robots (ANYmal B and C per paper abstract: 'two generations'); used in DARPA SubT. CONFLICT-risk: control rate — Fig. 4C labels the policy path 50 Hz and PD tracking 400 Hz, while supplement S2 states 'the neural network policy runs at 400 Hz on an onboard CPU'; surveys typically quote 50 Hz policy. The alphaXiv summary mentions 10 kg payload and zero locomotion failures in SubT; not verified against paper text here, so not placed in headlineResults.

name: Asymmetric actor-critic
resolvedTitle: Asymmetric Actor Critic for Image-Based Robot Learning
org: OpenAI; Carnegie Mellon University
problem: Training image-based policies with RL is hard because of partial observability and high input dimensionality, while training on full state requires reliable state estimators at deployment; simulators provide full state but it is unused by pixel policies.
keyIdea: In an actor-critic algorithm, give the critic the full simulator state (and goal state) while the actor sees only rendered RGBD images; the critic is discarded at test time, so the pixel policy transfers to the real robot, aided by visual domain randomization.
architecture: DDPG + HER. Critic: MLP with 3 hidden layers of 512 ReLU units on (state, goal state, action). Actor: CNN with 4 conv layers (64 filters, 2x2 kernels) applied to current observation and goal observation, concatenated then 3 FC layers of 512 units, tanh output. Optional bottleneck layer in actor regressed to full state.
inputs: Actor: RGB(D) image (100x100x3 or 100x100x4) and goal image. Critic (training only): full state, goal state, action.
outputs: Continuous action; for Fetch: 4-D (relative gripper xyz + finger distance).
actionRepr: Single-step continuous 4-D action (delta gripper position + gripper opening), deterministic DDPG policy.
trainingData: Simulated MuJoCo environments (Particle, Reacher, Fetch Pick) with sparse rewards, HER relabeling and texture/lighting/camera/depth domain randomization; no real-world training data.

headlineResults.comparedTo: Asym DDPG 0/5, Sym HER 0/5, Vanilla BC 0/5, DAgger BC 3/5
Asym DDPG 0/5, Sym HER 0/5, Vanilla BC 1/5, DAgger BC 0/5

whatChangedVsParent: Relative to symmetric DDPG/HER on images, the critic receives privileged full state instead of images, giving better value estimates and actor gradients.
limitations: Evaluated on simple block tasks with 5 real trials each; the imitation baseline plateaus only because the expert relies on state not visible in images; paper does not address dynamics (physics) gap, only visual gap via randomization.

keyEquations.tex: L_c = (Q(s_t, a_t) - y_t)^2, \quad y_t = r_t + \gamma Q(s_{t+1}, \pi(s_{t+1}))
keyEquations.meaning: Critic Bellman loss, computed on full state s (and goal) in the asymmetric variant.
Actor loss (deterministic policy gradient); actor input is image o, critic input is state s.

symbols.meaning: actor; in AAC takes observation o_t and goal observation g_o

keyEquations.meaning: Sparse goal-reaching reward used with HER.

algorithmSteps: Sample goal g and initial state s0; render goal image g_o.
Each step render o_t from s_t; act a_t = behavioural policy(o_t, g_o).
Store (s, o, a, r, s', o', g, g_o) in replay buffer with HER relabeled goals.
Update critic on {s, a, r, s', g}.
Update actor on {o, a, r, o', g_o} via critic gradient.
Deploy actor alone on real RGBD camera images.
ablations: Removing domain randomization: policies 0/5 on all three real tasks despite perfect sim performance.
Removing viewpoint randomization only: Pick 0/5, Forward Push 0/5, Block Move 4/5.
Adding a state-predicting bottleneck in the actor speeds and stabilizes training (large gains on Particle/Reacher, lower variance on Fetch Pick).
hyperparams: DDPG with 16 parallel rollouts, 40 optimization steps per iteration, minibatch 128, replay buffer 1e5, Polyak 0.98, Adam lr 1e-3, gamma 0.98, horizon T = 50; exploration: 20% uniform random actions, else Gaussian noise with std 5% of action range.
notes: Uses DDPG as base optimizer but the method is stated to apply to any actor-critic algorithm; now standard in legged RL (e.g., ASAP uses asymmetric actor-critic with PPO).

name: GAT (grounded action transformation)
resolvedTitle: Grounded Action Transformation for Robot Learning in Simulation (Hanna & Stone, AAAI 2017)
org: The University of Texas at Austin (Learning Agents Research Group)
problem: Policies optimized in simulation exploit simulator inaccuracies and fail on the real robot; many simulators cannot have their internal parameters modified.
keyIdea: Treat the simulator as a black box and ground it by transforming the agent's action: a learned real-world forward model predicts the next state, and a learned simulator inverse dynamics model finds the sim action that reproduces it; policy is then improved in the grounded simulator.
architecture: Two supervised networks: deterministic forward model of the real world f_real(s,a) and inverse dynamics model of the simulator f_sim^{-1}(s, s'); composed into an action transformer g(s,a) wrapped around the unmodified simulator. (Follow-up SGAT uses 2 hidden layers of 64 units for both models.)
inputs: State s_t and policy action a_t.
outputs: Transformed action â_t executed in the simulator.
trainingData: Small amount of real robot trajectories (for f_real) plus simulated trajectories (for f_sim^{-1}); original work: SoftBank NAO walking with SimSpark simulator.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real NAO bipedal walk (reported in SGAT, 2008.01281)
headlineResults.comparedTo: state-of-the-art hand-coded gait it was based on

parents: Grounded Simulation Learning (GSL, Farchy et al. 2013)
whatChangedVsParent: Unlike GSL, which adjusts simulator parameters, GAT grounds a black-box simulator by transforming actions using learned forward and inverse models.
limitations: Deterministic forward model captures only the most likely next state, so GAT fails in stochastic target environments (shown by SGAT follow-up: GAT NAO policy fell 10/10 on uneven ground after second grounding step).

keyEquations.meaning: Action transformer: find the sim action that reproduces the predicted real next state.

symbols.meaning: learned forward model of real-world dynamics
learned inverse dynamics model of the simulator

algorithmSteps: Deploy current policy on real robot; collect real transitions.
Train forward model f_real on real data.
Collect sim transitions; train inverse model f_sim^{-1}.
Compose g(s,a) and wrap simulator (grounded simulator).
Freeze g; improve policy by RL/optimization in grounded simulator.
Repeat until real-world performance stops improving.
notes: SURVEY-LEVEL: the original AAAI 2017 paper is not on arXiv and could not be retrieved (Semantic Scholar blocked). Equation, algorithm loop and the '43% faster' NAO result are taken from the direct follow-up by the same group, 'Stochastic Grounded Action Transformation for Robot Learning in Simulation' (Desai, Karnan, Hanna, Warnell, Stone, IROS 2020, arXiv 2008.01281), which restates GAT in Section II-C. A journal version exists: Hanna et al., 'Grounded action transformation for sim-to-real reinforcement learning', Machine Learning 110(9):2469-2499, 2021 (not read). SGAT result for context: on uneven ground, SGAT NAO fell 1/10 vs GAT 10/10 after grounding step 2. Related variants: RGAT (reinforced GAT, IROS 2020), GARAT (imitation-from-observation view, 2020).

name: ASAP
resolvedTitle: ASAP: Aligning Simulation and Real-World Physics for Learning Agile Humanoid Whole-Body Skills
org: Carnegie Mellon University; NVIDIA
problem: Agile whole-body humanoid skills fail on hardware due to sim-to-real dynamics mismatch; SysID needs predefined parameter spaces and torque sensing, domain randomization yields conservative policies, and learned dynamics had not been shown for humanoids.
keyIdea: Pre-train motion-tracking policies in sim, roll them out on the real robot, then train an RL 'delta action' model that adds corrective actions inside the simulator so replayed real actions reproduce real states; fine-tune the policy in this aligned simulator and deploy without the delta model.
architecture: Phase-conditioned motion-tracking policy trained with PPO and asymmetric actor-critic (critic gets reference global positions and root linear velocity). Delta action model pi_Delta(s_t, a_t) is a separate RL policy outputting residual actions injected into the simulator. Human video -> TRAM (SMPL) -> MaskedMimic sim cleaning -> shape-and-motion retargeting to Unitree G1.
inputs: Actor: 5-step history of joint positions (23), joint velocities (23), root angular velocity, projected gravity, last actions, plus time-phase variable phi in [0,1]. Delta model: state s_t and action a_t.
outputs: 23-D target joint positions tracked by PD controller; delta model outputs Delta a_t (4-DoF ankle subset in real-world experiments).
actionRepr: Single-step 23-D target joint positions (PD targets) for whole-body motion tracking; not chunked.
trainingData: Retargeted human-video motions (43 motions in easy/medium/hard for sim eval); real-world: 100 motion clips (5 tasks, 30 executions each) plus 10 minutes of locomotion data on Unitree G1, recorded with motion capture.
parents: DeepMimic-style phase tracking + Reference State Initialization
whatChangedVsParent: Instead of learning a residual state (delta dynamics) or tuning parameters (SysID), ASAP learns a residual action with RL that aligns simulator physics, then RL-fine-tunes the policy in that aligned simulator.
limitations: Agile motions break hardware (two G1 robots broke; motor overheating) limiting data; real-world data collection needs MoCap; full 23-DoF delta model needs 400+ clips so only a 4-DoF ankle model was trained on hardware.

keyEquations.meaning: Delta action model outputs corrective action from state and nominal action.
Replay real actions with correction in sim; reward matches s_{t+1} to recorded real state.

keyEquations.tex: s_{t+1} = f^{ASAP}(s_t, a_t) = f^{sim}(s_t, a_t + \pi^{\Delta}(s_t, a_t))
keyEquations.meaning: Aligned simulator used to fine-tune the tracking policy (delta model frozen).

algorithmSteps: Reconstruct human video motions to SMPL, clean in sim, retarget to G1.
Pre-train phase-based tracking policy with PPO, asymmetric critic, termination curriculum (1.5 m to 0.3 m), RSI, DR.
Deploy on real robot; record states (MoCap + onboard) and actions.
Train delta action model with PPO: initialize sim at real state, apply a^r + Delta a, reward state match minus action norm.
Freeze delta model inside simulator.
Fine-tune tracking policy with the pre-training rewards.
Deploy fine-tuned policy on hardware without delta model.
ablations: Dataset size: closed-loop MPJPE improvement saturates, only 0.65% decrease going from 4300 to 43000 samples.
Training horizon: open-loop best at 1.5 s, closed-loop best at 1.0 s; action-norm weight best at 0.1.
RL fine-tuning beats RL-free uses of the delta model (fixed-point iteration, gradient-based), which performed worse than baseline; ASAP also beats fine-tuning with random action noise.
hyperparams: Termination tolerance curriculum 1.5 m -> 0.3 m; 5-step proprioceptive history; 23 DoF actions; delta-action reward: action norm weight -0.2 in Table II (ablation best 0.1), action rate -0.01; 4-DoF ankle delta model on hardware; delta training horizon 1.0 s best for closed loop.
notes: Sim-to-sim evaluation: IsaacGym -> IsaacSim and IsaacGym -> Genesis; ASAP reported 100% success at all difficulty levels there (per summary; per-cell numbers not extracted). Open-source multi-simulator codebase (LeCAR-Lab/ASAP). Humanoid, not manipulation.

name: DAgger
topicName: Behavior cloning and why it breaks
resolvedTitle: A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning
org: Carnegie Mellon University (Robotics Institute; Machine Learning Dept.)
problem: Supervised imitation (behavior cloning) violates the i.i.d. assumption: the learner's own mistakes lead to unseen states, so error compounds quadratically in horizon T; prior fixes (Forward Training, SMILe, SEARN) give non-stationary or stochastic policies and need many iterations.
keyIdea: Iteratively run the current learned policy (optionally mixed with the expert), have the expert label the states actually visited, aggregate all data and retrain; this is Follow-The-Leader no-regret online learning and yields a deterministic stationary policy with error linear in T.
architecture: Meta-algorithm: any supervised learner as subroutine (paper uses linear ridge regression for Super Tux Kart, 4 linear SVMs for Super Mario Bros.).
inputs: States/observations visited by the mixed policy; expert action labels queried at those states.
outputs: A stationary deterministic policy (best of the sequence on validation).
actionRepr: Depends on base learner; experiments: continuous steering in [-1,1] (Tux Kart) and 4 binary buttons (Mario), both at 5 Hz.
trainingData: Tux Kart: ~1000 data points (1 lap) per iteration for 20 iterations; Mario: 5000 data points per iteration for 20 iterations; OCR handwriting benchmark.

headlineResults.comparedTo: SMILe ~2 falls/lap after 20 iterations; supervised does not improve with more data
outperforms SMILe (alpha=0.1), SEARN (best alpha=0.4) and supervised

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike SMILe/SEARN (stochastic policy mixtures) or Forward Training (T non-stationary policies), DAgger aggregates datasets and trains one deterministic stationary policy with linear-in-T guarantees.
limitations: Requires an interactive expert that can label arbitrary learner-visited states; guarantees rely on no-regret / strongly convex surrogate loss assumptions; the bound factor u can be O(T) in worst case when the expert cannot recover.

keyEquations.meaning: Behavior cloning bound: per-step error epsilon under expert distribution compounds quadratically.

symbols.meaning: surrogate (0-1) loss under expert state distribution

keyEquations.meaning: Data-collection policy at iteration i mixes expert and current learner.

symbols.meaning: expert mixing probability; beta_i = I(i=1) often best

keyEquations.meaning: DAgger bound (Thm 3.2): linear in horizon T when N is O~(uT).

symbols.meaning: max increase in cost-to-go from one deviating action
loss of best policy in hindsight on aggregated data

algorithmSteps: Initialize D empty and pi_hat_1 arbitrary.
For i = 1..N: set pi_i = beta_i pi* + (1 - beta_i) pi_hat_i.
Sample T-step trajectories with pi_i.
Label every visited state with expert action pi*(s) to form D_i.
Aggregate D <- D U D_i.
Train pi_hat_{i+1} on D.
Return best pi_hat_i on validation.
ablations: Mario: beta_i = 0.5^(i-1) scored 3030 vs 2980 for beta_i = I(i=1); beta_i = 0.9^(i-1) converged significantly slower.
Supervised BC performance stagnates as more expert data is added (Tux Kart and Mario), while iterative methods keep improving.
SEARN with alpha = 1 (pure policy iteration) was unstable on Mario but comparable to DAgger on OCR.
hyperparams: beta_i = I(i=1) default (parameter-free); 20 iterations in games; Tux Kart ridge lambda = 1e-3; Mario SVM lambda = 1e-4, 27152 sparse binary features.
notes: Published at AISTATS 2011 (arXiv v1 Nov 2010). Robotics variants that relax the labeling burden: HG-DAgger (human-gated interventions, used by BC-Z), EIL. Teacher-student locomotion (Lee 2020) uses DAgger to train the student. OCR 83.6% -> 85.5% figures come from the alphaXiv summary and were not re-verified in the retrieved page text.

name: BC-Z
topicName: Behavior cloning and why it breaks
resolvedTitle: BC-Z: Zero-Shot Task Generalization with Robotic Imitation Learning
org: Robotics at Google; Everyday Robots; UC Berkeley; Stanford University
problem: Imitation-learned manipulation policies generalized to new objects or goals but not to entirely new tasks; scaling data collection and handling distribution shift on real robots was the bottleneck.
