keyIdea: Scale interactive imitation (expert demos plus HG-DAgger shared-autonomy interventions) to 100 tasks, and condition a single ResNet policy via FiLM on a task embedding from pretrained language or from human video, enabling zero-shot execution of unseen tasks from a new sentence.
architecture: ResNet-18 image torso with FiLM layers in each of 4 ResNet blocks conditioned on a 512-D task embedding; action heads are MLPs (2 hidden layers of 256, ReLU) for delta XYZ, delta axis-angle and gripper angle. Task encoder: frozen Multilingual Universal Sentence Encoder (language) or ResNet-18 over 20 frames tiled 4x5 (video), trained with BC loss plus cosine regression to language embedding.
inputs: Monocular RGB head-camera image; task command (language string or human video). No proprioception (found not to help).
outputs: End-effector delta XYZ, delta axis-angle, gripper angle; plus auxiliary open-loop prediction of next 10 actions (only first executed).
actionRepr: Single-step 7-DoF end-effector action (delta position, delta axis-angle, gripper) defined as adaptive state differences N>1 steps ahead; auxiliary 10-step open-loop prediction, executed closed-loop at 10 Hz.
trainingData: 25,877 robot demonstrations (11,108 expert-only + 14,769 HG-DAgger over 16 iterations), 125 hours, 100 tasks, 12 robots, 7 operators; 18,726 human videos. Dataset open-sourced on Kaggle.

headlineResults.comparedTo: zero robot demos of those tasks
one-hot 45%; single-task 1000 demos 5%; no adaptive state-diff 3%

whatChangedVsParent: Scales BC with HG-DAgger interventions to 100 real tasks and replaces one-hot task IDs with pretrained language / video embeddings to get zero-shot task generalization.
limitations: Performance on novel tasks varies widely; language commands limited to simple '(verb) (noun)' structure; video-conditioned policy is much weaker; low-level control errors remain a major bottleneck.

keyEquations.tex: \min \sum_{i}\sum_{(s,a)\sim D^i_e,\, w_h\sim D^i_h \cup D^i_e} -\log \pi(a \mid s, z^i) + D_{cos}(z^i_h, z^i_\ell)
keyEquations.meaning: Behavior cloning plus cosine regression of video embedding onto the task's language embedding.
Per-head action loss weights from Algorithm 1.

algorithmSteps: Collect expert-only teleoperated demos and train initial multi-task policy.
Deploy policy in shared autonomy; human grips override switch to correct failures (HG-DAgger).
Aggregate interventions and retrain; repeat (16 iterations).
Encode task: frozen sentence encoder or video encoder trained with BC + language cosine loss.
At test time embed a new sentence (or average of a few human videos) and run policy closed-loop at 10 Hz, executing only first predicted action.
ablations: HG-DAgger vs manual at equal data: 1-task 53% vs 27%; 8-task 47% vs 23%.
Multi-task language 52% vs single-task (1000 demos) 5% on 'place the bottle in the ceramic bowl'.
Removing adaptive state-diff actions (N=1): 3% vs 45% for one-hot multi-task.
hyperparams: Task embedding 512-D; 10 auxiliary future actions; video 20 frames tiled 4x5; video encoder batch 28 per GPU on 18 V100s, lr 2.45e-4; single-task models: batch 32 per worker on 10 GPUs, lr 2.5e-4.
notes: Published at CoRL 2021 (arXiv Feb 2022). Paper finds intervention rate correlates negatively with success, usable as live metric. Precursor to RT-1 lineage at Google. Summary claim of 37% video-conditioned success not verified in retrieved text; paper says video generalizes to nine novel tasks with non-zero success.

name: ACT
resolvedTitle: Learning Fine-Grained Bimanual Manipulation with Low-Cost Hardware
org: Stanford University; UC Berkeley; Meta
problem: Fine-grained bimanual tasks need precise closed-loop control; low-cost arms are imprecise, and imitation learning suffers from compounding errors at high control frequency and from noisy, multimodal, non-Markovian human demonstrations.
keyIdea: Predict chunks of k future joint-position actions with a transformer trained as a conditional VAE, and smooth execution by querying every step and temporally ensembling overlapping chunk predictions; paired with the ALOHA low-cost bimanual teleoperation rig.
architecture: CVAE. Encoder (training only): BERT-like transformer over [CLS], joint positions and k-step action sequence -> diagonal Gaussian style variable z. Decoder/policy: ResNet-18 per camera (4 cams, 480x640 -> 15x20x512 features, 2D sinusoidal pos-emb), transformer encoder over 1202x512 tokens (1200 image + joints + z), transformer decoder with k fixed positional queries -> MLP to k x 14 actions. ~80M parameters.
inputs: 4 RGB images (480x640x3) and 14-D joint positions of two follower arms; z = 0 at test time.
outputs: k x 14 tensor of absolute target joint positions for both arms (leader-arm joint positions as labels).
actionRepr: Chunk of k = 100 absolute 14-DoF joint-position targets per query, decoded deterministically (z = prior mean) from a CVAE transformer; temporally ensembled at 50 Hz.
trainingData: Per-task from scratch: 50 human demos per real task (100 for Thread Velcro), 8-14 s episodes (400-700 steps at 50 Hz), about 10-20 min of data per task; sim tasks: 50 scripted or 50 human demos.

headlineResults.benchmark: Open Cup / Thread Velcro / Prep Tape / Put On Shoe (real)

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike single-step BC/BeT/RT-1 with discretized or single actions, ACT predicts continuous multi-step action chunks with a CVAE and temporal ensembling, cutting effective horizon k-fold.
limitations: Some tasks exceed robot or algorithm capability (e.g., buttoning a dress shirt); perception fails on low-contrast small objects (Thread Velcro 20%); trained per task from scratch.

keyEquations.meaning: Action chunking: policy outputs next k actions instead of one, reducing effective horizon k-fold.

keyEquations.tex: L = L_{reconst} + \beta L_{reg}, \quad L_{reg} = D_{KL}(q_\phi(z \mid a_{t:t+k}, \bar{o}_t) \,\|\, \mathcal{N}(0, I))
keyEquations.meaning: CVAE objective: reconstruction (L1 in final implementation) plus KL to unit Gaussian prior.

symbols.meaning: CVAE encoder over actions and proprioception

keyEquations.tex: a_t = \sum_i w_i A_t[i] / \sum_i w_i, \quad w_i = \exp(-m \cdot i)
keyEquations.meaning: Temporal ensemble: weighted average of all chunk predictions for current timestep; w_0 is oldest.

symbols.meaning: decay; smaller m incorporates new observations faster

algorithmSteps: Train: sample o_t and a_{t:t+k}; encode z ~ q(z | a, joints).
Decode a_hat_{t:t+k} from images, joints, z; loss = L1 reconstruction + beta KL.
Inference: at every timestep predict a_hat_{t:t+k} with z = 0.
Append predictions to per-timestep FIFO buffers B[t:t+k].
Execute exponentially weighted average of all predictions for current t.
PID in Dynamixel motors tracks target joint positions.
ablations: Chunk size (no temporal ensemble, avg over 4 sim settings): 1% success at k=1 to 44% at k=100, slight dip at k=200/400.
Removing CVAE on human data: success drops from 35.3% to 2% (scripted data almost unchanged, -1%).
Temporal ensemble adds +3.3% for ACT, +4% for BC-ConvMLP, -20% for VINN; user study: 5 Hz teleop is 62% slower than 50 Hz.
hyperparams: Chunk size 100; beta 10; 4 encoder / 7 decoder layers; hidden 512; feedforward 3200; 8 heads; dropout 0.1; lr 1e-5; batch 8; L1 loss; ~5 h training on one RTX 2080 Ti; ~0.01 s inference.
notes: Algorithm 1 box writes MSE for L_reconst but Section IV-C states L1 is used ('L1 loss leads to more precise modeling'); treat L1 as the final choice. ALOHA hardware <$20k, two ViperX 6-DoF follower arms, WidowX leader arms, fully open-sourced (code/hardware). Delta joint positions as actions degraded performance vs absolute targets. ACT is also the default policy in LeRobot (X2).

name: Diffusion Policy
resolvedTitle: Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion
org: Columbia University; Toyota Research Institute / Google DeepMind (per v5 affiliations); MIT
problem: Behavior cloning policies struggle with multimodal demonstrations, high-dimensional action sequences, and (for implicit/energy-based policies like IBC) unstable training from negative sampling.
keyIdea: Represent the visuomotor policy as a conditional DDPM over an action sequence: the network predicts noise (the score / gradient of an energy) conditioned on observations and iteratively denoises Gaussian noise into actions, executed with receding-horizon control.
architecture: Noise-prediction network eps_theta is either a 1D temporal CNN (U-Net from Janner et al.) with FiLM conditioning on observation features and diffusion step k, or a minGPT-style time-series diffusion transformer with causal self-attention over action tokens and cross-attention to observation embeddings. Vision encoder: ResNet-18 trained from scratch, spatial-softmax pooling and GroupNorm instead of BatchNorm; one encoder per camera view.
inputs: Last To (=2) steps of observations: RGB images (one or more views) and/or low-dim state, plus robot proprioception.
outputs: Sequence of Tp future actions (end-effector position commands), of which Ta are executed before replanning.
actionRepr: Chunk of Tp=16 (CNN) continuous actions (position control; 6D rotation representation for pose actions) generated by DDPM/DDIM denoising; Ta=8 executed per inference.
params: CNN noise net ~256M (sim tasks; 67M on real-world tasks); transformer noise net 9M (80M for Kitchen/real Push-T); ResNet-18 vision encoder ~22M per setup (45M for Transport).
trainingData: Task-specific human teleop demos: Robomimic (Lift, Can, Square, Transport, ToolHang; PH and MH), Push-T, Multimodal Block Pushing, Franka Kitchen; real world e.g. 136 demos for real Push-T, 50 demos each for sauce pouring/spreading; bimanual tasks. 15 tasks across 4 benchmarks.

headlineResults.metric: average success-rate improvement over best baseline

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike Diffuser (which diffuses a joint state-action trajectory for planning), it models only p(A_t|O_t) with observations as conditioning, and closes the loop via receding-horizon action chunks.
limitations: Inherits BC limitations (needs adequate demonstrations; performance bounded by demo quality) and is computationally heavier / higher latency than single-step policies due to iterative denoising; transformer variant is sensitive to hyperparameters and the CNN variant over-smooths high-frequency (velocity) action changes.
notes: Code, data and training details released at diffusion-policy.cs.columbia.edu. Extended IJRR version (v5) adds bimanual Egg Beater, Mat Unrolling, Shirt Folding (55-75% success per the paper summary) and a control-theory section. In simulation, 100 iDDPM iterations were used for both training and inference; real world used DDIM with 16 inference iterations (Table 7) while Sec 3.4 cites 10 inference iterations for 0.1 s latency on 3080. Position control consistently beat velocity control, contrary to prior BC practice. Observation horizon of 2 found best for vision policies. Square-cosine noise schedule (iDDPM) worked best. Affiliations differ across arXiv versions (v1: Columbia/TRI/MIT; v5 lists Google DeepMind).

Noise-prediction net (1D CNN + FiLM or diffusion transformer)

algorithmSteps: Encode the latest To=2 observation frames with the vision encoder once (not per denoising step).
Sample A_t^K ~ N(0, I) of length Tp.
For k = K..1: predict noise eps_theta(O_t, A_t^k, k) and apply the DDPM/DDIM update.
Take the denoised sequence A_t^0 and execute the first Ta actions open-loop.
Observe again and replan (optionally warm-starting from the previous prediction).
Training: sample demo chunk, random k, add noise, regress noise with MSE; vision encoder trained end-to-end.
ablations: Action execution horizon: performance peaks around Ta = 8 steps (balance of temporal consistency vs responsiveness).
Position control consistently outperforms velocity control for Diffusion Policy (opposite to baselines).
Robust to simulated latency: maintains peak performance up to 4 steps of delay; pretrained CLIP ViT-B/16 fine-tuned reaches 98% on Square (ph) in 50 epochs.
hyperparams: To=2, Tp=16, Ta=8 (CNN); 100 training diffusion iterations; 100 inference iterations in sim, 16 (DDIM) on real robot; square-cosine noise schedule; lr 1e-4; batch 256 (state) / 64 (image); actions min-max normalized to [-1,1].

name: DP3
resolvedTitle: 3D Diffusion Policy: Generalizable Visuomotor Policy Learning via Simple 3D Representations
org: Shanghai Qi Zhi Institute; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Tsinghua University (IIIS); Shanghai AI Lab
problem: Image-based diffusion policies need 100-200 real demonstrations per task and generalize poorly across space, viewpoint, appearance and instance; prior 3D policies (PerAct, Act3D) rely on keyframe prediction and are slow.
keyIdea: Condition a Diffusion Policy on a compact 64-d feature from a sparse, colorless single-view point cloud encoded by a tiny MLP+max-pool encoder, giving data-efficient, generalizable and fast visuomotor control.
architecture: Perception: single-view depth (84x84) -> point cloud, cropped to a workspace box, farthest-point-sampled to 512 or 1024 points (xyz only) -> DP3 Encoder (3-layer MLP 3-64-128-256 with LayerNorm+ReLU, max-pool, projection 256->64). Robot pose via 2-layer MLP to 64-d; concatenated 128-d conditioning. Decision: convolutional (U-Net) Diffusion Policy backbone.
inputs: Single-view point cloud without color (from depth camera, e.g. RealSense L515) and robot proprioception; Nobs=2 observation steps.
outputs: Sequence of H=4 future actions (joint/end-effector commands; up to 22-d for Allegro hand, 52-d Shadow in sim).
actionRepr: Chunk of H=4 continuous actions via DDIM diffusion (sample prediction), Nact=3 executed per inference.
trainingData: Mostly 10 demos per sim task across 72 tasks / 7 domains (Adroit, Bi-DexHands, DexArt, DexDeform, DexMV, HORA, MetaWorld; DexArt/HORA use 100); demos from RL experts, scripted policies, or human teleop (DexDeform). Real: 40 demos per task on 4 tasks (Allegro hand + Franka gripper).

headlineResults.benchmark: 4 real-robot tasks (Roll-Up, Dumpling, Drill, Pour), 40 demos each

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces Diffusion Policy's 2D image ResNet encoder with a lightweight point-cloud MLP encoder producing a 64-d 3D feature, and shortens the horizon (H=4) with sample prediction.
limitations: Authors note the optimal 3D representation for control is still open and extremely long-horizon tasks remain a challenge; relies on a calibrated depth camera and workspace cropping.
notes: Code: github.com/YanjieZe/3D-Diffusion-Policy (weights/code released; 'openWeights' refers to code release, checkpoints availability not verified). Real robots: Allegro hand on Franka arm and Franka gripper, one RealSense L515. DP3 had a near-zero safety-violation rate in real experiments vs frequent violations by 2D baselines. CONFLICT (inter-paper): 3D Diffuser Actor reports DP3 at only 0.31 avg length on CALVIN ABC->D after re-implementing it with language attention and two-camera point clouds; that is a different setting from DP3's own evaluations. DP3 paper reports 3D Diffuser Actor runs at 1.67 FPS vs DP3 581 ms for 4 actions on CALVIN (per footnote measured by 3DDA authors).

keyEquations.meaning: Reverse diffusion step conditioned on the compact 3D feature and robot pose.

symbols.meaning: noisy action sequence at step k

keyEquations.meaning: Denoising objective (implemented with sample prediction rather than epsilon prediction).

algorithmSteps: Capture single-view depth, back-project to xyz point cloud (no RGB).
Crop to workspace bounding box and farthest-point-sample 512/1024 points.
Encode with DP3 Encoder to a 64-d vector; encode robot pose to 64-d; concatenate.
Sample Gaussian noise for an H=4 action sequence and denoise with 10 DDIM steps conditioned on the 128-d feature.
Execute Nact=3 actions, then re-observe.
Training: end-to-end (encoder + diffusion) on demos with 100 diffusion timesteps, sample-prediction target.
ablations: Removing point-cloud cropping drops 6-task average from 78.3 to 45.3; w/o sample prediction 67.0; adding color 72.0; replacing DDIM with DPM-solver++ 48.3.
Standard PointNet encoder scores 15.7 avg on the 6 ablation tasks; removing T-Net and BatchNorm (DP3-style) raises it to 72.5.
Long horizon (H=16, Nact=8) gives 78.2 vs 78.3 for H=4 on DP3 (no significant difference).
hyperparams: H=4, Nobs=2, Nact=3; 512 or 1024 FPS points; 64-d point feature (+64-d pose); DDIM, 100 train / 10 inference steps, sample prediction; batch 128; 1000 epochs (MetaWorld) / 3000 epochs (others); actions and obs min-max normalized to [-1,1].

name: 3D Diffuser Actor
resolvedTitle: 3D Diffuser Actor: Policy Diffusion with 3D Scene Representations
org: Carnegie Mellon University
problem: Diffusion policies used 2D or low-dim scene representations, while 3D policies (PerAct, Act3D, RVT) used deterministic classification/regression objectives that handle multimodality poorly; the two had not been combined.
keyIdea: A 3D relative denoising transformer that denoises end-effector trajectories whose tokens live in the same 3D space as lifted image-feature scene tokens, using rotary relative-position attention for translation equivariance, conditioned on language and proprioception.
architecture: CLIP ResNet50 2D features lifted to 3D scene tokens using depth and camera parameters (multi-view aggregated); CLIP language encoder tokens; proprioception token; noised trajectory tokens (MLP embedding + 3D position from noisy location). 3D relative denoising transformer: rotary-embedding relative self-attention among 3D tokens, cross-attention to language. MLP heads predict location noise, rotation noise and gripper openness.
inputs: One or more posed RGB-D images, language instruction, current end-effector pose (proprioception).
outputs: Trajectory of future end-effector 3D locations and 6D rotations over horizon T, plus binary gripper open/close per step (or next keypose on RLBench).
actionRepr: End-effector pose trajectory (3D location + 6D rotation) denoised by DDPM with separate schedulers for position (scaled-linear) and rotation (square cosine); gripper open via BCE head. On RLBench only next keypose is predicted and a BiRRT motion planner executes it.
trainingData: RLBench multi-view (18 tasks, PerAct setup) and single-view (10 tasks, GNFactor setup) keypose demos; CALVIN ABC->D (24 h teleoperated play, 35% language-annotated); real world: 12 tasks, 15 demos per task on a Franka with Azure Kinect.

headlineResults.value: close box 100%, put duck in bowl 100%, press stapler 90%

whatChangedVsParent: Keeps Act3D-style tokenized 3D scene features but replaces its deterministic ghost-point classification with a diffusion objective that denoises full pose trajectories through a relative 3D transformer.
limitations: Requires calibrated cameras and depth; evaluated on quasi-static tasks (not dynamic/velocity control); slower than non-diffusion policies because of iterative denoising.
notes: Project: 3d-diffuser-actor.github.io; code and checkpoints released (not verified here). RLBench numbers use keyposes + low-level BiRRT planner; CALVIN has no motion planner, so trajectories are predicted and replanned. Authors argue tokenized 3D scene representations beat DP3's holistic pooled 1D embedding because scene changes only affect local tokens. Robust to mild depth noise (sigma 0.01): 72.4% on RLBench multi-view (per paper appendix summary).

keyEquations.meaning: Forward noising of the clean end-effector trajectory.

symbols.meaning: clean trajectory of 3D locations and 6D rotations

keyEquations.meaning: L1 noise loss on location and rotation plus BCE on gripper openness.
DDPM sampling step used at inference.
Rotary relative 3D attention: weights depend only on relative 3D positions (translation equivariance).

nodes: Execute (trajectory) or motion planner to keypose
edges: Execute (trajectory) or motion planner to keypose

algorithmSteps: Encode each RGB-D view with CLIP ResNet50, lift patch features to 3D using depth and camera parameters; aggregate views.
Encode language with CLIP; make a proprioception token at the current end-effector position.
Sample tau^N ~ N(0,1) for the future trajectory (locations + 6D rotations).
For i = N..1: embed noisy poses as 3D tokens, run relative 3D transformer, predict location/rotation noise, apply DDPM step.
Read gripper openness from the i=1 prediction.
Execute the trajectory (CALVIN/real) or send the predicted keypose to a motion planner (RLBench), then replan.
ablations: 2D Diffuser Actor (per-view pooled 2D features) reaches only 47.0% vs 81.3% on RLBench multi-view.
Absolute instead of relative 3D attention: 71.3% vs 81.3% (still above all prior methods).
Separate schedulers (scaled-linear for position, square-cosine for rotation) reported to improve performance (appendix B.7).
hyperparams: 100 diffusion timesteps (RLBench), 25 (CALVIN); image size 256 (RLBench) / 200 (CALVIN); embedding dim 120 (RLBench) / 192 (CALVIN); FPS keeps 20% (RLBench) / 33% (CALVIN) of scene tokens; loss weights w1=30, w2=10; action space absolute pose (RLBench) / relative displacement (CALVIN).

name: Consistency Policy
resolvedTitle: Consistency Policy: Accelerated Visuomotor Policies via Consistency Distillation
org: Stanford University; Princeton University
problem: Diffusion Policy needs many sequential denoising steps (DDPM 100 steps, ~1 s per action on a T4), too slow for resource-constrained robots and dynamic tasks.
keyIdea: Distill a pretrained EDM-style Diffusion Policy teacher into a student that can jump along the probability-flow ODE in one or a few steps, by enforcing self-consistency (CTM-local objective) plus a denoising score matching loss.
architecture: Teacher: EDM diffusion model using Diffusion Policy's 1D convolutional U-Net with FiLM conditioning on observations and time. Student g_theta(x_t, t, s; o): same U-Net with expanded (zero-initialized) FiLM blocks for the stop time s, warm-started from the teacher.
inputs: Two frames of observations (wrist + third-person camera images and end-effector pose), as in Diffusion Policy; state-based for Push-T and Kitchen.
outputs: Sequence of end-effector pose actions (Diffusion Policy action-chunk format).
actionRepr: Action chunk (Diffusion Policy format) generated in 1 step (or 3 chained steps) by a consistency-distilled student of an EDM teacher.
trainingData: Robomimic Lift, Can, Square, Tool Hang (image obs, proficient-human data, 200 demos per task); Push-T (200 expert demos, state obs); Franka Kitchen (state); real world: Trash Clean Up, Plug Insertion (Franka Panda), Microwave (mobile manipulator).

headlineResults.comparedTo: DDIM 15 steps 11 ms, DDPM 100 steps 110 ms

headlineResults.benchmark: Real-world Trash Clean Up (laptop RTX 3070 Ti)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces Diffusion Policy's DDPM/DDIM sampler with an EDM teacher distilled via a CTM-local consistency objective so actions are generated in 1-3 network evaluations.
limitations: Distilling a deterministic ODE loses some of Diffusion Policy's multimodality (e.g., favors one side in Push-T); training is slightly less stable and takes longer (teacher + distillation), and it slightly underperformed DDIM on the long-horizon Microwave task.
notes: Project page consistency-policy.github.io. Baselines were given optimistic ParaDiGMS speedups (DDPM NFE 100->27, DDIM 15->9). Paper reports NFE 1 or 3 vs 9/27 for baselines. Dropout 0.2. Note on variance: Sec. III says single-step sampling uses z ~ N(0, I) instead of the standard unnormalized N(0, T^2 I); Sec. IV ablation phrases the same choice in normalized units as N(0, 1/T^2) vs N(0, 1). Both describe the same reduced-variance initialization. The alphaXiv auto-summary garbled this; the numbers here come from the PDF (Table VI). Exact Table I per-task success numbers for Push-T/Tool Hang/Kitchen were not extracted.

keyEquations.tex: \mathcal{L}_{DSM}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t,x_0,x_t\mid x_0}\left[d\left(x_0, s_\phi(x_t, t; o)\right)\right],\quad d(x,y)=\sqrt{\|x-y\|_2^2 + c^2} - c
keyEquations.meaning: Denoising score matching with pseudo-Huber metric: predict clean action from noisy one.

symbols.meaning: action noised to time t (x_0 + t*eps)

keyEquations.tex: \mathcal{L}_{CTM} = d\left(g_\theta(x_s^{(t)}, s, 0; o),\, g_\theta(x_s^{(u)}, s, 0; o)\right),\ x_s^{(t)} = g_\theta(x_t, t, s; o),\ x_s^{(u)} = g_\theta(x_u, u, s; o)
keyEquations.meaning: Two points on the same ODE trajectory must map to the same result when jumped to s then 0.

symbols.meaning: student jumping from time t to earlier time s
obtained from x_t by teacher ODE steps (u = t-1)

keyEquations.meaning: Total Consistency Policy distillation objective.

algorithmSteps: Train an EDM teacher Diffusion Policy with DSM (pseudo-Huber) loss.
Initialize student from teacher; add zero-initialized FiLM inputs for stop time s.
Sample t, set u = t-1 (via teacher ODE step) and s < u on the discretized mesh; compute CTM-local + DSM loss with stopgrad on all but the t->s jump.
Inference (1-step): sample low-variance initial noise, compute x = g_theta(z, T, 0; o), execute.
Inference (3-step): denoise T->0, re-noise to t_{2N/3}, denoise to 0, re-noise to t_{N/3}, denoise to 0.
ablations: Consistency objective on Square: Consistency Distillation 0.88, CTM 0.91, CTM-local 0.92 (CTM trains >40% slower).
Low initial-sample variance on Square: 1-step 0.92 vs 0.90, 3-step 0.96 vs 0.91; discretized vs continuous chaining on Tool Hang 0.77 vs 0.72.
Teacher-free Consistency Training reaches only 0.55 on Square vs 0.92 for distilled CP; removing dropout on s->0 drops 0.92 to 0.86; a 0.84 teacher still yields a 0.88 student.
hyperparams: EDM teacher with Heun solver and EDM discretization; CTM-local (u=t-1, arbitrary s<u); 1 or 3 NFE; 3-step chaining at t_{2N/3}, t_{N/3}; dropout 0.2; pseudo-Huber c=0.00054 sqrt(D); two observation frames; Diffusion Policy action-chunk format.

name: VQ-BeT
resolvedTitle: Behavior Generation with Latent Actions
org: New York University; Seoul National University
problem: BeT's k-means action tokenizer does not scale to high-dimensional actions or action chunks and has no gradients, while diffusion policies capture multimodality but need many forward passes at inference.
keyIdea: Learn a hierarchical residual-VQ tokenizer for actions (or action chunks), then train a GPT-style transformer to predict primary and secondary codes plus a continuous offset in a single forward pass.
architecture: Stage 1: Residual VQ-VAE (encoder phi, Nq=2 residual codebook layers updated by EMA, decoder psi). Stage 2: frozen RVQ; MinGPT transformer over observation (and optional goal) sequence with a code-prediction head (focal loss, primary and weighted secondary codes) and an offset head (L1). Image envs use ResNet18 encoder; real world uses HPR encoder.
inputs: Observation window o_{t-h:t} (state or image features); optional goal observation sequence for conditional generation.
outputs: Action or action chunk a_{t:t+n} = decoded code sum + predicted continuous offset.
actionRepr: Discrete residual-VQ codes (2 layers, codebook size 8-16) decoded to continuous actions plus a continuous offset; chunk length 1 in most envs (5 on PushT, 10 UR3, 6 nuScenes).
trainingData: Simulated: PushT (state/image), Franka Kitchen (state/image), Multimodal Ant, BlockPush, UR3 BlockPush; nuScenes driving (GPT-Driver preprocessing); real world: Hello Robot Stretch kitchen tasks with Dobb-E-style data collection.

headlineResults.comparedTo: DiffusionPolicy-C 100.7 ms, DiffusionPolicy-T 98.6 ms (10 diffusion iterations)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces BeT's non-differentiable k-means action bins with a learned two-layer residual-VQ tokenizer (hierarchical primary/secondary codes), keeping the offset head.
notes: ICML 2024. Code: github.com/jayLEE0301/vq_bet_official. Claims 5x speedup over diffusion policies in simulation and 25x on real robots. Real-robot finding: Diffusion Policy with receding-horizon execution (n=3) scored 0/30 on the low-cost Stretch vs 47/60 closed-loop (n=1), attributed to controller noise. VQ-BeT beat baselines in 5/7 unconditional and 6/7 conditional sim environments; it lost to DiffusionPolicy-T on BlockPush and DiffusionPolicy-C on Image Kitchen. Limitations section not extracted; field left empty.

keyEquations.meaning: Residual VQ-VAE tokenizer loss: reconstruction + codebook + commitment terms.
Focal loss on primary code plus beta-weighted loss on secondary codes.

symbols.meaning: code prediction head of the transformer

keyEquations.meaning: Total loss: code prediction plus L1 offset around decoded code centroid.

algorithmSteps: Stage 1: train residual VQ-VAE (Nq=2) on action chunks with reconstruction + VQ losses; EMA codebook updates; freeze it.
Stage 2: feed observation window (and optional goal) to MinGPT.
Predict categorical distributions over primary and secondary codes (optionally autoregressively) and a continuous offset.
Inference: sample codes, sum their codebook vectors, decode with psi, add offset.
Execute action in a single forward pass per step (closed loop).
ablations: Vanilla VQ instead of residual VQ hurts (Fig. 5 completed goals 3.22 -> 2.99 and 3.78 -> 3.65 on the two task panels; beta=1 gives 2.93 and 3.67).
Removing the offset head causes the largest drop (3.78 -> 0.52 completed goals on one panel; nuScenes L2 0.73 -> 1.41).
Weighting primary/secondary codes equally (beta=1) and action chunking both reduced performance in sim.
hyperparams: Nq=2 residual layers; codebook size 8-16; VQ latent dim 512 (256 BlockPush); lambda_commit=1; beta 0.1-0.6; MinGPT 6 layers, 6 heads, 120-d (4/4/72 for BlockPush); obs window 1-100 depending on env; chunk length 1 (5 PushT, 10 UR3, 6 nuScenes).

name: AdaFlow
resolvedTitle: AdaFlow: Imitation Learning with Variance-Adaptive Flow-Based Policies
org: The University of Texas at Austin
problem: Diffusion policies capture multimodal actions but need many recursive steps at inference; BC is fast but not diverse; rectified flow can reach one step only after costly reflow/distillation.
keyIdea: Train a state-conditioned rectified-flow policy and a small network predicting the conditional variance of the flow loss; since zero variance implies straight ODE paths, use variance to set adaptive Euler step sizes, giving one-step generation at unimodal states and more steps at multimodal ones.
architecture: Velocity network v_theta: Diffusion Policy CNN (U-Net) backbone (Diffusion Policy-C for RoboMimic/LIBERO). Variance network sigma_phi: small 4-layer MLP (SiLU, hidden 512) on U-Net bottleneck features, trained in a second stage with Gaussian NLL.
inputs: State or images (76x76 crops for RoboMimic/LIBERO), 2 observation frames.
outputs: Action chunk (prediction horizon 16, execute 8) plus predicted variance used only for step-size selection.
actionRepr: Chunk of 16 continuous actions generated by rectified flow with variance-adaptive Euler solver (average 1.17-1.56 NFE).
trainingData: 1D toy regression; D4RL Maze2D navigation (4 mazes); RoboMimic (Lift, Can, Square, Transport, ToolHang, PH/MH) and Push-T following Diffusion Policy setup; LIBERO subset of 6 Kitchen tasks.

headlineResults.comparedTo: Diffusion Policy NFE 20: 0.88; NFE 1: 0.00; Rectified Flow (reflow) 0.88

whatChangedVsParent: Adds a learned conditional-variance estimate to a rectified-flow policy and uses it to adapt ODE step size, avoiding reflow/distillation needed by standard rectified flow for one-step sampling.
notes: NeurIPS 2024. No real-robot experiments found in extracted pages. RoboMimic results obtained by fine-tuning from Diffusion Policy's open-sourced pretrained model for 500 epochs due to compute cost. BC matches speed (NFE 1) but lacks behavioral diversity. Joint vs two-stage training of variance net reported comparable. Explicit limitations section not extracted.

keyEquations.tex: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim D,\,x_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)}\left[\int_0^1 \|a - x_0 - v_\theta(x_t, t\mid s)\|_2^2\,dt\right],\quad x_t = t a + (1-t)x_0
keyEquations.meaning: State-conditioned rectified flow (flow matching) objective on linear noise-to-action interpolation.
Gaussian NLL trains variance net to predict residual variance of the flow loss.
Adaptive step size: large steps where variance is low, one step when zero.
Local Euler discretization error bounded by conditional variance (justifies step rule).

algorithmSteps: Stage 1: train v_theta with state-conditioned rectified-flow loss.
Stage 2: fine-tune small variance MLP sigma_phi on bottleneck features with Gaussian NLL.
Inference: sample z_0 ~ N(0, I), set t = 0.
While t < 1: eps_t = Clip(eta / sigma_phi(z_t, t|s), [eps_min, 1 - t]).
Update z_t <- z_t + eps_t v_theta(z_t, t|s); t <- t + eps_t.
Execute action chunk a = z_1.
ablations: Without variance estimation (plain Euler), maze success drops (Maze1 0.78 vs 0.98, Maze4 0.80 vs 0.86).
Robust to eta: eta=1.5 gives NFE 1.56, eta=2.5 gives NFE 1.12 with similar success on mazes.
Diffusion Policy needs >3 NFE to perform well; at NFE 1 it scores 0.00-0.32 on mazes and 0.00 on LIBERO.
hyperparams: Action prediction horizon 16, execution horizon 8, 2 observation frames; eta=1.5 (maze) / 1.0 (RoboMimic, LIBERO); eps_min set via 5 (maze) / 10 (RoboMimic/LIBERO) in Table 7 (likely 1/N_max steps); variance MLP 4 layers, hidden 512; lr 1e-4 AdamW.

name: FAST
resolvedTitle: FAST: Efficient Action Tokenization for Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Physical Intelligence; UC Berkeley; Stanford
problem: Autoregressive VLAs use per-dimension, per-timestep binning, which on high-frequency action chunks yields many highly correlated tokens with little marginal information, so next-token training stalls (e.g., models just copy the last token).
keyIdea: Compress action chunks before tokenization: apply a per-dimension DCT, scale-and-round the coefficients, flatten low-frequency-first across dimensions, and compress with BPE into a small number of dense tokens.
architecture: Tokenizer only (no learned network except BPE vocabulary): quantile normalization -> DCT per action dimension -> round(gamma*C) -> column-first flattening -> BPE. Used with the pi0 VLA backbone (PaliGemma-3B) as pi0-FAST, replacing least-used VLM vocabulary tokens with action tokens; also tested with OpenVLA (Prismatic 7B).
inputs: For the tokenizer: 1-second normalized action chunks. For pi0-FAST: images + language instruction (+ state).
outputs: Variable-length sequence of discrete action tokens, decoded invertibly back to a continuous action chunk.
actionRepr: 1-second action chunk compressed via DCT + quantization + BPE (vocab 1024) into roughly 30 tokens per arm, decoded autoregressively by the VLA.
params: pi0-FAST: PaliGemma-3B based VLA (paper cites 2B-parameter language backbone used for autoregressive decoding).
trainingData: FAST+ universal tokenizer: ~1M one-second action chunks from single-arm, bimanual and mobile robots; policies trained on LIBERO, table bussing, T-shirt folding, DROID, and up to 10k hours of robot data (pi0 mixture).
controlRateHz: Evaluated datasets: DROID 15 Hz, bussing/grocery 20 Hz, T-shirt/laundry/toast 50 Hz, BridgeV2 5 Hz

headlineResults.benchmark: Token count per 1 s chunk (T-shirt fold, 14-d, 50 Hz)
Token count per 1 s chunk (DROID, 7-d, 15 Hz)

headlineResults.metric: training time to match diffusion pi0

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces RT-2/OpenVLA per-dimension 256-bin tokenization with DCT+BPE compressed tokens, enabling autoregressive VLAs (pi0-FAST) to train on high-frequency dexterous data.
limitations: Autoregressive decoding is slow (~750 ms per chunk vs ~100 ms for diffusion pi0) because 30-60 tokens must be decoded through the full language backbone; tokenization is slightly lossy (scale gamma trades fidelity vs compression).
notes: FAST+ tokenizer released as HuggingFace AutoProcessor 'physical-intelligence/fast'. Only two hyperparameters (rounding scale 10, BPE vocab 1024). Naive binning failed to make progress on Table Bussing (20 Hz) and T-shirt folding (50 Hz). FAST+ reduces token count by at least ~2x on all datasets tested. pi0-FAST trained on DROID gave the first zero-shot DROID policy evaluated in unseen environments by language prompting alone. Ablation: removing BPE hurts (many repeated zero tokens, slower inference) but still beats naive tokenization. CONFLICT: the alphaXiv summary describes FSQ as 'a previous frequency-space quantization method' and quantization to '256 levels'; the paper instead uses FSQ (finite scalar quantization, learned VQ-like) as a compression baseline and quantizes by scale-and-round (gamma=10), not 256 bins.

keyEquations.meaning: Per-dimension DCT of the action chunk, then scale-and-round quantization of coefficients.

symbols.meaning: action dimension i over the H-step chunk
j-th frequency coefficient of dimension i

keyEquations.meaning: Low-frequency-first flattening across dimensions, then BPE compression into final tokens.

symbols.meaning: variable number of output action tokens

algorithmSteps: Normalize each action dimension so 1st/99th quantiles map to [-1, 1].
Apply DCT to each action dimension of the 1 s chunk.
Multiply coefficients by gamma and round to integers (sparse matrix).
Flatten column-first (all dimensions' lowest frequencies first).
Train BPE on the flattened sequences (once per dataset, or use FAST+), then encode into tokens.
Train the VLA with next-token prediction on these tokens; at inference decode tokens autoregressively and invert BPE, rounding scale and DCT.
ablations: Removing BPE lowers table-bussing and T-shirt performance (many repeated zero tokens, slower inference) but still beats naive binning.
OpenVLA + FAST+ trains effectively on 50 Hz T-shirt folding where OpenVLA's naive tokenization fails (backbone-independence).
FAST roughly matches FSQ-based compressed tokenization while being simpler; FAST+ universal tokenizer closely matches per-dataset FAST.
hyperparams: 1-second chunks; rounding scale gamma=10; BPE vocabulary 1024; ~30 tokens per arm per chunk; naive baseline 256 bins per dimension per step; FAST+ trained on ~1M chunks.

name: OpenVLA-OFT
resolvedTitle: Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success
org: Stanford University
problem: Autoregressive VLAs like OpenVLA are too slow (3-5 Hz) for high-frequency control (25-50+ Hz) and fine-tune poorly to bimanual robots; there was little empirical guidance on how to fine-tune VLAs for a new robot.
keyIdea: An Optimized Fine-Tuning (OFT) recipe: parallel decoding with bidirectional attention + action chunking, continuous actions from an MLP head, and a plain L1 regression loss; OFT+ adds FiLM language conditioning inside the vision transformers.
architecture: OpenVLA (fused SigLIP+DINOv2 vision encoder, Llama-2 7B decoder) fine-tuned via LoRA; empty action embeddings with a bidirectional mask replace teacher-forced tokens; the LM output layer is replaced by a 4-layer ReLU MLP action head; proprio projected by a 2-layer MLP; optional FiLM (gamma, beta from averaged language embedding) in every ViT block.
inputs: 1-3 RGB images (224x224; third-person + wrist), optional robot proprioceptive state, language instruction.
outputs: Chunk of K continuous normalized actions in one forward pass.
actionRepr: Chunk of K continuous actions predicted in parallel via L1 regression (K=8 x 7-D delta EEF on LIBERO; K=25 x 14-D absolute joint angles on ALOHA), executed open-loop.
trainingData: Base: OpenVLA pretrained on 1M OXE episodes. Fine-tune: LIBERO 500 demos per suite; ALOHA 20-300 demos per task; also scaled to BridgeData V2 (50,365 demos).
controlRateHz: 25 (ALOHA); throughput 109.7 Hz (LIBERO, 1 image), 77.9 Hz (ALOHA, 3 images) on A100

headlineResults.comparedTo: pi0 93.33; DP 79.17; RDT-1B 73.33; ACT 71.25; OFT without FiLM 35.00

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces OpenVLA's autoregressive 256-bin discrete tokens + cross-entropy with parallel-decoded continuous action chunks trained by L1, plus multi-view/proprio inputs and FiLM.
limitations: L1 regression may fail to model truly multimodal action distributions; unclear whether OFT carries over to large-scale pretraining; OpenVLA without FiLM showed poor language grounding on ALOHA for unclear reasons.
notes: Paper reports 'up to 15% (absolute)' higher average success than baselines on ALOHA (Fig. 4 is a bar chart; per-task rubric tables in App. F). Fold shorts: all methods 100. Diffusion variant with 50 DDIM steps matched L1 on LIBERO (95.4 vs 95.3 avg) but latency 1.907 s. Abstract says 26x (LIBERO) and 43x (ALOHA) throughput vs base OpenVLA. Removing OpenVLA robot pretraining (fine-tuning Prismatic directly) drops LIBERO avg 97.1 -> 91.9. Code and checkpoints released at openvla-oft.github.io.

keyEquations.meaning: Mean L1 between predicted and ground-truth continuous action chunk (paper states in words, not as numbered equation).
Language-derived scale/shift applied per hidden unit across all ViT patch embeddings.

symbols.meaning: visual features in a ViT block
affine projections of averaged language embedding

algorithmSteps: Encode each camera view with fused SigLIP+DINOv2 (FiLM-modulated by language in OFT+).
Project visual patches and proprio into LLM embedding space; concatenate with language tokens.
Append K*D empty action embeddings (differ only by position).
Single bidirectional forward pass through Llama-2.
MLP head maps action-position hidden states to continuous normalized actions.
Train with L1 against ground-truth chunk (LoRA fine-tuning).
At test time execute the full chunk open-loop, then requery.
ablations: PD+AC with discrete tokens raises LIBERO avg 76.5 -> 90.2 (+14 abs); continuous L1 adds ~5 more (95.3).
Diffusion head: 50 test steps 91.1% LIBERO-Long at 4.2 Hz; 1 step 0.0%; L1 90.7% at 109.7 Hz.
Removing FiLM on ALOHA drops language following to 33% (chance) and scoop score 100 -> 35.
