name: Real-Time Chunking (RTC)
resolvedTitle: Real-Time Execution of Action Chunking Flow Policies
org: Physical Intelligence; UC Berkeley
problem: Large VLAs have inference latency longer than the control period, so synchronous chunking pauses and naive asynchronous switching causes mode-jumping/jerky discontinuities at chunk boundaries; temporal ensembling can average multimodal actions into invalid ones.
keyIdea: Treat asynchronous chunking as inpainting: while executing the current chunk, generate the next one with training-free guidance that freezes the actions that will execute during the delay and softly attends to the rest of the previous chunk.
architecture: Inference-time wrapper around any diffusion/flow policy: PiGDM-style gradient guidance added to the learned velocity field at each denoising step (vector-Jacobian product via autodiff), with a soft exponentially decaying mask and guidance-weight clip beta; background inference thread plus controller thread (Algorithm 1).
inputs: Current observation, remaining unexecuted actions of the previous chunk, estimated inference delay d, execution horizon s.
outputs: New action chunk of length H consistent with the committed prefix.
actionRepr: Chunk of H continuous actions from a flow-matching policy (H=50 at 50 Hz for pi0.5 real robot; H=8 in Kinetix), executed asynchronously.
params: Base pi0.5 (not RTC-specific); latency table cites 3B VLM backbone + 300M action expert for pi0 architecture
trainingData: None (training-free). Kinetix: 1M-transition datasets per env from RPO experts; real: pi0.5 fine-tuned policies.

headlineResults.value: best at +0/+100/+200 ms, no degradation with delay
headlineResults.comparedTo: Synchronous degrades linearly; TE sparse/dense fail at +100/+200 ms (protective stop)

headlineResults.value: RTC highest at all delays; gap widens with d
headlineResults.comparedTo: BID, naive async, TE, hard-mask RTC

headlineResults.value: succeeds with inference delays in excess of 300 ms (>30% of horizon)

parents: PiGDM / Pokle et al. training-free inpainting
whatChangedVsParent: Adds guided inpainting with soft masking and a guidance clip so that flow VLAs can run asynchronously without retraining.
limitations: Adds compute overhead vs plain sampling (2.5x per denoising step due to backprop); only applies to diffusion/flow policies; real-world tests do not include highly dynamic settings like legged locomotion.
notes: Kinetix simulation code released (github.com/Physical-Intelligence/real-time-chunking-kinetix); method is a sampling algorithm, not a model. Real-time delay d ~ 6/11/16 steps at +0/+100/+200 ms injected latency. Total system latency 108.76 ms (non-mobile) / 138.98 ms (mobile). Beta ablation: no benefit beyond beta=5; high beta diverges with 5 steps. Exponential decay mask best, linear close; guidance beats Diffuser-style overwrite inpainting. NeurIPS 2025.

keyEquations.meaning: Guided velocity: learned flow plus clipped pseudoinverse guidance pulling the denoised estimate toward previous-chunk actions.

symbols.meaning: noisy chunk at flow time tau

keyEquations.meaning: One-step estimate of the clean chunk and the variance term used in guidance weight.

keyEquations.tex: W_i = \begin{cases} 1 & i < d \\ c_i \frac{e^{c_i}-1}{e-1} & d \le i < H-s \\ 0 & i \ge H-s \end{cases},\quad c_i = \frac{H-s-i}{H-s-d+1}
keyEquations.meaning: Soft mask: frozen prefix, exponentially decaying overlap, fresh tail.

algorithmSteps: Controller calls GetAction every dt, consuming the next action and supplying the newest observation.
Background thread waits until at least s_min actions executed since last inference start.
Take remaining previous-chunk actions A_prev and latest observation; estimate delay d as max of recent delays.
Build soft mask W (Eq. 5); right-pad A_prev to H; sample A^0 ~ N(0,I).
For each of n denoising steps: compute clean estimate, weighted error vs A_prev, vector-Jacobian product, and integrate v + min(beta, ...) * g.
Swap in the new chunk as soon as ready; reindex t; push observed delay to buffer.
ablations: Soft masking beats hard masking, especially at small delays d (Kinetix).
Guidance clip beta: no marginal benefit beyond 5; large beta with 5 steps diverges and increases jerk.
BID (N=16) latency 115-223 ms vs RTC 97 ms, and BID underperforms RTC in simulation.
hyperparams: n=5 denoising steps; H=50 (real), 8 (sim); s_min=25; beta=5; delay buffer b=10; dt=20 ms.

name: UMI
resolvedTitle: Universal Manipulation Interface: In-The-Wild Robot Teaching Without In-The-Wild Robots
org: Stanford University; Columbia University; Toyota Research Institute
problem: Teleoperation is costly and lab-bound while human video has a large embodiment gap; prior hand-held gripper data could not transfer dynamic, bimanual or precise skills due to narrow FoV, imprecise SfM actions, latency mismatch and weak policy classes.
keyIdea: A hand-held GoPro-instrumented gripper plus a hardware-agnostic policy interface (latency matching, relative-trajectory actions and proprioception, Diffusion Policy) so human demos collected anywhere transfer directly to robot arms.
architecture: Data side: 3D-printed soft-finger gripper, wrist GoPro with 155-deg fisheye, side mirrors for implicit stereo, IMU-aware ORB-SLAM3 tracking, fiducial-based gripper width. Policy: Diffusion Policy with CLIP-pretrained ViT (B/16 or L/14) or ResNet-34 vision encoder.
inputs: Wrist fisheye RGB (224x224, with mirror views), relative EE pose history, gripper width; for bimanual, relative inter-gripper pose.
outputs: Sequence of desired relative EE poses (SE(3)) and gripper widths.
actionRepr: Chunk of relative SE(3) EE poses (relative to current EE pose at inference start) plus continuous gripper width, generated by DDIM diffusion (50 train / 16 inference steps).
trainingData: Per-task human demos with UMI grippers: e.g., 250 (cloth folding), 258 (dish washing); in-the-wild cup: 1400 demos in 30 locations with 15 cups (18 training cup styles bought).

headlineResults.comparedTo: no fisheye 11/20; absolute action 5/20; delta action 16/20

parents: Hand-held gripper data collection (e.g., Dobb-E, grabber-based)
whatChangedVsParent: Adds fisheye+mirror observation, IMU-SLAM metric actions, latency matching and relative-trajectory action/proprio so Diffusion Policy trained on hand-held data deploys on real arms.
limitations: Relies on kinematic filtering rather than embodiment-aware learning; SLAM needs visual texture; collection is slower than bare human hands due to gripper weight/bulk and fewer DoF.
notes: Hardware and software open-sourced (umi-gripper.github.io); checkpoint release not stated in paper. Gripper BoM $73 + GoPro/accessories $298; 780 g. SLAM accuracy: ATE 6.1 mm / 3.5 deg; inter-gripper RPE 10.1 mm / 0.8 deg. Fig. 5 example execution latencies: arm 100 ms, gripper 120 ms. UMI data collection >3x faster than SpaceMouse teleop for cup arrangement. Hyperparameter table obs horizon 2 (1 for ViT-L in-the-wild); action horizon column extracted as '6' (likely 16, unverified). Policy speed 0.5x of demo for quasi-static tasks. Cross-robot: 18/20 on Franka.

keyEquations.meaning: Relative-trajectory action: each future EE pose expressed in the frame of the EE pose at inference start (paper defines in words).

symbols.meaning: EE pose in SLAM world frame at t

nodes: UMI hand-held gripper (GoPro fisheye + mirrors + IMU)
edges: UMI hand-held gripper (GoPro fisheye + mirrors + IMU)
send ahead of time, drop outdated

algorithmSteps: Map scene with a mapping video, then record demos relocalized to the same map.
Recover metric 6DoF EE trajectories via IMU-aware SLAM and gripper width via fiducials; filter by target robot kinematics.
Train Diffusion Policy on relative EE trajectories + width with 2-step obs history.
At deployment, align camera/proprio streams to camera capture time using measured latencies.
Sample action sequence; convert relative poses to robot frame using current EE pose.
Discard actions whose timestamps have passed; send remaining commands early by execution latency.
ablations: Relative trajectory 20/20 vs delta 16/20 vs absolute 5/20 (cup arrangement).
Latency matching off: tossing 87.5% -> 57.5%.
In-the-wild data vs narrow-domain data (same CLIP ViT): 72% vs 0% in unseen environments.
hyperparams: Diffusion Policy, DDIM 50 training / 16 inference steps; obs horizon 2 (image and proprio); 10 Hz (20 Hz tossing); vision CLIP ViT-B/16 or ViT-L/14 (lr 3e-5) or ResNet-34; action lr 3e-4.

name: CrossFormer
resolvedTitle: Scaling Cross-Embodied Learning: One Policy for Manipulation, Navigation, Locomotion and Aviation
org: UC Berkeley; Carnegie Mellon University
problem: Cross-embodiment policies previously required shared or manually aligned observation and action spaces, limiting them to similar robots (e.g., single arms or ground navigators).
keyIdea: Cast cross-embodied imitation as sequence modeling: tokenize any set of observations into a sequence, insert embodiment-specific action readout tokens, and decode with per-action-type heads so one set of weights controls arms, bimanual rigs, wheeled robots, quadrupeds and drones.
architecture: Causal decoder-only transformer (12 layers, 8 heads, 512 emb, MLP 2048) shared across embodiments; ResNet-26 image tokenizers shared per camera type; linear proprio tokenizers; FiLM language conditioning or channel-stacked goal images; readout tokens feed 4 linear action heads.
inputs: Any subset of workspace, navigation and wrist images; quadruped or bimanual proprio; language or goal image; 5-step history.
outputs: Embodiment-specific action chunks from the matching head.
actionRepr: Continuous actions via L1 regression per head: single-arm 7-D Cartesian deltas chunk 4; nav 2-D waypoints chunk 4; bimanual 14-D joint positions chunk 100; quadruped 12-D joints, no chunking.
trainingData: 900K trajectories, 20 embodiments: OXE single-arm subset (Octo mix), DROID, 7K ALOHA trajectories, 60 h GNM navigation, 25 min Go1 walking, 200 Franka-tabletop trajectories; target datasets up-weighted.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real eval average across 6 settings (116 trials)
headlineResults.comparedTo: single-robot dataset same arch 0.68; best prior method 0.51

whatChangedVsParent: Extends Octo's readout-token design to heterogeneous action heads and far more diverse embodiments, with no manual action-space alignment.
limitations: No significant positive transfer across embodiments yet; hand-picked dataset sampling weights; inference speed of large transformers limits very high-frequency control.
notes: openWeights from project release (crossformer-model.github.io), not stated in the fetched pages. Training 300K steps, batch 512, TPU v5e-256; main text says 47 h, appendix says 80 h (internal inconsistency). Figure 1 says '30 Embodiments' while text says 20. Yang et al. policy scored 0% on WidowX. Sampling weights: Bridge 17%, GNM 17%, ALOHA-multi-task 17%, Fractal 17%, Go1 8.5%, Franka-tabletop 8.5%.

keyEquations.meaning: Input token sequence: per-timestep image, proprio and readout tokens under block-causal mask.
L1 regression of the embodiment-head output on readout embeddings (stated in words).

algorithmSteps: Chunk trajectories into 5-step observation windows.
Tokenize available images (ResNet-26) and proprio; mask missing observation types in fixed slots.
Insert readout token groups after each timestep's observations.
Run block-causal transformer.
Apply the action head for the robot's action type to readout embeddings.
Train with L1 on action chunks; randomly mask language vs goal image.
At test time sample the correct head and execute the chunk at robot's control rate.
ablations: Co-trained CrossFormer vs same-architecture single-robot training: 0.73 vs 0.68 average (no negative transfer).
Vs manually aligned cross-embodiment policy (Yang et al.): WidowX 0% for Yang vs 25-75% per task for CrossFormer.
5 steps of history needed for good navigation; kept for all embodiments without harm.
hyperparams: 12 layers, 8 heads, emb 512, MLP 2048; context 2135 tokens (5 timesteps); AdamW lr 3e-4, 2000 warmup, rsqrt schedule, wd 0.1, clip 1; batch 512, 300K steps; chunk sizes 4/4/100/1.

name: UniAct
resolvedTitle: Universal Actions for Enhanced Embodied Foundation Models
org: AIR Tsinghua University; SenseTime Research; Shanghai AI Lab; BAAI; Peking University; BUPT
problem: Crowd-sourced robot data has heterogeneous action spaces (different embodiments, control interfaces, operators); prior VLAs either treat them as equivalent (conflicting encodings) or hand-align them, and latent actions from video capture non-causal visual changes.
keyIdea: Learn a discrete Universal Action Space: a VLM selects a code from a shared vector-quantized codebook of atomic behaviors given observation and goal, and lightweight embodiment-specific heads decode that code into each robot's native commands.
architecture: LLaVA-OneVision-0.5B as universal action extractor producing p(u|o,g) over a 256 x 128 codebook; Gumbel-softmax selection; per-domain MLP decoder heads taking the universal action plus shared vision-backbone features (ACT head for bimanual).
inputs: Third-person image, language instruction (plus proprio/extra views for some heads).
outputs: Embodiment-specific control signals (EEF position/velocity or joint position) from the domain head.
actionRepr: Discrete universal action token (1 of 256 codes, 128-D) decoded by an MLP head into continuous embodiment-specific actions.
trainingData: ~1M demonstrations from 28 embodiments (OXE, LIBERO, DROID), action heterogeneity preserved (EEF position, EEF velocity, joint position).

headlineResults.benchmark: Bimanual AIRBOT with ACT head (fold towel)

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike LAPA-style latent actions inferred from frame changes, codes are selected by a VLM from task progression and supervised through real action losses via per-embodiment decoders.
limitations: Evaluated mainly on single-arm platforms; decoder heads are simple MLPs; scaling laws for universal action training not studied.
notes: openWeights from project page (2toinf.github.io/UniAct) not stated in fetched text. LIBERO results only in a bar figure (UniAct > Octo, CrossFormer, OpenVLA, LAPA in all 5 suites); numbers not extracted. Paper claims UniAct-0.5B 'reaches/outperforms 14x larger' OpenVLA-7B and LAPA-7B, but on semantic (3.9 vs 4.8) and language grounding (7.3 vs 8.8) OpenVLA is higher. At least 40% of 256 codes decode to consistent behaviors across robots. STE instead of Gumbel caused codebook collapse. Training 64 A100 x 10 days.

keyEquations.meaning: Extractor picks the universal action most relevant to task progress.

keyEquations.tex: u^* = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i u_i,\quad w_i = \frac{\exp((\log p(u_i\mid o,g)+\epsilon_i)/\tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{n}\exp((\log p(u_k\mid o,g)+\epsilon_k)/\tau)}
keyEquations.meaning: Gumbel-softmax relaxation for differentiable code selection; tau annealed.

keyEquations.tex: \hat a^{(k)} = h_k(u^*, o), \qquad \min_{U,\theta}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{a_i\in\tau_i,\tau_i\in D_k} \mathcal{L}_k(\hat a^{(k)}, a^{(k)}_i)
keyEquations.meaning: Per-embodiment heads decode the universal action; joint BC loss over all domains.

symbols.meaning: domain BC loss (CE, MSE, Huber or diffusion)

algorithmSteps: Sample batch from domain k.
VLM outputs log-probabilities over 256 universal codes given image and instruction.
Gumbel-softmax (annealed tau) forms u* as weighted codebook mix.
Head h_k maps (u*, visual features) to native action.
Backprop domain BC loss into head, codebook and VLM.
Adapt to new robot: freeze codebook and extractor, train a new lightweight head.
ablations: Straight-through estimator instead of Gumbel-softmax led to severe codebook collapse.
Bimanual AIRBOT with ACT head: UniAct 45/62.5/50/65 vs raw LLaVA-OV-0.5B 7.5/20/2.5/15 on four tasks.
Same task across robots gives similar code-usage distributions (low JS divergence); different tasks on the same robot differ.
hyperparams: Codebook 256 x 128; Gumbel temperature decayed; MLP heads; 1M demos / 28 embodiments; 64 A100, DeepSpeed, 10 days; adaptation with 100 demos (AIRBOT) or 250 demos/task (bimanual).

name: SpatialVLA
resolvedTitle: SpatialVLA: Exploring Spatial Representations for Visual-Language-Action Model
org: Shanghai AI Laboratory; Fudan; SJTU; Zhejiang University; ShanghaiTech; NWPU
problem: VLAs consume 2D images and lack 3D spatial understanding; cross-robot observations are not 3D-aligned and heterogeneous action statistics make spatial actions hard to learn.
keyIdea: Inject egocentric 3D positions (from monocular depth) into visual tokens, and tokenize actions with adaptive action grids fitted to the data distribution so each step is 3 spatial tokens; re-fit grids for new robots.
architecture: PaliGemma 2 backbone (SigLIP vision tower + Gemma2 decoder); ZoeDepth predicts depth, back-projected to egocentric 3D points, sinusoidally encoded + MLP and added to SigLIP patch tokens; spatial action token embeddings (V=8194) share the LLM embedding table.
inputs: 224x224 RGB image(s) and language instruction (camera intrinsics for back-projection).
outputs: Autoregressive spatial action tokens (translation, rotation, gripper) de-tokenized to continuous 7-D actions.
actionRepr: 3 discrete tokens per step: translation in polar coords (phi, theta, r) and rotation (roll, pitch, yaw) each binned with Gaussian equal-probability grids, plus 2 gripper tokens; 4 actions (12 tokens) per inference.
trainingData: 1.1M real robot episodes: OXE subset + RH20T (28 datasets), DROID removed for final 40k of 200k steps.
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces OpenVLA-style 7 uniform 256-bin tokens with 3 data-adaptive spatial grid tokens and adds Ego3D position encoding to visual tokens.
limitations: Gaussian fitting of action distributions may be suboptimal (grid clustering, noise sensitivity); autoregressive decoding slower than diffusion chunk decoding; weak on long-horizon tasks; OXE data quality varies.
notes: SimplerEnv/LIBERO avg numbers taken from paper's main tables via structured report (Tables not directly re-extracted); ablation tables were extracted directly. Paper's text gives both 20 Hz and 21 Hz for inference. Paper claims 3 tokens per action, while deployment outputs 4 actions / 12 tokens per inference (action chunk of 4 with ensembling of horizon 1 or 4). Bins: theta 16, phi 32, r 8; roll/pitch/yaw 16 each. Pretrain 64 A100 x 10 days, batch 2048, lr 2e-5. ZoeDepth frozen, 8.6% of params. Open-sourced code and HF weights.

keyEquations.meaning: Ego3D encoding: sinusoidal-MLP of back-projected 3D positions added to SigLIP features.
Grid edges chosen so each bin has equal probability under fitted Gaussian.

symbols.meaning: Gaussian pdf N(mu_a, Sigma_a) fit to normalized actions

keyEquations.tex: V = M_{trans} + M_{rot} + 2, \quad M_{trans}=M_\phi M_\theta M_r,\; M_{rot}=M_{roll}M_{pitch}M_{yaw}
keyEquations.meaning: Spatial action vocabulary size (8194 in the final model).
Cross-entropy next-token loss over spatial action tokens.

algorithmSteps: Normalize actions; convert translation to polar (phi, theta, r).
Fit Gaussian per variable over the whole mixture; split into equal-probability bins via CDF/PPF; linearize 3D grids to token ids.
Pretrain from PaliGemma 2 with next-token CE, text embeddings frozen, spatial embeddings and Ego3D MLP trained.
For a new robot: fit new Gaussians, rebuild grids, initialize new token embeddings by trilinear interpolation of pretrained ones (spatial embedding adaption).
Fine-tune (LoRA preferred on small data).
Inference: predict 3 tokens per step, map ids back to grid centers, unnormalize.
ablations: Linear 256-bin discretization vs adaptive grids: Pick Coke Can variant aggregation 40.7% vs 81.6%.
Removing Ego3D encoding: Pick Coke Can VA 81.6% -> 68.9%, Move Near VA 79.2% -> 66.7%.
Spatial embedding adaption with LoRA on LIBERO: +4.6/+5.1/+2.2/+5.4 points on Spatial/Object/Goal/Long.
hyperparams: V=8194 action tokens; bins theta 16, phi 32, r 8, roll/pitch/yaw 16 each; 3 tokens per action, 4 actions per inference; 224x224 input; pretrain batch 2048, lr 2e-5, 160k + 40k steps.

name: Gato
resolvedTitle: A Generalist Agent
org: DeepMind
problem: Agents were specialized per domain; the question was whether one sequence model with one set of weights could handle text, vision-language and control across many embodiments.
keyIdea: Serialize every modality (text, image patches, discrete and continuous observations/actions) into one flat token stream and train a single decoder-only transformer with masked next-token prediction, using prompt demonstrations for task conditioning.
architecture: 1.2B decoder-only transformer (24 layers, emb 2048, FFN 8196); text/discrete/continuous tokens via lookup embeddings; 16x16 image patches embedded by a ResNet block with within-image position encodings; local timestep position encodings.
inputs: Text, images (patches), proprioception and other observations, plus an optional prompt episode.
outputs: Next tokens: text, discrete actions, or discretized continuous actions.
actionRepr: Per-dimension discretized tokens: continuous values in [-1,1] binned into 1024 uniform bins (shifted to ids 32000-33024), sampled autoregressively; for the real robot, all action tokens of a step sampled in one pass.
trainingData: 604 tasks; control data ~1.5T tokens from 596 tasks (DM Lab, Atari, BabyAI, DMC, Meta-World, Procgen, RGB Stacking sim/real, Modular RL, etc.), filtered to >=80% expert return; plus MassiveText, M3W, ALIGN, LTIP, COCO, CC, OKVQA, VQAv2.
controlRateHz: 20 (RGB stacking real robot; overran by ~0.01 s)

headlineResults.benchmark: Real 'stack blue on green' after fine-tune on 500 demos

headlineResults.metric: games at or above average human

whatChangedVsParent: Extends sequence-model control to a single multi-modal, multi-task, multi-embodiment model with one weight set, including real-robot control.
limitations: Pure imitation of expert data; 1024-token context limits history, especially with images; transfer fails for visually distinct domains (Atari boxing); safety and value-alignment concerns for embodied generalists.
notes: Real-robot deployment used context length 1 and parallel sampling of all action tokens (trained with zeroed action tokens), run on RTX 3090s. Model scaling 79M -> 364M -> 1.18B improves normalized return. Fine-tuning recovers expert on RGB stacking with 10 episodes. Skill Mastery result used an earlier architecture variant (local transformer patch embedding). Sawyer arm: 3-DoF Cartesian velocity + 1 DoF + discrete gripper. TMLR 11/2022.

keyEquations.meaning: Autoregressive factorization over the serialized multimodal token sequence.
Masked NLL: loss only on text and action tokens.

symbols.meaning: 1 if token is text or logged action, else 0

keyEquations.meaning: Mu-law companding of continuous observations before 1024-bin discretization.

algorithmSteps: Tokenize a prompt demonstration and append to context.
Receive observation; tokenize (text, image patches, tensors) and append with separator.
Autoregressively sample action tokens until the action vector is complete (single pass on the real robot).
Detokenize and send action to environment.
Append action tokens and repeat; keep 1024-token window (Transformer-XL memory in deployment).
ablations: Scaling 79M -> 364M -> 1.18B consistently improves aggregate in-distribution performance at equal tokens.
Fine-tuning: larger models adapt with fewer RGB-stacking episodes; 364M overfits on 1 episode.
No benefit from pretraining on Atari boxing; random init did better.
hyperparams: 24 layers, emb 2048, FFN 8196; context 1024 tokens; 1024 bins for continuous values; mu=100, M=256; batch 512, 1M steps, 16x16 TPU v3, ~4 days; 25% of sequences prompt-conditioned.

name: VIMA
resolvedTitle: VIMA: General Robot Manipulation with Multimodal Prompts
org: Stanford, NVIDIA, Caltech, UT Austin, Macalester/AI2, Tsinghua
problem: Robot task specification (language, one-shot video demos, visual goals, constraints) is handled by separate specialised models, giving siloed systems that do not combine or generalize.
keyIdea: Express many manipulation tasks as multimodal prompts that interleave text and images, and train one encoder-decoder transformer that reads the prompt and outputs motor actions autoregressively.
architecture: Frozen pretrained T5-base encoder (last two layers fine-tuned) encodes interleaved text and object tokens; object tokens come from a domain-fine-tuned Mask R-CNN (bounding box via MLP + crop via ViT). A causal transformer decoder alternates cross-attention to the prompt with self-attention over the interaction history.
inputs: Multimodal prompt (text + object images / scene images / video frames); frontal and top-down RGB observations parsed into object tokens; past actions
outputs: High-level motor primitive parameters (pick-and-place or push: two SE(2) end-effector poses)
actionRepr: Two SE(2) poses per step (pick/place or push start/end), each decoded by independent discrete heads (x 50 bins, y 100 bins, rotation 50 bins), mapped to continuous via affine transform; one action per decision step
trainingData: VIMA-Bench (Ravens/PyBullet, UR5): 17 tasks, 50K trajectories per task, 650K successful scripted-oracle trajectories

headlineResults.comparedTo: best baseline VIMA-Gato, same training data

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces Gato-style decoder-only conditioning on image patches with object-centric tokens and cross-attention prompt conditioning in an encoder-decoder design.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation (VIMA-Bench) with high-level pick-and-place/push primitives and a domain-fine-tuned object detector; all methods still degrade strongly on L4 novel tasks (about 49% at best).
notes: Open-sources simulator, dataset, code and checkpoints (vimalabs.github.io). Abstract says 600K+ trajectories; body says 650K. Object augmentation injects false-positive detections with p={0:0.95,1:0.05}. Not a VLA in the RT-2 sense: no web-pretrained VLM backbone, only a frozen T5 text encoder.

keyEquations.meaning: Behaviour-cloning negative log-likelihood of actions given prompt and history.
Cross-attention: history queries attend to prompt keys/values in each decoder layer.
A prompt is an ordered sequence of interleaved text and image elements.

algorithmSteps: Tokenize prompt: text via T5 embeddings; images parsed by Mask R-CNN into object tokens (bbox + crop).
Encode prompt with T5 encoder (MLPs adapt non-text tokens).
At each step, parse current observation into object tokens and append with previous action tokens to history.
Run decoder: per layer cross-attend to prompt, then causal self-attend over history.
Decode last token with independent discrete heads into two SE(2) poses.
Execute primitive in simulator; repeat until episode ends.
Training: behaviour cloning NLL on 650K oracle trajectories with object augmentation.
ablations: Mask R-CNN object tokens lose little vs oracle boxes; raw-pixel tokenizers (patches, Perceiver, single image) and Object Perceiver (fixed #tokens) are clearly worse (Fig. 6).
Cross-attention beats GPT-style concatenation, mainly at small model sizes and on L4 novel tasks (Fig. 7).
T5 encoder size barely matters: L4 49.1 (small) / 48.6 (base) / 49.3 (large) with 200M controller.
hyperparams: 7 sizes 2M-200M (200M: dim 768, 11 blocks, 24 heads); action bins x50/y100/rot50; LR 1e-4, 7K warmup, cosine 17K steps, dropout 0.1; T5-base prompt encoder; 8x V100 nodes, largest run ~1 day

name: RT-1
resolvedTitle: RT-1: Robotics Transformer for Real-World Control at Scale
org: Robotics at Google, Everyday Robots, Google Research Brain Team
problem: Robot policies are trained per task on narrow data; it was unclear whether one high-capacity model trained on large, diverse real-robot data could absorb it and generalize zero-shot to new tasks, objects and environments while running in real time.
keyIdea: An efficient transformer that tokenizes a short image history (FiLM-conditioned EfficientNet + TokenLearner) and outputs per-dimension discretized action tokens, trained on 130k real demonstrations across 700+ instructions.
architecture: ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet-B3 conditioned on a Universal Sentence Encoder embedding via FiLM produces 9x9x512 = 81 tokens per image; TokenLearner compresses to 8 tokens per image (48 for 6 images); a decoder-only transformer (8 self-attention layers, 19M params) outputs action tokens. 35M params total.
inputs: History of 6 images (300x300) + natural-language instruction
outputs: Discretized action tokens for arm, base and mode
actionRepr: One action per step: 11 dims (7 arm: x,y,z,roll,pitch,yaw,gripper; 3 base: x,y,yaw; 1 mode: arm/base/terminate), each discretized into 256 uniform bins; not autoregressive over dims
trainingData: ~130k teleoperated demonstrations, 700+ instructions, 13 Everyday Robots mobile manipulators over 17 months; experiments also mix 518k sim trajectories and 209k Kuka IIWA (QT-Opt) episodes
whatChangedVsParent: Versus Gato/BC-Z: early language fusion via FiLM, TokenLearner compression, discrete per-dimension action bins and non-autoregressive actions for real-time inference, trained on far more diverse real data.
limitations: Imitation learning cannot exceed demonstrator performance; generalization limited to new combinations of seen concepts, not new motions; tasks are not highly dexterous.
notes: Paper states code is open-sourced; RT-1-X checkpoint released later via Open X-Embodiment (openWeights=true refers to that). Inference 15 ms network time (Gato-sized 37M: 129 ms). Mixing sim data: real tasks 92->90%, sim-only objects in real 23->87%. Mixing Kuka data: bin-picking eval 22->39%. CONFLICT: the Open X-Embodiment paper describes RT-1 as taking a history of 15 images and producing 81 vision-language tokens fed to the transformer; the RT-1 paper uses 6 images and TokenLearner (8 tokens/image).

keyEquations.meaning: Policy samples each action from instruction and all images so far (closed-loop).
Dataset of successful demonstration episodes used for behaviour cloning (NLL / categorical cross-entropy).

algorithmSteps: Embed instruction with Universal Sentence Encoder.
Encode each of last 6 images with FiLM-conditioned EfficientNet-B3 (81 tokens each).
Compress to 8 tokens/image with TokenLearner (reuse tokens across overlapping windows).
Feed 48 tokens to decoder-only transformer.
Read out 11 discrete action tokens (non-autoregressive).
De-tokenize and execute; repeat at 3 Hz until terminate or time limit.
Training: categorical cross-entropy with causal masking on 130k demos.
ablations: Continuous Gaussian actions instead of 256-bin discrete: seen 97->68, unseen 76->43.
No ImageNet pretraining: unseen 76->43, distractors 83->60.
Autoregressive actions: no benefit (seen 85) and inference 15->36 ms; no history: distractors 83->50.
hyperparams: 6-frame history; 81->8 tokens per image via TokenLearner; 8-layer transformer; 256 bins x 11 action dims; 3 Hz control; ~15 ms network inference

name: RT-2
resolvedTitle: RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control
org: Google DeepMind
problem: VLMs were used in robotics only for high-level planning, so low-level controllers did not benefit from web-scale semantic knowledge.
keyIdea: Express robot actions as text tokens and co-fine-tune a large pretrained VLM on robot trajectories plus web vision-language data, creating a vision-language-action (VLA) model that directly outputs low-level actions.
architecture: Two instantiations: RT-2-PaLI-X (ViT-22B vision encoder + 32B encoder-decoder UL2-like backbone; 5B and 55B variants) and RT-2-PaLM-E (12B, ViT-4B projecting into a decoder-only PaLM LLM). No new parameters; actions are output tokens. Served from a multi-TPU cloud.
inputs: Robot camera image + text instruction in VQA format ('Q: what action should the robot take to [task]? A:')
outputs: String of 8 action tokens (or natural language on VQA tasks)
actionRepr: One step per query: terminate flag + 6-DoF end-effector delta (pos, rot) + gripper extension; continuous dims discretized into 256 uniform bins -> 8 integer tokens (PaLI-X: integer tokens; PaLM-E: 256 least-frequent tokens overwritten)
trainingData: RT-1 robot demonstration data (13 robots, 17 months, office kitchen) co-fine-tuned with WebLI-based VLM mixture (~10B image-text pairs filtered to 1B); robot data ~50% of mixture for PaLI-X, ~66% for PaLM-E

headlineResults.benchmark: Emergent skills (symbol, reasoning, person recognition) avg

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces RT-1's 35M purpose-built network with a web-pretrained VLM (5B-55B) whose output vocabulary doubles as the action vocabulary, co-fine-tuned on web + robot data.
limitations: Web pretraining does not add new motions: physical skills stay limited to those in the robot data; large models are computationally expensive (cloud inference, 1-3 Hz for 55B), and few VLMs were available to build on.
notes: Output constraint: when prompted with a robot task, decoding is restricted to valid action tokens. Chain-of-thought variant (PaLM-E) adds a 'Plan:' step before actions, fine-tuned a few hundred steps. Failure cases: grasping by specific parts, novel motions (wiping, tool use), dexterous motions like folding. ~6,000 evaluation trials. Training: PaLI-X-55B LR 1e-3, batch 2048, 80K steps; PaLM-E-12B LR 4e-4, batch 512, 1M steps.

keyEquations.tex: \text{``terminate } \Delta pos_x\ \Delta pos_y\ \Delta pos_z\ \Delta rot_x\ \Delta rot_y\ \Delta rot_z\ \text{gripper\_extension''}
keyEquations.meaning: Action serialized as a space-separated token string, e.g. '1 128 91 241 5 101 127'.

algorithmSteps: Discretize each continuous action dim into 256 bins; map bins to existing VLM tokens.
Format robot data as VQA: image + 'what action should the robot take to [task]?' -> action string.
Co-fine-tune the VLM on a batch mix of web VL data and up-weighted robot data with next-token loss.
At inference, send image + instruction to cloud TPU service.
Decode 8 tokens restricted to the action vocabulary.
De-tokenize to end-effector deltas/gripper/terminate and execute; repeat closed-loop.
ablations: From scratch (5B): 9% unseen avg vs 44% co-fine-tuned.
Fine-tune only vs co-fine-tune: 5B 42 vs 44; 55B 52 vs 63.
Scale: 55B co-fine-tuned 63 vs 5B 44 (unseen average).
hyperparams: 256 bins per dim, 8 action tokens, 1 step per inference (no chunking); 55B: LR 1e-3, batch 2048, 80K steps; robot data ~50% (PaLI-X) / ~66% (PaLM-E) of mixture

name: Open X-Embodiment / RT-X
resolvedTitle: Open X-Embodiment: Robotic Learning Datasets and RT-X Models
org: Open X-Embodiment Collaboration (21 institutions; Google DeepMind, Stanford, UC Berkeley and others)
problem: Robot learning trains a separate model per robot, task and environment, and individual robot datasets are too narrow; it was unknown whether pooling many embodiments gives positive transfer.
keyIdea: Pool 60 existing datasets from 22 embodiments into one standardized (RLDS) dataset and train RT-1 and RT-2 on a multi-robot mixture with a coarsely aligned 7-DoF end-effector action space, showing positive transfer (RT-X).
architecture: No new architecture: RT-1-X = RT-1 (35M, FiLM EfficientNet + transformer); RT-2-X = RT-2-PaLI-X (ViT + UL2), 55B and 5B, co-fine-tuned about 1:1 with VLM data.
inputs: History of images from one canonical camera (resized) + language instruction
outputs: Tokenized 7-DoF end-effector action + terminate
actionRepr: 8 dims (terminate + x,y,z,roll,pitch,yaw,gripper, or their rates), each discretized into 256 uniform bins after per-dataset normalization; coordinate frames not aligned across robots
trainingData: OXE: 1M+ real trajectories, 22 embodiments, 60 datasets from 34 labs / 21 institutions, 527 skills (160,266 tasks). RT-X trained on a 9-manipulator mixture (RT-1, QT-Opt, Bridge, Task Agnostic Robot Play, Jaco Play, Cable Routing, RoboTurk, NYU VINN, Austin VIOLA, Berkeley Autolab UR5, TOTO, Language Table)

headlineResults.benchmark: 5 small-data domains (Kitchen Manip., Cable Routing, NYU Door, Autolab UR5, Robot Play)
headlineResults.comparedTo: Original Method and RT-1 trained per-dataset; beats Original Method on 4 of 5

headlineResults.benchmark: Emergent skills (Bridge skills on Google Robot)

whatChangedVsParent: Same RT-1/RT-2 architectures, but trained on pooled multi-embodiment data instead of a single robot's data.
limitations: Does not consider robots with very different sensing/actuation, does not test generalization to new robots, and does not characterize when positive transfer happens; RT-1-X underfits large-data domains.
notes: openWeights=true covers the dataset and RT-1-X checkpoint only; RT-2-X weights are closed. 3600 evaluation trials across 6 robots. RT-1-X underperforms RT-1 on data-rich domains (Bridge IRIS 27 vs 40; Google Robot 73 vs 92) -> capacity matters. Ablations: history 2 vs none (5B) 44.4 vs 14.5 emergent; no web pretraining 0%; co-fine-tune vs fine-tune similar (44.4 vs 48.7 emergent, 52 vs 47 generalization) unlike RT-2. Octo later reports OXE ~1.5M episodes and RT-X used a 350K-episode subset; OpenVLA reports 70+ datasets and 2M+ trajectories at its writing, so dataset size numbers vary by version. CONFLICT: this paper describes RT-1 as taking 15 images and producing 81 tokens, whereas the RT-1 paper uses 6 images and TokenLearner (8 tokens/image).

keyEquations.meaning: Coarsely aligned 7-DoF end-effector action, normalized per dataset then discretized (transcribed from prose).

algorithmSteps: Convert each dataset to RLDS tfrecords.
Pick one canonical camera per dataset; resize to common resolution.
Convert actions to 7-DoF end-effector (or rate) + terminate; normalize per dataset; discretize 256 bins.
Train RT-1-X on the robotics mixture; co-fine-tune RT-2-X ~1:1 with VLM data (cross-entropy).
At inference, predict tokens and de-normalize with the target robot's statistics.
Run at the robot's native rate (RT-1-X local, RT-2-X via cloud).
ablations: Removing Bridge from RT-2-X training: emergent skills 75.8 -> 42.8.
55B vs 5B RT-2-X: emergent skills 75.8 vs 44.4.
5B without web pretraining (from scratch): 0% emergent, 1% generalization.
hyperparams: 256 bins x 8 dims; per-dataset action normalization; RT-2-X ~1:1 VLM:robot co-fine-tuning; history of 2 images in best 5B ablation

name: Octo
resolvedTitle: Octo: An Open-Source Generalist Robot Policy
org: UC Berkeley, Stanford, CMU, Google DeepMind
problem: Existing generalist robot policies restrict inputs (e.g. one camera), lack support for finetuning to new observation/action spaces, and the strongest ones (RT-2-X) are closed.
keyIdea: A transformer-first policy with modular tokenizers, block-wise masked attention and readout tokens feeding a small diffusion action head, pretrained on 800k OXE trajectories and designed to be finetuned to new sensors, action spaces and robots.
architecture: Language tokenized by frozen t5-base (111M, 16 tokens); images by a shallow CNN then 16x16 patches (256 tokens 3rd-person, 64 wrist). Transformer backbone (Octo-Small 12 layers/384 dim/27M; Octo-Base 12 layers/768 dim/93M) with block-wise causal masking and learned readout tokens; diffusion action head = 3-layer MLP (hidden 256, residual, layernorm).
inputs: Language instruction and/or goal image; 3rd-person and wrist RGB (missing views zero-padded); 2-frame observation history
outputs: Chunk of future continuous actions (delta end-effector in pretraining; new heads for joint control on finetune)
actionRepr: Chunk of continuous actions sampled by a DDPM diffusion head (20 steps) conditioned on readout embedding; e.g. 14-D ALOHA joints with chunk 64 / execute 12 when finetuned to bimanual
trainingData: 800k trajectories from 25 curated Open X-Embodiment datasets; hindsight goal relabeling; language or goal randomly dropped

headlineResults.comparedTo: RT-1-X 35M; similar to RT-2-X 55B on WidowX and RT-1 Robot

whatChangedVsParent: Versus RT-1-X: transformer-first ViT-style backbone, diffusion head over action chunks instead of 256-bin tokens, flexible task/obs tokens and heads that can be added at finetune time, and a larger 800k-episode mix.
limitations: Struggles to use wrist cameras (only 27% of data has them) and language conditioning lags goal conditioning (56% of data has language); trained only on optimal demonstrations; novel skills zero-shot are weak (novel skill 5%).
notes: Octo-Base pretraining: 300k steps, batch 2048, TPU v4-128, 14 hours; finetuning ~5 h on one A5000 (24GB), 50k steps. Did not work: MSE heads (hedging/slow), 256-bin discrete heads (imprecise), proprioception input (causal confusion), finetuning or larger T5. Pretraining action chunk length not confirmed in the pages read (left out). CONFLICT to watch: surveys sometimes call Octo a VLA; it has no web-pretrained VLM backbone (only a frozen T5 text encoder).

keyEquations.meaning: One DDPM denoising step of the action chunk, conditioned on transformer readout embedding.

symbols.meaning: noisy action chunk at denoising step k

keyEquations.meaning: Sampling starts from Gaussian noise; K denoising steps run only in the small head.

nodes: New obs tokenizer / new action head (finetune)
edges: New obs tokenizer / new action head (finetune)

algorithmSteps: Tokenize language (t5-base) or goal image, and current + previous observation images (CNN patches).
Run one transformer forward pass with block-wise masked attention; read out embedding e.
Sample Gaussian noise x^K for the action chunk.
Apply K=20 denoising steps inside the diffusion head conditioned on e.
Execute the chunk with receding-horizon control, then repeat.
Finetune: add new tokenizers/heads as needed, update full model with the same diffusion loss (~100 demos, 50k steps).
ablations: Training objective (WidowX, Octo-Small): diffusion 83% vs MSE 35% vs discretized 18%.
Data: 25-dataset Octo mix 83% vs RT-X 11-dataset mix 60% vs Bridge-only 43%.
Architecture: ViT transformer-first 83% vs ResNet-50 + Transformer 70% on full OXE mix (ResNet better from scratch on ~100 demos).
hyperparams: Patch 16x16; 2-frame history; DDPM, cosine schedule, 20 diffusion steps; AdamW, inverse-sqrt LR, wd 0.1, clip 1.0; batch 2048, 300k steps; ALOHA finetune chunk 64 / execute 12

name: OpenVLA
resolvedTitle: OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model
org: Stanford, UC Berkeley, Toyota Research Institute, Google DeepMind, Physical Intelligence, MIT
problem: State-of-the-art VLAs (RT-2, RT-2-X) are closed, and there were no established recipes for efficiently fine-tuning VLAs to new robots and tasks on commodity hardware.
keyIdea: Fine-tune an open 7B VLM (Prismatic: fused DINOv2+SigLIP vision, Llama 2 7B) to predict RT-2-style discretized action tokens on 970k OXE episodes, and release weights, code and efficient LoRA/quantization recipes.
architecture: Prismatic-7B: 600M-parameter vision encoder concatenating DINOv2 and SigLIP patch features channel-wise; 2-layer MLP projector; Llama 2 7B language model. Vision encoder is fine-tuned during VLA training.
inputs: Single third-person RGB image (224x224) + language instruction
outputs: 7 discrete action tokens
actionRepr: One 7-DoF end-effector delta action per step (no chunking); each dim discretized into 256 bins spanning the 1st-99th percentile; the 256 least-used Llama tokens overwritten as action tokens
trainingData: 970k real robot episodes from Open X-Embodiment (single-arm, >=1 third-person camera; Octo mixture weights; DROID at 10% removed for final third); all-zero no-op actions filtered
controlRateHz: ~6 Hz inference on RTX 4090 (bf16); finetune setups at 5 Hz and 15 Hz
whatChangedVsParent: Same action-as-token recipe as RT-2 but with an open 7B backbone, fused DINOv2+SigLIP vision encoder, quantile-based bins, larger cleaned OXE mix, robot-only fine-tuning (no web co-training), plus LoRA and 4-bit quantization recipes.
limitations: Only single-image observations (no history, wrist or proprioception); inference throughput too low for high-frequency control (e.g. 50 Hz); success rates still below very high reliability; Diffusion Policy remains smoother on narrow dexterous tasks.
notes: Training: 64 A100s for 14 days (21,500 A100-hours), batch 2048, fixed LR 2e-5, 27 epochs (until action-token accuracy >95%). Needs 15GB bf16 for inference. RT-2-X beats OpenVLA on semantic generalization (web co-training). LoRA r=32 trains 1.4% of params (97.6M), 68.2% vs full FT 69.7%, 10-15 h on one A100. int4 71.9% vs bf16 71.3% at 7.0 vs 16.8 GB. Limitation wording taken from the paper summary report, not a verbatim page read.

keyEquations.meaning: Per-dimension uniform discretization between 1st and 99th action quantiles (transcribed from prose).

symbols.meaning: 1st and 99th percentile of training actions in that dimension

keyEquations.meaning: Next-token cross-entropy evaluated on action tokens only (transcribed from prose).

algorithmSteps: Discretize each action dim into 256 bins over 1st-99th quantile; map to last 256 Llama tokens.
Curate OXE mixture (single-arm, 3rd-person cam, Octo weights), filter no-op actions.
Fine-tune full Prismatic-7B (incl. vision encoder) with next-token loss on action tokens, 27 epochs.
Inference: encode image with DINOv2+SigLIP, project, prompt Llama 2 with instruction.
Decode 7 action tokens autoregressively and de-tokenize.
Execute one action; re-query each step.
Adaptation: LoRA r=32 on all linear layers with 10-150 demos, optionally serve in 4-bit.
ablations: Fine-tuning strategy (Franka-Tabletop): full FT 69.7%, LoRA r=32 68.2%, sandwich 62.1%, frozen vision 47.0%, last layer only 30.3%.
Quantization (BridgeData V2 subset): bf16 71.3%, int8 58.1% (slower inference), int4 71.9%.
OpenX pretraining matters: OpenVLA (scratch, base Prismatic fine-tuned) 43.4% vs OpenVLA 67.2% on Franka-Tabletop; 224px vs 384px no difference but 3x cheaper.
hyperparams: 224x224 input; 256 bins/dim (1st-99th quantile); fixed LR 2e-5, no warmup; batch 2048; 27 epochs; LoRA rank 32; 1 action per step, no history

name: RDT-1B
resolvedTitle: RDT-1B: a Diffusion Foundation Model for Bimanual Manipulation
org: Tsinghua University (Institute for AI, BNRist, Tsinghua-Bosch Joint ML Center)
problem: Bimanual foundation models face scarce dual-arm data, multi-modal action distributions from coordinating two arms, and heterogeneous action spaces across robots that make multi-robot pretraining hard.
keyIdea: A 1.2B Diffusion Transformer policy with robot-specific modifications, pretrained on 46 multi-robot datasets via a physically interpretable 128-D unified action space, then fine-tuned on 6K+ bimanual ALOHA episodes.
architecture: DiT backbone (28 layers, hidden 2048, 32 heads) with QKNorm + RMSNorm, nonlinear MLP decoder, and Alternating Condition Injection (image and language tokens injected in alternating cross-attention layers). Frozen SigLIP image encoder and frozen T5-XXL language encoder with MLP adaptors; low-dim inputs (proprio, noisy action chunk, control frequency, diffusion step) via MLPs with Fourier features.
inputs: Language instruction; 3 RGB views (exterior, right wrist, left wrist) x 2 frames (384x384); proprioception; control frequency
outputs: Denoised action chunk in unified action space
actionRepr: Chunk of 64 continuous actions in a 128-D physically interpretable unified space (joint/EEF pos, vel, gripper, base) with 0-1 padding mask; diffusion (DDPM 1000 train steps; DPM-Solver++ 5 steps at inference)
trainingData: Pretrain: 46 datasets, 1M+ trajectories, 21TB (OXE, RT-1, DROID, RH20T, Mobile ALOHA, RoboSet, BridgeData V2...). Fine-tune: self-collected ALOHA dataset, 6K+ trajectories, 300+ tasks, 100+ objects, 15+ rooms, 3M+ frames; GPT-4-Turbo instruction augmentation
controlRateHz: 6 Hz action-chunk inference (381 actions/s average) on onboard RTX 4090
whatChangedVsParent: Scales a diffusion policy to a 1.2B DiT with QKNorm/RMSNorm, MLP decoder and alternating image/text cross-attention, and replaces dataset-specific action spaces with a 128-D unified physical action space enabling pretraining on nearly all gripper-arm robots.
limitations: Paper states no dedicated limitations section; it notes the pretrained model still needs target-robot fine-tuning because of the embodiment gap, and key ablations were run without pretraining due to compute limits.
notes: Paper claims 56% average success-rate improvement over baselines. Pretraining: 48 H100 for one month, 1M steps; fine-tuning 3 days, 130K steps (started from the 500K checkpoint). Physical quantities are unit-aligned (m, rad) rather than normalized, to preserve cross-robot meaning; 6D rotation for EEF. Historical proprioception excluded to avoid shortcuts. Each modality masked independently with 10% probability. Fig. 1 summary: RDT 68.2% vs baselines up to 12.2% (metric aggregated per App. H). Evaluated only on one target robot (ALOHA).

keyEquations.meaning: Denoising loss: the network predicts the clean action (chunk) from a noised one.
DDPM reverse step, with a_t^0 replaced by the network estimate f_theta.

symbols.meaning: product of alpha_i up to k-1
standard Gaussian noise (0 at final step)

keyEquations.meaning: Policy models the conditional distribution of an action chunk of length T_a.

nodes: Noisy action chunk + proprio + freq + step k
Images: exterior, R-wrist, L-wrist x2 frames
edges: Noisy action chunk + proprio + freq + step k
Images: exterior, R-wrist, L-wrist x2 frames

algorithmSteps: Map each robot's proprio/actions into the 128-D unified space (unit-aligned, 6D rotation), concat 0-1 availability mask.
Pretrain on 46 datasets (sqrt-size sampling weights) with the denoising MSE loss on 64-step chunks.
Fine-tune on 6K+ ALOHA bimanual episodes with augmentation.
Inference: encode 2 frames x 3 views (SigLIP) and instruction (T5-XXL).
Start from Gaussian noise; run 5 DPM-Solver++ denoising steps through the DiT.
Decode 64-step action chunk via MLP decoder; execute; re-plan at ~6 Hz.
ablations: Diffusion vs regression: RDT (regress) 12.5/50/12.5 vs RDT 50/62.5/100 (unseen object/scene/instruction following).
No pretraining: RDT (scratch) 0/25/62.5; without MLP decoder or ACI (no pretrain) dexterity/instruction following drop from 32/62.5 to 12/12.5 (Fig. 4b).
hyperparams: T_img=2, T_a=64, 128-D unified action space (256-D with mask); DiT 28 layers, hidden 2048, 32 heads; DDPM 1000 steps (squaredcos_cap_v2) train, DPM-Solver++ 5 steps inference; AdamW LR 1e-4 constant, batch 32x48, bf16

name: π0
resolvedTitle: π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control
org: Physical Intelligence
problem: Autoregressive VLAs (RT-2, OpenVLA) discretize actions and cannot produce high-frequency action chunks needed for dexterous tasks; generalist robot policies lacked both scale and a pre-/post-training recipe for complex, long-horizon dexterity.
keyIdea: Attach a separate-weights 'action expert' to a pre-trained VLM (PaliGemma) and train it with conditional flow matching to emit 50-step continuous action chunks; pre-train on ~10k hours of cross-embodiment data, then post-train on curated high-quality task data.
architecture: Single transformer with two sets of weights (mixture-of-experts style): PaliGemma 3B (SigLIP + Gemma 2B, width 2048, depth 18) processes images and text; a ~300M action expert (width 1024, mlp 4096) processes proprioceptive state and noisy action tokens, interacting only via self-attention. Blockwise causal mask with 3 blocks [images+text], [state], [actions].
inputs: 2–3 RGB images, language command, proprioceptive state (joint angles)
outputs: Action chunk A_t = [a_t … a_{t+H-1}], H = 50 continuous actions (zero-padded to largest robot's action dim)
actionRepr: chunk of H=50 continuous actions (joint-space, padded to max embodiment dim) via conditional flow matching, 10 Euler steps
trainingData: Pre-training mixture: π dataset of 903M timesteps from 7 robot configurations and 68 tasks, plus OXE Magic Soup subset / Bridge v2 / DROID (9.1% of mixture); >10,000 hours of robot data total. Task-robot combos weighted by n^0.43. Post-training on task-specific curated data (1 h to larger datasets).
controlRateHz: up to 50 Hz (20 Hz UR5e/Franka, 50 Hz others); inference every 0.8 s (16 actions) at 20 Hz or 0.5 s (25 actions) at 50 Hz

headlineResults.benchmark: Out-of-box eval (shirt folding, bussing easy/hard, grocery bagging, toast)
headlineResults.value: best on all tasks; near-perfect on shirt folding and bussing easy (numbers in Fig. 7 bar chart only)
headlineResults.comparedTo: OpenVLA (7B), Octo (93M), π0-small, π0 parity (160k steps)

headlineResults.value: pre-trained π0 often ~2x better than training from scratch (text statement; per-task numbers in figures)
headlineResults.comparedTo: π0 scratch, ACT, Diffusion Policy, OpenVLA, Octo

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces autoregressive discretized action tokens of RT-2/OpenVLA with a flow-matching action expert (separate weights) that outputs 50-step continuous chunks at up to 50 Hz.
limitations: Unclear how pre-training data should be composed or weighted; not all tasks work reliably and it is hard to predict how much data is needed for near-perfect performance; unknown how far positive transfer extends to very different domains (driving, navigation, legged locomotion).

keyEquations.meaning: Conditional flow-matching loss: regress the action expert's vector field onto the denoising field.

symbols.meaning: action chunk of H=50 future actions

keyEquations.meaning: Linear-Gaussian (optimal-transport) probability path and its target vector field.
Forward-Euler sampling from noise (τ=0) to actions (τ=1); δ=0.1 → 10 steps.
Timestep sampling emphasizing low τ (noisier actions); no τ above cutoff s.

algorithmSteps: Encode 2–3 camera images with the vision encoder and embed language prompt
Run prefix forward pass over [images, text] and [state]; cache keys/values
Sample A^0 ~ N(0, I) for 50 action tokens
For 10 steps: action expert computes v_θ(A^τ, o_t) attending to cached prefix; A ← A + 0.1·v_θ
Output 50-step chunk; execute 16 (20 Hz robots) or 25 (50 Hz robots) actions open-loop (no temporal ensembling)
Re-observe and repeat
ablations: π0-parity (160k steps) still beats OpenVLA and Octo trained ≥160k/320k steps; even 470M π0-small (no VLM init) beats OpenVLA and Octo out of the box
VLM initialization strongly improves language-following vs π0-small, which translates into gains with human/high-level-policy guidance
Temporal ensembling (ACT) was tried and hurt performance; chunks executed open-loop instead
hyperparams: H=50 chunk; 10 Euler flow steps (δ=0.1); τ ~ shifted Beta(1.5,1), s=0.999; action expert width 1024 / mlp 4096; 700k pre-training steps; data weighting n^0.43
notes: Pre-training timestep count (903M) and '>10,000 hours' are both stated. Survey figures that list π0 control as '50 Hz' are consistent with 'up to 50 Hz'. Knowledge Insulation paper later reports that π0's action-expert gradients degrade VLM language following and that π0 needs 7.5x more steps than π0-FAST to converge. openWeights: released via the openpi repository (general knowledge, not stated in paper).

name: π0.5
resolvedTitle: π0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization
org: Physical Intelligence
problem: VLAs had not shown that end-to-end policies can generalize to entirely new real homes for long-horizon, dexterous tasks; robot data alone lacks the breadth needed for open-world generalization.
keyIdea: Co-train one VLA on heterogeneous sources (mobile-manipulator data, other robots, lab cross-embodiment data, high-level subtask prediction, web VLM data, verbal instructions) and use hierarchical inference in the same model: first predict a text subtask, then an action chunk conditioned on it.
architecture: π0-style VLA: SigLIP (400M) + Gemma (2B) VLM backbone; pre-training uses discrete FAST action tokens only; post-training adds a randomly initialized 300M flow-matching action expert. Same model outputs text (subtasks, VQA answers, boxes) and continuous actions; discretized proprio state input as text tokens.
inputs: Up to 4 cameras (front, rear, 2 wrists; high-level uses all four, low-level uses wrist+front), proprio state (as text tokens), high-level task prompt
outputs: High-level text subtask ℓ̂ (e.g., 'pick up the pillow') then continuous action chunk for 18–19 DoF (two 6-DoF arms + grippers, base velocity, torso lift)

name: Knowledge Insulation
resolvedTitle: Knowledge Insulating Vision-Language-Action Models: Train Fast, Run Fast, Generalize Better
org: Physical Intelligence
problem: Grafting a randomly initialized continuous action expert (diffusion/flow) onto a pre-trained VLM, as in π0, slows training and degrades the VLM's semantic knowledge and language following; autoregressive FAST VLAs keep knowledge but infer slowly (~750 ms per 1 s chunk).
keyIdea: Train the VLM backbone with next-token prediction on FAST-discretized actions plus VLM co-training data, while simultaneously training a flow-matching action expert whose gradients are stopped from flowing into the backbone.
architecture: π0 architecture: 3B VLM backbone + 300M action expert interacting only through attention. Stop-gradient is applied on backbone keys/values when the action expert attends to them; FAST tokens and continuous action tokens are masked from attending to each other.
inputs: Multi-view images, proprioceptive state (text or continuous), language instruction
outputs: Continuous action chunk from action expert at inference (FAST tokens and text only used as training targets / for language outputs)
actionRepr: continuous action chunk via flow-matching action expert (few integration steps); FAST discrete tokens as representation-learning target during training only
trainingData: Single-embodiment specialist mixes and a generalist mixture across many robots incl. non-action VLM data (captioning, VQA, bounding boxes, robot planning); evaluated on real tasks (table bussing, shirt folding, items in drawer, mobile manipulation) plus DROID and LIBERO.

headlineResults.benchmark: DROID (real, tabletop tasks from π0-FAST paper)

headlineResults.value: trains as fast as π0-FAST; π0 needs 7.5x as many steps

whatChangedVsParent: Formalizes π0.5's two-stage recipe into a single stage: joint FAST + flow-matching training with a stop-gradient insulating the VLM from the action expert, plus VLM data co-training.
limitations: Training with both continuous and discrete outputs adds ~20% training compute (offset by faster convergence); language following improves but is still far from perfect due to training-data correlations. Worse than OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO-10.

keyEquations.meaning: Joint next-token loss (text + FAST action tokens) and masked flow-matching loss for the action expert.

keyEquations.tex: \begin{bmatrix}P_{bb} & 0\\ P_{ab} & P_{aa}\end{bmatrix} = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\begin{bmatrix} Q_b(X_b)K_b(X_b)^T & 0 \\ Q_a(X_a)\,\mathrm{sg}(K_b(X_b)^T) & Q_a(X_a)K_a(X_a)^T\end{bmatrix} + A\right)
keyEquations.meaning: Attention with stop-gradient on backbone keys when action-expert tokens attend to backbone.
Value aggregation, also stop-gradient on backbone values for action-expert queries.

algorithmSteps: Tokenize actions with FAST; build mixed batches of robot action data, language+action data, and VLM-only data
Backbone predicts text and FAST tokens with cross-entropy (masked per example)
Action expert denoises continuous action chunk, attending to backbone KV through stop-gradient
FAST tokens and continuous action tokens cannot attend to each other
Sum losses (α=1) and update: backbone gets only AR gradients; expert gets flow gradients
At inference, skip AR action decoding; run a few flow steps in the action expert
ablations: Removing stop-gradient (joint-training) harms language following on 'items in drawer' similarly to π0; VLM data co-training partly compensates
Freezing the VLM backbone gives 0% on some tasks (representations insufficient for robotics)
Naive binning tokens as representation target beat continuous-only but underperform FAST; stride-5 subsampling better than dense naive tokens
hyperparams: α=1 with stop-gradient; FAST tokenizer for discrete target; 300M expert; ~20% training-compute overhead
notes: Survey mention of KI as part of π0.5 lineage is consistent: paper says π0.5 first trains FAST-only then adds action expert, KI makes it single-stage. π0.7 (2604.15483) explicitly uses the KI recipe. The paper quotes π0 at 10 Hz control vs 1.3 Hz for autoregressive VLAs (Sec. 4).

name: GR00T N1
resolvedTitle: GR00T N1: An Open Foundation Model for Generalist Humanoid Robots
org: NVIDIA
problem: No internet-scale humanoid dataset exists; embodiment-specific robot data forms isolated 'data islands', and a humanoid foundation model needs both semantic reasoning and fast motor control.
keyIdea: Dual-system VLA: an Eagle-2 VLM (System 2, 10 Hz) feeds middle-layer embeddings via cross-attention to a flow-matching DiT (System 1, 120 Hz actions), trained on a 'data pyramid' of web/human video, synthetic (simulation + neural video) and real robot data, with latent actions / IDM pseudo-labels for action-less video.
architecture: Eagle-2 VLM (SigLIP-2 + SmolLM2), 224x224 images → 64 tokens/frame, features taken from the 12th LLM layer; DiT with alternating cross-attention (to VL tokens) and self-attention (state + noisy action tokens), adaLN timestep conditioning; embodiment-specific MLP state/action encoders and action decoder. Language component frozen during training.
inputs: Image observation(s), language instruction, robot state (joint positions/velocities, EEF poses, base position…)
outputs: Action chunk of H=16 motor actions via embodiment-specific decoder
actionRepr: chunk of 16 continuous actions (embodiment-specific dimensions) via flow matching, K=4 Euler steps
trainingData: Data pyramid: human egocentric videos (latent actions), web data; simulation (DexMimicGen, 540k demos for GR-1 tabletop) and ~827 h neural trajectories from fine-tuned image-to-video models (expanding 88 h in-house teleop ~10x); real GR-1 humanoid teleop, OXE, others. ~50,000 H100 GPU hours pre-training, up to 1024 GPUs; batch 16,384, 200k steps.

headlineResults.benchmark: Pre-trained zero-shot GR-1 (bimanual handover; novel object)

whatChangedVsParent: Uses cross-attention from a DiT to middle-layer VLM features (instead of π0's MoE shared self-attention) plus embodiment-specific encoders/decoders and pseudo-labeled human/neural video in pre-training.
limitations: Focused mainly on short-horizon tabletop manipulation; long-horizon loco-manipulation needs better hardware, architecture and data; synthetic data generation struggles to be diverse, counterfactual and physically plausible.

keyEquations.tex: \mathcal{L}_{fm}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\tau\left[\left\| V_\theta(\varphi_t, A_t^\tau, q_t) - (\epsilon - A_t)\right\|^2\right],\quad A_t^\tau = \tau A_t + (1-\tau)\epsilon
keyEquations.meaning: Flow-matching loss for the DiT action module conditioned on VL tokens and state.
K-step forward-Euler denoising at inference; K=4.

algorithmSteps: Label action-less human/neural videos with latent actions (VQ-VAE encoder) or IDM pseudo-actions; treat as extra embodiments
Pre-train end-to-end with flow-matching loss over the whole data pyramid (language part of VLM frozen)
Post-train per embodiment (optionally co-train 1:1 with neural trajectories)
Inference: encode images+instruction with Eagle-2, take layer-12 embeddings
Sample A^0 ~ N(0,I); run 4 Euler steps of the DiT with state and VL cross-attention
Decode 16-step chunk with embodiment-specific decoder and execute

Middle-layer (12th) LLM embeddings gave faster inference and higher success than final-layer embeddings (qualitative statement)

name: SmolVLA
resolvedTitle: SmolVLA: A vision-language-action model for affordable and efficient robotics
org: Hugging Face; Sorbonne University; valeo.ai; ENS Paris-Saclay
problem: Existing VLAs have billions of parameters, costly training and poor deployability, and ignore community-collected data from low-cost robots.
keyIdea: A ~0.45B VLA built from a truncated SmolVLM-2 (first half of LLM layers, 64 visual tokens/frame) plus a flow-matching action expert with interleaved cross- and causal self-attention, pretrained on <30k community episodes, with an asynchronous inference stack.
architecture: SmolVLM-2 (SigLIP + SmolLM2) with layer skipping (use first N=L/2 layers; 16 layers), no image tiling, pixel shuffle to 64 tokens/frame; state projected to a single token in the VLM prefix. Action expert (~100M, hidden 0.75×d) alternates cross-attention to VLM KV and causal self-attention among action tokens. VLM frozen; only expert trained.
inputs: Multiple RGB images, language instruction, sensorimotor state
outputs: Chunk of n=50 continuous actions
actionRepr: chunk of 50 continuous actions via flow matching, 10 steps
trainingData: <30k episodes from publicly available community datasets (LeRobot/SO100); 200k pretraining steps, batch 256; ~30k GPU hours for the whole project.

headlineResults.metric: avg task time; cubes in fixed time

whatChangedVsParent: Shrinks π0's recipe ~7x: small VLM with half its layers, 64 visual tokens, interleaved CA/causal-SA expert, frozen VLM, community data and asynchronous chunked inference.
limitations: Pretraining data comes from a single robot type (SO100), limiting cross-embodiment training; dataset diversity is limited.

keyEquations.tex: L^\tau(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p(A_t|o_t),\,q(A_t^\tau|A_t)}\left[\left\| v_\theta(A_t^\tau, o_t) - u(A_t^\tau|A_t)\right\|^2\right],\ A_t^\tau = \tau A_t + (1-\tau)\epsilon,\ u = \epsilon - A_t
keyEquations.meaning: Flow-matching loss on action chunks conditioned on N-th-layer VLM features.

algorithmSteps: Robot client streams observation (images, state) to policy server
VLM encodes images (64 tokens each), text and state token through first N=L/2 layers
Action expert runs 10 flow-matching steps with interleaved cross-attn to VLM features and causal self-attn
Return 50-action chunk to client queue
Client executes actions while server computes the next chunk from a fresh observation (async)
Merge/overwrite queue with the newest chunk
ablations: Interleaved CA+SA 85.5 avg LIBERO vs CA 79.0 vs SA 74.5; causal SA 74.5 vs bidirectional 67.5

Chunk size 10 → 84.0, 50 → 80.3, 1 → 50.0, 100 → 74.5; pretraining on community data raises SO100 avg 51.7 → 78.3
hyperparams: n=50 chunk; 10 flow steps; N=16 LLM layers; expert width 0.75×d; 64 visual tokens; 512×512 images; 200k steps batch 256, lr 1e-4 cosine → 2.5e-6, AdamW (0.9, 0.95)

name: π0.7

trainingData: Demonstrations across many static/mobile, single/bimanual platforms in lab, home-like and in-the-wild homes; autonomous policy-evaluation data (incl. π*0.6 RL rollouts), human interventions, open-source robot datasets, egocentric human video, web data (localization, VQA, text, video captioning). name: CogACT
resolvedTitle: CogACT: A Foundational Vision-Language-Action Model for Synergizing Cognition and Action in Robotic Manipulation
org: Tsinghua University; Microsoft Research Asia; USTC; Institute of Microelectronics CAS
problem: VLAs like RT-2/OpenVLA quantize actions into bins, limiting precision, while regression heads ignore multimodality; resulting task success rates remain low.
keyIdea: Componentize the VLA: a 7B VLM produces a single 'cognition feature' that conditions a dedicated diffusion transformer (DiT) action module predicting a 16-step action sequence, plus an adaptive action ensemble at inference.
architecture: Prismatic-style VLM (DINOv2 + SigLIP vision, 256 visual tokens; LLaMA-2 7B) with an appended learnable cognition token; its output feature f^c_t conditions a DiT action module (default DiT-Base 89M; up to DiT-Large 308M) over noisy actions; total ~7.6B.
inputs: Single RGB image observation, language instruction
outputs: Sequence of current + 15 future 7-DoF end-effector actions
actionRepr: chunk of 16 (current + N=15 future) 7-DoF delta-EEF actions [Δx,Δy,Δz,Δφ,Δθ,Δψ,g] via DDPM-style diffusion (DDIM 10 steps, CFG 1.5), fused with adaptive action ensemble
trainingData: OXE subset (25 datasets, ~0.4M trajectories, 22.5M frames; excludes Language Table and DROID), initialized from OpenVLA weights; 135K iterations, batch 256, 16 A100s ~5 days.

headlineResults.comparedTo: RT-1 by +22.4 points; RT-2-X (55B) and OpenVLA lower

headlineResults.value: >35% over OpenVLA in sim, >55% in real; +18% absolute over RT-2-X in sim

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces OpenVLA's discretized autoregressive action tokens with a cognition-token-conditioned DiT diffusion action module and multi-step prediction with adaptive ensembling.
limitations: No explicit limitations section retrieved; action space restricted to 7-DoF single-arm gripper control and evaluation mostly on SIMPLER plus small real-robot sets.

keyEquations.meaning: Diffusion noise-prediction loss for the DiT action module, trained end-to-end with VLM.

symbols.meaning: predicted noise at denoising step i

keyEquations.tex: \hat a_t = \sum_{k=0}^{K} w^{ada}_k \cdot a_t|o_{t-k},\qquad w^{ada}_k = \exp\big(\alpha\cdot\langle a_t|o_t,\ a_t|o_{t-k}\rangle\big)
keyEquations.meaning: Adaptive action ensemble: weight past predictions by cosine similarity to current prediction.

symbols.meaning: action for time t predicted from observation t−k

algorithmSteps: Encode image with DINOv2+SigLIP into 256 tokens
Feed visual + language tokens + cognition token through LLaMA-2; read cognition feature
DiT denoises 16-step action sequence from noise conditioned on cognition feature (DDIM, 10 steps, CFG 1.5)
Cache predictions; gather predictions for time t from last K observations
Weight by exp(0.1·cosine similarity) and sum to get final action
Execute action; repeat each step
ablations: Action module: DiT-Large 308M 64.8 avg vs DiT-Base 89M 62.5 vs DiT-Small 58.5 vs 7-layer MLP (89M) 52.5 vs 3-layer MLP 50.6; success ~linear in log(module size)
Adaptive ensemble 62.5 vs temporal ensemble 58.9 vs action chunking 50.7; CFG 1.5 → 62.5 vs 1.0 → 55.7
hyperparams: N=15 future steps (17-token DiT context); DiT-Base 12 layers/768 dim; 8 diffusion steps per sample in training; DDIM 10 steps + CFG 1.5 at inference; ensemble α=0.1, K=2 (Google) / 7 (WidowX); lr 2e-5 constant, 135K iters

name: RT-H
resolvedTitle: RT-H: Action Hierarchies Using Language
org: Google DeepMind; Stanford University
problem: As multi-task datasets become semantically diverse ("pick coke can" vs "pour cup"), mapping high-level task language directly to actions shares data poorly and needs much more demonstration data.
keyIdea: Insert an intermediate layer of fine-grained 'language motions' (e.g. "move arm forward", "rotate arm right") between task and action: predict the language motion first, then the action conditioned on it. Humans can correct the robot by overriding language motions, and the model can be fine-tuned on those corrections.
architecture: Single RT-2-style VLM (PaLI-X 55B encoder-decoder, 22B ViT image encoder frozen during co-training) queried twice: a language-motion query (pi_h) and an action query (pi_l) where the language motion is fed to the encoder. Co-trained with the PaLI-X web mixture.
inputs: RGB image, task instruction in language (and, for the action query, the language motion)
outputs: Language motion (text) from query 1; tokenized robot action from query 2
actionRepr: Single-step discretized action tokens (each dimension into 256 bins, as in RT-2): end-effector delta position, delta axis-angle rotation, gripper open/close, termination flag
trainingData: Kitchen dataset (RT-1/RT-2; 70K demos, 6 semantic task categories) + new Diverse dataset (30K demos, 24+ semantic task categories) = Diverse+Kitchen; language motions auto-labeled from proprioception (>2500 language motions); co-trained 50/50 with the PaLI-X pre-training mixture

headlineResults.value: RT-H outperforms RT-2 by 15% on average (about 40% vs 25%)
RT-H 24.9 / 23.6; RT-H with GT language motion 17.9 / 17.8

whatChangedVsParent: RT-2 maps (image, task) directly to action tokens; RT-H first predicts a language motion and then the action conditioned on it, using the same VLM with two queries.
limitations: Absolute success rates still leave room for improvement even after corrections; only one intermediate hierarchy level was tested and the best abstraction level is open; systematic language-motion errors (e.g. repeatedly predicting "close gripper") can cause oscillatory or stuck behaviour.
notes: Automated labeling maps 9 action dims (3 delta pos, 3 delta rot, 2 base, 1 gripper) to spatial words, drops dims below a small-action threshold, orders by magnitude. Experiments use an 'asynchronous querying' variant. RT-H-Intervene updates only the language-motion query on correction data (correction samples upweighted ~50x). Paper reports RT-H outperforming IWR-style correction learning 'by 50%' in the intro.

keyEquations.tex: \pi(a, z \mid o, g) = \pi_h(z \mid o, g)\,\pi_l(a \mid o, g, z)
keyEquations.meaning: Action hierarchy: high-level policy picks language motion, low-level policy decodes it into an action.

algorithmSteps: Auto-label language motions for each timestep from end-effector deltas
Co-train one VLM on language-motion query, action query and web VQA data
At run time, query 1: 'What skill should the robot do to [task]?' -> language motion
Query 2: 'What action ... with current skill: [motion]?' -> action tokens
Detokenize and execute action
Optionally, human types/says a corrected language motion that replaces query-1 output
Collect corrections and fine-tune only the language-motion query (RT-H-Intervene)
ablations: RT-H-OneHot (integer class labels instead of language motions) performs much worse than RT-H, showing language structure matters.
RT-H-Cluster (K-means, 256 clusters) is slightly worse on average but better on the most precise tasks (open/close pistachio jar).
RT-H-Joint (single autoregressive query) performs comparably online but has higher MSE (25.44 vs 23.6 on Diverse).
hyperparams: Action dims discretized to 256 bins; training mix 50% web pre-training, 25% language-motion query, 25% action query; lr 1e-3, batch 1024; K-means ablation uses 256 clusters; 30 correction episodes per task.

name: Hi Robot
resolvedTitle: Hi Robot: Open-Ended Instruction Following with Hierarchical Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Physical Intelligence; Stanford University; UC Berkeley
problem: Flat VLAs follow simple atomic commands but cannot handle complex prompts, user constraints and mid-task feedback ("that's not trash"); out-of-the-box VLM planners lack grounding in the robot's skills and observations.
keyIdea: A 'System 2' high-level VLM reads images plus the open-ended prompt/interjection and emits an atomic language command (and optional spoken reply) for a 'System 1' pi0 VLA; the high level is trained on real skill-segmented data plus synthetic user prompts generated by a large VLM.
architecture: Two models both initialized from PaliGemma-3B: high-level policy fine-tuned for next-token prediction of commands/utterances; low-level policy is pi0 (PaliGemma-3B + flow-matching action expert). Speech via Whisper large-v2, TTS via Cartesia API.
inputs: Multi-view camera images, user prompt/interjection (text or transcribed speech), robot joint/gripper state (low level only)
outputs: High level: low-level language command + optional verbal utterance; low level: continuous action chunk
actionRepr: Action chunk A_t of the next H continuous actions from pi0 flow matching (7-dim UR5e, 14-dim bimanual ARX, 16-dim mobile ARX)
trainingData: Teleoperated demos per task segmented into 1-3 s skills (D_labeled) plus heuristic movement primitives; synthetic prompts/utterances D_syn generated by a large VLM; separate D_syn and high-level policy per task domain. Dataset sizes not stated.
controlRateHz: High level re-run every 1 s or on user interjection; low level ~10 Hz inference, 50 Hz control with action chunking

headlineResults.benchmark: Table bussing / sandwich making / grocery shopping (20 trials per task per method)
headlineResults.comparedTo: GPT-4o high-level with same pi0 low level
Flat VLA trained with the same synthetic data

whatChangedVsParent: Adds a fine-tuned VLM high-level policy trained on synthetic interaction data on top of pi0, replacing an out-of-the-box LLM planner (SayCan-style) or a single flat VLA.
limitations: Synthetic data generation relies on prompt engineering; high and low levels are trained separately and are unaware of each other's capabilities; no memory for long-context instructions; low level can temporarily ignore instructions near salient objects.
notes: Evaluated on UR5e (single-arm), bimanual ARX and mobile ARX (Mobile ALOHA based). Exact per-task IA/TP numbers only shown in bar charts; only the stated gaps are recorded here. Prompt a large VLM with images + skill label to generate user prompts and robot replies
