keyEquations.tex: a_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left( a_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}} s_\theta(o, a_t, o', t, 0) \right) + \sigma_t \delta_t
keyEquations.meaning: Inverse dynamics: condition on a clean next observation by fixing its timestep to 0.

keyEquations.tex: o'_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left( o'_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}} s_\theta(o, a, o'_t, 0, t) \right) + \sigma_t \delta_t
keyEquations.meaning: Forward dynamics: condition on clean action (t_a=0) and denoise the next observation.

algorithmSteps: Sample (o, a, o') from robot data; sample t_a and t_o' independently from U(0,T); noise both modalities; minimize Eq. 1.
For action-free video samples, fix t_a = T and impute actions with Gaussian noise; same loss (co-training).
Pretrain 100K steps on DROID subset (or LIBERO-90), then fine-tune on task demos.
Policy inference: set t_o' = T with o'_T ~ N(0,I); DDIM-denoise the action chunk over 10 steps.
Execute the first 8 of 16 actions and replan.
Other modes: t_a=0 for forward dynamics, t_o'=0 for inverse dynamics, t_a=T for video prediction.
ablations: Registers on LIBERO Book-Caddy / Soup-Cheese: 8 registers 0.88 / 0.90; 4 registers 0.83 / 0.86; none 0.81 / 0.85; cross-attention instead of AdaLN 0.78 / 0.86.
Reconstruction target (Stack-Bowls / Block-Cabinet): future obs 0.86 / 0.76 vs current obs 0.70 / 0.66 vs DP (none) 0.48 / 0.60.
Co-training data: robot videos 0.92 / 0.84, internet videos (Kinetics-400 + SSv2) 0.88 / 0.80, robot data only 0.86 / 0.76.
hyperparams: Obs length 2; action length 16, rollout 8; images 224x224x3 -> latent 28x28x4, patch 4x4x2; embed 768, depth 12, 12 heads; 8 registers; squaredcos_cap_v2 schedule, 100 train / 10 DDIM inference steps; w_a = w_o' = 1.0; lr 1e-4; 24 h on 4 A100 for 100K steps.
notes: Inverse dynamics trajectory tracking on LIBERO (Book-Caddy / Soup-Cheese, trajectory-length budget): 0.65 / 0.55 vs policy 0.47 / 0.26. Trained from scratch UWM and DP perform similarly; UWM gains more from pretraining. FLARE later uses UWM as a baseline (60.8% RoboCasa, 29.5% GR1 sim). Code released per paper.

name: FLARE
resolvedTitle: FLARE: Robot Learning with Implicit World Modeling
org: NVIDIA (GEAR), University of Maryland, Nanyang Technological University, UT Austin
problem: Joint world-model + policy methods that generate future frames are computationally heavy, add latency, and split model capacity between pixel fidelity and action modeling.
keyIdea: Future LAtent REpresentation Alignment: add a few learnable future tokens to a flow-matching DiT policy and align their intermediate-layer activations (cosine similarity) with a frozen/EMA embedding of the future observation, giving an implicit latent world model with no reconstruction.
architecture: GR00T N1-style flow-matching DiT (8 layers, alternating self- and cross-attention to vision-language embeddings); input sequence = state token + noised action chunk tokens + M=32 learnable future tokens; at layer 6 the future-token activations are MLP-projected and aligned to an action-aware VL embedding model (SigLIP-2 vision+text encoders, 4 fusion transformer layers, Q-former compressing to 32 query tokens) pretrained with an 8-block DiT action head.
inputs: Current multi-view RGB images + language instruction (via Q-former VL embedding), proprioceptive state
outputs: Action chunk; auxiliary predicted future-observation embeddings (training only)
actionRepr: chunk of H continuous actions via flow matching with K=4 Euler denoising steps
trainingData: Embedding model pretrained on ~2,000 hours of cross-embodiment data: GR00T N1 simulated + real GR1 humanoid tabletop data, in-house data, and 7 Open X-Embodiment datasets (DROID, Fractal, Bridge, PLEX, Language Table, Roboset, Mutex). Benchmarks: 24 RoboCasa tasks, 24 GR1 sim tasks; real GR1 with 100 trajectories per task; 150 GoPro human egocentric demos per novel object.

headlineResults.comparedTo: policy-only 61.9%; UWM 60.8%; GR00T N1 scratch 60.6%; Diffusion Policy 51.7%
GR00T N1 scratch 45.1%; policy-only 44.0%; DP 40.9%; UWM 29.5%
~14% higher on average than policy-only baseline

headlineResults.benchmark: Real GR1 novel objects (10 demos/object + human ego video)
headlineResults.comparedTo: roughly double the action-only baseline; 60% with 1 demo/object

whatChangedVsParent: Instead of reconstructing future frames/latents like UWM/UVA, FLARE only aligns DiT hidden states of extra future tokens to a compact future embedding, a REPA-style loss applied to future rather than current observations.
limitations: Focused mainly on imitation learning of pick-and-place on a real humanoid; still needs a small number of expert demonstrations; human egocentric video was collected in controlled settings with head-mounted GoPros - larger, in-the-wild egocentric data is future work.

keyEquations.tex: \mathcal{L}_{fm}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\tau\left[ \| V_\theta(\phi_t, A^\tau_t, q_t) - (\epsilon - A_t) \|^2 \right], \quad A^\tau_t = \tau A_t + (1-\tau)\epsilon
keyEquations.meaning: Flow-matching action loss (pi0 / GR00T N1 style).
Align DiT future-token activations with the embedding of the future observation.

symbols.meaning: DiT activations of the M future tokens at layer L (after MLP)

keyEquations.meaning: Total loss; lambda = 0.2. Action-free video uses only L_align.
EMA update of the target embedding model toward the policy's encoder; rho = 0.995.

algorithmSteps: Pretrain the action-aware VL embedding model (SigLIP-2 + fusion layers + Q-former) with a flow-matching action head on ~2,000 h of cross-embodiment data.
Initialize the policy's VL encoder and the target embedding from it; add M learnable future tokens to the DiT input.
Per batch: noise the action chunk, run DiT; compute L_fm on action tokens and cosine L_align between layer-6 future-token features and target embedding of o_{t+H}.
For action-free human video, apply only L_align.
Update target embedding by EMA (rho = 0.995).
Inference: drop future-token outputs; sample an action chunk with K=4 Euler steps from Gaussian noise.
ablations: Target embedding on GR1 sim: no FLARE loss 43.9%; SigLIP2 tokens 49.6%; SigLIP2 avg-pooled 50.9%; action-aware embedding 55.0%.
EMA coefficient on RoboCasa (24x300 trajectories): baseline 60.1%; rho 0.99 63.5%; 0.995 66.4%; 0.999 65.7%; 1.0 (frozen) 64.6%.
Applying the alignment loss too early (layer 4 of 8) notably hurts; layer 6 used. Policy-only for 160K steps stays at 44.1%, so gains are not from extra training.
hyperparams: K=4 flow denoising steps; DiT 8 layers, alignment at layer 6; M=32 future tokens / Q-former queries; lambda=0.2; EMA rho=0.995; future target at t+H (t+16 in SigLIP2 ablation); 80K steps, batch 1024 on 32 H100.
notes: Uses UWM as its main video-action baseline, extended to 400K steps. With the cross-embodiment pretrained embedding (never saw RoboCasa), 1000-traj RoboCasa result is 71.3% vs 70.2% for an in-domain embedding; +10% over policy-only at 100 trajectories per task. The paper's name expands to 'Future LAtent REpresentation Alignment'.

name: CoT-VLA
resolvedTitle: CoT-VLA: Visual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
org: NVIDIA, Stanford University, MIT
problem: VLAs map observations directly to actions without intermediate reasoning, lacking temporal planning, and cannot exploit action-less video.
keyIdea: Visual chain-of-thought: the VLA first autoregressively generates a subgoal image n frames ahead, then generates an action chunk conditioned on the observation, instruction and that subgoal; subgoal generation can be trained on action-less video.
architecture: Built on VILA-U 7B, a unified autoregressive multimodal model with a discrete (residual-quantized, depth-4) vision tower, projector, LLM backbone and RQ depth transformer; causal attention for image/text tokens, full attention within the action chunk (hybrid attention); vision tower frozen.
inputs: Current RGB image (256x256), language instruction
outputs: Subgoal image tokens (16x16x4 residual tokens), then a chunk of discretized 7-DoF actions
actionRepr: chunk of 10 actions, each 7 tokens with 256 bins per dimension (1st-99th percentile), predicted in parallel with full attention
trainingData: Pretraining on a curated Open X-Embodiment subset (Bridge 24.14%, RT-1, TOTO, VIOLA, RoboTurk, Jaco Play, Berkeley UR5, Berkeley Fanuc) plus action-less EPIC-KITCHENS-100 and Something-Something V2 (3.45% each); 11K A100 GPU hours. Fine-tuning on LIBERO, Bridge-V2 (45k trajectories), Franka-Tabletop (10-150 demos per task).
controlRateHz: Not stated; generating 256 image tokens before actions causes a ~7x slowdown vs direct action generation (chunk size 10)

headlineResults.comparedTo: 53.7% fine-tuning base VILA-U without robot/video pretraining

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike OpenVLA (direct token-level action prediction) and SuSIE (separate image-editing model + goal-conditioned policy), a single unified VLA both generates the subgoal image and the action chunk, with full attention over action tokens.
limitations: Image-token generation adds large overhead (256 tokens, ~7x slowdown); autoregressive image quality is below diffusion models; action chunking causes discontinuities between chunks and lacks high-frequency feedback (grasp failures on Bridge); visual reasoning does not yet generalize to entirely new tasks.

keyEquations.meaning: Visual chain-of-thought step: sample a subgoal image n frames ahead.
Generate an action chunk conditioned on observation, instruction and subgoal.
Residual-token image loss via the depth transformer.

symbols.meaning: d-th residual code at visual position j

keyEquations.meaning: Cross-entropy on discrete action tokens; total loss sums both.

algorithmSteps: Pretrain VILA-U on OpenX robot demos (subgoal + action) and action-less video (subgoal only); vision tower frozen.
Fine-tune on target-robot demonstrations with the same objectives.
At test time, sample subgoal image s_{t+n} ~ P(s | l, s_obs_t) autoregressively (causal attention).
Sample the 10-action chunk in parallel with full attention, conditioned on l, s_obs_t and the subgoal.
Execute all m actions, capture a new observation, repeat.
ablations: On LIBERO-Spatial/Goal, adding action chunking, then hybrid attention, then visual CoT each improves over a vanilla VILA-U VLA (numbers shown only in a figure).
Pretraining on OpenX + action-less video: Franka-Tabletop 53.7% -> 78.8% (46.7% relative).
Ground-truth vs generated goal images on OOD long-horizon tasks: 60% vs 20% and 40% vs 0% (40% absolute gain), showing visual reasoning is the bottleneck.
hyperparams: Image 256x256 -> 16x16x4 tokens (RQ depth 4); action chunk 10, 7 tokens/action, 256 bins; subgoal horizon sampled per dataset (e.g., Bridge 5-10 frames, TOTO 20-24); pretrain lr 1e-4 cosine, batch 2048, 10 epochs; fine-tune lr 1e-5 constant, 150 epochs.
notes: Abstract claims +17% over SOTA VLA in real world and +6% in simulation. Venue: CVPR 2025 (general knowledge, not verified). Bridge-V2 underperformance vs OpenVLA attributed to grasp failures from action chunking, not visual reasoning.

name: WorldVLA
resolvedTitle: WorldVLA: Towards Autoregressive Action World Model
org: DAMO Academy (Alibaba Group), Hupan Lab, Zhejiang University
problem: VLAs treat actions only as outputs and lack an understanding of action consequences, while world models predict future frames but cannot output actions; naive autoregressive action chunking in MLLM-based VLAs suffers error propagation.
keyIdea: A single autoregressive model with a shared token vocabulary for text, images and actions, trained on a mix of action-model data (predict actions) and world-model data (predict next frame from image + action), plus an attention mask that hides earlier actions in a chunk so each action depends only on text and images.
architecture: Initialized from Chameleon (unified image understanding/generation LLM); VQ-GAN image tokenizer (compression 16, codebook 8192; 256 tokens at 256x256, 1024 at 512x512); BPE text tokenizer (65,536 vocab incl. 8192 image and 256 action tokens); action tokenizer with 256 bins per dimension.
inputs: Language instruction + M=2 historical images (action model); image + action + fixed prompt (world model)
outputs: Discrete action tokens (policy) or next-frame image tokens (world model)
actionRepr: chunk of K discrete actions (K=5, or 10 for LIBERO-Long), each 7 tokens (3 rel. position, 3 rel. angle, 1 absolute gripper) with 256 bins, generated with action-masking attention
params: Not stated in retrieved text (Chameleon backbone)
trainingData: LIBERO only (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long; LIBERO-90); failed trajectories and no-op actions filtered; 90/10 train/val split for ablations, all data for the main table; no large-scale robot pretraining.
controlRateHz: Not stated in Hz; 3.13 FPS with 2 frames + chunking (Table 5)
whatChangedVsParent: Adds action-conditioned next-frame prediction (world model) to an OpenVLA-style discrete-token VLA on a Chameleon backbone, and replaces the causal mask over action chunks with one that masks prior actions.
limitations: Discrete image tokenizer has limited perceptual expressiveness; performance still degrades with overly long action chunks; scaling data/model size and auxiliary action heads are left for future work; evaluated only on LIBERO.

keyEquations.tex: a_t = \pi_\theta(a_t \mid o_{t-h:t}, l), \qquad o_t = f_\phi(o_t \mid o_{t-h:t-1}, a_{t-h:t-1})
keyEquations.meaning: Action model and world model sub-tasks unified in one autoregressive model M_psi.
Cross-entropy on action tokens plus down-weighted cross-entropy on generated image tokens.

symbols.meaning: balance weight, 0.04 (image tokens far outnumber 7 action tokens)

algorithmSteps: Tokenize text, images and actions into one vocabulary.
Build action-model sequences [text][M images][K actions] with loss on action tokens only.
Build world-model sequences ['Generate the next frame...'][image][action][next image] with loss on image tokens only.
Train on the mixture with L = L_action + 0.04 L_world.
At inference, generate K action tokens where each action attends to text and images but not previous actions in the chunk.
De-tokenize and execute the chunk; repeat.
ablations: Adding world-model data: 62.8% -> 67.2% avg (no chunking) and 76.6% -> 78.1% (with chunking + mask).
Naive autoregressive chunking drops avg SR 62.8% -> 54.0% (Spatial 77.8 -> 36.7); the proposed action attention mask recovers to 76.6%.
History frames (with chunking): 1 frame 74.0% @3.67 FPS, 2 frames 84.4% @3.13 FPS, 4 frames 84.7% @2.78 FPS; world-model pretraining alone lifts 62.8% -> 66.8%.
hyperparams: M=2 input images; K=5 action chunk (10 for LIBERO-Long); N=1 world-model round; alpha=0.04; 256 action bins; VQ-GAN codebook 8192; 256x256 or 512x512 images.
notes: World model beats a video-prediction (action-unconditioned) auxiliary objective for helping the policy. Code on GitHub (alibaba-damo-academy/WorldVLA); weight release not verified. LIBERO table lists baselines Seer 78.7/87.7 (scratch/pretrained, LIBERO-Long) and UVA 93.0 LIBERO-Long - CONFLICT: UVA's own paper reports 0.90 on 'Libero10' (a success/reward average), so WorldVLA's 93.0 figure for UVA differs from UVA's paper.

name: F1
resolvedTitle: F1: A Vision-Language-Action Model Bridging Understanding and Generation to Actions
org: Shanghai AI Laboratory; Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)
problem: VLAs map current state to action reactively, which makes them short-sighted and brittle in dynamic and long-horizon scenes; video-prediction policies anticipate the future but lack VLM semantic grounding.
keyIdea: Add a generation expert that predicts a goal-conditioned foresight image of the next observation via VAR-style next-scale prediction, then treat action generation as foresight-guided inverse dynamics.
architecture: Mixture-of-Transformer with three experts: understanding expert (PaliGemma, inherited from pi0), generation expert (Gemma backbone, randomly initialized, with a pretrained residual VQ-VAE from VAR), and action expert (Gemma, inherited from pi0). UGA progressive attention: generation attends to understanding, action attends to both, no reverse flow.
inputs: Language instruction, current image o_t plus history {o_{t-m}..o_{t-1}}, proprioception q_t
outputs: Foresight image o_hat_{t+1} (VQ tokens, next-scale) and action chunk a_{t:t+k}
actionRepr: Continuous action chunk via flow matching (chunk 50 on real robots, 4 on LIBERO, 8 on SimplerEnv), 10 denoising steps
trainingData: ~330k trajectories (330.9K trajs, 73.8M frames) across 136 tasks and 5 embodiments: AgiBot-World (187K), OXE-Fractal (87.2K), OXE-Bridge-v2 (53.2K), LIBERO (1.7K), plus in-house Genie-G1 / Franka / ARX LIFT II demos

headlineResults.benchmark: Dynamic conveyor-belt grasping (ARX LIFT II, 47 demos)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds a next-scale visual foresight generation expert between pi0's VLM and action expert so actions are conditioned on a predicted future image.
limitations: Paper lists future work rather than explicit limitations: scaling foresight to more embodiments and task families (locomotion, dexterous, multi-agent), adding physics-informed or structured world models, and adding RL / online adaptation.
notes: Code: github.com/InternRobotics/F1-VLA; weights on HuggingFace InternRobotics/F1-VLA. Training: Stage I 512K steps, batch 1280, generator predicts 10 scales; Stage II 100K steps, batch 2880, loss weight Gen:Act = 0.1:1. At inference, foresight is restricted to 4 scales. Motus describes F1 as merging VLA and IDM but excluding world model / video generation modes.

keyEquations.meaning: Stage I teacher-forced NLL on residual-VQ tokens of the next frame.

symbols.meaning: j-th VQ token of the foresight image

keyEquations.meaning: Stages II/III: autoregressive next-scale prediction conditioned on the model's own predicted tokens.
Flow-matching velocity loss for the action chunk.
Joint objective; Gen:Act weight 0.1:1 in practice.

symbols.meaning: balance between generation and action losses

algorithmSteps: Stage I: freeze understanding expert (from pi0); train generation expert with teacher forcing to predict next-frame VQ tokens over 10 scales.
Stage II: pretrain all three experts jointly on public robot data with autoregressive next-scale loss + flow-matching action loss (0.1:1).
Stage III: post-train on task-specific demos for embodiment adaptation.
Inference: encode instruction and current image with understanding expert.
Generation expert autoregressively predicts foresight tokens for 4 scales from history + instruction.
Action expert attends to understanding and foresight tokens plus proprioception and denoises an action chunk (10 steps).
ablations: Removing the generation expert (No-Gen) drops LIBERO+SimplerEnv average from 77.5% to 60.3%.
Freezing the generation expert after Stage I (Frozen-Gen) drops average to 73.8%; skipping Stage II robot pretraining (Cotrain-Scratch) drops to 74.2%.
Foresight scales: 2 scales 73.4%, 4 scales 77.5%, 6 scales 75.8%.
hyperparams: Foresight: next-scale VAR, 10 scales in Stage I, 4 at inference; gen resolution 256x256, und resolution 224x224; action chunk 50 (real) / 4 (LIBERO) / 8 (Simpler); 10 flow denoising steps; loss weight Gen:Act 0.1:1.

name: Motus
resolvedTitle: Motus: A Unified Latent Action World Model
org: Tsinghua University; Peking University; Horizon Robotics
problem: Embodied models are fragmented into separate VLA, world model, IDM, video generation and joint video-action models, and action experts cannot be pretrained on the large amount of action-less video.
keyIdea: Unify five modeling modes in one Mixture-of-Transformers of pretrained experts with a UniDiffuser-style scheduler (separate timesteps per modality), and pretrain the action expert on optical-flow-derived latent actions.
architecture: MoT with Tri-model Joint Attention linking three experts: video generation expert (Wan 2.2 5B), action expert (Transformer of same depth as Wan, AdaLN for flow timestep), understanding expert (on top of Qwen3-VL-2B last-layer tokens). Latent-action VAE: DPFlow optical flow -> DC-AE (4x512 tokens) -> lightweight encoder to a 14-dim latent action.
inputs: Current image o_t, language instruction, (proprioception); latent actions or real actions during training
outputs: Future video frames and/or action chunk, depending on inference mode (VLA, WM, IDM, VGM, joint)
actionRepr: Chunk of 48 actions at 30 Hz via rectified-flow denoising (10 inference steps), jointly with 8 video frames at 5 Hz
params: 8B total (VGM 5.00B, VLM 2.13B, action expert 641.5M, understanding expert 253.5M)
trainingData: Six-level embodied data pyramid: web data, egocentric human videos (e.g. EgoDex), synthetic data, task-agnostic Curobo random-action data, multi-robot trajectories (e.g. AgiBot, RDT, RoboTwin), target-robot data. Latent-action VAE trained with 90% unlabeled + 10% labeled data.
whatChangedVsParent: Unlike UWM (trained from scratch), Motus builds the unified video-action diffusion on pretrained VGM and VLM experts and pretrains the action expert on optical-flow latent actions.
limitations: Paper gives future directions only: more advanced unified architectures, more universal motion priors, and learning latent actions from internet-scale general videos.
notes: Project page motus-robotics.github.io/motus. RoboTwin setting: 2500 clean + 25000 randomized demos, 40k finetuning steps. The abstract's '+15% over X-VLA, +45% over pi0.5' refers to RoboTwin 2.0 randomized absolute gains. Motus in VLA mode reaches 83.90 vs 87.02 in joint mode on RoboTwin randomized; as IDM its action MSE is 0.014 vs 0.044 (ResNet18+MLP) and 0.122 (DINOv2+MLP). LingBot-VA reports Motus RoboTwin numbers as 88.7/87.0 (Easy/Hard), matching.

keyEquations.tex: \text{VLA: } p(a_{t+1:t+k}\mid o_t,\ell);\ \text{WM: } p(o_{t+1:t+k}\mid o_t,a_{t+1:t+k});\ \text{IDM: } p(a_{t+1:t+k}\mid o_{t:t+k});\ \text{VGM: } p(o_{t+1:t+k}\mid o_t,\ell);\ \text{Joint: } p(o_{t+1:t+k},a_{t+1:t+k}\mid o_t,\ell)
keyEquations.meaning: The five distributions one Motus model covers by choosing per-modality noise timesteps.
Latent-action VAE loss: flow reconstruction, weak alignment to real actions, KL regularization.

keyEquations.tex: a^{\tau-1}_{t+1:t+k} = a^{\tau}_{t+1:t+k} + v_a\,d\tau,\quad (v_o,v_a)=\mathrm{Model}_\theta(o^0_t, o^{T_\tau}_{t+1:t+k}, a^{\tau}_{t+1:t+k}, T_\tau, \tau, \ell)
keyEquations.meaning: VLA-mode sampling: video kept at full noise T_tau while actions are integrated.

algorithmSteps: Train latent-action VAE: DPFlow optical flow -> DC-AE -> 14-dim latent, with 10% labeled action supervision.
Stage 1: adapt the Wan 2.2 video generator on human videos, synthetic data and multi-robot trajectories.
Stage 2: train all three experts (VLM frozen) on video + language + latent actions.
Stage 3: SFT on target-robot trajectories with real actions.
Inference: choose mode by setting per-modality timesteps (e.g. VLA keeps video at pure noise).
Integrate rectified-flow velocities for 10 steps to output an action chunk (and optionally video).
ablations: RoboTwin randomized: w/o pretrain 77.00%, Stage-1 only 81.86%, full Stage-2 Motus 87.02% (+10.02).
RoboTwin clean: w/o pretrain 77.56%, Stage-1 82.26%, full 88.66% (+11.10).
VLA mode 83.90 vs joint video-action mode 87.02 on RoboTwin randomized.
hyperparams: Video 8 frames @5Hz; action chunk 48 @30Hz; 10 flow inference steps, logit-normal sampling; action expert hidden 1024, 30 layers; latent action 14-d from 4x512 DC-AE tokens; lambda_a=1.0, beta=1e-6.

name: Cosmos Policy
resolvedTitle: Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning
org: NVIDIA; Stanford University
problem: Video-model policies usually need multiple post-training stages and new action modules (separate action diffusers or IDMs), while unified video-action models are trained from scratch and miss pretrained spatiotemporal priors.
keyIdea: Fine-tune a pretrained video diffusion model in a single stage with no architecture changes by encoding actions, proprioception and values as extra latent frames ('latent injection') in the diffusion sequence, so one model is policy, world model and value function.
architecture: Cosmos-Predict2-2B-Video2World latent video diffusion transformer (EDM denoising, Wan2.1 VAE tokenizer, T5-XXL text). Sequence of 11 latent frames: blank, proprio, wrist, two third-person images, action chunk, future proprio, future images, future value. Non-image modalities are normalized to [-1,1] and duplicated to fill a latent volume.
inputs: Multi-view camera images (wrist + third-person), robot proprioception, task description
outputs: Action chunk, future state (proprio + images) at t+K, and value V(s') (expected return)
actionRepr: Action chunk encoded as a latent frame and generated by EDM diffusion: 16 steps (LIBERO), 32 with 16 executed (RoboCasa), 50 at 25 Hz (ALOHA); 5-10 denoising steps
trainingData: Target-platform demos only: LIBERO (500 demos per suite), RoboCasa (50 human demos per task, 24 tasks), ALOHA 185 demos over 4 tasks; plus policy rollouts for planning fine-tuning.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real ALOHA with model-based planning (2 hard tasks)

whatChangedVsParent: Turns Cosmos-Predict2 into a policy + world model + value function purely by injecting new modalities as latent frames, with a single post-training stage and no new modules.
limitations: Model-based planning is slow (about 5 s per action chunk), limiting dynamic tasks; effective planning needs substantial rollout data; planning is only best-of-N with one search layer.
notes: Released code, checkpoints and training data (research.nvidia.com/labs/dir/cosmos-policy). Inference latency: 0.61 s (5 steps), 0.95 s (10 steps), 0.16 s (1 step) per chunk on 1 H100; 1-step still gets 66.4% on RoboCasa. Planning: best-of-N with N=8 on 8 H100s; 3 world-model samples x 5 value samples per proposal aggregated by 'majority mean'. pi0.5 slightly beats Cosmos Policy on ALOHA OOD trials (92.5 vs 89.3).

keyEquations.meaning: EDM denoising loss of the base video model, reused unchanged for all injected modalities.

symbols.meaning: clean latent sequence (images, actions, proprio, value)

keyEquations.tex: p(a, s', V(s') \mid s),\quad p(s', V(s') \mid s, a),\quad p(V(s') \mid s, a, s')
keyEquations.meaning: Policy, world model, value function trained in one model via 50/25/25 batch split and conditioning masks.

algorithmSteps: Encode proprio, images, actions and value as latent frames in the Cosmos sequence (s, a, s', V(s')).
Train jointly: 50% of batch trains policy p(a,s',V|s) on demos; 25% world model; 25% value function on rollouts.
Direct policy: denoise actions, future state and value in parallel (5-10 steps), execute the chunk, discard the rest.
Planning: collect rollouts, fine-tune a planning checkpoint (90% world model/value, 10% policy).
Sample N action proposals from the policy checkpoint.
Planning checkpoint predicts future state (x3) and value (x5) per proposal; aggregate by majority mean.
Execute the highest-value action chunk in full.
ablations: LIBERO: removing auxiliary targets (predict only p(a|s)) drops average from 98.5% to 97.0%.
LIBERO: training from random init instead of the pretrained video model drops to 94.6%.
ALOHA fold shirt: from-scratch variant scores 80.8, 18.7 points lower than full model, with jerky motions.
hyperparams: Action chunk 16 (LIBERO) / 32 exec 16 (RoboCasa) / 50 at 25 Hz (ALOHA); 5 denoising steps (sim), 10 (ALOHA); planning N=8, 10 action / 5 state / 5 value steps; full fine-tune of all weights.

name: LingBot-VA
resolvedTitle: Causal World Modeling for Robot Control
org: Robbyant (Ant Group)
problem: Chunk-based or open-loop video-action models have a reactivity gap, limited long-term memory, and non-causal bidirectional attention, and large video models are too slow for closed-loop control.
keyIdea: Autoregressive diffusion over an interleaved video-action token sequence with causal masking and a KV cache, fed with real observations each step, plus noisy-history augmentation for partial video denoising and asynchronous inference.
architecture: Dual-stream Mixture-of-Transformers with shared attention: video stream = Wan2.2-5B (hidden 3072, 30 layers); action stream same depth, hidden 768 (~350M params), initialized by copying scaled video weights. Wan2.2 causal VAE (4x16x16) + patchify, 192 spatial tokens per frame; frozen T5 text encoder via cross-attention; single-layer MLP action encoder/decoder.
inputs: Multi-view video observations (concatenated along width), language instruction, past actions (KV cache)
outputs: Next video-latent chunk (partially denoised) and action chunk, autoregressively
actionRepr: Unified 30-dim dual-arm action (per arm: 7 EEF + 7 joints + 1 gripper), chunks of K (sampled 1-4 in training) generated by flow matching with 10 Euler steps
trainingData: ~16K hours of robot manipulation data: AgiBot, RoboMind, InternData-A1, OXE (OpenVLA subset), UMI data, RoboCOIN, plus internal demos; pretrained for 1.4T tokens. Post-training with 50 demos per real task.
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces chunk-wise bidirectional video-action diffusion with causal autoregressive interleaved generation, KV-cached history and real-observation feedback each step.
limitations: Future work notes the heavy computational overhead of video compression / generation and the absence of tactile, force or audio inputs for contact-rich tasks.
notes: Code github.com/robbyant/lingbot-va, checkpoints on HuggingFace robbyant/lingbot-va. Inference: video 3 Euler steps integrating to s=0.6, action 10 steps to s=1.0 (Algorithm 1 text says video to s=0.5; minor inconsistency in paper). Video CFG 5.0, action CFG 1.0; noise augmentation p=0.5, s_aug~U[0.5,1.0]. Conclusion states 92.0% on RoboTwin 2.0 while tables give 92.93/91.55. RoboTwin video downsampled 50 Hz -> 12.5 Hz with actions kept at 50 Hz. Fast-WAM quotes LingBot-VA as 92.90/91.50 on RoboTwin.

keyEquations.meaning: Video dynamics flow-matching loss conditioned on noisy-augmented history and past actions.
Inverse-dynamics flow loss: action conditioned on current and next video latents.
Total objective; lambda = 1 in pretraining.

algorithmSteps: Encode initial observation into video latent and initialize KV cache.
Generate next video-latent chunk by partial flow integration conditioned on cache.
Generate action chunk by full flow integration conditioned on predicted video and cache.
Execute actions; encode newly received real observations.
Append real video latents and executed actions to the KV cache.
Asynchronously predict the next chunk while the current one executes (FDM-grounded async).
ablations: Deployment on RoboTwin Easy: full model 92.9; FDM-grounded async 90.4; naive async 74.3 (Horizon-3 tasks 32.9).
Initializing from WAN (Wan2.2-5B) instead of LingBot-VA pretraining: 80.6 vs 92.9 on RoboTwin Easy.
Asynchronous inference matches synchronous success while completing tasks 2x faster.
hyperparams: Chunk size K ~ U[1,4] in training; video 3 Euler steps (to s=0.6), action 10 steps; video CFG 5.0, action CFG 1.0; noisy-history aug p=0.5, s_aug in [0.5,1]; sequences packed up to 10K tokens; 192 spatial tokens/frame.

name: DreamZero
resolvedTitle: World Action Models are Zero-shot Policies
org: NVIDIA
problem: VLAs generalize semantically but fail on unseen motions and novel environments, and need repetitive task-specific demos; large video-diffusion policies are too slow for closed-loop control.
keyIdea: A 14B autoregressive World Action Model built on a pretrained image-to-video diffusion model that jointly denoises video and action chunks with a shared objective, uses ground-truth observations in the KV cache, and is optimized to run at about 7 Hz.
architecture: Wan2.1-I2V-14B-480P DiT backbone made autoregressive over chunks, with added state encoder, action encoder and action decoder; multi-view images concatenated into one frame; text encoder, image encoder and VAE frozen. Teacher-forcing chunk-wise training with attention masks.
inputs: Visual context (current + past frames via VAE), language instruction, proprioceptive state
outputs: Future video chunk and aligned action chunk
actionRepr: Relative joint positions; action horizon 48 steps at 30 Hz (1.6 s per chunk) for bimanual robots; flow matching with shared video/action timestep
trainingData: ~500 hours AgiBot G1 teleoperation (7.2K episodes, 22 environments, mean 4.4 min and 42 subtasks per episode, diverse non-repetitive); separately DROID for Franka. Cross-embodiment: 12 min human / 20 min YAM video-only; 30 min YAM play data for adaptation.
controlRateHz: ~7 (action chunk generation); 30 Hz low-level action execution

headlineResults.benchmark: AgiBot G1 seen tasks, unseen environments

whatChangedVsParent: Single end-to-end autoregressive joint video-action denoiser at 14B scale with shared timestep, trained on diverse non-repetitive data, plus a 38x inference-speedup stack.
limitations: Pretrains separately per embodiment (multi-embodiment left to future work); failures mostly stem from video generation errors; memory-dependent tasks not evaluated; naive inference is ~5.7 s per chunk without the optimization stack.
notes: Open-source weights, inference code and DROID/PolaRiS eval code (github.com/dreamzero0/dreamzero). Speedups (cumulative on GB200): CFG parallelism 1.8x, DiT caching 5.4x, torch compile + CUDA graphs 10.9x, kernel opts 14.8x, NVFP4 16.6x, DreamZero-Flash 38x. DiT caching cuts effective steps 16 -> 4. Coined the term 'World Action Model (WAM)' used by later papers (Fast-WAM follows [4] = DreamZero).

keyEquations.tex: \pi_0(o_{l:l+H}, a_{l:l+H} \mid o_{0:l}, c, q_l) = \pi_0(o_{l:l+H} \mid o_{0:l}, c, q_l)\;\pi_0(a_{l:l+H} \mid o_{0:l+H}, q_l)
keyEquations.meaning: Joint video-action prediction decomposes into video prediction times an inverse dynamics model.

keyEquations.tex: z^k_{t_k} = t_k z^k_1 + (1-t_k) z^k_0,\quad a^k_{t_k} = t_k a^k_1 + (1-t_k) a^k_0
keyEquations.meaning: Per-chunk linear interpolation with a shared timestep for video and action.

keyEquations.tex: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} w(t_k)\left\| u_\theta\left([z^k_{t_k}, a^k_{t_k}]; \mathcal{C}_k, c, q_k, t_k\right) - v^k\right\|^2\right]
keyEquations.meaning: Teacher-forced chunk-wise joint flow-matching loss conditioned on clean previous chunks.

algorithmSteps: Training: sample trajectory, noise each chunk's video latents and actions with an independent shared-per-chunk timestep.
Denoise current noisy chunk attending to clean previous chunks (teacher forcing) with joint flow-matching loss.
Inference: jointly denoise next video and action chunk using KV cache (4 effective steps via DiT caching; 1 step with Flash).
Execute the action chunk asynchronously while next inference runs on the latest observation.
Replace predicted frames with real observations in the KV cache to prevent compounding error.
ablations: Data diversity: diverse data 50% vs repetitive data 33% task progress (PnP Easy, same hours).
Model scale: 14B 50% vs 5B 21%; VLA baselines at 5B/14B score 0% on the same data.
DreamZero-Flash at 1 step keeps 74% vs 52% for plain 1-step (83% at 4 steps), 150 ms vs 350 ms.
hyperparams: Backbone Wan2.1-I2V-14B-480P; 100K steps, batch 128; action horizon 48 @30Hz; 16 diffusion steps nominal, 4 with DiT caching, 1 with Flash; target latency <200 ms; ~150 ms achieved; relative joint positions.

name: Fast-WAM
resolvedTitle: Fast-WAM: Do World Action Models Need Test-time Future Imagination?
org: IIIS, Tsinghua University; Galaxea AI
problem: Imagine-then-execute WAMs pay large test-time latency for iterative video denoising, and it is unclear whether their gains come from video co-training or from explicit future imagination at inference.
keyIdea: Keep video prediction as a training-time co-objective but skip future generation at test time: the video DiT encodes only the current frame in one forward pass and an action expert denoises actions from that latent world representation.
architecture: MoT with shared attention: Wan2.2-5B video DiT (with its T5 text encoder and VAE) plus an action-expert DiT (hidden 1024, ~1B). Structured attention mask: action tokens see clean first-frame tokens but never future video tokens; first-frame tokens attend to nothing else.
inputs: Current frame (multi-camera images concatenated), language instruction
outputs: Action chunk (future video only during training)
actionRepr: Chunk of 32 actions via flow matching, 10 denoising steps, CFG 1.0
trainingData: No embodied pretraining; trained per benchmark: LIBERO (500 demos per suite, 20k steps), RoboTwin 2.0 (2,500 clean + 25,000 randomized demos, 30k steps), real towel folding (60 h teleop on Galaxea R1 Lite, 30k steps).
whatChangedVsParent: Removes test-time future video denoising from MoT WAMs like LingBot-VA/Motus while keeping the video flow-matching co-training loss.
limitations: Pretrained pi0.5 remains best on the real towel-folding task; effect of larger-scale pretraining and model scaling left for future work; outer autoregressive loop omitted in the study.
notes: Project page yuantianyuan01.github.io/FastWAM. Latency measured on a single RTX 5090D V2 32GB. Towel folding: w/o video co-training drops to 10% success. Results compare against LingBot-VA/Motus 'from WAN2.2' (no embodied pretraining): 80.6 and 77.3 on RoboTwin.

keyEquations.meaning: Imagine-then-execute factorization used by most prior WAMs.
Fast-WAM: actions from a single-pass latent world representation, no future sampling.

symbols.meaning: video-DiT features of current frame and instruction

keyEquations.meaning: Flow-matching loss applied to both actions and future video latents.

symbols.meaning: action chunk or future video latents

keyEquations.meaning: Action loss plus video co-training loss.

edges: shared attention to first-frame tokens only

algorithmSteps: Training: encode current frame (clean) and future frames (noised) with the VAE; noise the action chunk.
Apply structured mask: video tokens see first frame; action tokens see first frame but not future video.
Optimize L_act + lambda * L_vid with flow matching.
Inference: drop the future video branch; run the video DiT once on first-frame tokens (KV cached).
Denoise the 32-step action chunk with the action DiT in 10 steps.
ablations: RoboTwin: Fast-WAM 91.8 vs Fast-WAM-Joint 90.6 vs Fast-WAM-IDM 91.3; w/o video co-training 83.8.
LIBERO: Fast-WAM 97.6 vs Joint 98.5 vs IDM 98.0; w/o video co-training 93.5.
Real towel folding: w/o video co-training drops to 10% success; latency 190 ms vs 580 ms (Joint) and 810 ms (IDM).
hyperparams: Action horizon h=32; 9 video frames per chunk (4x temporal downsampling); 10 denoising steps, CFG 1.0, logit-normal t; action expert hidden 1024; AdamW lr 1e-4, wd 0.01, cosine.

name: mimic-video
resolvedTitle: mimic-video: Video-Action Models for Generalizable Robot Control Beyond VLAs
org: mimic robotics; Microsoft Zurich; ETH Zurich; ETH AI Center; UC Berkeley
problem: VLAs are built on static image-text pretraining, so physical dynamics must be learned from scarce robot data; prior video-model policies require generating full future frames at each control step.
keyIdea: Video-Action Model: condition a flow-matching action decoder (an inverse dynamics model) on intermediate-layer features of a pretrained video diffusion model at a partially denoised flow time, so no full video generation is needed.
architecture: Cosmos-Predict2 2B latent video DiT (LoRA-finetuned on robot video, then frozen) with 5-frame context; action decoder DiT that cross-attends to layer-k (k=19) video hidden states h_tau_v, self-attends over action tokens, with AdaLN on both flow times tau_v and tau_a.
inputs: Past video frames (5), language instruction, proprioceptive state
outputs: Action chunk A_t (video plan optional)
actionRepr: Action chunk of relative end-effector poses (6-D rotation) + gripper/hand joints via flow matching with independent video/action flow times
params: 2B video backbone + action decoder (size not stated)
trainingData: Per-benchmark: BridgeDataV2 (SIMPLER), LIBERO-Spatial/Object/Goal (50 demos per task); real bimanual mimic hands: video backbone on a 200-hour corpus, action decoders on 1h33m (512 episodes) sorting and 2h14m (480 episodes) stowing.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real bimanual dexterous: Packing / Package handover

headlineResults.value: 10x (matches VLA max with 10% data; 77% avg with 1 episode/task)

whatChangedVsParent: Swaps the VLM backbone of a pi0.5-style VLA for a pretrained video diffusion model and decodes actions from its partially denoised latent plan.
limitations: Single-view video backbone restricts policies to one fixed workspace view; no large-scale cross-embodiment VAM trained yet; real-world experiments cover a focused set of tasks.
notes: Default tau_v = 1 (pure noise) gives the best average and needs one backbone forward pass; action reconstruction MSE on noisy ground-truth video is lowest near tau_v ~0.4. Coins the term 'Video-Action Model (VAM)'; DreamZero groups it under WAMs. Action flow-time schedule T_a proportional to sqrt(tau_a - 0.001) following pi0; video flow time logit-normal. Convergence ~2x faster than the VLA decoder.

keyEquations.meaning: Hidden states at layer k of the video model at partial flow time tau_v condition the action decoder.
Flow sampling from noise; stopping at intermediate tau gives partial denoising.
Action decoder flow-matching loss with independently sampled video and action flow times.

algorithmSteps: Stage 1: LoRA-finetune the video backbone on robot videos.
Stage 2: freeze backbone; sample tau_v (logit-normal) and tau_a independently; train action decoder on layer-k features of noised ground-truth future latents.
Inference: sample future video noise and action noise.
Integrate the video flow from 1 to tau_v (skipped when tau_v = 1).
Run the first k video layers to extract h^{tau_v}.
Fully denoise the action chunk with the decoder conditioned on h and proprioception.
ablations: tau_v sweep on SIMPLER: best policy success at high noise (tau_v = 1 default); per-task tau_v tuning lifts average from 46.9% to 56.3%.
Action MSE with noisy ground-truth video latents is minimized at tau_v ~0.4 and rises sharply toward fully clean latents.
Video source layer k=19 best; 5-frame observation horizon beats 1 frame.
hyperparams: Video backbone Cosmos-Predict2 2B, 5 context frames, source layer k=19, tau_v=1 default; action flow time schedule ~ sqrt(tau_a - 0.001); images 480x640; 6-D rotation representation.

name: VideoVLA
resolvedTitle: VideoVLA: Video Generators Can Be Generalizable Robot Manipulators
org: Xi'an Jiaotong University (IAIR); Microsoft Research Asia; Fudan University
problem: VLAs built on pre-trained vision-language understanding models still generalize poorly to unseen tasks, objects and settings.
keyIdea: Turn a large pre-trained video generator (CogVideoX-5B) into a VLA by adding actions as an extra output modality and jointly denoising future video latents and an action chunk in one multimodal DiT; imagined futures act as visual foresight tied to the actions.
architecture: Multi-modal Diffusion Transformer initialized from CogVideoX-5B; T5 text encoder (226 tokens) and CogVideoX 3D-causal video VAE; language tokens + first-frame latent are conditions, noisy future-frame latents and noisy 7-D actions are denoised jointly with DDPM loss (timestep via adaLN). Video decoder optional, only for visualization.
inputs: Language instruction + current RGB observation (encoded as first video latent); no proprioception
outputs: Action chunk of K 7-D actions + future frame latents (13 latents = 49 frames in sim; 4 latents = 13 frames in real)
actionRepr: chunk of 6 continuous 7-D end-effector actions (3 rotation, 3 translation, 1 binary gripper), untokenized, jointly denoised with video latents via DDPM; first 3 executed
trainingData: OXE subset (~22.5M frames, as in Octo/OpenVLA/CogACT) for pre-training; 5,824 teleoperated Realman 7-DoF samples (pick/stack/place) for real-world fine-tuning
controlRateHz: ~3 Hz effective (real-world: 10 DDIM steps, ~1.1 s per inference on one H100)

headlineResults.benchmark: SIMPLER (all 12 tasks, WidowX VM + Google VM/VA)
SIMPLER Google robot novel objects (YCB/GSO, 10 objects)
Real cross-embodiment skill transfer (WidowX-only skills on Realman)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces the VLM backbone of VLAs (e.g., CogACT/pi0) with a pre-trained video diffusion transformer that predicts both actions and future video in one denoising process.
limitations: Inference is slow because it relies on a 5B general-purpose video generator (~1.1 s per step, ~3 Hz control); authors suggest smaller robot-oriented generators, one-step/shortcut denoising or distillation.
notes: NeurIPS 2025. Imagination quality correlates with success: when generated futures match real outcomes, actions succeed more often. Uses 50 DDIM steps in sim experiments, 10 in real deployment. Training: 100K pre-train + 15K fine-tune iterations on 32 AMD MI300X, batch 256, lr 1e-5.

keyEquations.meaning: Joint prediction targets: K-step 7-D action chunk and N future frames (predicted as latents).
Causal VAE latents; V_1 encodes only the current observation, V_2..V_n are future latents denoised with A.

algorithmSteps: Encode instruction with T5 into 226 tokens
Encode current observation alone with causal VAE to get V1
Concatenate text tokens, flattened V1, noisy future latents and noisy 7-D actions into one sequence
Jointly denoise video latents and actions with DDIM (50 steps sim / 10 steps real)
Execute first 3 of the 6 predicted actions
Observe new frame and repeat until task done
ablations: Backbone (SIMPLER Google VM avg): pre-trained CogVideoX-5B 80.4 vs OpenSora-1.1 50.2 vs CogVideoX-5B from scratch 12.6
Predicted future frames: 13 -> 75.2, 25 -> 77.4, 49 -> 80.4 avg success
Synchronous joint video+action diffusion 80.4 vs async-train/sync-infer 73.8 vs async-train/async-infer (video first then action) 71.0; causal mask 75.5
hyperparams: 6-action chunk (execute 3); 13 future latents/49 frames (sim) or 4 latents/13 frames (real); DDIM 50 steps sim, 10 steps real; AdamW lr 1e-5, wd 1e-4; batch 256

name: DreamGen
resolvedTitle: DreamGen: Unlocking Generalization in Robot Learning through Video World Models
org: NVIDIA (GEAR); University of Washington; KAIST; UCLA; UCSD; UT Austin et al.
topicName: World models as simulator, evaluator and data engine
problem: Teleoperation data must be collected for every new task and environment, and simulation-based synthetic data needs heavy engineering and suffers sim-to-real gap.
keyIdea: Use fine-tuned image-to-video world models as synthetic data generators: generate robot videos of familiar or novel behaviors/environments, label them with pseudo-actions (IDM or latent actions) to form 'neural trajectories', and train visuomotor policies on them.
architecture: 4-stage pipeline: (1) LoRA fine-tune a video world model (WAN2.1 by default) on target-robot teleop data (multi-view concatenated into a 2x2 grid); (2) roll out with new initial frames + language prompts; (3) pseudo-label actions with an IDM (DiT + SigLIP-2, flow matching, two frames in, action chunk out) or LAPA latent actions (VQ-VAE); (4) train a policy (Diffusion Policy, pi0 or GR00T N1).
inputs: Initial frame + language instruction (world model); two frames (IDM)
outputs: Synthetic robot videos with pseudo-action labels (neural trajectories) used to train policies
actionRepr: Pseudo-action chunks: IDM-predicted H-step robot actions (sliding window) or continuous pre-quantized LAPA latent actions; downstream policy action format depends on the policy (e.g., GR00T N1)
trainingData: GR1 humanoid: 2,884 pick-and-place trajectories in one lab environment; RoboCasa: world model trained on 1,200 demos, up to 240k neural trajectories (333x); Franka: world model/IDM on 49,895 DROID examples; SO-100 tasks with 10-13 real trajectories

headlineResults.benchmark: GR1 real, 14 novel behaviors in seen environment
headlineResults.comparedTo: GR00T N1 trained on pick-and-place only: 11.2

headlineResults.benchmark: GR1 real, 13 tasks in 10 unseen environments
RoboCasa 24 tasks, 300 real traj + 240k neural traj (GR00T N1)
RoboCasa 24 tasks, neural trajectories only (IDM actions)
Real-world data augmentation (4 GR1 / 3 Franka / 2 SO-100 tasks)

whatChangedVsParent: Uses video world models offline as synthetic data generators (not real-time planners) and trains standard policies on IDM- or latent-action-labeled generated videos.
limitations: Tasks are relatively simple and cover a limited part of the robot's kinematic range; generation is compute-heavy (240k RoboCasa samples took 54 hours on 1,500 L40 GPUs); relies on manually captured initial frames.
notes: Also introduces DreamGen Bench (instruction-following + physics-alignment scores via Qwen2.5-VL, GPT-4o, VideoCon-Physics, human); benchmark score positively correlates with RoboCasa success from neural-trajectory-only training (7K neural traj per model). Log-linear scaling of policy success with number of neural trajectories. Co-training ratio 1:1 real:neural; neural trajectories have zero state input. In DreamGen Bench, Cosmos-sft and WAN2.1-sft score best. NVIDIA later released this as the 'GR00T-Dreams' blueprint (general knowledge, not from paper).

keyEquations.meaning: IDM labels H actions between two frames; slid one step at a time over generated video.
Policy trained on neural trajectories from image observation and instruction (state zeroed).

algorithmSteps: LoRA fine-tune an image-to-video model on target-robot teleop videos
Collect new initial frames (randomized objects, new environments) and write prompts incl. novel verbs
Generate many robot videos from frame + instruction
Train IDM (or use LAPA) and pseudo-label actions with a sliding window
Train policy on neural trajectories alone or co-trained 1:1 with real data
Deploy policy on real robot
ablations: RoboCasa: co-training with neural trajectories helps in low (720), mid (2.4k) and high (7.2k) real-data regimes, with a log-linear trend vs number of neural trajectories
IDM and LAPA latent actions give similar gains; IDM used as default because it allows neural-only training
DreamGen Bench: zero-shot video models score near 0 on instruction following; fine-tuned WAN2.1/Cosmos score highest and yield best downstream RoboCasa policies
hyperparams: WAN2.1 LoRA fine-tuning; multi-view as 2x2 grid; LAPA conditioned on frames 1 s apart; 50 neural trajectories per novel behavior task; 1:1 co-training ratio

name: World-Env
resolvedTitle: World-Env: Leveraging World Model as a Virtual Environment for VLA Post-Training
org: Sun Yat-sen University; AMap, Alibaba Group
topicName: World models as simulator, evaluator and data engine
problem: Imitation-trained VLAs degrade with few demos, RL post-training needs resettable environments (costly/unsafe in real world), and VLAs lack a task-completion detector so they keep acting after success.
keyIdea: Replace the physical environment with a world-model simulator for RL post-training, and use a VLM-guided 'instant reflector' that outputs a continuous success probability both as reward and as an early-termination signal.
architecture: World simulator: U-Net video diffusion model conditioned on a projected action map (end-effector pose rendered on black background) + memory-bank reference frame, with geometry-aware VGGT features and CLIP features injected via cross-attention. Instant reflector: frozen LLaVA + trainable reward head (sigmoid). Policy: OpenVLA-OFT with an added Laplace scale head for stochastic exploration.
inputs: RGB observation, proprioceptive state (6D EE pose + 1D gripper), language instruction
outputs: Continuous action (policy); next observation (simulator); step-wise success probability in [0,1] (reflector)
actionRepr: continuous 7-D action from OpenVLA-OFT action head (mean) with a Laplace scale head for sampling during RL
trainingData: LIBERO with only 5 demos per task for the policy; world simulator trained on LIBERO demos plus self-explored rollouts from SFT OpenVLA-OFT with Laplace-perturbed actions; real world: 10 trajectories per task

headlineResults.benchmark: LIBERO without GT termination, full horizon
Real world, 4 tasks (clean table, put green/red/orange toy)

whatChangedVsParent: Moves RIPT-VLA-style RLOO/PPO post-training of OpenVLA-OFT from a physics simulator into a learned video world model with a learned continuous VLM reward and termination.
limitations: Both the world simulator and reflector need diverse training data for fidelity and accurate evaluation; policy optimization is slower than concurrent methods due to simulator trajectory-generation cost.
notes: Code at github.com/amap-cvlab/world-env. Reflector threshold eta=0.5 (accuracy 0.925, F1 0.896). Reward used sparsely: single reward at termination step. Training on 8 H20 GPUs ~48 h; LoRA rank 32; N=8 rollouts; PPO clip 0.1. Next proprio state from forward kinematics.

keyEquations.meaning: Instant reflector: success probability from pooled VLM embedding; terminate when > eta=0.5.

keyEquations.tex: b_n = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j\neq n} R_j,\quad A_n = R_n - b_n
keyEquations.meaning: RLOO leave-one-out baseline and trajectory advantage.
Clipped PPO update with Laplace action likelihood ratios.
Laplace NLL to train the scale head for exploration.

algorithmSteps: Set behavior policy to current policy + scale head
Sample context (instruction, o_1, s_1) and generate N rollouts
Each step: predict mean and log-scale, sample a_t from Laplace
Compute s_{t+1} by forward kinematics; world simulator predicts o_{t+1}
Stop when reflector R(o_{1:t+1}, g) > 0.5 or at T; reward = R at end
Compute RLOO advantages; update policy and scale head with clipped PPO for K steps
ablations: No extra data + no reward head: 68.4/75.2/73.2/42.2 (Goal/Object/Spatial/Long) vs both: 86.4/86.6/87.6/57.8
Extra simulator data alone: 79.8/81.8/78.4/44.6; reward head alone: 68.8/76.4/74.4/43.8
Reflector threshold: eta=0.5 gives F1 0.896 vs 0.8 at eta=0.2 and 0.75 at eta=0.8
hyperparams: N=8 rollouts; PPO clip 0.1; eta=0.5; LoRA rank 32 lr 1e-4, heads lr 1e-5; batch 4; reflector samples 32 frames at 384x384

name: VLA-RFT
resolvedTitle: VLA-RFT: Vision-Language-Action Reinforcement Fine-tuning with Verified Rewards in World Simulators
org: Westlake University; Zhejiang University; OpenHelix Team; Fudan University; Hebei University of Technology et al.
topicName: World models as simulator, evaluator and data engine
problem: Imitation-learned VLAs compound errors under distribution shift, while RL needs costly real interaction or suffers sim-to-real gaps and simulator RL needs millions of interactions.
keyIdea: Use a small data-driven autoregressive world model as a simulator and reward policy rollouts by comparing world-model rollouts of policy actions with rollouts of ground-truth actions (L1 + LPIPS), then fine-tune a flow-matching VLA with GRPO via an SDE (sigma-net) policy.
architecture: World model: 138M LLaMA-style autoregressive Transformer (12 layers, hidden 768) over VQGAN-like image tokens and discretized action tokens (iVideoGPT-inspired). Policy: lightweight VLA-Adapter (Qwen2.5-0.5B VLM + DiT flow-matching action head); VLM frozen during RFT, action head + a DiT-like Sigma Net trained.
inputs: Initial image, language instruction, robot state
outputs: Action chunk (policy); predicted future frames (world model)
actionRepr: chunk of T continuous 7-D actions from a flow-matching head, made stochastic by a Sigma Net (Gaussian per Euler step, K=10 steps)
params: World model 138M; policy based on Qwen2.5-0.5B VLA-Adapter
trainingData: LIBERO datasets for both world model (150K steps) and base policy (150K SFT steps); RFT only 400 steps
whatChangedVsParent: Moves GRPO fine-tuning of a flow-matching VLA from a physics simulator into a learned world model with verified (trajectory-similarity) rewards, needing only 400 RFT steps.
limitations: Reward is similarity to expert trajectories, so the policy cannot surpass expert quality; small world model limits OOD generalization; world model not used for planning; only flow-matching policies studied.
notes: CONFLICT (internal): Fig.1 and Table 2 report 91.1 average while the text says 91.3 (+4.7); use 91.1. Paper calls GRPO 'Generalized Reinforcement Policy Optimization'. Reward type ablation: action-L1 reward (no WM) +1.1; WM vs real images +0.5; WM-vs-WM rollouts (ours) +4.5. Trained on 4x A800 with VERL.

keyEquations.meaning: Autoregressive action-conditioned world model pretrained by maximum likelihood.
SDE-policy: each Euler flow step becomes Gaussian with learned variance, giving log-likelihoods.

name: WMPO

org: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; ByteDance Seed
topicName: World models as simulator, evaluator and data engine
problem: IL-trained VLAs cannot learn from failures or self-correct, while real-robot RL is sample-inefficient and latent-space world models mismatch VLAs pretrained on real images.
keyIdea: Do on-policy GRPO for a VLA entirely inside a pixel-space action-conditioned video diffusion world model, aligned to the policy's own behavior (including failures), with a learned binary success reward model.
architecture: World model: OpenSora-based video diffusion with SDXL 2D VAE (instead of 3D VAE), frame-level action control via extended AdaLN, noisy-frame conditioning; pretrained on OXE, fine-tuned on policy rollouts. name: Ctrl-World

org: Stanford University; Tsinghua University
topicName: World models as simulator, evaluator and data engine
problem: Evaluating and improving generalist policies needs many costly real rollouts and expert corrections; prior action-conditioned world models are single-view, imprecise in control and drift over long horizons, so they cannot host policy-in-the-loop rollouts.
keyIdea: Adapt a pretrained video diffusion model into a multi-view, action-controllable world model with pose-conditioned memory retrieval so that generalist VLAs (pi0, pi0-FAST, pi0.5) can roll out in imagination for evaluation and for synthesizing successful trajectories for fine-tuning.
architecture: Initialized from 1.5B Stable Video Diffusion (spatial-temporal transformer); only new module is a 3-layer MLP projecting 7-D Cartesian actions to 1024-D. Joint prediction of 3 camera views (2 third-person + wrist) concatenated along tokens; sparse history frames (k=7) with their arm poses and future action poses injected via frame-level cross-attention.

name: GPC (generative predictive control)
resolvedTitle: Strengthening Generative Robot Policies through Predictive World Modeling (v4 retitled: Inference-Time Enhancement of Generative Robot Policies via Predictive World Modeling)
org: Harvard University (SEAS); Georgia Institute of Technology (v4)
topicName: World models as simulator, evaluator and data engine
problem: Behavior-cloned generative policies suffer distribution shift and lack precision/test-time correction, while predictive control needs accurate dynamics models that are hard to obtain for contact-rich, vision-based manipulation.
keyIdea: At inference time, couple a frozen diffusion policy (proposal generator) with an action-conditioned world model trained on expert plus random-exploration data, and rank (GPC-RANK) and/or gradient-optimize (GPC-OPT) the proposed action chunks by predicted reward.
architecture: Diffusion Policy (ResNet18 + UNet, DDPM) proposes chunks; world model is an MLP (state-based) or a recursive single-step conditional image diffusion model (EDM-style UNet denoiser as in DIAMOND, N_d=3 steps, noise frozen to 0 at inference) rolled out T times; reward is a differentiable ResNet18+MLP pose/registration predictor or a VLM (GPT-4o) selector.
inputs: Observation history (states or images, H=2 for policy, H=4 for visual world model)
outputs: Selected or optimized action chunk
actionRepr: diffusion-policy chunk (prediction horizon 16, action horizon 8-9; T=32 in real Push-T) of 2-D pusher velocities for Push-T, re-ranked/optimized by world-model lookahead
trainingData: Push-T sim: 500 expert demos + 6x500 perturbations + 7 long-horizon random demos; other sim tasks 30-100 expert + 100 perturbations; real: 100 expert demos per task + 5 random-play videos

headlineResults.comparedTo: Diffusion Policy 0.642; GPC-RANK K=100 0.739; GPC-OPT M=25 0.791

headlineResults.benchmark: 4 vision sim tasks, GPC-RANK (Push-T / Triangle / Block Stacking / Cube&Sphere)

whatChangedVsParent: Keeps Diffusion Policy frozen and adds MPC-style lookahead through a learned (visual diffusion) world model trained with random exploration data to rank/refine its proposals.
limitations: Inference-time cost: diffusion world-model rollouts dominate runtime (~90-95%); ~3 s per decision cycle for real-world GPC-RANK, and GPC-RANK+OPT takes ~374 s per cycle in vision Push-T sim.
notes: Numbers above are from v4 (RA-L 2026, retitled) unless marked v1; v1 (Feb 2025) focused on planar pushing incl. collisions with 'A'/'R' blocks and reported offline-RL baseline worse than BC. Freezing the diffusion noise is essential: without it GPC-OPT fails. Planning-only baselines without policy prior (MPPI, CEM, pure gradient ascent) score <0.2 on vision Push-T. Random exploration data improves performance by about 10%.

name: WorldEval
resolvedTitle: WorldEval: World Model as Real-World Robot Policies Evaluator
org: Midea Group; East China Normal University
topicName: World models as simulator, evaluator and data engine
problem: Real-world evaluation of generalist manipulation policies is slow, unsafe and does not scale with task count; real-to-sim evaluators (SIMPLER-style) correlate poorly with real performance, and feeding raw actions or VQ/one-hot action codes into a video model fails to produce action-following videos.
keyIdea: Policy2Vec: use the evaluated policy's own latent action embedding (taken just before its action decoder) as the control signal for a fine-tuned image-to-video model, then judge generated rollouts with a VLM (Gemini-2.0) so that policy rankings in video match real-world rankings.
architecture: Wan 2.1 14B image-to-video DiT, LoRA fine-tuned; policy latent actions pass through a projection layer, are scaled by a learnable weight alpha and added to the language embedding that conditions the DiT. Success detector is Gemini-2.0 on the generated video; FID used as a cheap proxy metric.
inputs: Initial frame (top camera), language instruction, latent action embedding extracted from the policy under test
outputs: Generated rollout video (81 frames, 480x480) and a binary success judgement from Gemini-2.0
trainingData: 1,400 real-world robot trajectories on a bimanual AgileX ALOHA-style robot (14-D state/action, teleop at 50 Hz); each trajectory sampled 3x into 81-frame clips at 480x480.
controlRateHz: 50 (data collection teleop frequency of the evaluated robot)

limitations: Relies only on policy action latents as control; artifacts (object deformation, hallucinated/disappearing objects, arm ghosting) appear especially for low-performing policies; dependence on pretrained generative models limits adaptability to very novel scenarios; the world model does not fully recover latent actions from generated video.

name: WorldGym
resolvedTitle: WorldGym: World Model as An Environment for Policy Evaluation
org: Stanford University; NYU; Google DeepMind
topicName: World models as simulator, evaluator and data engine
problem: Real-robot policy evaluation is costly and risky, handcrafted simulators need heavy manual effort and suffer a sim-to-real gap, and classical OPE assumes full observability; there was no single learned environment for evaluating many policies across tasks and robots from images.
keyIdea: Train one autoregressive action-conditioned video world model on multi-robot Open-X data, roll policies out inside it by Monte Carlo from a single real start frame, and score rollouts with a VLM (GPT-4o) reward; align the diffusion prediction horizon with each policy's action-chunk size.
architecture: Latent Diffusion Transformer (SD3 VAE latents, 16 layers, hidden 1024, 16 heads) trained with Diffusion Forcing; per-frame 7-D actions linearly projected and added to diffusion-timestep embeddings, injected via AdaLN-Zero; causal temporal attention interleaved with spatial attention; action dropout + classifier-free guidance for action adherence.
inputs: Initial RGB frame (256x256), language goal (for policy and reward), per-step 7-D actions from the policy (6-D end-effector + binary gripper)
outputs: Autoregressively generated future frames; VLM reward in {0, 0.5, 1} per rollout
trainingData: 9 Open-X Embodiment datasets with unifiable action spaces (incl. Bridge V2, RT-1); action components normalised by aligning 10th/90th percentiles to RT-1; 300k training steps on 2x A100 80GB.

limitations: Generating highly realistic object interactions remains challenging; not all emulated interactions are realistic, so it is positioned as a pre-deployment sanity check rather than a replacement for real evaluation; per-task success rates still differ from real ones.

algorithmSteps: Initialise observation history with the real first frame o0 and a null action
Query policy on latest frame and goal to get action chunk a_pred
Set world-model prediction horizon h = |a_pred|
Condition on the last 20 frames/actions and denoise h future latent frames in parallel
Append generated frames and actions to history; feed latest frame back to the policy
Repeat until rollout length reached
Send the generated video plus instruction to GPT-4o with a success/partial-credit rubric

End-effector control sweeps (single-axis moves, gripper open/close) not in training data are followed faithfully (qualitative)

name: DROID
resolvedTitle: DROID: A Large-Scale In-The-Wild Robot Manipulation Dataset
org: Stanford, UC Berkeley, Toyota Research Institute, CMU, UT Austin, Google DeepMind and 10 other institutions
problem: Even the most general manipulation policies are trained on data from few, lab-like scenes with limited task diversity; aggregations like OXE total only ~300 scenes, limiting generalization to new scenes, objects and viewpoints.
keyIdea: Collect demonstrations 'in the wild' with one standardised, portable Franka setup replicated 18 times across labs and continents, with a protocol (randomised task prompts, scene augmentations, frequent scene changes) that maximises scene, task, viewpoint and interaction-location diversity.
architecture: Dataset + hardware platform: Franka Panda 7-DoF, Robotiq 2F-85 gripper, two adjustable Zed 2 stereo cameras + wrist Zed Mini, Oculus Quest 2 teleop, Polymetis controller, on a wheeled height-adjustable desk. Evaluation policy: Robomimic diffusion policy (ImageNet ResNet-50 per external camera, frozen DistilBERT language, proprio -> MLP [1024,512,512] -> U-Net diffusion head, DDIM).
inputs: Per episode: 3 stereo RGB streams (1280x720), depth, calibrated extrinsics, joint/EE/gripper states, 1-3 crowdsourced language instructions
outputs: Recorded actions in joint and end-effector spaces (dataset); evaluation policy outputs absolute EE translation, rotation and gripper
actionRepr: Evaluation diffusion policy: 16-step action sequences (absolute EE pose + gripper), first 8 executed open-loop
trainingData: 76k successful demonstration trajectories (~350 h) across 564 scenes, 52 buildings, 86 verbs/tasks, 1,417 camera viewpoints; ~16k additional 'not successful' trajectories released but not counted; 50 collectors, 18 robots/labs, 13 institutions, 12 months.

headlineResults.benchmark: 6 real tasks in 4 locations (lab, office, household), in-distribution

whatChangedVsParent: Moves from single-lab, few-scene collection (Bridge V2: 24 environments, one institution) to a distributed, standardised platform giving an order of magnitude more scenes and 1,417 viewpoints.
limitations: Paper frames open questions rather than listing limitations: how best to combine DROID with other datasets, how to achieve zero-shot performance in new scenes without in-domain data, and when to train on the full dataset versus slices; single embodiment (Franka) only; manual calibration can be inaccurate, hence post-hoc automatic recalibration.

Place and calibrate the two exterior cameras
Enter scene-appropriate tasks; GUI prompts a random one per episode
Teleoperate with Quest 2 controllers; mark success
Periodically apply GUI-prompted scene augmentations
After ~100 trajectories (~20 min) move to a new scene

Use: co-train policies with batches mixed 50/50 between in-domain demos and DROID

DROID co-training outperforms OXE co-training by 22% (in-distribution) and 17% (OOD) absolute average success

Scene = substantial workspace change (2,080 raw scene IDs de-duplicated to 564). Scene types labelled with GPT-4V. Run a heavily randomised scripted pick-and-place policy to add autonomous data
Crowdsource post-hoc language descriptions
Train goal-conditioned methods with goals sampled uniformly from future timesteps; train language-conditioned methods on labels
Evaluate on seen tasks, unseen objects/environments, and a second institution
ablations: Skill diversity: 13-skill (27k) vs 3-skill (28k) training set -> 0.65 vs 0.30 on unseen pick-and-place (20 trials)
Dataset size and diversity: GCBC on BridgeData V2 averages 0.70 vs 0.08 on V1+PTR (13k traj, 15 envs, 11 skills) on two unseen tasks
Model capacity: GCBC with ResNet-18 < ResNet-34 < ResNet-50 encoders; larger strictly better on spoon task (figure)
hyperparams: 5 Hz control; 128x128 obs (RT-1 320x256, seq len 15, 256 action bins); ACT chunk 5 (vs 100 original); GCBC/D-GCBC/CRL/LCBC Adam lr 3e-4 with 2000-step linear warmup; CRL GCBC-regularisation 0.2
notes: Robot setup ~ $4,000, parts turnaround < 2 weeks. Composition reported as 84% human / 16% scripted in own Table 1 (DROID's table lists 85/15). Many views/depth only for part of the data (cameras added during collection). Dataset and pre-trained models publicly shared (openWeights=true refers to released pre-trained policy checkpoints). Widely used as the Bridge component of OXE and in SIMPLER/WorldGym evaluations.

name: Mobile ALOHA
resolvedTitle: Mobile ALOHA: Learning Bimanual Mobile Manipulation with Low-Cost Whole-Body Teleoperation
org: Stanford University
problem: Imitation learning results were mostly tabletop; bimanual mobile manipulators cost >$200k and lacked whole-body teleoperation, and it was unclear whether BC recipes scale to coupled base-plus-arm control where small base errors cause large end-effector drift.
keyIdea: Mount ALOHA on a wheeled base with a waist-tethered operator who backdrives the base while puppeteering both arms (whole-body teleop, $32k), then train standard BC on a concatenated 16-D action and co-train with 825 static ALOHA episodes (base actions zero-padded).
architecture: Hardware: two ViperX 300 follower arms (+ leader arms for teleop) on an AgileX Tracer AGV, two wrist cameras + one top camera, onboard laptop and 1.62 kWh battery. Policies: ACT (ResNet-18, 4 enc / 7 dec layers, chunk 45), Diffusion Policy (ResNet-18 + UNet, chunk 64, DDIM) and VINN + chunking (BYOL features).
inputs: Two wrist RGB cameras, one egocentric top RGB camera, arm joint positions
outputs: 16-D action: 14 arm target joint positions (incl. 2 grippers) + base linear and angular velocity
actionRepr: Chunk of k 16-D actions (ACT k=45; Diffusion Policy k=64); to handle base latency d, execute first k-d arm actions and last k-d base actions
trainingData: Per task 20-50 Mobile ALOHA demos (7 tasks) + 825 static ALOHA episodes (disjoint tasks, from RT-X release); sampled 50/50 per batch.
controlRateHz: 50 (implied: Wipe Wine demos are 1300 steps = 26 s)

headlineResults.benchmark: Push Chairs (50 demos, ACT; 4th/5th chair OOD)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds a mobile base and whole-body teleop to static ALOHA, extends the action to 16-D, and shows co-training on static bimanual data transfers to mobile tasks despite different arm mounting and tasks.
limitations: Footprint 90x135 cm too wide for some paths; fixed arm height makes low cabinets, ovens and dishwashers hard to reach; Cook Shrimp only 40% (20 demos, low-contrast bowl); co-training gives mixed results for VINN since only its representation is co-trained.

keyEquations.meaning: Co-training objective: imitation loss on mobile task data plus static ALOHA data with zero-padded base actions.

symbols.meaning: Mobile ALOHA demos for task m

nodes: Operator tethered at waist, backdrives base
Zero-pad base actions, drop front cam
50/50 batch sampling, normalise by mobile stats
edges: Operator tethered at waist, backdrives base
Zero-pad base actions, drop front cam
50/50 batch sampling, normalise by mobile stats
Zero-pad base actions, drop front cam
50/50 batch sampling, normalise by mobile stats
50/50 batch sampling, normalise by mobile stats
first k-d arm, last k-d base

algorithmSteps: Collect 20-50 whole-body teleop demos per task on Mobile ALOHA
Load static ALOHA data; zero-pad base actions and ignore its extra front camera
Normalise all actions with Mobile ALOHA statistics
Train with each batch sampled 50/50 from mobile and static data (batch 16 for ACT)
At inference predict an action chunk of length k from 3 cameras + joints
Execute arm actions 1..k-d and base actions d+1..k to compensate base delay d
ablations: Data efficiency (Wipe Wine, ACT): with co-training, 35 demos beat no-co-training at 50 demos (70% vs 50%)
Mix ratio robust: 30% / 50% / 70% static data -> 95% / 95% / 90% on Wipe Wine
Co-training 95% vs pre-train-then-finetune 40% vs no co-train 50% (Wipe Wine)
hyperparams: ACT: lr 2e-5, batch 16, chunk 45, 4 enc/7 dec layers, hidden 512, ff 3200, 8 heads, beta 10, ResNet-18. Diffusion Policy: lr 1e-4, batch 32, chunk 64, DDIM 50 train / 10 test steps, UNet. VINN: BYOL encoder, chunk 100, state weight 5. Co-train sampling 0.5/0.5
notes: Hardware specs: 14+2 DoF, 75 kg, payload 750 g per arm, 12 h battery (1620 Wh), max pulling force 100 N at 100 cm, $32k including onboard power and compute; open-source hardware and software tutorial. Open-loop replay of demos yields zero whole-task success (base velocity control error >10 cm on a 180-degree 1 m-radius turn). User study: 8 participants; completion time Wipe Wine 46 s -> 28 s, Use Cabinet 75 s -> 36 s over 5 trials. CONFLICT: the alphaXiv summary said 10 study participants and that co-training raised Wipe Wine from 20% to 40% at 25 demos -- not in the paper text read (paper: 8 participants; exact 25-demo numbers only in Fig. 4). Diffusion Policy co-training: Wipe Wine 65% vs 35%, Push Chairs 100% vs 80%.

name: MimicGen
resolvedTitle: MimicGen: A Data Generation System for Scalable Robot Learning using Human Demonstrations
org: NVIDIA; The University of Texas at Austin
problem: Human teleoperated demonstrations are costly, and much of a large dataset repeats the same manipulation behaviour in different contexts; small datasets yield policies that fail on broad initial-state distributions, new objects or new arms.
keyIdea: Split a few source demos into object-centric subtask segments, re-express each segment's end-effector target poses relative to the relevant object, transform them to the object's new pose in a fresh scene, stitch with interpolation, execute, and keep only successful rollouts.
architecture: Data-generation system (not a policy) in robosuite/MuJoCo simulation plus a real Franka; policies trained on generated data with BC-RNN (robomimic) from image or low-dim observations.
inputs: ~10 source human demos per task (delta-EE actions), known object-centric subtask sequence, object poses at the start of each subtask (during generation only)
outputs: Large sets of successful demonstrations across new initial-state distributions (D1, D2), object instances (O) and robot arms (R)
actionRepr: 7-D delta end-effector pose (3 translation + 3 axis-angle rotation) + gripper open/close
trainingData: 175 source demos (10 per task for 16 sim tasks, 25 for Mobile Kitchen) -> ~50K generated demos across 18 tasks: 36K (1000 x 36 task variants) + 12K robot transfer + 2K object transfer; real robot: 20 source -> 200 generated.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Stack / Coffee (10 source demos, broad D1)

whatChangedVsParent: Generalises one-demo self-replay/segment-transform ideas into a scalable data generator across many tasks, broad reset distributions, object instances and robot arms, producing datasets for offline imitation rather than direct replay.
limitations: Needs known object-centric subtask sequence and object poses at each subtask start; one reference object per subtask; naive success-only filtering can bias data; linear interpolation is not collision-aware and longer interpolation hurts learning; quasi-static rigid tasks and same-category objects only; mobile base actions copied not transformed.

keyEquations.meaning: Re-target each source controller pose so its pose relative to the subtask object is preserved.

symbols.meaning: 4x4 pose of frame A w.r.t. frame B
controller target pose frame at step t (source)
object frame at segment start in source / new scene

keyEquations.meaning: Invariance constraint: target-to-object relative pose is copied from source to new scene.

symbols.meaning: source target pose relative to object

nodes: Observe object pose at subtask start
Transform segment to new object frame
Linear/slerp interpolation from current EE pose

Transform segment to new object frame
