algorithmSteps: Parse each source demo into segments, one per object-centric subtask
Sample a new start state (possibly new object instance or robot arm)
For each subtask: choose a source segment (random or nearest-neighbour by object pose)
Observe the reference object pose and transform the segment's controller poses to it
Prepend an interpolation segment from the current EE pose (n_interp steps, then hold n_fixed)
Convert target poses to delta-pose actions, add Gaussian noise (sigma=0.05), execute with source gripper actions
After all subtasks, keep the trajectory only if the task succeeded
Train BC-RNN on the generated dataset
ablations: Action noise: removing noise raises generation rate (Threading D0 51.0 -> 84.5%) but lowers image-agent success (Threading D0 98.0 -> 59.3%)
Replay-with-noise on same configurations gives Square 42.0% / Threading 74.0% vs MimicGen 90.7% / 98.0%
Removing nearest-neighbour / per-subtask selection cuts generation rate (e.g., Stack Three D0 71.3 -> 26.7%) but agent success mostly unchanged (88.0 -> 81.3%)
hyperparams: Default: action noise sigma=0.05; n_interp=5, n_fixed=0; random selection with per-subtask=False; 1000 generated demos per task variant; real robot uses 50 interpolation steps for safety; real cameras 120x160
notes: Agent performance on MimicGen data is reported to be comparable to an equal number of additional human demos. Transfers to Sawyer, IIWA, UR5e from Panda source demos. Datasets and sim environments released at mimicgen.github.io (no trained policy weights emphasised). Used downstream by RoboCasa (100K generated trajectories).

name: RoboCasa
resolvedTitle: RoboCasa: Large-Scale Simulation of Everyday Tasks for Generalist Robots
org: The University of Texas at Austin; NVIDIA Research
problem: Real robot data is too scarce and costly to scale, and existing simulators lack the combination of realism, room-scale scene/object/task diversity and accompanying large demonstration datasets needed to train generalist home robots.
keyIdea: A room-scale kitchen simulator on robosuite/MuJoCo whose diversity comes from generative AI (text-to-3D objects, text-to-image textures, LLM-proposed composite tasks), paired with human demos expanded by MimicGen into 100K+ trajectories.
architecture: robosuite (MuJoCo physics, OSC controllers) extended to mobile manipulators, humanoids and quadrupeds with arms; optional NVIDIA Omniverse photorealistic rendering. Benchmark policy: robomimic BC-Transformer (visuomotor).
inputs: Simulated RGB camera views + proprioception, task language (benchmark policies)
outputs: Scenes, tasks and demonstration datasets; BC-Transformer outputs end-effector (+ base) actions
trainingData: 120 kitchen scenes (10 floor plans x 12 styles) with 100 AI-generated textures each for walls/floors/counters/cabinets; 2,509 objects in 153 categories (1,592 from Luma.ai text-to-3D, rest Objaverse); 100 tasks (25 atomic, 75 LLM-guided composite); 50 human demos per task (1,250 atomic) + 100K+ MimicGen trajectories (72K in Generated-3000 over 24 atomic tasks, plus 28K with AI-generated objects).
controlRateHz: 20 (sim controller; real DROID-based robot runs at 15)

headlineResults.benchmark: 24 atomic tasks, unseen objects, 5 eval scenes
Real kitchen, 3 pick-place tasks, seen objects

whatChangedVsParent: Extends tabletop robosuite/MimicGen to room-scale mobile manipulation with generative-AI assets and LLM-generated tasks, and ships a 100K-trajectory multi-task dataset.
limitations: Composite-task performance stays low even with fine-tuning; generated trajectories can be jerky or colliding; LLM task creation still needs human-written implementations; kitchens only; no highly dexterous, deformable or bimanual skills; MimicGen cannot yet generate navigation trajectories.
algorithmSteps: Build 120 kitchen scenes from 10 floor plans x 12 styles, randomise AI-generated textures
Populate with articulated appliances and 2,509 objects
Prompt LLMs for kitchen activities, then concrete tasks; implement 75 composite tasks in code
Collect 50 human demos per atomic task in random kitchens
Annotate subtask boundaries with per-skill metrics and run MimicGen in parallel to generate thousands of demos per task
Train multi-task BC-Transformer; evaluate on unseen objects in 5 fixed scenes (2 unseen styles)
Fine-tune on composite tasks or co-train with real demos
ablations: Data scaling: Human-50 (1,250) -> Generated-100 (2,400) -> Generated-300 (7,200) -> Generated-3000 (72,000) increases overall atomic success steadily, reaching 47.6% vs 28.8%
Skill difficulty: door/drawer opening easiest; pick-and-place (dozens of categories) and insertion hardest
Composite tasks: scratch non-zero on 1/5 tasks vs fine-tuned non-zero on 4/5 (e.g., RestockPantry 0% -> 6%, PrepareCoffee 0% -> 0%)
hyperparams: Human-50 / Generated-100/300/3000 per task; 50 eval trials per task across 5 scenes; Franka Panda on Omron mobile base (Omni-Frankie-like) for atomic experiments; real co-training averaged over 3 seeds
notes: Real-world transfer used a Franka on the DROID hardware stack (non-OSC controller, 15 Hz) vs simulated OSC at 20 Hz. Relative real-world improvement 79% on seen objects. Cross-embodiment support: single-arm mobile platforms, humanoids, quadrupeds with arms. Open-source code/datasets on robocasa.ai; trained policy weights not stated. Later RoboCasa versions (e.g., RoboCasa365) may have different counts -- this card reflects arXiv v1 (June 2024).

name: GELLO
resolvedTitle: GELLO: A General, Low-Cost, and Intuitive Teleoperation Framework for Robot Manipulators
org: UC Berkeley
problem: Imitation learning is bottlenecked by demonstration quality and scale; high-fidelity bilateral teleop costs tens of thousands of dollars, while cheap devices (3D mouse, VR) work in abstract end-effector space and hide the robot's kinematic constraints, causing self-collisions and singularities.
keyIdea: Build a miniature, kinematically equivalent replica of the target arm from 3D-printed parts and cheap servos used as joint encoders; read its joint angles and send them directly as joint commands to the full-size arm.
architecture: Hardware leader device: target arm's DH parameters scaled by alpha = 0.5, 3D-printed links, DYNAMIXEL XL330-288T servos (12-bit encoders, 0.088 deg resolution) at each joint, passive springs/rubber bands as joint regularizers. Software: DYNAMIXEL Python API reads joints, robot Python APIs command the follower, ZMQ for message passing.
inputs: Human hand motion on the GELLO leader arm (joint angles from servo encoders)
outputs: Joint-position commands to the follower robot (UR5, xArm7, Franka Panda); teleoperated demonstrations
trainingData: Not a learned model. User study: 12 novice participants, bimanual UR5 station, 5 tasks, 3 devices.

headlineResults.benchmark: User study: plug in USB cable

headlineResults.comparedTo: 3D mouse $150, VR $300, robot-to-robot teleop $30,000, haptic Omega7 $40,000

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike ALOHA, which uses a full extra robot arm as the leader and is tailored to one arm, GELLO uses a scaled 3D-printed replica with cheap servo encoders and generalizes the recipe to UR5, xArm7 and Franka.
limitations: No force feedback because of limited motor torque, which limits contact-rich teleoperation; the user study only covered inexperienced users with brief practice.
notes: Not a learned policy: openWeights=false only because there are no weights; all hardware (BOM, CAD, assembly) and software are open-sourced at wuphilipp.github.io/gello. Authors state 'the ideas behind GELLO are not new'; contribution is practical designs, user study, open-sourcing. No control rate is stated. No defining equations in the paper (keyEquations intentionally empty).
algorithmSteps: Take the target arm's DH parameters and scale link lengths by alpha (0.5 used).
3D-print links; mount DYNAMIXEL XL330-288T servos at each joint as encoders (highest gear ratio for damping).
Add springs/rubber bands to the joints most loaded by gravity (joints 2 and 3 for UR).
At runtime, read joint angles from the servos via the DYNAMIXEL Python API.
Send the angles directly as joint-position commands to the follower robot (no inverse kinematics).
Record robot observations and commands as demonstrations.
ablations: Without joint regularization the force needed to hold the device against gravity is roughly constant at about 1.9 N; with regularization it varies with height, giving restorative feedback away from singularities.
Failure counts across all tasks: timeouts GELLO 1 vs 3D mouse 9 vs VR 5; self-collisions 1 vs 5 vs 5; environment collisions 3 vs 6 vs 6.
GELLO gave the fastest completion times on all tasks among successful trials (plotted, no single number).
hyperparams: Scale alpha = 0.5; XL330-288T servos, 12-bit encoders (0.088 deg); BOM < $300; user study: 5-min practice per device, time limits 45 s (hat) and 90 s (other tasks).

name: Time-Contrastive Networks (TCN)
resolvedTitle: Time-Contrastive Networks: Self-Supervised Learning from Video
org: Google Brain; University of Southern California
problem: Robots cannot be given labels for every task-relevant attribute (e.g., liquid level, tilt, contact), and imitating humans from third-person video needs a representation that is invariant to viewpoint and embodiment.
keyIdea: Metric-learn an embedding with a triplet loss where simultaneous frames from different viewpoints are attracted and temporally nearby frames from the same video are repelled, so the embedding keeps what changes over time and discards viewpoint and nuisance factors.
architecture: ImageNet-pretrained Inception up to Mixed_5d, then 2 conv layers, a spatial softmax layer and a fully-connected 32-unit embedding layer. Downstream: embedding distance as RL reward (PILQR), or a joints decoder trained by self-regression for pose imitation.
inputs: Single RGB frame (training uses synchronized multi-view video)
outputs: 32-d embedding; downstream a reward signal or robot joint vector
trainingData: Multi-view unlabeled video: pouring set 133 training sequences (~11 min), 17 val, 30 test; robot pouring TCN trained on ~20 min of human pouring plus ~20 min of humans manipulating cups, plus robot videos; multi-view human/robot random-motion video for pose imitation.

headlineResults.benchmark: Pouring video alignment (model selected by val loss)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces generic ImageNet or temporal-order self-supervision with a multi-view time-contrastive triplet signal that directly targets viewpoint invariance plus temporal sensitivity.
limitations: Needs multi-viewpoint video for training, which is far less available than standard web video; a separate TCN is trained per task (pouring, pose) rather than one universal embedding.
notes: Code and dataset released (sermanet.github.io/imitate); weight release not confirmed. Single-view variant: positive within 0.2 s, negatives beyond 2x that range. Multi-view TCN reached better accuracy with 15x less training time than single-view in Table IV selection. Real robot: 7-DoF KUKA learned bead pouring from a single third-person human video via PILQR; state = joint angles + velocities + TCN features. This is the 'time-contrastive' ancestor later reused inside R3M and contrasted with VIP's implicit version.

keyEquations.meaning: Triplet constraint: same-time other-view positive must be closer than a temporal-neighbour negative by a margin.

symbols.meaning: embedding of image x in R^d (d=32)

keyEquations.meaning: RL reward: squared plus Huber-style distance between robot and demo embeddings at each step.

symbols.meaning: TCN embedding of human demo frame t
TCN embedding of robot camera frame t

algorithmSteps: Record synchronized multi-view videos (e.g., two smartphones) of the task and related interactions.
Sample anchor and positive as simultaneous frames from two views; negative from another time in the same sequence.
Train the embedding with the triplet loss (margin 0.2).
For object tasks: embed a single third-person human demo and the robot's camera frames; compute R(v_t, w_t).
Optimize a time-varying linear-Gaussian policy with PILQR using state = joints + velocities + TCN features.
For pose imitation: train a joints decoder on the robot's own images (self-regression), then feed human images.
ablations: Multi-view vs single-view TCN: alignment error 18.8% vs 25.8%, classification error 21.4% vs 24.3% (Table I).
Metric losses are comparable: multi-view npairs 18.1%/22.2%, lifted 18.0%/19.6% alignment/classification error.
Adding the time-contrastive signal always helps pose imitation: Self 38.8% -> TC+Self 32.1% joints error; self-supervised TC+Self beats human-supervised Human (33.4%).
hyperparams: Embedding dim 32; triplet margin (gap) 0.2; single-view positive range 0.2 s, negative multiplier 2; Inception to Mixed_5d, ImageNet init; shuffle & learn baseline tmax 60, tmin 15.

name: R3M
resolvedTitle: R3M: A Universal Visual Representation for Robot Manipulation
org: Stanford University; Meta AI
problem: Robots are usually trained tabula rasa on in-domain data, which is data-hungry and generalizes poorly; robotics lacks an off-the-shelf pretrained visual backbone like ImageNet or BERT.
keyIdea: Pretrain an image encoder on diverse egocentric human video (Ego4D) with time-contrastive learning, video-language alignment and L1/L2 sparsity, then use it frozen as the perception module for behaviour cloning.
architecture: ResNet-50 encoder F_phi (ResNet-18/34 also released) producing a single-frame embedding; a 5-layer MLP language-prediction head G_theta scoring (initial frame, future frame, DistilBERT sentence embedding). Downstream policy: 2-layer MLP with input BatchNorm on [embedding, proprioception].
inputs: Single RGB image (224x224) plus robot proprioception for the downstream policy
outputs: Frozen visual embedding z = F_phi(I); downstream BC policy outputs continuous actions
trainingData: Ego4D egocentric video with per-clip language narrations (dataset has >3500 h from >70 locations; R3M uses clips paired with annotations). Downstream: 5/10/25 demos (MetaWorld, Franka Kitchen), 25/50/100 (Adroit); 20 demos per real task.

headlineResults.benchmark: 12 sim tasks (MetaWorld, Franka Kitchen, Adroit), frozen-encoder BC
headlineResults.comparedTo: authors report >10% over CLIP, MoCo(345) PVR, supervised ImageNet and >20% over scratch

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Franka, 5 household tasks, 20 demos each
Real: putting lettuce in pan / folding towel

whatChangedVsParent: Moves time-contrastive learning from small task-specific multi-view video to large in-the-wild Ego4D, and adds video-language alignment and sparsity to make a reusable manipulation backbone.
limitations: Evaluated only for behaviour cloning with few demos (may not be the best representation for RL); provides only a single-frame state representation and does not exploit video for rewards or task specification.
notes: Released at github.com/facebookresearch/r3m (resnet18/34/50). The ~62% all-domain average appears as 62.4% in Table 1. In VC-1's CortexBench, R3M remains best frozen PVR on Adroit, MetaWorld and DMControl, but weak on navigation. VIP's appendix Table 4 shows R3M 55.9 vs VIP 53.6 as a pure encoder for visual imitation, i.e., R3M is a slightly better BC encoder even though VIP is a much better reward.

keyEquations.tex: L_{tcn} = -\sum_{b\in B} \log \frac{e^{S(z^b_i, z^b_j)}}{e^{S(z^b_i, z^b_j)} + e^{S(z^b_i, z^b_k)} + e^{S(z^b_i, z^{\neq b}_i)}}
keyEquations.meaning: InfoNCE: frames closer in time are more similar than farther frames or other videos.

symbols.meaning: frame indices sampled from one clip
negative from a different video in the batch

keyEquations.tex: L_{language} = -\sum_{b\in B} \log \frac{e^{G_\theta(z^b_0, z^b_{j>i}, l^b)}}{e^{G_\theta(z^b_0, z^b_{j>i}, l^b)} + e^{G_\theta(z^b_0, z^b_i, l^b)} + e^{G_\theta(z^{\neq b}_0, z^{\neq b}_{j>i}, l^b)}}
keyEquations.meaning: Language score must rise over the clip and be higher for matching video-text pairs.
Total R3M objective: time contrast + language alignment + L1/L2 sparsity.

algorithmSteps: Sample a batch of 16 Ego4D clips; take 5 frames each (initial, final, and 3 ordered frames i<j<k).
Encode frames with F_phi (same random crop per video).
Compute L_tcn with 3 negatives from other videos.
Score (z_0, z_future, l) with G_theta and compute L_language with negatives.
Add L1 and L2 penalties; update with Adam (lr 1e-4) for 1M steps (1.5M for released models).
Freeze F_phi; train BC policy on [F_phi(I_t), proprio] with ||a_t - pi||^2 for 20k steps.
ablations: Removing language alignment: 62.4% -> 53.2% all-domain (Adroit 65.0 -> 45.6).
Removing L1 sparsity: 62.4% -> 59.4% (but Adroit improves 65.0 -> 66.5).
Removing crop augmentation: 62.4% -> 60.4%; same-data MoCo-Ego4D is ~10% worse, MVP ~20% worse.
hyperparams: lambda1=1, lambda2=1, lambda3=lambda4=1e-5; batch 16 clips x 5 frames; initial/final frames from first/last 20% of clip; 3 negatives; Adam lr 1e-4; 1M steps (1.5M released); 224x224 input; BC: 2-layer MLP + BatchNorm, 20k steps, 3 seeds.

name: VIP
resolvedTitle: VIP: Towards Universal Visual Reward and Representation via Value-Implicit Pre-Training
org: FAIR, Meta AI; University of Pennsylvania
problem: Pretrained visual representations from human video help as encoders, but their embedding distance to a goal image makes a poor reward, so real-world reward specification still needs manual engineering.
keyIdea: Treat pretraining on action-free human video as offline goal-conditioned RL and optimize the Fenchel-dual value objective, which needs no actions; with V defined as negative embedding distance, this becomes an implicit time-contrastive loss that yields smooth goal-distance rewards.
architecture: ResNet-50 visual encoder phi with a 1024-d FC output; value V(phi(o); phi(g)) = -||phi(o) - phi(g)||_2 (no separate value network). Downstream: frozen phi provides both the state embedding and the reward for MPPI, NPG, or reward-weighted regression.
inputs: RGB observation and goal image (224x224)
outputs: 1024-d embedding; dense reward R(o_t, o_{t+1}; phi, g)
trainingData: Same preprocessed Ego4D subset as R3M: ~72,000 clips of 10-150 frames, ~4.3M frames. Real robot: ~20 demos per task (CloseDrawer: 10 demos + 20 failures), 50 steps at 25 Hz.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Franka few-shot offline RL: CloseDrawer
FrankaKitchen visual online RL (NPG), VIP as reward + representation
headlineResults.comparedTo: VIP (Sparse) with ground-truth sparse reward solves no task

headlineResults.benchmark: FrankaKitchen trajectory optimization (MPPI), larger optimizer budget
headlineResults.comparedTo: baselines (R3M, ResNet) often degrade with more compute (reward hacking)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces R3M's explicit time contrast plus language with a fully self-supervised value objective that attracts initial and goal frames and implicitly repels intermediate frames via one-step TD, producing temporally smooth goal distances.
limitations: Embedding rewards still show local minima where large embedding distance maps to lower true reward; tasks are specified by a single goal image (paper lists language goals, asymmetric distances for irreversible tasks and navigation as future work).
notes: Project page sites.google.com/view/vip-rl; checkpoints public. As a pure BC encoder VIP scores 53.6 vs R3M 55.9 (Appendix Table 4), so its advantage is as a reward, not as an encoder. VIP rewards correlate with FrankaKitchen state rewards up to R^2=0.95 on at least one view for 8/12 tasks. The paper's intro says 'up to ~45%' while Fig. 5 text says 44%; 44% used here.

keyEquations.meaning: VIP loss: pull initial frame toward goal; log-sum-exp of one-step TD error over intermediate transitions.

symbols.meaning: goal frame (last frame of sampled sub-trajectory)

keyEquations.tex: R(o_t, o_{t+1}; \phi, \{g\}) := S_\phi(o_{t+1}; g) - S_\phi(o_t; g), \quad S_\phi(o_t; g) := -\|\phi(o_t) - \phi(g)\|_2
keyEquations.meaning: Downstream reward: decrease in embedding distance to goal (shaped progress reward).

symbols.meaning: negative L2 embedding distance to goal

keyEquations.meaning: Reward-weighted regression for few-shot real-world offline RL using VIP reward.

algorithmSteps: Sample B video sub-trajectories; first frame = initial state, last frame = goal.
Sample an intermediate transition (o_k, o_k+1) plus 3 negatives from other videos.
Compute L(phi) = (1-gamma)/B sum ||phi(o_t) - phi(o_T)|| + log mean exp(||phi(o_k)-phi(o_T)|| - delta - gamma ||phi(o_k+1)-phi(o_T)||).
Update phi with Adam (lr 1e-4, batch 32).
Downstream: freeze phi; specify task by goal image(s) (mean embedding of goal frames).
Use R = S(o_{t+1};g) - S(o_t;g) as reward for MPPI, NPG, or RWR with phi(o) as policy input.
ablations: LSTD value pretraining with the same parameterization beats prior baselines on Easy FrankaKitchen but is far weaker on Hard, showing the initial-to-goal term matters.
In-domain VIP trained only on ~20 task demos: 0% on all 4 real tasks (mostly stopped by safety checks), so Ego4D pretraining is necessary.
VIP reward histogram on robot data: about +20% more counts than R3M in the first positive-reward bin and about -100% extreme rewards (smoother landscape).
hyperparams: ResNet-50, FC output 1024; Adam lr 1e-4; batch 32; gamma 0.98; L1 weight penalty 0.001; 3 extra negatives; 224x224 input; MPPI horizon 12, 32 proposals; RWR tau 0.1 (1 for CloseDrawer); policy MLP [256,256], lr 1e-3, batch 32, 20k steps.

name: MVP
resolvedTitle: Masked Visual Pre-training for Motor Control
org: UC Berkeley
problem: End-to-end RL from pixels is sample-inefficient and overfits to a scene, and supervised ImageNet encoders transfer poorly to manipulation.
keyIdea: Pretrain a ViT with masked autoencoding on in-the-wild human-object-interaction frames, freeze it, and train small task-specific controllers on top with RL.
architecture: ViT-Small/16 encoder (384 hidden, 6 heads, 12 blocks, ~4.6 GFLOPs at 224x224) pretrained with MAE; CLS-token features projected to 128-d and concatenated with a 128-d projection of proprioception; 4-layer MLP actor (hidden [256,128,64], SeLU) and separate critic trained with PPO.
inputs: Wrist-camera RGB image (224x224) + joint positions and velocities
outputs: Delta joint angles
actionRepr: Single-step continuous delta joint-angle command (joint position control at 60 Hz), Gaussian PPO policy
params: ViT-Small encoder (ViT-Base tried, no clear gain)
trainingData: HOI dataset of ~700K frames: Epic-Kitchens (sampled 1 fps), Something-Something (0.3 fps), 100 Days of Hands (100K); also ImageNet for comparison. No labels or temporal info used.

headlineResults.metric: success rate vs supervised ImageNet encoder
headlineResults.value: better on 7/8 tasks, up to 80% absolute

whatChangedVsParent: Brings MAE self-supervision on in-the-wild interaction images to motor control and keeps the encoder frozen, instead of learning features from environment experience (CURL/RAD) or ImageNet labels.
limitations: Unfreezing the encoder for end-to-end RL was unstable (NaN) and gave 0 success; the scale distractor test fails (~50%, chance) due to single-camera scale ambiguity; larger ViT-B gave no clear gains; environment-trained encoders with enough data might do better.
notes: Released PixMC benchmark (IsaacGym), pretrained models and code. CONFLICT: surveys and VC-1 describe 'MVP' as trained on ~4.5M egocentric+ImageNet frames with ViT-B/ViT-L; that is the follow-up 'Real-World Robot Learning with Masked Visual Pre-training' (Radosavovic et al., arXiv 2210.03109). This original MVP paper uses ViT-S on ~700K HOI frames in simulation with RL. Check which paper the survey means. No new equation (standard MAE pixel-reconstruction loss), so keyEquations is empty.
algorithmSteps: Build HOI image set (~700K frames) from egocentric and YouTube interaction video.
Pretrain ViT-S with MAE (high masking, 1600 epochs on 16 GPUs).
Freeze the encoder; extract CLS features from the wrist camera each step.
Concatenate projected image features with projected proprioception.
Train MLP actor and critic with PPO in IsaacGym (256 envs x 32 steps per iteration, 10 epochs, 4 minibatches).
Execute delta joint-angle actions at 60 Hz.
ablations: HOI pretraining beats ImageNet pretraining on 7 of 8 PixMC tasks.
Random frozen encoder: zero or near-zero success on 6 of 8 tasks.
End-to-end (unfrozen) encoder: unstable training and flat 0% on FrankaPick across seeds; ViT-B no clear gain over ViT-S.
hyperparams: MAE mask ratio 75% (MAE default cited), 1600 epochs; crop ratio [0.2,1.0] ImageNet, [0.1,0.75] HOI; ViT-S/16; PPO: 256 envs x 32 steps, 10 epochs, 4 minibatches (2048 per update), lr searched in {5e-4, 1e-3, 1.5e-3} x 5 seeds, cosine decay; 500/1000/2000 iterations for reach/cabinet/pick.

name: VC-1
resolvedTitle: Where are we in the search for an Artificial Visual Cortex for Embodied Intelligence?
org: Georgia Tech; Meta AI (FAIR); UPenn; Stanford; UC Berkeley
problem: Prior pretrained visual representation (PVR) studies for embodied AI used different objectives, data and tasks, so nobody knew whether a single general 'visual cortex' existed or whether scaling data and model helps everywhere.
keyIdea: Build a 17-task benchmark (CortexBench), evaluate existing PVRs, then scale MAE pretraining of ViTs over curated egocentric + navigation + ImageNet data; the best (VC-1, ViT-L on Ego4D+MNI) wins on average, and task-specific adaptation closes the rest.
architecture: ViT-L (307M) encoder pretrained with MAE (ViT-B 86M also studied); used frozen, or adapted by end-to-end fine-tuning (large-scale IL/RL tasks) or continued MAE on in-domain frames (few-shot IL tasks). Task policies follow each benchmark's standard protocol.
inputs: RGB image (plus proprioception/goal depending on task)
outputs: Visual embedding for downstream policies
trainingData: Ego4D+MNI: 5,621,987 frames = Ego4D + 100DOH + Something-Something v2 + Epic Kitchens (manipulation) + RealEstate10K + OpenHouse24 (navigation) + ImageNet; >4,000 h of egocentric video from 7 sources. Training all models took >10,000 GPU-hours.

headlineResults.comparedTo: Ego4D+MN ViT-L 3.1; MVP ViT-L 2.1 among the existing-PVR table only

whatChangedVsParent: Same MAE recipe as MVP but a larger and more diverse dataset (adding navigation video and ImageNet) at ViT-L scale, evaluated systematically across manipulation, locomotion and navigation.
limitations: Presents no new technique; VC-1 does not dominate every benchmark (R3M still wins on Adroit, MetaWorld, DMControl), scaling does not help universally, and end-to-end fine-tuning hurts in few-shot IL domains.
notes: Code and models open-sourced at eai-vc.github.io. Mean rank values in the existing-PVR table (Table 2) and the scaling table (Table 4) are computed over different model sets, so they are not directly comparable; VC-1's 2.4 is from Table 4. VC-1 beats CLIP on every benchmark despite a ~70x smaller dataset. Scaling findings: Ego4D+N (navigation) helps more than Ego4D+M at similar size; adding ImageNet adds +1.5 (ViT-L). Real-robot TriFinger/Franka experiments: VC-1 and adapted VC-1 beat MVP (exact numbers not extracted). No new equation (MAE).

nodes: CortexBench (17 tasks: Adroit, MetaWorld, DMC, TriFinger, ObjectNav, ImageNav, MobilePick)
edges: CortexBench (17 tasks: Adroit, MetaWorld, DMC, TriFinger, ObjectNav, ImageNav, MobilePick)
CortexBench (17 tasks: Adroit, MetaWorld, DMC, TriFinger, ObjectNav, ImageNav, MobilePick)
CortexBench (17 tasks: Adroit, MetaWorld, DMC, TriFinger, ObjectNav, ImageNav, MobilePick)

algorithmSteps: Curate CortexBench: 17 tasks from 7 benchmarks with fixed community-standard policy learning.
Evaluate existing frozen PVRs (CLIP, R3M, MVP, VIP) and random ViTs.
Assemble 5 pretraining datasets of increasing size/diversity (2.79M to 5.62M frames).
Pretrain ViT-B and ViT-L with MAE on each dataset.
Pick VC-1 = ViT-L on Ego4D+MNI by mean rank/success.
Adapt: E2E fine-tune for large-scale IL/RL tasks; continue MAE on task frames then freeze for few-shot IL.
ablations: Adding navigation data beats adding manipulation data at similar size: Ego4D -> Ego4D+N 63.5 -> 67.1 (ViT-L) vs Ego4D -> Ego4D+M 63.5 -> 64.4.
Adding ImageNet helps: Ego4D+MN -> Ego4D+MNI 67.2 -> 68.7 (ViT-L), 64.1 -> 66.2 (ViT-B).
ViT-B -> ViT-L improves average on every dataset, but ViT-B beats ViT-L on MetaWorld and TriFinger with Ego4D+MNI.
hyperparams: ViT-L/16 (307M) MAE; Ego4D+MNI 5,621,987 frames; >10,000 GPU-hours total across models; adaptation: E2E fine-tuning or MAE continued pretraining on in-domain frames.

name: LAPA
resolvedTitle: Latent Action Pretraining from Videos
org: KAIST; University of Washington; Microsoft Research; NVIDIA; Allen Institute for AI
problem: VLA pretraining needs action-labeled teleoperation data, which limits scale; internet and human videos have no robot action labels and a large embodiment gap.
keyIdea: Learn discrete latent actions between frames with a VQ-VAE-style model (no action labels), pretrain a VLM to predict these latent actions from image + instruction, then finetune on a small labeled robot set to map to real actions.
architecture: Latent action quantization model (~300M, C-ViViT-style): encoder with spatial + causal transformers takes x_t and x_{t+H}, quantizes d = e_{t+H} - e_t to codebook tokens via NSVQ; decoder (spatial transformer) reconstructs x_{t+H} from x_t (stop-gradient) cross-attending to the latent action. Policy: 7B Large World Model (LWM-Chat-1M) with a single-MLP latent action head; vision encoder frozen, LM unfrozen. Finetuning swaps in an action head over discretized robot actions.
inputs: Current RGB image + language instruction
outputs: Pretraining: latent action tokens; after finetuning: discretized delta end-effector actions
actionRepr: Pretraining: 4 latent tokens from an 8-code vocabulary (8^4 space) per step; finetuning: per-dimension binned delta end-effector actions (OpenVLA/RT-2 style)
trainingData: Pretraining (no action labels): Bridgev2, Open X-Embodiment, or Something-Something V2 human videos (220K videos); Language Table 181k/440k trajectories. Finetuning: 150 teleoperated trajectories per real task; 100 SIMPLER trajectories; 1k/7k Language Table.
whatChangedVsParent: Uses a Genie-style latent action model not for world simulation but to pseudo-label action-free video, so a monolithic VLA can be pretrained without ground-truth actions, unlike OpenVLA/RT-2 which need labeled robot actions.
limitations: Underperforms action-pretrained models on fine-grained motions such as grasping; real-time inference latency as with other VLAs; not yet explored beyond manipulation video (driving, navigation).
notes: Paper states checkpoints and code will be open-sourced (latentactionpretraining.github.io). Window H: 0.6 s ahead for robot video, 2.4 s for human video (Bridgev2 at 5 Hz -> H=3). In real pick-and-place LAPA fails mostly by early grasping but has higher reaching success (83.33% vs 66.67% OpenVLA). Pairwise win rate vs OpenVLA ignoring ties 65.4%. Decoder can be used as a world model for closed-loop latent rollouts (qualitative only). No control rate is stated.

keyEquations.meaning: Latent action: nearest codebook vector to the embedding difference between two frames.

symbols.meaning: encoder embeddings of x_1 and x_2 (= x_{t+H})

keyEquations.meaning: NSVQ: replace quantization with scaled noise so gradients pass and codebook does not collapse.
Decoder reconstructs the future frame from current patches cross-attending to the latent action; L2 loss.

algorithmSteps: Train the latent action quantization model on frame pairs (x_t, x_{t+H}) with the VQ/NSVQ + L2 reconstruction objective.
Use its encoder as an inverse dynamics model to label every frame with latent action tokens.
Pretrain the 7B VLM (vision encoder frozen) to predict latent tokens from image + instruction with a new MLP head (single epoch sufficient).
Discard the latent head; attach an action head over per-dimension binned robot actions.
Finetune on a small labeled set (e.g., 150 trajectories per task).
At inference, predict and de-bin delta end-effector actions from the current image and instruction.
ablations: Scaling latent model size, pretraining data and latent action space (sequence length, vocabulary) all improve SIMPLER success; 8^4 used by default.
Human-video data scaling: 10% of SSv2 gives 50.0 vs full SSv2 52.1 avg SIMPLER success.
Window size H is robust on Bridgev2 except very large windows, where the ~300M quantizer struggles.
hyperparams: Latent space 8^4 (vocab 8, 4 tokens); H = 0.6 s (robot), 2.4 s (human), H=3 for 5 Hz Bridgev2; latent model ~300M; LWM-Chat-1M 7B backbone; pretraining 8 H100 x 34 h, batch 128; finetune batch 128 with image augmentation.

name: MimicPlay
resolvedTitle: MimicPlay: Long-Horizon Imitation Learning by Watching Human Play
org: Stanford, NVIDIA, Georgia Tech, UT Austin, Caltech
problem: Long-horizon imitation learning needs an unattainable amount of teleoperated robot demos; robot play data is slow to collect.
keyIdea: Hierarchical IL: learn a goal-conditioned latent planner from cheap human play videos (predicting 3D hand trajectories) and a low-level visuomotor controller from a small number of robot teleop demos conditioned on the latent plans.
architecture: High-level latent planner: two ResNet-18 image encoders + MLP encoder to a latent plan p_t + MLP GMM decoder (K=5) predicting 3D hand trajectory. Low-level policy: GPT-style transformer (4 layers, 4 heads) over tokens [wrist-cam feature, proprioception, latent plan] with a GMM action head.
inputs: Current third-person image, goal image (from a one-shot human or robot prompt video), 3D hand/end-effector location; wrist camera image and proprioception for the low-level policy
outputs: 6-DoF end-effector (OSC) and gripper commands
actionRepr: Single-step 6-DoF end-effector + gripper action sampled from a GMM head (autoregressive transformer), OSC control
trainingData: 10 min of single-hand human play video per environment (~36k frames at 60 fps, 3D hand tracked with two calibrated cameras; stated ~equivalent to 3 h of robot teleop) + 20 (or 40) robot teleop demos per task collected with RoboTurk
controlRateHz: 17 (whole system incl. planner); robot arm 17-20 Hz, gripper 2 Hz

headlineResults.benchmark: Kitchen env, long horizon (>=3 subgoals), 20 demos, ALL
Kitchen env, long horizon, 40 demos, ALL
Study Desk, trained tasks ALL (20 demos)
Study Desk, unseen subgoal compositions ALL

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike LMP/C-BeT, which learn plans and actions end-to-end from robot play, the planner is trained on human play hand trajectories and decoupled from a plan-conditioned low-level policy.
limitations: Latent planner is learned from scene-specific human play data (not Internet-scale); tasks limited to tabletop; cross-embodiment representation learning (beyond the KL loss) leaves plenty of room for improvement.
notes: Code released at github.com/j96w/MimicPlay. 14 tasks in 6 real environments on a Franka Emika arm; task horizons 2000-4000 steps (100-200 s). Baselines get an extra 10 min of robot demos to match data-collection time. KL loss increased human/robot feature-distribution overlap by 23% (t-SNE area). EgoMimic later reports MimicPlay (reimplemented with ACT low-level, no goal conditioning) underperforming a unified co-training policy.

symbols.meaning: mixture weight, mean, std of component k

keyEquations.tex: \mathcal{L}_{KL} = D_{KL}(Q^r \,\|\, Q^h),\quad Q^h = E(o^h),\ Q^r = E(o^r)
keyEquations.meaning: Align batch feature distributions (mean, variance) of human and robot frames through the visual encoder; unpaired.
Total latent-planner training loss.

algorithmSteps: Collect ~10 min human play per scene; reconstruct 3D hand trajectory from two calibrated cameras.
Stage 1: train goal-conditioned latent planner to predict future 3D hand trajectory with GMM NLL + KL feature alignment to unpaired robot frames.
Freeze planner.
Stage 2: train transformer policy on 20-40 robot demos per task; goal = frame H in [200,600] steps (10-30 s) ahead.
Inference: take a one-shot human or robot prompt video; feed its frames sequentially as goal images (start at frame 200, advance 1 per step).
Planner outputs latent plan p_t; policy consumes [wrist, proprio, p_t] and samples action from GMM.
Run closed loop at 17 Hz, enabling replanning after disturbances.
ablations: Removing human play data (0% human): Study Desk trained-task success 0.55 -> 0.20; unseen 0.47 -> 0.10.
Without GMM: trained 0.28, unseen 0.07 (worse than 0% human on unseen).

hyperparams: GMM K=5; goal offset H uniform in [200,600] steps (10-30 s); planner and policy each 100k iterations (~12 h on one GPU); policy transformer 4 layers x 4 heads; human video 60 fps; control 17 Hz OSC.

name: ATM (any-point trajectory modeling)
resolvedTitle: Any-point Trajectory Modeling for Policy Learning
org: UC Berkeley, Tsinghua IIIS, Stanford, Shanghai AI Lab, Shanghai Qi Zhi Institute, CUHK
problem: Action-labeled demos are expensive; prior video pretraining either learns static features (R3M) or pixel-level video prediction (UniPi) that is costly, hallucinates, and runs open-loop.
keyIdea: Pretrain a Track Transformer on action-free videos to predict future 2D trajectories of arbitrary query points conditioned on image and language; use the predicted tracks as dense closed-loop subgoals for a policy trained on few action-labeled demos.
architecture: Track Transformer: tokens for masked future point tracks, image patches (50% masked, MAE-style auxiliary reconstruction), and BERT language embedding in one transformer. Policy: ViT-T style spatial transformer (image patches + track tokens + CLS) then causal temporal transformer; tracks fused early (tokens) and late (concatenated with action CLS before MLP head).
inputs: Multi-view RGB (base + wrist, 128x128 in LIBERO), proprioception, 32 grid query points; language only for the Track Transformer
outputs: Predicted 16-step point tracks (Track Transformer); 7-D end-effector action in LIBERO (policy)
actionRepr: Per-step 7-D continuous action (translation, rotation, gripper) regressed with MSE by an MLP head; ATM Diffusion Policy variant conditions a diffusion policy on the tracks
trainingData: LIBERO: 10 action-labeled demos + 50 action-free videos per task (500 videos per 10-task suite); tracks labeled with CoTracker. Real UR5: 50 action-labeled + 250 action-free videos; human-to-robot: 10 robot demos + 100 human videos per task; robot-to-robot: 160 Franka videos + 10 UR demos

headlineResults.comparedTo: best prior video-pretraining baseline 37% (>80% relative improvement)
BC 42.50; UniPi 11.83; R3M-finetune 5.33; BC full trainset (oracle) 76.33

headlineResults.benchmark: Real UR5 human-to-robot (fold cloth / put tomato / sweep toys)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces UniPi's pixel-level video subgoals with predicted point trajectories, making subgoal generation cheap (0.015 s vs 8.14 s per generation) and closed-loop.
limitations: Still needs a small set of action-labeled demos (authors suggest RL for the track-following stage as future work); scaling to in-the-wild video with multimodality and camera motion is left open; long tracks become noisy for precision tasks.
notes: Policy does not take language; tracks alone specify the task. Track Transformer trained with CoTracker pseudo-labels plus variance filtering of static points (1000 random points, filter, resample). Compute: ATM 1.56 TFLOPs, 0.015 s per generation vs UniPi 39.29 TFLOPs, 8.14 s (V100). ATM Diffusion Policy improves DP on all suites (e.g., LIBERO-90 33.85 -> 62.89). All methods in Table V use 20% of demos except the oracle. Published RSS 2024.

keyEquations.meaning: Track Transformer predicts future positions of query points from current image, initial points and language.

symbols.meaning: 2D positions of query points at time t

keyEquations.meaning: Track-guided policy maps observation and predicted tracks to action; trained with MSE on few demos.

algorithmSteps: Label action-free videos with CoTracker; filter static points by track variance and resample around moving points.
Train Track Transformer to reconstruct masked future tracks (and 50%-masked image patches) given image, initial points, language.
Freeze Track Transformer.
At each policy step, query 32 grid points on each view and predict 16-step future tracks.
Feed image patches + track tokens to spatial transformer (early fusion); causal temporal transformer over CLS/proprio/action tokens.
Concatenate action CLS with predicted tracks (late fusion) and regress action with MLP.
Execute and repeat closed-loop.
ablations: With only 4% of action-labeled demos ATM is comparable to BC with 20%; at 20% it approaches BC with 100%.
Track length 16 best on average; shorter tracks hurt LIBERO-Goal/Long most; 32-64 steps degrade (noisier).
Removing late fusion causes the largest drop; removing 50% image masking causes a slight decline except on LIBERO-Spatial.
hyperparams: 32 points, track length 16, track patch size 4, image mask ratio 0.5; policy frame stack 10; AdamW (track lr 1e-4, policy lr 5e-4), 100 epochs; 128x128 images in LIBERO.

name: EgoMimic
resolvedTitle: EgoMimic: Scaling Imitation Learning via Egocentric Video
org: Georgia Tech, Stanford
problem: Prior human-video methods only extract high-level intent for a planner, so performance stays capped by a low-level policy trained only on teleop data.
keyIdea: Treat egocentric human data (Project Aria video + 3D hand tracks + SLAM) as first-class embodied demonstrations and co-train one unified ACT-based policy on human and robot data, with frame, distribution and appearance alignment.
architecture: ACT-based transformer encoder-decoder (4 enc / 7 dec layers, hidden 512, 8 heads) with shared ResNet-18 visual encoder and CVAE style token; shallow modality-specific input heads; two linear output heads: pose head (human + robot) and joint-action head (robot only).
inputs: Egocentric Aria image (SAM-masked, red-line overlay), normalized hand/EEF pose proprioception; robot additionally wrist-camera images and joint positions
outputs: Action chunk of camera-frame EEF/hand poses and (robot) joint-space actions; robot is controlled with joint actions
actionRepr: Chunk of future poses/joint positions over a 4 s horizon (ACT, L1 loss); first 1 s executed receding-horizon; bimanual 2x7 joint actions incl. gripper
trainingData: Per task human/robot: Object-in-Bowl 1400 human demos (60 min) + 270 robot demos (120 min); Groceries 160 (80 min) + 300 (300 min); Laundry 590 (100 min) + 430 (300 min)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces MimicPlay's hierarchical human-planner/robot-controller split with a single end-to-end ACT policy whose shared trunk is supervised by both human hand poses and robot actions.
limitations: Needs joint-space prediction because the 6-DoF ViperX arms handle Cartesian control poorly; human data lacks grasp (gripper) signal so grasping is learned only from robot data; generalization to new robot embodiments or behaviors seen only in human data is future work.
notes: Hardware: two ViperX 300 S arms in inverted configuration, RealSense D405 wrist cams, Aria glasses mounted as the robot's main camera. Human data slowed by 0.25 to match robot speed. One hour of human data = 1400 demos vs 135 robot demos. Relative score improvement 34-228% over ACT; absolute SR +8-33%. Novel scene: EgoMimic 63 points vs MimicPlay 4. Phantom later notes EgoMimic averages ~41% robot data and needs >=2 h robot data.

name: Phantom
resolvedTitle: Phantom: Training Robots Without Robots Using Only Human Videos
org: Stanford University
problem: Human-video methods still co-train with robot data or depend on object tracking, which bottlenecks scaling and fails on deformables or multiple objects.
keyIdea: Convert human RGBD videos into robot observation-action pairs: estimate hand pose to get end-effector actions, inpaint out the human arm and overlay a rendered robot; train a policy on the edited data and deploy zero-shot with a matching virtual-robot overlay at test time.
architecture: Data pipeline: HaMeR hand keypoints/mesh refined with SAM2 mask + depth ICP; E2FGVI video inpainting; MuJoCo (Menagerie) robot rendering with depth-aware occlusion. Policy: Diffusion Policy (DDIM).
inputs: Third-person RGB image (edited: rendered robot overlaid) from a fixed, known-extrinsics viewpoint
outputs: End-effector position, 6D rotation, normalized gripper width
actionRepr: Diffusion Policy chunk of 8 actions (T_a=8, T_o=2), each = 3D position + 6D rotation + gripper width in [0,1]; OSC (Franka) or IK (Kinova) low-level
trainingData: Human video only: 250-350 demos per in-distribution task (e.g., 313 book, 268 stack, 279 sweep, 307 rope, 283 box); 950 demos across diverse indoor/outdoor scenes for Kinova sweep. Zero robot data.

Red Line and Vanilla editing: 0.0 on all in-distribution tasks.
Hand Mask augmentation (random mask shift) raises Stack Cups 0.40 -> 0.52.
hyperparams: Diffusion Policy with DDIM, 100 train / 10 inference steps; T_o=2, T_a=8; image res 240; batch 200 (Franka) / 256 (Kinova); lr 1e-4.

name: Being-H0
resolvedTitle: Being-H0: Vision-Language-Action Pretraining from Large-Scale Human Videos
org: Peking University, Renmin University of China, BeingBeyond
problem: Dexterous VLAs lack data: teleop data is small, simulation has a sim-to-real gap, and implicit human-video pretraining (contrastive, MAE, latent actions) has not produced large gains.
keyIdea: Physical instruction tuning: pretrain an LMM to explicitly generate MANO hand motion as discrete tokens from large-scale human videos (treating the human hand as a foundation manipulator), align heterogeneous camera spaces, then post-train on robot data.
architecture: InternVL3 backbone (InternViT-300M vision encoder, 2-layer MLP projector, LLM) with vocabulary extended by motion codes and <MOT>/</MOT> tokens; part-level GRQ-VAE motion tokenizer (separate wrist and finger codebooks). Post-training: learnable action queries + MLP proprio projector + MLP regression head (non-autoregressive).
inputs: Image (448x448), text instruction, optional prior hand motion; robot proprioception for post-training
outputs: Pretraining: hand motion token sequences (MANO-D162 at 15 FPS). Robot: action chunk of end-effector poses + dexterous hand joint positions
actionRepr: Pretraining: discrete motion tokens (128 tokens per hand per second, GRQ). Post-training: chunk of continuous EE poses + hand joints regressed via learnable queries with L1 loss
trainingData: UniHand: millions of motion-instruction instances curated from mocap (e.g., OakInk2, HOI4D), VR (EgoDex) and pseudo-labeled RGB video (HaMeR); pretraining uses UniHand-2.5M subset. Post-training: 50-100 teleop trajectories per task (Franka + Inspire hand).

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Franka + Inspire hand: Pick-Place-Toy seen / unseen / clutter
Visual-grounded hand motion generation (head / tail split)

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike GR00T N1.5's implicit latent actions from human video, Being-H0 explicitly tokenizes 3D MANO hand motion and trains the LMM to generate it autoregressively before robot post-training.
limitations: Robot control transfer uses a simple MLP projection with learnable queries; more adaptive human-to-robot transfer, richer physical cues (depth, tactile), tool use and multi-object interaction are left to future work.
notes: Tokenizer: part-level GRQ, 8 RQ layers, group size 2, codebooks K_w=K_f=4096 per part, code dim 512, temporal downsample 4 -> 128 tokens per second. Part-level MANO-D162 reconstruction MPJPE 0.573 cm, PA-MPJPE 0.129 cm (millimeter-level). Data efficiency: with 25% of teleop data Being-H0 matches InternVL3 at 100% on Pick-Place-Toy; Close-Lid at 25% data Being-H0 15% vs baseline 0%. Each real task 20 trials. Total UniHand size: the alphaXiv summary states >150M pairs (and elsewhere 165M); not verified in the paper text read, abstract says 'millions of motion-based instructional instances'; pretraining used the 2.5M-sample subset.

keyEquations.tex: M = \{m_1, \dots, m_T\} \mapsto \lceil T/\alpha \rceil \text{ token embeddings},\quad m = \{\theta, r^{rot}, \tau, \beta\}
keyEquations.meaning: GRQ tokenizer compresses T frames of MANO hand features into discrete tokens with temporal downsampling alpha.

keyEquations.tex: H_{v,t,m} = [H_v; H_t; H_m] \rightarrow Q_{v,t,m}, K_{v,t,m}, V_{v,t,m}
keyEquations.meaning: Vision, text and motion tokens share one attention stack; trained with next-token prediction.

symbols.meaning: hidden states of vision, text, motion tokens

algorithmSteps: Curate UniHand: standardize all hand labels to MANO; pseudo-label RGB-only videos with HaMeR.
Map frames to a unified weak-perspective camera space; augment with depth scaling and in-plane rotation.
Train part-level GRQ tokenizer on MANO-D162 features (wrist and fingers separately).
Generate instruction data: motion generation, motion translation, contextual motion prediction.
Pretrain InternVL3 with next-token prediction plus vocabulary-level logit masking (P=50%) and token-level loss filtering.
Post-train on 50-100 teleop demos: project proprio via MLP, learnable queries attend to context, MLP regresses action chunk with L1.
ablations: Part-level tokenizer on MANO-D162: MPJPE 0.573 cm vs 0.704 (4-groups) and 1.054 (16-layer RQ).
Adding hand shape parameters degrades reconstruction; auxiliary joint positions help.
Removing motion-translation or contextual-prediction data degrades generation metrics; performance scales with data up to 2.5M samples.
hyperparams: Temporal downsample alpha=4; 8-layer GRQ, group size 2, codebooks 4096 per part, dim 512; 128 motion tokens per hand per second; MANO-D162 at 15 FPS; image 448x448; logit masking P=50%, token loss filter [15%,95%] percentile; AdamW lr 1e-5, batch 128, 32 A800 GPUs.

name: villa-X
resolvedTitle: villa-X: Enhancing Latent Action Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Microsoft Research, Tsinghua University, Wuhan University, HKUST, Nanjing University
problem: Visual-only latent action models miss subtle but control-critical motions (rotations, gripper), and existing ways of plugging latent actions into VLAs (LAPA init, Go-1 separate planner) transfer information poorly.
keyIdea: Ground latent actions with a proprioceptive forward dynamics decoder (conditioned on embodiment context) and jointly diffuse latent-action and robot-action chunks, with robot actions conditioned on latent plans via block-causal attention.
architecture: LAM: ST-Transformer IDM (12 blocks) over 8-frame clips, VQ codebook size 32 (continuous centers used downstream), ViT-B visual FDM, 2-layer MLP proprio-FDM. ACT: PaliGemma 3B VLM + ACT-latent expert + ACT-robot expert (each 18-layer transformer, ~300M params, hidden 1024, 8 heads), optional wrist-cam ResNet-18 via cross-attention, HPT-style per-embodiment state/action projections.
inputs: Third-person image (224x224), language instruction, proprioceptive state, embodiment context (dataset ID + control frequency); optional wrist image
outputs: Latent action plan (6 latents) and robot action chunk (4 steps)
actionRepr: Joint flow matching over a chunk of 4 continuous robot actions and 6 continuous latent actions (codebook centers)
trainingData: Robot: 1.6M trajectories / 223.5M frames (OpenX mixture + AgiBot World Beta); human: 3.6M clips (Ego4D/EgoHOD, EPIC-KITCHENS, Something-Something V2, HoloAssist, RH20T, HOI4D, EgoPAT3D, EGTEA Gaze+, HO-Cap)

headlineResults.comparedTo: pi0 58.7; pi0-FAST 61.9; GR00T-N1.5 57.9; MoTo 59.2; w/o latent 36.5

whatChangedVsParent: Adds a proprio-FDM so latent actions encode physical dynamics, and replaces LAPA-style weight initialization / Go-1-style separate autoregressive planner with joint latent+robot flow matching.
limitations: The latent expert's planning ability is not fully explored; e.g., sampling multiple latent plans and rejecting ones that do not follow the instruction with a VLM-based critic is left to future work.
notes: Code at github.com/microsoft/villa-x. Pretraining: LAM ~4 days on 128 A100; ACT ~4 days on 64 A100. Stochastic attention masking: 50% of the time all robot-to-latent attention masked, otherwise 50% of latent tokens masked. Tau sampled from different beta distributions for latent vs robot actions (latents biased noisier). Ablation SIMPLER numbers (Table 1) come from a reduced mixture (10% Fractal, 10% Bridge, 100% SSv2), not the full model. Realman: 375 teleop trajectories at 10 Hz; XHand: ~4000 trajectories, no dexterous data in pretraining.

keyEquations.meaning: Standard latent action model: infer latent from frame pair, reconstruct future frame.

keyEquations.tex: (\hat q_{t+1}, \dots, \hat q_{t+K}, \hat a_{t+1}, \dots, \hat a_{t+K}) = \text{proprio-FDM}(q_t, z_t, c_e)
keyEquations.meaning: Auxiliary decoder predicts future robot states and actions from latent, grounding it physically.

symbols.meaning: embodiment context f(dataset ID, control frequency)

keyEquations.tex: \pi(a_{t:t+m-1}, z^K_{t:t+(n-1)K} \mid o_t, l, q_t, c_e) = \pi_{robot}(a_{t:t+m-1} \mid z^K_{t:t+(n-1)K}, o_t, l, q_t, c_e)\cdot \pi_{latent}(z^K_{t:t+(n-1)K} \mid o_t, l)
keyEquations.meaning: Policy factorized into latent planner and latent-conditioned robot action expert.

keyEquations.tex: \mathcal{L}_\tau(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{p(x_t\mid O_t), q(x^\tau_t\mid x_t)} \left\| v^\theta_\tau(x^\tau_t, O_t) - u(x^\tau_t \mid x_t) \right\|^2,\quad x^\tau_t = \tau x_t + (1-\tau)\epsilon,\ u = \epsilon - x_t
keyEquations.meaning: Conditional flow matching loss jointly over latent and robot action chunks.

algorithmSteps: Stage 1: pretrain LAM on robot + human clips with visual reconstruction, proprio prediction (robot only) and VQ losses.
Label all pretraining data with continuous latent actions from the IDM.
Stage 2: pretrain ACT (VLM + latent expert + robot expert) with joint flow matching; human clips supervise only latents.
Apply stochastic robot-to-latent attention masking during training.
Stage 3: finetune on target embodiment (reinitialize state/action encoders/decoders).
Inference: jointly denoise latent plan and robot action chunk from noise conditioned on image, language, proprio, embodiment context.
ablations: Proprio-FDM: SIMPLER avg Google 58.5 vs 57.4 (wo/pp), WidowX 40.8 vs 32.3; no latent actions: 35.0 / 33.1.
Integration style: LAPA-style 43.8 / 1.0 and Go-1-style 32.8 / 14.8 vs ours 58.5 / 40.8.
Removing attention mask: 53.2 / 34.0; removing embodiment context: 49.1 / 38.5; context lowers visual/proprio FDM loss by 16.2% / 10.3%.
hyperparams: LAM: 8-frame clips 224x224, patch 14, 12 ST-blocks hidden 768; VQ codebook 32; ACT experts 18 layers, hidden 1024, 8 heads; latent sequence N=6, robot action chunk M=4; lr 5e-5 with 200-step warmup, grad clip 1.0; wrist view dropout 50%.

name: Dex-Net (ambidextrous grasping)
resolvedTitle: Learning ambidextrous robot grasping policies (Dex-Net 4.0), Science Robotics 4(26):eaau4984, 2019
org: UC Berkeley (AUTOLAB)
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
notes: Not on arXiv; alphaXiv title search resolved to an unrelated paper (Sim-Grasp, 2405.00841) and Semantic Scholar was not reachable, so the primary paper was not read. Authors per citation in Sim-Grasp: J. Mahler, M. Matl, V. Satish, M. Danielczuk, B. DeRose, S. McKinley, K. Goldberg. SECONDARY (from Sim-Grasp, 2405.00841, Table I): Dex-Net 4.0 dataset listed as 2D grasp labels from analytic models, 3-10 objects per scene, 1.6K objects, 2.2M labels, simulated. Level 1-4 object difficulty rubric originates in Dex-Net 4.0. GENERAL KNOWLEDGE (unverified, do not cite as numbers): Dex-Net 4.0 trains separate GQ-CNN grasp-quality networks for a suction cup and a parallel-jaw gripper on millions of synthetic depth images with domain-randomized analytic/physics-based robustness labels, and an 'ambidextrous' policy picks the gripper and grasp with highest predicted quality; bin-picking evaluations reported high reliability (~95%) and >300 mean picks per hour, but verify against the Science Robotics paper before stating figures.

topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
name: GG-CNN
resolvedTitle: Closing the Loop for Robotic Grasping: A Real-time, Generative Grasp Synthesis Approach
org: Australian Centre for Robotic Vision, Queensland University of Technology
problem: Deep grasp detectors of the time sampled and ranked grasp candidates, taking ~0.2 s to tens of seconds, so they ran open-loop and failed when objects moved or robot control was inaccurate.
keyIdea: A tiny fully convolutional net maps a depth image directly to per-pixel grasp quality, angle and width maps (a 'generative' one-to-one mapping), so the best grasp is an argmax and can be recomputed fast enough for closed-loop visual servoing.
architecture: Fully convolutional encoder-decoder (conv + transposed conv) on a 300x300 depth image with 62,420 parameters; outputs Q, cos(2Phi), sin(2Phi) and W maps. Best of 95 architecture variants (filter/stride combinations).
inputs: Single 300x300 inpainted, mean-subtracted depth image (wrist-mounted RealSense SR300).
outputs: Pixel-wise grasp map G = (Phi, W, Q): quality in [0,1], angle in [-pi/2, pi/2], width in [0,150] px; best grasp converted to a planar (top-down) 4-DoF grasp in robot frame.
actionRepr: Not a policy; outputs a planar antipodal grasp (x,y,z, yaw, width); closed-loop PBVS converts it to a 6D end-effector velocity v = lambda(T_g - T_f).
trainingData: Cornell Grasping Dataset (885 RGB-D images, 5110 positive / 2909 negative grasps), augmented with random crops/zooms/rotations to 8840 depth images with 51,100 grasp examples; only positive grasps used.
controlRateHz: up to 50 Hz (pipeline 19 ms; network 6 ms on GTX 1070); depth images at 30 Hz in closed-loop trials

headlineResults.benchmark: Real robot, adversarial objects (8 Dex-Net objects), dynamic (moved during grasp)
Real robot, household objects (12 APB/YCB), dynamic

parents: Cornell grasp rectangle detection (Lenz et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces sample-and-rank grasp CNNs with a pixel-wise generative FCN that is orders of magnitude smaller, enabling closed-loop grasping.
limitations: Planar (top-down, 4-DoF) grasps only; camera cannot update the grasp within ~70 mm of the object; fails on black/reflective objects without valid depth and on objects under 15 mm tall; not trained on clutter.
notes: Code at github.com/dougsm/ggcnn. An extended IJRR 2019 version ('Learning robust, real-time, reactive robotic grasping') introduced GG-CNN2 (cited by GR-ConvNet at 84% on Jacquard). On GraspNet-1Billion (CVPR 2020 Table 3), GG-CNN scores AP 15.48/16.89 on seen (RealSense/Kinect), showing rectangle-metric accuracy overestimates quality.

keyEquations.meaning: Image-space grasp mapped to robot frame via camera intrinsics and hand-eye calibration.
Network regresses the full grasp map from depth; trained with L2 loss.
Angle decoded from two unit-circle components to handle the +-pi/2 symmetry.
PBVS velocity command driving gripper pose toward the tracked best grasp.

algorithmSteps: Capture depth image; crop to square, resize to 300x300, inpaint invalid pixels, subtract mean
Run GG-CNN to get Q, cos2Phi, sin2Phi, W maps
Gaussian-filter Q
Find top 3 local maxima; keep the one nearest the previously tracked grasp (global max at start)
Read angle and width at that pixel; convert to robot-frame grasp
Issue 6D velocity v = lambda(T_g - T_f) and servo gripper width
Stop updating within ~70 mm of object; close gripper and lift
ablations: Closed-loop vs open-loop under simulated kinematic error: 68%/73% vs 38% worst case
Dynamic objects (83%/88%) within 95% CI of static results; open-loop cannot succeed once objects move
Dynamic clutter drop only 5% vs static clutter, compared to 12% for Viereck et al.
hyperparams: Input 300x300 depth; width capped 150 px (scaled 1/150); Q label = centre third of positive rectangles; 95 architectures x 100 epochs; 80/20 split; PBVS stops at ~70 mm; gripper width limited to ~70 mm.

topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
name: GR-ConvNet
resolvedTitle: Antipodal Robotic Grasping using Generative Residual Convolutional Neural Network
org: Rochester Institute of Technology (MABL); OSARO Inc.
problem: Grasp detectors either classify sampled candidates (slow) or used shallow generative nets like GG-CNN with limited accuracy; needed a fast, accurate, modality-flexible pixel-wise grasp generator.
keyIdea: Extend the GG-CNN pixel-wise quality/angle/width formulation with a deeper residual encoder-decoder that takes n-channel input (RGB, depth or RGB-D), trained with a smooth-L1 loss.
architecture: 3 conv layers -> 5 residual blocks -> transposed conv upsampling (feature map 56x56 back to 224x224), producing 4 output maps (quality, cos2Theta, sin2Theta, width). About 1.9M parameters.
inputs: n-channel 224x224 image (RGB, depth, or RGB-D); depth inpainted.
outputs: Pixel-wise grasp map G = (Theta, W, Q); highest-quality pixel gives a planar antipodal grasp.
actionRepr: Not a policy; outputs planar antipodal grasp (x, y, Theta, W, Q) converted to robot frame and executed by an IK/ROS trajectory planner.
trainingData: Cornell (1035 RGB-D images, 240 objects, 8019 grasps; augmented to ~51k grasp examples) and Jacquard (54k RGB-D images, 1.1M simulated grasps; 90/10 split).
controlRateHz: ~20 ms inference (GTX 1080 Ti); paper states suitable for closed-loop up to 50 Hz

headlineResults.benchmark: Real robot household objects (35 objects, 350 attempts, Baxter)
Real robot adversarial objects (10 objects, 100 attempts)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds residual blocks and n-channel (RGB-D) input to GG-CNN's generative pixel-wise formulation, with smooth-L1 loss, raising Cornell accuracy from 73% to 97.7%.
limitations: Planar antipodal grasps only; transparent/reflective objects fail due to bad depth; failures from slipping and gripper collision with neighbours; authors list suction and multi-finger grippers as future work.
notes: Code: github.com/skumra/robotic-grasping (inference) and skumra/baxter-pnp (control). Published at IROS 2020. Widely used as the default baseline in Grasp-Anything and later language-driven grasp datasets. Paper also writes the objective as a negative log-likelihood (Eq. 5) though the practical loss is smooth L1.

keyEquations.meaning: Robot-frame grasp obtained from image-frame grasp via camera and hand-eye transforms.
Per-pixel grasp map output by the network.
Smooth-L1 (Huber) loss between predicted and ground-truth grasp maps.

algorithmSteps: Acquire RGB and aligned depth; crop, resize to 224x224, normalize; inpaint depth
Forward n-channel image through GR-ConvNet
Decode angle from cos2Theta/sin2Theta; take pixel with max quality
Convert grasp to robot frame with hand-eye calibration
Plan trajectory via IK/ROS and execute pick-and-place
ablations: Input modality on Cornell IW/OW: depth 93.2/94.3, RGB 96.6/95.5, RGB-D 97.7/96.6
Jacquard: depth 93.7, RGB 91.8, RGB-D 94.6
Smooth L1 chosen over other losses to handle exploding gradients (no numbers given)
hyperparams: Input 224x224; bottleneck 56x56; 5 residual blocks; Adam lr 1e-3, batch 8; 3 random seeds averaged; rectangle metric IoU>25% and angle<30 deg.

topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
name: 6-DoF GraspNet
resolvedTitle: 6-DOF GraspNet: Variational Grasp Generation for Object Manipulation
org: NVIDIA
problem: 6-DoF grasp methods either evaluate candidates from hand-designed samplers (e.g. GPD, which misses thin rims) or regress a single grasp, lacking diversity needed for kinematic feasibility.
keyIdea: Learn a VAE grasp sampler conditioned on the object point cloud to generate diverse SE(3) grasps, then score them with a PointNet++ evaluator and refine them by gradient ascent on the evaluator's success probability.
architecture: VAE encoder/decoder and evaluator all PointNet++ (3 set-abstraction layers + 2 FC layers of 1024). Decoder outputs unit quaternion + translation. Evaluator takes merged object + rendered-gripper point cloud with a binary membership feature.
inputs: Segmented partial object point cloud from a depth camera (grasps expressed in frame at point-cloud centroid).
outputs: Set of 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasps (R, T) with success probabilities.
actionRepr: Not a policy; outputs SE(3) grasp poses; a motion planner executes the highest-scored feasible one.
trainingData: Simulated in NVIDIA FleX on 206 ShapeNet objects (boxes, cylinders, bowls, bottles, mugs): 10,816,720 candidates sampled, 7,074,038 simulated, 2,104,894 successful grasps. No real data.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Franka Panda, 17 unseen objects x 3 poses (51 trials)

headlineResults.value: 0.04 s VAE+evaluator forward; 0.3 s per refinement iteration

parents: GPD (grasp pose detection, ten Pas et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces heuristic surface-normal grasp sampling with a learned VAE sampler and adds gradient-based refinement through a differentiable evaluator.
limitations: Generates grasps for a single segmented object without considering surrounding objects or robot reach (handled separately by planner); grasps in unconstrained SE(3) space; tangent-finger grasps can push rather than grasp.
notes: PyTorch reimplementation with pretrained models at github.com/NVlabs/pytorch_6dof-graspnet (from general knowledge). Follow-up Murali et al. 2020 added CollisionNet for clutter; Contact-GraspNet reports 6-DOF GraspNet at 62.7% and +CollisionNet at 80.39% in clutter.

keyEquations.tex: P(G \mid X) = \int P(G \mid X, z; \Theta) P(z)\, dz
keyEquations.meaning: Grasp likelihood marginalised over latent z with prior N(0,I).

keyEquations.tex: L_{vae} = \sum_{z\sim Q, g\sim G^*} L(\hat{g}, g) - \alpha D_{KL}[Q(z|X,g), \mathcal{N}(0,I)]
keyEquations.meaning: VAE objective: grasp reconstruction plus KL regularisation of latent.
Reconstruction loss on transformed predefined gripper points, coupling rotation and translation.
Refinement step: gradient of evaluator success w.r.t. rigid grasp pose.

nodes: Plane fit + clustering -> object point cloud X
edges: Plane fit + clustering -> object point cloud X
Plane fit + clustering -> object point cloud X

algorithmSteps: Segment object point cloud (table-plane removal, clustering)
Sample 200 latent z from N(0,I); decode to grasps
Score each grasp with evaluator on merged object+gripper point cloud
Refine each grasp by gradient ascent on success (eta caps translation at 1 cm)
Repeat evaluation/refinement ~10 iterations
Discard grasps below threshold; check kinematics/collision with motion planner; execute best
ablations: Latent dimension: 2D gives best success-coverage AUC; 1D lacks capacity, 3D/4D overfit
Refinement raises both success and coverage; AUC plateaus after 10 iterations
VAE sampler significantly beats geometric surface-normal sampler on success and coverage (esp. rims/thin structures)
hyperparams: Latent dim 2; KL weight alpha=0.01; 64 grasps per training batch; evaluator batches 30% pos/30% neg/40% hard neg (perturb +-0.6 rad, +-3 cm); Adam lr 1e-4; 200 samples, 10 refinement iters; eta caps 1 cm.

topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
name: Contact-GraspNet
resolvedTitle: Contact-GraspNet: Efficient 6-DoF Grasp Generation in Cluttered Scenes
org: NVIDIA; German Aerospace Center (DLR); TU Munich; University of Washington
problem: Prior 6-DoF clutter grasping (e.g. 6-DOF GraspNet + CollisionNet) used multi-stage pipelines sensitive to segmentation errors, ignored scene context, and regressed in unconstrained SE(3).
keyIdea: Treat observed points as grasp contacts: for each point predict contact success, approach and baseline directions and width, reducing 6-DoF grasp learning to a 4-DoF problem rooted in the scene point cloud.
architecture: Asymmetric U-shaped PointNet++ (set abstraction + feature propagation) with 4 heads (two 1D conv each): contact score, z1, z2 (Gram-Schmidt to baseline b and approach a), 10-bin width.
inputs: Raw depth / scene point cloud (20,000 points), optionally a local region around a segmented target; unknown-object instance segmentation used only to filter grasps.
outputs: Per-point 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasp poses with widths and confidences for 2048 farthest-point-sampled points.
actionRepr: Not a policy; outputs 6-DoF grasps; most confident reachable, collision-free grasp executed via a motion planner.
trainingData: ACRONYM: 8872 ShapeNet meshes with 17.7M simulated grasps; 10,000 table-top scenes of 8-12 objects rendered from random virtual cameras.
controlRateHz: 0.28 s per full scene, ~0.19 s per local region

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Franka, 9 cluttered scenes / 51 unseen objects (Murali et al. protocol)

parents: Murali et al. 6-DoF grasping in clutter (CollisionNet)
whatChangedVsParent: Predicts grasps densely on full scene points anchored to observed contacts in a single network, instead of per-object VAE sampling plus a separate collision network.
limitations: Parallel-jaw only; requires at least one visible contact; thick objects near max width and small objects get low-confidence predictions; trained purely in simulation.
notes: Code and checkpoints released (NVlabs/contact_graspnet). Loss weights alpha=1, beta=10, gamma=1. The alphaXiv summary's 'approximately twice the success rate' is not in the paper; the paper says it cuts the failure rate in half vs. a recent SOTA method.

keyEquations.tex: t_g = c + \frac{w}{2} b + d a, \qquad R_g = [\, b \;\; a\times b \;\; a \,]
keyEquations.meaning: Grasp pose reconstructed from contact point, baseline, approach and width.
In-network Gram-Schmidt makes approach orthonormal to baseline.
Confidence-weighted symmetric gripper-point distance to nearest ground-truth grasp.
Total loss: top-k BCE on contacts, pose loss, weighted binned-width BCE.

nodes: Scene point cloud / local region crop
Per-point contact score, a, b, width
edges: Scene point cloud / local region crop
Scene point cloud / local region crop
Per-point contact score, a, b, width
Per-point contact score, a, b, width

algorithmSteps: Back-project depth; optionally crop a cube (0.3-0.6 m) around target segment centroid
Sample 20,000 points, center at mean
Run network; predict for 2048 FPS points: contact score, a, b, width bin
Build 6-DoF grasps via t_g = c + w/2 b + d a
Associate grasps to object segments by their contact points
Keep contacts above 0.23 confidence (fallback 0.19); FPS for coverage
Execute most confident kinematically reachable, collision-free grasp
ablations: Without weighted width binning, width predictions collapse to narrow grasps and success and coverage drop
add-s loss raises success at high-confidence contacts (coverage 0-0.1) and improves calibration
Training on the small 6-DOF GraspNet dataset (5 categories) instead of ACRONYM fails to generalize; skipping local regions lowers coverage
hyperparams: 20,000 input points, 2048 output points; 10 width bins; contact radius r=5 mm; top-k=512 BCE; loss weights 1/10/1; Adam lr 1e-3 -> 1e-4; batch 3, 144k iterations (~40 h on one V100); confidence threshold 0.23.

topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
name: GraspNet-1Billion
resolvedTitle: GraspNet-1Billion: A Large-Scale Benchmark for General Object Grasping
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University
problem: Grasp methods used incompatible representations (rectangles vs 6D) and metrics, and datasets were either small human-labelled real data or large simulated data with a visual domain gap.
keyIdea: Capture real RGB-D images of cluttered scenes and annotate them densely by analytic force-closure computation on object meshes projected via annotated 6D poses; evaluate any grasp online with the same analytic metric. Also proposes an end-to-end point-cloud grasp network with decoupled approach/operation prediction and grasp affinity fields.
architecture: Baseline net: PointNet++ backbone -> ApproachNet (graspability + 300-view classification per seed) -> cylinder grouping -> OperationNet (12 in-plane rotation bins, width, score per 4 depth bins) -> ToleranceNet (grasp affinity fields: perturbation tolerance).
inputs: Scene point cloud from a single RGB-D view (RealSense D435 or Kinect 4 Azure).
outputs: Dense 6-DoF grasps G = [R t w] with scores.
actionRepr: Not a policy; 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasp poses.
trainingData: 97,280 RGB-D images of 190 cluttered scenes (512 images each from 2 cameras, 256 viewpoints), 88 objects (32 YCB, 13 Dex-Net adversarial, 43 own), 3-9M grasps per scene, over 1.1 billion grasp poses; 100 train / 90 test scenes (30 seen, 30 similar, 30 novel).

headlineResults.benchmark: Label validation on real Flexiv arm (10 objects, 100 grasps each)

whatChangedVsParent: Moves from rectangle labels and per-method metrics to dense analytic 6-DoF labels on real sensor data with a unified force-closure AP metric.
limitations: Only parallel-jaw grippers (multi-finger and suction left to future work); 88 known objects; motion planning and real gripper/arm collisions not modelled; requires manual 6D pose annotation.
notes: Resolved CVPR 2020 paper via CVF open access; arXiv 1912.13470 is an earlier version with 87,040 images, 170 scenes, 370M grasps and no baseline network, so numbers differ by version. AP = mean Precision@k for k=1..50, averaged over friction mu=0.2..1.0; score s = 1.1 - mu. Dataset, API and graspnet-baseline code at graspnet.net. Basis for GSNet and AnyGrasp.

keyEquations.meaning: Grasp label score from smallest friction coefficient at which force closure holds.
6-DoF parallel-jaw grasp representation.
ApproachNet loss: graspability classification plus view-score regression.

algorithmSteps: Place ~10 objects; capture 256 viewpoints with RealSense and Kinect on a robot arm
Annotate 6D object poses in first frame; propagate via camera poses
Sample grasp points, views, depths and in-plane rotations per object mesh; score by force closure (s=1.1-mu)
Project to scene with 6D poses; remove colliding grasps
Train baseline: backbone -> ApproachNet -> cylinder grouping -> OperationNet + ToleranceNet
At inference, bin grasps by score (10 bins) and re-sort within bins by predicted tolerance
Evaluate with pose-NMS then Precision@k over friction levels
ablations: Replacing classification with regression for approach/rotation drops Kinect-seen AP 29.88 -> 23.74
Removing ToleranceNet drops AP 29.88 -> 28.53 (AP0.4 19.31 -> 16.33)
Rectangle methods (GG-CNN, Chu et al.) score lowest, indicating rectangle-metric accuracy is overestimated
