topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
name: AnyGrasp
resolvedTitle: AnyGrasp: Robust and Efficient Grasp Perception in Spatial and Temporal Domains
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University
problem: Existing grasp detectors were slow sampling-based or static-scene-only and, when trained in simulation, needed high-precision depth sensors; dynamic (moving-object) grasp tracking was largely unexplored.
keyIdea: Dense 7-DoF grasp prediction (GSNet-based) trained on real sensor data with analytic labels, extended with centre-of-gravity-aware stable scores, implicit obstacle awareness, and a temporal association module that tracks grasp correspondences across frames.
architecture: Geometry processing module = GSNet (3D sparse-conv backbone, graspable FPS of M=1024 seeds, graspable probabilistic view selection over 300 views, cylinder grouping, MLP predicting 12 rotations x 5 depths scores/widths + 12 stable scores). Temporal association module concatenates seed, grasp, colour features and pose into a C=256 embedding; cosine-similarity correspondence matrix.
inputs: Single-view point cloud (with RGB for the temporal module) from a commercial depth camera (RealSense D415/D435, L515).
outputs: Dense 7-DoF grasps G = [R t w] with quality scores; per-grasp embeddings for temporal association.
actionRepr: Not a policy; outputs 7-DoF parallel-jaw grasps; top-100 go to a grasp planner; dynamic grasping servos toward tracked (momentum-extrapolated) grasp.
trainingData: GraspNet-1Billion training set plus 168 extra scenes with 104 new objects: 268 scenes, 144 objects, 256 viewpoints each, real sensor data with analytic dense labels; extra 0.5 cm depth, stable-score and temporal-association labels.
controlRateHz: ~100 ms grasp perception; post-processing 80 ms for 100 grasps; total decision under 200 ms

headlineResults.benchmark: Catching swimming robot fish (5 runs, 8 fish)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds COG-aware stable score, 0.5 cm approach depth, implicit collision awareness and a contrastively trained temporal association module on top of GSNet, trained on expanded real data.
limitations: Visual-only open-loop grasping is fragile to occlusion during closed-loop tracking and lacks tactile in-hand adjustment; parallel gripper only; performance drops on smooth adversarial 3D-printed objects; fish-catching failures from slip, speed changes and correspondence switching.
notes: Published in IEEE T-RO 2023. Released as the AnyGrasp SDK (licensed binary; weights not openly downloadable, per general knowledge); GSNet/graspnet-baseline code is open. Humans achieved 1,000-1,200 MPPH on average. Widely used as the off-the-shelf grasp module in open-vocabulary mobile manipulation systems (e.g. OK-Robot) per general knowledge.

keyEquations.meaning: 7-DoF grasp: orientation, centre, width.
Grasp distance in object frame used to label temporal associations.
Cosine similarity between grasp embeddings across frames.
Supervised contrastive loss pulling together same-grasp pairs across adjacent views.

algorithmSteps: Voxel-downsample input point cloud (5 mm)
Predict graspness, sample 1024 seeds, pick best view per seed
Predict scores/widths for 12 rotations x 5 depths plus stable scores; rescore by (1 - stable score)
Rank grasps; explicit collision check and gripper centering on top-100 (80 ms)
For dynamic scenes: embed grasps, match to previous-frame buffer by cosine similarity, extrapolate with momentum
Send selected grasp to planner/servo; store features in temporal buffer
ablations: Stable score on a long heavy object: 11 in-hand slippages (2 failures) vs 16 (3 failures) without, over 25 attempts each
Training on simulated depth (even with Gaussian noise) gives a large AP gap vs real data, especially on novel objects, and worse real bin picking
Downsampling grasp-annotation density 10x/50x hurts about as much as downsampling images; downsampling scenes hurts most (fails to converge with 2 scenes)
hyperparams: M=1024 seeds, 300 views, 12 in-plane rotations, 5 approach depths (0.5,1,2,3,4 cm), C=256 embedding, K=16 cylinder points, sigma=0.1, tau=0.1, gamma=0.1, w_max=0.01 m; Adam lr 1e-3 poly decay; geometry module trained first then frozen.

topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
name: Grasp-Anything
resolvedTitle: Grasp-Anything: Large-scale Grasp Dataset from Foundation Models
org: FPT Software AI Center; TU Wien / AIT; Imperial College London; HUST; Ton Duc Thang Univ.; University of Liverpool
problem: Grasp datasets cover few objects, lack natural-language scene descriptions, and use lab/bin arrangements, limiting zero-shot generalization of grasp detectors.
keyIdea: Synthesize a 1M-image grasp dataset with foundation models: ChatGPT writes diverse scene descriptions, Stable Diffusion renders them, OFA + Segment-Anything produce masks, and a pretrained detector proposes rectangle grasps that are filtered with an analytic torque-ratio quality metric.
architecture: Data pipeline, not a model: ChatGPT (prompt engineering with self-reinforcing prompt buffer) -> Stable Diffusion 2.1 -> OFA grounding + SAM masks -> RAGT-3/3 grasp proposals -> Kamon-style quality evaluation on mask convex hull. Evaluated with GR-ConvNet, Det-Seg-Refine and GG-CNN.
inputs: Text prompts generated by ChatGPT.
outputs: 1M RGB images with scene descriptions, object masks, and 2D rectangle grasp labels (~600M grasps).
trainingData: 1M samples, ~3M objects, ~600M grasps, 236 LVIS categories (runner-up VMRD 115); ~1.5M POS tags in descriptions.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real KUKA + Robotiq 2F-85, single object (60 trials), GR-ConvNet
Real robot cluttered scene (15 objects, 60 trials)

whatChangedVsParent: Shifts from model-centric to data-centric: replaces lab-captured/simulated object sets with foundation-model-synthesized scenes at 1M-image scale plus language descriptions.
limitations: Creation took ~3 months on three Quadro 8000 GPUs and depends on the commercial ChatGPT API; only 2D rectangle grasps, no 3D point clouds; grasp evaluation needs accurate segmentation masks.
notes: Dataset + code at grasp-anything-2023.github.io (openWeights refers to dataset/code release). This is a dataset paper; it has no new grasp model. Follow-ups (Grasp-Anything-6D, language-driven grasp detection) by the same group exist (general knowledge). Note: the topic label 'grasp-anything models' refers to the dataset line; this paper itself introduces no model.

keyEquations.tex: T = (\tau_1 + \tau_2) - R M g, \quad \tau_i = K\mu_s F \cos\alpha_i
keyEquations.meaning: Net torque: contact resistance minus gravitational torque about grasp line.
Physics-free grasp quality; positive values labelled positive grasps.

symbols.meaning: set to -1 for a missing contact

nodes: Torque-ratio evaluation on mask convex hull
edges: Torque-ratio evaluation on mask convex hull
Torque-ratio evaluation on mask convex hull

algorithmSteps: Initialize ChatGPT with directives and template (sentence + object list); seed prompt buffer with 50 manual samples
Repeatedly feed 10-15 buffered samples to generate new scene descriptions until 1M
Render each description with Stable Diffusion 2.1
Ground and segment each listed object with OFA + SAM
Propose rectangle grasps with pretrained RAGT-3/3
Score each grasp with T~ = (cos a1 + cos a2)/R on mask convex hull; T~>0 is positive
ablations: Generalized zero-shot (GR-ConvNet, H on Cornell/VMRD/OCID): 0.62/0.31/0.39 trained on Grasp-Anything vs 0.51/0.13/0.21 on Jacquard
Cross-dataset transfer improves ~9-29% over other training sets
Models score lower on Grasp-Anything's own base-to-new split, showing it is harder
hyperparams: 1M prompts; Stable Diffusion 2.1; base/new split = top 70% / remaining 30% LVIS labels; rectangle metric IoU>0.25, angle<30 deg.

name: Grasp-Anything++ / LGD
resolvedTitle: Language-driven Grasp Detection
org: FPT Software AI Center; TU Wien; Imperial College London; Ton Duc Thang University; University of Liverpool
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Existing grasp datasets (Cornell, Jacquard) have no language, and language-conditioned datasets are small or lack part-level instructions, so there is no way to train a model that grasps 'the handle of the steak knife' among arbitrary objects.
keyIdea: Build Grasp-Anything++ (1M synthetic images, 3M+ objects, 10M+ object- and part-level grasp instructions) with foundation models, and cast language-driven grasp detection as conditional diffusion over the 5-D grasp rectangle, adding a contrastive loss that ties the image-text attention map estimate x~0 to the noisy grasp.
architecture: ResNet-50 vision encoder + CLIP (or BERT) text encoder fused by ALBEF (6 attention layers); the ALBEF attention map serves as the estimate x~0. MLPs embed timestep, fused text-image feature and noisy grasp x_{t+1}; concatenation -> MLP predicts x_t (signal prediction). ~5.18M trainable params reported.
inputs: Single RGB image (224x224) + natural-language grasp instruction (object or part level)
outputs: 2D rectangle grasp {x, y, w, h, theta} for the referred object/part
trainingData: Grasp-Anything++: 1M Stable-Diffusion images generated from ChatGPT scene descriptions, >3M objects, >10M grasp instructions, 236 LVIS categories; grasps auto-annotated from OFA/SAM/VLPart masks and filtered by an antipodal surrogate score; no real images.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real robot (KUKA LBR iiwa R820, 20 objects, 30 runs/scenario)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds language conditioning and object-part instructions to the synthetic Grasp-Anything pipeline, and replaces regression-style grasp heads with a diffusion denoiser guided by an explicit contrastive term.
limitations: Dataset has no depth images (RGB-only, 2D rectangle grasps), creation depends on paid ChatGPT API; language-driven success rates remain low (<0.5) and failures come from misaligned text-attention maps.
notes: Grasp-Anything++ extends the earlier Grasp-Anything dataset (ICRA 2024; ~1M images, per VCoT-Grasp ~33M grasp poses). Success metric: IoU>25% and angle error <30 deg. Base/new split = 70%/30% of LVIS labels by frequency. VCoT-Grasp later reports that Grasp-Anything's automatic labels are noisy (mislabeled/distorted objects) and re-filters them. Paper venue: CVPR 2024.

keyEquations.meaning: Conditional diffusion bound split into constant, contrastive and denoising-score terms.
Approximates the intractable contrastive term; pushes estimate x~0 toward ground truth.
Signal-prediction denoising loss conditioned on the estimate x~0.
Training objective.

algorithmSteps: Encode image with ResNet-50 and instruction with CLIP/BERT
Fuse with ALBEF; take attention map as x~0 and joint embedding z*_vl
Sample x_T ~ N(0,I) over 5 grasp parameters
For t = T..1: x_{t-1} = MLP([MLP(t), MLP(z*_vl), MLP(x_t)])
Output x_0 as rectangle (x,y,w,h,theta)
Robot: lift to 6-DoF pose with depth and execute with trajectory planner
ablations: Removing x~0 prediction: H drops 0.45 -> 0.10 (Seen 0.15, Unseen 0.08)
Without contrastive loss: H 0.42 vs 0.45 with it
BERT text encoder: H 0.41 vs CLIP 0.45
hyperparams: Image 224x224, N=196 patches, M=5 grasp params, ALBEF 6 layers, l=1024, d_ts=32, d_vl=256, d_df=256; CLIP text dim 512 / BERT 768.

name: Grasp-Anything-6D
resolvedTitle: Language-Driven 6-DoF Grasp Detection Using Negative Prompt Guidance
org: FPT Software AI Center; TU Wien / AIT; Imperial College London; Physical Intelligence; University of Arkansas; Ton Duc Thang University; University of Liverpool
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Prior language-driven grasping was limited to 2D rectangles, single objects, or multi-view scenes; there was no large dataset or model for language-driven 6-DoF grasps in cluttered single-view point clouds.
keyIdea: Lift Grasp-Anything to 3D (Grasp-Anything-6D: 1M point-cloud scenes, ~200M language-associated 6-DoF grasps) and train LGrasp6D, a diffusion model over se(3)+width grasps that learns a negative prompt embedding of the unwanted objects and uses compositional (classifier-free style) guidance to steer away from them.
architecture: Denoiser: MLP grasp encoder, PointNet++ scene encoder (n_s scene tokens), frozen CLIP ViT-B/32 text encoder, sinusoidal time embedding; unified query = concat(time, grasp+text) cross-attends to scene tokens; MLP predicts noise. A side branch (scene tokens minus text embedding, averaged, MLP) outputs the negative prompt embedding t~.
inputs: Single-view 3D point cloud of cluttered scene + natural-language grasp prompt
outputs: 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasp poses (se(3) vector + width); 64 sampled per scene-prompt in evaluation
trainingData: Grasp-Anything-6D: 1M point clouds built from Grasp-Anything RGB via ZoeDepth monocular depth (55 deg FoV assumed), 2D rectangles lifted to 6-DoF (max width 202.1 mm, Robotiq 2F-140), collision/mask filtered; ~200M grasps. 80/20 train/test split.
whatChangedVsParent: Moves from 2D rectangle grasps on RGB (LGD) to 6-DoF grasps on point clouds, and replaces contrastive conditioning with learned negative-prompt guidance at sampling time.
limitations: Still fails by grasping wrong objects, colliding or mis-targeting; no part-level or task-level grasping yet, single end-effector type, and not integrated end-to-end with low-level control.
notes: Venue ECCV 2024. Model name is LGrasp6D; 'Grasp-Anything-6D' is the dataset. Real-robot cluttered success equals LGD (0.42), so the 3D advantage is mainly on vision metrics. Text says 'outperforming the next best, LGD (0.42)' though numbers tie. Ablation table on w shows w=0.2 row CR 0.6649 while main table reports 0.6694 (minor inconsistency in paper).

keyEquations.meaning: Standard DDPM noise-prediction loss conditioned on scene and prompt.
Pull learned negative embedding toward text embedding of some other object in scene.
Factorization: include target prompt, exclude negative prompt.
Guided denoising step used in reverse sampling.

algorithmSteps: Encode scene tokens (PointNet++) and prompt embedding (CLIP) once
Compute negative prompt embedding t~ from scene tokens minus prompt
Sample g_T ~ N(0,I)
At each step compute eps with no text, target text, and t~
Combine: eps(empty) + w(eps(t) - eps(t~))
DDPM update to g_{t-1}; repeat to g_0
Map se(3)+width to end-effector pose; plan and execute
ablations: Negative prompt guidance: CR 0.5459 -> 0.6694, EMD 0.6262 -> 0.4013
Guidance scale: w=0.2/0.5 best (CR 0.6649/0.6607); w=2.0 drops to 0.6372
Loss ratio zeta: 0.1 best (CR 0.6733); 0.4 drops to 0.5833; CLIP beats BERT, PointNet++ beats Point Transformer
hyperparams: T=200 linear beta 1e-4..0.02; w=0.2; p_mask=0.1; L=0.9 L_noise + 0.1 L_negative; 200 epochs, 8xA100, batch 128, Adam lr 1e-3, wd 1e-4; 512-d text/negative embeddings.

name: GraspGPT
resolvedTitle: GraspGPT: Leveraging Semantic Knowledge from a Large Language Model for Task-Oriented Grasping
org: Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech); Georgia Institute of Technology
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Task-oriented grasping methods (e.g., GCNGrasp) rely on closed-world knowledge graphs and cannot generalize to object classes or tasks outside the pre-defined concept set.
keyIdea: Query an LLM (GPT-3) for natural-language descriptions of novel object classes and tasks, and inject them via cross-attention into the instruction embedding so a grasp evaluator can relate novel concepts to ones seen in training, zero-shot.
architecture: Two-stage sample-then-evaluate: Contact-GraspNet samples task-agnostic grasps; evaluator = PointNet++ on object+gripper points (1024-d), frozen BERT-Base encoding instruction and LLM description paragraphs, a 2-layer transformer-decoder Task-Oriented Grasp Evaluator (object-description layer then task-description layer, cross-attention from instruction to descriptions), mean-pool, concat with shape embedding, MLP+sigmoid score.
inputs: Partial object point cloud (4096 pts) + candidate grasp + language instruction; LLM-generated object-class and task description paragraphs
outputs: Task-compatibility success score per grasp candidate (top-scored grasp executed)
trainingData: LA-TaskGrasp: TaskGrasp (250K task-oriented grasp annotations, 56 tasks, 75 classes, 191 instances) augmented with 6000 object-class and 2240 task description records (750 / 560 paragraphs) and 53 instruction templates (222,600 possible sentences), generated with text-davinci-003.
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces GCNGrasp's closed-world knowledge graph with open-ended LLM-generated descriptions injected by cross-attention, enabling zero-shot novel classes/tasks.
limitations: LLM descriptions are used unfiltered and can conflict (task descriptions hurt held-out class); two-stage sample-and-evaluate bound by the sampler; manipulation uses rule-based primitives and cannot model tool-target relative pose.
notes: Venue RA-L 2023. Code, data and appendix released at project site. Open-world gains over GCNGrasp: +21.84/+29.69/+39.17 mAP (held-out task), +6.78/+5.43/+5.26 (held-out class). BERT-Small/Medium/Base give similar results (task mAP 71.90/72.02/72.34). Uses LLM only offline for knowledge, not as the policy.

keyEquations.meaning: Factorized into task-agnostic grasp sampling and task-oriented grasp evaluation.
Instruction tokens attend to description paragraph tokens.
Grasp score from shape and language embeddings.
Binary cross-entropy against grasp success labels.

algorithmSteps: Segment object (SAM) and get single-view point cloud
Sample 50 grasps with Contact-GraspNet
Parse instruction; prompt LLM for descriptions of novel class/task
Encode instruction and descriptions with frozen BERT
Inject descriptions into instruction via 2 cross-attention layers
Score each grasp from PointNet++ features + instruction embedding
Execute top grasp (optionally followed by motion primitive)
ablations: No descriptions (w/o D): held-out task task-mAP 68.14 vs 72.34 full
Held-out class: object-only descriptions (w/o TD) 73.76 task mAP beats full 72.84
BERT size barely matters: task mAP 71.90 (Small) vs 72.34 (Base)
hyperparams: 4096 points; 50 grasp candidates; BERT-Base frozen; 2 TGE layers, 128-d attention; Adam lr 1e-4, wd 1e-4, batch 32, 50 epochs.

name: ThinkGrasp
resolvedTitle: ThinkGrasp: A Vision-Language System for Strategic Part Grasping in Clutter
org: Northeastern University; Boston Dynamics AI Institute
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Language-conditioned grasping systems fail in heavy clutter where the target is partly or fully occluded, and many need task-specific training data.
keyIdea: Training-free, closed-loop modular pipeline: GPT-4o reasons over the scene to pick either the goal object/part or an occluder to remove first, plus a preferred 3x3 grid cell; LangSAM/VLPart segment it, and an off-the-shelf 6-DoF grasp generator proposes grasps ranked by proximity to the preferred cell and grasp quality.
architecture: GPT-4o (high-level selection + 'imagine segmentation' + 3x3 grid region) -> LangSAM (GroundingDINO+SAM) for objects or VLPart for parts -> cropped point cloud -> GraspNet-1Billion (sim) or FGC-GraspNet (real) candidates -> score by force-closure quality and distance to preferred region -> execute; re-observe and repeat.
inputs: RGB-D observation (224x224 sim, 640x480 real) + natural-language instruction
outputs: 6-DoF parallel-jaw grasp on the selected object or object part per step (multi-step until goal grasped)
trainingData: None (zero-shot composition of pretrained GPT-4o, LangSAM, VLPart, GraspNet-1Billion/FGC-GraspNet).

headlineResults.benchmark: PyBullet heavy clutter (up to 30 unseen objects, 50 attempts)

headlineResults.metric: Step1 remove occluder / Step2 grasp target

headlineResults.benchmark: Real UR5 'I want to cut something' (knife by handle)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces trained language-grasp policies (VLG, VL-Grasp) with GPT-4o strategic reasoning plus decoupled segmentation, adding occluder removal and part-level grid targeting without training.
limitations: Single-view point clouds cause interpenetration/collisions, cannot distinguish identical objects, only grasping (no other manipulation); real failures from single-image data, low-quality downstream grasps and UR5 control variation.
notes: Venue CoRL 2024. Not a learned policy: a modular VLM-orchestrated pipeline; ~$0.01 per GPT-4o API step at 224x224. Selection formalized as o_t = argmax_o f_select(g, O^c_t, o). Top-10 closest grasps to target point are re-ranked by score. Surveys that list it as a 'grasp foundation model' should note it has no trained weights of its own.

Candidate grasps from cropped point cloud.
Force-closure grasp quality; lower friction needed = better.

GPT-4o selects goal or occluding object/part, crop box, and 3x3 preferred cell
Segment named object with LangSAM (or part with VLPart, LangSAM fallback)
Crop point cloud around all segmented instances
Generate 6-DoF grasp candidates

name: RT-Grasp
resolvedTitle: RT-Grasp: Reasoning Tuning Robotic Grasping via Multi-modal Large Language Model
org: Rutgers University; Baidu Research USA (Robotics and Autonomous Driving Lab)
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Multimodal LLMs give verbose text and cannot output precise numbers such as grasp poses, while CNN grasp detectors give fixed predictions that cannot reason about object semantics or be refined by users.
keyIdea: Reasoning Tuning: fine-tune LLaVA to emit a short category-based reasoning sentence (shape, grasp strategy) before emitting the numeric grasp (x, y, theta) as text, so predictions are grounded in LLM prior knowledge and refinable through dialogue.
architecture: LLaVA-7B-v0 (LLaMA-7B + CLIP ViT-L/14 + projection). Two training strategies: projection-only 'pre-training', or LoRA (rank 64, alpha 32) on all LLM linear layers plus projection; vision encoder and base LLM frozen.
inputs: RGB image + text instruction (optionally follow-up refinement request)
outputs: Text: reasoning phase + grasp point [x, y] (normalized) and rotation angle theta (radians); width fixed to gripper max
actionRepr: Grasp pose p={x,y,theta} generated as text tokens autoregressively
trainingData: Reasoning Tuning VLM Grasp dataset: 885 Cornell images (240 objects, 74 manual categories) augmented to 76k image-text samples; GPT-3.5-generated and manually verified per-category reasoning templates.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Franka Panda, 27 unseen household objects x5

whatChangedVsParent: Turns a general multimodal LLM into a numeric grasp predictor by inserting a reasoning phase before the numbers during instruction tuning.
limitations: Accuracy still below CNN detectors on Cornell and slightly below GR-ConvNet in the real world; single-object, planar grasps with width assumed max; validated only on Cornell-derived data.
notes: Venue IROS 2024. Rectangle metric: IoU>25% and angle <30 deg (ground-truth width used to build rectangle). Reasoning tuning improves accuracy by 8.7-26.7% vs No Reasoning-A and 1.5-14.9% vs No Reasoning-B. VCoT-Grasp later reimplements RT-Grasp on PaliGemma (non-reasoning-B setting) and argues it overweights text over vision.

keyEquations.meaning: Planar grasp: normalized center and rotation in (-pi/2, pi/2).
Autoregressive likelihood: reasoning text first, then numeric grasp tokens.

algorithmSteps: Build per-category reasoning templates with GPT-3.5, verify manually
Pair Cornell images (augmented) with instruction + reasoning + ground-truth grasp text
Train projection only, or projection + LoRA, with next-token loss
Inference: model writes reasoning sentence then numbers
Parse [x,y], theta; use max gripper width
Optionally refine via follow-up instruction (e.g., avoid metal tip)
ablations: LoRA: RT-Grasp 84.05 IW vs No Reasoning-A 58.44 and No Reasoning-B 69.15
Pre-training: 74.41 IW vs 65.70 (A) / 72.94 (B)
LoRA beats projection-only by ~10 points IW (84.05 vs 74.41)
hyperparams: LLaVA-7B-v0; pre-train batch 32 lr 2e-3; LoRA r=64, alpha=32, lr 5e-4, batch 32; 5-fold cross-validation.

name: VCoT-Grasp
resolvedTitle: VCoT-Grasp: Grasp Foundation Models with Visual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Language-driven Grasp Generation
org: Xi'an Jiaotong University; Zhejiang University; Westlake University; BAAI
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Language-driven grasp models either lack reasoning (feature fusion), rely on heavy modular LLM pipelines, or, like RT-Grasp, overemphasize text reasoning and fail in clutter and single-object settings.
keyIdea: Visual chain-of-thought: a VLM first predicts the target's bounding box, crops and resizes that region, then re-reads both the full and zoomed image in a second turn to predict the grasp rectangle.
architecture: PaliGemma2-3B (frozen SigLIP image encoder, linear projector, Gemma2 LLM). Two-turn inference; grasp decoded by LM head over 1024 discretized location tokens (best), or MLP / DiT diffusion head on dummy-token features.
inputs: RGB image (224x224 to model) + language instruction naming the target
outputs: Intermediate bounding box, then 5-D rectangle grasp [x, y, w, h, theta]
actionRepr: Grasp rectangle, each dimension discretized into 1024 tokens (reusing PaliGemma <loc> tokens)
trainingData: VCoT-GraspSet: Grasp-Anything re-filtered with YOLO-World (IoU<0.25 removed) and crowdsourced checks: >190K images at 416x416, >1.36M grasps, 388 categories (367 seen: ~186K train / ~3K test; 21 unseen ~1.5K test); plus ~450 real images of 30 objects with >1.2K grasps.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Kinova Gen3, 15 seen objects x5
Real Kinova Gen3, 15 unseen objects x5
Real robot, zero-shot (no real fine-tune), unseen objects

name: GraspVLA

org: Galbot; Peking University; The University of Hong Kong; BAAI
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: VLA models depend on costly real-world teleoperation data; whether a VLA can be trained entirely on synthetic action data and still transfer zero-shot to the real world was unexplored.
keyIdea: Pre-train a grasping VLA only on SynGrasp-1B (a billion rendered frames) and co-train with internet grounding data through Progressive Action Generation: a chain of thought that first emits a 2D bounding box, then a 3D grasp pose, then a flow-matching action chunk.
architecture: VLM: InternLM2 1.8B LLM (trainable), vision encoder fusing frozen DINOv2 + SigLIP, trainable projector; autoregressively outputs bbox tokens and grasp-pose tokens. Action expert: conditional flow-matching model attending to the VLM KV cache, outputting chunked end-effector delta actions; proprioception from the last two timesteps tokenized before grasp pose.
inputs: Two RGB views (front + side), language instruction, proprioception (last 2 steps)
outputs: 2D bbox tokens, grasp pose in robot base frame (synthetic data), chunk of end-effector delta actions + discrete gripper open/close

name: DexGraspNet
resolvedTitle: DexGraspNet: A Large-Scale Robotic Dexterous Grasp Dataset for General Objects Based on Simulation
org: Peking University (PKU-EPIC), BIGAI, Tsinghua University
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Dexterous grasping lacked a large-scale dataset: the only robotic-hand dataset (DDG, 6.9K grasps on 565 objects, from GraspIt!) was small and low-diversity, and the differentiable force-closure synthesis of Liu et al. [19] was too slow, low-yield and mesh-sensitive to scale.
keyIdea: Accelerate and robustify differentiable force-closure grasp optimization (better initialization, reverse penetration energy, self-penetration and joint-limit terms, plain gradient descent) and validate every grasp in Isaac Gym, producing 1.32M ShadowHand grasps on 5355 objects.
architecture: Not a policy: an optimization-based synthesis pipeline. Energy over grasp tuple (T, R, theta, contact points x) minimized with gradient descent; signed distances via modified Kaolin (replacing DeepSDF); grasps filtered by Isaac Gym (PhysX) physics validation.
inputs: Object mesh (normalized, 5 scales, remeshed watertight; CoACD collision mesh); hand URDF
outputs: Static grasp poses g = (T, R, theta) for ShadowHand (22 joint angles), plus variants for MANO and Allegro
trainingData: Objects: 3980 from ShapeNetCore/ShapeNetSem (133 categories) + 1375 scanned (YCB, BigBIRD, Grasp, KIT, Google Scanned Objects) = 5355 objects; output 1.32M grasps, >200 per object
parents: Differentiable force closure grasp synthesis (Liu et al. 2021)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces random init + MALA with convex-hull-based open-hand initialization + gradient descent, uses reverse (object-to-hand) penetration energy and adds self-penetration/joint-limit energies, giving ~50x speedup and robustness to thin meshes.
limitations: Optimization pulls all contact candidates to the surface, so grasps are almost always contact-rich power grasps; precision grasps rarely appear, and without semantic guidance it cannot produce functional grasps (e.g., mug by handle).
notes: Released dataset and generation code (incl. MANO and Allegro synthesis). Speedup detail: 10,000 valid grasps went from 400 GPU hours to 7 GPU hours; ~18% of optimized grasps valid vs ~3% for [19]; converges in <6000 iterations vs 10000. Benchmark validity criterion (1 of 6 gravity directions, pen<5mm) is looser than the dataset filter (all 6 directions, pen<=0.1cm). Existing learners (DDG, GraspTTA) cannot match both its diversity and a high success rate. Dex1B later reports ~90% of DexGraspNet grasps would collide with a table (free-floating setting).

keyEquations.meaning: Differentiable force-closure: contact normals must be able to cancel net wrench.

keyEquations.tex: E_{dis} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} d(x_i, O), \quad E_{pen} = \sum_{v \in S(H)} [v \in O]\, d(v, O)
keyEquations.meaning: Attraction of contacts to object surface and penetration penalty (DexGraspNet reverses it: object points vs hand mesh).

symbols.meaning: surface point cloud of hand mesh H

keyEquations.tex: E_{spen} = \sum_{p \in P(H)} \sum_{q \in P(H)} [p \neq q] \max(\delta - d(p,q), 0), \quad E_{joints} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \left(\max(\theta_i - \theta_i^{max}, 0) + \max(\theta_i^{min} - \theta_i, 0)\right)
keyEquations.meaning: New self-penetration and joint-limit penalties.

keyEquations.tex: E = E_{fc} + w_{dis}E_{dis} + w_{pen}E_{pen} + w_{spen}E_{spen} + w_{joints}E_{joints}
keyEquations.meaning: Total energy minimized by gradient descent; w_dis=100, w_pen=100, w_spen=10, w_joints=1.

edges: keep if holds under 6 gravity dirs & pen<=0.1cm

algorithmSteps: Normalize object to unit sphere, scale to 5 sizes, remesh watertight, build CoACD collision mesh
Jitter canonical open hand pose; sample point on convex hull inflated by 0.2m; orient palm toward nearest object point with cone jitter
Sample n=4 contact points from 140 hand contact candidates each iteration
Minimize E_fc + weighted E_dis, E_pen (reverse), E_spen, E_joints by gradient descent (<6000 iters)
Validate in Isaac Gym: squeeze contact links along normals, apply gravity in 6 axis directions for 100 steps
Keep grasps that stay in contact in all 6 directions and penetrate <=0.1cm
ablations: Throughput: 10,000 grasps x 6000 steps in 74 min on A100 with ~18% valid, vs original [19] 512 grasps x 10000 steps in 37 min on 3090 with ~3% valid
Training DDG on DexGraspNet vs DDGdata lowers max penetration on DexGraspNet test set from 0.353 to 0.173 cm
GraspTTA trained on DexGraspNet: success 24.5% vs 17.1% on DexGraspNet test set
hyperparams: n=4 contact points from 140 candidates; w_dis=100, w_pen=100, w_spen=10, w_joints=1; delta=1cm sphere radius; <6000 GD iterations; convex hull inflated by 0.2m; validation 100 sim steps x 6 gravity directions, max pen 0.1cm

name: Dex1B
resolvedTitle: Dex1B: Learning with 1B Demonstrations for Dexterous Manipulation
org: UC San Diego (Xiaolong Wang lab)
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models
problem: Dexterous demonstration sources are each limited: human demos are costly and imprecise, optimization is slow and init-sensitive, RL lacks diversity, and generative models produce infeasible samples and merely interpolate the training distribution.
keyIdea: An iterative data engine: optimize a small high-quality seed set, train a geometry-aware CVAE (DexSimple) to propose far more demonstrations, post-optimize, filter in simulation, debias by sampling under-represented object points, retrain, and repeat up to ~1B demonstrations for grasping and articulation.
architecture: DexSimple: CVAE with MLP encoder/decoder (layers 256-512-256, latent 256) conditioned on a PointNet object feature (256-d) and optionally on a local point feature for debiasing; trained with reconstruction, KL, sphere-point SDF and distance losses. Seed generation uses Warp-accelerated energy optimization with sphere-approximated hand links; motion planning by smoothness+SDF optimization.
inputs: Object point cloud (full mesh samples for data generation; single-view depth for deployment); optional hand root rotation/translation/joint conditions; optional 3D point condition
outputs: Hand pose trajectory (N_frame x N_DOF) for grasp-and-lift or articulation
actionRepr: CVAE-sampled hand pose sequence of N_frames x N_DOF (key-frame grasp + planned reach/lift or articulation trajectory); executed open-loop
trainingData: Dex1B: ~1B (950M successful) demonstrations; grasping on DexGraspNet's 5751 object assets (tabletop-stable subset; 3,491 train / 933 test in lifting), articulation on 650+ assets from DexArt and ManiSkill (43 train / 21 test); three hands (Shadow, Inspire, Ability); seed 5M -> 50M -> 500M -> 950M
whatChangedVsParent: Moves from pure optimization (DexGraspNet) to an optimization-seeded generative loop with SDF-constrained CVAE, simulation filtering and debiased conditional sampling, scaling from 1.32M static grasps to ~1B full trajectories incl. articulation.
limitations: Real-world deployment is open-loop and thus sensitive to sim-to-real, control and observation errors; simulation filtering remains a runtime bottleneck; only single-object scenes are considered.
notes: Real-world (from paper text via alphaXiv report, not re-verified in the page extract): direct sim-to-real on xArm+Ability Hand and Unitree H1+Inspire Hand, 96% success on 10 unseen objects vs retrained DexDiffuser 58%. Their pure-optimization grasp generator is 30x faster than DexGraspNet (2 min for 2000 grasps x 6000 steps on one RTX 3090, 27% vs 20% success) and ~700x faster with network initialization (CVAE + 100 post-opt steps). Without post-opt/filter DexSimple SR 63.7 is slightly below regression-based DDG 67.5 but with much higher diversity (8.53 vs 5.68). Appendix notes the DexGraspNet entropy uses 10000 bins and prior papers' descriptions were inaccurate (DexGraspNet text says 100 bins). Baseline BC w. PointNet predicts 50-frame action chunks merged with ACT temporal weighting.

keyEquations.meaning: CVAE over hand poses conditioned on PointNet object feature.

symbols.meaning: hand pose (T, R, theta) or trajectory

keyEquations.meaning: Point-sphere penetration loss: object points must stay outside hand spheres.
DexSimple base training loss (plus distance loss L_D in full model).

keyEquations.meaning: Light post-optimization of sampled poses (100 steps), dropping force-closure/wrench terms.

algorithmSteps: Generate ~5M seed demos by Warp-accelerated energy optimization (force closure for grasping, task-wrench-space for articulation) and verify in simulation
Train DexSimple CVAE with reconstruction, KL, point-sphere SDF and distance losses
Sample ~10x more hand poses, conditioning on object points inversely proportional to their frequency in the current dataset
Post-optimize each pose with E_post for ~100 steps
Plan reach trajectory (smoothness + SDF), then lift or rotate/translate along joint axis

Retrain DexSimple on enlarged set; repeat 5M -> 50M -> 500M -> 950M

Removing distance loss L_D drops success to 42.0% and Q1 from 0.075 to 0.044
Both losses barely change diversity (H mean 8.53-8.65)

name: DAPG (Rajeswaran)
resolvedTitle: Learning Complex Dexterous Manipulation with Deep Reinforcement Learning and Demonstrations
org: University of Washington, OpenAI, UC Berkeley, IIT
problem: Model-free deep RL had not been shown to scale to high-dimensional (24-DoF) dexterous hands, needed laborious reward shaping, was too sample-inefficient for hardware, and produced unnatural, brittle behaviors.
keyIdea: Demo Augmented Policy Gradient: initialize with behavior cloning on ~25 VR demonstrations, then fine-tune with natural policy gradient using an augmented gradient that adds a decaying demonstration log-likelihood term, learning from sparse rewards.
architecture: Gaussian MLP policy trained with Natural Policy Gradient (Fisher-preconditioned, normalized step) in MuJoCo; ADROIT 24-DoF anthropomorphic hand; demos collected with MuJoCo HAPTIX VR (CyberGlove III + HTC Vive).
inputs: Low-dimensional state: hand joint angles, object pose, target information
outputs: Desired joint positions for the ADROIT hand (position control)
actionRepr: Single-step continuous 24-DoF desired joint positions from a stochastic Gaussian policy
trainingData: 25 successful human VR demonstrations per task + on-policy RL rollouts (each iteration 200 trajectories of 2 s) in 4 MuJoCo tasks: object relocation, in-hand pen reorientation, door opening, hammer

headlineResults.comparedTo: 98 (NPG shaped reward); never with sparse reward

whatChangedVsParent: Adds BC pretraining and a decaying demonstration term to the NPG gradient so on-policy RL can learn 24-DoF dexterous tasks from sparse rewards ~30x faster than shaped-reward NPG.
limitations: All results are in simulation; success on real hardware remains to be demonstrated. Future work named: learning on real hardware, novelty-based exploration, learning from raw vision and touch.
notes: Paper states models and code are released (sites.google.com/view/deeprl-dexterous-manipulation); the task suite became the ADROIT/D4RL hand benchmarks. DDPG and DDPGfD failed to make progress on these tasks. DAPG policies were more robust to object mass/size variation than shaped-reward NPG and could learn on an ensemble of environments where RL from scratch failed. BC alone was usually unsuccessful due to distribution shift.

keyEquations.meaning: Normalized natural policy gradient step.
Behavior cloning pretraining on demonstrations.
Augmented gradient mixing RL advantage and weighted demo likelihood.
Heuristic demo weight decaying with iteration k.

algorithmSteps: Collect 25 demonstrations per task in VR with MuJoCo HAPTIX
Pretrain policy by maximum-likelihood behavior cloning
Roll out current policy (200 trajectories of 2 s per iteration) with sparse task reward
Estimate advantages on policy data
Form g_aug with demo term weighted by lambda0*lambda1^k*max advantage
Apply normalized NPG update with Fisher preconditioning; repeat
ablations: NPG/DDPG with sparse rewards never succeed (except pen); DDPG fails even with shaped rewards
Pen task: DAPG 30 iterations (3.33 h) vs NPG sparse 2900 iterations (322 h)
BC alone usually fails; BC init + NPG helps but DAPG's augmented loss is best (Fig. 10)
hyperparams: lambda0=0.1, lambda1=0.95; 25 demos/task; 200 trajectories of 2 s per NPG iteration; success scored on 100 trajectories

name: PDDM
resolvedTitle: Deep Dynamics Models for Learning Dexterous Manipulation
org: Google Brain
problem: Model-free RL for dexterous hands needs huge data and yields task-specific policies, while prior model-based RL had not scaled to high-DoF, contact-rich fine-motor tasks.
keyIdea: Online Planning with Deep Dynamics Models: learn an ensemble of neural dynamics models and plan with MPC using an MPPI-style reward-weighted update over temporally filtered (smoothed) action samples, replanning every step.
architecture: Ensemble of E=3 MLP dynamics models (2 hidden layers x 500, ReLU) predicting state deltas, trained with MSE; MPC planner with filtering + reward-weighted refinement; real-world ball tracking via KeypointNet-style dilated CNN on stereo RGB.
inputs: Low-dimensional state (joint positions, object positions/orientations; e.g., 40-d for Baoding) and task reward function
outputs: Joint position commands for the hand
actionRepr: MPC: optimize H=7-step action sequence (normalized to [-1,1]) and execute only the first action each step
trainingData: Self-collected on-policy interaction data only (no demos, no sim for real hardware): ~1-2 h per simulated task (Baoding sim 100,000 datapoints ~2.7 h); ~4 h real-world Shadow Hand data
controlRateHz: 10 (real Shadow Hand planner; 1 kHz low-level PD)

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Shadow Hand Baoding balls, 90 deg
Real Shadow Hand Baoding balls, 180 deg

headlineResults.comparedTo: SAC, NPG, MBPO, PETS, Nagabandi et al. did not succeed

whatChangedVsParent: Combines PETS-style ensembles with an MPPI-style soft reward-weighted update and temporally correlated (filtered) action noise instead of random shooting/CEM, scaling model-based RL to 24-DoF hands.
limitations: Planning is short-horizon so sparse-reward or long-horizon tasks need planning at other abstraction levels; models use low-dimensional state only, and integrating vision and touch is left to future work.
notes: Tasks: valve turning (9-DoF D'Claw), in-hand cube reorientation, handwriting, Baoding balls (24-DoF Shadow Hand). With 8 goal angles for reorientation, model-free methods stall while PDDM keeps working because it models interactions rather than goal-specific trajectories. The Baoding model trained on 100-step rollouts runs for 1000 steps at test time and can be repurposed (single ball, clockwise) without retraining. Real setup: Franka arm auto-reset; tracker ~5 mm error, 20 ms latency. General knowledge (not from paper): code released as google-research/pddm.

keyEquations.meaning: Gaussian dynamics model whose mean is a neural network; ensemble of E models.

keyEquations.tex: \mu_t = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{N} e^{\gamma R_k} a_t^{(k)}}{\sum_{j=0}^{N} e^{\gamma R_j}} \quad \forall t \in \{0 \dots H-1\}
keyEquations.meaning: Reward-weighted soft update of mean action sequence.

symbols.meaning: ensemble-mean predicted return of sample k

keyEquations.tex: u_t^i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma), \quad n_t^i = \beta u_t^i + (1-\beta) n_{t-1}^i, \quad a_t^i = n_t^i + \mu_t
keyEquations.meaning: Temporally filtered noise produces smooth candidate action sequences.

symbols.meaning: current mean action at step t

algorithmSteps: Randomly initialize ensemble of dynamics models; empty dataset
At each step, sample N action sequences of length H with filtered noise around mean mu
Predict each sequence with every ensemble member; score by mean predicted reward
Update mean with exponential reward weighting (gamma)
Execute first action, observe next state, append transition to D; replan
After R rollouts, train models on D for E epochs; repeat
ablations: Model size: 2x500 hidden layers needed; 2x64 performs much worse on Baoding
Horizon: intermediate H=7 best; H=2 greedy and H=15 suffers compounding error
Controller: filtering + reward weighting greatly beats CEM and random shooting; medium gamma best
hyperparams: Ensemble M=3; MLP 2x500 ReLU; Adam lr 1e-3, batch 500; H=7; Baoding N=700, gamma=20, beta=0.7; reorientation N=700, gamma=50, beta=0.7; valve N=200, gamma=10, beta=0.6; handwriting gamma=0.5, beta=0.5; dt 0.1 s for Shadow Hand tasks

name: Learning dexterous in-hand manipulation (Dactyl)
resolvedTitle: Learning Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
org: OpenAI
problem: Vision-based in-hand object reorientation on a real 24-DoF Shadow Hand was out of reach: real-world RL is too sample-hungry and sim-trained policies failed to cross the reality gap.
keyIdea: Train an LSTM policy with large-scale distributed PPO entirely in a heavily domain-randomized MuJoCo simulation (physics, unmodeled effects, noise) plus a CNN pose estimator trained only on randomized Unity renders, then deploy zero-shot on the real hand.
architecture: Policy and value nets: normalization + dense 1024 ReLU layer + LSTM 512, separate weights; asymmetric actor-critic (critic sees privileged state). Vision: 3-camera CNN (2 conv, max-pool, 4 ResNet blocks, spatial softmax, shared weights) regressing object position and orientation. Trained on OpenAI's Rapid distributed RL system (same as OpenAI Five).
inputs: Policy: fingertip positions (15D), object position (3D), relative target orientation (4D quaternion) from PhaseSpace mocap or vision CNN (3 RGB cameras)
outputs: Relative desired joint-angle changes for 20 actuated joints
actionRepr: 20-D discrete action, 11 bins per coordinate, relative joint targets, EMA-smoothed (coefficient 0.3 per 80 ms), one action per 80 ms step
trainingData: Pure simulation, no demonstrations: ~100 years of simulated experience (~50 h wall-clock) for fully randomized env; vision CNN on 1M simulated states rendered with randomized appearance
controlRateHz: ~12 (80 ms per policy step; low-level PD ~1 kHz)
parents: Domain randomization (Tobin et al.; Peng et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Scales domain randomization with memory-based policies and massive distributed PPO to achieve the first sim-to-real vision-based in-hand reorientation on a 24-DoF anthropomorphic hand.
limitations: A clear reality gap remains (real median 13 vs sim 50); failures from dropping when rotating the wrist downward and objects snagging on screw holes; frequent hardware breakage; sphere manipulation failed and a unified multi-object policy was left to future work.
notes: Reward: r_t = d_t - d_{t+1}, +5 on goal (0.4 rad tolerance), -20 on drop. Episode ends after 50 consecutive goals, 8 s without reaching a goal (sim) or a drop; physical evaluation timeout 80 s. Discrete actions worked much better than Gaussian. LSTM hidden state after 5 s predicts whether the block is larger/smaller than average in 80% of cases. Emergent grasps: tripod, palmar pinch, tip pinch, quadpod, 5-finger precision, power; policy favors little finger (extra DoF). Vision errors: 2.71 deg / 3.12 mm on Unity renders, 5.01 deg / 9.27 mm on real images (from alphaXiv report). Scaling: 8 GPU/6144 cores was 5.5x faster than 1 GPU/768 cores to 20 consecutive goals (from report). Surveys often call this 'Dactyl'; the paper itself does not use that name in the title.

symbols.meaning: rotation angle between desired and current object orientation

keyEquations.meaning: Clipped PPO objective used to train the LSTM policy.

algorithmSteps: Calibrate MuJoCo Shadow Hand model (264 parameters) against recorded real trajectories
Each episode sample physics randomizations, unmodeled effects (backlash, delays, random forces), and observation/action noise
Collect experience with distributed workers running the LSTM policy; critic receives privileged state
Optimize PPO on 8 GPUs until robust across randomizations (~100 simulated years)
Train vision CNN on 1M simulated states rendered with randomized appearance
Deploy: CNN (or PhaseSpace) pose + fingertips -> LSTM policy -> EMA-smoothed relative joint targets

Observation noise matters with vision: median drops 11.5 -> 3.5 without it (state: 13 -> 8.5)

name: DeXtreme
resolvedTitle: DeXtreme: Transfer of Agile In-hand Manipulation from Simulation to Reality
org: NVIDIA (with University of Toronto, USC, Snap)
problem: OpenAI's in-hand reorientation results relied on an expensive Shadow Hand, marker-based motion capture and large CPU clusters, making them hard to reproduce; few others had shown sim-to-real transfer for this task.
keyIdea: Train LSTM PPO policies for an affordable Allegro Hand in GPU-parallel Isaac Gym with vectorized Automatic Domain Randomization (VADR), random network adversary and pose injection, and pair them with a keypoint-based pose estimator trained on 5M synthetic Replicator images from three RGB cameras.
architecture: Actor: LSTM 1024 (layer norm) + MLP 512-512 (ELU); critic: LSTM 2048 + MLP 1024-512 with privileged 265-D input (asymmetric actor-critic). Perception: Mask-RCNN-style network predicting bbox, mask and 8 cube-corner keypoints per camera, followed by PnP, consistency filtering, triangulation and model registration.
inputs: Policy (50-D): noisy object position and orientation, target pose, relative target orientation, last actions, 16 hand joint angles; object pose from 3 Intel D415 RGB cameras
outputs: PD position targets for the 16 Allegro joints

limitations: Noticeable sim-to-real gap remains (manual DR ~35 consecutive successes in sim vs ~15 real); ADR policies do not consistently reach OpenAI ADR(XXL) levels; pose estimation still has a sim-to-real gap, preventing easy physics calibration of the cube; VADR does not model joint distributions over parameters.
notes: Reward (Table 2): 1/(d+0.1) weight 1.0; object-to-target position distance weight -10; action penalty -0.001; action delta -0.25; joint velocity -0.003; +250 goal bonus when d<0.1. Training reaches goal at 0.1 rad but testing uses 0.4 rad. Discount 0.998 essential for LSTM training. From alphaXiv report (not re-verified in extracted pages): 700K frames/s on 8 A40 GPUs; median consecutive successes 26.6 for best policy; comparisons to OpenAI 2019 ADR(XL) state-based mean 16.0 and ADR(XXL) mean 32. Paper page 13: manual DR takes ~24 hours to reach average 35 consecutive successes in sim. Hardware quirks: Allegro fragile, works even with partially malfunctioning thumb; best npd ~ -0.2. Real-world max streak progression (Appendix A.5): 10 (manual DR) -> 43 (pose injection + RNA) -> 70 (ADR) -> 112 (ADR + deeper nets).

keyEquations.meaning: Nats per dimension: average entropy of ADR ranges, a proxy for randomization amount.
Random network adversary actions blended into policy actions; alpha set by ADR.

keyEquations.tex: pose_{obs} = pose \cdot (1 - m) + random\_pose \cdot m, \quad m \sim \mathrm{Bern}(p)

algorithmSteps: Initialize DR ranges from calibration/best guesses; run thousands of Isaac Gym envs per GPU
Dedicate 40% of envs to evaluate one ADR bound at a time; queue consecutive-success counts (N=256)
Widen a bound if mean successes > 20, tighten if < 5; clear queue on change
Train LSTM actor-critic with PPO under physics, noise, latency, RNA and pose-injection randomizations
Train keypoint pose network on 5M randomized synthetic images; mine hard real configurations and re-render
Deploy: 3-camera keypoints -> PnP/filter/triangulate -> pose at 15 Hz -> policy at 30 Hz -> EMA 0.1 -> Allegro PD
ablations: ADR vs manual DR on hardware: mean consecutive successes 27.8 vs 14.8 (from report); ADR better at recovering from stuck states
Real max streak rose 20 -> 31 with larger networks, -> 43 with random pose injection + RNA, -> 112 with ADR + deeper networks
Real-world best EMA 0.1 balanced agility vs hardware safety
