name: Variational Integrator Networks
resolvedTitle: Variational Integrator Networks for Physically Structured Embeddings
org: Imperial College London; Microsoft Research; University College London
problem: Black-box networks and Euler-discretized ResNets/neural ODEs do not conserve physical quantities, harming long-term prediction; loss-based physics priors (HNN, DeLaN, PINN) need data covering configuration space.
keyIdea: Build the network architecture from a structure-preserving variational (symplectic) integrator of a learned Lagrangian, so the latent embedding is itself a physical dynamical system that conserves momentum/energy by construction.
architecture: Residual-like network whose layers follow Stormer-Verlet or velocity-Verlet updates with learned potential U_theta (single-hidden-layer MLP) and optional learned mass matrix; Lie-group (SO(2)) variant for rotations; embedded in a VAE (MLP encoder + LSTM for initial condition, MLP decoder) for pixel observations.
inputs: Noisy position/velocity observations, or 28x28 pixel image sequences
outputs: Future latent states q_t (and p_t); decoded images in the VAE setting
trainingData: Ideal pendulum and mass-spring: 25 trajectories (750 points) or 5 trajectories (150 points) with noise sigma 0.1; pixel setting 6 s at 10 Hz (60 images) split into 1 s windows
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces the Euler discretization of neural ODEs with a symplectic variational integrator derived from Euler-Lagrange equations, enforcing conservation architecturally rather than via loss.
limitations: Only time-invariant Lagrangians studied; evaluated on simple systems (pendulum, mass-spring); mass matrix not identifiable from pixels; VIN-VV drifts out of phase around 15-20 s.
notes: AISTATS 2020. Code on GitHub (steindoringi/Variational_Integrator_Networks). Authors suggest robotics/RL as future application.

keyEquations.meaning: Separable Newtonian learned Lagrangian
Stormer-Verlet network layer (VIN-SV)

keyEquations.tex: q_{t+1} = q_t + hM_\theta^{-1}\dot q_t - \frac{h^2}{2}M_\theta^{-1}\frac{\partial U_\theta(q_t)}{\partial q_t},\; p_{t+1} = p_t - \frac{h}{2}\left(\frac{\partial U_\theta(q_t)}{\partial q_t}+\frac{\partial U_\theta(q_{t+1})}{\partial q_{t+1}}\right)
keyEquations.meaning: Velocity-Verlet network layer (VIN-VV)

algorithmSteps: Encode observed sequence to posterior over initial latent state
Sample initial condition
Propagate through stacked variational-integrator layers using learned potential/mass
Decode each latent state to observation
Maximize ELBO jointly over encoder, dynamics, decoder
At test time roll out integrator arbitrarily far and decode
ablations: Low-data (5 trajectories): HNN overfits noise and mispredicts; VIN outperforms HNN and NN in both low and moderate data
ResRNN latent spirals away from initial condition while VINs stay on a bounded submanifold
VIN-SO(2) improves log-likelihood over VIN-VV (-3.2 vs -13.4 x10^2); RMSE inconclusive
hyperparams: Network depth 10 (1 s windows at 10 Hz), latent step size 1.0, dynamics MLP 1000 tanh units (pixels) / 200 tanh units (noisy obs), Adam lr 3e-4 (VAE) / 1e-3

name: PINN (Raissi)
resolvedTitle: Physics Informed Deep Learning (Part I): Data-driven Solutions of Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
org: Brown University; University of Pennsylvania
problem: Solving and identifying nonlinear PDEs from small, noisy data; Gaussian-process approaches need prior assumptions/linearization and are brittle for nonlinear problems.
keyIdea: Approximate the PDE solution u(t,x) with a neural net and penalize the PDE residual f = u_t + N[u], computed by automatic differentiation at collocation points, in addition to data fit.
architecture: Fully connected tanh MLP u(t,x); physics-informed network f(t,x) obtained by autodiff of u. Discrete-time variant: multi-output net predicting all q implicit Runge-Kutta stages.
inputs: Space-time coordinates (t, x)
outputs: Solution value u(t,x) (or RK stage values in discrete-time model)
trainingData: Burgers: N_u=100 initial/boundary points + N_f=10,000 collocation points (Latin hypercube); Schrodinger: N_0=50, N_b=50, N_f=20,000

headlineResults.comparedTo: ~2 orders of magnitude lower than prior GP work

headlineResults.benchmark: Burgers (discrete time, 500-stage IRK, single step t=0.1->0.9)

parents: Gaussian-process PDE solvers (numerical GPs, hidden physics models)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces GP priors with deep nets and enforces the PDE as a soft residual loss at collocation points via autodiff.
limitations: Continuous-time models need many collocation points, growing exponentially in high dimensions; no convergence guarantee to global minimum; uncertainty quantification not captured; not a replacement for classical solvers.
notes: Name ambiguity: the widely cited PINN paper is the 2019 J. Comput. Phys. article combining Part I (1711.10561) and Part II (1711.10566, data-driven discovery). This card reads Part I. Code: github.com/maziarraissi/PINNs.

keyEquations.meaning: PDE residual network obtained by autodiff of the solution network
Data loss on initial/boundary points plus physics residual at collocation points

algorithmSteps: Sample N_u initial/boundary data and N_f collocation points (Latin hypercube)
Define u(t,x) as MLP
Compute PDE residual f by autodiff
Minimize MSE_u + MSE_f with full-batch L-BFGS
Evaluate u anywhere in domain (mesh-free)
ablations: N_f=0 is a plain NN; accuracy improves with N_u given sufficient N_f (e.g. N_u=100, N_f=10000: 6.7e-4)
Deeper/wider nets reduce error (2 layers x 10 neurons 7.4e-2 vs 8 x 40: 5.6e-4)
Low RK stage counts (q=1,2) fail for dt>0.2; q>=32 resolves Burgers in a single dt=0.8 step
hyperparams: Burgers: 9 layers x 20 tanh neurons, L-BFGS; Schrodinger: 5 layers x 100 neurons; discrete-time Burgers: 4 x 50, q=500 IRK stages, dt=0.8

name: SINDy
resolvedTitle: Discovering governing equations from data: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems
org: University of Washington; Institute for Disease Modeling
problem: Symbolic regression for discovering governing equations is expensive, scales poorly and can overfit; classical system ID assumes model form and is mostly linear.
keyIdea: Assume dynamics are sparse in a library of candidate nonlinear functions and use sparse regression (sequentially thresholded least squares) to select the few active terms, giving parsimonious interpretable equations.
architecture: Not a neural net: build library Theta(X) (constant, polynomial, trigonometric terms) from state snapshots; solve Xdot = Theta(X) Xi with sparsity-promoting regression; cross-validate lambda on the Pareto front. Extensions: discrete-time, high-dimensional (POD reduction), parameterized, forced/controlled systems.
inputs: Time history of states X and derivatives Xdot (or finite-differenced / TV-regularized)
outputs: Sparse coefficient matrix Xi defining symbolic ODEs xdot = f(x)
trainingData: Simulated canonical systems: damped oscillators, Lorenz, fluid wake behind cylinder (DNS, POD modes), logistic map, Hopf normal form

headlineResults.value: correct terms at eta=0.01 and eta=10 noise

headlineResults.comparedTo: took the community ~30 years to resolve

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces combinatorial genetic-programming search with convex/thresholded sparse regression over a fixed function library.
limitations: Relies on choosing good coordinates and a library that contains the true terms; noisy derivatives may require filtering; when noise is too large structure identification fails.
notes: PNAS 2016. Classic system-ID baseline; SINDy with control (SINDYc) extends to forced systems. Not a policy.

keyEquations.meaning: Derivatives expressed as sparse combination of candidate library functions
LASSO sparse regression; paper mainly uses sequential thresholded least squares
Identified symbolic model

algorithmSteps: Collect states X and derivatives Xdot (denoise if needed)
Build library Theta(X)
Least-squares initial Xi
Zero coefficients with |Xi| < lambda
Re-regress on remaining terms; repeat until converged (~10 iters)
Select lambda by cross-validation at Pareto elbow
ablations: Lorenz: correct terms identified for noise eta=0.01 and eta=10; error grows with eta but attractor preserved
hyperparams: Single sparsity knob lambda; polynomial library up to 5th order in examples; 10 thresholding iterations

name: Port-Hamiltonian on SE(3) (Duong & Atanasov)
resolvedTitle: Port-Hamiltonian Neural ODE Networks on Lie Groups For Robot Dynamics Learning and Control
org: University of California San Diego
problem: Hand-designed robot models are inaccurate, black-box learned models need lots of data and violate energy conservation and Lie-group (SE(3)) kinematic constraints; prior Hamiltonian nets used vector states and ignored dissipation.
keyIdea: Structure a neural ODE as port-Hamiltonian dynamics on a matrix Lie group, learning mass, potential, dissipation and input matrices, then design an energy-shaping/damping-injection (IDA-PBC) tracking controller directly from the learned model.
architecture: Five MLPs learn inverse mass blocks M_v^-1(q), M_w^-1(q) (via Cholesky + epsilon I for positive definiteness), potential V(q), dissipation D(q,p) (Cholesky), and input matrix B(q), optionally added to nominal values; integrated by a neural ODE solver on vectorized SE(3) states.
inputs: State-control trajectories: pose q in SE(3) (position + rotation), twist zeta, control u (thrust/torques)
outputs: Predicted state trajectories; control input u from IDA-PBC controller
trainingData: Pendulum: D=5120 trajectories (N=5, 0.05 s); PyBullet Crazyflie: 18 trajectories, D=1080; real PX4 quadrotor: 12 trajectories, D=10000

headlineResults.benchmark: Real quadrotor with payload after 100-step update

parents: Hamiltonian-based Neural ODE Networks on SE(3) (Duong & Atanasov, RSS 2021)
whatChangedVsParent: Generalizes their earlier SE(3) Hamiltonian neural ODE to general matrix Lie groups and port-Hamiltonian form with a learned dissipation term (friction/drag) compensated in the tracking controller.
limitations: Single rigid body only; future work needed for multi-rigid-body dynamics, contact, and online adaptation; Lie-group neural ODE training not used due to lack of open-source Lie-group integrators (embedding in R^{nxn} instead).
notes: IEEE T-RO 2024. Code/videos at thaipduong.github.io/LieGroupHamDL. Name in batch says 'Port-Hamiltonian on SE(3)'; the earlier RSS 2021 paper (arXiv 2106.12782) is the Hamiltonian (non-port) SE(3) version without dissipation. Momentum scale-invariance: learned M, V, D, B identifiable only up to a common factor beta.

keyEquations.tex: \begin{bmatrix}\dot q\\ \dot p\end{bmatrix} = (\mathcal{J}(q,p) - \mathcal{R}(q,p))\begin{bmatrix}\partial H/\partial q\\ \partial H/\partial p\end{bmatrix} + G(q,p)u
keyEquations.meaning: Port-Hamiltonian dynamics: energy storage, dissipation, and control input ports
Structured Hamiltonian with learned inverse mass and potential
Training loss on orientation (Lie log), position and twist
IDA-PBC: inject energy so desired Hamiltonian has minimum at target / tracking error zero

algorithmSteps: Collect state-control trajectories (e.g. PID flights to random poses)
Parameterize M^-1, V, D, B as MLPs (+ nominal priors), Cholesky for PD
Roll out port-Hamiltonian dynamics with neural ODE (zero-order-hold u)
Minimize SO(3)-log, position and twist loss
Construct desired Hamiltonian on tracking error and match via control law u = B^dagger(...)
Track trajectory; fine-tune model quickly (100 steps) if dynamics change
ablations: Structured vs unstructured Hamiltonian vs black-box (pendulum): training loss 2.3e-7 vs 6.3e-5 vs 0.037; energy std 0.003 vs 0.163 vs 13557
Quadrotor: black-box violates SO(3) constraints (||RR^T - I|| avg 29336.7) vs 1.3e-6 structured
Payload update: 100 fine-tuning steps improve tracking 1.5-4x over previously learned model
hyperparams: eps_v = eps_w = 0.01; horizon N=5 (sim) / N=1 (real); real PX4 nets 4x20 tanh; PyBullet nets 400-unit tanh; 5000 iterations (pendulum, real), 500 (Crazyflie)

controlRateHz: 100 (state estimate and MPC solve per new estimate)
name: Neural SDE (Djeumou)
resolvedTitle: How to Learn and Generalize From Three Minutes of Data: Physics-Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Neural Stochastic Differential Equations
org: University of Texas at Austin (Center for Autonomy)
problem: Physics-constrained learned dynamics models (neural ODEs, Lagrangian/Hamiltonian nets) are deterministic and cannot estimate their own uncertainty, which model-based RL/MPC needs to avoid model exploitation; ensembles ignore physics and cost multiple models.
keyIdea: Learn a neural SDE whose drift composes known physics with learned unknown terms and whose diffusion is a distance-aware uncertainty estimate: minimal near training data (zero-gradient + local strong convexity losses) and saturating at a maximum far from it.
architecture: Drift f_theta = F(x,u,g_theta1..g_thetad) with known differentiable F (e.g., 6-DoF rigid-body equations) and small MLP unknowns (residual forces/moments, motor map, mass, inertia); diffusion Sigma = Sigma_max * h_phi(eta_psi(x,u)) with eta_psi a sigmoid MLP (2x32 swish) and mu_zeta MLP for convexity constants; integrated with Euler-Maruyama / Milstein.
inputs: State x and control input u (hexacopter: position, velocity, quaternion, body rates; motor commands)
outputs: Sampled future state trajectories (distribution); used in MPC or as offline RL simulator
trainingData: Hexacopter: 3 manually flown trajectories, 203 s total at 100 Hz; spring-mass-damper: 5 noisy 5 s trajectories; cartpole: 100 trajectories x 200 steps (random or PPO on-policy)

headlineResults.benchmark: Real hexacopter lemniscate tracking (MPC + neural SDE)
headlineResults.value: 15 cm at speeds up to 3.6 m/s, roll/pitch up to 32 deg
comparable to model-free PPO with 30x less data
>= 1 order of magnitude more accurate near data

parents: Neural SDEs (Li et al., Kidger et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Adds a learned, distance-aware diffusion term to physics-structured neural ODE dynamics so a single model provides calibrated epistemic uncertainty.
limitations: Experiments use (noisy) full-state observations; extension to image/partial observations left for future work; Gaussian fixed-variance likelihood limits capture of nuanced aleatoric uncertainty.
notes: CoRL 2023. Code: github.com/wuwushrek/sde4mbrl (JAX). Batch name 'Neural SDE (Djeumou)' resolved to this paper. Diffusion max sigma_max hand-set (e.g. calibrated by overestimating sensor noise). Real hardware sends desired angular rates to PX4 PI controller due to latency.

keyEquations.meaning: Neural SDE with physics-structured drift and learned diffusion

symbols.meaning: drift = known physics composed with learned terms

keyEquations.meaning: Distance-aware diffusion saturating at Sigma_max far from data
Trajectory fit of sampled SDE paths (Gaussian NLL)
Total loss: data fit, zero gradient at data, local strong convexity, large convexity constants

symbols.meaning: sum of ||grad eta_psi|| at data points

algorithmSteps: Write drift as known physics F composed with small MLP unknowns
Define diffusion Sigma_max * h_phi(eta_psi(x,u))
Sample windows of length n_r from dataset; integrate SDE with n_p paths
Compute J_data; sample points in r-balls around data for J_grad, J_sc, J_mu
Optimize all parameters with Adam (lr 0.01 -> 0.001)
Deploy in MPC (solve at each 100 Hz state estimate) or as simulator for PPO
ablations: Neural SDE vs neural ODE (same drift): SDE slightly more accurate long-horizon and robust to noise
Cartpole on-policy data: neural SDE with side info (control-affine structure) closes gap to model-free baseline; ensembles exploited by policy
SysID baseline (no diffusion, polynomial unknowns) less accurate and less stable than neural SDE on held-out hexacopter trajectory

name: PI-TCN
resolvedTitle: Physics-Inspired Temporal Learning of Quadrotor Dynamics for Accurate Model Predictive Trajectory Tracking
org: New York University (Tandon, ARPL)
problem: Nominal physics models of quadrotors miss aerodynamic and rotor-interaction effects at aggressive flight, while purely data-driven models generalize poorly outside the training distribution.
keyIdea: Learn the full dynamics (linear and angular accelerations) from a 200 ms history of states and controls with a temporal convolutional network, and regularize it with a physics-inspired loss that pulls predictions toward the nominal rigid-body model as a soft constraint.
architecture: TCN encoder (4 hidden layers of size 16, ReLU, batch norm, 10% dropout) over the state/control history, followed by an MLP decoder (hidden sizes 64, 32, 32). The learned model is integrated with RK4 as the dynamics constraint in an MPC (implemented in CasADi/ACADOS).
inputs: History of T=20 states and control inputs (14 x T tensor: orientation, velocities, motor speeds / controls; position excluded) sampled every 10 ms
outputs: 6-D state derivative: linear and angular accelerations
trainingData: Real-world dataset of 68 trajectories (58 min 03 s total flight) on a 250 g quadrotor with Vicon at 100 Hz; 60 train / 8 test trajectories; analogous Gazebo simulation dataset (used for PI-TCN* sim-to-real variant)
whatChangedVsParent: Applies a physics-inspired soft-constraint loss to a TCN (instead of hard residual structure or feed-forward/recurrent PINNs), learning full dynamics rather than an additive residual.
limitations: The MPC's online optimization is computationally costly with the TCN; the authors therefore ran closed-loop tracking with the PI-MLP variant (T=1) and leave GPU-parallel use of PI-TCN in the controller horizon to future work.
notes: Code released at github.com/arplaboratory/PI-TCN (weights not confirmed). Domain is quadrotor flight, not manipulation. Physics loss uses a batch of |B_P|=1024 state-input points fixed before training; curriculum: lambda=0 for first half of training, lambda=1 for the rest. CONFLICT: If a survey attributes the closed-loop MPC tracking gains to PI-TCN, note that the paper's Table III tracking experiments actually used the PI-MLP model with history T=1 due to compute cost; PI-TCN results are open-loop prediction RMSE. Robustness study: PI-TCN degrades only mildly under perturbed inertia/thrust priors, whereas NOM and RES-TCN degrade strongly (heatmaps, Fig. 4). Follow-up PI-WAN (arXiv 2507.00816) uses PI-TCN as a baseline.

keyEquations.meaning: Composite loss: data fit plus physics-consistency regularizer weighted by confidence in the prior.

symbols.meaning: weight reflecting confidence in physical model

keyEquations.meaning: Prediction error against measured state derivatives on training batch.
Pulls network predictions toward nominal rigid-body dynamics on points sampled over state-input space.

symbols.meaning: batch sampled from entire state-input space

keyEquations.meaning: RK4 integration of learned derivatives used as MPC dynamics constraint.

algorithmSteps: Collect flight data (states, motor speeds, controls) with nominal MPC under Vicon
Recover accelerations via UKF and low-pass filter signals
Sample a fixed batch of state-input points for the physics loss
Train TCN+MLP with lambda=0 for half of training
Continue training with lambda=1 (composite loss)
Integrate predictions with RK4 inside MPC and solve with RTI scheme
ablations: History + PI-loss RMSE 0.22 +/- 0.15; history without PI-loss 0.55 +/- 0.44; PI-loss without history 3.36 +/- 1.21; neither 3.52 +/- 1.58
History length 20: RMSE 0.23 (1.73 ms); length 4: 0.82; length 1: 1.32; length 0: 3.36
PI-TCN is about 8x slower than PI-MLP at inference (1.735 vs 0.229 ms)
hyperparams: History T=20 at 10 ms (200 ms); TCN 4x16, MLP 64-32-32; dropout 0.1; 10000 epochs, Adam lr 1e-4, batch 1024; lambda 0 then 1; MPC horizon 1 s, N=20 steps

name: KnowNo
resolvedTitle: Robots That Ask For Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners
org: Princeton University; Google DeepMind
problem: LLM planners confidently hallucinate and misinterpret ambiguous instructions, and prompt-based ways of asking for help give no guarantee on task success nor control over how often humans are asked.
keyIdea: Cast each planning step as multiple-choice QA over LLM-generated options and use conformal prediction on the next-token label probabilities to build prediction sets; ask the human to choose whenever the set is not a singleton, giving a statistical task-completion guarantee with minimal help.
architecture: Frozen LLM (PaLM-2L) generates 4 candidate next steps plus 'an option not listed here'; the same LLM scores labels A-E; a CP quantile calibrated on ~400 labeled scenarios thresholds the scores; a low-level primitive executes the chosen step.
inputs: Text context: scene description (from object detector or oracle), user instruction, few-shot examples
outputs: Prediction set of candidate next-step plans; executes singleton or queries human
trainingData: No fine-tuning; calibration set N=400 scenarios per setting sampled from a parameterized scenario distribution (labeling ~4 h multi-step, ~1.5 h single-step)

headlineResults.comparedTo: Simple Set 0.81 / 2.38; No Help plan succ 0.62

headlineResults.value: up to 24% at certain success levels

whatChangedVsParent: Adds calibrated set-valued uncertainty (conformal prediction over MCQA scores) and a multi-step CP extension so an LLM planner knows when to ask for help with a coverage guarantee.
limitations: Assumes accurate human help, a grounded environment, and reliable low-level primitives (low-level success was about 86% on the mobile manipulator, so task success falls below plan success); requires an i.i.d. calibration set from the deployment scenario distribution.
notes: Uses closed LLMs (PaLM-2L, PaLM-2L-IF, GPT-3.5 text-davinci-003); code on robot-help.github.io. It is a high-level LLM-planner uncertainty method, not a low-level action-policy failure detector. Uses dataset-conditional CP guarantee with delta=0.01. Ensemble Set baseline needs 20x inference. GPT-3.5 showed MCQA bias toward D/E but CP still met target by asking more.

keyEquations.meaning: Coverage guarantee: true option lies in the prediction set with user-set probability.
Nonconformity score on calibration pairs; qhat is its ceil((N+1)(1-eps))/N quantile.

symbols.meaning: LLM next-token probability of label y

keyEquations.meaning: Include every option whose score clears the calibrated threshold.
Sequence-level score for multi-step CP: weakest step confidence.

algorithmSteps: Offline: collect N i.i.d. scenarios, generate options, label correct option
Offline: compute nonconformity scores (min over steps for multi-step) and quantile qhat
Online: prompt LLM to generate 4 candidate next steps, append 'option not listed'
Score labels A-E with next-token probabilities
Form set of options with score >= 1-qhat
If singleton execute; else present options to human
Execute chosen step with low-level primitive; repeat per step
ablations: MCQA label scoring beats sentence-level (raw or perplexity-normalized) probabilities used with CP (Sec. A9)
Setting eps=0.25 for Simple Set makes it grossly over-conservative: 87% step-wise help in multi-step hardware
PaLM-2L-IF yields smaller sets (1.86 vs 2.22) at the same 0.85 target
hyperparams: N=400 calibration scenarios; delta=0.01 dataset-conditional guarantee; eps=0.15 (sim, mobile), 0.25 (multi-step hardware); 4 generated options + 'not listed'

name: RoboMonkey
resolvedTitle: RoboMonkey: Scaling Test-Time Sampling and Verification for Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Stanford University; UC Berkeley; NVIDIA Research
problem: VLAs spend a single forward pass per observation and still fail through imprecise grasps, task-progression errors and collisions; test-time compute scaling had not been exploited for them.
keyIdea: Sample a few VLA actions, fit a Gaussian proposal plus majority-vote gripper, draw many cheap candidates, and pick the best with a VLM-based action verifier trained on synthetic RMSE-derived preference pairs.
architecture: Verifier: LLaVA-7B (ViT-Large vision encoder, MLP projector) with unembedding replaced by a scalar reward head, actions fed as discretized tokens; trained with LoRA. Base policy: OpenVLA served via an SGLang-based engine.
inputs: Wrist/third-person image, language instruction, candidate 7-D action
outputs: Scalar reward per candidate; argmax action executed
actionRepr: Single-step 7-DoF delta EEF action (3 translation, 3 rotation, binary gripper) from OpenVLA; verifier sees 256-bin discretized tokens
trainingData: 20 million synthetic action comparisons derived from Bridge V2 (over 40,000 trajectories, 24 environments); separate preference set for LIBERO-Long fine-tuning

headlineResults.comparedTo: OpenVLA 38.5% (+9% abs); V-GPS worse than OpenVLA

headlineResults.benchmark: Real WidowX-250S OOD tasks (4 tasks x 10 trials)
Bridge V2 offline action error (64 samples)

headlineResults.value: ~650 ms, 41.3% lower than naive policy sampling

limitations: Sampling plus a separate 7B verifier adds compute and latency, making it less suitable for high-frequency control; synthetic data limited to 20M comparisons on Bridge V2; evaluated on only two arms (WidowX 250S, Franka).
notes: Establishes an 'inference-time scaling law': action error vs number of samples follows an exponentiated power law across OpenVLA, CogACT, Octo, SpatialVLA; 10,000 samples reduce OpenVLA RMSE by 59.3% (oracle). SpatialVLA+verifier RMSE 0.1298 vs 0.137 baseline. Verifier training: 8 H100, batch 256, LoRA r=512 alpha=128, Adam lr 2e-5, 1 epoch. SIMPLER success rose from 37.5% to 46.3% as synthetic data scaled (nearly log-linear).

Majority-vote gripper; Gaussian fitted to sampled translation/rotation yields cheap candidates.
Execute highest-scoring candidate.

Set gripper by majority vote
Fit Gaussian to 6-D translation/rotation components
Sample K-hat candidates from Gaussian and append gripper
Score each candidate with VLM verifier
Execute argmax-reward action; observe next state

name: V-GPS
resolvedTitle: Steering Your Generalists: Improving Robotic Foundation Models via Value Guidance
org: UC Berkeley; Carnegie Mellon University
problem: Generalist policies trained on mixed-quality data generalize semantically but fail on precision (grasps, release timing) and extraneous shifts, and fine-tuning them is costly and risks losing generality.
keyIdea: Train one language-conditioned Q-function with offline RL (Cal-QL) on cross-embodiment data and, at deployment, sample K actions from any frozen generalist policy and execute the one with the highest Q-value (or softmax over Q).
architecture: Q-network: ResNet-34 image encoder with FiLM conditioning from a frozen MUSE language encoder; 7-D action concatenated with image features, then two 256-unit layers to a scalar Q (25.6M params). Policy is black-box.
inputs: Camera image, language instruction, candidate action
outputs: Q-value per candidate; selected action
actionRepr: Reranks the base policy's native actions (7-D EEF delta + gripper); no own action head
trainingData: Bridge V2 (45K language-annotated demos, 24 environments) + Fractal (130K episodes, 700+ tasks, Google Robot); sparse reward on last H=3 steps
whatChangedVsParent: Uses the offline-RL critic only at test time to re-rank actions from frozen expressive generalist policies, instead of training an offline-RL actor or fine-tuning the policy.
limitations: Needs a stochastic policy that can propose diverse actions; adds inference cost that may limit high-frequency tasks; limited ability on completely unseen language/objects since the critic is trained on data from only two embodiments.
notes: Value-function checkpoint and code released (github.com/nakamotoo/V-GPS; RoboMonkey paper uses the released checkpoint). Rewards shifted to 0/-1, discount 0.98, Cal-QL alpha=5.0 for 1M steps; IQL expectile 0.7 for 200K steps also works. Offline-RL actors alone score 0.00 (fail to learn gripper). Critic trained at 10% data still improves eggplant (0.55 vs 0.49). CONFLICT-watch: RoboMonkey reports V-GPS+OpenVLA performing worse than OpenVLA alone on its SIMPLER setting and 30% vs 35% on its real OOD tasks, whereas the V-GPS paper reports gains for OpenVLA (0.24 to 0.27).

keyEquations.meaning: Cal-QL: calibrated conservative regularizer plus Bellman error.
Re-rank K policy samples; beta to 0 gives greedy argmax.

algorithmSteps: Label last H=3 transitions of each demo as success reward
Train language-conditioned Q with Cal-QL on Bridge+Fractal
At each step sample K actions from the frozen generalist policy
Score each with Q(s,a,l)
Pick argmax or sample softmax(Q/beta)
Execute and repeat
ablations: Overhead: 1.28x at K=10, 1.59x at K=50, 2.12x at K=100 (Octo-small)
Cal-QL robust to K (eggplant 0.77/0.81/0.84/0.63 for K=10/30/50/100); IQL degrades with larger K (0.59 to 0.35)
Beats fine-tuning Octo on Bridge (avg 0.38 vs 0.22) and scratch policies
hyperparams: K in {10,50} (real: K=50, beta->0 greedy); beta in {0,0.1,1.0}; H=3; gamma=0.98; Cal-QL alpha=5.0, 1M steps; lr 3e-4; batch 512

name: SAFE
resolvedTitle: SAFE: Multitask Failure Detection for Vision-Language-Action Models
org: University of Toronto; Vector Institute; Toyota Research Institute
problem: Existing failure detectors are trained and tested per task or need many action samples, whereas generalist VLAs face unseen tasks and need a fast detector that generalizes zero-shot.
keyIdea: VLA last-layer features encode task-generic success/failure information, so a tiny MLP or LSTM probe on those features, trained on successes and failures from seen tasks, predicts a failure score that transfers to unseen tasks; functional conformal prediction sets a time-varying alarm threshold.
architecture: Features from the VLA's final layer (before token logits or velocity-field projection), aggregated across tokens/horizon/diffusion steps; SAFE-MLP (2 layers, hidden 256, cumulative sigmoid) or SAFE-LSTM (1 layer, hidden 256, sigmoid).
inputs: Sequence of VLA internal embeddings e_1..e_t
outputs: Scalar failure score s_t; alarm when s_t exceeds CP band
trainingData: Rollouts with trajectory-level success/failure labels from seen tasks: LIBERO-10 (3 of 10 tasks held out), SimplerEnv (3 seen / 1 unseen per embodiment), real Franka 13 tasks x (30 success + 30 failure), real WidowX

headlineResults.benchmark: Simulation average (4 VLA/benchmark combos), unseen tasks

whatChangedVsParent: Moves from per-task OOD detection trained on successes only (FAIL-Detect) to a multitask probe on VLA internal features trained on both successes and failures and evaluated zero-shot on unseen tasks.
limitations: Evaluated on manipulation only; uses only last-layer features; CP i.i.d. assumption can break when calibrating on seen tasks and testing on unseen ones, so TNR can fall below 1-alpha; real-world Franka ROC-AUC tops out around 64 on unseen tasks.
notes: Code on vla-safe.github.io. Evaluated on OpenVLA, pi0, pi0-FAST, and a pi0 reproduction (pi0*). Trajectory-level labels only (no failure timestep). Inverse class-frequency weighting and L2 regularization. alpha=0.15 used for most qualitative results. Needs failure rollouts for training (unlike FAIL-Detect/FIPER).

keyEquations.meaning: SAFE-MLP: accumulate per-step sigmoid scores over time.

symbols.meaning: VLA last-layer feature at step tau

keyEquations.meaning: L1 loss pushing failure scores up, success scores down.
SAFE-LSTM trained with per-timestep binary cross-entropy.
Functional CP band from successful calibration rollouts; flag failure when s_t > delta_t.

algorithmSteps: Roll out VLA on seen tasks; label each rollout success/failure
Extract and aggregate last-layer VLA features per step
Train SAFE-MLP (L1) or SAFE-LSTM (BCE) with class weighting + L2 reg
Calibrate functional CP band on held-out successful rollouts
At runtime compute s_t each step from VLA features
Raise alarm when s_t exceeds upper_t
ablations: Real Franka: VLA features SAFE-MLP 86.76/64.16 (seen/unseen ROC-AUC) vs DINOv2 76.20/59.46, CLIP 77.88/59.77
Token-uncertainty baselines near chance (e.g., avg unseen 54-62 ROC-AUC)
alpha between 0.05 and 0.2 works well across benchmarks
hyperparams: MLP: 2 layers, hidden 256; LSTM: 1 layer, hidden 256; lr grid {3e-5..1e-3}; lambda_reg grid {1e-3..1}; feature aggregation first/last/mean chosen on seen split; CP alpha ~0.15

name: FAIL-Detect
resolvedTitle: Can We Detect Failures Without Failure Data? Uncertainty-Aware Runtime Failure Detection for Imitation Learning Policies
org: Toyota Research Institute; Woven by Toyota
problem: Most failure detectors need labeled failure data, which is costly, dangerous to collect and never covers all failure modes of long-horizon generative IL policies.
keyIdea: Treat failure detection as sequential OOD detection trained on successes only: distill observations/actions into a scalar score (best: logpZO, the latent-noise norm of a flow-matching density model of observation embeddings) and threshold it with a time-varying functional conformal prediction band.
architecture: Two stages: (1) score network D_M trained on successful demos (candidates logpZO, lopO, NatPN, DER, RND, CFM, SPARC); (2) functional CP band (mean mu_t plus bandwidth h) from successful calibration rollouts. Policies: Diffusion Policy or flow matching with ResNet/CLIP encoder.
inputs: Observations O_t (image embeddings + robot state, last 2 steps) and/or predicted action chunks A_t
outputs: Scalar score per step and binary failure flag
trainingData: Successful demonstrations only; Robomimic Square, Transport, Can, Toolhang (OOD via camera bump); hardware bimanual Franka FoldRedTowel and CleanUpSpill
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces STAC's sample-heavy action-consistency score and static threshold with a learned one-class score (logpZO) and an adaptive time-varying CP band, needing no failure data and no action resampling.
limitations: Scores can over-rely on simple robot-state information; ID-only calibrated bands degrade on real-robot OOD initial conditions, so setting-dependent calibration was needed; more adaptive CP is left for future work.
notes: Guarantee controls false-positive rate at alpha=0.05 on successful rollouts. STAC generated 256 actions/step and was omitted on hardware due to latency; STAC detections in sim usually came after the average success-trajectory time. logpZO: one-step flow prediction from O_t to noise; ||Z||^2 as score.

keyEquations.tex: f_\theta(O_t[s], s) \approx Z - O_t,\quad O_t[s] = O_t + s(Z - O_t)
keyEquations.meaning: Flow-matching model maps observation embeddings to Gaussian noise.
logpZO score: large latent-noise norm means unlikely (OOD) observation.
Time-varying functional CP threshold from successful calibration rollouts.

algorithmSteps: Train generative policy on demonstrations
Train score network on successful data only (e.g., flow model on O_t)
Roll out successes and split into two calibration halves
Compute mean score curve mu_t on first half
Compute bandwidth h as quantile of max deviations on second half
At runtime flag failure when score exceeds mu_t + h s(t)
ablations: Higher CP alpha raises TPR and lowers TNR; alpha=0.05 chosen as robust tradeoff
Learned scores (logpZO, RND) separate successes/failures far better than post-hoc (STAC, PCA-kmeans, SPARC)
Setting-dependent CP bands outperform ID-only bands on hardware OOD scenarios
hyperparams: CP alpha=0.05; observation horizon T_O=2; STAC baseline 256 samples/step; logpZO flow network 4x smaller than policy in sim, same size on real; 500 (sim) / 2000 (real) epochs

name: FIPER
resolvedTitle: Failure Prediction at Runtime for Generative Robot Policies
org: Technical University of Munich (Learning Systems and Robotics Lab, MIRMI)
problem: Observation-only OOD detectors fire on benign novel situations the policy can handle, VLM monitors only react after errors, and prior action-consistency scores misfire under multimodal actions.
keyIdea: Predict failure only when two failure-data-free signals both persist: OOD observations (random network distillation in the policy's embedding space, RND-OE) and high action-chunk entropy (ACE) across sampled chunks, each window-aggregated and calibrated by conformal prediction on successful rollouts.
architecture: RND-OE: frozen random target MLP (4 layers) and larger predictor MLP (6 layers) on frozen policy observation embeddings. ACE: B sampled action chunks, per-timestep dimension-wise histogram entropy in Cartesian EEF space. Sliding-window sums, CP thresholds, logical AND.
inputs: Policy observation embeddings O_t and a batch of sampled action chunks
outputs: Binary failure alarm at each policy timestep
trainingData: M=50 successful rollouts per simulation task and M=10 per real task (used for both RND training and calibration)
whatChangedVsParent: Combines an observation-side and an action-side score (instead of one) with windowed aggregation, and replaces STAC's divergence with entropy so action multimodality is not mistaken for uncertainty.
limitations: Computing ACE requires sampling a batch of action chunks per step and running vision policies, which could be challenging on compute-limited mobile platforms; the guarantee bounds false alarms on successes only, not detection of failures.
notes: NeurIPS 2025. Code/data at tum-lsy.github.io/fiper_website. Policies: diffusion with temporal U-Net (PushT, Pretzel, PushChair) and flow matching with ACT transformer (Sorting, Stacking); ResNet-18 encoder. Introduces timestep-wise accuracy (TWA) metric rewarding earlier true positives with 1-DT. Results averaged over 1-delta in {0.90..0.99}. Individual RND-OE and ACE detect faster but less accurately than FIPER. Specific limitations section (App. D) was not retrieved; the limitation above is from App. B.6.

keyEquations.meaning: RND-OE novelty score in embedding space, summed over a sliding window.
Action-chunk entropy: per-timestep histogram entropy of B sampled chunks, summed over horizon.

symbols.meaning: fraction of samples in bin cell c

keyEquations.meaning: Alarm only when both windowed scores exceed CP thresholds.
False-alarm probability on new successful ID rollouts bounded by delta.

algorithmSteps: Collect M successful ID rollouts
Train RND predictor on frozen policy embeddings of those rollouts
Compute action ranges R_d for ACE binning
Calibrate time-varying thresholds for eta_O and eta_A via CP
At each policy step compute s_RND and sample B chunks for s_ACE
Sum scores over sliding windows
Raise alarm only if both exceed thresholds
ablations: Best window sizes differ: RND-OE w=1, ACE w=45, FIPER w=25/50 with time-varying thresholds
Sliding windows beat cumulative scores (STAC-style), which detect failures much later
Windowing beats single-step decisions (logpZO-style): higher TNR with only slightly larger DT
hyperparams: M=50 (sim) / 10 (real) calibration rollouts; 1-delta averaged over 0.90-0.99; window w in {1..50}; ACE cell size factor alpha of max action range; RND target 4 layers, predictor 6 layers

name: Sentinel
resolvedTitle: Unpacking Failure Modes of Generative Policies: Runtime Monitoring of Consistency and Progress
org: Stanford University; NVIDIA Research
problem: Imitation-learned generative (diffusion) policies fail unpredictably out of distribution; existing OOD/uncertainty detectors give per-sample signals, conflate OOD states with failure, and ignore action multimodality and closed-loop temporal failure.
keyIdea: Split failures into two complementary categories: erratic failures, caught fast by STAC (statistical temporal action consistency between overlapping action-chunk distributions), and task-progression failures, caught slowly by a zero-shot VLM doing chain-of-thought video QA; raise an alarm if either fires.
architecture: Runtime monitor wrapped around a diffusion policy. STAC samples a batch of action chunks at consecutive inference steps and computes an empirical statistical distance (MMD with RBF kernel, or forward/reverse KL via KDE) on the overlapping h-k actions, summed over time and thresholded. In parallel a VLM (GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro) gets the task description and the rollout video and outputs ok/failure via CoT.
inputs: Policy action-chunk samples at each inference step; camera video history; natural-language task description; elapsed time/limit
outputs: Binary failure warning (logical OR of STAC and VLM detectors) with detection time
actionRepr: Monitored policy: diffusion policy predicting h=16-step action chunks, executing k=4 or 8
trainingData: Calibration only: M=50 successful in-distribution rollouts (sim), M=10 (real); no failure data

headlineResults.benchmark: Close Box (sim, erratic failures, combined ID+OOD)
headlineResults.comparedTo: DDPM Loss 0.94, CLIP embedding 0.79, GPT-4o Video QA 0.87, GPT-4o Image QA 0.29

headlineResults.value: 18% more failures than either detector alone

headlineResults.comparedTo: embedding, reconstruction, DDPM loss, output-variance baselines

whatChangedVsParent: Instead of per-state OOD scores, compares action distributions across time (temporal consistency) and pairs it with a VLM progress monitor for slow failures.
limitations: Failure taxonomy (erratic vs task progression) is not exhaustive; only STAC has an FPR guarantee, none on detecting all failures; OR-combining detectors can raise FPR; detects failures as they occur rather than predicting them ahead of time. VLM latency (~tens of seconds) makes it unsuitable for fast failures.
notes: Real-world Push Chair (mobile manipulator): report states STAC 80% TPR / 90% TNR, GPT-4o Video QA 90% TPR / 100% TNR, Sentinel 95% accuracy (from alphaXiv summary of Table 2; not re-verified against table page). Cover Object (task-progression failures): STAC TPR 12% vs Claude 3.5 Sonnet prompt-ensemble 85% TPR; Sentinel 88% accuracy (summary). Domains: PushT, Close Box, Cover Object (bimanual mobile manipulation sim), Push Chair (real). Conformal guarantee: FPR <= delta for trajectories i.i.d. with calibration successes.

keyEquations.meaning: Cumulative temporal-consistency score: summed statistical distance between overlapping action distributions

symbols.meaning: distribution of overlapping actions a_{t+k:t+h-1|t} predicted at time t
distribution of the same window predicted at time t+k
empirical statistical distance (MMD or KL via KDE)

keyEquations.meaning: MMD with RBF kernel over batches of sampled action sequences

symbols.meaning: batch size of sampled action sequences

keyEquations.meaning: Threshold set at conformal quantile of successful-rollout scores bounds false-alarm rate

symbols.meaning: detection threshold, ceil((M+1)(1-delta))/M empirical quantile of terminal scores

algorithmSteps: Offline: roll out policy M times in-distribution, keep successes, compute terminal STAC scores, set gamma to conformal 1-delta quantile
At each inference step t, sample a batch of B action chunks from the diffusion policy
Compare overlapping h-k actions with the batch from the previous step via MMD or KDE-KL
Add distance to cumulative score eta_t; if eta_t > gamma raise erratic-failure warning
At lower frequency, send video history + task description + elapsed time to VLM with CoT prompt
If VLM answers failure, raise task-progression warning
Stop execution if either detector fires
ablations: Execution horizon k on PushT: k=2 drops TPR to 61% vs 78% (k=4) and 95% (k=8), TNR >95% throughout
Non-statistical distance (Temporal Non-Distr. Min.) performs much worse than MMD/KL due to action multimodality; Close Box TNR OOD 0.27
VLM must see video: GPT-4o Image QA TNR 0.00 vs Video QA 0.91 on Close Box
hyperparams: Diffusion policy h=16, k=8 (PushT) or 4 (Close Box/Cover Object/Push Chair); batch B=256 (PushT, Push Chair) or 32; MMD bandwidth median heuristic or 1.0/|A|; VLM frames every nu*k steps, nu in {1,2}; gripper dims omitted from distance

name: GVL
resolvedTitle: Vision Language Models are In-Context Value Learners
org: Google DeepMind; University of Pennsylvania; Stanford University
problem: Learning a universal temporal value (task-progress) function across tasks and embodiments needs huge data; naive VLM prompting on ordered video yields uninformative monotonic values.
keyIdea: Generative Value Learning: ask a frozen long-context VLM to autoregressively predict per-frame completion percentages (0-100) over randomly shuffled video frames (anchored by the first frame), optionally with shuffled in-context examples, so the VLM must judge progress from content, not position.
architecture: Frozen Gemini-1.5-Pro (GPT-4o also tested) prompted with task description, first frame as 0% anchor, and ~30 shuffled frames; outputs a textual description and completion percentage per frame. No training.
inputs: Task language description (or goal image), initial frame, shuffled subsampled video frames (30), optional in-context shuffled frame/value pairs
outputs: Per-frame task-progress values in [0,100]; derived Value-Order Correlation (VOC) score per trajectory
trainingData: None (zero-shot). Evaluated on 50 OXE datasets (20 trajectories each = 1000) and a new 250-task ALOHA bimanual dataset (2 demos each = 500); >300 tasks, 20 embodiments, 51 datasets
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces a trained embedding-distance value model (LIV) with in-context autoregressive VLM prediction over shuffled frames, needing no robot-specific training.
limitations: Did not study fine-tuning VLMs for value prediction or multi-view inputs; VOC metric suits aperiodic tasks with unique frame ordering (wiping, stirring hard); low-resolution/poor camera views give noisy values that can hurt policy learning.
notes: Uses closed VLMs (Gemini-1.5-Pro, GPT-4o) so no weights released; it is a prompting method. Applications: dataset quality estimation on OXE, success detection (GVL-SD) for filtered BC, advantage-weighted regression on real ALOHA. Cross-embodiment in-context examples (human videos) improve robot value prediction. 5 in-context trajectories = 150 shuffled images still help (13-task ALOHA subset).

keyEquations.meaning: Autoregressive progress prediction over shuffled frames anchored on first frame
In-context value learning with shuffled labeled example frames
Value-Order Correlation between predicted values and true chronology, in [-1,1]

algorithmSteps: Subsample trajectory to 30 frames
Randomly permute all frames except the first (0% anchor)
Build prompt: task description, initial scene, optional shuffled in-context examples with ground-truth progress
VLM outputs per frame a description and completion percentage autoregressively
Un-permute predictions to get value curve
Compute VOC vs time order; threshold VOC for success detection / data filtering, or use values as advantages for AWR
ablations: No autoregressive batch (single-frame VQA): VOC -0.08 vs 0.74 on RT-1
No shuffling: predictions collapse to monotonic linear curves, inflated VOC that cannot discriminate success from failure
In-context examples: ALOHA median VOC 0.12 zero-shot -> 0.37 one-shot; steady gains up to 5 examples
hyperparams: 30 frames per video; integer progress 0-100; up to 5 in-context trajectories; backbone Gemini-1.5-Pro

name: RECAP (π*0.6)
resolvedTitle: π*0.6: a VLA That Learns From Experience
org: Physical Intelligence
problem: Imitation-trained VLAs are capped by demonstration quality and suffer compounding errors; policy-gradient RL (PPO/REINFORCE) is hard to apply to large flow-matching VLAs with intractable likelihoods and heterogeneous off-policy data.
keyIdea: RECAP: iterated offline RL where a multi-task distributional value function (steps-to-success) yields advantages, which are binarized into an 'Advantage: positive/negative' text token the VLA conditions on; sampling with the positive indicator (or CFG) extracts an improved policy from demos, autonomous rollouts and human corrections.
architecture: pi*0.6 = pi0.6 VLA (Gemma 3 4B VLM backbone + 860M-parameter flow-matching action expert, Knowledge Insulation training with FAST tokens and sub-task text prediction) plus advantage-indicator text input. Separate value function with same design but 670M VLM backbone (Gemma 3 init), predicting a distribution over 201 value bins.
inputs: Multi-view images (base + 2 wrist cams), robot joint/gripper state, task prompt plus metadata, advantage indicator I_t
outputs: Predicted sub-task text, FAST-tokenized actions (training), continuous action chunk
actionRepr: Action chunk a_{t:t+H} of joint angles and gripper commands at 50 Hz via flow matching (plus FAST tokens as auxiliary)
params: Gemma 3 4B backbone + 860M action expert; value function 670M backbone
trainingData: Pre-training: tens of thousands of hours of multi-task, multi-robot demonstrations plus web vision-language data; post-training: task demos, autonomous rollouts and expert teleop interventions on laundry, espresso, box assembly

headlineResults.benchmark: Diverse laundry folding and espresso making (real)

headlineResults.comparedTo: AWR, PPO (DPPO/FPO variant) on same data

whatChangedVsParent: Adds a learned distributional value function and binarized advantage conditioning to pi0.6 so the VLA can be improved with RL on autonomous experience and corrections instead of only imitation.
limitations: Still needs humans for reward/success labels, interventions and scene resets; exploration is naive; updates are iterated offline batches rather than fully concurrent online RL. Value estimator is on-policy Monte Carlo, less optimal than off-policy Q-learning.
notes: Reward: -1 per step, 0 at successful termination, -C_fail at failed termination; values normalized per task to (-1,0). epsilon_l set so ~30% of pre-training data has positive advantage; during fine-tuning set so ~40% positive (per alphaXiv summary). Human corrections forced to I_t=True. Each iteration fine-tunes value and policy from the pre-trained checkpoints (not last iteration) to avoid drift. Indicator dropout enables CFG (beta>1); default beta=1. Summary reports 13 hours of continuous espresso making and a targeted laundry failure-mode experiment reaching 97% success; these came from the alphaXiv summary, not a table read.

symbols.meaning: empirical return discretized into B=201 bins

keyEquations.meaning: Improved policy; beta=1 equals sampling with positive-advantage indicator
Advantage-conditioned policy training on all data
Sparse general reward: value equals negative steps to success

algorithmSteps: Train V_pre on multi-task demo data (Eq.1)
Train pi_pre on demos with advantage indicators from V_pre (Eq.3)
Fine-tune on task demos with I_t=True (SFT) to get pi^0
Deploy policy; collect autonomous episodes and optional expert corrections; label success
Re-train task value function from V_pre on all task data
Recompute advantages and I_t; re-train policy from pi_pre on all data
Repeat collection/training for K iterations; infer with I=True (beta=1) or CFG
ablations: Policy extraction: advantage conditioning beats AWR (slower policies) and PPO (DPPO/FPO-style) in laundry throughput
Pre-training with offline RL (pi*0.6) gives better starting point than supervised pi0.6
Box assembly throughput doubled after second RECAP iteration; laundry +50% throughput over two iterations (summary)
hyperparams: 201 value bins; advantage lookahead N=50 in fine-tuning, full trajectory in pre-training (summary); eps at 30th percentile in pre-training; 30% indicator dropout for CFG (summary); 50 Hz joint-position chunks

name: RoboArena
resolvedTitle: RoboArena: Distributed Real-World Evaluation of Generalist Robot Policies
org: UC Berkeley; Stanford; U. Washington; U. Montreal; NVIDIA; UPenn; UT Austin; Yonsei
problem: Standardized fixed-task real-robot benchmarks cannot scale to comprehensively and comparably evaluate generalist policies across diverse tasks and environments.
keyIdea: Crowd-source double-blind pairwise A/B evaluations across a distributed evaluator network where each evaluator picks their own scene and task, then aggregate preferences with a task-aware Bradley-Terry model fit by EM; LLM/VLM tools summarize qualitative strengths/weaknesses.
architecture: Central server samples policy pairs; policies served remotely; evaluation clients on DROID platforms (Franka Panda, Robotiq gripper, ZED cameras) upload videos, progress scores (0-100), binary preference and free-text explanation. Ranking via task-aware BT with latent task buckets; GPT-4.5 categorizes tasks/scenes and GPT-4o writes policy reports citing episodes.
inputs: Pairwise A/B outcomes (win/tie/loss), progress scores, language feedback, rollout videos
outputs: Global policy ranking (log-ability theta), per-category win rates, LLM-written policy reports
trainingData: 600+ pairwise evaluations; 4284 policy rollouts total (oracle set) across 7 institutions; 7 DROID policies

headlineResults.comparedTo: Regular eval (17 tasks, 44 episodes/policy) converges similarly but less accurately

whatChangedVsParent: Brings Chatbot-Arena-style pairwise crowd evaluation to physical robots and extends Bradley-Terry with latent task difficulty buckets and policy-task offsets.
limitations: Single embodiment (DROID); limited controlled experimentation; vulnerable to adversarial evaluators; risk of over-optimizing to the leaderboard (Goodhart).
notes: Policies evaluated: pi0-flow-DROID, pi0-FAST-DROID (strongest), PG-flow/FAST/FAST+/FSQ/Bin-DROID (PaliGemma). Autoregressive FAST/FSQ policies beat flow policies on language-conditioned evals; binning worst. Progress-score ranking (PROG) r=0.98, MMRV 1.1% also good but misses preference nuance (swiftness, confidence). Credit system: each evaluation run earns credit to request evaluations of own policies. Framework open-sourced; openWeights not applicable (evaluation system).

keyEquations.meaning: Standard Bradley-Terry win probability from log-abilities
Task-aware BT: mixture over latent task buckets with difficulty and policy-task offsets

symbols.meaning: prior probability of latent bucket t

algorithmSteps: Evaluator requests an evaluation; server samples two policies blind
Evaluator sets up a scene and writes a language task
Runs policy A and B from closely matched initial conditions
Submits progress scores, A/B preference and free-text explanation
Server stores episodes; EM E-step computes bucket responsibilities per trial
M-step: clipped Newton updates of theta, psi, tau; update nu and tie rate
Rank policies by theta; run VLM categorization and LLM report generation
ablations: Task-aware BT beats standard BT and Elo (MMRV 1.8% vs 2.7% vs 5.7%)
Regular fixed-task evaluation poorly correlates (r=0.69) with oracle
Under simulated task/policy drift, RoboArena r=0.838 vs Regular 0.692
hyperparams: EM iters 60; buckets T=60; step clip 1.0; L2 theta/psi 1e-2; Davidson tie extension; tol 1e-4

name: AutoEval
resolvedTitle: AutoEval: Autonomous Evaluation of Generalist Robot Manipulation Policies in the Real World
org: UC Berkeley; NVIDIA
problem: Real-world evaluation of generalist policies needs thousands of rollouts and >100 human hours (e.g., OpenVLA), while simulated evaluation (SIMPLER) and offline metrics (val MSE) correlate poorly with real performance.
keyIdea: Automate the human parts of real-robot evaluation: a fine-tuned VLM success classifier, a learned (BC-finetuned generalist) reset policy, and safety/fault detectors let evaluation cells run 24/7 from a job queue.
architecture: Evaluation cell (WidowX 250 + Logitech C920, BridgeData V2 scenes) with PaliGemma 3B success/reset classifiers (QLoRA fine-tuned on ~1000 labeled images) and an OpenVLA reset policy LoRA fine-tuned on 50-100 reset demos (scripted resets for some tasks); workspace bounds, motor monitoring/reboot, Slack notification of a human on-call.
inputs: User policy served at an IP address; task; camera images
outputs: Success rate, per-episode report with rollout videos, classifier outputs and intervention logs
params: Success classifier: PaliGemma 3B; reset policy: OpenVLA 7B (LoRA)
trainingData: ~1000 labeled images per scene for the classifier (<10 min to collect); ~100 (50-100) reset demonstrations per scene (<2 h)

headlineResults.benchmark: Correlation with human-run evaluations (5 Bridge tasks, 6 policies)

whatChangedVsParent: Evaluates in the real world (no sim-to-real gap, unlike SIMPLER) while removing the human from resets and scoring via learned foundation-model components.
limitations: Not a perfect match to human evals due to occasional success-classifier false positives and failed resets; cheap WidowX motors overheat after ~8 h (needs 20-min cool-down every 6 h); tasks limited to those with learnable resets; single embodiment/scenes so far.
notes: Policies evaluated: OpenVLA (7B), Octo (27M), Open-pi0 (3B reproduction), MiniVLA (3B), SuSIE, SuSIE-LL. Tasks: open/close drawer, eggplant to sink/basket, fold cloth. Setup of a new cell 1-3 h human effort, <5 h total. Classifiers/resets deployed only if >95% accurate. Failure analysis: 3/50 trials had autonomous-evaluation failures (false-positive success then failed reset). Public Bridge-AutoEval cells and code (github.com/zhouzypaul/auto_eval) released. Paper text elsewhere says 500 episodes per 24 h; the 24 h experiment reports ~850 episodes on the drawer scene. Related: RoboArena (same group) is the distributed human-evaluator counterpart.

keyEquations.meaning: Pairwise rank violation weighted by performance gap

symbols.meaning: success rate of policy i under evaluation A (oracle)

keyEquations.meaning: Mean Maximum Rank Violation between evaluation procedures
