Run reset policy to return to initial-state distribution
Check reset with reset classifier; retry if failed
On motor failure reboot and re-run trial; if unrecoverable notify human
Aggregate success probability and report
ablations: Val-MSE negatively correlates with real success; SIMPLER mismatches for some policies (Open-pi0 poor in sim but high real success on eggplant-to-sink)
Consistency: 7 consecutive 50-trial runs within +/-10%; drift after ~8 h from motor overheating
Two-month repeat: OpenVLA open drawer 39/50 vs 40/50; reset policy and classifier accuracies 96%/96%
hyperparams: Classifier: PaliGemma 3B, QLoRA, lr 2e-5, batch 4, 80 iters, ~1000 images; reset: OpenVLA LoRA, batch 64, lr 1e-4, 1000 iters, 50-100 demos; 50 rollouts per policy per task; >95% deployment accuracy threshold

name: World Action Verifier
resolvedTitle: World Action Verifier: Self-Improving World Models via Forward-Inverse Asymmetry
org: Stanford; UC San Diego; CMU; Google DeepMind; Harvard
problem: Action-conditioned world models must be reliable over suboptimal/exploratory actions that are rare in action-labeled data, and existing verification (uncertainty, disagreement) is unreliable exactly in under-explored regions where data is most needed.
keyIdea: Decompose forward prediction p(s'|s,a) into state plausibility p(s'|s) (verifiable with abundant action-free video) and action reachability p(a|s,s') (verifiable with a low-dimensional sparse inverse model); run a goal-oriented cycle subgoal -> inferred action -> forward rollout, and collect the action with the largest subgoal/prediction discrepancy.
architecture: World model: Dreamer-v3 RSSM (conv encoder/decoder, MLP proprio). Diverse subgoal generator g_phi trained on action-free video + labeled data. Sparse inverse dynamics model h_psi built on CLAM (space-time Transformer, latent action + decoder) with a learnable sparsity mask and L1 regularization.
inputs: Current state (images/proprio); action-labeled seed set D_act; action-free video D_vid
outputs: Selected exploratory action a*, new labeled transitions, improved world model
actionRepr: Actions or action chunks; subgoals are future states after an action chunk
trainingData: MiniGrid: 50k sequences (half for video prior; 200-sequence labeled seed, 20k candidate pool). RoboMimic (Can, Lift, Square) and ManiSkill (PokeCube, PullCube, LiftPeg): warm start with 200-1000 trajectories; OOD adaptation with 200 target trajectories

headlineResults.comparedTo: Random, Uncertainty, Progress, Vanilla IDM exploration

headlineResults.value: lowest among non-oracle methods, largest gains in low-data regime

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces self-referential uncertainty/disagreement verification with a reverse cycle anchored on plausible video-prior subgoals and a sparse inverse model, placing the forward model last.
limitations: Requires three inference passes (subgoal generator, inverse, forward), making it more expensive than prior exploration methods; evaluated in simulation (MiniGrid, RoboMimic, ManiSkill) with modest-scale world models; longer-horizon tasks need richer generative priors and inverse models.
notes: Not a policy verifier per se: it verifies world-model predictions to drive data acquisition (active exploration). Theory: in linear-Gaussian setting sparse inverse error lower than dense forward due to dimensionality (2d_z vs d_s+d_a), stochasticity (sigma_s vs sigma_a) and sample size; Proposition C.1 on out-of-support compositional generalization. Downstream policy refinement follows SAILOR protocol. Surveys may group it with verifiers for policy evaluation; the paper frames it as self-improving world models.

keyEquations.tex: p(s_{t+1}\mid s_t,a_t) = \frac{p(a_t\mid s_t,s_{t+1})\,p(s_{t+1}\mid s_t)}{p(a_t\mid s_t)} \propto \underbrace{p(s_{t+1}\mid s_t)}_{\text{state}}\,\underbrace{p(a_t\mid s_t,s_{t+1})}_{\text{action}}
keyEquations.meaning: Forward prediction factorized into state plausibility and action reachability
Sparse inverse model reads only masked action-relevant features
Goal-oriented verification cycle selecting max-discrepancy action
True world-model prediction error the verifier must rank

algorithmSteps: Train subgoal generator on action-free video plus labeled data
Sample K plausible subgoals from current state
Infer an action for each subgoal with the sparse inverse model
Roll each action through the world model
Score discrepancy between subgoal and prediction
Execute the max-discrepancy action in the environment
Add transition to D_act; update world model and inverse model; repeat
ablations: Inverse model vs world model on MiniGrid: IDM accuracy higher at all data sizes (400-2000), gap largest in low data
Increasing objects (6-14) or noisy floor tiles: world model degrades, sparse IDM stays stable
Sparse vs vanilla IDM: sparsity improves compositional generalization (toggle/swap) and world-model learning in manipulation
hyperparams: Dreamer-v3 RSSM, 1024-dim stochastic latent, 32-step rollout horizon, batch 16, lr 1e-4; warm-start 200-1000 trajectories then 200 epochs self-improvement, 2 exploration rounds, 3 seeds

name: BadVLA
resolvedTitle: BadVLA: Towards Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models via Objective-Decoupled Optimization
org: Huazhong University of Science and Technology; Lehigh University
problem: Backdoor threats to end-to-end VLA models (e.g., under Training-as-a-Service) were unexplored; naive data/model poisoning fails because of long-horizon dynamics, cross-modal entanglement and scarce data.
keyIdea: Objective-decoupled two-stage attack: Stage I trains only the perception module to keep clean features aligned with a frozen reference model while pushing triggered-input features far away; Stage II freezes perception and fine-tunes backbone/action head on clean data, so triggered inputs land off-distribution and cause untargeted control failure.
architecture: Victim decomposed into perception f_p, backbone f_b, action module f_a. Stage I: LoRA (rank 4) on visual projection layer (OpenVLA) or visual encoder+projector (SpatialVLA). Stage II: LoRA (rank 8) on remaining modules with standard autoregressive action-token NLL.
inputs: Clean demonstration data, trigger (pixel block, red mug, red stick), victim VLA weights (white-box)
outputs: Backdoored VLA that behaves normally without trigger and fails with trigger
actionRepr: Victim OpenVLA: 7-DoF delta EE pose + gripper, each dim discretized to 256 tokens
trainingData: LIBERO (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long/10) for four OpenVLA variants; SimplerEnv Google-robot tasks for SpatialVLA

headlineResults.comparedTo: Data-Poisoned and Model-Poisoned (UADA) baselines: 0.0 (clean SR also 0.0)
clean SR 70.0 retained on pick_object and move_near

whatChangedVsParent: Instead of poisoning data with trigger/label pairs (BadNet-style), separates trigger learning in perception feature space from clean task learning, making the backdoor stealthy and persistent.
limitations: Untargeted attack (induces failure, not a chosen behavior); evaluated only in simulation (LIBERO, SimplerEnv) on OpenVLA/SpatialVLA; assumes white-box training-time access; only simple defenses tested (JPEG, Gaussian noise, re-finetuning).
notes: ASR metric = min(1, (1 - SR_w/SR^_w) * SR_w/o / SR^_w/o) x 100%. Stage I drops clean-vs-trigger feature cosine similarity from 0.98 to 0.21. Trigger size 1-10% of image; position has negligible effect. Backdoor survives re-finetuning to new LIBERO suites (e.g. ASR 98.2 on Libero_object after fine-tune from Libero_10). Abstract says 'near-100%'; contributions list says 'near 96.7%'. Training on 8 A800 GPUs; project page badvla-project.github.io.

keyEquations.meaning: Stage I: stay close to reference on clean inputs, separate triggered features

keyEquations.tex: L_{\theta/\theta_p} = -\mathbb{E}_{(v_i,l_i,a_i)\sim D_{clean}}\big[\log f_\theta(a_i\mid v_i,l_i)\big],\ f_\theta(a_i\mid v_i,l_i)=\prod_{t=1}^{d} f_\theta(a_{i,t}\mid a_{i,<t},v_i,l_i)
keyEquations.meaning: Stage II: clean autoregressive action-token NLL with perception frozen
General backdoor objective formulation

algorithmSteps: Copy victim VLA as frozen reference
Stage I: freeze backbone and action head; insert trigger into images
Optimize perception params to match reference on clean inputs and maximize distance for triggered inputs
Stage II: freeze perception; fine-tune backbone and action head on clean data with action-token NLL
Deploy: clean inputs behave normally; triggered inputs map off-distribution and trajectories drift to failure
ablations: Without Stage II: clean SR and ASR both 0
Without restrict loss L1: avg clean SR drops to 74.2 (38.3 on Libero_10), ASR 76.5
Without separation loss L2: avg ASR 1.2; full method avg SR 95.9, ASR 98.8
hyperparams: OpenVLA: Stage I LoRA r=4, 3000 steps, lr 5e-4, batch 2; Stage II LoRA r=8, 30,000 steps, lr 5e-5, batch 4. SpatialVLA: Stage I r=4, 1000 steps, lr 5e-4, batch 4; Stage II r=8, lr 5e-5, batch 16, 100 epochs. Triggers 1-10% image area

name: FlowHijack
resolvedTitle: FlowHijack: A Dynamics-Aware Backdoor Attack on Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Zhejiang University; Beijing Key Laboratory of Intelligent Space Robotic Systems Technology and Applications; Huzhou Institute of Industrial Control Technology
problem: Backdoor vulnerability studies built for token-based VLAs do not transfer to flow-matching VLAs, whose actions come from ODE integration of a learned vector field; prior triggers are visually conspicuous and their induced motions are kinematically anomalous and detectable.
keyIdea: A backdoor-robustness study that targets the vector field of a flow-matching policy: a loss applied only to the early (low-tau) phase of the flow associates a context-aware trigger with a target action, and a dynamics-mimicry regularizer keeps the triggered motion's velocity magnitude close to benign so it is hard to detect.
architecture: Fine-tunes pi0 (PaliGemma VLM backbone + flow-matching action head) via LoRA. Three components: context-aware visual triggers (object-state / scene-semantic), a tau-conditioned vector-field hijacking loss, and a dynamics-mimicry regularizer.
inputs: RGB observation + language instruction + proprioceptive state (o_t); flow-matching time variable tau in [0,1]
outputs: Continuous action chunk A in R^(d x H) via ODE integration of the vector field
actionRepr: Continuous action chunk generated by flow matching (delta end-effector pose + gripper), same as pi0
params: pi0 base (~3.3B); attack adds LoRA adapters (VLM rank 16/alpha 16, flow head rank 32/alpha 32)
trainingData: LIBERO (Spatial, Object, Goal, LIBERO-10 suites; 50 demos/task); poisoning rate 10% (5 poisoned demos per task)
whatChangedVsParent: Where BadVLA separates VLM features for discrete-token VLAs, FlowHijack instead corrupts the continuous vector field only in the early flow phase and adds a mimicry term so triggered motions stay kinematically indistinguishable.
limitations: Assumes a white-box fine-tuning-poisoning threat model (adversary controls fine-tuning and releases the model); evaluated mainly on pi0 and LIBERO plus a single Franka real-world setup; the Pose-Locking variant is filterable by target-position checks.
notes: Cited by P13 (Safety of Embodied AI survey), which describes it as 'tau-conditioned vector-field injection with a dynamics-mimicry regularizer, producing kinematically indistinguishable triggered actions where prior autoregressive backdoors do not transfer' -- consistent with the paper. Two target strategies: Pose-Locking (constant target pose) and Initial-Perturbation (small persistent offset amplified by the ODE solver). Ablation: removing L_FM gives 100% ASR but 0% clean SR (catastrophic forgetting); removing L_BD gives 0% ASR; removing L_mimic keeps high ASR but loses behavioral stealth.

keyEquations.meaning: Linear interpolation defining the noisy action along the flow path
Standard conditional flow-matching loss matching the target velocity field
Trigger-conditioned loss redirecting the field to a target action, only for tau in [0,tau_0]
Matches triggered field magnitude to benign field magnitude for kinematic similarity

algorithmSteps: Take pretrained pi0; build poisoned set by adding a context-aware trigger to selected clean samples and assigning a target action A* (pose-lock or benign+offset).
For clean samples, apply standard flow-matching loss L_FM.
For poisoned samples, sample tau ~ U[0, tau0=0.4] and apply hijacking loss L_BD toward u(A^tau|A*).
Add dynamics-mimicry regularizer L_mimic matching triggered vs benign field magnitude.
Optimize weighted total L_total = (1-a-b)L_FM + a L_BD + b L_mimic via LoRA (a=b=0.05).
At inference the backdoor stays dormant; when the trigger appears the early-flow error is amplified by the ODE solver into a large final deviation.
ablations: Remove L_FM: ASR 100% but clean SR collapses to 0% (catastrophic forgetting).
Remove L_BD: ASR 0% (no backdoor learned).
tau0 window: ASR 23.9% @0.1, 57.4% @0.2, 100% @0.4 on LIBERO-Goal (Ours-IP) -- too-small window fails.
hyperparams: tau0=0.4 injection window; loss weights alpha=0.05, beta=0.05; poisoning rate 10%; LoRA VLM rank16/alpha16, head rank32/alpha32; 30k steps, batch 8, peak lr 2.5e-5, cosine schedule

name: SilentDrift
resolvedTitle: SilentDrift: Exploiting Action Chunking for Stealthy Backdoor Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
org: University of Southern California; University of Central Florida; Illinois Institute of Technology
problem: Prior VLA backdoor studies induce abrupt behaviors (sudden gripper release, target redirection) that create kinematic discontinuities easily flagged by trajectory validators or human review, limiting their realism.
keyIdea: A backdoor-robustness study identifying an 'intra-chunk visual open-loop': combining action chunking with delta-pose representation means small per-step perturbations integrate uncorrected over a chunk. Perturbations shaped by a Smootherstep (quintic) function give C2-continuous drift that satisfies kinematic-consistency checks, injected only at keyframes (final approach) to stay stealthy.
architecture: Black-box data-poisoning framework, model-agnostic; needs only the ability to inject poisoned demonstrations. Smootherstep-modulated perturbation generator + keyframe selection based on end-effector-to-target distance.
inputs: RGB observations + language instruction (poisoned trajectories); visual trigger a small red circular patch
outputs: Poisoned delta-pose action chunks that accumulate smooth trajectory drift
actionRepr: Delta-pose action chunks (7-DoF relative EE pose + gripper), chunk size K
params: Attack is model-agnostic; evaluated on VLA-Adapter (0.5B) and pi0
trainingData: LIBERO (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long); poisoning rate ~2% (one poisoned episode per task)

headlineResults.comparedTo: confirms open-loop drift scales with K

whatChangedVsParent: Instead of abrupt discontinuous perturbations, it uses C2-continuous Smootherstep drift confined to keyframes, exploiting the action-chunking open-loop so failures look like natural near-misses.
limitations: Authors note dual-use risk as the main limitation; low ASR when the trigger activates too late (0.05m) because the remaining trajectory is too short for drift to accumulate; evaluated only in LIBERO simulation.
notes: Metric definition: ASR = (CTSR - SR_trigger)/CTSR (normalized performance degradation under trigger). Trigger: red circular patch r=5px, alpha=1.0, perturbation magnitude 0.3m, activated when EE within 0.15m of target. Temporal-ensembling analysis (Appendix) shows Smootherstep drift passes ensemble filtering nearly unattenuated while i.i.d. noise is suppressed by sqrt(K) -- the smoothing filter acts as camouflage.

keyEquations.meaning: Delta-pose state update; errors in u_t integrate over time
Poisoned action adds perturbation only when trigger present
Accumulated drift over a K-step chunk grows linearly with chunk size
Smootherstep quintic giving C2-continuous drift (zero velocity/accel at boundaries)

algorithmSteps: Parse instruction to identify target object and ground its position in the first frame.
Find t_start: first step where EE is within distance d_th of the object (critical approach phase).
Set attack window [t_start, t_start+T_window].
Add visual trigger to frames in the window.
Add Smootherstep-modulated drift alpha*d*S(tau_norm) to each clean delta action in the window.
Fine-tune the VLA on the poisoned dataset (~2% poison).
At deployment, monitor EE-to-object distance and activate the backdoor at the point of no return so open-loop drift makes recovery impossible.
ablations: Chunk size: ASR rises 56.1% (K=1) -> 95.6% (K=8) -> 96.2% (K=16), matching E_accum ~ K theory.
Perturbation function: Smootherstep ASR 95.6% comparable to constant/smoothstep but far stealthier kinematically.
Poison ratio: 1% -> 68.7% ASR, 2% (default) -> 95.6%, 4% -> 97.3% (saturates).
hyperparams: chunk size K (up to ~50-100); poison ratio 2% (1 episode/task); drift magnitude 0.3m; trigger r=5px alpha=1.0; activation distance 0.15m; fine-tune up to 15,000 steps on 6x RTX A6000

name: FreezeVLA
resolvedTitle: FreezeVLA: Action-Freezing Attacks against Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Fudan University; Shanghai AI Lab; Sea AI Lab
problem: Adversarial studies on VLAs mostly induce incorrect actions; the opposite failure -- inaction/freezing -- is overlooked yet dangerous because it mimics standby/completion, evades safety monitors, and (unlike wrong actions) keeps a fixed viewpoint so the perturbation stays effective.
keyIdea: A robustness study formulating 'action-freezing' as a min-max bi-level problem: an inner maximization finds 'hard prompts' (synonym-substituted instructions resistant to freezing) and an outer minimization crafts a single adversarial image that forces the freeze token across all of them, yielding strong cross-prompt transfer.
architecture: White-box (to model) / black-box (to user prompt) attack. Inner loop: gradient-based word selection + greedy WordNet synonym substitution over a reference prompt set. Outer loop: PGD-style image update aggregating gradients over the hard-prompt set.
inputs: Camera image (perturbed within L-inf budget eps) + user language instruction
outputs: Adversarial image that makes the VLA emit its inaction token (<eos> for SpatialVLA/pi0, 'do nothing' token for OpenVLA)
trainingData: LIBERO-10, LIBERO-Goal, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Spatial (validation sets); 20 reference prompts (random or o3-generated)
whatChangedVsParent: Adds a min-max bi-level formulation with learnable multi-prompts (hard-prompt search) so one adversarial image transfers across diverse unseen instructions, rather than optimizing against a single prompt.
limitations: White-box threat model (needs model gradients); evaluated only in LIBERO simulation, no real-world test; extending to black-box and dynamic real environments is future work.
notes: Code at github.com/xinwong/FreezeVLA. 'freeze' token differs by tokenizer: <eos> terminates action chunking in SpatialVLA/pi0; OpenVLA uses a special 'do nothing' token. Perturbation budget eps=4/255, 100 image iterations, step 1/255. P13 survey describes it as 'generates cross-prompt adversarial images to induce action-freezing behaviors across diverse user instructions' -- consistent.

keyEquations.meaning: White-box objective driving output toward target (freeze) action tokens
Outer image update aggregating gradients over the hard-prompt set
Min-max bi-level view: prompts resist freezing, image forces it anyway

nodes: inner: gradient word selection + WordNet synonym swap
edges: inner: gradient word selection + WordNet synonym swap
inner: gradient word selection + WordNet synonym swap

algorithmSteps: Initialize adversarial image x' = x and generate a reference prompt set P via an LLM.
Inner maximization: for each prompt find the highest-gradient word and greedily swap it with a WordNet synonym that lowers the freeze probability; accept if it reduces freeze likelihood.
Collect the refined hard-prompt set P*.
Outer minimization: update x' by sign-gradient ascent aggregating the freeze-loss gradients over all p* in P*.
Repeat inner/outer for K outer iterations.
Evaluate the final image on unseen instructions; success = consistent paralysis.
ablations: Multi-Prompt vs single-prompt PGD: OpenVLA avg ASR jumps 17.0% -> 92.0%.
Adding GPT-generated prompts: SpatialVLA 49.0% -> 70.1% (Multi-Prompt) and further with FreezeVLA.
More reference prompts (1->20) steadily raises ASR; default 100 image steps + 10 prompt steps balances cost/effectiveness.
hyperparams: eps=4/255, step alpha=1/255, K=100 image iters, M=10 inner prompt iters, |P|=20 reference prompts, WordNet synonyms; 32x A800-80GB

name: RoboPAIR
resolvedTitle: Jailbreaking LLM-Controlled Robots
org: University of Pennsylvania
problem: LLM jailbreaks were studied for harmful text, but LLM-controlled robots can take physical actions; no algorithm existed to assess whether robots can be induced (via prompts) to produce grounded, executable harmful actions rather than mere text.
keyIdea: A robot-safety red-teaming study adapting the PAIR chatbot-jailbreak loop to robots by (1) giving the attacker/judge robot-specific system prompts with the robot's API and in-context examples, and (2) adding a syntax-checker LLM that scores whether generated code is executable on the target's API -- so prompts elicit grounded, runnable actions.
architecture: Four LLM modules: Attacker, Target (the robot's own LLM), Judge, SyntaxChecker (Attacker/Judge/SyntaxChecker are GPT-4). Iterates K rounds; terminates when both judge and syntax scores exceed thresholds.
inputs: Robot's control interface (text/voice prompts); robot API; harmful-action task description
outputs: Prompt that elicits an executable action plan/code from the robot's LLM
trainingData: Three new red-team datasets of harmful robotic actions (7 actions each) for NVIDIA Dolphins self-driving LLM, Clearpath Jackal UGV, Unitree Go2
whatChangedVsParent: Adds robot-specific system prompts (API + in-context harmful examples) and a syntax-checker so returned prompts yield grounded, executable robot actions instead of ungrounded fictional text.
limitations: Jailbreaks assessed across three specific platforms; static in-context/template/API jailbreaks are already near-100%, raising the question of whether the automated algorithm is even needed -- authors argue LLM-controlled robots are fundamentally unaligned because harm is context/situation-dependent. Ethical release aimed at spurring defenses.
notes: First successful jailbreak of a deployed commercial robot (Unitree Go2). Judge/SyntaxChecker follow LLM-as-a-judge (score 1-10); thresholds t_J=t_S=10, K=10 iterations. P13 groups it under jailbreak/prompt attacks on embodied agents. Also demonstrates an 'API jailbreak' composing existing motion primitives (e.g., disabling obstacle avoidance) to reach 100% ASR.

keyEquations.meaning: Attack success rate metric
Termination rule requiring both harmfulness and executability thresholds

nodes: Attacker LLM (GPT-4, robot API + in-context examples)
edges: Attacker LLM (GPT-4, robot API + in-context examples)
Attacker LLM (GPT-4, robot API + in-context examples)

algorithmSteps: Initialize robot-specific system prompts for Attacker, Target, Judge, SyntaxChecker; empty CONTEXT.
Attacker proposes a candidate prompt from CONTEXT.
Target (robot LLM) produces a response / action code.
Judge scores harmfulness; SyntaxChecker scores API-executability.
If both scores exceed thresholds, return the prompt; else append (prompt, response, scores) to CONTEXT.
Repeat for up to K=10 rounds.
ablations: PAIR vs RoboPAIR on Go2: 17/35 -> 35/35 by adding robot system prompts + syntax checker.
In-context and template static jailbreaks alone reach ~89-97% ASR across robots.
RoboPAIR reaches 100% ASR regardless of whether the Go2 uses GPT-3.5 or GPT-4.
hyperparams: K=10 iterations; judge/syntax thresholds t_J=t_S=10; Attacker/Judge/SyntaxChecker = GPT-4; 5 trials per action; 7 harmful actions per robot

name: BADROBOT
resolvedTitle: BadRobot: Jailbreaking Embodied LLM Agents in the Physical World
org: Huazhong University of Science and Technology; Beihang University; Griffith University
problem: Existing LLM jailbreaks (text-based) largely fail to transfer to embodied LLMs, which add an action-planning space; no paradigm existed to make embodied LLMs actually perform unsafe physical actions via ordinary voice/text interaction.
keyIdea: A safety-evaluation study (ICLR 2025) identifying three risk surfaces of embodied LLMs and three matching attack forms: (1) contextual jailbreak that cascades a compromised LLM into malicious commands, (2) safety misalignment where the model verbally refuses but still emits the unsafe action (function) output, and (3) conceptual deception that rephrases a harmful goal into seemingly innocent steps the model executes.
architecture: No-box paradigm (voice/text I/O, no gradients). Three attack algorithms operating on the embodied LLM stack (task planner + action pool + world model). Includes a benchmark of 277 physical-world malicious queries across 7 harm categories.
inputs: Voice/text user instruction (optionally with jailbreak prompt p, suffix s, or semantic rephrasing)
outputs: Unsafe action plans (JSON/YAML/code) executed by downstream robot control
trainingData: Benchmark of 277 malicious physical-action queries (Physical Harm, Privacy, Pornography, Fraud, Illegal Activity, Hateful Conduct, Sabotage); tested on GPT-4-turbo, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o, LLaVA-1.5-7B, Yi-vision and frameworks VoxPoser, Code as Policies, ProgPrompt, Visual Programming
parents: VoxPoser / Code as Policies / ProgPrompt (embodied LLM frameworks)
whatChangedVsParent: Moves jailbreaking from eliciting harmful text to eliciting harmful physical actions by exploiting the action-output space and language-action misalignment unique to embodied LLMs.
limitations: Hand-crafted contextual prompts can be patched point-to-point by commercial LLMs; the paper frames prompts as a class of ideas rather than optimal. World-model fine-tuning only partially mitigates (helps conceptual deception, worsens jailbreak/misalignment). Human-in-the-loop suggested as final safeguard.
notes: First jailbreak of a real robotic-arm system (Elephant/UR arm). Metric MSR = Manipulation/Malicious Success Rate; also a GPT-4 Judge harmfulness score (1-5). Safety-misalignment key finding: aligned LLMs refuse in the 'response' field but still populate the 'function' field with the unsafe action. P13 survey references its three-risk taxonomy (also echoed by POEX's related work).

keyEquations.meaning: Threat objective: minimize action-safety score (i.e., force unsafe actions) over malicious queries
Safety misalignment: safe language output but unsafe action output

symbols.meaning: suffix instruction forcing structured action output

keyEquations.meaning: Contextual jailbreak: both language and action outputs compromised

algorithmSteps: Build a benchmark of 277 physical-world malicious queries across 7 harm categories.
Contextual jailbreak: prepend a role-play/sandbox prompt p aligned with the robotic-assistant system prompt, then the malicious query.
Safety misalignment: append suffix s ('ensure structured, complete action output') to exploit weaker scrutiny of code/function outputs.
Conceptual deception: use an LLM to rephrase the harmful query into innocuous-seeming steps preserving intent.
Feed to the embodied LLM; count success when the action output is unsafe (S_A=0).
Evaluate MSR across LLMs and against VoxPoser/CaP/ProgPrompt/VisProg, plus a real robot arm.
ablations: Contextual/Safety-Misalignment/Conceptual raise avg MSR by +215.9%/+193.8%/+213.7% over vanilla.
World-model fine-tuning (LLaVA-1.5-7B) lowers conceptual-deception MSR but raises contextual-jailbreak and misalignment MSR.
Prompt-design insights: incorporate role-play/disguised intent, minimize conflict with the robot system prompt, keep prompts short.
hyperparams: 277-query benchmark; 7 harm categories; MSR + GPT-4 Judge (1-5); multiple contextual-jailbreak prompt variants averaged; no gradient optimization (no-box)

name: POEX
resolvedTitle: POEX: Policy Executable Embodied AI Jailbreak Attacks
org: Zhejiang University
problem: Traditional LLM jailbreaks produce harmful text that does not necessarily yield harmful policies in embodied AI, and even when a harmful policy is generated it is often non-executable (hallucinated/illogical); no method ensured both jailbreak success and real-world executability.
keyIdea: A safety-analysis study proposing a policy-executable jailbreak: optimize a readable word-level adversarial suffix appended to a harmful instruction, using a four-module loop (mutator/constraint/selector/evaluator) where a fine-tuned LLM policy-evaluator scores executability, so the resulting policy both bypasses safety and runs on the robot's API.
architecture: White-box (to planning LLM). Modules: initialization (readable suffix), mutator (greedy coordinate gradient restricted to English tokens), constraint (perplexity filter), selector (weighted reference + policy-executability loss), evaluator (prefix matching + fine-tuned LLM policy evaluator scoring 0-4).
inputs: Harmful instruction + optimized adversarial suffix + system prompt/context; pre-defined API primitives
outputs: Executable harmful policy (sequence of API/composer calls) for the embodied AI
params: Policy evaluator fine-tuned on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (LoRA) and GPT-4o-mini; attacks Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B, Vicuna-13B (white-box) plus black-box transfer to GPT-4-Turbo, Mixtral-8x22B, Llama-3.1-70B
trainingData: Harmful-RLbench: 25 hand-crafted task scenarios, 126 correct + 136 harmful instructions on RLbench/Franka Panda; evaluator fine-tuned on ~5500 instruction-policy-score sets
whatChangedVsParent: Constrains the suffix to readable English words (low perplexity, voice-injectable) and adds a fine-tuned policy-executability evaluator into the optimization loop, so jailbreaks yield runnable policies, not just harmful text.
limitations: White-box access to the planning LLM assumed; harmful instructions released only on request for ethics; defenses (safety-constrained prompts, pre-/post-checks, HarmBench-with-context) partially mitigate. Focused on LLM-planner embodied stacks, not end-to-end VLAs.
notes: Harmful-RLbench is the first general-purpose manipulation dataset with harmful task scenarios (knives, fragile vases) on a Franka Emika Panda in RLbench, transferable to real hardware via unified Pyrep interfaces. Metrics: ASR (non-refusal rate), PSR (policy success rate = executable+harmful), PPR, WER. Defense: HarmBench-with-context reaches ~81-94% precision, far above Llama Guard. P13 cites it among jailbreak attacks on LLM-planning embodied agents.

keyEquations.meaning: Selector loss balancing jailbreak (reference) loss and policy-executability loss
Executability loss from the fine-tuned policy evaluator score Q in [0,4]
Normalized inverted-gradient score ranking token replacements (English-only)

symbols.meaning: gradient of cross-entropy loss for token j at position i

keyEquations.meaning: Perplexity constraint keeping the suffix stealthy/readable

algorithmSteps: Initialize a low-perplexity adversarial suffix (repeated English word or pre-trained suffix).
Mutator: compute GCG gradients, restrict to English tokens, randomly swap one token from the top-k.
Constraint: filter candidate suffixes above the perplexity threshold.
Selector: score candidates by weighted reference loss + policy-executability loss, keep the lowest.
Evaluator: prefix-match against API names and score executability with the fine-tuned evaluator.
If both jailbreak-success and executable, stop; else repeat mutation/constraint/selection/evaluation.
ablations: POEX vs GCG/AutoDAN: much higher PSR (e.g., Vicuna 78.68% vs 26.47%/10.29%) and far lower WER.
Transferability: combining suffixes from 3 white-box models reaches 100% ASR / 63.24% PSR on Mixtral-8x22B.
Defenses: HarmBench-with-context precision 80.95-94.39% vs Llama Guard 2/3 much lower.
hyperparams: suffix length 5; 64 mutations/step; batch 16; top-256 gradient tokens; temperature 0.01; evaluator LoRA on Llama-3-8B (lr 5e-5, max len 1024, bf16); 2x A800

name: BYOVLA
resolvedTitle: Run-time Observation Interventions Make Vision-Language-Action Models More Visually Robust (Bring Your Own VLA)
org: Princeton University (Dept. of Mechanical & Aerospace Engineering)
problem: State-of-the-art VLAs are brittle to task-irrelevant visual details (distractor objects, background color changes) that leave task difficulty unchanged yet drop success rates by up to 40%; fine-tuning to fix this is costly and needs model weights.
keyIdea: A run-time (test-time) defense/robustness intervention: identify task-irrelevant regions with a VLM, probe which of them the VLA is actually sensitive to by perturbing them and measuring action change, then minimally edit (inpaint objects / recolor backgrounds) only the sensitive-and-irrelevant regions -- no fine-tuning or weight access.
architecture: Model-agnostic pipeline orchestrating GPT-4o (task-irrelevant region proposals), Grounded-SAM2 (segmentation masks), a visual-sensitivity probe, and Inpaint Anything (image editing). Wraps any off-the-shelf VLA.
inputs: RGB observation o_t + language instruction l
outputs: Transformed observation rho_f(o_t) fed to the unchanged VLA, which then outputs its action chunk
actionRepr: Does not change action representation; VLA outputs action chunk (a_t..a_{t+Ta}) of relative EE displacement + gripper
params: No added trainable params; wraps Octo-Base (93M) and OpenVLA (7B)
trainingData: None (run-time only); thresholds calibrated on 60 BridgeData V2 environments; tasks 'put carrot on yellow plate', 'put eggplant in pot'
controlRateHz: Octo-Base 13Hz, OpenVLA 6Hz base; object-distraction steps 1-3 add ~2s (GPT-4o query <3s once at init)

headlineResults.benchmark: Octo-Base, object distractions ('carrot on yellow plate')
headlineResults.comparedTo: distractors drop it by 40%; GradCAM/BYOVLA\Sens fail to recover

whatChangedVsParent: Rather than domain-randomization at training time or masking all irrelevant regions, it edits only regions the model is provably sensitive to, at run time, keeping edited observations realistic and preserving nominal performance.
limitations: Relies on orchestrating multiple foundation models (integration challenges); GPT-4o sometimes misses irrelevant objects (e.g., stovetop lids), so OpenVLA does not fully regain nominal; object/background distinction and the sensitivity threshold tau are hand-tuned; only static environments tested.
notes: Website aasherh.github.io/byovla with code. Sensitivity probe perturbs a region (Gaussian blur for objects, Gaussian noise for backgrounds) and measures weighted L2 change in the action chunk; intervene if above threshold. Thresholds tau=2mm (objects), 1mm (backgrounds) from BridgeV2 third-quartile calibration. P13 lists it as a defense/robustness intervention (VLSA-adjacent run-time protection). This is a defense paper, not an attack.

keyEquations.meaning: VLA acts on the intervened observation instead of the raw one
Visual sensitivity of the VLA to region r (weighted L2 action change under perturbation)

nodes: visual sensitivity probe (perturb region, measure action change)
edges: visual sensitivity probe (perturb region, measure action change)
visual sensitivity probe (perturb region, measure action change)

algorithmSteps: Query GPT-4o (few-shot) once to list task-irrelevant object and background regions.
Each step, use Grounded-SAM2 to get pixel masks for those regions.
For each region, perturb it (blur for objects, noise for backgrounds) and sample K action chunks to compute sensitivity Delta_f.
If Delta_f >= threshold tau, edit the region: inpaint objects with Inpaint Anything, or recolor background until Delta_f < tau.
Feed the transformed observation to the unchanged VLA to get the action chunk.
ablations: vs BYOVLA\Sens (edit all irrelevant regions, no sensitivity probe): probe needed to retain nominal SR on Octo.
vs GradCAM sensitivity: GradCAM misses regions Octo is sensitive to and fails to recover nominal SR.
Running the probe every step ('-Full') gives no extra benefit in static scenes; sampling K observations vs K actions is roughly equivalent.
hyperparams: tau=2mm (objects), 1mm (backgrounds); K=5 rollouts (Octo, Ta=3), K=1 (OpenVLA, no chunking); Gaussian blur kernel 25 for objects, Gaussian noise N(0,sqrt(0.075)) for backgrounds; Grounded-SAM2 conf 0.4; inpaint mask dilation 10

name: VLSA
resolvedTitle: VLSA: Vision-Language-Action Models with Plug-and-Play Safety Constraint Layer
org: Tsinghua University (Dept. of Automation; Institute for Embodied Intelligence and Robotics); TetraBOT; DAMO Academy, Alibaba
problem: VLA models have no explicit collision-safety guarantee; RL-based safety (e.g. SafeVLA) needs costly retraining and treats safety as a soft reward penalty rather than a hard constraint.
keyIdea: VLSA architecture: add a training-free, plug-and-play safety constraint (SC) layer after any VLA's action output. The concrete instance AEGIS uses a VLM + open-set detector to find the task-relevant obstacle, fits ellipsoids, and minimally corrects the VLA action with a control-barrier-function QP.
architecture: Base VLA (pi0.5-LIBERO in sim, pi0.5-DROID zero-shot on real) -> SC layer = (1) vision-language safety assessment: VLM (GLM-4.5V) names the single most critical obstacle, GroundingDINO localizes it, depth/point cloud (DBSCAN filtering) gives geometry fitted with minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoids (MVEE); (2) safety-guaranteed control: ellipsoid-ellipsoid CBF with a virtual supporting-hyperplane state, solved as a convex QP with one linear constraint.
inputs: Agent-view RGB, depth/point cloud, language instruction, nominal VLA action
outputs: Safe end-effector action u_safe = [v, omega, gripper] (identical to the VLA action when no risk is detected)
actionRepr: Post-hoc filter on the base VLA's end-effector velocity commands (translational v, rotational omega, gripper g); base pi0.5 produces flow-matching action chunks
trainingData: None (training-free). Evaluated on SafeLIBERO: 16 LIBERO tasks x 2 obstacle levels = 32 scenarios, 50 episodes each = 1,600 episodes.
controlRateHz: 20 Hz in simulation (OSC_POSE, Robosuite); real robot: VLA inference 15 Hz, low-level controller 1 kHz
whatChangedVsParent: Unlike SafeVLA's constrained-RL retraining, safety is enforced at inference as a hard CBF constraint on top of an unmodified pretrained VLA.
limitations: 100% collision avoidance is not reached because of upstream perception errors (misidentified obstacles, bad grounding, over-aggressive point-cloud filtering) and because only the end-effector (not other links) is constrained; safety corrections can push the policy into out-of-distribution states (e.g. higher altitudes) where it fails the task. Dynamic obstacles and whole-body avoidance are left to future work.
notes: Paper's method name is AEGIS (Action Execution Guarded by Invariant Safety); VLSA = Vision-Language-Safe Action architecture class. Theorem 1 guarantees end-effector collision-freedom assuming accurate assessment, filtering and enclosing ellipsoids (via Nagumo's theorem). Code/benchmark released at vlsa-aegis.github.io (training-free, so 'open weights' means code + benchmark). Hyperparameters: alpha(h)=10h, reference control coefficient k=10, end-effector MVEE Q_ef = diag(0.06, 0.12, 0.11) m, horizons 300 steps (Spatial/Goal/Object) and 550 (Long). Real-world: Franka Panda + Robotiq 2F-85, ZED 2 + ZED Mini, qualitative comparison only (video).

keyEquations.meaning: Safe set is the superlevel set of the barrier function h over ellipsoid geometry plus virtual state.

symbols.meaning: ellipsoid geometric parameters plus virtual auxiliary state

keyEquations.meaning: QP minimally modifies the VLA action so the safe set stays forward-invariant.

algorithmSteps: Base VLA predicts nominal action u_vla from image and instruction.
VLM is prompted to name the single most critical non-robot obstacle given instruction + agent-view image.
GroundingDINO grounds the name to a bounding box; depth gives a filtered obstacle point cloud.
Fit minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoids for obstacle and end-effector.
Build ellipsoid CBF h(x) via a virtual supporting hyperplane state.
Solve convex QP: minimize ||u - u_vla||^2 subject to hdot >= -alpha(h).
Execute u_safe (equals u_vla when constraint inactive).
ablations: CBF value h(x) stays strictly positive over all four SafeLIBERO suites (constraint evolution plots).
SC layer adds 0.356 ms/step, about 1/47 of VLA inference time, keeping 20 Hz loop.
Long suite, translational: CAR 79.6% vs pi0.5 12.8%, TSR 43.8% vs 35.8%.
hyperparams: alpha(h)=10h; k=10; Q_ef=diag(0.06,0.12,0.11) m; dynamics pdot=0.2u; 20 Hz; horizons 300/550 steps

name: SafeVLA
resolvedTitle: SafeVLA: Towards Safety Alignment of Vision-Language-Action Model via Constrained Learning
org: Peking University (Institute for AI; PKU-PsiBot Joint Lab; State Key Lab of General AI); Zhongguancun Academy
problem: VLA training (imitation or RL fine-tuning) optimizes task success with no explicit physical-safety constraints, and LLM-style safety alignment does not address concrete physical hazards.
keyIdea: Integrated Safety Approach (ISA): model safety as predicates in a CMDP, elicit risks with safety-critical scene components (Safety-CHORES), constrain the VLA with Lagrangian PPO (min-max over policy and multipliers), then assure safety with test-time, long-tail and extreme-failure evaluation.
architecture: Base VLA is SPOC (DINOv2 variant): pretrained text encoder (SigLIP) for goals, goal-conditioned transformer encoder fusing navigation + manipulation camera RGB with language (3 layers, 512 hidden, 8 heads), causal transformer decoder (3 layers, 512 hidden, 8 heads) with 100-step context predicting discrete actions. Fine-tuned with PPO-Lagrangian using separate reward and cost advantages.
inputs: History of RGB observations (two cameras) + proprioception, language instruction
outputs: Discrete mobile-manipulation actions
actionRepr: Discrete actions from a causal transformer decoder (SPOC action space), one per step
trainingData: RL in AI2THOR on ProcTHOR scenes (150K procedural houses) with Objaverse assets (800K); 15M env steps for Safety-ObjNav/PickUp, 25M for Safety-Fetch; 8x H100.
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces FLaRe's task-only RL fine-tuning of SPOC with constrained (Lagrangian) RL on explicit safety-predicate costs in a risk-eliciting benchmark.
limitations: Relies primarily on simulation (AI2THOR) with only a small sim-to-real demonstration; cost assignment from predicates can be refined; setting is mobile manipulation with discrete actions, not continuous-control VLAs.
notes: Published NeurIPS 2025. Five safety-critical components: corners, blind spots, fragile collections, critical points, dangerous equipment. Cost threshold b = 20% of baseline (FLaRe) converged cost (e.g. 11.5982 on ObjNav). Data, models, benchmark released at pku-safevla.github.io. Also tested PID- and Augmented-Lagrangian variants (Table 11). CONFLICT-watch: surveys may call it a 'VLA safety' method generally; it is evaluated on navigation+pick mobile manipulation (Safety-ObjNav/PickUp/Fetch), not tabletop continuous control.

keyEquations.meaning: Maximize instruction-conditioned return over policies satisfying every expected-cost limit.

symbols.meaning: reward return conditioned on instruction l

keyEquations.meaning: Lagrangian relaxation into a min-max over policy parameters and multipliers.
Combined PPO surrogate mixing reward and cost clipped objectives, normalized by 1+lambda.

symbols.meaning: PPO clipped surrogate with reward advantage
PPO clipped surrogate with cost advantage

keyEquations.meaning: Dual ascent: multiplier grows when expected cost exceeds the limit.

algorithmSteps: Initialize from IL-pretrained SPOC-DINOv2.
Roll out policy in procedurally generated Safety-CHORES scenes with safety-critical components.
Label steps with reward and with costs from state-action (cost at violating step) and trajectory predicates (cost at end of violating segment).
Compute reward and cost advantages (GAE, gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95).
Update theta with the combined clipped PPO loss weighted by 1/(1+lambda).
Update lambda by dual ascent on (J_C - b).
Repeat for 15M-25M steps; evaluate SR and cumulative cost.
ablations: Without risk elicitation (no safety-critical components): SR 0.64, CC 5.01 vs full ISA SR 0.86, CC 1.85 (FLaRe-RS 0.75 / 4.75).
Cost threshold 10% / 20% / 50% of FLaRe cost: CC 1.16 / 1.85 / 5.91 with SR 0.82 / 0.86 / 0.87.
Dynamic Lagrange multipliers beat all fixed-penalty baselines that meet the same cost limit (Fig. 6).
hyperparams: PPO clip 0.1, lr 2e-5, gamma 0.99, GAE 0.95, 128 steps/update, 4 update repeats; initial lambda 0.001, lambda lr 0.035; b = 20% of FLaRe cost; 100-step context

name: SafeDreamer
resolvedTitle: SafeDreamer: Safe Reinforcement Learning with World Model
org: Peking University (Institute of AI); Beihang University
problem: Lagrangian SafeRL fails to reach near-zero cost (or sacrifices the task) at low cost thresholds, especially from vision-only input, due to model/critic inaccuracy and poor sample efficiency; MPC planners are short-sighted without cost critics.
keyIdea: Extend DreamerV3 with a cost decoder and cost critic, and combine Lagrangian methods with safety-reward planning inside the learned world model, either online (constrained CEM, OSRP / OSRP-Lag) or in the background to train a safe actor (BSRP-Lag).
architecture: DreamerV3 RSSM world model (GRU sequence model, discrete latents 48x48) with observation, reward and cost decoders; actor, reward critic and cost critic on model state s_t = {h_t, z_t}. Three variants: OSRP (constrained CEM planning), OSRP-Lag (CEM with PID-Lagrangian sorting key), BSRP-Lag (actor trained on imagined rollouts with augmented Lagrangian).
inputs: Images (64x64 vision tasks) or low-dimensional vectors; reward and cost signals
outputs: Continuous actions
actionRepr: Single continuous action per step (action repeat 4); OSRP executes the first action of a planned H=15 trajectory
trainingData: Online interaction in Safety-Gymnasium (5 vision tasks, 2 low-dimensional tasks), plus MetaDrive, Car-Racing, FormulaOne; e.g. results after 2M steps for vision tasks.

headlineResults.metric: Cost vs LAMBDA at similar reward

whatChangedVsParent: Adds cost decoder, cost critic and Lagrangian-constrained safety-reward planning (online CCEM or background actor training) to DreamerV3.
limitations: Cost threshold cannot be exactly zero for planning variants because learned cost models/critics are never exactly zero (2.0 used for vision tasks); OSRP is slow for real-time use and limited in planning length/samples for dexterous behavior; evaluated in simulation navigation/driving, not robot manipulation.
notes: ICLR 2024. Code at github.com/PKU-Alignment/SafeDreamer. Claimed first to reach near-zero cost on vision-only Safety-Gymnasium. OSRP beats BSRP-Lag on dynamic SafetyPointButton1; BSRP-Lag better on SafetyPointPush1. Same PKU-Alignment group (Yaodong Yang, Jiaming Ji, Borong Zhang) as SafeVLA. Not a manipulation method; cited as safe world-model RL.

keyEquations.meaning: Lagrangian relaxation of reward maximization under world-model-estimated cost constraint.

symbols.meaning: reward return under world model P_phi

keyEquations.tex: C^\lambda(s_t) = \begin{cases} C_\phi(s_t) + \gamma\left((1-\lambda)V_{\psi_c}(s_{t+1}) + \lambda C^\lambda(s_{t+1})\right) & t<H \\ V_{\psi_c}(s_t) & t=H \end{cases}
keyEquations.meaning: TD(lambda) cost return from cost model and cost critic along imagined rollout.
BSRP-Lag actor loss: maximize reward return and entropy, minus augmented-Lagrangian cost penalty.

keyEquations.tex: L(\phi) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \alpha_q KL[z_t \| \mathrm{sg}(\hat{z}_t)] + \alpha_p KL[\mathrm{sg}(z_t)\|\hat{z}_t] - \beta_o \ln O_\phi(o_t|s_t) - \beta_r \ln R_\phi(r_t|s_t) - \beta_c \ln C_\phi(c_t|s_t)
keyEquations.meaning: World model loss: KL regularization/prediction plus observation, reward and cost likelihoods.

algorithmSteps: Sample B trajectories from replay; train world model with Eq. 9.
Imagine latent rollouts from replay states; train reward and cost critics.
OSRP: sample N=500 Gaussian + actor trajectories over H=15 in the world model; estimate reward return (TD-lambda) and cost J^C' = (J^{C,H}/H)L.
If fewer than N_s trajectories are safe, rank by -cost; else rank safe set by reward (OSRP) or reward - lambda_p cost (OSRP-Lag).
Refit Gaussian to top-k elites; iterate J=6 times; execute first action.
BSRP-Lag instead: update safe actor with augmented-Lagrangian loss and act from it directly.
Update lambda_p from episode cost (PID Lagrangian or augmented Lagrangian rule).
ablations: Lower cost limit (1.0 / 0.1 / 0.01) pushes cost closer to zero but reduces reward (SafetyPointGoal1/2).
Removing reconstruction loss slows reward convergence and cost fails to decrease.
Larger stochastic latent (48x48 vs 32x32 vs 16x16) gives larger cost reduction; higher cost-loss weight helps under unbalanced cost.
hyperparams: Latents 48x48; batch 64 x length 16; planning horizon H=15; N=500 samples; J=6 CCEM iterations; PID Kp 0.1, Ki 0.01, Kd 0.01; imagination horizon 15; gamma 0.997; cost threshold 2.0 (vision) / 0 (vector); action repeat 4

name: LIBERO-Plus
resolvedTitle: LIBERO-Plus: In-depth Robustness Analysis of Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Fudan University (OpenMOSS); Tongji University; Shanghai Innovation Institute; National University of Singapore
problem: Near-perfect VLA scores on LIBERO are measured under static ideal conditions and hide brittleness to realistic variation.
keyIdea: Systematically perturb LIBERO along 7 dimensions (object layout, camera viewpoint, robot initial state, language, lighting, background texture, sensor noise; 21 sub-dimensions, 5 difficulty levels) to diagnose 10 open VLAs, and release a 10,030-task robustness benchmark plus a 20K-trajectory generalization training set.
architecture: Benchmark/diagnostic, not a policy. Automated perturbation generator on LIBERO -> 14,000 candidate tasks filtered to 10,030 and stratified into L1-L5 by success of 4 reference models; compositionality analysis via conditional covariance with chi-square tests; baseline fine-tune of OpenVLA-OFT on generalized data.
inputs: Evaluated VLAs' standard inputs (third-person and wrist RGB, language, proprio)
outputs: Success rates per perturbation dimension and difficulty level
trainingData: Generalization training set: 22,400 collected trajectories (replaying LIBERO state-action pairs in perturbed scenes), >20,000 successful kept; fine-tune OpenVLA-OFT 100K steps on 8x A100.
whatChangedVsParent: Extends LIBERO from fixed ideal-condition tasks to 10,030 perturbed tasks across 7 factors and 5 difficulty levels with fine-grained failure diagnosis.
limitations: Built in LIBERO simulation only; language-robustness numbers are 'deceptive' because models ignore language; perturbation levels are defined relative to four reference models.
notes: Key findings: most fragile to camera viewpoint and robot initial state; relatively robust to lighting/background; wrist camera gives illumination and viewpoint robustness (OpenVLA-OFT vs third-view-only OFT_w camera 59.7 vs 16.8); models largely ignore language (blank-instruction and goal-replacement tests); negative compositionality gap for all perturbation pairs (Finding 9), from 2000 trials per condition with OpenVLA-OFT. Language perturbation had second-smallest average drop (-25.3). Abstract headline: performance drops from 95% to below 30% under modest camera/robot perturbations. Released on GitHub and HuggingFace (sylvestf/LIBERO-plus). Slight table inconsistency in paper: text says 79.6% total, Table 2 shows 79.5%.

keyEquations.tex: \Delta_{ij} \triangleq \mathrm{Cov}(D_i, D_j \mid Y=1) = p(D_i=1, D_j=1 \mid Y=1) - p(D_i=1 \mid Y=1)\, p(D_j=1 \mid Y=1)
keyEquations.meaning: Compositionality gap: negative means combined perturbations hurt more than independent effects predict.

symbols.meaning: indicator that perturbation i is applied

keyEquations.tex: p(D_i = d_i, D_j = d_j \mid Y = 1) = \frac{s(D_i=d_i, D_j=d_j)}{\sum_{a,b \in \{0,1\}} s(D_i=a, D_j=b)}
keyEquations.meaning: Share of successes under each perturbation combination, from measured success rates.

algorithmSteps: Apply single-dimension perturbations to LIBERO evaluation episodes for 10 open VLAs.
Run targeted probes: object-layout decomposition, all-black / third-view-black images, blank instruction, goal replacement.
Measure pairwise-perturbation success over 2000 trials and compute compositionality gap with chi-square test.
Generate 14,000 perturbed tasks; filter and balance to 10,030.
Stratify into five difficulty levels using OpenVLA-OFT, pi0, pi0-fast, UniVLA.
Build 20K+ perturbed-scene trajectories and fine-tune OpenVLA-OFT; evaluate on LIBERO-Plus.
ablations: Third-view-only OpenVLA-OFT_w vs OpenVLA-OFT with wrist camera: camera 16.8 vs 59.7, noise 51.4 vs 76.7.
Pairwise perturbations: e.g. camera+robot joint success 9.64% vs independence-predicted 10.86% (gap -1.22); all pairwise gaps negative.
Generalized-data fine-tuning: +37.2 points on camera, +11.6 total over OpenVLA-OFT_m.
hyperparams: 7 factors / 21 sub-dimensions / 5 levels; 10,030 test tasks; fine-tune lr 5e-4, 100K steps, effective batch 16, AdamW wd 0.1, cosine schedule

name: LIBERO
resolvedTitle: LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning
org: The University of Texas at Austin; Sony AI; Tsinghua University
problem: Lifelong learning benchmarks focus on declarative knowledge in vision/NLP; decision-making needs transfer of procedural knowledge too, and no manipulation benchmark disentangles the two.
keyIdea: A procedurally generated lifelong robot-manipulation benchmark (Robosuite) with task suites that isolate spatial, object and goal knowledge transfer, plus 50 human teleop demos per task and LLDM metrics (FWT, NBT, AUC).
architecture: Benchmark: procedural generation pipeline (behavior templates from Ego4D -> instructions; PDDL initial-state distributions; goal as conjunction of predicates). Baseline policies: ResNet-RNN, ResNet-T, ViT-T (BERT language embedding; GMM action head), trained with behavior cloning; LL algorithms SeqL, ER, EWC, PackNet, MTL.
inputs: RGB images (workspace + wrist), proprioception, language instruction
outputs: Continuous end-effector actions
actionRepr: Single continuous end-effector action per step sampled from a GMM head (baseline policies)
trainingData: 130 tasks in four suites (LIBERO-Spatial 10, -Object 10, -Goal 10, LIBERO-100 = LIBERO-90 + LIBERO-Long 10), 50 human-teleoperated demos per task (3Dconnexion SpaceMouse).
whatChangedVsParent: Adds procedural task generation and suites that disentangle declarative vs procedural knowledge transfer for lifelong learning in manipulation.
limitations: Sequential finetuning gives the best forward transfer (LL algorithms hurt FWT); naive supervised pretraining on LIBERO-90 can hurt downstream lifelong learning; results sensitive to task ordering; language embeddings act like task IDs.
notes: NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks. Evaluation: 20 rollouts per task, max 600 steps, every 5 epochs; 50 epochs per task; Adam, batch 32, cosine LR 1e-4 -> 1e-5. CONFLICT-watch: LIBERO was designed as a lifelong-learning benchmark; VLA papers use the four suites (Spatial/Object/Goal/Long) as a multitask success-rate benchmark, where scores are now near-saturated (e.g. OpenVLA-OFT 97.1% avg per LIBERO-Plus) - that usage is not the paper's original protocol. Control rate not stated in paper (Robosuite default commonly 20 Hz per VLSA/SafeLIBERO; not from LIBERO paper).

keyEquations.meaning: Forward transfer: average success on new task k across training checkpoints.

symbols.meaning: success on task k after e epochs of training on it

keyEquations.meaning: Negative backward transfer: forgetting of task k after learning later tasks.

symbols.meaning: best success on task k when learned
success on task k after learning task tau

keyEquations.meaning: Area under success curve combining learning speed and retention.

symbols.meaning: number of tasks in the sequence

algorithmSteps: Generate instruction from Ego4D-derived behavior template.
Sample scene and specify initial object layout/status in PDDL.
Specify goal as conjunction of unary/binary predicates; episode ends when all hold.
Collect 50 teleoperated demos per task.
Train policy by BC on tasks sequentially (50 epochs each) with an LL algorithm.
Evaluate every 5 epochs (20 rollouts) and on all previous tasks; compute FWT, NBT, AUC.
ablations: SeqL has best FWT on all suites (e.g. Long 0.54 vs ER 0.48) but worst forgetting (NBT 0.63).
Transformer temporal backbones beat RNN: LIBERO-Long ER AUC ResNet-T 0.32 vs ResNet-RNN 0.08.
Pretraining on LIBERO-90 can reduce downstream LIBERO-Long lifelong performance (Fig. 5).
hyperparams: 4 suites / 130 tasks; 50 demos per task; 50 epochs per task; eval 20 rollouts, max 600 steps; ER buffer up to 1000 traj, 32 replayed; EWC lambda 5e4, gamma 0.9; PackNet keeps 25%

name: CALVIN
resolvedTitle: CALVIN: A Benchmark for Language-Conditioned Policy Learning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Tasks
org: University of Freiburg; University of Technology Nuremberg
problem: No standard open benchmark combined natural-language conditioning, multimodal high-dimensional sensing, 7-DoF continuous control and long-horizon chained manipulation with zero-shot generalization.
keyIdea: Four structurally related PyBullet tabletop environments (A-D) with ~24h of unscripted teleoperated play data, 1% language-annotated, and evaluations of 34 tasks and 1000 chains of 5 instructions, including zero-shot transfer to an unseen environment (ABC->D).
architecture: Benchmark: Franka Panda with parallel gripper, desk with sliding door, drawer, button/LED, switch/lightbulb, three colored blocks; automatic task detector from state change. Baseline MCIL: seq2seq CVAE latent plan model with per-modality encoders (conv for gripper cam, ResNet-18 for tactile), early-fusion depth.
inputs: Static RGB-D (200x200), gripper RGB-D (84x84), vision-based tactile (120x160x2), proprioception, language instruction
outputs: Continuous 7-DoF arm actions + gripper
actionRepr: Absolute Cartesian pose, relative Cartesian displacement, or joint positions + gripper (baseline uses absolute Cartesian), one per step at 30 Hz
trainingData: ~24h teleoperated play (6h per environment, ~2.4M interaction steps); 389 unique crowd-sourced instructions (~11 per task) for 34 tasks, automatically aligned; only 1% of data language-labeled; precomputed MiniLM embeddings.

headlineResults.benchmark: CALVIN MTLC (34 tasks), D->D, static RGB

parents: MCIL / Language from Play (Lynch et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Versus Lynch et al.'s play setup: 34 vs 18 subtasks, 5 vs 4 instruction chains, multi-sensor suite, four environments with zero-shot evaluation and unseen instructions.
limitations: Objects are simplified unicolored primitive shapes; baseline MCIL performs poorly on long horizons and does not benefit from extra sensors; policy performance depends on initial robot pose (possible causal confusion with proprioception).
notes: RA-L 2022. Standard metric later used by VLA papers is average chain length (0-5) over 1000 LH-MTLC chains, computed from the per-step success rates; that 'avg len' metric is not reported in this paper, which reports per-position success percentages. Robot reset to neutral pose after each chain. Tasks listed in Fig. 6 with success criteria (e.g. slider moved >=12 cm, drawer >=10 cm, lift >=5 cm). Baseline: Adam lr 1e-4, KL beta 0.001, windows 16-32. openWeights refers to benchmark/data/code release.

keyEquations.meaning: Goal-conditioned imitation on hindsight-relabeled play windows (MCIL baseline basis).

algorithmSteps: Collect unscripted teleop play in environments A-D.
Sample 64-frame windows; task detector checks a task is solved at the end but not in the first half; attach one of ~11 synonymous instructions.
Train policy (MCIL baseline) on relabeled goal-image and language windows.
MTLC: 10 rollouts per task from valid unseen start states with unseen instructions.
LH-MTLC: 1000 feasible 5-instruction chains; advance only when detector confirms success; reset to neutral pose per chain.
ablations: Adding gripper RGB: D->D MTLC 51.8% vs 53.9% static-only (no gain).
Adding tactile: D->D MTLC 54.2%, LH first instruction 28.5% vs 48.9%.
All RGB-D cameras: ABC->D MTLC 30.8% vs 38.6% static RGB.
hyperparams: 34 tasks; 1000 chains of 5; 30 Hz; 1% language annotation; static 200x200, gripper 84x84; MCIL lr 1e-4, KL beta 0.001, windows 16-32

name: SIMPLER
resolvedTitle: Evaluating Real-World Robot Manipulation Policies in Simulation
org: UC San Diego; Stanford University; UC Berkeley; Google DeepMind
problem: Real-world evaluation of generalist manipulation policies is expensive, slow and irreproducible, and validation action MSE is a poor proxy for real performance.
keyIdea: Real-to-sim evaluation: build simulated replicas of common real setups (Google Robot, WidowX/BridgeData V2) that close the control gap via system identification and the visual gap via green-screening + texture matching (Visual Matching) or randomized variants (Variant Aggregation), then validate with paired sim/real evaluations using a new rank metric (MMRV).
architecture: Evaluation suite on SAPIEN (reproduced in Isaac Sim): URDF robots, Objaverse/scanned object assets with CoACD collision meshes, simulated controllers matched to real via system ID (Ruckig motion planning for Google Robot), green-screen real backgrounds, baked real textures, multiple tuned arm colors; Gym API.
inputs: Policy under test receives simulated RGB (Google Robot head camera or Bridge third-view) + instruction
outputs: Simulated success rates; MMRV and Pearson r vs real
trainingData: N/A (evaluation). Policies evaluated: RT-1 (Begin/15%/Converged), RT-1-X, RT-2-X, Octo-Base, Octo-Small; ~1500 paired evaluation episodes.
controlRateHz: Policy control 3 Hz (Google Robot) and 5 Hz (WidowX); simulation 500-501 Hz

headlineResults.benchmark: Google Robot tasks (avg of Pick Coke Can, Move Near, Drawer)

whatChangedVsParent: Instead of sim-to-real training, evaluates real-trained policies in sim and shows ranking fidelity without building full digital twins.
limitations: Focused on rigid-object, relatively short-horizon tasks whose physics current simulators handle; simplified physical properties (mass, friction, center of mass); residual visual gaps; articulated-object modeling needs manual effort.
notes: Name expands to Simulated Manipulation Policy Evaluation for Real Robot Setups (RSS 2024). Google Robot tasks: pick coke can, move near, open/close drawer, open top drawer and place apple; Bridge: spoon on towel, carrot on plate, stack green block on yellow, eggplant in basket. Octo-Base success 0% with untuned sim arm vs 29.3% with tuned arm, predicting real arm-texture sensitivity. CONFLICT: the alphaXiv overview renders MMRV as (1/N^2) sum_i sum_j max(0,(r_i-r_j)(s_j-s_i)); the paper's actual definition (Eq. 1-2) is the mean over policies of the maximum real-performance-weighted rank violation, used here. Released as pip-installable simpler_env (code open; 'openWeights' refers to environments).

name: RLBench
resolvedTitle: RLBench: The Robot Learning Benchmark & Learning Environment
org: Dyson Robotics Lab, Imperial College London
problem: No standard benchmark existed for comparing vision-guided manipulation methods across RL, imitation, multi-task and few-shot learning; existing RL suites (Gym, DM Control) were toy-like and few-shot robotics work used very narrow task distributions.
keyIdea: 100 hand-designed manipulation tasks on a common simulated Franka Panda, each with variations, language descriptions and an infinite supply of motion-planned demonstrations generated from task waypoints.
architecture: Benchmark/learning environment built on V-REP (CoppeliaSim) via the PyRep toolkit. Each task = a V-REP model file (.ttm) with scene and demo waypoints + a Python file defining variations, success conditions and behaviours; demos come from OMPL motion planning.
inputs: RGB, depth and segmentation masks from an over-the-shoulder stereo camera and an eye-in-hand monocular camera; proprioception (joint angles, velocities, torques, end-effector/gripper pose); per-variation text descriptions.
outputs: Sparse +1 reward on task completion; success/terminate signal.
actionRepr: Selectable action modes: absolute or delta joint velocities, joint positions, joint torques, end-effector velocities, or end-effector poses (7-DoF Franka Panda + gripper).
trainingData: 100 tasks; each task has one or more variations, each variation yields unlimited episodes; demos generated on the fly or pre-generated (motion planner, OMPL). Demo lengths range from 100 to 1000 timesteps (avg of 5 demos over 75 tasks).
whatChangedVsParent: Moves from toy continuous-control suites to 100 visually-guided, multi-stage manipulation tasks with language variations and unlimited scripted demos.
limitations: Not photorealistic and physics not fully realistic (authors cannot claim full photorealism or general realistic physics); simulation-only, sacrificing real-world data for scalable task creation. No baseline results reported in the paper.
notes: Benchmark paper, not a policy. Proposes the RLBench Few-Shot Challenge v1.0: 10% of the 100 tasks held out as meta-test; report 1-shot, 5-shot and 20-shot success on new episodes of unseen tasks. Arm can be swapped with one line of code; domain-randomised rendering option for sim-to-real. Every task starts with nothing grasped (tools must be grasped first). Open-source code (github.com/stepjam/RLBench). Later work (PerAct, RVT, 3D Diffuser Actor, etc.) typically evaluates on an 18-task RLBench subset with 100 demos; that protocol is NOT from this paper. ManiSkill3 notes RLBench is CPU-only simulation.

name: Meta-World
resolvedTitle: Meta-World: A Benchmark and Evaluation for Multi-Task and Meta Reinforcement Learning
org: Stanford, UC Berkeley, Columbia, USC, Robotics at Google
problem: Meta-RL benchmarks used very narrow task distributions (e.g. different running velocities), so meta-trained policies could not be expected to generalise to genuinely new behaviours.
keyIdea: 50 qualitatively distinct (non-parametric) tabletop manipulation tasks on a shared Sawyer arm, each with parametric variation of object/goal positions, plus a graded protocol (ML1, MT1, MT10, MT50, ML10, ML45) and per-task success metrics.
architecture: MuJoCo tasks with Multiworld/OpenAI Gym interfaces; shared 39-dim observation and 4-dim action space; structured multi-component shaped reward (reach + grasp + place) in [0,10]. Baselines run in the garage RL library.
inputs: 39-dim state: end-effector 3D position, normalised gripper opening, positions + quaternions of up to two objects, previous measurements, and goal position (zeroed when absent/hidden).
outputs: Shaped reward in [0,10] and binary success (distance-to-goal threshold).
actionRepr: 4-dim continuous in [-1,1]: 3D end-effector displacement + normalised gripper torque (Sawyer robot).
trainingData: 50 tasks; ML1 = 50 train / 50 held-out goal positions for one task; MT10/MT50 = 50 goals x 10 / 50 environments (500 / 2,500 training tasks); ML10 / ML45 meta-train on 10 / 45 tasks and test on 5 held-out tasks.
parents: MAML / RL2 / PEARL meta-RL evaluations (goal-velocity tasks)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces single-task parametric variation (e.g. running direction) with 50 non-parametrically distinct manipulation tasks, each still parametrically varied.
limitations: State-based (object poses assumed known) with shaped rewards; authors list image observations and sparse rewards, compositional long-horizon tasks, reduced resets and online meta-learning as future extensions. Current methods fail to even fit the meta-training tasks.
notes: Benchmark paper. Text says MAML and RL2 reach '35% and 31%' on ML10 test, whereas Table 1 gives MAML 31.6% and RL2 35.8% (the prose appears to swap them); Table 1 values used above. arXiv v2 (2021) updates the CoRL 2019 version with v2 environments. Success threshold typically ~5 cm (per-task thresholds in Appendix Table 12). Single-task SAC can solve all 50 tasks to some degree; PPO most. Code: github.com/rlworkgroup/metaworld (now Farama-Foundation).

keyEquations.meaning: Multi-task RL objective: task-conditioned policy maximises expected return averaged over the task distribution.
Success: task-relevant object within threshold (e.g. 5 cm) of goal.

algorithmSteps: Pick an evaluation mode (ML1, MT1, MT10, MT50, ML10, ML45)
Multi-task: train one policy with one-hot task ID over fixed object/goal positions
Meta-RL: meta-train on 10 or 45 tasks with randomised positions, no task ID
At meta-test, adapt on the 5 held-out tasks with a few trajectories
Report average maximum success rate over tasks (10 seeds)
ablations: Scaling MT10 -> MT50 drops MT-SAC from 68.3% to 38.5%
RL2 fits ML10 meta-train (86.9%) but only 35.8% meta-test, showing a generalisation gap
PEARL is weak on both ML10 (13%) and ML45 (22%) meta-test
hyperparams: Obs 39-dim; action 4-dim in [-1,1]; reward in [0,10]; success thresholds per task (mostly 0.02-0.08 m); 10 seeds; ML10/ML45 hold out 5 test tasks.

name: robomimic
resolvedTitle: What Matters in Learning from Offline Human Demonstrations for Robot Manipulation
org: Stanford University, UT Austin
problem: Lack of open human-demonstration datasets and reproducible implementations made it unclear which design choices matter when learning manipulation offline from human data (vs machine-generated offline-RL data).
keyIdea: A study + open framework: 6 offline learning algorithms evaluated on 5 simulated and 3 real multi-stage tasks with datasets of varying quality (machine-generated, proficient-human, multi-human), deriving lessons on history dependence, batch RL, observation spaces, dataset size and policy selection.
architecture: robomimic framework on robosuite (MuJoCo). Algorithms: BC, BC-RNN, HBC, IRIS, BCQ, CQL. Default BC-RNN uses an RNN policy with GMM action head; image agents use a conv encoder over external + wrist cameras.
inputs: 'low-dim': end-effector pose, gripper finger positions and ground-truth object poses; 'image': same proprio but object info replaced by external and wrist camera images.
outputs: Robot actions (end-effector control) per timestep.
actionRepr: Per-step continuous end-effector actions from a GMM head (BC-RNN default) or deterministic head; one action per step (no chunking).
trainingData: Tasks: Lift, Can, Square, Transport (bimanual), Tool Hang (sim); Lift, Can, Tool Hang (real). PH = 200 demos from one proficient operator; MH = 300 demos from 6 operators (50 each: 2 better, 2 okay, 2 worse); MG = 300 rollouts per RL-agent checkpoint (Lift 225k transitions, Can 585k). Collected via RoboTurk.
whatChangedVsParent: Evaluates offline IL/RL on human (not machine-generated) multi-stage manipulation data, showing batch-RL methods that excel on D4RL-like data fail on human demos.
limitations: Policies are selected by best online-evaluated checkpoint, which is infeasible in the real world; offline policy selection remains open. Batch RL results may improve with newer pixel-based offline RL methods; complex tasks may need more data than collected.
notes: 'robomimic' is the name of the framework/datasets released with this paper. Five lessons: (1) observation history matters (BC-RNN >> BC, especially long-horizon and multi-human); (2) batch RL (BCQ, CQL) performs poorly on human data though BCQ is strong on MG; (3) observation space/hyperparameters matter a lot; (4) dataset size: simple tasks need a fraction of data, complex ones benefit from more; (5) policy selection by validation loss or last checkpoint loses much performance. Datasets, trained models and code are open-sourced. Later Diffusion Policy (Chi et al. 2023) popularised the robomimic Lift/Can/Square/Transport/ToolHang PH/MH suite as a standard benchmark.

hyperparams: Binary task-completion rewards; low-dim N=2000 epochs x M=100 steps, eval every 50; image N=600 x 500, eval every 20; 50 eval rollouts; 3 seeds; eval horizons 400-1100 steps by dataset.

name: ManiSkill3
resolvedTitle: Demonstrating GPU Parallelized Robot Simulation and Rendering for Generalizable Embodied AI with ManiSkill3
org: UC San Diego, Hillbot, CMU, TU Dresden, Tsinghua, King's College London
problem: Existing simulators support narrow task ranges, lack heterogeneous parallel simulation and fast parallel rendering, so visual RL and large-scale data generation for manipulation are too slow; CPU frameworks (RLBench, RoboCasa, etc.) are orders of magnitude slower.
keyIdea: Open-source GPU-parallelised simulation + rendering (PhysX + SAPIEN parallel renderer) with heterogeneous per-environment scenes, low GPU memory, 12 task categories, 20+ robots, demo generation pipelines and RL/IL baselines.
architecture: Built on SAPIEN (PhysX GPU simulation, rasterised parallel rendering); object-oriented, batched API; supports RGB/depth/segmentation, point clouds and voxels; demos from motion planning, RL and teleoperation (incl. VR); online-IL pipeline (RLPD, RFCL) to scale few demos.
inputs: State, RGB, depth, segmentation, point cloud or voxel observations plus proprioception (task-dependent).
outputs: Batched observations, rewards (dense/sparse), success flags at up to 30,000+ FPS.
actionRepr: Multiple controllers incl. delta joint position, joint position, delta end-effector pose; sim2real demo uses target delta joint position at 30 Hz with +/-0.05 rad per joint.
trainingData: Millions of demonstration frames from motion planning, RL and teleoperation; IL baselines use 100 or 1000 motion-planning demos per task.
controlRateHz: Benchmarks at sim 120 Hz / control 60 Hz; Koch sim2real at 30 Hz

headlineResults.benchmark: GPU memory, 128 parallel envs (Cartpole, realistic camera)

headlineResults.value: state ~1 min (15x faster); RGB ~10 min (8x faster)

whatChangedVsParent: Moves ManiSkill2's CPU simulation to GPU-parallel simulation and rendering with heterogeneous scenes, giving order-of-magnitude faster visual RL.
limitations: Complex scenes (room-scale) run fewer parallel envs per GPU; soft-body and vision-tactile environments are not batched; sim2real demo needed reward engineering, static cameras and green-screening, and is far from solving sim2real. Speed comparison vs Isaac Lab is not apples-to-apples (rasterisation vs ray tracing).
notes: Framework/benchmark paper (RSS 2025 demo; Apache-2.0). 12 task categories: tabletop, mobile manipulation, room-scale scenes (ReplicaCAD, AI2-THOR, RoboCasa), locomotion, humanoid/bimanual, multi-agent, drawing/cleaning, dexterous, vision-tactile, classic control, digital twins, soft body. Hosts GPU-parallel SIMPLER digital twins evaluating Octo/RT-X at 60-100x real-world speed (~10x faster than original SIMPLER). Supports evaluating Octo, RT-X, RDT-1B and training PerAct. Diffusion Policy was best IL baseline, especially with few demos. RGB with 100 demos: DP PickCube 0.76 vs ACT 0.28.

For sim2real: domain-randomise camera pose, lighting, cube size/colour/friction; green-screen background; deploy zero-shot
ablations: Isaac Lab ~2-4x higher GPU memory than ManiSkill3 in sim+render tests; ManiSkill3 ~2x faster at realistic camera settings (1x640x480, 3x320x180)

name: WorldSimBench
resolvedTitle: WorldSimBench: Towards Video Generation Models as World Simulators
org: CUHK-Shenzhen, Shanghai AI Laboratory, Beihang University, HKU
problem: Existing video-generation benchmarks score aesthetics/feature similarity and cannot judge whether generated videos are physically plausible and actionable for embodied agents.
keyIdea: Define a hierarchy of predictive models (S0 text -> S3 actionable video, 'World Simulators') and evaluate S3 models two ways: Explicit Perceptual Evaluation with a human-preference evaluator trained on fine-grained human feedback, and Implicit Manipulative Evaluation by converting generated videos to actions in closed-loop simulators.
architecture: (1) HF-Embodied Dataset + Human Preference Evaluator (video MLLM fine-tuned on human scores) across hierarchical dimensions (Visual Quality, Condition Consistency, Embodiment). (2) Closed-loop: video generator predicts future video from observation + instruction, a video-to-action model (Steve-1-style goal policy for Minecraft, SuSIE-style policy for CALVIN, LMDrive-style for CARLA) executes it, regenerate every k steps.
inputs: Text instruction (+ current image observation for TI2V models).
outputs: Human-preference scores per dimension; closed-loop task metrics (Minecraft item counts/distance, CARLA DS/RC/IS etc., CALVIN success / avg length).
actionRepr: Robot Manipulation uses CALVIN's 7-DoF arm action space produced by a video-to-action policy from generated frames.
trainingData: HF-Embodied: 35,701 tuples with multi-dimensional scores and feedback over 3 scenarios and 20 dimensions (OE 8,401 videos, AD 15,870, RM 11,430). Video models fine-tuned on VPT/Minecraft, nuScenes, RH20T-P (perceptual) and CALVIN ABC, CARLA (implicit).

headlineResults.benchmark: HPE vs GPT-4o alignment, Robot Manipulation

whatChangedVsParent: Adds embodiment-specific human-preference scoring and closed-loop action-level evaluation on top of aesthetic/feature-similarity video benchmarks.
limitations: Evaluates physics/3D content only from an embodied-robotics perspective; world simulators apply to many other scenarios with other physical properties needing further evaluation. Findings: current video models still fail to capture many physical rules.
notes: Evaluates 8 video generators: Open-Sora-Plan (T2V and TI2V), Lavie, ModelScope, OpenSora, AnimateDiff, DynamiCrafter, EasyAnimate. In RM, models do well on perspectivity/consistency but score poorly on Instruction Alignment (IA mostly 1.0-2.6 of 5), often generating aimless actions. Image conditioning hurt Minecraft closed-loop performance. Explicit and implicit rankings mostly agree but diverge on long-horizon tasks (Open-Sora-Plan more robust than DynamiCrafter on CALVIN tasks 4-5). Uses CALVIN train A,B,C -> test D; SuSIE policy without extra fine-tuning.

algorithmSteps: Define hierarchical evaluation dimensions per scenario (OE, AD, RM)
Generate videos from prompt list with fine-tuned video models; collect human scores + reasons -> HF-Embodied
