name: EWMBench
resolvedTitle: EWMBench: Evaluating Scene, Motion, and Semantic Quality in Embodied World Models
org: AgiBot, SJTU, MMLab-CUHK, HIT
problem: General video-generation benchmarks (e.g. VBench) measure perceptual quality but not whether an embodied world model keeps the scene static, moves the robot along a correct trajectory and follows task logic.
keyIdea: Benchmark embodied world models on robot manipulation from a unified initialisation (initial frames + instruction [+ optional 6D action trajectory]) with metrics over three axes: scene consistency, end-effector motion correctness vs ground truth, and semantic alignment/diversity.
architecture: Evaluation toolkit: fine-tuned DINOv2 (ViT-B/14-reg4) patch features for scene consistency; fine-tuned YOLO-World + BoT-SORT end-effector tracker for trajectory metrics (HSD, nDTW, DYN); video MLLM captions (global, key steps, logic errors) scored with BLEU/CLIP; CLIP video features for diversity.
inputs: Up to 4 initial scene images, step-level language instruction, optional action trajectory (sequence of 6D poses).
outputs: Normalised scores for SceneC, HSD, DYN, nDTW, Diversity, BLEU, CLIP, Logics and overall sum.
trainingData: Curated from AgiBot World: 10 tasks (household/industrial, e.g. toaster, pour water, hang showerhead), each decomposed into 4-10 sub-actions; 10 diverse GT episodes per task selected by greedy voxel-IoU diversity; 2,100 generated videos evaluated (7 models x 100 episodes x 3).

headlineResults.comparedTo: LTX_FT 4.5493, Kling 3.8698, Hailuo 3.4125, COSMOS 3.2872, OpenSora 3.1392, LTX 2.9676

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces perceptual-only video metrics with trajectory-grounded (end-effector) motion metrics against ground truth plus embodied scene-consistency and logic-error checks.
limitations: Only tracks the end-effector trajectory (not full-arm state); fixed-viewpoint scenes only; manipulation tasks only (navigation and mobile manipulation left for future). Only image-text-to-video models evaluated since no open-source action-conditioned video models were available.
notes: Dataset and evaluation tools released at github.com/AgibotTech/EWMBench. Intro says '30 candidate samples across ten tasks' while the experiment section says 10 tasks x 10 GT episodes (and Appendix samples 100 instances per task, then greedily selects 10); treat 10 tasks x 10 episodes as the evaluation set. Best-of-3 generation per episode selected by Hausdorff distance. Domain-adapted models sometimes show 'empty grasping'; COSMOS and LTX bias toward human hands. VBench background consistency stays high (0.88-0.91) even under camera drift, which EWMBench's fine-tuned DINOv2 metric detects. Trajectory metrics are complementary: reversal only hurts nDTW; outliers hurt HSD and DYN; repeated frames raise nDTW but lower DYN.

keyEquations.meaning: Evaluated video: normalised output of the world model on preprocessed image, language, trajectory inputs.
Reciprocal symmetric Hausdorff distance between GT and generated EEF trajectory.

Normalise videos to 640x480, 30 FPS

name: A Walk in the Park
resolvedTitle: A Walk in the Park: Learning to Walk in 20 Minutes With Model-Free Reinforcement Learning
org: UC Berkeley (BAIR)
problem: Deep RL was believed too sample-inefficient to train legged locomotion directly in the real world, pushing work toward large-scale simulation, demonstrations, model-based RL or motion primitives.
keyIdea: Careful implementation of an existing off-policy actor-critic (SAC with regularization/normalization, i.e., DroQ-style, high update-to-data ratio) plus careful MDP design lets a quadruped learn to walk from scratch in the real world in about 20 minutes.
architecture: Separate fully-connected networks for policy and a Q-function ensemble, trained in JAX; SAC augmented with LayerNorm (and/or dropout) and 20 critic updates per environment step, trained synchronously on a single-GPU laptop.
inputs: Proprioception only: roll/pitch, root angular velocity, estimated linear velocity (Kalman filter), joint angles and velocities, binary foot contacts, previous action.
outputs: PD position targets for 12 joints within a constrained offset range around default angles.
actionRepr: single-step continuous 12-D joint PD targets (bounded offsets), 20 Hz
trainingData: No simulation or demos for the real-world runs; ~1 min of random-action data then online RL; ~20,000 real samples (~20 min wall-clock) per terrain on a Unitree A1.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real-world A1 walking (flat ground, mattress, mulch, lawn, hiking trail)
headlineResults.comparedTo: Wu et al. 72k samples/1 h; Haarnoja et al. 160k/2 h (Table I)

headlineResults.value: 2400 (JAX, jitted) vs 7.5 Hz effective control for best PyTorch impl.

whatChangedVsParent: No new algorithm; combines DroQ/SAC with LayerNorm, high UTD, synchronous per-step JAX updates and a constrained action space to make real-world training fast.
limitations: Paper frames itself as an empirical demonstration using existing components; limited to forward walking with proprioception, and requires human repositioning of the robot during training.
notes: Code released to reproduce results (project site). Emphasises that a variety of regularization methods (dropout, LayerNorm, REDQ ensembles) give similar gains. Limitations sentence is partly inferred from setup; the paper has no explicit limitations section.

name: Q-Transformer
resolvedTitle: Q-Transformer: Scalable Offline Reinforcement Learning via Autoregressive Q-Functions
org: Google DeepMind
problem: High-capacity Transformer robot policies are usually trained by imitation and are capped by demonstration quality; training Transformers with offline RL on mixed-quality real data at scale was hard.
keyIdea: Discretize each action dimension and treat each dimension as a separate token/time-step, learning per-dimension Q-values autoregressively with a Transformer via offline TD backups, a conservative regularizer that pushes down unseen actions, and Monte-Carlo plus n-step returns.
architecture: RT-1-derived: Universal Sentence Encoder language embedding + FiLM-EfficientNet image tokenizer + 8 self-attention layers; sigmoid output gives Q-values in [0,1] per action bin; previously chosen action dimensions fed back as one-hot embeddings.
inputs: Head-mounted RGB images (downsampled to 320x256, history window) and a language instruction.
outputs: Q-values for 256 bins of each of 8 action dimensions; greedy argmax per dimension.
actionRepr: 8-D action (3D position, 3D axis-angle orientation, gripper, terminate), each discretized into 256 bins and decoded autoregressively per dimension
trainingData: ~38,000 successful RT-1 teleop demos (max 100 per task, 700+ tasks) + ~20,000 failed autonomous episodes (~58k episodes) from a fleet of 13 robots; scaling experiment with ~300,000 episodes (115k successes, 185k failures).
whatChangedVsParent: Keeps the RT-1 Transformer backbone but trains it as an autoregressive per-dimension Q-function with offline conservative Q-learning instead of behavior cloning.
limitations: Focuses on sparse binary rewards; per-dimension discretization grows sequence length and inference time with action dimensionality (e.g., humanoids) and uniform bins struggle with mixed coarse/fine motions; offline only, no online fine-tuning.
notes: Mobile manipulator with 7-DoF arm and parallel gripper (Everyday Robots). Claims ~70% improvement over the best prior method's average. n-step returns reach similar performance with ~4x fewer gradient steps.

name: MT-Opt
resolvedTitle: MT-Opt: Continuous Multi-Task Robotic Reinforcement Learning at Scale
org: Robotics at Google
problem: Single-task real-world RL (e.g., QT-Opt grasping needing 500k+ trials) is too expensive to scale to a generalist robot with many skills learned from scratch in isolation.
keyIdea: Learn many vision-based manipulation tasks simultaneously with one multi-task Q-function, sharing data across related tasks (task impersonation + re-balancing), using easier tasks to bootstrap harder ones, and specifying rewards via learned multi-task visual success detectors.
architecture: Distributed off-policy multi-task Q-learning built on QT-Opt: a single network conditioned on camera image and one-hot task ID; actions chosen by optimizing the Q-function (QT-Opt style); separate multi-task success-detector network trained from user-provided outcome examples.
inputs: Robot camera images + one-hot task encoding.
outputs: Arm position/orientation and gripper commands plus a TERMINATE action.
actionRepr: continuous end-effector pose + gripper commands selected by Q-function optimization (QT-Opt)
trainingData: 800,000+ episode offline dataset collected by 7 KUKA robots over time (scripted, epsilon-greedy and on-policy); ~5,000 labeled images per task for success detectors; 12 evaluation tasks.
whatChangedVsParent: Extends single-task QT-Opt to a shared multi-task Q-function with task-conditioned inputs, success-detector rewards, and data-sharing/re-balancing across tasks.
limitations: Tasks must be judged from the final image with sparse rewards; success detectors need continued manual labeling for out-of-distribution images; underrepresented tasks still perform poorly without more targeted data collection.
notes: Also shows fine-tuning to new tasks (lift-cloth, cover-object). Paper states the data-sharing strategy yields up to ~10x improvement on some tasks and ~3x average over baselines.

name: Eureka
resolvedTitle: Eureka: Human-Level Reward Design via Coding Large Language Models
org: NVIDIA, UPenn, Caltech, UT Austin
problem: Reward design for RL is manual trial-and-error and often suboptimal; prior LLM reward methods needed task-specific prompts or reward templates and could not learn complex low-level dexterous skills.
keyIdea: A coding LLM (GPT-4) reads raw environment source code and writes executable reward functions, which are improved by evolutionary in-context search guided by 'reward reflection' (text summaries of per-component training statistics).
architecture: Loop: sample K=16 reward programs from GPT-4 given env code + task description; train PPO policies in GPU-accelerated IsaacGym to score them; feed best reward and its reflection back as context; 5 iterations x 5 restarts.
inputs: Environment source code (state/action variables) + natural-language task description; optional human textual feedback.
outputs: Python reward function code (then used to train RL policies).
trainingData: No training data for the LLM; policies trained with PPO in IsaacGym on 29 tasks (9 Isaac + 20 Bidexterous Manipulation tasks), 10 robot morphologies.

headlineResults.metric: Tasks where Eureka beats expert human rewards

headlineResults.comparedTo: Human rewards; L2R lags on high-dim tasks

headlineResults.metric: Drop in avg normalized score without reward reflection

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike L2R, uses no reward templates or task-specific prompts; generates free-form reward code and refines it by evolutionary search with reward reflection.
limitations: Relies on a simulator exposing source code and a task fitness function to evaluate candidate rewards, requiring many RL training runs; performance degrades with weaker LLMs (GPT-3.5).
notes: Uses gpt-4-0314. First simulated Shadow Hand pen-spinning via Eureka rewards plus curriculum. Prompts, environments and generated rewards open-sourced. Simulation only (real-world transfer addressed in DrEureka). Limitations sentence is a synthesis; the paper has no explicit limitations section.

name: DrEureka
resolvedTitle: DrEureka: Language Model Guided Sim-To-Real Transfer
org: UPenn, NVIDIA, UT Austin
problem: Sim-to-real transfer requires manual, iterative design of both reward functions and domain-randomization (DR) parameters, which is slow and labor-intensive.
keyIdea: Use an LLM to automate both: Eureka-style reward generation with added safety instructions, then a Reward-Aware Physics Prior (RAPP) that finds feasible physics-parameter ranges by rolling out the initial policy, which the LLM uses to propose DR configurations.
architecture: Three stages with GPT-4: (1) Eureka reward search with safety prompt; (2) RAPP: per-parameter sweep in simulation to get feasible lower/upper bounds; (3) LLM samples 16 DR configurations within RAPP bounds; PPO policies trained in IsaacGym for each.
inputs: Environment code, task description and safety instruction; RAPP ranges for DR prompting.
outputs: Reward function code and DR configurations; resulting PPO policies output joint position targets.
trainingData: Simulation only (IsaacGym, PPO; teacher-student for locomotion); Unitree Go1 quadruped and LEAP hand (16 DoF).

headlineResults.benchmark: Walking globe (yoga ball), real lab with support

whatChangedVsParent: Extends Eureka from simulation-only reward design to full sim-to-real by adding safety-regularized rewards and LLM-generated domain randomization grounded by RAPP.
limitations: Cannot select the best DR configuration in simulation, so all sampled policies are trained and evaluated in the real world; walking-globe dynamics are not faithfully simulated and real tests needed a human support point.
notes: Paper reports +34% forward velocity and +20% distance vs human-designed on locomotion, and ~300% more cube rotation. Ablations without RAPP prior mostly produced unsafe policies. Code at eureka-research.github.io/dr-eureka.

name: DPPO
resolvedTitle: Diffusion Policy Policy Optimization
org: Princeton, MIT, Toyota Research Institute, CMU
problem: Behavior-cloned diffusion policies are limited by suboptimal/narrow demonstrations, and policy-gradient RL was conjectured to be inefficient for fine-tuning diffusion-based policies.
keyIdea: Treat the denoising process as an inner MDP embedded in the environment MDP (a two-layer 'Diffusion Policy MDP') so each denoising step has a Gaussian likelihood, then fine-tune with PPO.
architecture: Diffusion Policy with MLP or UNet denoiser; PPO over the denoising chain, often fine-tuning only the last few denoising steps or DDIM; state-only value function; clipped denoising noise schedule for exploration.
inputs: State or pixel observations (plus proprioception).
outputs: Action chunks produced by denoising.
actionRepr: diffusion-denoised action chunks (e.g., Ta=4 or 8 executed, Tp up to 16 predicted)
trainingData: Pre-trained on D4RL (Gym, Franka Kitchen), Robomimic (300 state / 100 pixel demos), Furniture-Bench (50 sim demos); fine-tuned online in simulation with sparse or dense rewards.

headlineResults.comparedTo: Gaussian PPO 0% real (88% sim); Gaussian + BC loss 50% real

whatChangedVsParent: Applies PPO through the denoising chain of a pre-trained Diffusion Policy, with design choices (partial-step fine-tuning, noise clipping, state-only critic) that make PG fine-tuning stable.
limitations: Lower sample efficiency than off-policy methods; multi-step denoising costs wall-clock time (about 6x Gaussian when training from scratch); structured on-manifold exploration can hurt when aggressive exploration is needed.
notes: Code released at diffusion-ppo.github.io. Also compares against off-policy diffusion RL (DQL, IDQL, DIPO, QSM) and demo-augmented RL (RLPD, Cal-QL, IBRL); per-benchmark success numbers were not in the retrieved pages. openWeights=true refers to released code/checkpoints on project site.

name: SimpleVLA-RL
resolvedTitle: SimpleVLA-RL: Scaling VLA Training via Reinforcement Learning
org: Tsinghua University, Shanghai AI Lab, SJTU, Peking University, HKU
authorsShort: Li, Zuo, Yu, Zhang et al.
problem: Scaling VLA supervised fine-tuning needs scarce, expensive teleoperated trajectories and generalizes poorly under distribution shift.
keyIdea: DeepSeek-R1-style online RL for VLAs: sample groups of trajectories with a token-based VLA, give a binary outcome reward, and optimize with GRPO plus exploration enhancements (dynamic sampling, clip-higher, higher rollout temperature).
architecture: Built on veRL with VLA-specific interactive rollout, parallel multi-environment rendering and an integrated training-inference-rendering loop; policy is OpenVLA-OFT using action-token distributions.
inputs: RGB observations, proprioception, language instruction.
outputs: Action-token distributions decoded to action chunks.
actionRepr: discrete action tokens (OpenVLA-OFT) sampled per chunk; 7-D end-effector deltas + gripper
trainingData: SFT on LIBERO demos (full: 500 per suite; one-trajectory: 1 per task) and RoboTwin 1.0/2.0 sim trajectories (e.g., 1000 per task for sim-to-real); then online RL in simulation with 0/1 outcome reward.
whatChangedVsParent: Applies LLM-style outcome-reward GRPO RL (with DAPO-style exploration tricks) to fine-tune OpenVLA-OFT beyond SFT.
limitations: RL fails completely when the base model has zero initial task success (no successful trajectories to reward); gains depend strongly on the SFT prior.
notes: Reports an emergent 'pushcut' behaviour: RL policy pushes objects instead of the demonstrated grasp-move-place. Code at github.com/PRIME-RL/SimpleVLA-RL (released May 2025). Figure 1 shows LIBERO 91.0 -> 99.1 while text says 91% -> 99%.

name: RIPT-VLA
resolvedTitle: Interactive Post-Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
org: UT Austin, Nankai University
problem: VLA training relies on offline demonstrations and imitation, so policies never see consequences of their actions and degrade badly in low-data regimes.
keyIdea: Add a third 'Reinforcement Interactive Post-Training' stage using only sparse binary success rewards, optimized critic-free with LOOP (RLOO leave-one-out advantages + PPO) and dynamic rollout sampling that rejects context groups with all-identical rewards.
architecture: Model-agnostic: applied to QueST (20M, VQ-VAE skill tokens + GPT-style transformer) and OpenVLA-OFT (7B, continuous L1 head augmented with a learned Laplace scale head so log-probs are available); LoRA rank 32 for OpenVLA-OFT.
inputs: Images and language goal (as per base VLA).
outputs: Actions from the base VLA (discrete skill tokens or continuous actions sampled from Gaussian/Laplace).
actionRepr: base-model dependent: discrete skill tokens (QueST) or continuous action chunks with Laplace sampling (OpenVLA-OFT)
trainingData: LIBERO and MetaWorld ML45 with 50 demos per task for SFT (or 1-10 demos in few-shot), then interactive RL with binary rewards in simulation.
whatChangedVsParent: Extends LOOP with dynamic rejection of zero-advantage context groups to build uniform non-zero-advantage batches for stable VLA RL.
limitations: Requires the SFT model to have non-zero success on target tasks and a resettable environment with binary rewards; evaluated in simulation (LIBERO, MetaWorld).
notes: Code and models at ariostgx.github.io/ript_vla. ML45 full-data result 92.2% vs QueST 91.0%. Abstract says failure rate 3.3% -> 2.5% while body says 2.4% (minor internal inconsistency). Limitations sentence is synthesized; paper has no explicit limitations section.

name: ConRFT
resolvedTitle: ConRFT: A Reinforced Fine-tuning Method for VLA Models via Consistency Policy
org: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CASIA); UCAS
problem: Supervised fine-tuning of VLAs on small, inconsistent demonstration sets gives poor robustness, especially in contact-rich real-world tasks, while naive real-world RL is unsafe and sample-inefficient.
keyIdea: Two-stage reinforced fine-tuning with a unified consistency-policy objective: offline Cal-ConRFT (Cal-QL critic + consistency BC loss on 20-30 demos) then online HIL-ConRFT with task rewards and human-in-the-loop interventions.
architecture: Octo-small VLA backbone with a consistency-policy action head (2-layer MLP, hidden 256) and a critic; only the action head is fine-tuned while visual encoders and transformer backbone stay frozen.
inputs: Wrist (128x128) and side (256x256) RGB images, proprioception (EE pose, twist, force/torque, gripper), language instruction.
outputs: 6-D end-effector delta pose (+1-D binary gripper) for an impedance controller.
actionRepr: single-step continuous 6/7-D EE delta generated by a consistency policy head
trainingData: 20-30 teleoperated demos per task plus 45-90 minutes of real-world online interaction with human interventions on a Franka arm; reward from a learned binary success classifier.
whatChangedVsParent: Fine-tunes a pre-trained VLA (rather than training from scratch like HIL-SERL) with a unified consistency-based BC+Q objective across offline and online stages.
limitations: Relies on task-specific binary reward classifiers that are vulnerable to reward hacking and give sparse feedback; encoders and transformer backbone are frozen, limiting perception adaptation.
notes: Training time 45-90 min per task. Code on project website cccedric.github.io/conrft. Reward: +10 on success, -0.05 per step.

name: iRe-VLA
resolvedTitle: Improving Vision-Language-Action Model with Online Reinforcement Learning
org: Tsinghua University (IIIS), UC Berkeley, Shanghai Qi Zhi Institute
problem: Directly applying online RL to large VLA models is unstable (performance collapse) and computationally too heavy for local robot machines.
keyIdea: Iterate between an online RL stage that freezes the VLM and trains only a lightweight action head (plus critic head), and a supervised stage that fine-tunes the whole model (LoRA) on expert data plus RL-collected successful trajectories.
architecture: BLIP-2 3B VLM backbone with LoRA; action head = token learner + MLP regressing continuous actions; critic head of same structure. RL stage uses PPO in simulation and SACfD in the real world (VLM latents cached).
inputs: Image observation + language instruction.
outputs: Continuous end-effector pose change and gripper status.
actionRepr: single-step continuous action regressed by an MLP head
trainingData: MetaWorld expert set of 25 tasks x 50 trajectories; Franka Kitchen 5 expert tasks; real world 2,000 teleop/scripted trajectories on a Panda, plus online RL (~1 hour per new real task).
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces unstable end-to-end PPO on the full VLA with alternating frozen-backbone RL and full-model supervised distillation of successes.
limitations: Can only improve skills within seen skill types and cannot learn entirely new skills under sparse-reward online RL.
notes: Real-world RL stage run on a single RTX 4090 locally; supervised stage on 4 A100s remotely.

name: VLA-RL
resolvedTitle: VLA-RL: Towards Masterful and General Robotic Manipulation with Scalable Reinforcement Learning
org: Tsinghua University (Shenzhen), Nanyang Technological University
problem: Imitation-trained VLAs fail out of distribution because offline data covers limited states; online RL for large auto-regressive VLAs faces sparse rewards and scaling issues.
keyIdea: Formulate manipulation trajectories as multi-modal multi-turn conversation and fine-tune OpenVLA with PPO, densifying sparse rewards with a VLM-based Robotic Process Reward Model trained on automatically extracted pseudo-labels.
architecture: OpenVLA-7B policy (Llama-2-7B + SigLIP/DINOv2) with LoRA, a value model, a frozen robotic process reward model; vLLM inference GPU + Ray/FSDP learners, GPU-balanced vectorized environments, curriculum task selection, critic warmup.
inputs: Third-person image + language instruction.
outputs: Action token sequence detokenized into 7-DoF actions.
actionRepr: 7 discrete action tokens (one per DoF, binned) per step, auto-regressive
trainingData: Starts from OpenVLA SFT checkpoints on LIBERO; online PPO over 40 LIBERO tasks; ~48 GPU hours of RL training.

headlineResults.value: 90.2% full vs 85.8% without process reward model

whatChangedVsParent: Adds online PPO with a learned robotic process reward model and systems tricks on top of imitation-trained OpenVLA.
limitations: Heuristic pseudo-reward label extraction (gripper changes, velocity keyframes) may not capture nuances of dexterous tasks; only auto-regressive VLAs are addressed, and only in simulation.
notes: Claims 'early spark of inference scaling laws' as success rises with more RL training. The abstract says it 'matches' pi0-FAST, but the table shows 81.0% vs 85.5% average. CONFLICT-flag for surveys citing parity. Code at github.com/GuanxingLu/vlarl.

name: Pinto & Gupta (50K grasps)
resolvedTitle: Supersizing Self-supervision: Learning to Grasp from 50K Tries and 700 Robot Hours
org: Carnegie Mellon University (Robotics Institute)
problem: Learned grasping relied on small, semantically biased human-labeled datasets, and prior trial-and-error approaches used too little data to train high-capacity CNNs without overfitting.
keyIdea: Self-supervised large-scale trial-and-error data collection (50K grasps, 700 robot hours) to train a CNN that predicts graspability of an image patch at 18 angle bins, with multi-stage curriculum collecting hard negatives.
architecture: ImageNet-pretrained AlexNet conv layers + fc6 (4096) and fc7 (1024) + 18 binary angle classifiers; only the executed angle's loss is back-propagated.
inputs: 380x380 image patch around candidate grasp point (resized to 227x227).
outputs: 18 graspability scores for angles 0-170 degrees; best patch/angle executed as a planar grasp.
actionRepr: planar grasp (x, y, theta) chosen by patch sampling and 18-way angle classification
params: 18M new parameters in fully connected layers
trainingData: 50,567 grasp attempts (6,266 positive) on 150 objects with a Baxter robot over 700 robot hours, in clutter.

headlineResults.benchmark: Held-out test set (15 novel objects, ~3K grasps)

whatChangedVsParent: Scales self-supervised grasp data ~40x over prior work and reframes grasp prediction as 18-way per-angle binary classification with staged hard-negative mining.
limitations: Planar grasps only; Baxter arm imprecision causes failures; gains from more data saturate after about 20K points and multi-stage gains saturate after 3 stages.
notes: Not RL in the strict sense: it is self-supervised learning from trial-and-error, 'inspired by' RL. Dataset was to be released.

name: Zeng push-grasp synergies
resolvedTitle: Learning Synergies between Pushing and Grasping with Self-supervised Deep Reinforcement Learning
org: Princeton University, Google, MIT
problem: Pushing and grasping were studied in isolation or combined via hand-coded heuristics, making it hard to exploit their synergy in cluttered picking.
keyIdea: Visual Pushing for Grasping (VPG): learn push and grasp jointly from scratch with model-free Q-learning, using fully convolutional action-value functions that predict pixel-wise Q-values over a heightmap, self-supervised by grasp success.
architecture: Two FCNs (push and grasp), each with two parallel ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet-121 towers (RGB and cloned depth) + 1x1 convs + bilinear upsampling; input heightmap rotated into 16 orientations giving 32 pixel-wise Q maps; DQN-style training with Huber loss and prioritized replay.
inputs: RGB-D heightmap of the workspace (from a fixed RealSense SR300 in real, simulated camera in sim).
outputs: Pixel-wise Q-values for push (16 directions) and grasp (16 orientations); argmax gives primitive, location and angle.
actionRepr: discrete motion primitives (push or top-down parallel-jaw grasp) parameterized by pixel location x 16 rotations (224x224x32 actions)
trainingData: Self-supervised trial and error: <2000 transitions (~5.5 h wall-clock) on a real UR5 + RG2 gripper with toy blocks; also trained in V-REP simulation with 10 objects.
whatChangedVsParent: Combines Q-learning with pixel-wise affordance FCNs and adds a pushing primitive trained through future grasp rewards.
limitations: Motion primitives on a regular heightmap grid limit expressiveness; trained only on blocks with limited generalization to novel shapes (struggles with reflective objects lacking depth); only push and grasp primitives studied.
notes: Code, pre-trained models and simulation environments released at vpg.cs.princeton.edu. Discount gamma = 0.5; push reward 0.5 for detectable change, grasp reward 1.

name: Sim-to-real agile locomotion (Tan 2018)
resolvedTitle: Sim-to-Real: Learning Agile Locomotion For Quadruped Robots
org: Google Brain, X, Google DeepMind
problem: Policies learned in simulation for agile legged locomotion rarely transfer to real robots because of model discrepancies (actuators, latency, parameters) amplified by contact-rich dynamics.
keyIdea: Narrow the reality gap by both improving the simulator (system identification, learned-from-physics DC-motor actuator model, latency modeling) and learning robust policies (dynamics randomization, random perturbations, compact observations), then deploy zero-shot.
architecture: PPO with fully-connected policy and value networks (two hidden layers each); hybrid policy a(t,o) = open-loop reference gait + learned feedback, allowing from-scratch or user-guided gaits; PyBullet simulation of the Minitaur.
inputs: Compact proprioceptive observations: 4-D IMU (roll, pitch, their angular rates) for trotting; 12-D (IMU + motor angles) for galloping.
outputs: Leg swing and extension targets (added to an optional open-loop signal) for 8 motors.
actionRepr: single-step continuous leg pose (swing/extension) targets, optionally residual on a sinusoidal reference
trainingData: Simulation only: 7 million steps per policy, 25 parallel roll-outs; ~3-4 h learning time per gait; randomized mass, friction, inertia, motor strength, control step, latency, battery voltage, contact friction, IMU bias/noise.
whatChangedVsParent: Adds an accurate actuator model and latency simulation to system-identified PyBullet, showing these (not just randomization) are essential for transfer.
limitations: Uses a simple reward and flat ground only (maximize forward speed); no speed/direction changes and no vision for complex terrain; randomization trades optimality for robustness.
notes: Learned gaits use 35% (galloping) and 23% (trotting) less power than expert handcrafted gaits. Without either actuator model or latency simulation, controllers failed on the real robot. Minitaur environments open-sourced in Bullet.

name: ANYmal actuator net (Hwangbo 2019)
resolvedTitle: Learning Agile and Dynamic Motor Skills for Legged Robots
org: ETH Zurich (Robotic Systems Lab), Intel Intelligent Systems Lab
problem: RL for legged robots had mostly stayed in simulation because complex actuator dynamics (series-elastic actuators, delays, low-level controllers) are nearly impossible to model analytically, preventing transfer.
keyIdea: Learn an 'actuator net' from real robot data that maps joint position-error/velocity history to torque, plug it into a fast rigid-body simulator, train RL policies in this hybrid simulator, and deploy zero-shot on ANYmal.
architecture: Actuator net: MLP with 3 hidden layers of 32 units (softsign), inputs of current and two past joint states (t-0.01, t-0.02 s). Policy: MLP with two hidden layers trained with TRPO; outputs low-impedance joint position targets.
inputs: Gravity vector, base height, linear/angular velocity, joint positions/velocities, sparse joint state history, previous action, command.
outputs: 12 joint position targets for ANYmal.
actionRepr: single-step continuous 12-D joint position targets (impedance control)
trainingData: Actuator net: >1 million samples at 400 Hz collected in <4 minutes on the real robot. Policy: simulation only, ~a quarter billion transitions in ~4 h; all training on one CPU + one GPU PC, none longer than 11 h; 30 ANYmal models with randomized inertia.

headlineResults.comparedTo: Model-based controllers need ~2 orders of magnitude more onboard compute

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces analytical actuator models with a learned actuator network inside the simulator, enabling zero-shot RL transfer on a complex SEA-driven quadruped.
limitations: Still needs per-task cost function and initial-state design; a single network yields single-faceted behaviours that do not generalize across tasks; independent per-actuator models may fail for coupled actuation such as shared hydraulics.
notes: Published in Science Robotics (2019). Learned controller more precise and energy-efficient than the best existing model-based controller on ANYmal; policies ran for more than three months without modification.

name: Perceptive locomotion (Miki 2022)
resolvedTitle: Learning robust perceptive locomotion for quadrupedal robots in the wild
org: ETH Zurich (Robotic Systems Lab), KAIST, Intel
problem: Exteroception enables fast legged locomotion but is unreliable in the wild (snow, vegetation, reflective/transparent surfaces, occlusion), so the most robust controllers were blind (proprioceptive only) and slow.
keyIdea: A recurrent belief-state encoder with an attention gate that learns end-to-end how much to trust noisy elevation-map input versus proprioception, trained via teacher-student privileged learning with heavy height-map noise randomization.
architecture: Teacher: PPO policy with privileged terrain/state info. Student: GRU belief encoder + gated exteroceptive fusion + MLP (reused from teacher), trained by behavior cloning and reconstruction losses; adaptive terrain curriculum.
inputs: Proprioception + height samples from a robot-centric 2.5D elevation map (built at 20 Hz from LiDAR or depth cameras) + velocity command.
outputs: Joint position targets for ANYmal C.
actionRepr: single-step continuous 12-D joint position targets
trainingData: Simulation only with randomized terrains and a parameterized height-map noise model (nominal / large offset / large noise in 60/30/10% ratio); zero-shot deployment.

headlineResults.value: Completed hour-long hike in the recommended human time
0 falls over 1700+ m across tunnel/urban/cave courses

parents: Lee et al. 2020 (learning quadrupedal locomotion over challenging terrain)
whatChangedVsParent: Adds exteroception to the blind teacher-student framework via a gated recurrent belief encoder robust to perception failures.
limitations: Uses uncertainty only implicitly (may step off cliffs under occlusion); relies on an elevation-map intermediate and separate pose estimation; cannot do maneuvers very different from walking (e.g., freeing stuck legs, climbing high ledges).
notes: Published in Science Robotics (2022). Controller was the default in team Cerberus's DARPA SubT win; zero falls reported across deployments.

name: RL-CycleGAN
resolvedTitle: RL-CycleGAN: Reinforcement Learning Aware Simulation-To-Real
org: Google Brain, UC Berkeley, X
problem: GAN-based sim-to-real image translation is task-agnostic and may delete or alter task-relevant content, while randomization or task-specific losses need manual engineering.
keyIdea: Train a CycleGAN jointly with Q-functions and add an RL-scene consistency loss that forces Q-values to be invariant across original, translated and cycled images, giving task-aware sim-to-real translation.
architecture: CycleGAN (Sim2Real and Real2Sim generators + two discriminators) plus Q_sim and Q_real networks trained with QT-Opt TD loss; after training, freeze Sim2Real generator and retrain a Q-function from scratch.
inputs: Monocular RGB images + candidate action.
outputs: Realistic translated images for training; final QT-Opt Q-function for closed-loop grasping.
actionRepr: QT-Opt continuous actions: gripper xyz + top-down rotation, open/close and terminate, chosen by Q maximization
trainingData: Simulated grasping (Bullet) plus off-policy real episodes: 5,000 to 580,000 (Robot 1, KUKA) and 3,000 to 80,000 (Robot 2, mobile base, trash items).

headlineResults.benchmark: Robot 1 grasping, sim-only training + GAN (580k real episodes for GAN)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces task-specific constraints (GraspGAN segmentation, RCAN canonical scenes) with a generic Q-value consistency loss on CycleGAN translations.
limitations: Addresses only the visual sim-to-real gap, not physics; operates on single states rather than trajectories; generators are deterministic.
notes: With on-robot fine-tuning, 5k off-policy + 10k on-policy episodes reach 94%, matching RCAN with 28k on-policy episodes. Paper says 20x fewer real grasps (28k) to match performance of 580k real grasps.

name: Active DR
resolvedTitle: Active Domain Randomization
org: Mila (Universite de Montreal, Polytechnique Montreal), Element AI, CIFAR
problem: Uniform domain randomization samples all environment parameters equally, which yields suboptimal, high-variance policies and gives no insight when transfer fails.
keyIdea: Learn where to sample in the randomization space: SVPG particles propose environment parameters and are rewarded by a discriminator that detects when the agent's rollouts in randomized environments differ from those in a reference environment, focusing training on currently hard environments.
architecture: Agent policy trained with DDPG (400-300 MLP); SVPG sampler with A2C particles (100-unit layers) and RBF kernel; discriminator MLP (two 128-unit layers) scoring (s, a, s') tuples.
inputs: Environment state (task-specific) for the agent; randomization parameter vector for SVPG particles.
outputs: Agent actions (joint commands); proposed randomization parameters.
actionRepr: single-step continuous actions (DDPG)
trainingData: Simulation: LunarLander-v2, Pusher-3DOF, ErgoReacher (8 randomized parameters); zero-shot transfer to a real Poppy Ergo Jr. (ErgoReacher, ErgoPusher).

headlineResults.comparedTo: UDR fails on low main-engine strengths

headlineResults.value: Better or similar performance with lower spread (plotted)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces uniform sampling of randomization parameters with a learned, adaptive sampling strategy driven by a discriminator reward.
limitations: Requires a reference environment and predefined parameter ranges; degenerate ranges (e.g., unsolvable engine strengths) can make ADR focus on impossible environments until ranges are corrected.
notes: Results are reported mainly as plots; no single headline numbers in the text. Learned sampler and discriminator can bootstrap new agents. Limitations sentence partly synthesized from Appendix C.

name: DROPO
resolvedTitle: DROPO: Sim-to-Real Transfer with Offline Domain Randomization
org: Politecnico di Torino, Aalto University
problem: Choosing domain-randomization distributions is hard, and prior automatic methods need repeated real-world policy rollouts or collapse to point estimates.
keyIdea: Fit a DR distribution (means and variances of dynamics parameters) offline by maximizing the likelihood of real transitions under the simulator's next-state distribution induced by that DR distribution, using only a small pre-collected dataset (e.g., human demos).
architecture: Replay real (s, a) sequences in a black-box simulator under K sampled parameter sets, fit a Gaussian next-state distribution, compute log-likelihood of the real next state, and optimize the truncated-normal DR parameters with gradient-free CMA-ES; then train the policy with PPO or SAC under the learned DR.
inputs: Offline real state-action trajectories (any policy or kinesthetic demos).
outputs: Domain randomization distribution over dynamics parameters; downstream RL policy.
trainingData: As little as a single offline real trajectory (pushing task) or two trajectories (Hopper, 1000 transitions); evaluated on Hopper (sim), hockey-puck sliding and box pushing on a real Panda.

headlineResults.value: as close as 2 cm; consistently best (plotted)
Converged to ground truth with std at 1e-5 lower bound

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike DROID (optimizes means only with L2 loss), DROPO uses a likelihood objective and learns per-parameter variances, balancing system identification and randomization.
limitations: Limited to relatively low-dimensional parametric distributions (shown up to 18 dimensions) due to costly gradient-free optimization; needs data that excite the relevant dynamics and an epsilon hyperparameter trading observation noise vs parameter variance.
notes: Code released at github.com/gabrieletiboni/dropo. Published in Robotics and Autonomous Systems. Most results are plotted rather than tabulated.

name: IndustReal
resolvedTitle: IndustReal: Transferring Contact-Rich Assembly Tasks from Simulation to Reality
org: NVIDIA, USC, Stanford, University of Sydney, University of Washington
problem: Simulation had limited impact on robotic assembly: contact-rich, tight-clearance insertion is hard to simulate accurately, and RL agents exploit simulator artifacts, so policies rarely transfer.
keyIdea: Solve assembly with RL in Isaac Gym (Factory) using simulation-aware policy updates that down-weight episodes with interpenetration, SDF-based dense rewards, and a sampling-based curriculum, then deploy with a policy-level action integrator (PLAI) to cancel steady-state error.
architecture: PPO policies per phase (Reach, Pick, Place, Insert) trained in Isaac Gym/Factory; GPU interpenetration checking via Warp; deployment through IndustRealLib with a task-space impedance controller on a Franka Panda plus wrist RealSense D435 for detection.
inputs: Robot proprioception plus goal pose (from RGB-D detection); observation noise injected for Insert policies.
outputs: Relative end-effector pose actions integrated by PLAI into task-space impedance targets.
actionRepr: single-step relative EE pose increments, integrated at policy level (PLAI)
trainingData: Simulation only (no demos, no dynamics randomization, no real-world adaptation); evaluation over 265k simulated trials and 600 real trials.
whatChangedVsParent: Turns Factory's simulated assembly tasks into a full sim-to-real pipeline with SAPU, SDF reward, sampling-based curriculum and PLAI.
limitations: Tasks inspired by the NIST board only; real failures mostly from object slip in the gripper and wedging; no passive compliance or visuotactile sensing; relies on a high-accuracy simulator that may not suffice for harder tasks like elastic cables.
notes: Claims first RL-based sim-to-real system for end-to-end assembly (detection, grasp, transport, insertion) without real-world policy adaptation. Releases IndustRealKit (3D-printable parts) and IndustRealLib with policy weights for peg tasks. Part clearances 0.5-0.6 mm. PLAI later reused by ManipGen/Local Policies.

name: Bi-directional DA
resolvedTitle: Bi-directional Domain Adaptation for Sim2Real Transfer of Embodied Navigation Agents
org: Georgia Tech, Facebook AI Research
problem: Policies trained in simulation fail in reality due to both visual and dynamics gaps, and fine-tuning directly with scarce real data is very sample-inefficient.
keyIdea: Use the small real dataset to adapt the simulator rather than the policy: a real2sim CycleGAN observation adapter ('goggles') at test time, and a sim2real dynamics adapter that learns the residual between simulated and real transitions and resets the simulator accordingly during training.
architecture: Observation adapter: CycleGAN on unpaired RGB-D images. Dynamics adapter: 3-layer MLP predicting residual change in (x, y, theta). Policy: DD-PPO with ResNet50 encoder + 2-layer LSTM in Habitat.
inputs: Egocentric RGB-D + GPS/compass goal vector.
outputs: Discrete navigation actions (PointGoal navigation incl. STOP).
actionRepr: discrete navigation actions
trainingData: Base policy 100M steps in Gibson (Habitat); adapters trained with 100-5,000 target-domain (state, action, next-state) samples. Experiments are Sim2Sim (target simulator with added noise) as a stand-in for reality due to COVID-19.

headlineResults.metric: Target samples to match fine-tuned policy SPL

whatChangedVsParent: Combines real2sim visual adaptation with sim2real residual dynamics adaptation instead of fine-tuning the policy.
limitations: Evaluated Sim2Sim with synthetic noise models as a stand-in for real robots; residual dynamics model covers only 2D pose; underperforms oracle when no dynamics noise due to 'sliding disabled' getting agents stuck.
notes: Navigation (Habitat, LoCoBot dimensions), not manipulation. Also reports FID of real LAB images improving from 100.74 to 83.05 after real2sim adaptation. Limitations synthesized; no explicit limitations section.

name: Walk These Ways
resolvedTitle: Walk These Ways: Tuning Robot Control for Generalization with Multiplicity of Behavior
org: MIT (Improbable AI Lab)
problem: Learned locomotion policies adapt within the training distribution but have no fast way to be tuned when they fail out of distribution, forcing slow reward/environment redesign and retraining.
keyIdea: Multiplicity of Behavior (MoB): train one policy conditioned on 8 interpretable gait/behavior parameters so it solves the training task in many ways; a human can tune these parameters at deployment to generalize to unseen terrains and tasks.
architecture: MLP policy [512, 256, 128] (ELU) with a learned estimator MLP for body velocity and ground friction; 30-step history of observations, commands, behaviors, actions and gait timing variables; PPO in Isaac Gym; actuator network and 20 ms latency model for sim-to-real.
inputs: Joint positions/velocities, gravity vector, velocity command (vx, vy, yaw rate), behavior parameters (foot phase offsets, frequency, body height, pitch, stance width, footswing height), timing references.
outputs: 12 joint position targets tracked by PD (kp=20, kd=0.5).
actionRepr: single-step continuous 12-D joint position targets at 50 Hz
trainingData: Simulation only on flat ground (no terrain randomization) with dynamics randomization (payload, motor strength, calibration, friction, restitution, gravity); deployed on Unitree Go1.

headlineResults.value: Crawled under 22 cm bar (13 cm body)

parents: Siekmann et al. periodic reward composition
whatChangedVsParent: Adds behavior-parameter-conditioned auxiliary rewards so a single policy encodes a tunable family of gaits instead of one fixed solution.
limitations: MoB costs some in-distribution performance (flat-ground sprinting, high combined linear+angular velocity); behavior selection currently requires a human pilot.
notes: Open-source controller and code at gmargo11.github.io/walk-these-ways. Locomotion, not manipulation; relevant to sim-to-real design (actuator net, latency modeling). Note: arXiv 2212.03863 is an unrelated paper (X-Paste); correct ID is 2212.03238.

name: DCAC (random delay)
resolvedTitle: Reinforcement Learning with Random Delays
org: Mila, McGill University, Polytechnique Montreal, Universite de Montreal
problem: Real-world RL faces random action and observation delays that break the Markov assumption and make credit assignment hard; prior work assumed constant delays or planned with predictive models.
keyIdea: Formalize Random-Delay MDPs (state augmented with action buffer and delay values) and use partial trajectory resampling to turn off-policy sub-trajectories into on-policy ones, enabling unbiased multi-step value targets; instantiate as Delay-Correcting Actor-Critic (DCAC) on top of SAC.
architecture: SAC-style actor-critic with a soft state-value critic; multi-step value estimator over resampled sub-trajectories; actor trained via reparameterization with backprop through the action buffer.
inputs: Delayed observation + buffer of last K actions + observation and action delays.
outputs: Continuous control actions.
actionRepr: single-step continuous actions (SAC)
trainingData: Delay-augmented MuJoCo Gym tasks with constant delays and random delays sampled from a real WiFi delay dataset (20 ms steps).

headlineResults.value: Strong advantage over SAC and RTAC (plotted)
DCAC clearly dominates; only DCAC escapes local minima on HalfCheetah (plotted)

whatChangedVsParent: Generalizes RTAC from a fixed one-step delay to random observation/action delays, using delay-aware trajectory resampling for multi-step off-policy targets.
limitations: Requires delay measurements and a bounded maximum delay in the state; all tested methods fail on randomly delayed Ant; time-steps smaller than inference time need extra tricks.
notes: Published at ICLR 2021. Releases a Gym wrapper for adding delays (later rtgym). Results are plots only; no numeric headline values in text. Not robot-specific but used for sim-to-real latency handling.

name: Local Policies (Dalal)
resolvedTitle: Local Policies Enable Zero-shot Long-horizon Manipulation
org: Carnegie Mellon University, Apple
problem: Sim-to-real for open-world manipulation is hard because simulating every scene/task configuration and learning long-horizon behaviours needs intractable data.
keyIdea: ManipGen: train 'local policies' that observe and act only near the target object (invariant to absolute pose, skill order and scene layout), and chain them with a VLM task planner, pose estimation and neural motion planning for zero-shot long-horizon tasks.
architecture: Thousands of single-object state-based PPO experts in GPU simulation, distilled via multi-task DAgger into per-skill visuomotor policies (ResNet-18 + spatial softmax + 2-layer MLP); GPT-4o planner, Grounded-SAM pose estimation, Neural MP motion planner; skills: pick, place, grasp handle, open, close.
inputs: Local wrist depth (84x84), target segmentation mask of first frame, first-frame depth, proprioception relative to first frame; global RGB-D for planning.
outputs: End-effector delta position and rotation at 60 Hz via task-space impedance control with Leaky PLAI.
actionRepr: single-step continuous EE delta (dx, dtheta) at 60 Hz
trainingData: Simulation only: 3.5K UniDexGrasp objects for pick/place, 2.6K PartNet handles for articulated skills; PPO with 8192 parallel envs, 500 epochs; zero real-world data.

headlineResults.benchmark: 50 real-world long-horizon tasks (5 tasks, up to 8 stages)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces hand-engineered or BC skills in LLM-planning pipelines with sim-trained, locality-invariant RL policies distilled into visuomotor generalists.
limitations: Failures from open-set detection errors (Grounding DINO), imperfect motion planning collisions, and local policies failing from suboptimal initial poses; minimal skill library (5 skills).
notes: Method name is ManipGen. Paper states it outperforms SayCan, OpenVLA, LLMTrajGen and VoxPoser by 36%, 76%, 62%, 60% (absolute points). OpenVLA baseline was fine-tuned with 25 demos per task.

name: HG-DAgger
resolvedTitle: HG-DAgger: Interactive Imitation Learning with Human Experts
org: Stanford University; UIUC
topicName: Behavior cloning and why it breaks
problem: DAgger's robot-centric sampling hands control back and forth between novice and human stochastically, which degrades human label quality (perceived actuator lag) and compromises training-time safety.
keyIdea: Let the human expert act as the gating function: the novice drives until the human judges it unsafe, the human takes uninterrupted control to recover, and only those recovery labels are aggregated; also learns a doubt threshold from the novice ensemble's variance at intervention points.
architecture: Novice policy is an ensemble of neural networks; doubt = L2-norm of the diagonal of the ensemble output covariance; threshold tau = mean doubt over the last 25% of logged interventions.
inputs: Low-dimensional vehicle state (distance from median, heading, speed, lane-edge distances, distances to leading obstacles)
outputs: Steering angle and speed commands
actionRepr: single-step continuous 2-D command (steering, speed) regressed per timestep
trainingData: BC init on 10,000 expert labels, then 5 epochs of ~2,000 expert labels each; simulated and real (MG-GS test vehicle) driving with simulated obstacles

headlineResults.metric: Bhattacharyya distance of steering distribution to human (lower better)

headlineResults.benchmark: Simulation, init inside vs outside learned safe set
headlineResults.comparedTo: ~12x lower collisions, ~20x lower road departures inside

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces DAgger's stochastic beta-mixing gate with a human-controlled gate that gives the expert uninterrupted control, and learns the EnsembleDAgger doubt threshold from human interventions.
limitations: Relies on the human to spot and react to unsafe states, so unsuitable where experts cannot quickly identify danger; real-vehicle test data are limited, so statistical significance is low.
notes: Evaluated on autonomous driving, not manipulation; surveys use it as the canonical human-gated interactive IL method. Requires constant human monitoring (the burden ThriftyDAgger later targets).

name: ThriftyDAgger
resolvedTitle: ThriftyDAgger: Budget-Aware Novelty and Risk Gating for Interactive Imitation Learning
org: UC Berkeley (AUTOLAB)
topicName: Behavior cloning and why it breaks
problem: Human-gated interactive IL (e.g. HG-DAgger) requires continuous human monitoring, which does not scale to one human supervising many robots; prior robot-gated criteria need careful threshold tuning.
keyIdea: A robot-gated switching policy requests human help only in states that are novel (high ensemble action variance) or risky (low learned Q-value for reaching the goal set), with thresholds set automatically from a user-specified intervention budget alpha_h.
architecture: Bootstrapped ensemble of BC policies for novelty; a goal-reaching Q-function Q_G trained on offline + intervention data gives Risk = 1 - Q_G; hysteresis thresholds (stricter to cede control back).
inputs: Simulated state (peg insertion, block stacking) or 64x64x3 RGB images (physical cable routing)
outputs: Continuous actions (e.g. delta-(x,y) positions in cable routing)
actionRepr: single-step continuous actions (delta-position) regressed per timestep
trainingData: Physical cable routing: 25 offline demos (1,381 state-action pairs) + 1,500 environment steps with interventions; target intervention rate alpha_h = 0.01
whatChangedVsParent: Moves the gate from the human to the robot and adds a learned task-success risk signal on top of ensemble-novelty gating, with budget-derived thresholds.
limitations: Tends to request fewer but longer interventions, so it can need more total human actions (e.g. block stacking); assumes a goal-set indicator and shared human/robot action space; effect of the budget alpha_h left to future work.
notes: Abstract reports 58% (human) and 80% (robot) performance improvement over next-best algorithm in the fleet user study. Block stacking autonomous success 52/100 vs HG-DAgger 56/100 (comparable, not better).

name: One-shot imitation (Duan)
resolvedTitle: One-Shot Imitation Learning
org: OpenAI; UC Berkeley (BAIR)
topicName: Behavior cloning and why it breaks
problem: Imitation learning is typically trained per task and needs many demos or feature engineering; robots should generalize to a new task from a single demonstration.
keyIdea: Meta-learn a demonstration-conditioned policy: trained on pairs of demos of the same task, the network takes one full demo plus the current state and predicts the action from the other demo; soft attention over demo timesteps and over blocks enables generalization to unseen tasks.
architecture: Three modules: demonstration network (temporal dropout p=0.95, dilated temporal convolutions + neighborhood attention), context network (attention over demo then over current state, LSTM with untied weights), manipulation network (2x256 MLP).
inputs: One demonstration trajectory (observations only) + current state: (x,y,z) of each block relative to gripper and gripper open/closed
outputs: Action (distribution) for a 7-DoF Fetch arm
actionRepr: single-step action; l2 loss for continuous or cross-entropy for discrete actions
trainingData: Simulated block-stacking task family (towers of various heights); noise-injected scripted demonstrations; trained with BC or DAgger
whatChangedVsParent: Turns single-task BC into a meta-learned, demonstration-conditioned policy that generalizes to unseen tasks from one demo.
limitations: Only demonstrated on simulated block stacking with state (not image) inputs; success drops sharply as the number of stages grows; conditions on only one demo.
notes: BC performed on par with DAgger when noise was injected into demos; column labels in the paper's Tables 3-4 ('Demo' vs 'DAgger'/'BC') are architecture/training variants.

name: End-to-end visuomotor policies (Levine)
resolvedTitle: End-to-End Training of Deep Visuomotor Policies
org: UC Berkeley
topicName: Behavior cloning and why it breaks
problem: Policy search usually relies on hand-engineered perception and state estimation that are not adapted to the task; does training perception and control jointly end-to-end work better?
keyIdea: Guided policy search (BADMM formulation) turns policy search into supervised learning: local linear-Gaussian controllers trained with full state supervise a CNN policy that sees only images and robot configuration.
architecture: 7-layer CNN (~92,000 parameters): 3 conv layers, spatial softmax + expected 2-D position layer producing feature points, concatenated with robot configuration, then fully connected layers to torques; first layer initialized from ImageNet-trained model; conv layers pretrained on pose prediction.
inputs: Monocular RGB image (240x240) + robot configuration (joint angles, end-effector points, velocities)
outputs: Joint torques on a 7-DoF PR2 arm
actionRepr: single-step continuous joint torques (Gaussian policy)
trainingData: Real PR2 trials: 156-288 total trials per task (e.g. bottle cap 288); ~1,000 images for visual pretraining; only ~15 minutes of robot execution per task

headlineResults.benchmark: PR2 visuomotor tasks (coat hanger, shape cube, toy hammer, bottle cap)

whatChangedVsParent: Extends guided policy search to deep CNN policies from raw pixels with a spatial-softmax architecture and BADMM optimization.
limitations: Does not generalize to dramatically different scenes or occluding distractors; requires full state observability at training time (instrumentation).
notes: Not behavior cloning in the strict sense: supervision comes from RL-optimized local controllers, but training of the global policy is supervised. Origin of the spatial softmax layer used by later visuomotor policies (e.g. Diffusion Policy). End-to-end success-rate numbers vs pose-feature baseline are in the paper but were not retrieved here.

name: Behavior Transformers (BeT)
resolvedTitle: Behavior Transformers: Cloning k modes with one stone
org: New York University
topicName: Behavior cloning and why it breaks
problem: MSE-based behavior cloning assumes unimodal data and averages across modes; natural pre-collected human data is multimodal and unlabeled.
keyIdea: Discretize continuous actions with k-means into bins, predict a categorical bin with a transformer over observation history, and add a per-bin continuous residual offset (like object-detection box offsets).
architecture: minGPT transformer decoder with linear input projection; binning head (focal loss) and offset head (masked multi-task MSE); frozen ImageNet ResNet-18 encoder for visual observations (CARLA).
inputs: History of h observations (states, or 224x224 RGB in CARLA)
outputs: Categorical bin probabilities + k x dim(A) offsets
actionRepr: single-step continuous action = sampled k-means bin center + predicted residual offset (k = 24 to 64 depending on env)
trainingData: Offline demos: Point-mass, CARLA (100 demos), Block push, Franka Kitchen

headlineResults.benchmark: Ablation (relative to full BeT), Block push

headlineResults.metric: normalized success with MLP / LSTM trunk

headlineResults.comparedTo: IBC 52 ms; MLP 0.5 ms; Trajectory Transformer 867.86 ms

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces unimodal MSE regression with k-means-binned categorical prediction plus residual offsets on a transformer over history.
limitations: Evaluated mostly in simulation; can over-visit some task sequences relative to the demos in Kitchen; bin count k trades off classification and offset losses.
notes: Main success-rate table (Table 1) not retrieved; only ablation and timing numbers recorded. Paper states datasets, code and trained models will be released.

name: iDP3
resolvedTitle: Generalizable Humanoid Manipulation with 3D Diffusion Policies (Improved 3D Diffusion Policy, iDP3)
org: Stanford University; Simon Fraser University; UPenn; UIUC; CMU
problem: 3D Diffusion Policy (DP3) needs precise camera calibration and point-cloud segmentation in a world frame, which is impractical on humanoids with moving heads, and humanoid skills rarely generalize beyond the training scene.
keyIdea: Use egocentric (camera-frame) point clouds with no calibration or segmentation, scale up the number of sampled points, swap in a pyramid convolutional encoder and lengthen the prediction horizon so the diffusion policy learns from noisy human teleop data.
architecture: DP3-style diffusion policy with a Conv+Pyramid point-cloud encoder (replacing DP3's MLP), voxel + uniform point sampling (4096 points) instead of farthest point sampling; DDIM with 50 training / 10 inference steps.
inputs: Egocentric point cloud from head-mounted RealSense L515 LiDAR camera + proprioception (joint positions)
outputs: Target joint positions for 25-DoF upper body (head, waist, arms, Inspire hands) of Fourier GR1
actionRepr: diffusion-generated chunk of target joint positions, prediction horizon 16
trainingData: Apple Vision Pro whole-upper-body teleop in a single scene; 10 demos x 10 rollouts per task, 300 episodes across Pick&Place, Pour, Wipe
whatChangedVsParent: Moves DP3 from world-frame segmented sparse point clouds to egocentric dense point clouds with a pyramid conv encoder and longer horizon, removing calibration/segmentation needs.
limitations: AVP teleoperation is tiring so data are hard to scale; depth sensor point clouds are noisy; fine-grained skills are slow to collect; lower body disabled (robot on a cart).
notes: In the training scene DP with a finetuned R3M encoder beat iDP3 (99/147 vs 75/139); iDP3's advantage is generalization to new objects/views/scenes. More than 2,000 real rollouts reported (Table I lists 2,253). Code released per project site, weights not confirmed.

name: ScaleDP
resolvedTitle: Scaling Diffusion Policy in Transformer to 1 Billion Parameters for Robotic Manipulation
org: East China Normal University; Midea Group AI Research Center; Shanghai University; Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics
problem: The transformer variant of Diffusion Policy (DP-T) does not scale: adding layers lowers performance because cross-attention condition fusion produces large, unstable gradients.
keyIdea: Fuse timestep and observation conditions with adaptive LayerNorm (DiT-style AdaLN) instead of cross-attention and remove causal masking so action tokens attend to future actions, enabling stable scaling from 10M to 1B parameters.
architecture: Stack of AdaLN transformer blocks with non-causal self-attention over noisy action tokens; ResNet-50 encoders for multi-view images; five sizes Ti/S/B/L/H (10M, 33M, 130M, 457M, 1B).
inputs: Multi-view RGB images (global + wrist cameras) + proprioception
outputs: Denoised action sequence
actionRepr: DDPM-diffused chunk of 6-D end-effector pose actions (x,y,z,roll,pitch,yaw) plus gripper
trainingData: MetaWorld 50 tasks with 20 demos each; real: 100 trajectories per task (40 for close laptop) on Franka and bimanual UR5

headlineResults.metric: average success with vs without non-causal attention

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces DP-T's cross-attention conditioning and causal masking with AdaLN conditioning and bidirectional attention so the model scales with size.
limitations: Generalization to large lighting changes and added distractors remains limited (single-trial qualitative tests); scaling claims rest on MetaWorld and 7 real tasks.
notes: Abstract: +36.25% avg over DP-T on four single-arm tasks and +75% on three bimanual tasks. DP-T drops from 80.1% (8 layers) to 74.6% (14 layers) on MetaWorld in the motivation study.

name: MoDE
resolvedTitle: Efficient Diffusion Transformer Policies with Mixture of Expert Denoisers for Multitask Learning
org: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (Intuitive Robots Lab); MIT
problem: Diffusion-transformer policies are computationally expensive as they scale (many denoising steps through a large dense network), limiting real-time and on-board use.
keyIdea: Mixture-of-Experts diffusion transformer whose router is conditioned only on the noise level, so each denoising phase uses specialized experts and the routing can be precomputed and experts fused (expert caching) for cheap inference.
architecture: Causal transformer; each block = noise-conditioned self-attention (noise token added to all tokens) + sparse MoE of Swish-GLU MLP experts (4 experts, top-2 by default) with load-balancing loss; frozen CLIP text encoder, FiLM-ResNet-18/50 image encoders; EDM diffusion with 10 DDIM steps.
inputs: Static + wrist camera images, language goal
outputs: Denoised action chunk
actionRepr: EDM score-based diffusion over a chunk of future actions (end-effector control in LIBERO/CALVIN)
trainingData: Pretraining on 196k trajectories from six Open X-Embodiment datasets (300k steps, 6 GPUs, 3 days); evaluated on CALVIN and LIBERO (134 tasks across 4 benchmarks)

headlineResults.metric: average gain over CNN and Transformer Diffusion Policies

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces dense FFNs with noise-conditioned MoE experts and adds noise-conditioned attention, cutting compute via cached routing.
limitations: Slightly higher variance across seeds than baselines (router initialization sensitivity); expert collapse observed in some runs (only a subset of experts used).
notes: Code and demos released per abstract; pretrained weights availability inferred from project page but not confirmed in retrieved text. More than 4 experts degraded CALVIN performance.

name: SDP
resolvedTitle: Sparse Diffusion Policy: A Sparse, Reusable, and Flexible Policy for Robot Learning
org: UC Berkeley; Carnegie Mellon University; UNC-Chapel Hill
problem: A single dense policy for all tasks is computationally expensive and suffers catastrophic forgetting when new tasks are learned; adapters like LoRA grow active parameters.
keyIdea: Replace the FFNs of a transformer diffusion policy with Mixture-of-Experts layers and task-specific routers, so tasks sparsely activate and share experts; continual learning adds new experts/routers while freezing old ones; transfer tunes only the router.
architecture: Transformer-based Diffusion Policy with MoE layers (top-K experts per layer, task-specific routers), trained with BC loss minus a task-expert mutual-information term; also integrated into DP3 for point-cloud tasks.
inputs: Historical states/images (2D) or point clouds (3D, DP3 variant) + task identity
outputs: Sequence of future actions
actionRepr: diffusion-generated action chunk (Diffusion Policy style)
trainingData: MimicGen 8 tasks (1K-10K demos per task), DexArt and Adroit (3 tasks each), robomimic for continual learning, real FANUC arm 20-40 demos per task

headlineResults.metric: success on Can after stage 3 / active params

whatChangedVsParent: Adds sparse MoE layers with task-specific routers to Diffusion Policy for multitask, continual and transfer learning at near-constant active parameters.
limitations: Can fail if shared knowledge is too limited while the same experts are used by different routers; routers are task-specific, so it needs task identity rather than being a universal language-conditioned policy.
notes: Code released per abstract. Distinct from MoDE: SDP routes by task (state tokens + task-specific router), MoDE routes by noise level.

name: OneDP
resolvedTitle: One-Step Diffusion Policy: Fast Visuomotor Policies via Diffusion Distillation
org: NVIDIA; UT Austin
problem: Diffusion Policy's iterative denoising is slow (about 1.5 Hz by default), too slow for dynamic environments and constrained compute; prior Consistency Policy still needs several steps and converges slowly.
keyIdea: Distill a pretrained diffusion policy into a one-step action generator by minimizing reverse KL along the diffusion chain, whose gradient is a score difference between the frozen teacher and an auxiliary generator-score network (SDS/VSD-style).
architecture: Generator and generator-score network both initialized from the pretrained CNN U-Net Diffusion Policy with ResNet-18 vision encoder; stochastic (OneDP-S) and deterministic (OneDP-D, no auxiliary network) variants.
inputs: Two past RGB observations (+ proprioception)
outputs: Action chunk in one forward pass
actionRepr: one-step generated chunk of 16 actions (distilled from DDPM/EDM diffusion)
trainingData: Robomimic Square/Transport/ToolHang (PH and MH) and PushT (200 demos); 4 real Franka tasks; distillation 20 epochs after 1000-epoch pretraining (2-10% extra cost)

headlineResults.comparedTo: DP DDPM 100 steps 0.829; DP DDIM 10 steps 0.836; DP 1 step 0.000
DDPM 100 steps 660 ms; DDIM 10 steps 66 ms

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces multi-step denoising with a single-step generator distilled by KL/score-difference matching, achieving ~42x faster inference without losing success rate.
limitations: Requires a pretrained diffusion teacher; deterministic variant is slightly weaker; paper does not evaluate beyond single-arm and Robomimic-style tasks.
notes: Real completion time 25.81 s vs 36.36 s for DP (Figure 1).

name: ManiCM
resolvedTitle: ManiCM: Real-time 3D Diffusion Policy via Consistency Model for Robotic Manipulation
org: Tsinghua University (Shenzhen); University of Hong Kong; Nanyang Technological University
problem: 3D diffusion policies (DP3) need ~10 denoising steps with point-cloud conditioning, giving ~178 ms latency that blocks real-time closed-loop control.
keyIdea: Consistency distillation of a DP3 teacher into a point-cloud-conditioned consistency model that maps any point on the PF-ODE trajectory directly to the clean action, parameterized to predict the action sample (not noise) for fast convergence.
architecture: DP3-style MLP point-cloud encoder (512 FPS points) + pose encoder (64-d embeddings) conditioning a consistency function; online, EMA target and frozen DP3 teacher networks; DDIM solver with skip k=10.
inputs: Sparse point cloud from single-view depth (84x84) over 2 observation steps + robot pose
outputs: Action sequence (end-effector change + gripper) in one step
actionRepr: 1-step consistency-model sample of a 4-action chunk (2 executed)
trainingData: 10 expert demos per task on 31 tasks (Adroit 3, MetaWorld 28); RLBench 8 tasks (20 demos) multi-task; 3 real UR3e tasks

headlineResults.benchmark: Real UR3e (Slide Block / Stack Cube / Transfer Piece)

whatChangedVsParent: Distills DP3 into a 1-step consistency model with sample prediction, cutting latency ~10x at equal success.
limitations: Requires a pretrained diffusion teacher; scalability to distilling large pretrained diffusion policies left to future work.
notes: Noise-prediction variant collapses under consistency distillation (24.4% vs 78.5%).

name: FLOWER
resolvedTitle: FLOWER: Democratizing Generalist Robot Policies with Efficient Vision-Language-Action Flow Policies
org: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (Intuitive Robots Lab); Microsoft Research
problem: Diffusion/flow VLAs are multi-billion-parameter models needing massive pretraining compute; spending most parameters on the VLM starves the action head.
keyIdea: Intermediate-modality fusion: prune the VLM (drop Florence-2's decoder, ~50% of LLM layers) and feed intermediate VLM tokens into a large Flow Transformer via cross-attention, with a shared action-space Global-AdaLN plus LoRA for heterogeneous embodiments.
architecture: Florence-2-L encoder (ViT 360M + 205M VLM) + 18-layer, 1024-d Flow Transformer (339M) with cross-attention to VLM tokens, action-space Global-AdaLN-Zero, per-action-space encoders/decoders; 947M total, 1.85 GB VRAM.
inputs: Single static image (plus wrist/secondary cameras on some benchmarks), language instruction, embodiment/action-space metadata, proprio for bimanual
outputs: Continuous action chunk
actionRepr: rectified-flow chunk (10-100 steps depending on benchmark; 20 in pretraining) in delta-EEF or joint space, 4-8 integration steps
trainingData: OXE-soup of 8 public datasets, ~250k trajectories (Bridge, Fractal, DROID, etc.); 360k steps in 48 h on 4 H100 (~200 GPU-hours)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces late/early fusion with pruned-VLM intermediate fusion and a parameter-shared action-space AdaLN, yielding a <1B flow VLA trained with ~1% of OpenVLA's pretraining compute.
limitations: Still iterative sampling (slower than one-pass deterministic policies); validated mostly on three manipulation action spaces; weaker on SIMPLER Google Robot (32.2% vs 42.4%); 8 of 10 benchmarks are simulated.
notes: Pretraining GPU hours shown as 192 in Fig 1 vs OpenVLA 21,500 and RDT-1B 35,000. Intermediate fusion ablation: 93.4% LIBERO-Long vs 33.4% early and 61.8% late fusion.

name: Streaming Flow Policy
resolvedTitle: Streaming Flow Policy: Simplifying diffusion/flow-matching policies by treating action trajectories as flow trajectories
org: MIT
problem: Diffusion/flow policies sample a 'trajectory of trajectories', discarding intermediates and forcing the robot to wait for sampling to finish before executing any action.
keyIdea: Make flow time equal execution time: start from a narrow Gaussian around the last action (or current robot state) and integrate a learned velocity field in action space, streaming each action to the robot as it is generated; conditional flows include a stabilizing term that pulls back toward the demonstration.
architecture: Reuses diffusion-policy network architectures with input/output changed from A^T to A; velocity field v(a,t|h) trained by conditional flow matching on analytically constructed stabilizing flows (trajectory velocity minus k times deviation).
inputs: Observation history (images/state), current action or robot state, flow time
outputs: Action velocity, integrated into a streamed action sequence
actionRepr: streamed continuous actions (position setpoints) generated sequentially by ODE integration in action space; deterministic at test time (sigma0=0)
trainingData: Push-T and RoboMimic benchmarks; real Franka Research 3 tasks (apple pick, block reorientation)
whatChangedVsParent: Moves flow matching from trajectory space to action space so the flow path itself is the executed trajectory, enabling streaming without an action buffer.
limitations: Only matches per-timestep marginal action distributions, not the joint trajectory distribution, so sampled trajectories can compose segments of different demos and cannot capture global trajectory constraints.
notes: Paper reports performance comparable to Diffusion Policy with much lower per-action latency; exact benchmark numbers were not retrieved in this pass. CoRL 2025.

name: ManiFlow
resolvedTitle: ManiFlow: A General Robot Manipulation Policy via Consistency Flow Training
org: University of Washington; UC San Diego; NVIDIA; Allen Institute for AI
problem: Existing flow-matching policies are limited in efficiency, robustness and generalization for high-dimensional dexterous manipulation, and their architectures condition poorly on multiple input modalities.
keyIdea: Jointly train flow matching with a continuous-time consistency objective (shortcut-model style, no teacher) so 1-2 steps suffice, and use a DiT-X transformer whose AdaLN-Zero modulation also scales cross-attention to visual/language tokens.
architecture: DiT-X blocks: self-attention + adaptive cross-attention to visual/language tokens + FFN, all modulated by AdaLN-Zero from timestep, step size and low-dim inputs; ResNet-18 (2D) or DP3-style point encoder (3D).
inputs: 2D images or 3D point clouds, robot proprioception, optional language
outputs: Action sequence
actionRepr: flow-matching chunk of high-dimensional (up to dexterous-hand joint) actions, 1-2 inference steps
trainingData: Adroit, DexArt, RoboTwin 1.0 (12 tasks), MetaWorld 48 language-conditioned tasks, RoboTwin 2.0 (50 domain-randomized demos per task); 8 real tasks on Franka, bimanual xArm with Ability hands, Unitree H1 humanoid
whatChangedVsParent: Adds teacher-free consistency training to flow matching and replaces DiT/MDT blocks with DiT-X adaptive cross-attention conditioning.
limitations: Real-world success depends heavily on demonstration quality and diversity; not yet combined with RL; richer modalities (tactile, VLM conditioning) unexplored.
notes: As a drop-in head for 3D Diffuser Actor on CALVIN it raised avg length from 3.35 (DDPM 25 steps) to 3.67 (1 step) and 4.03 (10 steps). Unseen-object real success 67.4% vs DP3 31.1%.

name: MP1
resolvedTitle: MP1: MeanFlow Tames Policy Learning in 1-step for Robotic Manipulation
org: Peking University (Shenzhen Graduate School)
problem: Diffusion policies are slow (many denoising steps) while one-step flow policies such as FlowPolicy rely on explicit consistency constraints.
keyIdea: Adapt MeanFlow to point-cloud policies: learn the interval-averaged velocity via the MeanFlow identity so one network evaluation maps noise to the action trajectory, plus CFG and a Dispersive Loss that spreads latent state embeddings for few-shot generalization.
architecture: DP3-style point-cloud and state encoders conditioning a U-Net MeanFlow network; Dispersive Loss (InfoNCE-style, no positives) on down-sampling block features; classifier-free guidance baked into training.
inputs: Point cloud (512 or 1024 FPS points) + robot state, 2-step observation window
outputs: Action trajectory in one forward pass
actionRepr: 1-NFE MeanFlow-generated action chunk (prediction horizon 4 in sim, 16 in real)
trainingData: 10 expert demos per task on 3 Adroit + 34 MetaWorld tasks; 20 human demos per real task on ARX R5 dual-arm
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces FlowPolicy's consistency-constrained 1-step flow with a MeanFlow average-velocity objective and adds Dispersive Loss.
limitations: Evaluated with few demonstrations on Adroit/MetaWorld and five real tasks; flow ratio of 1.0 collapses performance, so the r != t sampling ratio matters.
notes: Code on GitHub (LogSSim/MP1). AAAI 2026. Dispersive Loss ablation gives roughly 4-5 point gains.

name: FlowPolicy
resolvedTitle: FlowPolicy: Enabling Fast and Robust 3D Flow-based Policy via Consistency Flow Matching for Robot Manipulation
org: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China; Megvii Technology
problem: Diffusion-based 3D policies (DP3) need many sampling steps, trading inference speed against action quality.
keyIdea: Condition Consistency Flow Matching on point clouds: learn velocity-consistent straight-line flows (two-segment) from noise to action so actions are generated in a single step without distillation.
architecture: DP3 backbone: single-view depth to point cloud, FPS downsampling, lightweight MLP encoder to a 64-d compact 3D representation plus robot state embedding, conditioning a flow network trained with two-segment Consistency-FM loss (EMA target).
inputs: Point cloud (512 Adroit / 1024 MetaWorld) from 2 most recent frames + robot state
outputs: Action trajectory in one step
actionRepr: 1-NFE consistency-flow-matching action chunk (straight-line flow, 2 segments)
trainingData: 10 expert demos per task on 37 tasks (3 Adroit + 34 MetaWorld) from scripted/heuristic experts

headlineResults.comparedTo: DP3 68.7%; Simple DP3 67.4%; Consistency Policy 50.1%; DP 35.2%
DP3 145.7 ms; Simple DP3 63.0 ms; DP 106.1 ms

whatChangedVsParent: Swaps DP3's 10-step DDIM diffusion for a 1-step conditional consistency flow-matching generator, ~7x faster.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation (Adroit, MetaWorld) with scripted demonstrations; gains over DP3 in success rate are small (+1.3 points) and it underperforms DP3 on MetaWorld Very Hard (36.6 vs 39.4).
