notes: AAAI 2025; code at github.com/zql-kk/FlowPolicy. MP1 later reports FlowPolicy at 71.6% / 12.6 ms under its own re-run on RTX 4090 (differs from FlowPolicy's own 70.0% / 19.9 ms on 2080Ti).

name: PointFlowMatch
resolvedTitle: Learning Robotic Manipulation Policies from Point Clouds with Conditional Flow Matching
org: University of Freiburg
problem: Imitation-learning design choices (observation modality, generative objective, 6-DoF rotation representation) interact, and CFM had not been systematically studied for policy learning.
keyIdea: Combine conditional flow matching (rectified flow) with point-cloud observations for non-hierarchical single-task policies, and compare Euclidean vs SO(3) flow formulations for end-effector orientation.
architecture: Modified PointNet encoder (no T-nets) on merged multi-camera point cloud (4096 points) + proprioception, conditioning a 1D conditional U-Net that predicts velocity; closed-loop receding-horizon execution.
inputs: Merged, voxel-downsampled point cloud from calibrated RGB-D cameras + robot end-effector pose history
outputs: Future end-effector trajectory
actionRepr: CFM-generated chunk of 10-D absolute actions (3-D position, 6-D rotation, gripper), integrated with k steps
trainingData: RLBench: 100 scripted demos per task, 8 tasks (Franka); real Franka with 2 RealSense cameras

headlineResults.comparedTo: OL-ChainedDiffuser 34.6%; 3D Diffusion Policy 28.5%; AdaFlow 19.0%; Diffusion Policy 18.7%

headlineResults.benchmark: RLBench, image vs point cloud input (ablation)
Real Franka open box / sponge on plate

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces diffusion with conditional flow matching on point-cloud inputs, showing CFM matches DDIM at 50 steps but is much better with few steps.
limitations: Iterative inference is slower than direct BC; cannot extrapolate beyond demonstrated corrections; needs calibrated depth cameras; single-task only, generalization not studied.
notes: CoRL 2024; code, models and videos released. Euclidean 6-D rotation formulation slightly beat the SO(3) formulation (67.8 vs 67.4). Conclusion text says 68.6% while Table 1 says 67.8% (internal inconsistency in the paper).

name: MaIL
resolvedTitle: MaIL: Improving Imitation Learning with Mamba
org: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (ALR and Intuitive Robots Lab)
problem: Transformer policies tend to overfit or learn poor representations when demonstrations are scarce.
keyIdea: Replace the transformer backbone of BC and diffusion policies with Mamba selective state-space models, including a novel encoder-decoder Mamba that aligns sequences with learnable action/state/time variables.
architecture: Decoder-only Mamba (D-Ma) or encoder-decoder Mamba (ED-Ma) stacks; ResNet-18 image encoder, CLIP language embeddings; used either as BC mean regressor or as DDPM denoiser (16 diffusion steps).
inputs: Images (1 or 5 history steps), optional language
outputs: Action sequence (denoised or regressed)
actionRepr: diffusion (DDPM, 16 steps) or Gaussian-BC action chunk; real robot: 8-D joint positions + gripper
trainingData: LIBERO suites with 20% of demonstrations (10 per task); real Franka tasks with 30-100 demos
whatChangedVsParent: Swaps transformer self/cross-attention backbones for selective state-space (Mamba) blocks in both BC and diffusion policies.
limitations: Advantage shrinks with full datasets (comparable, not better, than transformers); with short IL sequences, inference-speed advantage over transformers is negligible.
notes: CoRL 2024; code at github.com/ALRhub/MaIL. Not itself a new generative head: it is a backbone swap usable under BC or diffusion.

name: RoboMamba
resolvedTitle: RoboMamba: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Model for Robotic Reasoning and Manipulation
org: Peking University; AI2Robotics; BAAI
problem: VLA models reason poorly on complex robotic tasks and are expensive to fine-tune and run because of attention-based LLMs.
keyIdea: Build a VLA on the linear-complexity Mamba LLM: align a CLIP encoder to Mamba and co-train on general plus robotic (RoboVQA) instruction data, then freeze everything and fine-tune only a tiny MLP policy head for SE(3) pose prediction.
architecture: CLIP vision encoder + projection + Mamba 2.7B LLM (3.2B total); policy head of two MLPs (position, rotation) with 3.7M parameters (~0.1%).
inputs: Single RGB image (224 or 336) + language question/instruction
outputs: Language reasoning answers and end-effector pose (2-D contact pixel lifted with depth + 3x3 rotation; gripper state for grasping)
actionRepr: single-shot 6-DoF/7-DoF end-effector pose (contact point + rotation matrix) regressed by MLP head; not a trajectory
trainingData: LLaVA 558k alignment; 655k LLaVA mix / ShareGPT4V / LLaVA-Next + RoboVQA co-training; 10k SAPIEN pose samples for manipulation fine-tuning
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces attention LLM backbones of robotic MLLMs with Mamba and learns manipulation via a frozen-backbone tiny policy head.
limitations: 2.7B LLM limits complex reasoning relative to 7B/13B MLLMs; predicts single contact poses in open loop rather than closed-loop trajectories.
notes: NeurIPS 2024. Survey placement under 'generative policy heads' is loose: RoboMamba's action head is a deterministic MLP pose regressor, not generative.

name: FreqPolicy
resolvedTitle: FreqPolicy: Frequency Autoregressive Visuomotor Policy with Continuous Tokens
org: ShanghaiTech University; University of Hong Kong; NTU; CUHK
problem: Diffusion policies are slow while autoregressive policies discretize actions (losing precision) and accumulate errors; neither exploits that tasks need different amounts of high-frequency action detail.
keyIdea: Transform action chunks with the DCT and generate them coarse-to-fine across frequency levels autoregressively, using continuous tokens decoded by a small per-token diffusion MLP (MAR-style) instead of discrete tokens.
architecture: Masked encoder-decoder (FreqPolicy encoder/decoder) conditioned on observation features (DP or DP3 encoders), frequency index and lower-frequency reconstruction; diffusion-loss MLP head; frequency-aware masking from FAR.
inputs: Images (2D tasks) or point clouds (3D tasks) + robot state
outputs: Full-frequency action sequence, refined over N_iter frequency levels
actionRepr: action chunk generated in DCT frequency domain, low-to-high frequency autoregression with continuous diffusion-decoded tokens
trainingData: Robomimic, Push-T (2D); Adroit, DexArt, MetaWorld, RoboTwin (3D); real ShadowHand handover
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces temporal or discrete-token generation with frequency-domain coarse-to-fine autoregression over continuous tokens.
limitations: Condition-input designs were kept identical to DP/DP3 and not explored; room for improvement on 2D tasks; performance drops when frequency partitioning becomes too fine-grained.
notes: Code at github.com/4DVLab/Freqpolicy. Main per-benchmark success tables were not retrieved in this pass; only efficiency numbers recorded.

name: Wavelet Policy
resolvedTitle: Wavelet Policy: Imitation Policy Learning in Frequency Domain with Wavelet Transforms
org: Zhejiang University; Tsinghua University
problem: Imitation policies model action trajectories in the spatial/time domain and underuse frequency-domain structure, which may miss temporal information, especially on long-range tasks.
keyIdea: Apply a Haar wavelet transform to encoded visual features and decode each frequency band with its own transformer decoder (single encoder, multiple decoders), then reconstruct the action sequence by inverse wavelet transform; add learnable frequency-domain filters per band.
architecture: ResNet-18 feature extractor per camera with conv compression and embedding-dimension fusion; Haar DWT; SE2MD transformer (1 encoder, one decoder per wavelet band) with Learnable Frequency-Domain Filters (RBF/RBLF/EBF); IDWT to actions.
inputs: Multi-view RGB images (+ proprioception) in ALOHA-style simulated bimanual tasks
outputs: Action sequence (e.g. 40 x 7 per arm in figure)
actionRepr: deterministic action chunk reconstructed from wavelet-band decoder outputs (ACT-style regression, not generative)
trainingData: Simulated bimanual ALOHA tasks: Transfer Cube, Bimanual Insertion, plus two new tasks Transfer Plus and Stack Two Blocks

headlineResults.metric: insert success % without WT / without SE2MD

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces ACT's single transformer decoder with wavelet-band-specific decoders and learnable frequency filters at ~1/3 the parameters.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation on four bimanual tasks with single-task datasets; learnable-filter gains are modest; real-robot validation left to future work.
notes: Despite being listed under generative policy heads by the survey, Wavelet Policy is a deterministic (non-generative) chunk regressor; frequency is used on features, not on sampling. Abstract claims >10% over SOTA end-to-end methods.

name: DBPO
resolvedTitle: Drift-Based Policy Optimization: Native One-Step Policy Learning for Online Robot Control
org: University of Science and Technology of China; iFlytek
problem: Multi-step generative policies need tens to hundreds of NFEs per action, too costly for high-frequency control and online RL; existing one-step methods depend on distillation or auxiliary correction losses.
keyIdea: Drift-Based Policy (DBP) uses Drifting Models' fixed-point attraction-repulsion objective so iterative refinement is absorbed at training time and inference is natively 1-NFE; DBPO adds a stochastic interface for exact-likelihood PPO fine-tuning with an anchor loss to the pretrained policy.
architecture: Same U-Net backbone and point-cloud/image encoders as MP1/OMP (or Diffusion Policy) trained with drifting objective (kernel temperatures {0.02, 0.05, 0.2}); DBPO adds Gaussian exploration around the deterministic mean, PPO with value head and anchor regularization.
inputs: Low-dim states, RGB images, 3D point clouds, or multi-camera inputs
outputs: Action chunk in one forward pass
actionRepr: 1-NFE drifting-model generated action chunk; Gaussian noise added only during online RL
trainingData: Diffusion Policy sim suite (12 tasks); 37 Adroit/MetaWorld point-cloud tasks with 10 demos; RoboMimic and D4RL for online RL; 50 teleop demos per real UR5 task
parents: Generative Modeling via Drifting (Deng et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces distillation- or MeanFlow-based one-step policies with a drifting objective that is one-step by construction, and extends it to PPO fine-tuning.
limitations: Evaluations target tabletop manipulation and locomotion in structured scenes; DBPO sample efficiency from scratch and at larger scale not yet studied; real Transport task only 55%.
notes: Name resolved via keyword search; the survey's 'DBPO' is assumed to be this April 2026 paper (drift-based one-step policies), consistent with its neighbor 'Implicit Drifting Policy'. Point-cloud baselines quoted from OMP.

name: Implicit Drifting Policy
resolvedTitle: Implicit Drifting Policy: One-Step Action Generation via Conditional Expert Geometry
org: ShanghaiTech University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; CUHK; Morphi Robot
problem: One-step policies discard the intermediate correction of multi-step generation, and explicit drifting fields degenerate to plain MSE in behavior cloning because each observation has a single expert action.
keyIdea: Replace the explicit drifting field with an implicit, geometry-aware potential: weight action errors by a conditional expert geometry (covariance of expert actions under similar observations) relative to a global reference geometry, plus an expert-proximal terminal evaluation during training.
architecture: One-step generator (Transformer/CNN for 2D, DP3-style for 3D) trained with a potential weighted by ReLU 'geometry excess' of normalized local vs global precision per action dimension; neighbors found by observation similarity.
inputs: States, images or point clouds
outputs: Action chunk in one evaluation
actionRepr: 1-NFE generated action chunk trained with geometry-weighted implicit drifting objective
trainingData: Robomimic (Lift, Can, Square, Transport, ph/mh), Tool-Hang, PushT; 56 point-cloud tasks across Adroit, DexArt, MetaWorld; real single-arm ALOHA 'Pick Peach'

headlineResults.comparedTo: Naive Drifting 79.8%; MP1 (reproduced) 79.7%; DP3 (reproduced, 10 NFE) 79.4%; OFP 71.6%

whatChangedVsParent: Swaps the explicit drifting vector field for a static geometry-weighted potential derived from neighboring expert actions.
limitations: Single-step policies (including IDP) collapse to one mode on balanced bimodal demos; conditional geometry needs a reasonable density of expert actions under similar observations; underperforms MIP in the real state-based (qpos) setting.
notes: Preprint May 2026. 'Naive Drifting' baseline is the explicit Drifting Models objective applied to BC.

name: Chain-of-Action
resolvedTitle: Chain-of-Action: Trajectory Autoregressive Modeling for Robotic Manipulation
org: ByteDance Seed; University of Adelaide; NUS; CAS; CSIRO
problem: Forward, next-step action prediction (even with chunking) is myopic and accumulates compounding errors because it is not anchored to the task goal.
keyIdea: Generate the trajectory backward: first predict a keyframe (goal) action, then autoregressively decode earlier actions until reaching the current gripper state, giving goal-anchored global-to-local consistency.
architecture: ACT-like 4-layer transformer encoder / 7-layer decoder with causal mask; ResNet-18 per camera; continuous action tokens via linear encoder/decoder with latent consistency loss; multi-token prediction heads (5) at training; distance-based dynamic stop; reverse temporal ensemble.
inputs: Multi-view RGB (4 cameras in RLBench, single camera real) + gripper/proprioceptive state
outputs: Variable-length end-effector pose trajectory to the next keyframe
actionRepr: continuous-token reverse autoregressive trajectory of absolute end-effector poses, variable length with dynamic stop
trainingData: RLBench 60 tasks, 100 demos each (evaluated on 25); real Fetch robot 8 kitchen tasks with 35-81 demos
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces ACT's forward fixed-length chunk prediction with reverse autoregressive generation anchored on a predicted keyframe action.
limitations: Relies on keyframe heuristics (gripper change or near-zero joint velocity) to split trajectories, which may not generalize to diverse task types.
notes: Ablation: forward ordering 0.668, hybrid 0.600, reverse 0.756 on RLBench-10. Not a diffusion/flow head; it is a deterministic continuous-token autoregressive policy.

name: Bi-ACT
resolvedTitle: Bi-ACT: Bilateral Control-Based Imitation Learning via Action Chunking with Transformer
org: Osaka University
problem: ACT/ALOHA collect position-only data and cannot sense object hardness or weight, while prior bilateral-control imitation learning (position+force) used LSTMs and no images.
keyIdea: Combine ACT-style action chunking with four-channel bilateral (leader-follower, position+force) control: the policy predicts the leader's joint angle, velocity and torque, which the follower tracks via the bilateral controller.
architecture: ACT architecture (CVAE + transformer) with image inputs from two RGB cameras and an extended 15-D joint-state vector (angle, angular velocity, force for 5 joints); a disturbance observer / reaction-force observer based controller converts predictions to joint currents.
inputs: Two RGB images (gripper and overhead, 360x640) + follower joint angles, angular velocities and torques (15-D)
outputs: k x 15 chunk of leader joint angle, velocity and torque commands
actionRepr: Chunk of k future leader states (angle, velocity, torque for 5 joints = 15-D) executed at 100 Hz through bilateral control
trainingData: Real OpenMANIPULATOR-X data via bilateral control: 50 pick-and-place episodes (2 objects, >44,184 timesteps) and 50 put-in-drawer episodes (97,972 timesteps), downsampled to 100 Hz
parents: Bilateral control-based imitation learning (Sakaino et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Adds joint velocity and torque to ACT's inputs/outputs and executes via 4-channel bilateral control instead of pure position control.
limitations: Tested only on one 4-DoF arm (OpenMANIPULATOR-X) with two tasks; authors list robustness to lighting/dynamic scenes and cross-platform generalization as future work.
notes: Small-scale study; trials were 10 per object. No comparison against vanilla ACT, only an ablation without force.

name: ALOHA Unleashed
resolvedTitle: ALOHA Unleashed: A Simple Recipe for Robot Dexterity
org: Google DeepMind
problem: Unclear whether simply scaling imitation learning suffices for highly dexterous, contact-rich bimanual tasks with deformables (e.g. shoelace tying, shirt hanging).
keyIdea: Large-scale teleoperated data collection on ALOHA 2 plus a transformer encoder-decoder trained with a diffusion loss (Diffusion Policy on an ACT-like architecture) is enough to learn dexterous bimanual skills.
architecture: Four ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50s embed four camera views; an 85M transformer encoder fuses image tokens + proprioception; a 55M transformer decoder denoises a 50x14 action chunk by cross-attending to encoder latents (DDIM, 50 steps). Base model 217M params total.
inputs: 4 RGB images (480x640) + proprioceptive joint positions and gripper values
outputs: Chunk of 50 absolute joint-position actions (14-D: 2x6 joints + 2 grippers)
actionRepr: Chunk of 50 continuous 14-DoF absolute joint actions (1 s) via DDIM diffusion, executed open-loop without temporal ensembling
trainingData: Over 26,000 real teleoperated demos for 5 tasks on ALOHA 2 fleet plus over 2,000 simulated demos for 3 sim tasks; one policy per task; trained on 64 TPUv5e for 2M steps
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces ACT's CVAE/L1 regression with a diffusion loss on a scaled-up transformer encoder-decoder and trains on far more (non-researcher) teleop data.
limitations: Policies are single-task; replanning only every 1 s may be too slow for reactive tasks; requires many human demos per task.
notes: Inference 0.043 s per forward+denoising on an RTX 4090. First end-to-end policy claimed to tie shoelaces and hang t-shirts.

name: Dense Policy
resolvedTitle: Dense Policy: Bidirectional Autoregressive Learning of Actions
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Xidian University; Shanghai Innovation Institute
problem: Autoregressive policies (next-token or next-chunk) underperform holistic generative policies like Diffusion Policy because unidirectional prediction misses long-range dependencies, and discrete multi-scale tokenization (CARP) hurts precision.
keyIdea: Generate actions coarse-to-fine by bidirectional expansion: start from a single frame, then repeatedly upsample the sparse keyframe sequence and refine it with cross-attention to observations, doubling length each level for logarithmic-time inference in continuous action space.
architecture: Encoder-only (BERT-style, 4 encoder layers) action head that cross-attends to observation features; ResNet18 (GroupNorm) for 2D or sparse conv net for 3D point clouds; proprioception via MLP with random masking; L2 loss.
inputs: RGB images or point clouds + optional proprioception
outputs: Sequence of end-effector TCP poses over horizon T
actionRepr: Continuous action chunk built hierarchically in log2(T) dense-process levels (no tokenization)
params: Action head: less than half of ACT's; 9.19M more than DP's head (exact totals in a figure)
trainingData: Sim: 10 demos (Adroit, MetaWorld), 100 demos (DexArt); real-world tasks on a single arm
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces the diffusion action head with a bidirectional coarse-to-fine autoregressive expansion in continuous space, unlike CARP's VQ tokens.
limitations: Not yet extended to general-purpose autoregressive VLAs; stability when scaled to large foundation models is untested.
notes: Paper says code and example data would be released upon publication. Reported ~10x faster inference than DP's action head.

name: CARP
resolvedTitle: CARP: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Coarse-to-Fine Autoregressive Prediction
org: Westlake University; Zhejiang University
problem: Autoregressive policies are fast but miss global structure; diffusion policies are accurate but slow due to many denoising steps.
keyIdea: Reformulate autoregressive action generation as next-scale (coarse-to-fine) prediction over multi-scale action token maps, VAR-style.
architecture: Two stages: (1) multi-scale VQ-VAE action autoencoder with 1D temporal CNN encoder/decoder and shared codebook producing K token maps; (2) GPT-style transformer with scale-wise causal mask predicting token maps coarse-to-fine with cross-entropy, conditioned on observation embeddings.
inputs: State or image observations + proprioception (history)
outputs: Action sequence over horizon H decoded from token maps
actionRepr: Multi-scale discrete tokens (VQ) of the whole action chunk, decoded to continuous actions
trainingData: Robomimic (Lift, Can, Square), Franka Kitchen (566 demos), Push-T (200 demos), MimicGen multi-task, and real-world tasks
whatChangedVsParent: Swaps next-token AR (BET) and iterative denoising (DP) for next-scale AR over multi-scale action tokens.
notes: Claims up to 10% success improvement and ~10x faster inference with 1-5% of DP's parameters. Limitations section not retrieved.

name: EquiBot
resolvedTitle: EquiBot: SIM(3)-Equivariant Diffusion Policy for Generalizable and Data Efficient Learning
org: Stanford University
problem: Imitation-learned visuomotor policies need lots of data and generalize poorly to unseen object poses, scales and scenes; prior equivariant policy EquivAct was deterministic and could not handle multimodal data.
keyIdea: Make every denoising step of a diffusion policy SIM(3)-equivariant (rotation, translation, scale) so outputs transform with the input point cloud by construction.
architecture: SIM(3)-equivariant PointNet-style encoder (Vector Neurons, from EquivAct) + SO(3)-equivariant conditional 1D U-Net (CNN Diffusion Policy with vector-neuron FiLM layers); translation/scale canonicalization using predicted centroid and scale.
inputs: Single-view object-centric point cloud + robot proprioception
outputs: Sequence of end-effector actions: 6D velocity commands and gripper open/close
actionRepr: Chunk of end-effector velocity + gripper actions via DDPM diffusion
trainingData: 6 sim tasks; real: 15 human demonstration videos per task (~5 minutes) processed with hand detection and segmentation into point clouds, on Kinova Gen3 arms on holonomic mobile bases
whatChangedVsParent: Adds a diffusion head to EquivAct's SIM(3)-equivariant design (or equivalently makes Diffusion Policy's U-Net equivariant).
limitations: Does not handle nonlinear changes in object shape or dynamics, nor variations in relative placement of multiple objects; may fail under heavy occlusion or large camera-angle changes.
notes: CoRL 2024. Distinct from EquiDiff (Wang et al.), which is SO(2)-equivariant.

name: EquiDiff
resolvedTitle: Equivariant Diffusion Policy
org: Northeastern University; Boston Dynamics AI Institute
problem: Diffusion policies must learn a denoising function that is harder to learn than an explicit policy, which raises data requirements.
keyIdea: Embed SO(2) (rotation about gravity axis) symmetry into the denoising network so the diffusion policy is equivariant, with theory showing SO(2) equivariance applies to full 6-DoF control.
architecture: Equivariant observation and action encoders (escnn, regular representation of cyclic group C_u), a shared 1D temporal U-Net applied per group element, and an equivariant noise decoder; voxel or RGB input.
inputs: Voxel grid (from 4 cameras) or RGB images + proprioception
outputs: Denoised 6-DoF end-effector action trajectory (absolute or relative pose control)
actionRepr: Chunk of continuous 6-DoF end-effector poses + gripper via DDPM (sim) / DDIM 16 steps (real)
trainingData: MimicGen 12 tasks with 100/200/1000 demos; real-world 20-60 demos per task on 6 tasks
whatChangedVsParent: Makes the Diffusion Policy U-Net SO(2)-equivariant via group-wise shared processing and equivariant encoders/decoders.
limitations: Symmetry mismatch in the vision system (non-top-down cameras, arm in voxel grid, camera noise) partially breaks equivariance; incorrect equivariance may hurt when demos conflict with symmetry.
notes: CoRL 2024. Name collides with an unrelated 2023 trajectory-prediction paper also called EquiDiff (Chen et al., ITSC).

name: BEAST
resolvedTitle: BEAST: Efficient Tokenization of B-Splines Encoded Action Sequences for Imitation Learning
org: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology; Robotics Institute Germany; Microsoft Research
problem: Existing action tokenizers need separately trained encoders (VQ) or produce variable-length token sequences (FAST/BPE) that block parallel decoding, and ignore smoothness across chunk boundaries.
keyIdea: Encode each action chunk as B-spline control points, used directly as fixed-length discrete (quantized) or continuous tokens; no tokenizer training, smooth within chunks and continuous between chunks, enabling parallel decoding.
architecture: Tokenizer plugged into three architectures: BEAST-F (Florence-2-large 0.77B VLM, encoder-decoder, least-used 256 vocab tokens overwritten as action tokens, parallel decoding), BEAST-D (small decoder-only transformer with CLIP text + FiLM-ResNet-18), BEAST-ACT (continuous control-point tokens in ACT's CVAE).
inputs: RGB images, language instruction, proprioception
outputs: Fixed number of B-spline control-point tokens per DoF, decoded to a smooth action trajectory
actionRepr: B-spline control points (e.g. 5-10 bases per 1 s chunk), quantized to 256 bins or continuous; 4-8x fewer tokens than binning
trainingData: No large-scale robot pretraining for BEAST-F; trained per benchmark: CALVIN (24,000 language-annotated demos), LIBERO, ALOHA sim; 166 sim tasks and 8 real tasks on 3 robot setups
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces binning/DCT-BPE/VQ tokenization with training-free, fixed-length B-spline control-point tokens that guarantee smooth, continuous chunks.
limitations: Sensitive to the number of B-spline basis functions, whose optimum depends on trajectory smoothness and sampling rate (5-10 bases worked for 1 s trajectories).
notes: NeurIPS 2025. Code released per paper. Discrete tokens beat continuous BEAST tokens by 12.7% in an ablation.

name: ABPolicy
resolvedTitle: ABPolicy: Asynchronous B-Spline Flow Policy for Real-Time and Smooth Robotic Manipulation
org: Tianjin University
problem: Synchronous inference in raw action space causes intra-chunk jitter, inter-chunk discontinuities and stop-and-go execution, hurting smoothness and responsiveness to moving objects.
keyIdea: Predict continuous cubic B-spline control points with a flow-matching policy, jointly predict past+future actions (bidirectional prediction), and refit the first control points to the executed history so asynchronously generated chunks stitch smoothly.
architecture: DiT flow-matching policy with cross-attention to observations; frozen DINOv2 image encoder plus MLP over the last 8 robot states; Continuity-Constrained Refitting (least-squares on initial free control points); inference and control in separate threads.
inputs: RGB images from two fixed cameras + past 8 robot states
outputs: Continuous B-spline control points for an action chunk spanning 8 past and 32 future steps
actionRepr: Continuous cubic (C2) B-spline control points per action dim (joint angles + gripper), 10 flow-matching steps, asynchronous execution
trainingData: Real AgileX Piper 6-DoF arm: 100 demos per dynamic task, 200 per static task (7 tasks)
whatChangedVsParent: Keeps BEAST's B-spline idea but uses continuous control points with flow matching, and replaces RTC-style inpainting/weighted fusion with least-squares refitting for async continuity.
notes: Async inference improved dynamic-task success by 18.3% on average and cut static completion time by 14.2% with ~90 ms inference delay. BiAP ablation: 60% to 85% success on static block stacking. No explicit limitations section retrieved.

name: Q-chunking
resolvedTitle: Reinforcement Learning with Action Chunking
org: UC Berkeley
problem: Offline-to-online RL on long-horizon sparse-reward tasks struggles with exploration and slow, biased value propagation.
keyIdea: Run TD-based actor-critic RL directly in a chunked action space: the policy outputs an h-step action chunk executed open loop and the critic scores state + whole chunk, giving temporally coherent exploration and unbiased n-step backups.
architecture: Behavior flow-matching policy over action chunks with best-of-N sampling (QC) or FQL-style one-step policy (QC-FQL); critic ensemble Q(s, a_t:t+h) trained with standard TD loss.
inputs: State observations (OGBench, robomimic)
outputs: Chunk of h low-level actions
actionRepr: Action chunk of length h (critic evaluates the full chunk)
trainingData: OGBench 5 domains x 5 tasks (default play datasets; 100M dataset for cube-quadruple) and robomimic lift/can/square multi-human datasets; 1M offline + 1M online steps
whatChangedVsParent: Moves action chunking from imitation learning into TD-based offline-to-online RL, with a chunk-level critic for bias-free n-step backups.
notes: NeurIPS 2025. RL method evaluated in simulation only (state-based). Limitations section not retrieved. openWeights refers to code; no pretrained foundation weights. Code released at github.com/ColinQiyangLi/qc.

name: Qwen-RobotManip (semantic action slots)
resolvedTitle: Qwen-RobotManip Technical Report: Alignment Unlocks Scale for Robotic Manipulation Foundation Models
org: Qwen Team, Alibaba Group
problem: Manipulation data is heterogeneous across embodiments (different state/action layouts and coordinate frames), so naive pooling conflicts and prevents scaling.
keyIdea: Align data along representation, motion and behavior: an 80-D canonical state/action vector with semantically fixed slots and loss masks, end-effector actions as camera-frame delta poses, plus structured embodiment prompts, enabling a ~38,100-hour pretraining corpus.
architecture: Qwen3.5-4B natively multimodal backbone; flow-matching DiT action expert (10 blocks, hidden 768, 12 heads) alternating cross-attention to visual and language tokens of the VLM's last layer; proprioception via 2-layer MLP; camera and end-effector-type embeddings; 4 Euler steps at inference.
inputs: Multi-view images, language instruction, structured embodiment prompt, history state/actions
outputs: Action chunk in the 80-D canonical space
actionRepr: 80-D canonical vector: two 29-D per-arm blocks (7 joint, 9 EEF pose = 3 pos + 6D rot, 1 gripper, 12 dexterous-hand joints) + 22 reserved; joints absolute, EEF as camera-frame deltas; masked flow matching
params: Backbone 4B (Qwen3.5-4B) + DiT action expert (size not stated in retrieved pages)
trainingData: ~38,100 hours: open-source robot datasets, human-to-robot synthesized trajectories from egocentric human video across 15 platforms, synthetic data, plus VL co-training data

headlineResults.benchmark: Cross-embodiment skill transfer on ARX (4 novel tasks)

whatChangedVsParent: Keeps π-style VLM+flow-expert split but adds a semantically slotted 80-D action space with camera-frame EEF deltas so cross-embodiment data scales log-linearly.
notes: The survey label 'semantic action slots' maps to the paper's 80-D canonical state-action vector with fixed semantic groups and binary masks. GitHub repo github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-RobotManip listed; weight release not confirmed in retrieved pages. Distinct from RhinoVLA (Huixi, 72-D physical slot space, Qwen3-VL backbone), which the resolver first returned.

name: RoboFlamingo
resolvedTitle: Vision-Language Foundation Models as Effective Robot Imitators
org: ByteDance Research; Tsinghua University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; NUS
problem: RT-2-style VLAs rely on private models and costly co-fine-tuning on web + robot data; a cheap way to adapt open VLMs to low-level control was missing.
keyIdea: Use open-source OpenFlamingo for single-step vision-language understanding and add an explicit policy head (LSTM) that models observation history, fine-tuned only by imitation on language-conditioned manipulation data.
architecture: OpenFlamingo (ViT encoder + perceiver resampler + gated cross-attention into an LLM such as MPT-3B/9B); max-pooled per-step features fed to an LSTM + MLP policy head; only resampler, cross-attention and head are trained (~1B trainable params).
inputs: Two camera views (CALVIN), language instruction, history
outputs: 7-DoF end-effector relative pose + gripper open/close
actionRepr: Single-step continuous 6-DoF relative pose (MSE) + binary gripper (BCE); open-loop multi-step variant needs retraining
trainingData: CALVIN language-annotated subset (~24K annotated trajectories, ~1% of data); trained on a single 8xA100 server
whatChangedVsParent: Decouples perception (frozen-mostly VLM) from decision-making (explicit LSTM policy head) instead of RT-2's co-fine-tuned action tokens.
limitations: No real-robot deployment due to lack of real-robot data; fine-tuning degrades original VL abilities (co-training partially mitigates).
notes: Paper states codes and models will be public. Full-model fine-tuning (3B trainable) performed worse than partial fine-tuning.

name: HybridVLA
resolvedTitle: HybridVLA: Collaborative Diffusion and Autoregression in a Unified Vision-Language-Action Model
org: Peking University; BAAI; CUHK
problem: Autoregressive VLAs discretize actions and lose continuity; diffusion-head VLAs treat the VLM as a feature extractor and do not exploit its next-token reasoning.
keyIdea: Integrate diffusion denoising into the next-token prediction process of a single LLM, trained collaboratively, and adaptively ensemble diffusion and autoregressive actions based on autoregressive token confidence.
architecture: Single LLM backbone (7B and 2.7B variants, initialized from a Prismatic VLM) with a token sequence containing multimodal inputs, diffusion tokens and autoregressive action tokens linked by marker tokens; MLP projections for diffusion; DDIM with KV cache.
inputs: Single-view RGB (224x224), language, robot state (7-DoF end-effector pose)
outputs: 7-DoF end-effector action from diffusion, autoregression, or their ensemble
actionRepr: Continuous diffusion action + discrete binned AR action, fused; no action chunking in reported inference
trainingData: Pretraining on Open X-Embodiment, DROID and ROBOMIND (760K trajectories, >10K A800 GPU hours); fine-tuned on RLBench (100 trajectories/task) and self-collected real data
whatChangedVsParent: Moves diffusion inside the LLM's token stream rather than as a separate head after the VLM, and ensembles AR and diffusion actions.
limitations: Inference speed is limited by slow autoregressive generation; diffusion-only inference (9.4 Hz) is the workaround.
notes: Abstract claims +14% (sim) and +19% (real-world) mean success over prior SOTA VLAs.

name: DexVLA
resolvedTitle: DexVLA: Vision-Language Model with Plug-In Diffusion Expert for General Robot Control
org: Midea Group; East China Normal University; Shanghai University
problem: VLAs scale the VLM but leave the action expert small, and rely on huge datasets and external high-level planners for long-horizon tasks.
keyIdea: Pair a VLM with a 1B-parameter diffusion action expert (ScaleDP with per-embodiment heads) trained via a three-stage embodiment curriculum, and have the VLM generate sub-step reasoning that is injected into the expert.
architecture: Qwen2-VL-2B backbone emits reasoning tokens and action tokens; action tokens pass through a 2-layer projector; reasoning injected via FiLM; 1B ScaleDP diffusion transformer expert (32 layers, hidden 1280, 16 heads) with multi-head outputs per embodiment.
inputs: Multi-view RGB (3 cams), language instruction, robot state
outputs: Sub-step reasoning text + action chunk for the target embodiment (e.g. 14-D bimanual)
actionRepr: Continuous joint-space actions via diffusion (1B expert), embodiment-specific output heads
trainingData: ~100 hours of demonstrations over 91 tasks (mostly AgileX and Franka), Stage 1 cross-embodiment, Stage 2 embodiment-specific, Stage 3 task-specific; sub-step annotations every ~5 s

headlineResults.benchmark: Ablation: expert size on shirt folding

whatChangedVsParent: Scales the diffusion expert to 1B with per-embodiment heads, adds a 3-stage embodied curriculum and sub-step reasoning instead of an external SayCan-style planner.
limitations: Very long-horizon contact-rich tasks (crumpled shirts, continuous bin picking) remain hard; Stage 1 is required or the large expert fails to optimize.
notes: Outperforms π0 on laundry folding via direct prompting per abstract.

name: DiffusionVLA
resolvedTitle: Diffusion-VLA: Generalizable and Interpretable Robot Foundation Model via Self-Generated Reasoning
org: Midea Group; East China Normal University; Shanghai University
problem: Autoregressive VLAs give imprecise, slow actions; diffusion policies lack reasoning.
keyIdea: Keep a pretrained VLM's autoregressive reasoning (task decomposition text) and attach a diffusion policy head, with a reasoning-injection module that feeds the self-generated reasoning into the policy.
architecture: SigLIP visual encoder (shared across views) + Qwen2-VL backbone (2B/7B/72B); fixed number of action tokens projected by 2-layer MLP+LayerNorm into a standard Diffusion Policy head; reasoning embedded into the head (FiLM-style); per-embodiment MLP output layer.
inputs: Multi-view RGB, language instruction, robot state
outputs: Reasoning text + continuous joint-space actions
actionRepr: Continuous joint-space actions via diffusion head
trainingData: Pretrained on DROID; fine-tuned on self-collected Franka and bimanual AgileX data with reasoning annotations (pretraining trajectory count listed as 39K vs 970K for OpenVLA)
controlRateHz: 82 Hz (DiVLA-2B), 42 Hz (DiVLA-7B) on A6000 with vLLM
whatChangedVsParent: Adds autoregressive self-generated reasoning and injects it into a diffusion action head on a larger Qwen2-VL backbone.
limitations: Performance degrades significantly at 8-bit/4-bit quantization; grasp precision drops on novel instructions.
notes: ICML 2025. Referred to as DiVLA. Ablation without reasoning injection drops in-distribution avg from 83.6 to 50.3.

name: TinyVLA
resolvedTitle: TinyVLA: Towards Fast, Data-Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
org: East China Normal University; Midea Group; Shanghai University; Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics
problem: VLAs like OpenVLA are slow (large VLM + autoregressive action tokens) and need large-scale robot pretraining.
keyIdea: Use a small pretrained VLM (<1.4B, Pythia-based, LLaVA pipeline) fine-tuned with LoRA and attach a Diffusion Policy head, skipping robot-data pretraining.
architecture: Compact VLM (ViT + Pythia LLM, 70M-1.4B) with LoRA (~5% trainable) ; adaptive pooling + LayerNorm, concat with proprioception, 3-layer MLP conditioning a fully trained DP head.
inputs: Two camera views, language instruction, proprioception
outputs: 7-D actions: xyz position, roll/pitch/yaw, gripper width
actionRepr: Continuous 7-D end-effector action sequence via DDPM diffusion head
trainingData: No robot pretraining; 100 teleop trajectories per task (5 Franka tasks), bimanual UR5 tasks, MetaWorld 50 tasks with 50 demos
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces OpenVLA's 7B VLM and autoregressive action tokens with a sub-1.4B VLM and a diffusion policy head, without OpenX pretraining.
limitations: Smaller VLMs misinterpret instructions and localize poorly (failure analysis); performance scales strongly with VLM size.
notes: IEEE RA-L 2025. Claims 20x lower latency than OpenVLA with 5.5x fewer parameters. MLP head failed entirely in ablation; ACT head worse than diffusion.

name: ECoT
resolvedTitle: Robotic Control via Embodied Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
org: UC Berkeley; University of Warsaw; Stanford University
problem: VLAs map observations directly to actions without reasoning, and naive text chain-of-thought is ineffective with small open VLM backbones and ungrounded in the scene.
keyIdea: Train the VLA to autoregressively generate an embodied reasoning chain (task rephrase, plan, subtask, move primitive, gripper pixel position, object bounding boxes) before the action tokens, using synthetically generated labels.
architecture: OpenVLA (Prismatic: fused SigLIP + DINOv2 encoders, Llama 2 7B) fine-tuned to output reasoning tokens followed by 7 discretized action tokens; reasoning partially frozen for N steps or run asynchronously to save time.
inputs: Single third-person RGB image + language instruction
outputs: Textual embodied reasoning chain + 7-DoF end-effector velocity action (256-bin tokens)
actionRepr: Single-step 7-DoF end-effector delta action as 7 discrete 256-bin tokens (after ~350 reasoning tokens)
trainingData: Bridge V2 (60k demos, >2.5M transitions) auto-labeled with reasoning using open-vocabulary detectors and an LLM (7 days of generation)

headlineResults.benchmark: WidowX real generalization suite (ID view, 314 trials)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds grounded multi-step textual reasoning (plans, bounding boxes, gripper position) before OpenVLA's action tokens.
limitations: Reasoning chain structure is fixed regardless of task; reasoning makes inference slow (7 to ~350 generated tokens per step); ECoT data only for one embodiment (WidowX); real-to-sim gap hurt SIMPLER evaluation.
notes: Abstract states +28% absolute success over OpenVLA across generalization tasks. Fine-tuning released OpenVLA with ~13% ECoT data transfers reasoning to other embodiments.

name: GR-3
resolvedTitle: GR-3 Technical Report
org: ByteDance Seed
problem: VLAs struggle to follow out-of-distribution instructions with abstract concepts, need many demos to adapt, and are brittle on long-horizon dexterous tasks.
keyIdea: A mixture-of-transformers VLA (Qwen2.5-VL + flow-matching action DiT) co-trained with web-scale VL data, fine-tuned from few-shot VR human trajectories, with an auxiliary task-status output and extra RMSNorm for stability and language following.
architecture: Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct processes multi-view images and language; action DiT with half as many layers uses KV cache from the latter half of VLM layers; AdaLN timestep injection; causal attention within the chunk; RMSNorm after linear layers in DiT attention and FFN.
inputs: Multi-view RGB, language instruction, robot state (bimanual mobile robot ByteMini)
outputs: k-length action chunk plus task-status dimension (Ongoing/Terminated/Invalid)
actionRepr: Chunk of k continuous actions via flow matching, 5 Euler steps (Δτ = 0.2)
trainingData: Teleoperated robot trajectories (e.g. 35k trajectories/69 h pick-and-place, ~101 h table bussing, 116 h cloth hanging), curated VL datasets, and human VR trajectories (~450/hour collection; 450 traj ≈30 min for few-shot)
whatChangedVsParent: π0-style VLM + flow action expert on Qwen2.5-VL, adding VL co-training, few-shot human VR data, task-status supervision and DiT RMSNorm.
limitations: Still errs on unseen instructions with novel concepts/objects and unseen shapes; like other IL methods it can get stuck in OOD states without recovering; RL planned as future work.
notes: Without VL co-training GR-3 underperforms π0 on generalization, attributed to π0's large cross-embodiment pretraining. Introduces ByteMini bimanual mobile robot.

name: X-VLA
resolvedTitle: X-VLA: Soft-Prompted Transformer as Scalable Cross-Embodiment Vision-Language-Action Model
org: Tsinghua University (AIR); Shanghai AI Lab; Peking University
problem: Cross-embodiment VLA pretraining is destabilized by heterogeneity in action spaces, cameras and task distributions; per-embodiment output heads only address the final stage.
keyIdea: Give each data source a small set of learnable soft-prompt embeddings injected early into a plain transformer, absorbing hardware-specific variation; adapt to new robots by warming up new prompts then jointly fine-tuning.
architecture: Florence-Large VLM encodes main view + instruction; auxiliary (wrist) views through a shared vision encoder; proprioception, flow time and noisy action chunk concatenated and linearly projected; 24-layer, 1024-hidden self-attention transformer with soft prompts; domain-specific in/out linear projections (0.04% of params).
inputs: Main-view + optional wrist views, language, proprioception
outputs: Action chunk in a unified EEF space
actionRepr: Flow-matching action chunk: EEF xyz + absolute Rotate6D + binary gripper (MSE + BCE), temporally downsampled 'intention' targets
trainingData: 290K episodes from DROID, RoboMind and AgiBot spanning 7 platforms / 5 arm types; Soft-Fold dataset of 1,200 cloth-folding trajectories for adaptation
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces embodiment-specific heads / HPT-style projections with per-source soft prompts in a plain transformer backbone.
notes: Claims SOTA on 6 simulation benchmarks (incl. one autonomous driving) and 3 real robots. Limitations in Appendix N not retrieved. Soft-Fold dataset to be released.

name: Magma
resolvedTitle: Magma: A Foundation Model for Multimodal AI Agents
org: Microsoft Research; University of Maryland; UW-Madison; KAIST; University of Washington
problem: VLAs are trained per domain (UI or robots) and lose general multimodal understanding; action-free video and image data cannot easily supervise action.
keyIdea: Unify digital and physical agentic tasks with two surrogate labels: Set-of-Mark (numbered actionable regions) for action grounding and Trace-of-Mark (future point-track traces from CoTracker) for action planning, which also turns unlabeled video into action supervision.
architecture: ConvNeXt-XXLarge vision encoder + LLaMA-3-8B decoder-only LLM; all outputs (UI coordinates, robot actions, text) as tokens; robot actions via 256 least-used vocab tokens as in OpenVLA.
inputs: Images/video frames (with SoM overlays), task text
outputs: Text, marks/coordinates, traces, or 7-DoF robot action tokens
actionRepr: Single-step 7-DoF end-effector delta discretized into 256 bins (OpenVLA-style tokens)
trainingData: ~39M samples: OXE 970K trajectories (9.4M frames), ~2.7M UI screenshots (SeeClick, Vision2UI), >25M video samples (Ego4D, Epic-Kitchens, Something-v2, instructional), 1.2M image-text (ShareGPT4V, LLaVA-1.5)
whatChangedVsParent: Extends an OpenVLA-style action tokenization to a general multimodal agent pretrained with SoM/ToM surrogate action labels on images, UI and video.
notes: Paper states model and code are public. Also SOTA on UI navigation (Mind2Web, AITW). Limitations not retrieved.

name: RoboDual
resolvedTitle: Towards Synergistic, Generalized, and Efficient Dual-System for Robotic Manipulation
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; HKU; AgiBot; Shanghai AI Lab
problem: Generalist VLAs are slow, costly to adapt and limited to single RGB input; specialist policies are fast and precise but do not generalize.
keyIdea: Pair a slow OpenVLA generalist (outputs action chunks and latents) with a fast 20M-param diffusion-transformer specialist conditioned on those outputs plus extra sensors, rolling out multiple steps per generalist call.
architecture: Generalist: OpenVLA (Prismatic-7B, LLaMA-2) LoRA-finetuned to predict discretized action chunks (k_g). Specialist: 6-layer DiT (hidden 256, 8 heads) with cross-attention to generalist task/action latents and per-modality ViT encoders + perceiver resampler; DDIM 5 inference steps.
inputs: Generalist: third-view RGB + language; specialist: RGB, depth, gripper view, proprioception + generalist latents/actions
outputs: 7-D action chunks (k_s = 8) from the specialist
actionRepr: Generalist: discretized 256-bin action chunks; specialist: continuous 8-step chunk via diffusion (sample prediction), temporal aggregation
trainingData: OpenVLA pretraining corpus (OXE, Bridge, DROID); CALVIN ABC; real ALOHA tasks with 20-120 demos each

headlineResults.benchmark: CALVIN ABC→D with GPT-4 enriched instructions

whatChangedVsParent: Adds a lightweight fast DiT specialist that consumes OpenVLA's latents and coarse action chunks rather than using the VLA alone.
notes: Abstract: +26.7% over OpenVLA in real world, +12% on CALVIN. Code to be released. Latency-aware training conditions the specialist on delayed generalist outputs.

name: HiRT
resolvedTitle: HiRT: Enhancing Robotic Control with Hierarchical Robot Transformers
org: Tsinghua University (IIIS); UC Berkeley; Shanghai Qizhi Institute
problem: Billion-parameter VLAs run at low frequency with high latency, limiting them to quasi-static tasks.
keyIdea: Run a VLM slowly and asynchronously to produce latent task features that condition a lightweight high-frequency visual policy (System 1 / System 2 split).
architecture: InstructBLIP-7B (ViT + Q-Former + LLaMA, LoRA) with a MAP pooling block producing a latent; fast policy = EfficientNet-B3 + FiLM (~35M, sim) or ViT-B/16 + cross-attention (~150M, real) with prefix-conditioned MAP action head; latent buffer for asynchronous use; training samples stale VLM inputs for robustness.
inputs: VLM: single image + language; fast policy: recent image context (wrist/third-view) + latest VLM latent (no proprioception)
outputs: Relative end-effector pose + binary gripper status
actionRepr: Single-step continuous relative EEF action (MSE) + gripper (BCE)
trainingData: MetaWorld 20 tasks x 50 demos; Franka-Kitchen 5 tasks x 100 demos; ~2000 real Franka trajectories
controlRateHz: 9.8 Hz (vs 4.1 Hz Vanilla-VLA) in reported setting
whatChangedVsParent: Splits an RT-2-style VLA into a slow VLM latent producer and a fast latent-conditioned visual policy running asynchronously.
limitations: Not yet tested on harder dynamic tasks (catching fast-flying objects, rapid pose adjustment) due to data constraints.
notes: CoRL 2024. Vanilla-VLA baseline is an RT-2 reimplementation on the same backbone.

name: Fast-in-Slow
resolvedTitle: Fast-in-Slow: A Dual-System Foundation Model Unifying Fast Manipulation within Slow Reasoning
org: CUHK; Peking University; AI2 Robotics; BAAI
problem: Dual-system VLAs attach a separately trained System 1 head that lacks the VLM's pretrained knowledge and relies only on System 2 features.
keyIdea: Repurpose the final transformer blocks of the VLM's LLM as System 1 (sharing parameters) while the full VLM remains System 2, with asynchronous frequencies, heterogeneous inputs and a dual-aware co-training loss (diffusion + next-token).
architecture: Prismatic-initialized VLM: SigLIP + DINOv2 encoders, LLaMA-2 7B (32 blocks); System 1 = last 2 blocks conditioned on an intermediate System 2 latent plus robot state, 2D images and point-cloud tokens (lightweight 3D tokenizer through the shared vision encoder); MLPs for state, timestep, noisy actions.
inputs: System 2: 2D image + language (low frequency); System 1: current image, robot state, 3D point cloud (high frequency)
outputs: Continuous action chunk from System 1; discrete actions or language plans from System 2
actionRepr: Diffusion-generated continuous action chunk (7-DoF EEF sim; 14-DoF/16-DoF dual-arm real), System 2:1 frequency ratio 1:4
trainingData: Pretraining on >860K trajectories from OXE, DROID, ROBOMIND etc.; fine-tuned on RLBench (100 traj/task) and self-collected Agilex / AlphaBot dual-arm data
controlRateHz: 117.7 Hz with action chunk 8 (21.9 Hz with chunk 1) on RTX 4090
whatChangedVsParent: System 1 is carved out of the VLM's own final layers rather than a separate small policy.
limitations: Number of shared System 1 blocks and the System 2/System 1 frequency ratio are fixed statically rather than adapted to task demands.
notes: Ablation: removing the autoregressive (slow) loss drops RLBench mean from 69% to 62%. Ratio 1:4 and 2 shared blocks found best. Same group as HybridVLA.

name: Hume
resolvedTitle: Hume: Introducing System-2 Thinking in Visual-Language-Action Model
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai AI Lab; Fudan University; AgiBot; INSAIT; Zhejiang University; NWPU
problem: Existing dual-system VLAs are fast but their System 2 does not actually 'think' about which action is best; text CoT (ECoT) is slow.
keyIdea: System 2 samples N candidate action chunks at different noise levels and picks the best by a learned Q-value head (value-guided best-of-N); System 1 finishes the denoising of short segments of the chosen chunk in real time (cascaded denoising).
architecture: System 2: PaliGemma with flow-matching action expert (4B) plus a value-query head (query token + two critics + actor) trained by offline RL (Cal-QL); System 1: DINOv2-small encoder + lightweight transformer flow-matching denoiser (80M).
inputs: Multi-view RGB, language, robot state
outputs: Refined action sub-chunks for real-time control
actionRepr: Flow-matching action chunks (10 Euler steps in System 2) with partially denoised best-of-N candidate refined by System 1
trainingData: OXE mixtures for SimplerEnv; LIBERO; real WidowX, Franka and AgiBot G-1 data; rewards +1 on last 3 transitions for value learning
whatChangedVsParent: Adds a value-query head and best-of-N candidate selection to a π0-style System 2, plus a cascaded System 1 denoiser.
limitations: Bounded by quality of sampled candidates; learned values are not well aligned with semantics; the thinking scheme is simple (no tree search, self-correction or RL).
notes: Removing the value-query head drops LIBERO avg from 98.6 to 84.9. Real WidowX averages read from a bar chart (π0 0.79, OpenVLA 0.58 approx.).

name: OpenHelix
resolvedTitle: OpenHelix: A Short Survey, Empirical Analysis, and Open-Source Dual-System VLA Model for Robotic Manipulation
org: Westlake University; Zhejiang University; Xi'an Jiaotong University; HKUST(GZ)
problem: Dual-system VLAs (Helix-style) lack open-source implementations and systematic comparisons of design choices (MLLM training, integration, asynchrony).
keyIdea: Empirically compare design choices and release a simple dual system: frozen MLLM with a single prompt-tuned <ACT> token whose embedding conditions a pretrained 3D Diffuser Actor, plus an auxiliary action-prediction loss on the <ACT> embedding.
architecture: LLaVA-7B (frozen, only <ACT> token embedding trained) → linear projection (4096→512) → pretrained 3D Diffuser Actor diffusion policy (RGB-D 3D scene tokens, proprioception); two-stage training with projector pre-alignment.
inputs: MLLM: third-view RGB + instruction; policy: two RGB-D views (3D scene tokens) + proprioception + <ACT> latent
outputs: End-effector trajectory: 3D location, 6-D rotation, gripper open/close
actionRepr: Diffusion-denoised trajectory of EEF poses over horizon T (3D Diffuser Actor)
trainingData: CALVIN ABC→D; evaluated also on CALVIN-E (enriched instructions) and CALVIN-D (dynamic)

headlineResults.benchmark: CALVIN ablation: prompt tuning + auxiliary task

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces LCB's fine-tuned MLLM + CLIP-loss alignment with a frozen MLLM, prompt-tuned <ACT> token and an auxiliary action loss.
limitations: No real-robot deployment yet; latent <ACT> embeddings were found largely insensitive to visual changes (mostly encode instruction semantics); asynchronous inference steps (1-60) barely change performance.
notes: Technical report; project is open-source (github.com/OpenHelix-robot/OpenHelix). Without projector pre-alignment, all integration variants fail (0% success). Not a reproduction of Figure AI's Helix.

name: 3D-VLA
resolvedTitle: 3D-VLA: A 3D Vision-Language-Action Generative World Model
org: UMass Amherst, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, SCUT, Wuhan University, MIT, UCLA, MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab
problem: Existing VLAs rely on 2D inputs and learn a direct perception-to-action mapping, ignoring 3D structure and world dynamics (no imagination of future states).
keyIdea: Build a 3D-LLM-style embodied foundation model with interaction tokens (object, location, scene, action) and align pretrained embodied diffusion models so the LLM can imagine goal images/depth/point clouds and then plan actions.
architecture: 3D-LLM-style backbone initialized from BLIP2-FlanT5-XL with Q-Former over multi-view 3D features; RGB-D-to-RGB-D diffusion (from Stable Diffusion v1.4) and point-to-point diffusion (from Point-E) goal generators aligned to the LLM via a transformer projector and LoRA.
inputs: 3D scene features lifted from multi/single-view images (with estimated depth), language instruction
outputs: Text, 3D bounding boxes (location tokens), goal image/depth/point cloud, discrete action tokens
actionRepr: Discrete 7-DoF action tokens (<aloc0-255>, <arot0-255>, <gripper0/1>) for absolute arm location, rotation and gripper openness, separated by <ACT_SEP>
trainingData: Curated 3D embodied instruction-tuning dataset of 2M 3D-language-action pairs from 12 Open X-Embodiment datasets, Dobb-E, RH20T, RLBench, CALVIN, Epic-Kitchens, HOI4D; depth via ZoeDepth, flow via RAFT, 3D boxes via Grounded-SAM, prompts diversified with ChatGPT.

headlineResults.benchmark: RLBench (Put Knife / Take Umbrella / Pick up Cup / Pick up Cup unseen)
CALVIN ABC->D (tasks completed in a row, 1..5)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds 3D inputs, interaction/action tokens and aligned goal-generation diffusion decoders to a 3D-LLM-style model so it can imagine future states before acting.
limitations: Action planning evaluated only in simulation with open-loop control; the paper frames real-world deployment as future potential.
notes: Robot control evaluated on only 3 RLBench tasks + CALVIN; most results are reasoning/generation metrics. PointVLA paper notes 3D-VLA relies on simulation for robot control (sim-to-real gap).

name: BridgeVLA
resolvedTitle: BridgeVLA: Input-Output Alignment for Efficient 3D Manipulation Learning with Vision-Language Models
org: CASIA, ByteDance Seed, UCAS, FiveAges, Nanjing University
problem: 3D VLAs tokenize actions without spatial structure and feed 3D inputs that are misaligned with the VLM's 2D pretraining, leading to poor sample efficiency.
keyIdea: Align input and output in a shared 2D image space: project point clouds into orthographic multi-view images and predict 2D heatmaps for translation, after pretraining the VLM to output text-conditioned object-grounding heatmaps.
architecture: PaliGemma VLM backbone (SigLIP encoder frozen) whose image tokens are reshaped/upsampled into per-view heatmaps (RVT-2-style multi-view projection); remaining rotation/gripper/collision outputs predicted from features.
inputs: Colored point cloud rendered to 3 orthographic views (RGB only, no per-pixel 3D positions), language instruction
outputs: Per-view 2D heatmaps giving next keyframe translation, plus rotation, gripper and collision flag
actionRepr: Keyframe (next-best-pose) 3D end-effector action; translation from multi-view 2D heatmaps
trainingData: 2D heatmap grounding pretraining (~2 h on 8 A100, 3,800 steps); fine-tuned on RLBench (100 demos/task, 18 tasks), COLOSSEUM, GemBench and 10 real trajectories per task for 13 real tasks.
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces RVT-2's from-scratch multi-view transformer with a pretrained VLM and adds heatmap pretraining so VLM knowledge transfers while keeping 3D sample efficiency.
limitations: Fails on long-horizon GemBench L4 (0.0%); weakest on Place Cups due to occlusion in fixed orthographic views; keyframe-based, not continuous control.
notes: Ablation: adding per-pixel 3D position input drops RLBench from 88.2% to 56.2%. End-to-end inference ~0.21 s on RTX 4090. Project page bridgevla.github.io.

name: PointVLA
resolvedTitle: PointVLA: Injecting the 3D World into Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Midea Group, Shanghai University, East China Normal University
problem: Pretrained VLAs use only RGB, limiting spatial reasoning, but retraining them with scarce 3D data is prohibitive and would waste 2D pretraining.
keyIdea: Keep the VLM and vanilla action expert frozen and inject point-cloud features additively (via zero-initialized adapters) only into action-expert blocks found to be skippable by a skip-block analysis.
architecture: Built on DexVLA: 2B Qwen2-VL VLM + 1B ScaleDP diffusion action expert; lightweight hierarchical conv point-cloud encoder (iDP3-like) feeds a point cloud injector into selected blocks (e.g. blocks 12-16).
inputs: Multi-view RGB, language instruction, point cloud (e.g. RealSense L515)
outputs: Continuous action chunks
actionRepr: Diffusion (ScaleDP) action chunks, chunk size 50
params: ~3B (2B VLM + 1B action expert, inherited from DexVLA)
trainingData: DexVLA pretraining (100 h cross-embodiment); small 3D fine-tuning sets, e.g. 20 demos per task (80 total) for few-shot multi-tasking; RoboTwin sim with 20/50 demos.
whatChangedVsParent: Adds a point-cloud injector into skippable blocks of DexVLA's frozen action expert instead of retraining with 3D tokens.
limitations: Uses a simple point-cloud encoder (better encoders left for future work); 3D-aware pretraining at scale is future work.
notes: Few-shot multi-task: 4 tasks x 20 demos on bimanual AgileX. DexVLA serves as the no-3D ablation.

name: AgiBot World / GO-1
resolvedTitle: AgiBot World Colosseo: A Large-scale Manipulation Platform for Scalable and Intelligent Embodied Systems
org: The University of Hong Kong, AgiBot Inc., Shanghai Innovation Institute, Shanghai AI Lab
problem: Existing robot datasets are short-horizon, lab-controlled and of inconsistent quality, and generalist policies struggle to use heterogeneous action-free data.
keyIdea: Collect 1M+ quality-verified dual-arm trajectories on 100 homogeneous robots and train GO-1, a Vision-Language-Latent-Action (ViLLA) policy that predicts discrete latent actions (learned from videos) before decoding low-level actions.
architecture: InternVL2.5-2B VLM backbone; latent planner (24 transformer layers) predicts latent action tokens supervised by a VQ latent action model (Genie-style IDM encoder / FDM decoder, k=4 tokens); diffusion action expert with the same architecture outputs action chunks.
inputs: Multi-view images (head, left wrist, right wrist), language instruction, proprioception
outputs: Latent action tokens, then continuous low-level action chunk
actionRepr: Chunk of H=30 continuous actions via diffusion, conditioned on 4 discrete latent action tokens
trainingData: AgiBot World: 1,001,552 trajectories, 2,976.4 hours, 217 tasks, 87 skills, 106 scenes from 100+ AgiBot G1 robots; plus web vision-language data, Ego4D human videos and cross-embodiment robot data for LAM/latent planner.

headlineResults.benchmark: RDT pretrained on AgiBot World (beta) vs OXE, in-distribution
RDT pretrained on AgiBot World (beta) vs OXE, out-of-distribution
Wipe Table, verified vs all data (RDT)

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike LAPA, latent-action planning is kept at inference as an explicit latent planner between the VLM and a diffusion action expert.
limitations: All evaluations are real-world only; an aligned simulation environment for reproducible evaluation is still under development.
notes: Dataset under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 with model checkpoints and code on GitHub (OpenDriveLab/AgiBot-World). Abstract claims 30% gain over OXE pretraining and 32% over RDT. Robot: AgiBot G1 with dual 7-DoF arms, mobile chassis, 6-DoF dexterous hands, visuo-tactile sensors.

name: Gemini Robotics
resolvedTitle: Gemini Robotics: Bringing AI into the Physical World
org: Google DeepMind
problem: Frontier multimodal models lack the embodied reasoning and low-latency action grounding needed for dexterous, general robot control.
keyIdea: Extend Gemini 2.0 into Gemini Robotics-ER (embodied reasoning VLM: 3D detection, pointing, trajectories, grasps) and then into Gemini Robotics, a VLA that splits a distilled cloud backbone from an on-robot action decoder for fast control.
architecture: Cloud-hosted VLA backbone (distilled Gemini Robotics-ER, <160 ms query latency) plus a local action decoder on the robot's onboard computer; ~250 ms end-to-end latency from observations to action chunks.
inputs: Multiple scene images, text instruction, proprioception
outputs: Action chunks executed by the robot
actionRepr: Action chunks decoded by a local action decoder; effective control frequency 50 Hz
trainingData: Thousands of hours of teleoperated ALOHA 2 demonstrations collected over 12 months covering thousands of tasks, plus non-action data (web documents, code, image/audio/video, embodied reasoning and VQA data).

headlineResults.benchmark: Fast adaptation to new short-horizon tasks

whatChangedVsParent: Builds action generation on a frontier Gemini backbone with a cloud-backbone/local-decoder split, rather than a small open VLM like pi0's PaliGemma.
limitations: Gemini 2.0 may struggle to ground spatial relations across long videos and its numerical predictions (points, boxes) may not be precise enough for fine-grained control; multi-step reasoning combined with precise dexterity remains future work.
notes: Baselines: pi0 re-implement (trained on the same mixture; outperformed public openpi checkpoint) and a multi-task diffusion policy. Specialist Gemini Robotics trained from scratch on specialization data got 0% on long-horizon dexterous tasks, showing the value of generalist pretraining. Adaptation demonstrated to bi-arm Franka and Apptronik Apollo humanoid (humanoid per general knowledge of the report). Model card in Appendix A.

name: Large Behavior Models (TRI LBM)
resolvedTitle: A Careful Examination of Large Behavior Models for Multitask Dexterous Manipulation
org: Toyota Research Institute
problem: It is unclear how much of generalist-policy success actually comes from multitask pretraining, because real-world evaluation is rarely statistically rigorous.
keyIdea: Train diffusion-transformer LBMs on ~1,700 h of multitask data and compare finetuned LBMs vs single-task Diffusion Policy with blind, randomized A/B trials and Bayesian/sequential statistical tests in sim and real.
architecture: Diffusion Transformer (8 DiT blocks, embedding 768, adaLN) conditioned on CLIP ViT image CLS features (finetuned), frozen CLIP text encoder + projection, and proprioception over two observation timesteps; DDIM sampling.
inputs: Multiple camera images (2 scene + wrist cameras), language task description, proprioception
outputs: Bimanual end-effector action sequence
actionRepr: 16-step chunk of 20-dimensional continuous actions via DDIM diffusion; 8 steps executed before replanning
trainingData: Ramen mixture ~1,695 h: TRI-Ramen ~545 h (468 h real over 362 tasks/46,063 demos on 9 stations; 45 h sim; 32 h UMI) + OXE-Ramen ~1,150 h curated Open X-Embodiment.

headlineResults.metric: finetuning data needed to beat single-task (100% data)

whatChangedVsParent: Scales Diffusion Policy to a multitask language-conditioned DiT pretrained on sim+real+OXE data, and focuses on rigorous evaluation rather than architecture novelty.
limitations: Success rates on complex unseen tasks remain low; pretrained (non-finetuned) LBMs show language-steerability issues and can be slow to initiate motion; some sim/real discrepancies (e.g. Kiwi task) unexplained.
notes: Findings: pretraining reduces task-specific data needed, improves robustness under distribution shift, and performance improves with pretraining scale/diversity. Simulation benchmark lbm_eval built on Drake. Platform: two Franka FR3 arms.

name: MDT
resolvedTitle: Multimodal Diffusion Transformer: Learning Versatile Behavior from Multimodal Goals
org: Intuitive Robots Lab, Karlsruhe Institute of Technology
problem: Large imitation datasets are only sparsely language-annotated, so language-conditioned policies cannot use most of the data; most methods learn from a single goal modality.
keyIdea: A transformer encoder-decoder diffusion policy that learns a latent goal-conditioned state from both image and language goals, with two self-supervised auxiliary losses: Masked Generative Foresight (reconstruct masked future frames) and Contrastive Latent Alignment (align image- and language-goal embeddings).
architecture: Multimodal transformer encoder over static + wrist camera tokens (frozen Voltron + Perceiver for MDT-V, or ResNet-18 for MDT) and CLIP goal embeddings; GPT-style causal transformer decoder denoises actions with cross-attention and adaLN noise conditioning; continuous-time (Karras/EDM) score-based diffusion with DDIM sampling.
inputs: Static and wrist camera images, goal as language instruction (CLIP ViT-B/32) or goal image (CLIP ViT-B/16)
outputs: Action sequence of 10 steps
actionRepr: Chunk of 10 continuous delta end-effector (velocity-based) actions + gripper via score-based diffusion
trainingData: CALVIN play data (ABCD: 24 h, ~1% language-annotated; D: 6 h), LIBERO (5 suites, 130 tasks; variant with <2% language labels), real toy-kitchen play data (20 tasks).
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces U-Net / single-goal diffusion policies with an encoder-decoder diffusion transformer trained on mixed image/language goals plus foresight and contrastive auxiliary losses, beating a 3B VLM policy with <10% of its parameters.
limitations: MGF/CLA do not help on LIBERO-Long and their impact varies across benchmarks; diffusion needs multiple forward passes (slower inference); real-robot rollout lengths are short, partly due to camera self-occlusion.
notes: Code available at intuitive-robots.github.io/mdt_policy. Abstract claims 15% absolute gain over prior SOTA on CALVIN challenge. Evaluated on 184 tasks total.

name: Dita
resolvedTitle: Dita: Scaling Diffusion Transformer for Generalist Vision-Language-Action Policy
org: Shanghai AI Lab, Zhejiang University, CUHK MMLab, Peking University, SenseTime Research, Tsinghua University, HKISI CAS
problem: Generalist VLAs use compact action heads (discrete tokens or small diffusion MLPs conditioned on one fused embedding), which limits adaptation to heterogeneous cross-embodiment action spaces.
keyIdea: Denoise the continuous action chunk directly inside a large causal transformer with in-context conditioning, so noisy action tokens attend to raw visual tokens from historical observations rather than a single fused embedding.
architecture: LLaMA2-style causal transformer (12 blocks, hidden 768, trained from scratch); frozen CLIP text encoder; DINOv2 image encoder (finetuned) with a 4-layer Q-Former + FiLM selecting 32 image tokens; timestep embedding and noisy actions appended in context.
inputs: Language instruction and single third-person camera image (2 frames of history); wrist camera optional
outputs: Action chunk
actionRepr: Chunk of 16 continuous 7-D end-effector actions (3 translation, 3 rotation, 1 gripper) via DDPM training / DDIM (20 steps) inference
trainingData: Open X-Embodiment mixture (OpenVLA/Octo selection and weighting); pretrained 100k steps, batch 8192 on 32 A100s.

headlineResults.benchmark: SimplerEnv Google Robot, coke can (match / variant)

headlineResults.value: +0.45 over diffusion head; +1.23 over non-pretrained Dita

whatChangedVsParent: Moves denoising from a small per-token diffusion head (Octo/pi0 style) into the full transformer with in-context conditioning on image tokens.
limitations: 334M model lacks capacity to fully absorb the whole OXE mixture (authors suggest DROID may be better pretraining for LIBERO and scaling model size would help); uses only a third-person camera by default.
notes: Paper describes itself as an open-source baseline (robodita.github.io). Real robot: 10-shot finetuning for multi-task long-horizon tasks, robust to background, distractor and lighting changes.

name: BitVLA
resolvedTitle: BitVLA: 1-bit Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotics Manipulation
org: Key Laboratory of AI Safety, Institute of Computing Technology, CAS; University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
problem: Full-precision VLAs are too large in memory and latency for edge robots, and post-training quantization costs accuracy.
keyIdea: A fully native 1-bit (ternary {-1,0,1}) VLA built on the BitNet b1.58 2B4T LLM, with a Quantize-then-Distill stage that compresses the SigLIP encoder to 1.58-bit weights / INT8 activations under a full-precision teacher.
architecture: BitNet b1.58 2B4T ternary LLM backbone (causal attention kept); SigLIP-L vision encoder quantized to W1.58A8; full-precision 2-layer MLP connector; OpenVLA-OFT-style parallel-decoding action head with L1 regression.
inputs: Single- or multi-view images (e.g. wrist + external), proprioceptive state token, language instruction
outputs: Continuous action chunk in one forward pass
actionRepr: OFT-style chunk of continuous actions (K=8 on LIBERO, 10 real-world) regressed with L1 loss
trainingData: VLM stages on LLaVA-1.5-558k, 10M-sample MammoTH-VL subset, 5M-sample (up to 10B tokens) distillation set; VLA pretraining on >1M-sample Open X-Embodiment subset (200K steps, 16 H800s, 14 days).

headlineResults.comparedTo: OpenVLA-OFT+ 321 ms / 77.9 Hz; pi0 86 ms / 291.6 Hz

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces OpenVLA-OFT's full-precision 7B backbone with a ternary 2B LLM and ternary-distilled vision encoder, keeping the OFT action head.
limitations: Relies on quantization-aware training, so it is not a drop-in conversion for arbitrary full-precision backbones; pretrained on only ~1M samples, so broader generalization needs larger robot pretraining.
notes: Code at github.com/ustcwhy/BitVLA, weights at huggingface.co/lxsy/bitvla-bf16. Without robot pretraining it fails on real tasks (near-zero).

name: VLA-Cache
resolvedTitle: VLA-Cache: Efficient Vision-Language-Action Manipulation via Adaptive Token Caching
org: University of Sydney; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
problem: VLAs recompute all visual tokens every control step even though most of the scene is static between frames, wasting compute and limiting control frequency.
keyIdea: Training-free cross-frame KV caching: reuse KV entries for visually static tokens, but always recompute task-relevant tokens (high decoder attention), with a layer-adaptive reuse ratio based on attention entropy.
architecture: Plug-in to the LLM decoder of existing VLAs (OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, CogACT); patch-similarity static-token selection (tau=0.996, top-k=100), attention-based task-relevance filter, entropy-based per-layer reuse.
inputs: Same as host VLA (images + instruction)
outputs: Same as host VLA
trainingData: None (training-free); real-robot OpenVLA LoRA-finetuned on 150-200 teleop trajectories per task.
whatChangedVsParent: Unlike intra-frame token pruning (FastV, SparseVLM), exploits inter-frame temporal redundancy by reusing cached KV of static tokens.
limitations: Gains shrink in dynamic scenes with lots of motion; only tested on LLaMA2-based VLAs, applicability to other backbones (e.g. Gemma in pi0) is open.
notes: NeurIPS 2025. Abstract: up to 1.7x CUDA-latency speedup and 15% higher control frequency. FLOPs reduced 27.31% on OpenVLA/LIBERO. Code via vla-cache.github.io.

name: DeeR-VLA
resolvedTitle: DeeR-VLA: Dynamic Inference of Multimodal Large Language Models for Efficient Robot Execution
org: Tsinghua University; ByteDance
problem: Running a full MLLM for every robot action wastes compute, memory and latency, although most control situations are 'easy' and need a much smaller model.
keyIdea: Add intermediate exits to the MLLM and terminate early when consecutive exits' predicted actions agree (action-consistency criterion), with thresholds tuned to average/peak FLOPs and GPU memory budgets.
architecture: RoboFlamingo++ on OpenFlamingo 3B (MPT-1B + CLIP ViT-L/14) or 9B; exits after every 2 LLM layers (first 12 layers used, 6 exits); max-pooled exit features fed to a 4-layer LSTM + MLP action head; auxiliary heads used in training only.
inputs: RGB (static + gripper camera) images, language instruction, history
outputs: Per-step action (pose + gripper)
actionRepr: Single-step continuous end-effector pose (MSE) + binary gripper (cross-entropy) via LSTM action head
trainingData: CALVIN language-annotated subset (~24k trajectories, ~1% of data), settings D->D, ABC->D, ABCD->D.
whatChangedVsParent: Turns RoboFlamingo's fixed-depth LLM into a multi-exit dynamic network with budget-aware exit thresholds.
limitations: Only accelerates the LLM, not the visual encoder; evaluated only on a simulated benchmark (CALVIN).
notes: NeurIPS 2024. Code and checkpoints at github.com/yueyang130/DeeR-VLA. DeeR-S uses only ~2 GB LLM memory.

name: GR00T N1.5 / N1.6
resolvedTitle: GR00T N1: An Open Foundation Model for Generalist Humanoid Robots (N1.5 / N1.6 have no arXiv paper)
org: NVIDIA
problem: [From GR00T N1 paper] Humanoid robot data is scarce and fragmented into embodiment-specific 'data islands', blocking foundation-model-style pretraining.
keyIdea: [From GR00T N1 paper] Dual-system VLA: a VLM (System 2) interprets images and language, and a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer (System 1) generates actions, trained end-to-end on a data pyramid of web/human video, synthetic (sim + neural video) and real robot data.
architecture: [From GR00T N1 paper] NVIDIA Eagle-2 VLM (SmolLM2 + SigLIP-2), 12th-layer embeddings; DiT with alternating cross-/self-attention; embodiment-specific MLP state/action encoders and decoders; latent actions (VQ-VAE, LAPA-style) and IDM pseudo-labels for action-less video.
inputs: [N1] Images (224x224, 64 tokens/frame), language instruction, robot proprioceptive state
outputs: [N1] Motor action chunk
actionRepr: [N1] Chunk of H=16 continuous actions via flow matching (K=4 Euler denoising steps); embodiment-specific action dimensions
trainingData: [N1] Real (in-house GR-1 teleop, Open X-Embodiment subsets, AgiBot-Alpha 140k trajectories), simulation (DexMimicGen/MimicGen), ~300k neural trajectories (827 h) from finetuned WAN2.1 video model, human egocentric video with latent actions.
controlRateHz: [N1] System 2 at 10 Hz, System 1 at 120 Hz; 63.9 ms to sample a 16-action chunk on L40

headlineResults.benchmark: [N1] Real GR-1 humanoid (all tasks, full data)

notes: GR00T N1.5 and N1.6 are NVIDIA model releases (blog/model card/GitHub) with no arXiv paper found; all field values above are from the GR00T N1 paper (arXiv 2503.14734) and are marked [N1]. GENERAL KNOWLEDGE (unverified, not from a paper): N1.5 reportedly froze the VLM during training, upgraded to an Eagle 2.5-based VLM with better grounding, added a FLARE future-latent-alignment objective and learning from human ego videos; N1.6 reportedly moved to a Cosmos-Reason-based VLM and a larger DiT with relative actions. Treat these as unverified. N1-2B checkpoint, data and sim benchmarks were released publicly (GitHub/HuggingFace).

name: ProgPrompt
resolvedTitle: ProgPrompt: Generating Situated Robot Task Plans using Large Language Models
org: University of Southern California; NVIDIA
topicName: High-level planning with LLMs and VLMs (new)
problem: LLM planners either must score every possible next action or generate free-form text that may reference actions/objects not available to the robot in its current situation.
keyIdea: Prompt the LLM with a Pythonic program: import statements for available action primitives, a list of scene objects, and example task functions with comments and assert-based precondition checks with recovery actions; the LLM completes a new task function that is directly executable.
architecture: Few-shot prompted GPT-3 / Codex / davinci; generated plan executed by an interpreter; assertions checked by prompting the LLM with the environment state graph; real robot uses ViLD detection plus a pick-and-place policy (Contact-GraspNet, MPPI, SceneCollisionNet).
inputs: Task name (natural language as function name), available actions (imports), object list, example programs, state feedback
outputs: Executable Python-like plan of action primitive calls
