whatChangedVsParent: Collects multi-embodiment data (including humanoid dexterous hands) under a single standardized protocol with failure data and digital twin, rather than aggregating heterogeneous lab datasets.
limitations: Relatively simple background environments; lacks mobile manipulation scenarios.
notes: Benchmarks ACT, Diffusion Policy, BAKU (single-task) and OpenVLA, RDT-1B, CrossFormer (multi-task). Toolchain for LeRobot at github.com/x-humanoid-robomind.

name: DexUMI
resolvedTitle: DexUMI: Using Human Hand as the Universal Manipulation Interface for Dexterous Manipulation
org: Stanford University; Columbia University; J.P. Morgan AI Research; CMU; NVIDIA
problem: Transferring dexterous skills from human hands to diverse robot hands is hard because of kinematic, tactile and visual embodiment gaps; teleoperation suffers from spatial mismatch and lacks direct haptic feedback.
keyIdea: Use the human hand as the interface: a per-robot-hand wearable exoskeleton (optimized to share the robot's joint-to-fingertip mapping) records feasible joint actions with direct haptic feedback, and a software pipeline replaces the human hand/exoskeleton in video with an inpainted robot hand.
architecture: Hardware: optimized exoskeleton with joint encoders, fingertip tactile sensors matching the robot's, a 150-degree wrist camera (OAK-1) and iPhone ARKit wrist tracking. Software: SAM2 segmentation + ProPainter background inpainting + replayed robot-hand rendering composited with occlusion handling. Policy trained on the adapted data (diffusion policy per references; not restated in retrieved text).
inputs: Wrist-camera RGB (inpainted to show robot hand), optional fingertip tactile readings
outputs: Wrist pose (relative) and finger joint actions for the target robot hand
actionRepr: Relative wrist trajectory plus relative (delta) finger-joint trajectory; relative finger action outperformed absolute
trainingData: Exoskeleton demonstrations collected without the robot for 4 real tasks (Cube, Egg Carton, Tea, Kitchen) on Inspire (6-DoF) and XHand (12-DoF) hands; exact demo counts not in retrieved text

headlineResults.value: 3.2x teleoperation (36 vs 11 successful demos; bare hand 51)

headlineResults.metric: success, relative action + inpaint vs raw images

whatChangedVsParent: Extends UMI's robot-free handheld data collection from parallel grippers to multi-fingered hands via a robot-specific exoskeleton plus robot-hand inpainting, avoiding DexCap-style retargeting.
limitations: Exoskeleton must be designed per robot hand; installed tactile sensors were noisy/drifting, so tactile input often hurt performance except with relative actions on tasks with clean force profiles.
notes: CoRL 2025. Project site dex-umi.github.io. Tactile helped the salt-picking stage on XHand but not tweezer manipulation.

name: FastUMI
resolvedTitle: FastUMI: A Scalable and Hardware-Independent Universal Manipulation Interface with Dataset
org: Shanghai AI Lab; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Fudan University; HKU; et al.
problem: The original UMI is tightly coupled to specific hardware (e.g., WSG-50 gripper) and relies on a fragile GoPro VIO/SLAM pipeline that fails under prolonged occlusion and needs complex calibration.
keyIdea: Redesign UMI with decoupled, ISO-standard-compatible mounts and plug-in fingertips that fit many arms/grippers, and replace VIO with an off-the-shelf RealSense T265 tracker, plus a data verification ecosystem and algorithm adaptations.
architecture: Handheld device: GoPro for visuals, RealSense T265 for pose, ArUco fingertip markers for gripper width; robot-mounted mirror device. Policy adaptations: Smooth-ACT (GRU on ACT decoder), PoseACT (end-effector pose output), Depth-Enhanced DP (Depth Anything V2 pseudo-depth + CLIP ViT-B/16 encoder), dynamic TCP error compensation.
inputs: Wrist GoPro fisheye RGB (optionally estimated depth), proprioception
outputs: End-effector trajectories or joint trajectories, gripper width
actionRepr: Relative TCP pose trajectories (PoseACT / DP) or absolute joint chunks (ACT variants)
trainingData: Open-sourced dataset of over 10,000 real-world demonstrations across 22 everyday tasks
controlRateHz: Depth estimation runs at 20 Hz on RTX 4090 during DP rollout
whatChangedVsParent: Swaps UMI's GoPro-VIO SLAM for a T265 tracker and hardware-specific gripper for universal mounts/fingertips, making UMI-style collection robot-agnostic.
limitations: Single fisheye view lacks depth and full-arm visibility (hence the adaptations); future work needed on richer sensing modalities and more complex platforms.
notes: Dataset is open-sourced (HDF5, ACT-style layout). Per-task success numbers not captured in retrieved pages.

name: UMI on Legs
resolvedTitle: UMI on Legs: Making Manipulation Policies Mobile with Manipulation-Centric Whole-body Controllers
org: Stanford University; Columbia University; Google DeepMind
problem: Real-world teleoperation data is robot-specific and simulation lacks task diversity; legged manipulators need both expressive manipulation skills and robust whole-body control.
keyIdea: Combine robot-free UMI demonstrations (task-centric, real) with a simulation-trained RL whole-body controller (robot-centric), interfaced by task-frame end-effector trajectories.
architecture: High level: U-Net diffusion policy with CLIP vision encoder (UMI default) predicting camera-frame EE trajectories from GoPro RGB. Low level: MLP whole-body controller trained with RL in massively parallel sim, tracking task-frame EE pose targets with preview, outputting 18 joint targets (12 leg + 6 arm) to PD controllers. iPhone ARKit odometry.
inputs: Wrist GoPro RGB (policy); joint states, base orientation/angular velocity, previous action, target EE trajectory (controller)
outputs: Task-space EE trajectory (policy); joint position targets for legs and arm (controller)
actionRepr: Diffusion-predicted EE pose trajectory with action horizon 64, tracked by a 50 Hz RL controller
trainingData: UMI hand-held gripper demos (own data for pushing and tossing; UMI's cup-rearrangement checkpoint reused); controller trained in simulation on UMI trajectories
controlRateHz: Manipulation policy 1-5 Hz (2 Hz in figure); whole-body controller 50 Hz

headlineResults.comparedTo: policy originally trained for fixed-base arm

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces body-frame EE targets and velocity commands of prior legged WBCs with task-frame EE trajectory tracking with preview, allowing UMI policies to run on a quadruped.
limitations: Gripper-only manipulation inherited from UMI; embodiment-specific constraints are not fed back to the high-level policy; no collision avoidance or force control.
notes: Hardware: Unitree Go2 + ARX5 arm. Code, data released at umi-on-legs.github.io.

name: DexMimicGen
resolvedTitle: DexMimicGen: Automated Data Generation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation via Imitation Learning
org: NVIDIA Research; UT Austin; UC San Diego
problem: Collecting teleoperated demos for bimanual dexterous robots (e.g., humanoids) is especially costly, and MimicGen's single subtask sequence cannot handle independent and coordinated two-arm behaviors.
keyIdea: Extend MimicGen with per-arm subtask segmentation and a taxonomy of parallel, coordination and sequential subtasks, using asynchronous per-arm execution, synchronization and ordering constraints to synthesize large datasets from a handful of human demos in simulation.
architecture: Data-generation system on robosuite/MuJoCo: object-centric SE(3) transformation of source segments per arm, synchronized coordination with Transform or Replay schemes, finger motions replayed from source. Policies trained afterward: BC-RNN, BC-RNN-GMM, Diffusion Policy.
inputs: Images and proprioception (for trained visuomotor policies)
outputs: Per-arm end-effector pose commands plus hand joint commands
actionRepr: Per-arm EE pose command + dexterous hand joint positions (6-D per hand), via OSC (Panda) or IK controller (GR-1)
trainingData: 21K generated demos from 60 source human demos across 9 sim tasks and 3 embodiments (bimanual Panda grippers, bimanual Panda dexterous hands, GR-1 humanoid); 1000 generated demos per task in main experiments
whatChangedVsParent: Generalizes MimicGen's single-arm subtask stitching to two arms with dexterous hands via per-arm asynchronous segments plus synchronization and ordering constraints.
limitations: Inherits MimicGen assumptions: object-centric subtasks and object poses observable before contact; real-world use requires a digital twin and real2sim2real pipeline.
notes: Simulation environments and generated datasets released (dexmimicgen.github.io). Also applied to BiGym benchmark tasks.

name: InternData-A1
resolvedTitle: InternData-A1: Pioneering High-Fidelity Synthetic Data for Pre-training Generalist Policy
org: Shanghai AI Laboratory; Peking University
problem: Synthetic data had not been shown to match large-scale real-robot data for VLA pre-training; existing sim datasets are narrow (mostly pick-and-place, rigid objects) and need human operation.
keyIdea: Build a fully decoupled, autonomous, compositional simulation pipeline (assets, scripted skills, task composition, rendering) to generate a large photorealistic multi-embodiment dataset, and show pi0 pre-trained solely on it matches official pi0.
architecture: Data pipeline: asset library retrieval, composable scripted skill policies with collision-aware motion planning, domain randomization, decoupled planner/renderer with dynamic scheduling and stacked rendering. Policy: same architecture as pi0 (PaliGemma VLM + flow-matching action expert), pre-trained from PaliGemma weights.
inputs: Multi-view RGB, language, proprioception (pi0 setup)
outputs: Robot actions (pi0 flow-matching action chunks)
actionRepr: pi0 flow-matching action chunks
trainingData: 630k (637,498) trajectories, 7,433.9 hours, 401.4M frames, 4 embodiments (Genie-1, Franka, AgileX Split Aloha, ARX Lift-2), 18 skills, 70 tasks, 227 scenes; rigid, articulated, deformable and fluid objects

headlineResults.benchmark: Pre-training dataset comparison, 2 real tasks (Sort Rubbish / Pass Bottle)

whatChangedVsParent: First to show simulation-only pre-training matching the closed pi-dataset, with broader skills/object types than prior sim datasets like RoboTwin 2.0 or GraspVLA.
limitations: Physics simulators cannot yet model highly dexterous tasks such as tying shoelaces or threading a needle.
notes: Dataset released; generation pipeline to be open-sourced. Real-world regular tasks: +6.2% over pi-dataset; dexterous tasks comparable. Fewer than 1,600 sim samples matched 200 real samples on 4 aligned tasks.

name: GenSim / GenSim2
resolvedTitle: GenSim: Generating Robotic Simulation Tasks via Large Language Models (ICLR 2024); GenSim2: Scaling Robot Data Generation with Multi-modal and Reasoning LLMs (CoRL 2024)
org: MIT CSAIL; UC San Diego; Tsinghua; SJTU; UW; CMU (GenSim). Tsinghua IIIS; UCSD; SJTU; MIT CSAIL (GenSim2)
authorsShort: Wang et al. (GenSim); Hua, Liu, Macaluso et al. (GenSim2)
problem: Simulation data diversity is mostly scene-level, not task-level, because humans must design and verify each new task; GenSim2 further targets articulated, 6-DoF, long-horizon tasks and sim-to-real transfer.
keyIdea: Use LLMs to write simulation task code (goal-directed and exploratory modes) cached in a task library; GenSim2 adds multi-modal/reasoning LLMs (GPT-4V, o1) to generate keypoint-based kPAM planner configs to solve articulated tasks, and a point-cloud multi-task policy.
architecture: GenSim: GPT-4 prompt chain + task library + CLIPort policy on Ravens (UR5e suction, top-down RGB-D, affordance map). GenSim2: SAPIEN tasks, MLLM-generated kPAM constraints/actuation motions (plus RL solver), Proprioceptive Point-cloud Transformer (PPT): CLIP text, PointNext point-cloud encoder, MLP proprio encoder, transformer trunk, diffusion/transformer/MLP heads.
inputs: GenSim: top-down RGB-D + language. GenSim2: point cloud (no color), proprioception, language
outputs: GenSim: pick/place affordance poses. GenSim2: action sequences
actionRepr: GenSim: two end-effector poses (pick and place) via affordance maps. GenSim2: action chunks from diffusion or transformer head
trainingData: GenSim: 10 human CLIPort tasks expanded to over 100 GPT-4 tasks (120 generated in exploratory mode). GenSim2: up to 100 articulated tasks with 35 objects (200+ instances) incl. 50 long-horizon; 100 sim demos per real task plus 10 real demos
controlRateHz: GenSim2 inference latency 0.1 s on RTX 3080
whatChangedVsParent: GenSim2 moves from GenSim's top-down pick-and-place code generation to MLLM-generated planner solvers for 6-DoF articulated and long-horizon tasks, with a point-cloud policy for zero-shot sim-to-real.
limitations: LLM-generated code still has syntax errors/hallucinations and imperfect evaluation metrics needing some manual filtering; GenSim limited to tabletop pick-and-place; GenSim2 still needs minimal human involvement and only 6-DoF tasks with limited point clouds.
notes: Merged card for two papers. GenSim2 arXiv 2410.03645. GenSim released code, benchmark and model weights; GenSim2 weights status unknown.

name: RoboGen
resolvedTitle: RoboGen: Towards Unleashing Infinite Data for Automated Robot Learning via Generative Simulation
org: CMU; Tsinghua IIIS; MIT CSAIL; UMass Amherst; MIT-IBM AI Lab
problem: Building simulation environments (tasks, assets, scenes, rewards) requires heavy human effort, limiting scalable skill learning in simulation.
keyIdea: Generative simulation: an agent runs a propose-generate-learn cycle where foundation models propose tasks, generate scenes (asset retrieval + VLM verification), decompose tasks, write rewards, and pick the learning method (RL, motion planning, or trajectory optimization).
architecture: GPT-4 for task proposal, scene config, decomposition and reward generation; Objaverse retrieval with Sentence-BERT + Gemini-Pro verification; skill learning with SAC (MLP 256x3), BIT* motion planning primitives, Adam gradient-based trajectory optimization (soft bodies), CEM for locomotion; runs on Genesis simulator.
inputs: Low-level simulator state (for RL policies)
outputs: 6-D end-effector delta actions (RL), motion-planned trajectories, or optimized joint/trajectory actions
actionRepr: 6-D EE action (3 translation + 3 delta axis-angle) for RL; motion primitives; trajectory optimization
trainingData: Self-generated tasks: 106 tasks evaluated for diversity; covers rigid/articulated manipulation, soft bodies, legged locomotion
whatChangedVsParent: Unlike GenSim's LLM-written scripted demos for tabletop tasks, RoboGen generates scenes and rewards and selects RL/planning/trajectory optimization to learn skills across broader task types.
limitations: Large-scale verification of learned skills remains a challenge; intrinsically constrained by sim-to-real gaps (no real deployment).
notes: ICML 2024. RL-only ablation fails on most articulated tasks. GenSim2 notes RoboGen's RL data is slow and less transferable.

name: RoboTwin 2.0
resolvedTitle: RoboTwin 2.0: A Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark with Strong Domain Randomization for Robust Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
org: SJTU; HKU MMLab; Shanghai AI Lab; D-Robotics; SZU; Tsinghua; TeleAI; et al.
problem: Existing synthetic datasets for bimanual manipulation lack efficient scalable generation for new tasks, have oversimplified (clean) scenes, lack automated quality control, and ignore cross-embodiment differences.
keyIdea: Combine MLLM-based task-code generation with simulation-in-the-loop VLM feedback, structured domain randomization on five axes (clutter, lighting, background, tabletop height, language), and embodiment-aware grasp candidates to mass-produce robust dual-arm expert data.
architecture: Framework: RoboTwin-OD object library (731 objects, 147 categories, keypoint/axis annotations), skill API, code-generation agent + VLM observer, Curobo GPU motion planning, embodiment-adaptive grasp candidates. Policies benchmarked: ACT, DP, DP3, RDT, pi0.
outputs: Expert dual-arm trajectories (data generator); benchmark evaluation
trainingData: Over 100,000 pre-collected dual-arm trajectories across 50 tasks and 5 embodiments (Aloha-AgileX, ARX-X5, Piper, Franka, UR5)

headlineResults.benchmark: Real world, VLA with synthetic + 10 real demos
Robustness, 8 unseen sim tasks under randomization

whatChangedVsParent: Moves from RoboTwin 1.0's digital-twin replicas and clean scenes to MLLM code generation with VLM feedback, strong domain randomization, 50 tasks and 5 embodiments.
limitations: Pretrained VLAs still drop sharply (about 20-30 points) from clean to randomized settings; future work on real-world deployment and multi-object task complexity.
notes: Data generator, benchmark, dataset and code released (robotwin-platform.github.io). InternData-A1 later uses RoboTwin 2.0's 49 tasks as its sim benchmark.

name: EgoScale
resolvedTitle: EgoScale: Scaling Dexterous Manipulation with Diverse Egocentric Human Data
org: NVIDIA; UC Berkeley; University of Maryland
problem: It was unclear whether large-scale human data can support fine-grained high-DoF dexterous robot manipulation; prior human-to-robot work used tens to hundreds of hours and mostly grippers or low-DoF hands.
keyIdea: Pretrain a flow-based VLA on over 20k hours of action-labeled egocentric human video (relative wrist motion + retargeted 22-DoF hand joints), then mid-train on a small aligned human-robot play set, revealing a log-linear scaling law that predicts robot performance.
architecture: Flow-based VLA similar to GR00T N1: pretrained VLM backbone + DiT action expert with flow matching; learnable placeholder token replaces proprioception for human data; lightweight embodiment-specific MLP adapters for state and hand actions.
inputs: Egocentric (head) RGB plus two wrist cameras on robot, language instruction, proprioception (robot only)
outputs: Chunk of relative wrist (end-effector) motions and dexterous hand joint targets
actionRepr: Flow-matching action chunks: relative wrist SE(3) motion + 22-DoF retargeted hand joint angles (Sharpa hand)
trainingData: Stage I: 20,854 hours egocentric human video (9,869 scenes, 6,015 tasks, 43,237 objects) incl. 829 h EgoDex; Stage II: ~50 h aligned human + 4 h robot data over 344 tasks; Stage III task-specific robot demos

headlineResults.benchmark: 5 dexterous tasks on Galaxea R1Pro + 22-DoF hands
headlineResults.comparedTo: 0.02 no pretrain; 0.28 midtrain only; 0.38 human pretrain only

headlineResults.benchmark: Scaling law on human validation loss

whatChangedVsParent: Scales human pretraining over 20x beyond prior human-to-robot transfer work and supervises full retargeted high-DoF hand joints rather than wrist-only or fingertip targets.
limitations: Relies on noisy off-the-shelf SLAM/hand-pose labels and still needs a small aligned human-robot mid-training set; scaling of model capacity and unlabeled video left open.
notes: Paper abstract states 54% average success-rate improvement over no-pretraining baseline. Transfers to Unitree G1 with tri-finger hand (over 30% absolute improvement). Pretraining used 256 GB200 GPUs.

name: Re-Mix
resolvedTitle: Re-Mix: Optimizing Data Mixtures for Large Scale Imitation Learning
org: Stanford University; UC Berkeley
problem: Large heterogeneous robot datasets (e.g., Open X-Embodiment) are mixed with ad hoc, human-chosen domain weights; there is no principled way to choose data mixtures for generalist policy pre-training.
keyIdea: Learn domain mixture weights with group distributionally robust optimization over excess behavior-cloning loss relative to a reference model (DoReMi-style), adapted for robotics via per-domain Gaussian action normalization, action discretization, and aggressive early stopping.
architecture: ResNet-50 image encoder; discrete MLP action head for the reference model and Group DRO; final policies use a diffusion action head trained on the re-weighted mixture.
inputs: Third-person RGB images (goal-conditioned policies)
outputs: Domain weights (method); continuous actions (final diffusion policies)
actionRepr: Binned discrete actions for weight estimation; diffusion head for final policies
trainingData: Bridge V2 (50k demos, 32 scene domains) and the RT-X subset of Open X-Embodiment (350k demos, 11 datasets)

headlineResults.benchmark: RT-X mix, WidowX + Franka real tasks
headlineResults.value: +38% over uniform, +32% over human-selected RT-X weights

whatChangedVsParent: Adapts DoReMi's language-model data-mixture optimization to robotics by fixing unbalanced continuous action losses and overfitting.
limitations: Limited real-world embodiments evaluated; upweights datasets with abnormal action distributions (e.g., Toto); requires training on full data twice; not yet scaled to full OpenX.
notes: Code at github.com/jhejna/remix. Learned weights reusable across policy classes.

name: DemInf
resolvedTitle: Robot Data Curation with Mutual Information Estimators
org: Google DeepMind Robotics; Stanford University
problem: Robot data quality is rarely measured, and vision/language curation tools cannot reason about actions; group-level mixing (Re-Mix) cannot score individual demonstrations.
keyIdea: Score each demonstration by its average contribution to the mutual information between states and action chunks, favoring diverse yet predictable actions, estimated with k-NN (KSG) estimators on VAE latent embeddings.
architecture: Separate VAEs embed states and action chunks into low-dimensional latents; KSG k-nearest-neighbor mutual information estimator computed over randomized batches and several k; per-episode average score used to filter.
inputs: Demonstration dataset (states/images and action chunks)
outputs: Per-demonstration quality scores for filtering
trainingData: Evaluated on RoboMimic (MH datasets, state and image), RoboCrowd ALOHA datasets (40-100 demos), and Franka tasks
parents: Data Quality in Imitation Learning (Belkhale et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Moves from group-level mixture weights (Re-Mix) to unsupervised per-demonstration quality scores via non-parametric mutual information.
limitations: Ignores time evolution through dynamics; may prefer demos with pauses; greedy filtering; assumes all demos are successful; single-task setting.
notes: Name is from 'Demonstration Information Estimation'. Outperforms InfoNCE and MINE estimators, VIP and uncertainty baselines in partitioning by human quality labels. Code at jhejna.github.io/demonstration-info.

name: DataMIL
resolvedTitle: DataMIL: Selecting Data for Robot Imitation Learning with Datamodels
org: UT Austin; MIT; Stanford University
problem: Co-training with task-specific data plus subsets of large prior datasets helps, but heuristic similarity-based selection (visual, motion, state-action) ignores each sample's real effect on policy performance and can hurt it.
keyIdea: Apply the datamodels framework: estimate each prior datapoint's (cluster's) influence on policy performance with linear datamodels (regression or metagradient estimators), using a surrogate loss on target task data instead of rollouts, and select the top-scoring data for co-training.
architecture: Datamodel estimators: regression estimator (train on random subsets) and metagradient (MGD) estimator; clustering of prior data into (sub-)trajectories; final policy co-trained on selected + target data. Policies: MLP with Gaussian head (MetaWorld), Octo (LIBERO, OXE).
inputs: Prior dataset, small target dataset
outputs: Selected subset of prior data (influence scores)
trainingData: MetaWorld 50 tasks (scripted + SAC replay data), LIBERO-90 as prior for LIBERO-10, 24 OXE datasets from Octo's training mix for real-world tasks
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces similarity-heuristic retrieval with performance-aware influence estimation, made tractable in robotics via a rollout-free surrogate loss.
limitations: Datamodel estimation costs several times more than training on all data; sensitive to hyperparameters (selected size, cluster size); mainly single-task target settings.
notes: Exact MetaWorld/LIBERO percentages only in figures, not transcribed. Covers 60+ sim and real tasks.

name: Sirius
resolvedTitle: Robot Learning on the Job: Human-in-the-Loop Autonomy and Learning During Deployment
org: UT Austin
problem: Learned manipulation policies are not reliable enough for deployment and do not improve from deployment experience; existing human-in-the-loop methods do not fully exploit intervention signals.
keyIdea: Human-robot team with human-gated interventions during deployment; re-weight deployment data by intervention-derived class (demo, robot, intervention upweighted to 50%, pre-intervention set to 0) and train with weighted behavioral cloning, plus memory management (LFI).
architecture: BC-RNN backbone (LSTM) with ResNet-18 encoders on workspace and eye-in-hand images plus proprioception, GMM action output; weighted BC loss; rounds of deployment and policy update.
inputs: Workspace RGB, eye-in-hand RGB, proprioception
outputs: Task-space motor actions (GMM)
actionRepr: Single-step task-space actions from a GMM head (BC-RNN)
trainingData: Initial human demos plus deployment data over 3 rounds (Nut Assembly and Tool Hang in robosuite; real Gear Insertion and Coffee Pod Packing on Franka)
whatChangedVsParent: Refines IWR's two-class weighting into four intervention-guided classes, down-weighting pre-intervention robot samples and preserving demo ratio.
limitations: Requires continuous human monitoring; pre-intervention window length set heuristically from human reaction time (2 s, 15 steps); evaluated on a limited set of tasks.
notes: RSS 2023. Project site ut-austin-rpl.github.io/sirius.

name: Open-TeleVision
resolvedTitle: Open-TeleVision: Teleoperation with Immersive Active Visual Feedback
org: UC San Diego; MIT
problem: Teleoperation systems suffer from occlusion and poor spatial perception (direct view or static RGB), cannot combine remote operation with depth perception, and joint-copy systems cannot drive multi-finger hands.
keyIdea: Immersive VR teleoperation with an actuated head-mounted stereo camera that follows the operator's head, streaming stereoscopic video back to the headset, while arm and hand motions are retargeted to the robot.
architecture: Apple Vision Pro + Vuer web server streaming hand/head/wrist poses; IK and hand retargeting; ZED Mini stereo camera on 2-3 DoF neck. Policy: ACT with DinoV2 backbone on two stereo images plus joint-position proprioception.
inputs: Stereo RGB from active head camera, joint positions
outputs: Absolute joint positions for arms, hands/grippers and neck
actionRepr: ACT action chunks of absolute joint positions (28-D on H1: 7 per arm, 6 per hand, 2 neck; 19-D on GR-1); chunk size 60
trainingData: Teleoperated demos on 4 tasks (Can Sorting, Can Insertion, Folding, Unloading) on Unitree H1 and Fourier GR-1
controlRateHz: 60 Hz teleoperation loop and policy deployment

headlineResults.value: 2x faster training and inference vs wide-angle input

whatChangedVsParent: Adds active stereo first-person perception to VR hand-tracking teleoperation, enabling remote operation with depth, and swaps ACT's ResNet for DinoV2 on stereo inputs.
limitations: No haptic feedback; no mechanism to relabel expert data; only upper body used (mobile version left for future); ACT memory limited by chunk size.
notes: Open-sourced at robot-tv.github.io. Demonstrated coast-to-coast (Boston to San Diego) teleoperation.

name: AnyTeleop
resolvedTitle: AnyTeleop: A General Vision-Based Dexterous Robot Arm-Hand Teleoperation System
org: UC San Diego; NVIDIA
problem: Vision-based dexterous teleoperation systems are engineered for a specific robot, environment, or simulator and single operator, so they scale poorly for data collection.
keyIdea: A unified, modular, learning-free vision teleoperation server supporting any arm-hand URDF, any simulator or real robot, any camera configuration, remote web visualization and multi-operator collaboration.
architecture: Four modules: MediaPipe hand keypoint detection with RGB-D PnP or RGB-only weak-perspective wrist estimation; multi-camera fusion using SMPL-X shape confidence; optimization-based hand retargeting; CuRobo GPU collision-free motion generation; meshcat-based web viewer; Docker packaging.
inputs: RGB or RGB-D from one or more uncalibrated cameras of the human hand
outputs: Robot arm and hand joint commands
controlRateHz: Hand detection/retargeting 25 Hz; motion generation 120 Hz

headlineResults.value: higher on 8/10, equal on 2/10 (e.g., Two Cup Stacking 0.7 vs 0.3)

parents: From One Hand to Multiple Hands (Qin et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces robot-specific learned retargeting/collision models with generic optimization-based retargeting and CuRobo motion generation, generalizing across robots and realities.
limitations: Loses tracking during fast hand motion; unreliable hand pose under self-occlusion (mitigated with multiple cameras).
notes: RSS 2023. Teleoperation system, not a policy. Imitation learning comparison: better on 5/6 SAPIEN tasks.

name: DexCap
resolvedTitle: DexCap: Scalable and Portable Mocap Data Collection System for Dexterous Manipulation
org: Stanford University
problem: Hand mocap systems are not portable and vision-based hand tracking fails under occlusion and lacks accurate 3D; translating human mocap into robot policies is hard due to embodiment gaps.
keyIdea: A portable wearable mocap rig (EMF gloves + SLAM wrist tracking + chest LiDAR) captures 3D hand motion and scenes in the wild; DexIL retargets fingertips via IK and trains a point-cloud diffusion policy, with optional human-in-the-loop correction.
architecture: Hardware: Rokoko EMF gloves, three RealSense T265 SLAM cameras (moved to hand mounts), RealSense L515 chest LiDAR, Intel NUC backpack. DexIL: fingertip IK retargeting to LEAP hands, point clouds transformed to a world frame with robot-hand points merged, Diffusion Policy with Perceiver point-cloud encoder (DP-perc).
inputs: Colored point cloud (K points x 6) plus proprioception (wrist pose + finger joints)
outputs: Future sequence of arm end-effector poses and hand joint positions
actionRepr: Diffusion-generated trajectory of next states over d steps; 46-dim action (two 7-DoF arms + two 16-DoF LEAP hands) for bimanual
trainingData: About 30 minutes of mocap demonstrations per task, including in-the-wild data; optional 30 human correction trials
controlRateHz: Mocap tracking 60 Hz; robot arms and LEAP hands controlled at 20 Hz

headlineResults.benchmark: Sponge picking / Ball collecting / Plate wiping (mocap data only)
Packaging from in-the-wild data (subtask / all / unseen)

whatChangedVsParent: Brings UMI-style robot-free data collection to multi-fingered bimanual hands with 3D mocap and point-cloud diffusion policies.
limitations: No force information captured; objects can leave the chest camera view as the human moves; simple fingertip IK does not close all embodiment gaps (e.g., scissor grasp), requiring human corrections.
notes: RSS 2024. Project dex-cap.github.io. DexUMI criticizes DexCap for relying on retargeting and real robot data (corrections).

name: LIV
resolvedTitle: LIV: Language-Image Representations and Rewards for Robotic Control
org: University of Pennsylvania; Meta AI
problem: Robots need vision-language representations that align modalities, capture task progress as rewards, and can be both pre-trained on generic video and fine-tuned on small in-domain data.
keyIdea: Language-Image Value learning: extend VIP's dual-RL implicit value objective to language goals and show it generalizes CLIP's InfoNCE, yielding one objective (VIP-I + InfoNCE) for representation and dense language- or image-goal rewards.
architecture: CLIP-style dual encoder with ResNet-50 vision backbone initialized from CLIP; value implicitly defined as scaled cosine similarity between frame embedding and goal (image or text) embedding.
inputs: Video frames plus text annotations (pre-training); image observations and language goal (downstream)
outputs: Vision-language embeddings; dense goal-conditioned rewards
trainingData: EPIC-KITCHENS-100: 90k video segments, 20M frames, 20k unique text annotations; 200k gradient steps on 8 V100
whatChangedVsParent: Generalizes VIP from image-only goal values to joint vision-language values, recovering CLIP's contrastive objective as a special case.
limitations: Zero-shot rewards on robot videos are imperfect; evaluated with frozen or lightly fine-tuned ResNet-50 on limited simulated and real kitchen tasks.
notes: ICML 2023. Model and code released at github.com/penn-pal-lab/LIV.

name: Voltron
resolvedTitle: Language-Driven Representation Learning for Robotics
org: Stanford University; Toyota Research Institute
problem: Existing visual representations for robotics are inconsistent across tasks: masked autoencoding (MVP) captures low-level spatial features but misses semantics, while contrastive methods (R3M) capture the opposite.
keyIdea: Masked autoencoding on human video frames that either conditions on or generates the language caption (probability alpha), balancing low-level visual reconstruction with high-level semantic grounding; plus a five-task evaluation suite.
architecture: ViT-Small/16 (22M) or ViT-Base (86M) multimodal encoder jointly embedding visible patches and DistilBERT-initialized language tokens; MAE decoder plus causal language generator; variants V-Cond, V-Dual (two-frame context), V-Gen (alpha = 0.5); multihead attention pooling for downstream heads.
inputs: One or two video frames plus language caption
outputs: Visual (and language) representations for frozen downstream heads
trainingData: Something-Something-v2 (168K clips, 5 frames each, 844K frames per epoch), 400 epochs
whatChangedVsParent: Adds language conditioning and generation to MVP-style masked autoencoding, and multi-frame context, to capture both spatial and semantic features.
limitations: Trained at smaller data/compute scale than official MVP/R3M; no single variant best on all tasks (language generation hurts some control tasks).
notes: Models, pretraining code and evaluation suite released (github.com/siddk/voltron-robotics). V-Gen enables zero-shot intent scoring on WHiRL videos.

name: MPI
resolvedTitle: Learning Manipulation by Predicting Interaction
org: Shanghai AI Lab; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Renmin University; Peking University; et al.
authorsShort: Zeng, Bu, Wang, Xia et al.
problem: Prior human-video pretraining (contrastive, masked modeling, video prediction) ignores interactive dynamics between agent, objects and environment.
keyIdea: Given initial and final (or transition) keyframes plus language, predict the unseen interaction frame (how-to-interact) and detect the interaction object's box (where-to-interact), with mutually communicating prediction and detection transformers.
architecture: ViT encoder with frozen DistilBERT language encoder, deformable-attention causality module between two frames, MAP token aggregator; Prediction Transformer and Detection Transformer decoders (pre-training only); losses: MSE + L1/GIoU + InfoNCE.
inputs: Two keyframes plus language instruction (pre-training); images downstream
outputs: Visual representations for frozen downstream heads
trainingData: 93K clips from Ego4D Hand-Object Interaction subset with keyframe and box annotations
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces masked reconstruction / contrastive alignment with interaction-oriented keyframe prediction plus interaction-object detection.
limitations: Requires keyframe and bounding-box annotations (Ego4D HOI); evaluated only with frozen encoders.
notes: RSS 2024. Code and checkpoints at github.com/OpenDriveLab/MPI.

name: XIRL
resolvedTitle: XIRL: Cross-embodiment Inverse Reinforcement Learning
org: Stanford University; Robotics at Google; UC Berkeley
problem: Learning from videos of agents with different embodiments (e.g., humans) is hard because they solve tasks differently and frame-level correspondences or reference trajectories are unavailable.
keyIdea: Learn a task-progress-aware, embodiment-invariant visual embedding with temporal cycle-consistency (TCC) across demos from multiple embodiments, and use negative distance to the goal embedding as the RL reward.
architecture: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 encoder with 32-D embedding head trained with TCC loss; reward = negative embedding distance to goal frame; policies trained with SAC.
inputs: RGB frames (reward); state vector for RL policy in X-MAGICAL
outputs: Dense scalar reward
trainingData: X-MAGICAL benchmark: 1000 demos per agent for 4 embodiments; RLV human State Pusher videos; X-REAL real dataset of 93 videos with 9 embodiments

headlineResults.benchmark: State Pusher (human videos to sim Sawyer)
headlineResults.value: better than RLV and sparse reward, without paired frame labels

whatChangedVsParent: Uses TCC cross-video alignment to learn rewards that generalize to unseen embodiments, removing RLV's need for human-labeled paired frames.
limitations: Policy learning demonstrated only in simulation; no real-robot policy learning yet.
notes: CoRL 2021. Code and datasets at x-irl.github.io. Results are reported as learning curves, no single headline number transcribed.

name: DVD
resolvedTitle: Learning Generalizable Robotic Reward Functions from "In-The-Wild" Human Videos
org: Stanford University
problem: Generalist robots need reward functions that generalize across environments and tasks from on-board RGB, but diverse robot interaction data is scarce.
keyIdea: Domain-agnostic Video Discriminator: train a classifier to predict whether two videos (human or robot) perform the same task, using many in-the-wild human videos plus a few robot demos; condition on a human demo video to score robot behavior.
architecture: Pretrained (frozen) 3D-conv video encoder from Concept2Robot on Something-Something-v2, plus trainable fully connected similarity network; used as reward inside visual MPC (SV2P video prediction + CEM).
inputs: Two videos (human demo, candidate robot trajectory)
outputs: Task-similarity score used as reward
trainingData: Something-Something-v2 human videos from up to 15 tasks (853-3170 videos per task) plus 120 simulated robot demos per task for 3 tasks; 80 real robot demos per task for 2 tasks

headlineResults.benchmark: Real WidowX200, unseen env (+ unseen task)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces Concept2Robot's fixed 174-way classifier reward with a demo-conditioned same-task discriminator trained on mixed human and robot videos, enabling unseen-task rewards.
limitations: Learns only rewards (not policies or dynamics); needs some robot demos and task labels; tested on coarse tasks without fine-grained manipulation.

name: Vid2Robot
resolvedTitle: Vid2Robot: End-to-end Video-conditioned Policy Learning with Cross-Attention Transformers
org: Google DeepMind Robotics; Carnegie Mellon University; University of Toronto
problem: Text-conditioned multi-task policies struggle with polysemous or hard-to-describe tasks; video-conditioned policies lag behind and assume same-workspace demos.
keyIdea: End-to-end policy that takes a human (or robot) prompt video and current robot observations, fuses them via cross-attention, and outputs actions, with auxiliary contrastive losses aligning prompt and robot video representations.
architecture: Shared ViT-B/16 frame encoder + Perceiver Resampler (64 tokens) for prompt video (16 frames) and robot state (8 frames); 4-layer cross-attention state-prompt encoder; 4-layer cross-attention action decoder with action position queries; losses: action CE + TCC + video-video and video-text contrastive (SigLIP).
inputs: Prompt video (16 frames) and robot camera history (8 frames)
outputs: Discretized actions for mode, arm and base
actionRepr: 11 action dimensions, each discretized into 256 bins; prediction horizon 4
trainingData: About 100k robot videos and 10k human videos (Robot-Robot pairs >90%, Hindsight Human-Robot, Co-located Human-Robot) covering RT-1/RT-2 tasks

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Google Robot, 9 tasks with human prompt videos

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces BC-Z's FiLM-conditioned ResNet with large ViT encoders, Perceiver resamplers, cross-attention and contrastive alignment losses for video-conditioned control.
limitations: Failures from self-occlusion, grasping errors (transparent/deformable objects) and distractors; notable drop in grasping success; performance gap remains for video-conditioned policies.
notes: RSS 2024. Also demonstrates cross-object motion transfer. Exact per-task numbers in Table I not transcribed.

name: Track2Act
resolvedTitle: Track2Act: Predicting Point Tracks from Internet Videos enables Generalizable Robot Manipulation
org: Carnegie Mellon University; FAIR at Meta
problem: Generalizable goal-conditioned manipulation normally needs huge robot datasets or test-time training; web videos are abundant but lack robot actions.
keyIdea: Train a diffusion model on web videos to predict 2D point tracks from initial and goal images, convert tracks to 3D object rigid transforms (PnP) for an open-loop end-effector plan, and correct it with a small closed-loop residual policy.
architecture: Track predictor: DiT (24 blocks, hidden 1024, 16 heads) conditioned on ResNet-18 embeddings of initial and goal images, denoising tracks of 200-400 points. Rigid-transform solver from tracks + depth. Residual policy: DiT (12 blocks, hidden 512) predicting residual end-effector poses for h=4 steps.
inputs: Initial RGB(-D) image, goal image, current image
outputs: End-effector poses (open-loop plan plus residual corrections)
actionRepr: End-effector pose sequence = rigid-transform plan + predicted residuals over 4 future steps (first executed)
trainingData: About 400,000 web video clips (Something-Something-v2, Epic-Kitchens, RT-1, BridgeData) with CoTracker pseudo-labels; about 400 teleoperated Spot trajectories over 10 tasks for the residual policy

headlineResults.benchmark: Spot real-world, generalization levels MG / G / CG / TG

parents: Hand-object mask conditioned BC (Bharadhwaj et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Uses embodiment-agnostic point tracks (instead of hand-object masks or generated RGB video) as the interaction plan, enabling rigid-transform inference plus residual correction.
limitations: Short-horizon tasks manipulating a single object; failures from wrong grasp location and infeasible motions at higher generalization levels.
notes: ECCV 2024. Robot data is 3-4 orders of magnitude less than typical BC approaches (per paper).

name: VideoDex
resolvedTitle: VideoDex: Learning Dexterity from Internet Videos
org: Carnegie Mellon University
problem: Human videos are mostly used only for visual pretraining, but high-DoF dexterous hands suffer from very large action spaces that visual priors alone do not address.
keyIdea: Retarget human hand and wrist motion from Epic-Kitchens into the robot's embodiment to pretrain an action prior, combined with a visual prior (R3M) and a physical prior (Neural Dynamic Policies), then fine-tune on a few teleoperated demos.
architecture: R3M ResNet-18 visual encoder, 3-layer MLP, two Neural Dynamic Policy (DMP-based) streams for wrist and hand; retargeting via OpenPose + FrankMocap (MANO), PnP, ORB-SLAM3, gravity estimation from Detic + AdaBins surface normals, learned hand retargeting from Robotic Telekinesis.
inputs: Initial scene image
outputs: Open-loop wrist (xArm6) and 16-DoF LEAP hand trajectories
actionRepr: Open-loop smooth trajectories generated by Neural Dynamic Policies (second-order dynamical system) for wrist and hand
trainingData: 500-3000 Epic-Kitchens clips per task category for the action prior; about 120-175 teleoperated demos per task
whatChangedVsParent: Adds action priors from retargeted internet human videos on top of visual (R3M) and physical (NDP) priors.
limitations: Relies on noisy off-the-shelf hand pose detectors; retargeting must be recomputed per robot embodiment; policy is open-loop and cannot react to environment changes.
notes: CoRL 2022. Seven real tasks (pick, rotate, open, cover, uncover, place, push) on xArm6 + LEAP hand.

name: HRP
resolvedTitle: HRP: Human Affordances for Robotic Pre-Training
org: Carnegie Mellon University
problem: Visual representations pre-trained on human video with generic self-supervised objectives (MAE, TCN) often fail to beat a plain ImageNet MAE baseline for robot control and are sensitive to camera view.
keyIdea: Mine hand-object affordance labels (future contact points, future wrist pose, active-object box) from Ego4D with off-the-shelf detectors and distill them into an existing pre-trained encoder by regression, tuning only LayerNorm parameters.
architecture: ViT-B/16 encoder (any pre-trained init: ImageNet MAE, CLIP, DINO, MVP, VC-1, Ego4D MAE) plus three small affordance regression heads trained with weighted L2 losses; only LayerNorm gamma/beta fine-tuned. The resulting encoder feeds a behavior-cloning policy.
inputs: Single RGB image (policy also uses it via BC head)
outputs: Visual embedding (768-d); downstream BC policy outputs end-effector and gripper velocity (delta pose) actions
actionRepr: Representation method; downstream BC policy predicts delta end-effector pose / gripper velocity (also tested with Diffusion Policy U-Net head)
trainingData: ~150K Ego4D human-object interaction clips (subset from R3M's sampling) auto-labelled with 100DoH hand-object detector and FrankMocap; 50 teleop demos per downstream robot task

headlineResults.comparedTo: 56% with Chi et al.'s default ResNet encoder

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces purely self-supervised objectives with auto-mined affordance regression (hand, object, contact) fine-tuning only LayerNorms of an existing encoder.
limitations: Only tested in imitation-learning settings; extension to RL or model-based control left for future work. Contact labels are noisy and the contact loss only helps the Ego4D base model.
notes: RSS 2024. Ablations: object and hand losses critical; LayerNorm-only fine-tuning beats full fine-tuning. Used as a baseline in Masquerade.

name: OKAMI
resolvedTitle: OKAMI: Teaching Humanoid Robots Manipulation Skills through Single Video Imitation
org: UT Austin; NVIDIA Research
problem: Humanoid manipulation via imitation normally requires many whole-body teleoperation demos; prior single-video imitation methods (e.g. ORION) target single-arm grippers and ignore the human body motion.
keyIdea: Object-aware retargeting: build a reference plan from one RGB-D human video (task-relevant objects + SMPL-H body/hand motion per subgoal), then at test time warp the retargeted arm trajectory to the new object locations and map finger poses separately.
architecture: Two-stage pipeline: (1) GPT-4V names task-relevant objects, Grounded-SAM + Cutie segment/track them, SLAHMR extended with HaMeR hand init reconstructs SMPL-H motion, CoTracker keypoint velocity changepoints give subgoals; (2) test-time object localization, task-space arm retargeting + trajectory warping, IK for arms and direct finger joint mapping. Rollouts optionally distilled into ACT visuomotor policies.
inputs: One RGB-D human video; test-time RGB-D robot observation
outputs: Humanoid arm and dexterous-hand joint position commands
actionRepr: Joint position commands computed at 40 Hz and interpolated to 400 Hz (retargeting); ACT policy for distilled visuomotor variant
trainingData: Single human video per task; distilled policies trained on 50-100 successful OKAMI rollouts

headlineResults.benchmark: Visuomotor policies trained on OKAMI rollouts

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike ORION, conditions on and retargets the demonstrator's body and hand motion (SMPL-H) to a humanoid, warped to new object locations.
limitations: Upper-body only (no locomotion); needs RGB-D video with static camera so cannot use in-the-wild RGB web video; limited robustness to large object shape variations.
notes: CoRL 2024. Hardware: Fourier GR1 with two 6-DoF Inspire hands, D435i camera. 12 trials per task.

name: ZeroMimic
resolvedTitle: ZeroMimic: Distilling Robotic Manipulation Skills from Web Videos
org: University of Pennsylvania
problem: Imitation learning needs in-domain robot demos; prior human-video methods give representations/rewards/affordances that still need robot data, or need curated videos with known camera/depth.
keyIdea: Distill zero-shot deployable image-goal-conditioned skill policies purely from EpicKitchens by splitting skills into a grasp phase (VRB affordance + AnyGrasp) and a post-grasp phase (ACT policy predicting 6D wrist trajectories reconstructed with HaMeR + SfM camera poses).
architecture: Grasping: VRB contact point -> AnyGrasp grasp selection -> linear approach. Post-grasp: per-skill ACT policy taking current image, goal image and current wrist pose; wrist trajectories from HaMeR lifted to world frame via COLMAP/EPIC-Fields cameras.
inputs: RGB-D egocentric-like image, goal image, current wrist/end-effector pose
outputs: Future relative 6D wrist (end-effector) poses
actionRepr: Chunk of 10 relative 6D end-effector poses (relative translation + relative orientation) via ACT; one model per skill (9 skills)
trainingData: EpicKitchens (~100 hours, 20M frames) egocentric videos; no robot demonstrations

headlineResults.benchmark: Open Drawer / Pour Food from Bowl into Pan

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike H2R, grounds wrist trajectories in 3D via SfM camera poses and combines a learned affordance-grasp phase with a learned 6D post-grasp policy.
limitations: Simplified pre-grasp/post-grasp structure; retargets wrist motion without accounting for morphology; no in-hand, non-prehensile, gripper release or bimanual tasks; limited by upstream grasp/affordance/hand models and trained on only ~100 h of video.
notes: CONFLICT (internal): abstract says 71.0% real-world success while Sec. IV-C reports 71.9% with Franka. Failure breakdown of 87 real failures: 31.1% AnyGrasp, 24.1% VRB, 44.8% post-grasp policy. ACT vs Diffusion Policy performed similarly.

name: RAM
resolvedTitle: RAM: Retrieval-Based Affordance Transfer for Generalizable Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation
org: University of Southern California; Peking University; Stanford University
problem: Learning manipulation from in-domain demos is costly, and learning from abundant out-of-domain data (HOI video, robot data from other setups, web images) suffers from large domain shift.
keyIdea: Build an affordance memory of 2D contact points + post-contact waypoints from heterogeneous sources, hierarchically retrieve the most similar demo for a language instruction, transfer the 2D affordance by dense VFM correspondence, and lift it to an executable 3D contact point and direction.
architecture: Training-free pipeline: task retrieval (CLIP/GPT-4) -> CLIP semantic filtering -> geometric retrieval via Stable Diffusion features (Instance Matching Distance) -> SD-feature correspondence + RANSAC for 2D affordance -> sampling-based lifting with depth normals -> AnyGrasp/GSNet grasp + motion planner.
inputs: Monocular RGB-D image + language instruction
outputs: 3D affordance: contact point and post-contact direction, executed via grasp generator and motion planning
actionRepr: 3D contact point + post-contact direction (not a learned policy); optional ACT distillation (chunk size 60)
trainingData: Affordance memory from DROID (robot), HOI4D (human-object interaction) and manually annotated custom web images; no training
whatChangedVsParent: Extends Robo-ABC's contact-point retrieval to hierarchical retrieval over multi-source memory and transfers both contact and post-contact direction lifted to 3D.
limitations: The retrieved chunk did not include an explicit limitations paragraph; ablations show dependence on the visual foundation model and on geometric retrieval (SR drops 38.3% to 26.7% without it).
notes: CoRL 2024. Also demonstrated cross-embodiment on Unitree B1 + Z1 arm, one-shot visual imitation, and GPT-4V task decomposition. Not strictly a human-video method: human data enters via HOI4D.

name: Masquerade
resolvedTitle: Masquerade: Learning from In-the-wild Human Videos using Data-Editing
org: Stanford University
problem: Prior work using in-the-wild human video (representations, rewards, world models) leaves the visual human-robot embodiment gap to be learned implicitly, limiting transfer.
keyIdea: Edit in-the-wild egocentric videos into 'robotized' clips (HaMeR hand poses -> inpaint arms -> overlay rendered bimanual robot), pretrain a vision encoder to predict future 2D robot keypoints, and keep that auxiliary loss while co-training a diffusion policy on 50 robot demos.
architecture: Language-conditioned (FiLM, DistilBERT embeddings) ViT-Base encoder initialized from ImageNet, MLP head for 2D keypoint regression, Diffusion Policy action head; robot images also overlaid with rendered robot for consistency.
inputs: Egocentric RGB image + language annotation embedding
outputs: Bimanual Cartesian end-effector actions
actionRepr: Cartesian end-effector actions from a Diffusion Policy head (bimanual)
trainingData: 10K Epic Kitchens clips (675K edited frames) + 50 robot demos per task from one scene

headlineResults.benchmark: 3 long-horizon bimanual tasks x 3 unseen scenes (dual Kinova)

whatChangedVsParent: Extends Phantom's hand-inpainting/robot-overlay editing from curated single-hand fixed-camera demos to in-the-wild egocentric video, and adds pretrain + co-train with a 2D keypoint auxiliary loss.
limitations: Relies on monocular hand-pose estimation (fails on fast motion/occlusion); no depth so overlays mis-handle occlusion; egocentric camera motion forces heavy frame filtering; dexterous-to-parallel-jaw retargeting is imperfect.
notes: Ablations: both robot overlay and co-training indispensable; performance scales logarithmically with edited video amount.

name: AVID
resolvedTitle: AVID: Learning Multi-Stage Tasks via Pixel-Level Translation of Human Videos
org: UC Berkeley (BAIR)
problem: Robotic RL for long-horizon tasks needs reward specification and manual resets; imitation from human video is hindered by human-robot appearance differences.
keyIdea: Translate human demo frames into robot images with CycleGAN, use translated stage-completion 'instruction images' to train per-stage success classifiers as rewards, and learn each stage with latent-space model-based RL that automatically resets and retries.
architecture: CycleGAN (unpaired human->robot translation); structured latent variable model (VAE-style encoder, learned latent dynamics, CNN decoder) trained by ELBO; per-stage classifiers on latent states; MPC with CEM planning in latent space; human key-press success confirmation.
inputs: Raw robot RGB images; human demonstration videos
outputs: Robot arm actions from latent MPC-CEM planner
actionRepr: Low-level actions chosen by CEM model-predictive control in learned latent space (not a learned policy)
trainingData: Coffee making: 30 human demos (900 images) + 500 random human images; cup retrieval: 20 demos (600 images) + 300 random; plus random robot data; ~20 min human time per task

headlineResults.comparedTo: BC from teleop 90%; TCN 0%; full-video ablation 0%

whatChangedVsParent: Handles embodiment change via learned pixel-level translation and learns stage-wise with automatic resets instead of learning from full videos or needing robot demos.
limitations: Requires a separate CycleGAN per task/scene with human and robot data collection; stage instruction frames are manually selected; human key-press feedback needed during RL.
notes: RSS 2020. Evaluated on Sawyer arm.

name: Moto
resolvedTitle: Moto: Latent Motion Token as the Bridging Language for Learning Robot Manipulation from Videos
org: The University of Hong Kong; Tencent ARC Lab; CUHK; UC Berkeley
problem: Action-labelled robot data is costly; prior video pre-training for robotics focused on static frame-level features rather than motion, which is closer to low-level actions and hardware-agnostic.
keyIdea: Learn discrete latent motion tokens between consecutive frames with a VQ-VAE-style tokenizer, pre-train a GPT to autoregressively predict motion tokens from an initial frame and instruction, then co-fine-tune with action query tokens to output real robot actions.
architecture: Latent Motion Tokenizer: M-Former (8 queries, 4 layers) encoder + ViT decoder, VQ codebook of 128 codes (dim 32); Moto-GPT: 12-layer GPT (hidden 768) backbone with a 2-layer action head added at fine-tuning; action query tokens appended after motion tokens each step.
inputs: Static-camera RGB frame(s) + language instruction
outputs: Latent motion tokens (pre-training); low-level robot actions via action head (fine-tuning)
actionRepr: Discrete latent motion tokens (8 per frame pair, 128-code codebook) as pre-training target; continuous low-level actions from action query tokens (3 queries/step on SIMPLER, 5 on CALVIN)
trainingData: Pre-train: 109k OXE trajectory videos (SIMPLER/real) or CALVIN ABC play videos; optional 105k SSV2 human videos. Fine-tune: 73k RT-1 trajectories; 18k CALVIN trajectories; 90 real teleop demos

headlineResults.benchmark: SIMPLER Move Near with SSV2 human video

whatChangedVsParent: Autoregressively pre-trains on unsupervised latent motion tokens rather than future pixels (GR-1), then co-fine-tunes motion-token and action prediction jointly.
limitations: Latent motion tokenizer mainly trained on robot videos; human-video pre-training is preliminary (SSV2 subset); scaling data and improving fine-tuning left for future work.
notes: ICCV 2025 version. Pre-training uses no action labels. Log-likelihood of Moto-GPT separates successful/failed/random trajectories (possible reward signal).

name: IGOR
resolvedTitle: IGOR: Image-GOal Representations are the Atomic Control Units for Foundation Models in Embodied AI
org: Microsoft Research; Tsinghua University
problem: Interaction data is orders of magnitude scarcer than video; prior latent-action work (Genie, LAPO) targets 2D games rather than a shared action space across humans and many robots.
keyIdea: Compress the visual change between an image and its goal into a discrete latent action shared by humans and robots, use it to label internet video, and train a foundation policy (predicts latent actions from text+images) and a world model (generates frames from latent actions).
architecture: Latent action model: ViT + spatio-temporal transformer IDM with readout tokens and VQ, single-frame ViT FDM with different random crops; world model: Open-Sora-based rectified-flow ST transformer conditioned on latent actions; foundation policy: ST-transformer with ViT + text encoder; low-level policy head fine-tuned on robot actions.
inputs: Video frames + text task description
outputs: Latent actions (policy); future frames (world model); continuous robot actions via low-level policy
actionRepr: Discrete latent actions (N VQ tokens per image-goal pair) decoded by a low-level policy into chunks of continuous robot actions per latent action
trainingData: ~2.8M clips: ~0.8M robot trajectories (OXE mixture, RT-1 held out) + ~2.0M filtered human videos (Ego4D, SSV2, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA)

headlineResults.benchmark: SIMPLER Google robot tasks, fine-tuned on 1% of RT-1
headlineResults.value: higher or equal to from-scratch low-level policy (reported in figure only)
headlineResults.comparedTo: same low-level policy without latent actions

whatChangedVsParent: Moves latent-action learning from 2D games to open-world human+robot video with a single-frame FDM and crop augmentation for semantically consistent latent actions.
limitations: Cannot separate visual changes caused by the agent from other agents or camera shake (mitigated by filtering ~40% of open-world video and stabilising); world model not yet fine-tuned to robot action spaces.
notes: Mostly qualitative evaluation (motion migration between videos, human-to-robot). Latent actions shown more predictive of robot translation than rotation/gripper on RT-1.

name: UniVLA (Bu et al.)
resolvedTitle: UniVLA: Learning to Act Anywhere with Task-centric Latent Actions
org: The University of Hong Kong; OpenDriveLab; AgiBot
problem: VLAs depend on action-labelled data from a single embodiment; prior latent-action methods (LAPA, IGOR) reconstruct raw pixels and so encode task-irrelevant dynamics like camera shake and other agents.
keyIdea: Learn task-centric latent actions in DINOv2 feature space with a two-stage, language-conditioned latent action model that first captures task-irrelevant dynamics and then a separate task-centric codebook; pretrain a VLM to predict these tokens and decode them with a small action head per embodiment.
architecture: Latent action model: spatial-temporal transformer IDM encoder + spatial transformer FDM decoder over DINOv2 patch features, T5 instruction conditioning, VQ codebooks (|C|=16, N=4 tokens). Policy: Prismatic-7B (SigLIP+DINOv2, LLaMA-2) with vocabulary extended by latent-action tokens; attention-pooling action decoder; LoRA fine-tuning; past latent actions fed back as history.
inputs: Third-person RGB image + language instruction (+ history latent actions)
outputs: Latent action tokens decoded into embodiment-specific action chunks
actionRepr: 4 discrete latent action tokens (codebook 16) per ~1 s interval, decoded by a lightweight head into continuous action chunks
params: 7B (Prismatic-7B); ~123M trainable in post-training incl. 12.6M action head (abstract text also cites a 10.8M decoder)
trainingData: OXE subset (manipulation), GNM (navigation), Ego4D human video; 960 A100-hours pretraining
whatChangedVsParent: Unlike LAPA/IGOR, predicts in DINOv2 feature space and uses language to disentangle task-centric from task-irrelevant latent actions.
limitations: Fixed latent-action granularity and codebook size; evaluated mainly on single-arm manipulation (dual-arm/dexterous untested); relies on language annotations for disentanglement.
notes: RSS 2025. Fig. 1 reports CALVIN, SimplerEnv and real-world bars vs OpenVLA (e.g. 17.5 -> 47.1, 38.3 -> 81.7) but axis-to-benchmark mapping not verified from text; omitted. Distinct from 'UniVLA (Wang et al.)' unified VLA with world-model tokens.

name: CLAP
resolvedTitle: CLAP: Contrastive Latent Action Pretraining for Learning Vision-Language-Action Models from Human Videos
org: Tsinghua University; Astribot; HKU; MIT
problem: Latent action models trained by visual reconstruction entangle extraneous visual factors (background, deformation) and are not aligned with the robot's physical action space, limiting skill transfer from human video.
keyIdea: Quantize robot action chunks into an executable token vocabulary (Act-VAE), then contrastively align visual transitions from human and robot video to that vocabulary (VD-VAE) so human videos get physically grounded pseudo action tokens.
architecture: Act-VAE (transformer VQ-VAE, 150M) over 14-D bimanual action chunks; VD-VAE (200M) inverse dynamics over frozen DINO features with action codebook (frozen) + environment codebook, SigLIP contrastive loss and EMA teacher for human samples; CLAP-NTP autoregressive VLM policy; CLAP-RF rectified-flow action head with Knowledge Matching regularization.
inputs: RGB observation + language instruction
outputs: Subtask text + action tokens (NTP) or continuous action chunks (RF)
actionRepr: Discrete Act-VAE action tokens (8 codes per arm) for NTP; chunk of 32 continuous 14-D bimanual EE actions (pos, Euler, gripper per arm) via rectified flow for CLAP-RF
trainingData: Robot demos (Astribot S1, AgiBot) + Ego4D human videos (pseudo-labelled); CLAP-NTP pretraining ~3,800 A100-hours
whatChangedVsParent: Grounds the latent action codebook in robot actions and aligns video transitions contrastively instead of defining latent actions only by visual reconstruction.
limitations: Generalizes to novel objects in known tasks but not to entirely new tasks from human video alone; hand-to-gripper morphology gap causes latent ambiguity; multi-stage training pipeline.
notes: Resolved to arXiv 2601.04061 (v2 June 2026); code at github.com/LinShan-Bin/OpenCLAP. Name is ambiguous; confirm this is the CLAP the surveys cite. Task success numbers on LIBERO/real bimanual tasks not captured in retrieved pages.

name: EgoVLA
resolvedTitle: EgoVLA: Learning Vision-Language-Action Models from Egocentric Human Videos
org: UC San Diego; UIUC; MIT; NVIDIA
problem: Robot-data collection needs hardware and operators, capping scale and diversity; human egocentric video offers far richer scenes and tasks.
keyIdea: Pretrain a VLA on egocentric human video to predict future wrist poses and MANO hand parameters, treating the human action space as a unified space convertible to a humanoid via IK and hand retargeting, then fine-tune on a small set of robot demos.
architecture: NVILA-2B VLM backbone (SigLIP vision) with 30 action query tokens and a 300M transformer action head (6 layers, hidden 1536); proprioception via MLPs; MANO fingertip-fitting for robot->human retargeting and a small MLP for keypoints->robot hand joints.
inputs: 6 egocentric RGB frames (1 s history, 384x384), language instruction, wrist and hand pose proprioception
outputs: Future bimanual wrist poses (translation + rot6D) and MANO hand parameters (15 PCA), converted to robot arm IK and hand joint commands
actionRepr: Chunk of 30 future steps (1 s at 30 Hz) of bimanual wrist pose + 15-D MANO hand PCA per hand
trainingData: Ego-centric human dataset from HOI4D, HOT3D, HoloAssist (1/10 sampled) and TACO, ~500K image-action pairs; 100 robot demos per task for fine-tuning
controlRateHz: 30 Hz (benchmark control); actions predicted over 30 Hz horizon

headlineResults.benchmark: Ego Humanoid Manipulation Benchmark short-horizon, seen backgrounds

whatChangedVsParent: Pretrains the VLA on human egocentric hand/wrist actions in a shared MANO-based action space instead of robot action data.
limitations: Requires human data with hand and wrist pose annotations; cannot be deployed without fine-tuning on a moderate amount of robot data.
notes: Introduces the Ego Humanoid Manipulation Benchmark (Isaac Lab, Unitree H1 + Inspire hands, 12 tasks, 25 background combos). Evaluation is simulation-only. Data-mixture ablation: more diverse human data improves results.

name: H-RDT
resolvedTitle: H-RDT: Human Manipulation Enhanced Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
org: Tsinghua University; Horizon Robotics
problem: Cross-embodiment robot pre-training suffers from heterogeneous action spaces and still-limited robot data; prior human-video methods (EgoMimic, HAT) are small-scale and tied to one embodiment.
keyIdea: Pre-train a diffusion-transformer policy on large-scale egocentric human data (EgoDex) using a 48-D hand action representation, then fine-tune to each robot by re-initializing only modular state/action adapters and decoders.
architecture: 2B diffusion transformer (LLaMA-3 style, RMSNorm, SwiGLU) with DINOv2 + SigLIP vision encoders and T5-XXL language via cross-attention, AdaLN flow-time embedding, modular MLP action encoder/decoder; trained with flow matching, ODE sampling at inference.
inputs: Multi-view RGB, proprioceptive state, language instruction
outputs: Action chunk in target robot's action space (e.g. 14-D for dual 7-DoF arms)
actionRepr: Action chunk via flow matching; pretraining target is 48-D human action (bilateral wrist pos+6D rot = 18, fingertip positions = 30)
trainingData: EgoDex: 338K+ trajectories, 829 h, 194 tasks (pretraining); robot fine-tuning on RoboTwin 2.0 and real platforms (few-shot 1-5 demos per task in some experiments)
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces RDT's cross-robot pretraining with human-hand pretraining on EgoDex, switches to flow matching, and adds modular re-initialized action adapters for embodiment transfer.
limitations: No explicit limitations section in retrieved text; relies on datasets with accurate 3D hand-pose annotation (EgoDex).
notes: Abstract claims +13.9% (sim) and +40.5% (real) over training from scratch. Project page states code and pretrained models released.

name: HaMeR
resolvedTitle: Reconstructing Hands in 3D with Transformers
org: UC Berkeley; University of Michigan; New York University
problem: Monocular 3D hand mesh recovery was brittle in-the-wild (occlusion, egocentric views, hand-object interaction) and benchmarked mainly on controlled studio data.
keyIdea: Scale both data (many 2D/3D-annotated hand datasets combined) and model capacity (ViT-H backbone + transformer decoder) in a simple HMR-style regressor of MANO parameters.
architecture: ViT-H image backbone followed by a transformer decoder head (single query token cross-attending to ViT tokens) regressing MANO pose (48), shape (10) and camera translation.
inputs: RGB hand crop
outputs: MANO pose/shape parameters, 3D mesh (778 vertices), 21 joints, weak camera translation
trainingData: Combination of FreiHAND, HO-3D, DexYCB, InterHand2.6M, Panoptic, AssemblyHands (3D) plus COCO-WholeBody, Halpe, MPII-NZSL (2D); also introduces HInt (40.4K annotated hands from New Days, VISOR, Ego4D)
whatChangedVsParent: Applies HMR2.0's fully transformer design and data scaling to hands, replacing ResNet-based FrankMocap-style regressors.
limitations: Single-frame method (no temporal model); HInt only benchmarks 2D reprojection for in-the-wild images; egocentric performance improves further when trained on HInt, indicating limited egocentric training data.
notes: CVPR 2024. Perception tool, not a policy: widely used for hand-pose extraction in OKAMI, ZeroMimic, Masquerade.

name: CoTracker
resolvedTitle: CoTracker: It is Better to Track Together
org: Meta AI; University of Oxford (VGG)
problem: Point trackers (PIPs, TAPIR, PIPs++) track points independently, ignoring strong dependencies between points on the same object, hurting accuracy under occlusion.

trainingData: Synthetic TAP-Vid-Kubric (24-frame sequences); PointOdyssey for that benchmark

limitations: Online causal sliding-window design is disadvantaged on long slow-motion videos (RGB-S evaluated at reduced frame rate); trained only on synthetic data.
notes: ECCV 2024 version. Perception tool used in OKAMI (keyframe segmentation) and point-track based policies (e.g. ATM, Track2Act).

name: Real-time grasp detection (Redmon & Angelova)

org: University of Washington; Google Research
topicName: Grasping: analytic grasps to grasp-anything models

outputs: Oriented grasp rectangle {x, y, theta, h, w} for a parallel-plate gripper (optionally object class)
actionRepr: Single planar grasp rectangle (5-D) per image or per grid cell; not a closed-loop policy
trainingData: Cornell Grasping Dataset: 885 images of 240 objects, heavy augmentation (3000 examples per image)

name: OWG (open-world grasping)

org: University of Groningen

name: DexDiffuser

name: Dexterous Grasp Transformer

notes: CVPR 2024. Code at github.com/iSEE-Laboratory/DGTR. Limitation re complete point cloud is from problem formulation, not an explicit limitations section.

outputs: Action chunk of 26-D actions: 9-D relative end-effector position (3D) and orientation (6D) + 17-D hand joint position targets
actionRepr: Chunk of 26-D actions (relative EE pose 9-D + 17 absolute hand joint targets) generated by a diffusion U-Net
trainingData: 9,290 human demonstrations across 93 diverse environments collected with DexWild-System, co-trained with a smaller teleoperated robot dataset (xArm + LEAP Hand V2 Advanced); optimal robot:human ratio 1:2

headlineResults.benchmark: Cross-task pouring (no pour robot data), in-the-wild extreme

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces robot teleoperation as the main data source with glove-based in-the-wild human data aligned in observation and action space, and co-trains with a small robot dataset.
limitations: Still needs some teleoperated robot data; human demos rarely include error recovery so policies struggle to recover; uses only vision and kinematics (no tactile), limiting contact-rich tasks.
notes: Paper reports cross-embodiment improvement '5.8x' in abstract. Cross-hand transfer LEAP V2 Advanced to original LEAP: 65.3% vs 13.3%. Code and hardware instructions released on dexwild.github.io. Bimanual tasks: 68.1% vs 13% robot-only.

name: EgoDex
resolvedTitle: EgoDex: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Large-Scale Egocentric Video
org: Apple
problem: There is no internet-scale corpus for dexterous manipulation; teleoperation does not scale and existing egocentric datasets (e.g. Ego4D) lack native 3D hand pose annotation and do not focus on manipulation.
keyIdea: Collect a passively scalable egocentric dataset with Apple Vision Pro, where on-device SLAM and calibrated cameras give precise 3D tracking of every hand joint at recording time, and define benchmarks for hand trajectory prediction.
architecture: Dataset + benchmark paper. Baseline imitation policies (e.g. Dec+BC transformer decoder, default 200M params; 500M variant tested) predict hand trajectories from images, skeletal poses and language; a goal-image-conditioned (inverse dynamics) variant is also benchmarked.
inputs: Egocentric 1080p RGB video, skeletal joint poses, natural language description (optionally goal image)
outputs: Future hand trajectories (action chunks)
actionRepr: 48-D per step: for each hand, 3-D wrist position + 6-D wrist orientation + 3-D positions of 5 fingertips; predicted in chunks (horizon e.g. 30 or 90 frames) as relative trajectories in the current camera frame
params: 200M default baseline (500M variant gave identical results)
trainingData: 829 hours of 30 Hz 1080p egocentric video, 90M frames, 338k episodes, 194 tabletop tasks; 25 joints per hand plus upper body, camera intrinsics/extrinsics, confidence values, GPT-4-refined language annotations; 2.0 TB

headlineResults.comparedTo: 22% lower avg and 53% lower final distance than without goal

whatChangedVsParent: Scales egocentric video with paired 3D hand tracking from EgoMimic's ~4 hours (wrist-only) to 829 hours with full 25-joint hand annotation.
limitations: Scene diversity is limited to tabletop environments (focus is behavioural diversity); the embodiment gap to robots must still be bridged (no robot policy trained in the paper).
notes: ICLR 2026. Dataset publicly released at github.com/apple/ml-egodex. Abstract says 829 hours; Figure 1 rounds to '800 hours', '300K episodes', '200 tasks', '500 objects'. Dataset rather than method paper.

name: TriFinger
resolvedTitle: TriFinger: An Open-Source Robot for Learning Dexterity
org: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems (Tübingen); New York University
problem: Real-world dexterous manipulation research is hindered by the high cost of experimentation: robot hands are expensive, fragile and need human supervision, so there is no shared real-robot benchmark.
keyIdea: An inexpensive (~$5000), robust, open-source three-finger platform with 1 kHz torque control and software safety checks that allows unsupervised operation, including deep RL from scratch on hardware.
architecture: Hardware platform: three 3-DoF fingers built from the open-source quadruped actuator modules (brushless DC motors, transparent transmission, soft fingertips), aluminium frame, three high-speed cameras; robot-agnostic C++/Python real-time software with action queue + observation history interface and PyBullet simulation.
inputs: Proprioception (joint angles, velocities, torques) at 1 kHz; images from three cameras typically at 100 Hz
outputs: 9-D desired joint torque vector
actionRepr: 9-D joint torques at 1 kHz (not a learned policy)
parents: Open Dynamic Robot Initiative quadruped (Grimminger et al. 2020)
whatChangedVsParent: Reuses the 3-DoF open quadruped leg as a finger and adds a larger shared workspace, soft tips, cameras and safety-checked software for unsupervised learning.
limitations: Paper's experiments are illustrative rather than state of the art; each finger has only 3 DoF; the paper names the lack of standardized real benchmarks as motivation but the platform itself was a first step.
notes: Experiments: 1 kHz optimal control (cube pick with force optimization + impedance control), deep RL from scratch on hardware, throwing, writing, durability. Hardware and software are open-source. Later used as the basis of the Real Robot Challenge (not stated in this paper).

name: DexJoCo
resolvedTitle: DexJoCo: A Benchmark and Toolkit for Task-Oriented Dexterous Manipulation on MuJoCo
org: CASIA (NLPR & MAIS); SJTU; MBZUAI; PKU & Galbot; CUHK
problem: Existing dexterous benchmarks focus on hand-only in-hand manipulation or simple pick-and-place, lack high-quality human demonstrations, and lack standardized language instructions and data formats for modern VLA models.
keyIdea: A MuJoCo benchmark of 11 functionally grounded arm+hand tasks (tool use, bimanual, long-horizon, reasoning) with 1.1K human teleop demonstrations from a low-cost glove+tracker system, plus trajectory replay under domain randomization for robustness evaluation.
architecture: Benchmark: Franka arm + Allegro hand in RoboSuite-style scenes (MuJoCo Menagerie assets); data collected with Rokoko glove + HTC Vive tracker and an MLP retargeting network trained with direction/coverage/flatness/pinch/collision losses. Evaluates ACT, Diffusion Policy (DP-T, DP-C), pi0.5 and GR00T N1.5 (LoRA fine-tuned).
inputs: Third-person RGB, end-effector translation (3), quaternion (4), hand joint angles (16), optional language
outputs: 22-D (single arm) or 44-D (dual arm) absolute actions
actionRepr: Absolute EE translation (3) + rotation vector (3) + 16 hand joints = 22-D per arm, predicted as action chunks (DP-T 45, DP-C 43, ACT 100, pi0.5 30, GR00T 50)
trainingData: 1.1K human demonstration trajectories (100 per task, 11 tasks)
whatChangedVsParent: Moves from RL-oriented hand-only in-hand benchmarks to arm+hand, task-oriented, human-demonstration-based imitation/VLA evaluation with language and domain randomization.
limitations: Policies remain sensitive to visual variation and struggle with fine-grained interaction, bimanual coordination and long horizons; pretraining and multi-task training do not consistently help; VLAs show limited language generalization (paper's findings about evaluated models).
notes: Code at dexjoco.github.io. Assembly bimanual task near 0% for all policies. Inference latency on RTX 4090: ACT 7 ms, DP-C ~38-42 ms, DP-T ~34-36 ms, pi0.5 ~84-85 ms, GR00T 80-90 ms. Benchmark rather than method paper.

name: DexVerse
resolvedTitle: DexVerse: A Modular Benchmark for Multi-Task, Multi-Embodiment Dexterous Manipulation
org: UNC-Chapel Hill; The University of Hong Kong; UC Berkeley
problem: Existing dexterous benchmarks are limited in task/data diversity, embodiment coverage or controllable visual variation, hindering study of cross-task and cross-embodiment generalization.
keyIdea: A configuration-driven Isaac Lab benchmark with 100 dexterous tasks in 8 categories, 3 arms x 6 hands, configurable visual variation, parallel RL environments and a VR-teleoperated multimodal demonstration dataset.
architecture: Benchmark on Isaac Lab manager-based environments with task-family templates; arms: Franka Research 3, UR10e, xArm 7; hands: Sharpa Wave, WUJI, Shadow, Inspire, Allegro, LEAP. Apple Vision Pro teleop via CloudXR with dex-retargeting. Baselines: Diffusion Policy, DP3, OpenVLA, pi0.5.
inputs: Proprioception, RGB, depth, point cloud, simulator state (9 observation groups incl. contact forces)
outputs: Arm + hand joint targets (embodiment-specific)
trainingData: 3,180 VR-teleoperated demonstrations (56 single-goal tasks x 55 demos: 50 Shadow Hand + 1 per other hand; 5 long-horizon tasks x 20); baselines trained on 950 episodes (19 tasks x 50)
