whatChangedVsParent: Broadens dexterous benchmarks to 100 tasks with multiple arm-hand embodiments, controllable visual variation, demonstrations and parallel RL in a single platform.
limitations: Simulation-only in current release; demonstrations concentrated on the Shadow Hand; future work on real-robot transfer and broader cross-embodiment standardization.
notes: Name resolution: a title search first returned BiDexHD (2410.02477) - wrong paper; correct paper found via discovery. Findings: internet-scale VLA pretraining did not give a dexterous advantage; different method wins each skill family.

name: Jan et al. deformable RL
resolvedTitle: Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning for Deformable Object Manipulation
org: Imperial College London
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Deformable (cloth) manipulation lagged rigid manipulation; model-based approaches need heavy engineering and no prior work had tested whether deep RL policies for deformable objects could be learned in simulation and transferred to the real world.
keyIdea: Train cloth-manipulation policies entirely in simulation with an improved DDPG (seeded with 20 demonstrations, sparse reward) and heavy domain randomization, then deploy zero-shot on a real robot.
architecture: DDPG extended with prioritized replay, N-step returns, DDPGfD demo seeding and priority boost, behaviour cloning loss with Q-filter, reset-to-demonstration, TD3 twin critics, asymmetric actor-critic (actor sees RGB + joint angles, critics see full state), and auxiliary outputs (cloth corners, targets). Conv encoder (3x3, 32 filters) + FC layers.
inputs: 84x84 RGB image + joint angles and gripper position (actor); full low-dim state for critic at training time
outputs: 4-D action: 3-D end-effector velocity + gripper velocity
actionRepr: Continuous 4-D (EE velocity xyz + gripping velocity), gripper rotation fixed; Kinova Mico 7-DoF arm
trainingData: RL in PyBullet with domain randomization; 20 demonstrations per task; ~80k transitions; ~24 h per run on one GTX TITAN
whatChangedVsParent: Combines nine DDPG extensions (Rainbow-style) and applies them with domain randomization to deformable cloth tasks for the first sim-to-real transfer.
limitations: Deformable simulation support in PyBullet was rudimentary (fake grasp anchors); real cloth was stiffer than simulated, causing crumpling; grasp failures dominate; policy remained very sensitive to camera position.
notes: CONFLICT: survey P01 cites this as 'Jan et al. [262]', but Jan is the first author's given name; the first author is Jan Matas (Matas, James, Davison, CoRL 2018). Survey describes it as 'modified DDPG ... zero-shot sim-to-real via domain randomization', which matches.

name: DMfD
resolvedTitle: Learning Deformable Object Manipulation from Expert Demonstrations
org: University of Southern California
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Deformable manipulation is high-dimensional with hard-to-extract state; pure IL suffers covariate shift and is bounded by expert quality, while pure RL explores too slowly.
keyIdea: An asymmetric actor-critic LfD method that uses expert data three ways: pre-filling the replay buffer, an advantage-weighted loss augmented with an entropy/exploration term, and probabilistic reference state initialization.
architecture: Off-policy SAC/AWAC-style asymmetric actor-critic; for images, CNN actor with random-crop augmentation, critics receive image + state.
inputs: State (reduced state) or RGB images
outputs: End-effector actions for SoftGym pickers / robot arm
trainingData: SoftGym rope and cloth tasks plus two new Cloth Fold Diagonal environments; up to 8k expert episodes (ablation: 4k ~ 8k >> 1k); 1M steps (image) / 3M steps (state)

headlineResults.benchmark: Cloth Fold Diagonal Unpinned, real Franka (10 rollouts)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds an entropy-based exploration term to AWAC's advantage-weighted loss, extends it to images, and invokes reference state initialization probabilistically.
notes: RA-L 2022; code at github.com/uscresl/dmfd. Limitations not explicitly stated in the retrieved text.

name: DefGoalNet
resolvedTitle: DefGoalNet: Contextual Goal Learning from Demonstrations for Deformable Object Manipulation
org: University of Utah; NVIDIA
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Shape servoing methods (e.g. DeformerNet) require an explicit goal shape, obtained by laborious engineering or by manually deforming the object, which is impractical in many applications.
keyIdea: Learn to predict the goal point cloud of a deformable object from its current point cloud and a task-context point cloud using a few human demonstrations, then feed it to a pretrained shape-servoing policy.
architecture: Encoder-decoder: two identical PointConv encoders (3 layers) for current and contextual point clouds, concatenated to a feature vector, then FC decoder (256, 256, 3N) producing a 512-point goal cloud; trained with Chamfer + EMD loss. Output goes to DeformerNet (unchanged) which computes end-effector actions.
inputs: Current object partial-view point cloud + contextual point cloud (e.g. kidney, tube, human hand)
outputs: Goal point cloud (512 points); downstream DeformerNet outputs SE(3) end-effector displacement(s)
trainingData: Simulated demos in Isaac Gym (dVRK arm) with 10/100/1000/10000 demos for retraction, 10/100/1000 for tissue wrapping; 20 real human demos (15 train) for hand-conditioned retraction
whatChangedVsParent: Removes DeformerNet's need for a hand-specified goal shape by learning contextual goal prediction from demonstrations.
limitations: Assumes success is defined solely by the final object shape; trajectories that matter for success are not modeled (future work: sequences of goal shapes).
notes: ICRA 2024. Code and data published on project site.

name: MPD
resolvedTitle: Movement Primitive Diffusion: Learning Gentle Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects
org: Friedrich-Alexander-University Erlangen-Nürnberg; Karlsruhe Institute of Technology
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Policy learning for robot-assisted surgery needs data-efficient, multimodal methods that produce gentle, smooth motions on delicate deformable tissue; existing diffusion IL methods output jagged action sequences.
keyIdea: Combine score-based diffusion imitation learning with Probabilistic Dynamic Movement Primitives (ProDMPs): the denoiser outputs ProDMP weights that are decoded into smooth action sequences with guaranteed initial position/velocity.
architecture: Score-based generative model (EDM/BESO-style Probability Flow ODE, Euler solver) whose inner model is a transformer (6 layers, 4 heads, 256-d) outputting ProDMP weights (3 basis functions); ProDMP decoder maps weights to trajectories. Images encoded by ResNet-18 (no pretraining, 128-d).
inputs: Previous 3 observations: task state vectors or 256x256 RGB images (random-cropped to 224)
outputs: Action sequence of 12 steps (0.1 s spacing), decodable at arbitrary frequency (e.g. 0.005 s for real robot)
actionRepr: Chunk of 12 task-space actions (instrument DoFs: articulation, rotations/translations about remote center of motion) encoded as ProDMP weights via diffusion; decoded to high-frequency smooth trajectories
trainingData: Human demos via Xbox controller at 10 Hz: GLT 90, RT 200, BTM 150, LL 135 (sim, LapGym); BTM-RW 200, GLT/RT/LL-RW 45 each (real, xArm7 + laparoscopic graspers)

headlineResults.metric: success rate / motion quality / data efficiency
headlineResults.value: outperforms Diffusion Policy (DP-C, DP-T) and BESO

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces direct action-sequence output of diffusion policies with ProDMP-weight output, giving smooth, multimodal, high-frequency trajectories with guaranteed initial conditions.
limitations: Limited performance outside the demonstration distribution (e.g. failure to recover when rope bent severely in RT-RW); IL with no feedback-based continued training.
notes: RA-L 2024. Survey P01 describes MPD as 'generates movement primitives with diffusion models', consistent. Exact per-task success rates not captured in retrieved pages; see paper figures/tables.

name: DeformGS
resolvedTitle: DeformGS: Scene Flow in Highly Deformable Scenes for Deformable Object Manipulation
org: Carnegie Mellon University; Stanford University; NVIDIA; National University of Singapore; TU Munich
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Dense 3D tracking (scene flow) of highly deformable objects like cloth is hard due to self-occlusion, shadows and weak texture; prior dynamic Gaussian methods drift under large deformation.
keyIdea: Learn canonical 3D Gaussians plus a continuous deformation field (HexPlane neural-voxel encoding + MLP predicting position, rotation, shadow scalar) from multi-view video, with physics-inspired isometry and momentum regularizers and learned per-Gaussian dynamic masks.
architecture: Built on 4D Gaussian Splatting: canonical Gaussians, HexPlane voxel encoding, deformation MLP (outputs position, rotation, shadow; not opacity or scale), differentiable rasterizer; masks from SAM + XMem.
inputs: Time-synchronized multi-view RGB images with known intrinsics/extrinsics (+ noisy masks)
outputs: Dense 3D trajectories of scene points (scene flow) and novel-view renderings
trainingData: Per-scene optimization; 6 synthetic Blender cloth scenes (100 views x 40 timesteps = 4,000 images each); real: Robo360 dataset (17-20 training views)

headlineResults.value: 55.8% average vs state of the art

whatChangedVsParent: Adapts 4D-GS for tracking: fixes opacity/scale over time, adds shadow modeling, isometry + momentum regularization and learned dynamic masks.
limitations: Requires multiple synchronized calibrated cameras; not real-time; some Gaussians wander off; sensitive to regularization hyperparameters.
notes: WAFR 2024 per survey. Perception method (not a policy); robotics use shown as real2sim digital twin and task-relevant keypoint tracking for grasping.

name: Foresightful Affordance
resolvedTitle: Learning Foresightful Dense Visual Affordance for Deformable Object Manipulation
org: Peking University (CFCS); BAAI
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Multi-step deformable manipulation (rope, cloth) is prone to greedy actions that lead to local optima; RL struggles with complex states and imitation needs hand-crafted expert policies.
keyIdea: Learn dense per-pixel picking and placing affordance maps whose supervision includes estimated state 'values' (aggregated from future affordance, Bellman-style) so actions avoid local optima; trained stage-by-stage with self-supervised 'Fold to Unfold' reversed data collection.
architecture: Two fully convolutional networks M_pick and M_place producing dense affordance maps (placing conditioned on pick point); multi-stage training plus Integrated Systematic Training.
inputs: Top-down visual observation of the object
outputs: Pick point and place point (pick-and-place primitive)
actionRepr: Pick-and-place primitive: argmax pixels of dense pick and place affordance maps (no rotation)
trainingData: Self-supervised interaction data in simulation (DeformableRavens, SoftGym) collected via Fold to Unfold; real-world fine-tuning with Fold-to-Unfold data on Franka Panda
whatChangedVsParent: Extends one-step dense affordance to multi-step deformable manipulation by supervising with state values that account for future actions.
notes: ICCV 2023. Limitations not explicitly stated in retrieved text.

name: APS-Net
resolvedTitle: Learning Efficient Robotic Garment Manipulation with Standardization
org: Tongji University
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Garment unfolding methods focus on maximizing coverage and ignore standardization (shape and orientation alignment), which makes downstream folding, ironing and packing harder.
keyIdea: A self-supervised Action-Primitive Selector Network that chooses between dual-arm dynamic fling and single-arm pick-and-place via spatial action maps, trained with a factorized reward of coverage, IoU and keypoint distance, plus a spatial action mask and shoulder-keypoint Action Optimized Module.
architecture: Three encoders (coverage, IoU, keypoint rewards), each with fling and p&p decoder heads producing spatial value maps over 80 rotated/scaled copies of the input (16 rotations x 5 scales); spatial action mask filters invalid actions; DeepLabv3 keypoint detector + heuristic folding downstream.
inputs: Overhead RGB-D image (128x128), garment segmented with Grounded-SAM in real world
outputs: Primitive choice (fling or p&p) and parameters <x, y, theta, w> giving grasp/pick/place points
actionRepr: Spatial action map over pixels x 16 discrete rotations x 5 scales; fling = two grasp points + fixed fling trajectory, p&p = pick and place points
trainingData: Simulation (Cloth Action Gym on SoftGym/NVIDIA FleX, CLOTH3D meshes): 2000 training tasks + 50 test per garment category; 100k optimization steps; keypoint detector on 10,000 sim images fine-tuned on 1,100 real images

headlineResults.benchmark: Real long-sleeve unfolding (15 trials, dual UR5)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds garment standardization (IoU and keypoint rewards) and primitive selection between fling and pick-and-place, rather than coverage-only reward.
notes: ICML 2025. CONFLICT: survey P01 reference [328] lists authors starting 'Feng Luan, Shaoqiang Meng, ...', but the arXiv paper's first author is Changshi Zhou (Feng Luan second). Survey describes APS-Net as ranking 'standardized folding and flattening trajectories guided by affordance heatmaps'; the paper describes spatial action (value) maps selecting fling vs pick-and-place with heuristic keypoint-based folding. Limitations not explicitly stated.

name: GenDOM
resolvedTitle: GenDOM: Generalizable One-shot Deformable Object Manipulation with Parameter-Aware Policy
org: The University of Tokyo; Osaka University
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Deformable manipulation policies typically need hundreds of real demonstrations per object because dynamics differ across objects; Real2Sim2Real approaches still need much real data and are object-specific.
keyIdea: Condition the policy on physical parameters (Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio), train it on diverse simulated objects, and at test time estimate those parameters from one real demonstration via gradient-based optimization in a differentiable simulator matching point-cloud grid densities.
architecture: Simple MLP policy conditioned on task input and (Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio); Real2Sim parameter estimation in PlasticineLab-based differentiable MPM simulator using L1 loss between 64^3 grid densities of real and simulated point clouds (two RealSense D435i, xArm 7).
inputs: Goal coordinate (task-dependent) + estimated material parameters
outputs: Release coordinate (rope reaching), momentary action (rope casting) or acceleration parameter A (cloth spreading)
actionRepr: Single low-dimensional action parameter per task (not a closed-loop visuomotor policy)
trainingData: Simulated demonstrations with randomized Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio (e.g. 800-sample dataset for cloth); one real-world demonstration per new object for parameter estimation
whatChangedVsParent: Uses estimated material parameters as policy conditioning inputs rather than only as simulator parameters, enabling one-shot generalization across objects.
notes: ICRA 2024. Tasks are single-action dynamic manipulation (reach, cast, spread). Limitations not explicitly stated in retrieved text.

name: DeformNet
resolvedTitle: DeformNet: Latent Space Modeling and Dynamics Prediction for Deformable Object Manipulation
org: Tsinghua University (Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School; IIIS)
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Deformable objects (plasticine, clay, towels, grains) need a general state representation and accurate dynamics prediction; 2D CNN latents miss 3D deformation, and GNNs need predefined particle structure.
keyIdea: Encode multi-view RGB-D point clouds with PointNet into split deformation and appearance latents supervised by a conditional NeRF decoder, learn latent dynamics with a recurrent state-space model (RSSM), and plan with gradient-augmented iCEM MPC.
architecture: PointNet encoder -> latent split (deformation e_d for density, appearance e_a for color) -> conditional NeRF decoder; RSSM world model (Dreamer-V2 style) with reward predictor; gradient-based iCEM planning.
inputs: Multi-view RGB-D images (8 cameras in sim) converted to point clouds; goal observation
outputs: Parameterized end-effector actions (e.g. push start/end, pinch pose and gripper width)
actionRepr: Task-specific low-dimensional parameterized primitives (e.g. {x0,y0,x1,y1} for push/write, {x,y,z,rz,dg} for pinch) chosen by MPC
trainingData: ManiSkill2 MPM soft-body simulation: 100 random trajectories per task initially, plus iCEM-generated samples; 6 tasks (Push, Pinch, Write, Pile, Transport, Poke); real UR5 deployment
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces 2D-CNN latents in NeRF-RL/Dreamer with a PointNet-encoded 3D latent split into deformation and appearance parts, used by an RSSM world model for MPC.
notes: ICRA 2024. Assumes deterministic initial observation for all simulated tasks. Limitations not explicitly captured in retrieved text. Not to be confused with DeformerNet (Hu et al. 2019 / Thach et al.).

name: DoughNet
resolvedTitle: DoughNet: A Visual Predictive Model for Topological Manipulation of Deformable Objects
org: Columbia University; Stanford University
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Manipulating elastoplastic objects like dough involves topological changes (splitting, merging, changing genus) that prior predictive models, which treat deformation only as geometric change, cannot predict.
keyIdea: A Transformer-based denoising autoencoder encodes objects of varying topology as a set of latent codes decodable into per-component occupancy plus genus, and a visual predictive model does autoregressive set-to-set prediction of geometry and topology purely in latent space, used by a CEM planner.
architecture: Encoder: point-feature embedding + cross-attention to 256 learned queries (+ pooled code) -> 257x512 latent set + self-attention stack; dynamics: 4 stacks of self/cross-attention conditioned on end-effector geometry points at t and t+1; decoder: cross-attention interpolation + K+1 component occupancy masks and genus classifier. Trained only on MPM-simulated data.
inputs: Single partial RGB-D point cloud of initial state + end-effector (tool) geometry and planned trajectory
outputs: Predicted per-step geometry (component occupancy) and topology (number of components, genus); planner outputs tool choice, in-plane pose and opening width
actionRepr: Manipulator represented as sampled surface points at two timesteps; CEM samples in-plane translation, rotation and gripper type (narrow/regular/wide)
trainingData: Synthetic MPM-based simulation data with topological checking operations; real evaluation on 60 recorded scenes (15 frames each) with UR5 + WSG50 and Play-Doh

headlineResults.benchmark: Topological change detection from latent distance

whatChangedVsParent: Moves from particle/GNN geometric prediction (RoboCook) to latent set prediction that explicitly models topology (components and genus).
limitations: Human-defined goals with irregular geometry (fingers, curved palms) are only approximately reachable with the three flat robot tools; reconstruction from noisy partial views can be too wide.
notes: Survey P01 describes it as 'CEM for tool selection and manipulation', consistent. Preprint version (under review) read; final venue per survey: ECCV 2024.

name: MoMa
resolvedTitle: Causal Policy Gradient for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation (Causal MoMa)
org: The University of Texas at Austin; Sony AI
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Mobile manipulation RL faces a large action space and multi-objective composite rewards; prior work splits base and arm actions by hand, preventing whole-body motion and requiring domain knowledge.
keyIdea: Automatically discover causal dependencies between action dimensions and reward terms (via conditional mutual information tests on random exploration data), then use a causal policy gradient in PPO where each action dimension's advantage uses only causally related reward terms.
architecture: Two-step: action-reward causal discovery producing a binary bi-adjacency matrix; modified PPO with factored (causal) advantages. Policy inputs are proprioceptive/task vector + LiDAR scan.
inputs: Proprioceptive and task-related vector (25-D HSR / 27-D Fetch) + LiDAR scan (270-D HSR / 220-D Fetch); end-effector goal
outputs: Whole-body continuous actions for base, arm, head (and gripper)
actionRepr: Continuous whole-body velocity-level actions (base + arm + head)
trainingData: RL in Minigrid (discrete) and iGibson (Fetch, Toyota HSR); sim2sim to Gazebo; zero-shot sim-to-real on Toyota HSR

headlineResults.benchmark: Real HSR, dynamic goal + dynamic obstacles (9 runs)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces hand-coded action-reward factorization with automatically discovered causal structure for variance-reduced policy gradients.
limitations: Cannot handle very long-horizon causal dependencies (sparse rewards, assumption A4); reactive policy may fail to plan long trajectories around local minima; images are first converted to an end-effector goal rather than consumed directly.
notes: RSS 2023. CONFLICT/ambiguity: survey P01 Table 7 lists 'MoMa [268]' under mobile RL; reference [268] is this paper (Causal MoMa by Hu, Stone, Martín-Martín), not a method literally named 'MoMa'.

name: MOMA-Force
resolvedTitle: MOMA-Force: Visual-Force Imitation for Real-World Mobile Manipulation
org: ByteDance Research
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Learning-based mobile manipulation lacks action accuracy and robustness in contact-rich tasks (the 'last-centimeter' error can cause large forces), while classical control needs extensive tuning.
keyIdea: Imitate both kinematic actions and expert wrenches: retrieve the nearest expert frame in a pretrained visual embedding space to get action and target wrench, then track the pose with admittance whole-body control that regulates contact wrench.
architecture: Non-parametric retrieval (VINN-style) using a pretrained iBOT visual encoder with cosine similarity over expert frames; PID-based force (admittance) control producing pose corrections perpendicular to motion; QP whole-body controller (qpOASES) for base + arm.
inputs: Arm-mounted camera RGB image; force-torque sensor wrench; end-effector pose
outputs: SE(3) relative end-effector action, gripper action {-1,0,1}, target 6-D wrench, termination flag
actionRepr: Retrieved relative SE(3) EE pose delta + target wrench, executed via admittance whole-body control (differential-drive base + 7-DoF Kinova Gen2)
trainingData: 30 human expert demonstrations per task (6 tasks), collected by carrying the end-effector with HTC VIVE tracking and FT sensor

headlineResults.benchmark: 6 real contact-rich household tasks (10 trials each)

whatChangedVsParent: Extends retrieval-based visual imitation (VINN) to also imitate wrenches and executes via admittance whole-body control.
limitations: Failures mainly from inaccurate action prediction (visually similar frames make retrieval ambiguous, causing grasp failures); not evaluated on perturbed backgrounds or novel objects.
notes: IROS 2023. Visual encoder comparison: iBOT MSE lower than CLIP and MVP.

name: Skill Transformer
resolvedTitle: Skill Transformer: A Monolithic Policy for Mobile Manipulation
org: Georgia Tech; Meta AI (FAIR)
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Long-horizon mobile manipulation (rearrangement) is hard for end-to-end monolithic policies, while modular skill-chaining suffers hand-off errors and cannot adapt the skill sequence to disturbances.
keyIdea: A single causal-transformer policy trained end-to-end by imitation that first infers the current high-level skill and then predicts whole-body low-level actions conditioned on that skill, keeping modularity without separate hand-offs.
architecture: ResNet-18 depth encoder + MLP proprio encoder -> 512-d tokens; Skill Inference causal transformer (2 layers, context 30) outputs one-hot skill; Action Inference causal transformer consumes observation, previous action and skill tokens; total 16M parameters; auxiliary receptacle-prediction head during training.
inputs: 256x256 head depth image, joint angles, holding state, base egomotion, 3D start and goal positions of object
outputs: Skill ID (pick, place, navigate, open drawer, open fridge) + 12-D action: 7 arm delta joint positions, 2 base velocities, 3-way gripper (suction) state
actionRepr: Per-step whole-body action: 7-D delta arm joints (PD-controlled) + 2-D base velocity + discrete gripper command
trainingData: 10,000 demonstrations generated by an RL-trained M3 skill policy with oracle planner in Habitat 2.0 (Rearrangement Challenge train split: 50,000 object configurations across 63 scenes)

headlineResults.comparedTo: modular and end-to-end baselines (Mono RL, Decision Transformer, M3)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds an explicit skill-inference module to a transformer sequence policy so a monolithic policy retains skill modularity.
limitations: Geometric task specification makes it hard to identify the target object after its receptacle is manipulated (objects shift when drawers open), limiting success on hard rearrangement; simulation only.
notes: ICCV 2023. Exact absolute success rates not captured in retrieved pages.

name: TidyBot++
resolvedTitle: TidyBot++: An Open-Source Holonomic Mobile Manipulator for Robot Learning
org: Princeton University; Stanford University; Dexterity
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Mobile manipulation imitation learning lacks suitable research hardware: commercial bases are expensive, large and nonholonomic, which makes teleoperation and learning harder.
keyIdea: An inexpensive (~$5.4k) open-source holonomic base using powered casters (modified FRC swerve modules with caster offset) plus a WebXR mobile-phone teleoperation interface for easy demonstration collection.
architecture: Hardware: four powered-caster modules on a T-slot aluminum frame, Kinova Gen3 7-DoF arm, Intel NUC; powered-caster vehicle kinematics (Holmberg & Khatib) for base control in position mode. Policies: Diffusion Policy per task.
inputs: Camera images + robot state (for diffusion policies)
outputs: Base pose (x, y, theta) targets and arm end-effector commands
actionRepr: Diffusion Policy action sequences with base controlled in position mode (x, y, theta)
trainingData: Phone-teleoperated demos: 100 for open fridge, 50 for each other task (1-2 h per 50 episodes)

headlineResults.benchmark: Real apartment household tasks (10 trials each)
headlineResults.value: Open fridge 10/10, Wipe countertop 9/10, Load dishwasher 7/10, Take out trash 10/10, Load laundry 7/10, Water plant 6/10

headlineResults.benchmark: Wipe countertop, holonomic vs differential drive (50 demos each)

whatChangedVsParent: Provides a holonomic, low-cost, arm-agnostic open-source base with phone teleop, versus nonholonomic differential-drive platforms like Mobile ALOHA or Stretch.
limitations: Base does not backdrive well due to high steering friction (steer gear ratio 12.8, caster offset 14 mm).
notes: CoRL 2024. Hardware and software open-sourced (tidybot2.github.io). Odometry drift <1 cm per meter and <1 deg per 360 deg; 8 h runtime; 60 kg payload estimate.

name: Waste sorting RL (Herzog)
resolvedTitle: Deep RL at Scale: Sorting Waste in Office Buildings with a Fleet of Mobile Manipulators
org: Everyday Robots; Robotics at Google
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Deploying end-to-end deep RL for manipulation in the real world requires bootstrapping exploration, broad generalization to novel objects, and scalable data collection, which had not been shown on a large real-world task.
keyIdea: A data flywheel combining offline RL (PI-QT-Opt) on real data from a robot fleet, simulation bootstrapping with RetinaGAN sim-to-real, scripted policies, multi-task curriculum, LSTM memory and object masks from a vision system to sort recyclables, compost and landfill.
architecture: PI-QT-Opt (QT-Opt Q-learning with CEM action selection + predictive information auxiliary), recurrent (LSTM) critic, image + object-mask (ShapeMask-based) inputs; critic has 1.43M learnable parameters.
inputs: 640x512 RGB image + proprioception (tool height, target tool pose, gripper aperture) + object masks
outputs: 10-D action: end-effector 3D position and orientation deltas, gripper closedness, base x, y, yaw deltas, terminate
actionRepr: Whole-body delta pose targets (arm or base motion) chosen at 1 Hz via CEM over the learned Q-function
trainingData: 9,527 hours of robot experience over 24 months, 23 robots in 3 office buildings; 540k episodes in 'robot classrooms' (20 robots) plus 32.5k deployment episodes, plus simulation

headlineResults.comparedTo: no LSTM 69.57%, sim only 67.39%, no mask 58.7%, sim only + poor bootstrap 45.66%

headlineResults.benchmark: Intermediate eval in office buildings vs classrooms

whatChangedVsParent: Scales QT-Opt-style real-world RL from grasping to a deployed multi-building sorting task with sim bootstrapping, curriculum, memory and vision-system masks.
limitations: Still relies heavily on experience from controlled robot classrooms rather than deployment data; deployment data throughput is variable and low.
notes: Survey name 'Herzog' matches first author Alexander Herzog. Everyday Robots platform is not publicly available.

name: M-EMBER
resolvedTitle: M-EMBER: Tackling Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation via Factorized Domain Transfer
org: Stanford University; The University of Texas at Austin
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Long-horizon visuomotor mobile manipulation needs both perceptual and compositional generalization; real-world data cannot cover the activity distribution, and existing sim-to-real techniques target navigation or stationary manipulation.
keyIdea: Factorize a BEHAVIOR activity into primitive visual skills, reinforcement-learn each skill in photorealistic, domain-randomized iGibson with per-skill success detectors, and compose them with a symbolic planner at test time.
architecture: Per skill: VAE image encoder, success detector (learned binary reward) and Q-function; actions via CEM over Q-values (no latent dynamics model, unlike EMBER); success detectors also ground observations to symbolic state for a symbolic planner.
inputs: N camera images at 112x112 (+ in-view and masked object images) and 19 robot joint angles
outputs: Small changes in pose of two end-effectors (6D) and base (3D), plus head, torso and gripper joint positions
actionRepr: Delta end-effector and base poses selected by CEM on learned Q-functions
trainingData: RL in iGibson with photorealistic rendering and 14-dimension domain randomization; real TIAGo robot with cameras at 3 Hz

headlineResults.benchmark: Real cleaning kitchen activity, 3 kitchens (30 trials, 5 skills)
Ablation: without photorealism / with 50% domain randomization

whatChangedVsParent: Drops EMBER's latent dynamics model in favor of Q-function CEM, uses per-skill VAEs and adds skill factorization with symbolic planning for long-horizon mobile tasks.
limitations: Domain gap remains immense, reflected in low success rates and limited settings/activities; cannot use depth input; LiDAR only used as fail-safe.
notes: Authors explicitly acknowledge empirical weakness of their solution.

name: DribbleBot
resolvedTitle: DribbleBot: Dynamic Legged Manipulation in the Wild
org: MIT (Improbable AI Lab)
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Legged robot soccer previously required flat surfaces, external cameras or static dribbling; dribbling in the wild needs adapting to terrain-dependent ball dynamics and perceiving the ball with onboard cameras.
keyIdea: Sim-to-real RL of a whole-body dribbling policy commanded by global-frame ball velocity, with a ball drag domain randomization model, fisheye-camera YOLOv7 ball detection, and a separate fall-recovery policy.
architecture: PPO MLP policy [512, 256, 128] with a [256, 128] state-estimation regressor; inputs 15-step history; YOLOv7 fine-tuned on 254 fisheye images (TensorRT, 30 Hz); recovery MLP policy with finite-state switching.
inputs: Proprioception history, ball position (from fisheye detection), global yaw, commanded ball velocity, gait timing variables
outputs: 12 joint position targets (PD controller)
actionRepr: 12-D joint position targets at 50 Hz
trainingData: Isaac Gym, 4096 environments, 7 billion timesteps (~48 h on one RTX 3090); randomized robot and ball dynamics including drag coefficient 0-1.5

headlineResults.benchmark: Scripted real dribbling trajectory, full system
headlineResults.value: 4/4 on tile, grass, sand; 3/4 snow; 2/4 curb; 0/4 ramp
headlineResults.comparedTo: no YOLO fine-tuning 0/4 on all terrains

whatChangedVsParent: Extends sim-to-real legged locomotion RL to dynamic object manipulation (ball dribbling) with perception and ball-dynamics randomization.
limitations: Slow turning response; perception sensitive to bright sunlight/glare; imprecise at high speed on low-drag terrain; no geometry awareness (steep slopes, stairs, poles, walls).
notes: Unitree Go1 with two 210-degree fisheye cameras and onboard Jetson Xavier NX; code released per project page.

name: VBC
resolvedTitle: Visual Whole-Body Control for Legged Loco-Manipulation
org: UC San Diego
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Legged robots with arms could use legs to extend manipulation workspace, but prior whole-body loco-manipulation needed teleoperation or kept a fixed body height, and end-to-end visual learning is infeasible.
keyIdea: A hierarchical framework: an RL low-level whole-body policy tracks base velocity and end-effector pose commands; a high-level privileged RL teacher proposes commands and is distilled via DAgger into a depth-image visuomotor student; all trained in simulation and transferred zero-shot.
architecture: Low-level: RL MLP policy outputting 12 leg joint targets with arm commanded via IK from end-effector pose; high-level teacher: MLPs over PointNet++ shape latent (1024-d) + object pose + proprio; student: CNN over segmented depth + masks (TrackingSAM) from front and wrist cameras.
inputs: Segmented depth images and masks from two RealSense D435 cameras + proprioception
outputs: High-level: 9-D command (6-D gripper pose increment, 2-D base linear/yaw velocity, gripper open/close); low-level: 12 leg joint targets + IK arm joints
actionRepr: Hierarchical: high-level 9-D command at ~6-8 Hz; low-level leg joint targets at 50 Hz; arm IK at 800 Hz
trainingData: Simulation only (34 YCB-derived objects in 7 categories); zero real-world data; hardware Unitree B1 + Z1 arm (19 DoF)

headlineResults.metric: success rate (e.g. cup / square box / drill)

headlineResults.benchmark: Real pick-up of 14 objects at 0.0/0.3/0.5 m
headlineResults.value: higher than teleoperated-base baseline at all heights (baseline fails at 0.0 and 0.3 m)
headlineResults.comparedTo: Teleoperated default Unitree controller + stationary high-level policy

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces joint-space arm prediction of Deep WBC with end-effector pose + IK and adds an autonomous visual high-level policy distilled from a privileged teacher.
limitations: Visual tracking loss (most common failure), beak-like Z1 gripper, imprecise depth on reflective objects, compounding error across hierarchy; target object must be manually annotated before autonomous run.
notes: CoRL 2024. In Table 1 the teacher's square-box value is printed as '81.87 ± 0.02' (likely a typo for 0.8187) - not used above.

name: GAMMA
resolvedTitle: GAMMA: Graspability-Aware Mobile MAnipulation Policy Learning based on Online Grasping Pose Fusion
org: Peking University (CFCS); BAAI; Galbot; Tongji University
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: RL mobile-manipulation agents must observe a target while approaching it; prior scene priors (visibility, reachability) give only indirect guidance for grasping, and per-frame grasp predictions are noisy and redundant under occlusion.
keyIdea: Introduce 'graspability' as a scene prior: fuse per-frame predicted grasp poses online into a temporally consistent set, encode it as an RL state, and use its quantity/quality as an observe-to-grasp reward.
architecture: GSNet predicts grasp poses from gripper-camera depth RoI; an online grasping-pose fusion module (64^3 voxel grid, angle-threshold merging, cluster-based outlier removal) keeps fused poses; a PointNet-style encoder turns them into a graspability state fed with visual and joint states to a PPO policy.
inputs: Head and gripper RGB-D, fused grasp poses (graspability state), base/arm joint state, target object location
outputs: 3-DoF base SE(2)-type velocity, 6-DoF residual arm joint adjustment, 1-DoF gripper switch
actionRepr: Per-step continuous base velocity (3-DoF) + residual arm joint deltas (6-DoF) + binary gripper command, RL policy (PPO)
trainingData: RL in Habitat 2.0 (ReplicaCAD scenes, YCB objects; 1000 standard + 1000 self-built cluttered episodes) and Isaac Gym; ~36 A100 GPU-hours
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces reachability/visibility priors with an explicit, online-fused grasp-pose set (graspability) used both as state and reward.
limitations: Authors list highly dynamic environments and long-horizon tasks as future work; evaluated on single-object grasping.
notes: Name ambiguity: a different 2023 paper 'GAMMA: Generalizable Articulation Modeling and Manipulation for Articulated Objects' exists; this card assumes the mobile-manipulation GAMMA given the E3 (mobile manipulation) topic. Project page pku-epic.github.io/GAMMA; paper says episode data will be released. P01 Table 7 lists GAMMA [274] under Quadrupedal/RL, consistent with this paper (Unitree B1+Z1 robot dog).

name: Human2LocoMan
resolvedTitle: Human2LocoMan: Learning Versatile Quadrupedal Manipulation with Human Pretraining
org: Carnegie Mellon University; Google DeepMind; Bosch Center for AI
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Scalable, versatile manipulation for quadrupeds is hard: collecting robot data on high-DoF legged platforms is costly and the human-quadruped embodiment gap blocks use of human data.
keyIdea: Collect aligned human and LocoMan robot data via an XR (Apple Vision Pro) teleop system in a unified frame, pretrain a modular cross-embodiment Transformer on human data and finetune on a small amount of robot data.
architecture: Modularized Cross-embodiment Transformer (MXT): embodiment- and modality-specific tokenizers (cross-attention; ResNet image features, MLP for proprio) and detokenizers around a shared encoder-decoder Transformer trunk; whole-body controller (null-space + QP) tracks torso/EEF targets.
inputs: Egocentric main stereo image, optional wrist images, body/head pose, EEF poses, EEF-to-body pose, gripper state
outputs: Body (torso/head) 6D pose, EEF 6D poses, gripper actions
actionRepr: Action chunks of h future pose targets per modality (body pose, EEF poses, gripper), L1 behavior cloning loss
trainingData: New LocoMan robot dataset plus corresponding human dataset for six household tasks (unimanual and bimanual modes); human data for pretraining, robot data for finetuning
whatChangedVsParent: Unlike HPT's aggregated tokenizers, MXT splits tokenizers/detokenizers per fine-grained modality and treats the human as a separate embodiment for pretraining rather than co-training with normalization.
limitations: Teleop has a learning curve (head-to-torso control unintuitive); validated only on LocoMan; relies on per-task pretrain-finetune rather than multi-task co-training.
notes: Paper states code, hardware and data are open-sourced (human2bots.github.io); release of trained weights not explicitly verified.

name: WildLMa
resolvedTitle: WildLMa: Long Horizon Loco-Manipulation in the Wild
org: UC San Diego; MIT
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: In-the-wild quadruped mobile manipulation needs skills that generalize across objects/environments, long-horizon execution and manipulation beyond pick-and-place; modular methods are limited to pick-and-place and end-to-end policies generalize poorly.
keyIdea: Combine VR whole-body teleoperation (via a learned whole-body controller) with a library of language-conditioned ACT skills using frozen CLIP + MaskCLIP image-text cross-attention, composed by an LLM planner over a hierarchical scene graph.
architecture: WildLMa-Skill: ACT with frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 (MaskCLIP reparam) features and text cross-attention maps, plus an autonomous 'end' signal; low-level RL whole-body controller from VBC; WildLMa-Planner: GPT-4 coarse-to-fine planner over waypoint graph.
inputs: Head (Azure Kinect) and wrist (RealSense D405) RGB, robot state, task-specific text queries
outputs: Base velocity and end-effector pose commands (to whole-body controller), gripper, termination signal
actionRepr: ACT action chunks of base velocity + 6-DoF EE pose commands; policy at 10 Hz, whole-body controller aggregation at 50 Hz
trainingData: 30-60 VR teleop demonstrations per skill on Unitree B1 + Z1

headlineResults.benchmark: Real-world skills (tabletop grasp, button press, ground grasp)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds CLIP/MaskCLIP text-conditioned cross-attention and learned termination to ACT, and uses VBC's learned whole-body controller for VR teleop and deployment.
limitations: Planner relies on manually annotated waypoints/nodes; long-horizon success remains modest (3/10 shelf rearrangement); each skill trained separately.
notes: Whole-body control reported to reduce demonstration cost by 26.9% vs decoupled strategy.

name: QUAR-VLA
resolvedTitle: QUAR-VLA: Vision-Language-Action Model for Quadruped Robots
org: Westlake University; Zhejiang University
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Quadruped learning treated vision-only (goal image) and language-only tasks separately, limiting autonomy and fine-grained instruction following; no large quadruped VLA dataset existed.
keyIdea: Define the QUAR-VLA task and train QUART, an MLLM fine-tuned to output discretized high-level quadruped commands (velocity, gait, posture) from image + instruction, with the QUARD sim+real dataset and sim-real co-training.
architecture: QUART: pretrained Fuyu-8B decoder-only VLM; action bins mapped onto integer tokens (RT-2-style symbol tuning); detokenized commands passed to a low-level locomotion policy.
inputs: Single first-person RGB image + natural-language instruction
outputs: 11-dim high-level command (vx, vy, wz, 3 gait params, frequency, body height, pitch, foot width, foot height) + terminate flag
actionRepr: 12 discrete tokens, each continuous dim discretized into 256 bins (RT-2 style), autoregressive
trainingData: QUARD: ~259K simulated episodes + ~3K real-world episodes (perception, navigation, whole-body manipulation-like tasks)
whatChangedVsParent: Applies RT-2-style action tokenization to quadrupeds with a high-level command space (velocity, gait, body pose) instead of arm end-effector actions.
limitations: Limited data scale/diversity (no complex terrain or long-horizon tasks); 2 Hz inference too slow for tasks needing high-frequency control; sim-to-real handled only by co-training.
notes: Published at ECCV 2024. 'Manipulation' tasks are mostly whole-body (e.g. unload, crawl) rather than arm manipulation.

name: GeRM
resolvedTitle: GeRM: A Generalist Robotic Model with Mixture-of-experts for Quadruped Robot
org: MiLAB, Westlake University
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Imitation-learned VLA models for quadrupeds are limited by costly expert data and by demonstration quality; scaling RL policy parameters usually hurts performance.
keyIdea: Train a transformer VLA with offline RL (Q-Transformer-style CQL) on both demonstrations and auto-collected failed trajectories, and use a sparse Mixture-of-Experts decoder to raise capacity at fixed inference cost.
architecture: Universal Sentence Encoder text embedding -> FiLM-conditioned ImageNet EfficientNet-B3 over 6-image history -> TokenLearner -> 8-layer decoder-only Transformer with MoE FFNs (8 experts, top-2 routing) outputting discretized action tokens used as autoregressive Q-values.
inputs: History of 6 first-person images + language instruction
outputs: 12-dim quadruped command: vx, vy, wz, 3 gait params, frequency, body height, pitch, foot width, foot height, terminate
actionRepr: Per-dimension discretized action tokens (vocab 256) with autoregressive Q-functions (Q-Transformer), executed by a Walk-These-Ways low-level controller
trainingData: QUARD demonstrations (8,610 successful trajectories) + QUARD-Auto auto-collected sub-optimal data (2,766 failed trajectories used; QUARD-Auto totals ~257K trajectories in Isaac Gym), 5 task types / 99 sub-tasks; demo:sub-optimal ratio 75.69%:24.31%
whatChangedVsParent: Adds sparse MoE layers to a Q-Transformer-style VLA and trains on mixed-quality quadruped data rather than demonstrations only.
limitations: Evaluated only in simulation; real-world deployment and broader task categories left as future work.
notes: Paper claims GeRM outperforms RT-1, GeRM w/o RL and GeRM w/o MoE across all tasks (400 trajectories per model over 99 sub-tasks), but the per-task numeric table was not in the retrieved pages, so no headline numbers recorded. Reports an 'emergent' dynamic adaptive path-planning skill.

name: Soft DAgger
resolvedTitle: Soft DAgger: Sample-Efficient Imitation Learning for Control of Soft Robots
org: The BioRobotics Institute, Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna; National University of Singapore
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Imitation learning for soft robots suffers from compounding errors, while existing remedies (RL teacher agents or human intervention) are too sample-inefficient for real soft hardware.
keyIdea: Replace the RL teacher in DAgger/policy distillation with a learned dynamic behavioral map (DBM) of the soft arm that predicts corrective actuation for expert target states, and distill it into a student policy online.
architecture: DBM: LSTM network (2x128 units) mapping current/previous task-space states, next target state and previous pressures (66 inputs) to 6 chamber pressures, trained on 5 min of motor babbling; student policy trained with distillation loss; two variants (with/without periodic DBM re-optimization via an instantaneous buffer).
inputs: Target state from expert demonstration, current and previous 3D tip positions of the two modules
outputs: Pneumatic pressures for 6 chambers
actionRepr: Per-step continuous pressure commands (6-D) at 20 Hz
trainingData: 6,000-observation (300 s) motor-babbling dataset for the DBM; kinesthetic demonstrations from 14 human experts writing letters (B, M, Z, S, C), the word BRAIR and a star pattern in 3D

headlineResults.comparedTo: average RL approaches and a continuous IL algorithm, respectively

whatChangedVsParent: Uses a learned dynamics map of the soft arm, not an RL agent or human, as the DAgger teacher/supervisor.
limitations: Results are only qualitative; suited to reproducing demonstrations qualitatively rather than precise trajectory tracking; higher accuracy would need extra exploration, trading off sample efficiency.
notes: Published in MDPI Sensors 23(19):8278 (2023); not on arXiv. Read via PMC full text (PMC10574889). Platform: two-module pneumatic soft arm with Vicon motion-capture feedback.

name: KineSoft
resolvedTitle: KineSoft: Learning Proprioceptive Manipulation Policies with Soft Robot Hands
org: Carnegie Mellon University; Bosch Center for AI
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Imitation learning for underactuated soft hands lacks demonstration interfaces and meaningful state representations; strain signals during kinesthetic demonstration differ from those during tendon-actuated execution.
keyIdea: Collect demonstrations by kinesthetically deforming the soft hand, represent state as a sim-trained mesh shape estimate from embedded strain sensors, learn a diffusion policy over shape deformations, and track them with a shape-conditioned controller.
architecture: Proprioception network (signal encoder + deformation-field decoder over finger mesh vertices) trained on SOFA FEM data with CMA-ES domain alignment; diffusion policy with MLP shape encoder + DP3 point-cloud encoder; low-level shape-conditioned P-controller projecting vertex error onto tendon servo directions.
inputs: Estimated finger mesh vertices (from 4 strain sensors per finger), wrist RGB-D point cloud, end-effector pose
outputs: Changes in finger mesh vertices (target shapes) and end-effector pose
actionRepr: Diffusion-generated trajectory of vertex displacements + EE pose deltas, tracked by a 100 Hz shape controller driving tendon servos
trainingData: 50 kinesthetic demonstrations per task (per baseline description) on a three-finger MOE soft hand; large simulated SOFA dataset for shape estimation
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces raw strain signals with a geometric mesh-shape state so kinesthetic demonstrations and tendon-actuated execution share one representation.
limitations: No explicit limitations section in retrieved pages; paper frames the demonstration-execution gap (sensor signals under manual deformation vs tendon actuation) as the core challenge. Validated on one soft hand (MOE, 3 fingers) over six tasks.
notes: Paper says videos and code will be available at kinesoft-policy.github.io upon final decision.

name: SS-ILKC
resolvedTitle: Sensor-Space Based Robust Kinematic Control of Redundant Soft Manipulator by Learning
org: The University of Manchester
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Kinematic control of redundant soft manipulators breaks under unknown external loads, actuator saturation from poor null-space regulation, and confined environments.
keyIdea: Learn control in sensor space (spring-length targets) with a multi-goal RL policy trained in a sim-to-real pre-calibrated simulator for open space, plus GAIL from sparse physical demonstrations for confined spaces.
architecture: Multi-goal sensor-space RL (actor-critic) producing reference sensor signals tracked by a PID pressure controller; GAIL discriminator (with gradient penalty) provides learned reward for confined-space tasks; lightweight NN maps simulated to real EE poses for pre-calibration.
inputs: Current spring-sensor (inductance) readings and state-action history, goal 6D end-effector pose
outputs: Reference sensor (spring-length) values, converted to chamber pressures by PID
actionRepr: Per-step sensor-space setpoints (continuous) tracked by PID
trainingData: Simulation rollouts for open space; sparse expert demonstration poses recorded with motion capture (e.g. 16 points for path following)

headlineResults.comparedTo: w/o S2R & demo 21.01 mm; w/o demo 11.59 mm

headlineResults.benchmark: Path following with unknown loads (35-500 g)

whatChangedVsParent: Moves from gradient-based sensor-space IK to learned multi-goal RL with sim-to-real pre-calibration and GAIL demonstrations for confined spaces.
limitations: Demonstrated on a single three-section pneumatic manipulator; confined-space tasks need physical demonstrations and task-specific RL training.
notes: Acronym expands to 'Sensor-Space Imitation Learning Kinematic Control'. Robot: 3-section, 9-chamber pneumatic continuum arm (~4.7 kg) with conductive-spring inductive sensors. P01 survey describes it as combining multi-objective RL with adversarial IL; paper says 'multi-goal'.

name: BiGym
resolvedTitle: BiGym: A Demo-Driven Mobile Bi-Manual Manipulation Benchmark
org: Dyson Robot Learning Lab
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Existing benchmarks either use dense shaped rewards (unsuited to long-horizon tasks) or planner-generated demonstrations that are unnaturally narrow; performance on RLBench-style single-arm tasks is plateauing.
keyIdea: A MuJoCo benchmark of 40 mobile bi-manual household tasks on a Unitree H1 humanoid with sparse rewards and 50 human VR-teleoperated (noisy, multi-modal) demonstrations per task, for both IL and demo-driven RL.
architecture: Benchmark (not a policy): MuJoCo/dm_control scenes, Unitree H1 with two Robotiq 2F-85 grippers, 3 RGB-D cameras (head, both wrists), Gymnasium API, whole-body and bi-manual (floating-base) action modes, 46 reusable assets.
inputs: RGB and depth from head/left-wrist/right-wrist cameras (default 84x84), proprioception (76-D whole-body, 64-D bi-manual)
outputs: Joint-position actions: 23-D whole-body or 16-D bi-manual (arms + 4-D floating base deltas + grippers), absolute or delta
trainingData: 50 human VR demonstrations per task (40 tasks), recorded at 500 Hz and down-sampleable to 20-500 Hz
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces motion-planner demos and dense rewards (RLBench, HumanoidBench) with human-collected multi-modal demos and sparse rewards on a mobile bi-manual humanoid.
limitations: Parallel grippers only (dexterous hands left for future); RL baselines run with common hyperparameters, not tuned per task; tasks are simulation-only.
notes: Benchmark paper; baselines evaluated: BC, ACT, Diffusion Policy (IL) and DrQ-v2, AWAC, IQL, CQN (demo-driven RL). Per-task numbers are in Appendix C, not retrieved. Code released on the project website. Simulator runs ~400-1400 FPS single process. P01 Table 2 lists 2K demos (40 tasks x 50 demos), consistent.

name: SoftGym
resolvedTitle: SoftGym: Benchmarking Deep Reinforcement Learning for Deformable Object Manipulation
org: Carnegie Mellon University
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: No standard benchmark existed for deformable object manipulation; RL benchmarks assumed low-dimensional, fully observable state and rigid objects.
keyIdea: Open-source Gym benchmark on NVIDIA FleX with 10 rope, cloth and fluid tasks (SoftGym-Medium, -Hard, -Robot) and systematic evaluation of state-, image- and dynamics-oracle methods.
architecture: Benchmark: FleX particle/position-based dynamics; abstract 'picker' action space (sphere grippers) for rope/cloth, direct cup actuation for fluids; SoftGym-Robot uses Sawyer/Franka.
inputs: Ground-truth particle state, hand-defined reduced state, or RGB images depending on setting
outputs: Per-picker (dx, dy, dz, pick flag) actions (4n-D for n pickers); cup motion for fluid tasks
trainingData: 1000 task variations per task (800 train / 200 eval); algorithms trained for 1e6 steps (PlaNet 5e5)
whatChangedVsParent: First standardized RL benchmark covering high-dimensional, partially observable deformable objects (rope, cloth, fluid).
limitations: Image-based RL far below state-oracle performance; ground-truth rewards assumed; SoftGym-Robot release depended on NVIDIA permission; direct sim-to-real transfer of policies still expected to be challenging.
notes: CoRL 2020. Baselines: CEM-MPC (dynamics oracle), SAC on full/reduced state, CURL-SAC, DrQ, PlaNet, Wu et al. pick-and-place. Results reported only as normalized-performance plots, so no verbatim numbers recorded. Code open-sourced.

name: DaXBench
resolvedTitle: DaXBench: Benchmarking Deformable Object Manipulation with Differentiable Physics
org: National University of Singapore; Sea AI Lab
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Existing differentiable deformable-object simulators each cover one material type, and no general benchmark compared planning, IL and RL methods (with and without analytic gradients) across rope, cloth and liquid.
keyIdea: A JAX-based differentiable, parallelizable simulator (DaX) covering liquid, rope, cloth and elasto-plastic materials with Gym-wrapped tasks, including long-horizon low-level-control tasks, to benchmark eight DOM methods.
architecture: Benchmark: DaX simulator using MLS-MPM for liquid/rope and mass-spring for cloth, lazy active-region updates and gradient checkpointing; tasks with macro-actions (pick-and-place/push) and low-level velocity control.
inputs: Particle/mesh states (Transporter also tested with RGB)
outputs: Macro-actions (6-D start/end gripper positions) or low-level Cartesian velocity controls
trainingData: Expert demonstrations for IL; RL/planning in simulation
whatChangedVsParent: Adds differentiability, multi-material coverage and multi-GPU parallel simulation that SoftGym (non-differentiable) and PlasticineLab (single material) lack.
limitations: Differentiable-physics RL suffers from poor exploration on macro-action tasks and depends on smooth optimization landscapes; sim-to-real only checked qualitatively on a Push-Rope task.
notes: ICLR 2023. Code at github.com/AdaCompNUS/DaXBench. Benchmarked: CEM-MPC, Diff-MPC, Diff-CEM-MPC, PPO, SHAC, APG, Transporter, ILD. Task naming in RL table is 'Wipe Rope' vs 'Whip-Rope' elsewhere in paper.

name: ODYSSEY
resolvedTitle: ODYSSEY: Open-World Quadrupeds Exploration and Manipulation for Long-Horizon Tasks
org: Zhejiang University; Zhejiang University of Technology; CUHK-Shenzhen
topicName: Deformable, bimanual, mobile and soft manipulation
problem: Language-guided long-horizon mobile manipulation lacks planners grounded in egocentric perception, generalizable manipulation, and whole-body control that keeps both mobility and end-effector precision on rough terrain; no long-horizon mobile manipulation benchmark existed.
keyIdea: Combine a coarse-to-fine VLM/LLM planner (GPT-4.1 over an instance scene graph; Qwen2.5-VL-72B for geometry-constrained contact/pose) with a single RL whole-body policy trained with terrain-invariant end-effector sampling, plus a new benchmark.
architecture: Perception: LiDAR+RGB instance graph (RAM++, Grounding-SAM/MobileSAM, MaskCLIP); task planner decomposes into navigate/pick/place/push/pull/drag; local VLM predicts contact point + EE orientation under axis/surface constraints; two-stage RL unified whole-body policy outputs joint positions.
inputs: Language instruction, head RGB, wrist RGB-D, LiDAR; policy uses proprioception, gravity vector, height scan, base-velocity and EE pose commands
outputs: Joint position targets for 12-DoF Go2 legs and 6-DoF Arx5 arm
actionRepr: Per-step joint position targets from an RL whole-body policy at 50 Hz (PD at 200 Hz); high level emits atomic actions and EE target poses
trainingData: RL in simulation over diverse terrains; benchmark with 100+ assets, 10 scenes, 8 long-horizon tasks (246 indoor + 58 outdoor variations) plus 4 ARNOLD tasks
whatChangedVsParent: Unlike RoboDuet's dual locomotion/manipulation policies with base-centric sampling, uses one unified policy with terrain-invariant EE sampling that generalizes to stairs/rough terrain.
limitations: Real-world grasping of small objects sometimes fails due to EE tracking and perception errors; failures from gripper misalignment and localizing slim/occluded handles; objects beyond reach cause control failures.
notes: Hardware: Unitree Go2 + ARX5 arm. PerAct outperforms ODYSSEY on seen Pick Object; ODYSSEY stronger on novel splits. Real-world evaluation was qualitative (two tasks, five objects).

name: ExBody
resolvedTitle: Expressive Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Robots
org: UC San Diego
problem: Graphics-style full-body motion imitation does not transfer to real humanoids because of large DoF gaps (e.g. 69 vs 19) and unrealistically high actuator gains, while standard humanoid RL yields unexpressive motion.
keyIdea: Train one RL policy where only the upper body imitates retargeted human mocap (joint angles + keypoints) and the legs merely track a root-movement goal (velocity, roll/pitch, height), using mocap-derived goal distributions and reference state initialization.
architecture: Single goal-conditioned PPO policy in Isaac Gym; goal = expression goal (9 upper-body joint targets + 18-D arm keypoints) + root movement goal; observes proprioception only (no privileged linear velocity or height); outputs PD targets.
inputs: Proprioception (root angular velocity, roll, pitch, yaw error, joint positions/velocities, previous action) + expression and root-movement goals
outputs: 19 joint PD position targets on Unitree H1
actionRepr: Per-step 19-D joint position targets for PD controllers (RL policy)
trainingData: 780 retargeted CMU MoCap clips (~3.7 h; walk, dance, basketball, punch, others); motions can also come from MDM text-to-motion diffusion at test time
whatChangedVsParent: Relaxes lower-body imitation (tracking only root movement) so graphics-style motion imitation becomes deployable on a 19-DoF real humanoid.
limitations: Direct joint-angle retargeting to fewer DoF loses information; falls can break costly hardware, so protection/recovery is needed.
notes: Humanoid WBC, not manipulation per se, but underpins later loco-manipulation work (Mobile-TeleVision reuses its retargeting and rewards).

name: Mobile-TeleVision
resolvedTitle: Mobile-TeleVision: Predictive Motion Priors for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
org: UC San Diego; MIT
problem: RL whole-body humanoid policies give robust walking but imprecise, unpredictable high-DoF arm control; fully decoupling upper and lower body causes instability.
keyIdea: Control the upper body directly with IK/retargeting and train only the lower body with RL, conditioned on a CVAE-learned Predictive Motion Prior (PMP) latent that forecasts upcoming upper-body motion, plus an adaptive motion-amplitude curriculum.
architecture: CVAE (3-layer MLP prior, encoder, decoder; 64-D latent; 1 s window) trained on retargeted motion; PPO lower-body policy observes proprioception, locomotion command, gait signals and PMP latent; teleop via Apple Vision Pro (upper body) and joystick/pedals (legs).
inputs: Lower-body proprioception, velocity/rpy/height command, gait phase, PMP latent from past upper-body joint targets
outputs: 12 lower-body joint PD targets; upper-body joints set directly by IK/retargeting
actionRepr: Per-step lower-body joint position targets from RL; upper body open-loop joint targets
trainingData: Retargeted human motion dataset (following ExBody filtering); RL in simulation on Unitree H1 (real + sim) and Fourier GR1 (sim)
whatChangedVsParent: Takes arm control out of the RL policy (IK instead) and feeds a learned upper-body motion forecast to the RL leg policy.
limitations: Separating upper/lower control limits agility; humanoid hardware lacks DoF for agile whole-body tracking; multiple input commands raise teleoperator cognitive load.
notes: Paper reports ~40% better upper-DoF tracking than ExBody under disturbance and ~25% stability improvement from motion prior + curriculum. H1 fitted with 7-DoF arms and 6-DoF dexterous hands, active neck.

name: DiffuseLoco
resolvedTitle: DiffuseLoco: Real-Time Legged Locomotion Control with Diffusion from Offline Datasets
org: UC Berkeley; Simon Fraser University
problem: Online RL struggles to scale to many agile locomotion skills in one policy; offline learning for low-level legged control on real robots was largely unproven.
keyIdea: Train a transformer DDPM policy purely from offline multi-skill datasets (from source RL policies), with receding-horizon execution and delayed inputs so diffusion can run in real time onboard.
architecture: Transformer decoder denoiser with separate MLP encoders for state/action history and goals, causal cross-attention; DDPM sampling (not DDIM); TensorRT acceleration on an onboard RTX 4060 Mobile mini-PC.
inputs: Delayed h-step history of proprioceptive states, goals (velocity commands, base height) and previous actions
outputs: Sequence of future joint-level PD targets; only the first is executed (receding horizon)
actionRepr: Diffusion (DDPM) over n-step action sequence of joint PD targets, receding-horizon, 30 Hz
trainingData: Offline datasets generated by skill-specific source RL policies in simulation (5 skills: trotting, pacing, hopping, bipedal walking, etc. on Go1; walking/running on Cassie)

headlineResults.comparedTo: AMP 0; AMP w/ history 20; TF w/ RHC 40

whatChangedVsParent: Applies diffusion policies to high-frequency low-level legged control with delayed inputs and receding-horizon execution rather than interpolated action chunks.
limitations: Less robust than skill-specific RL to large external pushes; failed zero-shot sim-to-real on Cassie hardware (worked only in Simulink sim).
notes: Locomotion (not manipulation) paper cited in humanoid WBC context. Authors state code and checkpoints will be open-sourced upon acceptance.

name: AMP
resolvedTitle: AMP: Adversarial Motion Priors for Stylized Physics-Based Character Control
org: UC Berkeley; Shanghai Jiao Tong University
problem: Tracking-based motion imitation needs hand-designed pose-error objectives and a motion planner to select which clip to track, which scales poorly to large unstructured motion datasets.
keyIdea: Learn a style reward from an adversarial discriminator that distinguishes dataset state transitions from the character's, and combine it with a simple task reward in goal-conditioned RL, so clip selection and skill composition emerge automatically.
architecture: Policy pi(a|s,g) outputting PD targets, trained with goal-conditioned RL; a discriminator over state transitions (no actions needed) trained GAIL-style provides the style reward, combined with a task reward.
inputs: Character state and task goal; discriminator sees state transitions
outputs: Target positions for joint PD controllers
actionRepr: Per-step joint PD targets (RL policy)
trainingData: Unstructured motion clips (mocap and keyframe animation), e.g. CMU mocap and Sony-provided data
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces DeepMimic-style per-clip tracking and phase variables with an adversarial motion prior over state transitions from unstructured datasets.
limitations: Not stated in retrieved pages; later papers (ExBody, DiffuseLoco, PhysHOI) report mode collapse / unstable transfer as datasets grow and inaccurate object control in HOI.
notes: ACM TOG / SIGGRAPH 2021, computer-graphics simulated characters. Numeric results tables not in retrieved pages; paper claims quality comparable to tracking-based methods. Widely reused as a style reward for legged/humanoid robots (e.g. ExBody+AMP baseline, AMP locomotion).

name: PhysHOI
resolvedTitle: PhysHOI: Physics-Based Imitation of Dynamic Human-Object Interaction
org: Peking University; International Digital Economy Academy (IDEA); Tsinghua University; Carnegie Mellon University
problem: Physics-based human-object interaction (HOI) methods need hand-designed task-specific rewards per skill, and kinematic-only imitation rewards fall into local optima (e.g. not touching the object) in dynamic HOI.
keyIdea: Imitate kinematic HOI demonstrations with a task-agnostic multiplicative reward that adds a contact graph reward (binary contacts between body-part groups and objects) to body, object and interaction-graph kinematic rewards.
architecture: PPO policy in Isaac Gym controlling an SMPL-X whole-body humanoid with hands (52 bodies, 51x3 DoF); state = simulated HOI state + next reference HOI state (human motion, object motion, interaction graph, aggregated contact graph).
inputs: Simulated humanoid and object state, next-frame reference HOI state including contact graph
outputs: 51x3 joint PD targets (converted to torques by PD controllers)
actionRepr: Per-step joint PD targets (RL policy)
trainingData: 5 GRAB (S8) whole-body grasp sequences and the new BallPlay dataset (8 basketball skills with SMPL-X + ball motion + contact labels); 2048 parallel envs on one A100
whatChangedVsParent: Adds an explicit contact graph and contact-graph reward to kinematic HOI imitation rewards, removing need for task-specific rewards.
limitations: Fails with badly biased reference data; coarse CG nodes cause local optima for fine in-hand skills; minor penetrations from low frame rates; single-frame object reference insufficient for hands-off control (e.g. jump shots); no generalization to untrained HOIs.
notes: Simulation / character animation work (SMPL-X humanoid, 153 DoF); not deployed on a real robot. * = re-implemented baselines.

name: SFV
resolvedTitle: SFV: Reinforcement Learning of Physical Skills from Videos
org: UC Berkeley
problem: Physics-based character controllers rely on motion capture, which needs instrumented environments; monocular video is abundant but pose estimates are noisy and physically inconsistent.
keyIdea: Pipeline of per-frame 2D (OpenPose) and 3D (HMR) pose estimation, latent-space motion reconstruction for temporal consistency, then RL motion imitation with adaptive state initialization to learn skills from YouTube-style video.
architecture: Pose estimators trained with rotation augmentation; motion reconstruction optimizes an HMR latent trajectory with 2D reprojection, 3D consistency and smoothness losses; PPO-variant imitation policy (feedforward network) with adaptive initial-state distribution.
inputs: Monocular video clip and a simulated character model; policy observes character state (and reference motion phase)
outputs: Control policy producing joint actions for the simulated character
actionRepr: Per-step joint targets from an RL imitation policy
trainingData: Monocular video clips of skills (locomotion, acrobatics, martial arts, dance); pose estimators trained on in-the-wild image datasets (e.g. COCO) with rotation augmentation
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces mocap reference motions in DeepMimic-style imitation with reconstructed motions from monocular video, adding adaptive state initialization to cope with low-fidelity references.
limitations: Fails when pose estimation is wrong (kip-up, spinkick); artifacts like stiff postures; fast dance steps (Gangnam Style) remain hard; limited to clips with minimal camera motion due to root-translation estimation.
notes: ACM TOG (SIGGRAPH Asia) 2018, simulated characters; also retargets skills to a simulated Atlas robot and does physics-based motion completion from a single image. Quantitative tables not in retrieved pages.

name: Agile soccer (Haarnoja)
resolvedTitle: Learning Agile Soccer Skills for a Bipedal Robot with Deep Reinforcement Learning
org: Google DeepMind
problem: Whether deep RL can synthesize safe, agile, composable whole-body skills for a low-cost miniature humanoid in a dynamic multi-agent game, and transfer them zero-shot to hardware.
keyIdea: Two-stage training: separate get-up and soccer skill teachers, then distill them into one 1v1 agent with adaptive KL regularization while training via self-play against earlier snapshots; transfer zero-shot using system ID, domain randomization and perturbations.
architecture: Feed-forward Gaussian policy trained with Distributional MPO (off-policy actor-critic); critic conditioned on opponent ID; state-dependent KL regularization to the relevant skill with Lagrangian-adjusted weights.
inputs: Proprioception plus game state (ball, opponent, goal) tracked by motion capture in the real setup
outputs: Joint position targets for 20 actuated joints of a Robotis OP3
actionRepr: Per-step joint position targets, nominal 25 ms control step
trainingData: Simulation only (MuJoCo) with domain randomization and random pushes; get-up skill guided by key poses from a scripted get-up
whatChangedVsParent: Extends kickstarting to multiple mutually exclusive skill teachers with performance-adaptive regularization, combined with self-play for a real bipedal robot.
limitations: Relies on domain knowledge for rewards and get-up key poses; manual skill selection in distillation; no real data used; small robot only; motion-capture ball tracking is fragile; control loop often missed 25 ms deadline; unmodeled servos make behavior sensitive to battery level.
notes: Published in Science Robotics 2024. Also reports kicks 34% faster than scripted baseline. Locomotion/soccer rather than manipulation; cited as humanoid whole-body RL exemplar. controlRateHz derived from stated 25 ms nominal step; authors note it was often missed.

name: CooHOI
resolvedTitle: CooHOI: Learning Cooperative Human-Object Interaction with Manipulated Object Dynamics
org: Shanghai AI Laboratory; Tsinghua University; Beihang University; NTU; Carnegie Mellon University
problem: Multi-humanoid cooperative carrying of large objects lacks multi-person mocap data, and training multi-agent policies from scratch fails to converge.
keyIdea: First learn single-agent carrying with AMP from single-person motion priors, then transfer to cooperative carrying with MAPPO (CTDE), using each end's bounding-box dynamics as observation so object motion acts as implicit communication between agents.
architecture: AMP-style policy (actor-critic, CNN + MLP [1024,1024,512]) and discriminator; stage 2 initializes all agents from the single-agent policy with parameter sharing and MAPPO fine-tuning; stand-point and held-point rewards.
inputs: Humanoid proprioception, bounding-box state and velocity of the object (or of each end of a long object), task targets
outputs: Joint PD targets for a simulated humanoid
actionRepr: Per-step joint targets from RL policy at 30 Hz
trainingData: AMASS clips (9 walking, 5 pick-up, 4 carry, 5 put-down) plus backward/side walking; Isaac Gym, 4096 envs, 15,000 epochs (~15 h on one GPU)
whatChangedVsParent: Extends single-character AMP HOI (InterPhys) to multi-agent cooperation via skill transfer and object-dynamics observations instead of multi-person tracking.
limitations: No dexterous hands; relies on object bounding boxes (limits shape generalization); simulation only, no real-world deployment.
notes: NeurIPS 2024. Simulated characters (not real robots). InterPhys comparison includes weight info in observation; CooHOI without weight info handles 2-13 kg range.

name: HumanVLA
resolvedTitle: HumanVLA: Towards Vision-Language Directed Object Rearrangement by Physical Humanoid
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Tencent Robotics X
problem: Physics-based human-scene interaction methods handle only static objects or one object type and rely on privileged object/goal states unavailable in real deployment.
keyIdea: Train a privileged state-based teacher (goal-conditioned RL + AMP) for general object rearrangement, then distill it via DAgger into a vision-language-action student using egocentric images and language, with active rendering that steers head gaze toward the object.
architecture: Teacher: MLP actor/critic/discriminator with BPS object-geometry encoding, A* waypoints, carry curriculum. Student (HumanVLA): EfficientNet-B0 image encoder + frozen BERT-base text encoder + proprioception + last action -> 6-layer MLP action decoder.
inputs: Egocentric 256x256 RGB (90 deg FoV), language instruction, 223-D proprioception, last action
outputs: 28-D PD joint targets for a simulated humanoid (15 rigid bodies, 28 joints)
actionRepr: Per-step 28-D joint PD targets at 30 Hz, trained by behavior cloning (DAgger) from teacher
trainingData: Human-in-the-Room (HITR) dataset: 615 tasks (552 train / 63 test) in 4 room layouts, 50 static + 34 movable objects (HSSD assets), GPT-4V-generated instructions; ~30 min motion data from OMOMO + SAMP locomotion

headlineResults.comparedTo: Offline GC-BC 10.2%; w/o active rendering 56.7%; privileged InterPhys 59.5%

whatChangedVsParent: Moves from privileged-state AMP interaction controllers (InterPhys) to a language- and egocentric-vision-conditioned student policy via teacher-student distillation.
limitations: Humanoid uses spherical hands (no dexterous manipulation); single-object rearrangement; simulation only; future work: dexterous manipulation and long-horizon multi-object interaction.
notes: NeurIPS 2024; code at github.com/AllenXuuu/HumanVLA. Success threshold relaxed to 40 cm for vision-language policies vs 20 cm for state-based. Simulated character, not a real robot.

name: Humanoid-VLA
resolvedTitle: Humanoid-VLA: Towards Universal Humanoid Control with Visual Integration
org: Westlake University (MiLAB); Zhejiang University; Westlake Robotics
problem: Humanoid whole-body controllers are reactive (tracking given motions or text) and cannot perceive the scene to choose interactions; egocentric visuomotor humanoid data is scarce.
keyIdea: Pre-align language and motion in an LLM using body-part-tokenized motion from mocap, synthetic and video-extracted data with self-supervised pseudo-annotations (occlusion, track, time, state tasks), then add egocentric vision via parameter-efficient cross-attention fine-tuning, and execute with an RL whole-body controller.
architecture: Compositional VQ motion tokenizer (5 codebooks: legs, torso, arms) sharing vocabulary with an LLM; frozen copied transformer layers + visual encoder with cross-attention for vision conditioning; goal-conditioned PPO whole-body controller (following H2O/OmniH2O) outputs PD targets.
inputs: Language instruction, egocentric RGB video, optional motion conditions (trajectory, time, state)
outputs: Discrete motion tokens decoded to human-pose sequences, then 24 humanoid joint PD targets via the whole-body controller
actionRepr: Autoregressive discrete body-part motion tokens (VQ) -> kinematic pose targets tracked by RL WBC
trainingData: ~7,790 h motion: AMASS mocap (29K clips, 4.1 h), online video (0.8M clips, 7,515.7 h), synthetic (100K clips, 227.7 h); plus real mocap paired with egocentric video for fine-tuning

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Unitree G1, 8 vision tasks x10 trials

whatChangedVsParent: Adds egocentric visual conditioning and large-scale self-supervised motion-language pretraining on top of reactive motion-tracking whole-body controllers.
limitations: Paper does not report baselines for the vision tasks (claimed uniquely solvable); real-world evaluation is small-scale (10 trials per task); relies on retargeting to 15 SMPL joints.
notes: Limitations field partly editorial (inferred from evaluation setup, not an explicit limitations section in retrieved pages). Claims dataset is 25x larger than UH-1's. Backbone LLM size not stated in retrieved pages.

name: HumanoidBench
resolvedTitle: HumanoidBench: Simulated Humanoid Benchmark for Whole-Body Locomotion and Manipulation
org: UC Berkeley; Yonsei University
problem: Humanoid research is bottlenecked by costly, fragile hardware; existing simulated benchmarks focus on single arms or humanoid locomotion, not whole-body manipulation with dexterous hands.
keyIdea: A MuJoCo benchmark with a Unitree H1 plus two Shadow Hands (61-D action) covering 15 whole-body manipulation and 12 locomotion tasks, showing flat RL fails and hierarchical RL with robust pretrained low-level skills helps.
architecture: Benchmark: MuJoCo simulation, H1 + Shadow Hands (also G1, Digit, Robotiq, Unitree hands); state, egocentric stereo vision and whole-body tactile (448 taxels) observations; hierarchical RL baseline with MJX-pretrained PPO reaching policies.
inputs: Proprioception (151-D with hands) + object states; optional egocentric cameras and tactile
outputs: 61-D normalized position-control actions (19 body + 21 per hand)
