name: Coupled oscillator networks (CONs)
resolvedTitle: Input-to-State Stable Coupled Oscillator Networks for Closed-form Model-based Control in Latent Space
org: Delft University of Technology
problem: Latent-space dynamics models learned from pixels lack physical structure, stability guarantees and an invertible input-to-forcing map, so closed-form model-based controllers cannot be used on them.
keyIdea: Model latent dynamics as a network of damped harmonic oscillators with nonlinear tanh coupling, which is a Lagrangian system with provable global input-to-state stability, then control it with potential-force compensation plus saturated PID.
architecture: CNN (beta-VAE) autoencoder to a latent state; CON dynamics x'' = g(u) - Kx - Dx' - tanh(Wx+b) with MLP input map B(u); approximate closed-form integration (CFA-CON); learned forcing decoder approximating g^-1 for control.
inputs: 32x32 pixel images and control inputs
outputs: Predicted latent/observation trajectories; latent-space control inputs
params: 34-7048 trainable dynamics parameters depending on dataset (e.g., 34 on mass-spring, 246 on double pendulum)
trainingData: 6 simulated datasets: mass-spring, pendulum, double pendulum with friction; continuum soft robots (constant strain, 2- and 3-segment PCC)

headlineResults.benchmark: Latent-space trajectory tracking on simulated soft robot
headlineResults.comparedTo: pure feedback controller on latent NODE

whatChangedVsParent: Adds Lagrangian structure, ISS stability proof, an input decoder and closed-form integration to coupled-oscillator RNNs for control.
limitations: Best suited to mechanical systems with dissipation and a single attractive equilibrium (e.g., soft robots); multi-equilibrium or non-dissipative systems fit less well.
notes: NeurIPS 2024; code on GitHub (tud-phi). Control demo is on a simulated continuum soft robot with raw pixels as feedback.

name: MixNet
resolvedTitle: MixNet: Structured Deep Neural Motion Prediction for Autonomous Racing
org: Technical University of Munich
problem: Black-box neural motion predictors for opponent racecars give no quality guarantees, while physics-based predictors degrade beyond ~2 s.
keyIdea: LSTM encoder of opponent history and track boundaries, but the decoder outputs softmax weights to superimpose dynamically feasible base curves (boundaries, raceline, centerline) plus a piecewise-linear velocity profile, so predictions are smooth and inside the track by construction.
architecture: LSTM encoders for history (30 positions at 10 Hz) and left/right boundaries; linear latent; heads for base-curve weights (softmax), initial velocity and 5 accelerations; fuzzy-logic interaction model and plausibility checks.
inputs: 3 s of opponent 2D positions; sampled track boundaries (400 m ahead)
outputs: 5 s trajectory prediction (50 steps) per opponent
trainingData: Data from high-fidelity hardware-in-the-loop racing simulations (IAC); evaluated on 10 recorded interactive HIL scenarios

headlineResults.benchmark: Gaussian input noise sigma 1.0 m (both axes)
Compute, 4 vehicles on one CPU core

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces the LSTM decoder with a constrained superposition of track base curves plus a physically parameterized velocity profile.
limitations: Base curves are track-specific so it does not generalize to unseen tracks; rule-based interaction model scales poorly beyond ~4 cars; single constant weight set per prediction.
notes: Deployed on TUM's racecar in the Indy Autonomous Challenge 2021; code open-sourced (github.com/TUMFTM/MixNet). Published later in IEEE Access 2023 as 'MixNet: Physics Constrained Deep Neural Motion Prediction for Autonomous Racing' (the title P11 cites). Not a manipulation method.

name: Morphological symmetry (Ordoñez-Apraez)
resolvedTitle: Morphological Symmetries in Robotics
org: Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia; IRI CSIC-UPC; Heriot-Watt University; IHMC
problem: Data-driven robotics models need lots of data and ignore the structural symmetries of robot bodies (replicated limbs, symmetric mass) that analytical models implicitly respect.
keyIdea: Formalize morphological symmetries as a symmetry group acting on state, sensors and dynamics, showing equations of motion and optimal policies are equivariant; exploit this via data augmentation, equivariant networks and harmonic decomposition of joint-space dynamics.
architecture: Group/representation-theoretic framework; equivariant MLPs/CNNs built with ESCNN; Dynamics' Harmonics Analysis via isotypic decomposition; MorphoSymm library.
inputs: Robot state (q, qdot) and proprioceptive/exteroceptive sensor data
outputs: Task-dependent (centroidal momentum regression, contact-state classification)
trainingData: Synthetic centroidal momentum data (Pinocchio) for Solo quadruped and Atlas humanoid; real Mini Cheetah locomotion dataset (Lin et al. 2021) for contact detection

headlineResults.value: equivariant MLP and augmentation beat plain MLP (plots)

whatChangedVsParent: Extends the authors' earlier morphological symmetry work with existence conditions in rigid-body dynamics and harmonic analysis of joint-space dynamics.
notes: IJRR 2025; MorphoSymm repository released. Results are reported in plots; no single headline numbers were extracted. Applies to legged robots primarily, not manipulation.

name: GP-MPC racing (Kabzan)
resolvedTitle: Learning-Based Model Predictive Control for Autonomous Racing (Kabzan, Hewing, Liniger, Zeilinger; IEEE RA-L 2019)
org: ETH Zurich
notes: Primary paper not found via alphaXiv (title search resolved to unrelated racing MPC papers). From general knowledge (unverified, not from the paper): augments a nominal single-track vehicle model with a sparse Gaussian-process residual learned online from driving data, used inside an MPC for the AMZ Driverless race car, improving lap times; the GP uses a reduced feature set and a dictionary for real-time use. DOI given is from general knowledge and should be verified.

name: PhysDiff
resolvedTitle: PhysDiff: Physics-Guided Human Motion Diffusion Model
org: NVIDIA
problem: Motion diffusion models ignore physics and generate human motions with floating, foot sliding and ground penetration.
keyIdea: Insert a physics-based projection inside the diffusion sampling loop: an RL motion-imitation policy tracks the denoised motion in a simulator and the simulated (physically plausible) motion guides the next denoising step.
architecture: Plug-in to pretrained denoisers (MDM or MotionDiffuse) with DDIM-style sampling; projection = PPO-trained MLP imitation policy (1024-1024-512) controlling an SMPL character in IsaacGym with PD targets and residual forces; projections scheduled at the last few diffusion steps (e.g., End 4, Space 1).
inputs: Text prompt or action label
outputs: Physically plausible human motion sequences
trainingData: Imitation policy trained on AMASS; evaluated on HumanML3D (14,616 motions, 44,970 texts), HumanAct12, UESTC
whatChangedVsParent: Moves physics correction from post-processing into the diffusion loop, iterating physics projection and denoising.
limitations: Physics simulation makes sampling slower (2.5x slower than MDM for one motion); too many projections at early steps hurt motion quality.
notes: ICCV 2023. Human motion generation, not robot manipulation; P11 lists it under physically consistent world representations / VWMs as 'humanoid motions generated by a VWM', which is loose: it is a motion diffusion model, not a video world model. CONFLICT (minor): P11 describes the projection as onto trajectories from 'an imitation policy trained in a physics simulator' (correct) but frames it as a video world model.

name: Riemannian flow matching
resolvedTitle: Flow Matching on General Geometries
org: FAIR, Meta; Weizmann Institute of Science
problem: Generative models on manifolds need expensive simulation, scale poorly with dimension, or use biased approximations of scores.
keyIdea: Riemannian Flow Matching: define conditional vector fields from a premetric (geodesic distance on simple manifolds, spectral distances on general ones), giving simulation-free, divergence-free training of continuous normalizing flows on manifolds.
architecture: MLP vector field (512 hidden units, 6-12 layers, Swish) outputting tangent vectors; conditional flows via exp/log maps (simple geometries) or ODE simulation with biharmonic/diffusion spectral distances (meshes, manifolds with boundary).
inputs: Samples on a manifold (sphere, torus, SPD matrices, meshes)
outputs: Learned continuous normalizing flow / samples on the manifold
trainingData: Earth science datasets on the sphere (volcano, earthquake, flood, fire), protein torsion angles on tori, EEG covariance on SPD manifold, mesh distributions (Bunny, Spot), maze manifolds
whatChangedVsParent: Generalizes Euclidean conditional flow matching to Riemannian manifolds via premetric-defined conditional vector fields.
limitations: General manifolds still need simulation of x_t during training; spectral distances need eigenfunction solvers that can be costly on complex manifolds.
notes: ICLR 2024. Generic generative modeling, not a robot policy. CONFLICT: P11 says Chen & Lipman introduced RFM 'for navigation'; the paper targets general manifold generative modeling (earth science, proteins, meshes, SPD); the only navigation-like demo is transport through maze manifolds with boundaries. P11 also cites Chisari et al. (2024) for RFM-based manipulation policies from point clouds, which is the robotics application.

name: Reachable-set projection diffusion
resolvedTitle: DDAT: Diffusion Policies Enforcing Dynamically Admissible Robot Trajectories
org: UC Berkeley (ICON Lab, Hybrid Robotics Lab)
problem: Diffusion planners produce state sequences that underactuated robots cannot actually follow, forcing constant replanning.
keyIdea: Project each predicted next state onto a polytopic under-approximation of the reachable set of the previous state (built by applying extremal actions in a black-box simulator), and use these projections, with a noise-level curriculum, during both training and inference.
architecture: Diffusion Transformer (DiT) over trajectories of states, actions, or both; differentiable convex projections via cvxpylayers; partial/stochastic projection curriculum between sigma_min and sigma_max; 5 inference steps plus trajectory selection.
inputs: Initial state (and command, for quadrupeds); black-box simulator access for projections
outputs: Open-loop state and/or action trajectories (e.g., 500 steps at 50 Hz for GO2)
actionRepr: full-horizon trajectory of states and/or actions generated by diffusion, projected to be dynamically admissible
trainingData: Hundreds to 1000 simulated trajectories per system: Hopper, Walker, HalfCheetah (MuJoCo), quadcopter (MPC-generated), Unitree GO1/GO2 (joystick policy rollouts)

headlineResults.benchmark: Inference cost, Hopper (8 trajs x 300 steps, CPU)
Unitree GO2 hardware open-loop corridor walk
headlineResults.value: DDAT succeeds where vanilla diffusion policy fails

whatChangedVsParent: Enforces black-box dynamic admissibility inside diffusion training and sampling via reachable-set projections, instead of relying on replanning or learned inverse dynamics.
limitations: Projections are computationally costly and scale exponentially with action dimension; assumes convex reachable sets (violated with contacts); slow inference limits closed-loop use.
notes: RSS 2025; code on project site. Retrieved pages did not include the main quantitative admissibility tables, so few numbers are given. Name here is descriptive; P11 cites Bouvier et al. (2025) as 'projection to reachable sets with dynamics-consistency penalties' for quadrotor/quadruped.

name: Hamiltonian video world model
resolvedTitle: Physically Native World Models: A Hamiltonian Perspective on Generative World Modeling
org: Tsinghua University
problem: Video-generative, 3D scene-centric and JEPA-style world models produce visually plausible futures but with weakly structured latent transitions, leading to long-horizon drift, poor action-consistency and high data needs for embodied planning.
keyIdea: Encode observations into an entity-level latent phase space (q, p), evolve it with a learned Hamiltonian (kinetic + potential + interaction terms) extended with dissipation, control and a constrained residual term, then decode the latent rollout to video and use it for planning.
architecture: Position/perspective paper proposing a design: encoder to entity-level phase variables; learned Hamiltonian H = sum K(p_i) + sum U(q_i) + sum V(q_i,q_j); controlled-dissipative dynamics dz/dt = (J - R(z)) grad H + G(z) a + eps(z,a) with an L2 penalty on the residual; a video generative decoder conditioned on the predicted latent trajectory; and a sampling-based planning interface that scores M candidate action sequences.
inputs: Past observations and candidate action sequences.
outputs: Predicted latent phase-space trajectory and decoded future video frames; selected action via utility maximization.
trainingData: None reported (conceptual proposal, no experiments).
whatChangedVsParent: Moves HNN/HGN-style energy-structured latent dynamics from toy physical systems into a full action-conditioned video world model with dissipation, control and residual terms plus a planning interface.
limitations: Real embodied scenes are not conservative (friction, impacts, partial observability); inferring meaningful (q, p) from pixels is hard; contact-rich, articulated and deformable interactions may need hybrid or event-driven extensions; current evaluation protocols cannot show whether reusable physics was learned.
notes: Perspective/position paper with no experiments or numbers. P11 (Table 6) lists it as Cui and Ma (2026), 'Dynamics learning, VWM, physics-encoded, Manipulator, latent energy-based dynamics with Hamiltonian structure'. The paper itself contains no manipulator experiments; the 'Manipulator' label in P11 reflects intended application, not a demonstrated result.

name: Deep Koopman with physics lifting
resolvedTitle: Physics-Informed Adaptive Deep Koopman Operator Modeling for Autonomous Vehicle Dynamics
org: Chongqing University; Nanyang Technological University
problem: Deep Koopman models of vehicle dynamics are black-box, generalize poorly, and cannot track time-varying parameters (mass, road friction) during fast maneuvers.
keyIdea: Add a PINN-style acceleration-consistency loss (predicted vs IMU-measured acceleration) to deep Koopman training, and update the lifted-space A and B matrices online with sliding-window least squares (SWLS).
architecture: Autoencoder lifting: encoder MLP [3-128-128-128-12] and decoder [12-128-128-128-3]; lifted state = [x; Phi(x)] (15-dim); linear A (15x15) and B (2x15) layers without bias. Loss = linearity + reconstruction + prediction + acceleration loss. Online SWLS recursive update of [A B].
inputs: Vehicle states (Vx, Vy, yaw rate) plus measured accelerations (ax, ay); control inputs (torque T, front steering angle).
outputs: One-step-ahead predicted vehicle states via linear evolution in the lifted space.
trainingData: CarSim/Simulink co-simulation of an in-wheel-motor-driven vehicle: 1400 s at 0.025 s sampling = 56,001 snapshots (70% train / 30% test).

headlineResults.metric: RMSE reduction ALDK-SWLS vs ALDK (Vx / Vy / yaw rate)

parents: Deep Koopman operator (Xiao et al.; Wang et al.)
whatChangedVsParent: Adds a physics-informed acceleration loss to deep Koopman training and SWLS online adaptation of the lifted linear model.
limitations: Validated only in CarSim/Simulink simulation for vehicle planar dynamics; observer and stability-controller use left to future work.
notes: Name is ambiguous. P11's Table 5 cites 'Zhang et al. (2026) Koopman, Vehicle, acceleration-consistency physics loss' (Advanced Engineering Informatics 71: 104274), which matches this arXiv preprint (2503.23396). The phrase 'physics lifting' might instead point to Shi & Karydis (2022) ACD-EDMD, which builds Koopman lifting functions analytically from configuration-space topology (not deep); that one was not read. A follow-up, arXiv 2606.15094 (Wang et al., tire-force-driven Deep Koopman with PI-VSS-NLMS online update), also exists. Not a manipulation paper: it models vehicles.

name: Deep RL from human preferences (Christiano)
resolvedTitle: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
org: OpenAI; DeepMind
problem: Many RL tasks have goals that are hard to specify as a reward function, and using human feedback directly as a reward costs far too much human time for deep RL.
keyIdea: Ask non-expert humans to compare pairs of 1-2 second trajectory clips, fit a reward predictor to these preferences with a Bradley-Terry model, and optimize the policy with RL against the predicted reward, all running asynchronously.
architecture: Ensemble of reward predictors (each trained on bootstrap-resampled comparisons, independently normalized and averaged), with 10% assumed random-response rate in the preference likelihood; queries chosen by ensemble disagreement. Policies: A2C for Atari, TRPO for MuJoCo. Atari reward net: 4 conv layers (16 filters each) + FC 64 on 84x84x4 frames.
inputs: Observation-action trajectory segments; human pairwise preference labels.
outputs: Learned scalar reward r(o, a); policy trained on it.
trainingData: MuJoCo (8 simulated robotics tasks) and 7 Atari games in ALE; feedback on under 1% of agent interactions; 30 minutes to 5 hours of contractor time per task (several hundred to several thousand comparisons).

headlineResults.comparedTo: 350/700/1400 synthetic-oracle queries and RL on true reward

parents: Akrour et al. preference-based policy learning
Wilson et al. trajectory preference queries
whatChangedVsParent: Scales preference-based reward learning to deep RL with nonlinear reward models, short-clip comparisons, asynchronous training and ensembles.
limitations: Uncertainty-based query selection is a crude approximation and in some tasks hurt performance in ablations; on-policy RL is sample-inefficient.
notes: P14 places it under 'human preference' with a pairwise comparison interface. Not robot-hardware; MuJoCo and Atari only.

name: PEBBLE
resolvedTitle: PEBBLE: Feedback-Efficient Interactive Reinforcement Learning via Relabeling Experience and Unsupervised Pre-training
org: UC Berkeley
problem: Preference-based human-in-the-loop RL (Christiano et al.) relies on sample-inefficient on-policy RL, so it still needs a lot of human feedback.
keyIdea: Pre-train the agent with unsupervised state-entropy exploration so early queries show diverse behavior, then learn a preference reward model and train off-policy (SAC), relabeling the entire replay buffer every time the reward model updates.
architecture: SAC agent; ensemble of three reward models trained with Bradley-Terry preference loss; entropy-based query sampling; 10K steps of unsupervised pre-training with intrinsic state-entropy reward.
inputs: States/actions; binary preferences between two behavior clips (1 s video clips for humans).
outputs: Learned reward model and SAC policy.
trainingData: DeepMind Control Suite locomotion (Cheetah, Walker, Quadruped) and Meta-world manipulation; scripted teacher from ground-truth reward, plus author-provided human feedback (at most one hour).

headlineResults.comparedTo: Preference PPO (Christiano re-implemented with PPO) given up to 2100 queries fails to match PPO oracle

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces on-policy RL with off-policy SAC plus full replay relabeling, adds unsupervised pre-training, and uses entropy-based query sampling.
notes: Code released at the project site. Most experiments use a scripted teacher rather than real humans.

name: ConformalSTL (Lindemann)
resolvedTitle: Conformal Prediction for STL Runtime Verification
org: University of Southern California; University of Pennsylvania
problem: Predictive runtime verification of stochastic systems against signal temporal logic (STL) specifications gave no formal guarantees unless the predictor or distribution was tightly constrained.
keyIdea: Use any trajectory predictor (e.g. an LSTM) to forecast future states and wrap it with split conformal prediction, so the predicted STL robustness gives a distribution-free guarantee that the true run satisfies the specification with probability at least 1-delta.
architecture: Two algorithms. Direct: nonconformity score = predicted minus true STL robustness on calibration trajectories; the (1-delta) quantile C gives P(satisfied) >= 1-delta whenever predicted robustness > C. Indirect: per-timestep state prediction regions (with delta/H union bound) and worst-case robustness over those balls. Predictors are task-independent, so no retraining when the specification changes.
inputs: Observed state prefix; STL formula; calibration trajectories.
outputs: Lower bound on STL robustness and a verification verdict with confidence 1-delta.
trainingData: F-16 aircraft simulation and CARLA lane-keeping (1000 trajectories per controller: 700 train LSTM, 200 calibration, 100 test).

headlineResults.metric: test trajectories where predicted robustness > C implied satisfaction

whatChangedVsParent: First predictive runtime STL verification with formal guarantees that works with arbitrary learned trajectory predictors and no distributional assumptions.
limitations: Guarantees are marginal, not conditional on the calibration set; the indirect method needs more calibration data as the horizon grows; requires exchangeable (i.i.d.) calibration trajectories.
notes: Not a manipulation paper (aircraft and driving). P14 groups it with TGPO under temporal-logic scoring and as a calibrated safety/constraint verifier.

name: TGPO
resolvedTitle: TGPO: Temporal Grounded Policy Optimization for Signal Temporal Logic Tasks
org: MIT
problem: STL tasks are non-Markovian and give only sparse terminal robustness rewards, so standard RL fails, and prior RL-for-STL handles only limited fragments (up to two temporal layers).
keyIdea: Decompose an STL formula into timed reach subgoals and invariance constraints with free time variables; a high-level component samples time assignments (critic-guided Metropolis-Hastings) and a low-level time-conditioned policy learns them with dense stage-wise rewards.
architecture: Hierarchical model-free RL (PPO) over an augmented MDP (state + time index + progress flags + time variables); rewards combine STL score, invariance penalty, progress and distance terms; critic predicts STL satisfaction and guides MCMC over time allocations (500 iterations, 200 warm-up, 512 chains). At inference, pick the time allocation with highest critic value and roll out once.
inputs: System state, augmented with time and subgoal flags; STL specification.
outputs: Control actions satisfying the STL spec.
actionRepr: Continuous low-level control actions from a time-conditioned policy.
trainingData: Five simulated environments (Linear, Unicycle, Franka Panda, Quadrotor, 29D Ant); 10 STLs per environment; 512 parallel envs, 1000-4000 epochs, 7 seeds; JAX.

headlineResults.benchmark: Five environments, wide range of STLs
headlineResults.metric: task success rate vs best baseline

whatChangedVsParent: Grounds STL time variables into concrete subgoal schedules, turning a sparse non-Markovian objective into dense stage-wise rewards for general nested STLs.
limitations: No formal convergence guarantees; does not efficiently handle disjunctions or infinite-horizon patterns like G(F); tested with up to 5 time variables, so scalability is open.
notes: Code announced at github.com/mengyuest/TGPO. In P14 it appears as an uncalibrated specification verifier used as a dense reward.

name: RINSE
resolvedTitle: Learning from the Best: Smoothness-Driven Metrics for Data Quality in Imitation Learning
org: UCLA
problem: Behavior cloning treats all demonstrations equally, but real datasets mix skilled and noisy demos; existing curation needs policy training in the loop or manual labels.
keyIdea: Score each demonstration by trajectory smoothness alone: Spectral Arc Length (SAL, frequency-domain regularity of end-effector speed) and Trajectory-Envelope Distance (TED, DTW distance to a contact-aware Bezier-smoothed version of itself), then keep or upweight the smoothest demos.
architecture: No learned model. SAL = negative arc length of the log-magnitude spectrum of the speed signal. TED = contact-phase partitioning, greedy Bezier envelope fitting with corridor fallback, geodesic orientation smoothing, then normalized FastDTW distance. Used as a filter, a retrieval re-ranker (STRAP), or soft weights in Re-Mix.
inputs: Proprioceptive end-effector trajectories (TED also uses gripper contact/phase signal).
outputs: Per-demonstration smoothness scores; filtered or reweighted dataset.
trainingData: RoboMimic (Square, Tool Hang, Transport), RTIS modality benchmark, 7 Open X-Embodiment domains (Re-Mix), LIBERO-10 (STRAP), real xArm-7 tasks; policies are Diffusion Policy or BC Transformer.

headlineResults.metric: Spearman rho vs learned Re-Mix allocations

whatChangedVsParent: Brings a clinically validated smoothness metric plus a new contact-aware envelope metric into robot demonstration curation, with no policy training needed.
limitations: Smoothness is necessary but not sufficient: smooth yet suboptimal demos exist; assumes demos are pre-filtered for success; TED may still penalize task-necessary abrupt motions.
notes: P14 describes RINSE as geometry-based scoring that trains on the highest-scoring subset, and notes that its scores agree closely with Re-Mix mixture weights, which matches the paper. A first alphaXiv title search resolved to an unrelated paper (2312.15346, single-demo dishwashing); resolved correctly via P14's description.

name: Code-as-Monitor
resolvedTitle: Code-as-Monitor: Constraint-aware Visual Programming for Reactive and Proactive Robotic Failure Detection
org: Beihang University; Peking University; BAAI; Galbot
problem: VLM-based failure detectors work as slow, coarse VQA on single images and only react after failure; open-set proactive detection (catching failures before they happen) was largely unaddressed.
keyIdea: Cast both reactive and proactive failure detection as spatio-temporal constraint satisfaction: a VLM writes monitor code over compact geometric 'constraint elements' (points, lines, surfaces) that are tracked in real time, so the VLM is called once per subgoal rather than every frame.
architecture: Constraint Generator (GPT-4o) proposes next subgoal plus during/upon-completion textual constraints; Constraint Painter uses ConSeg (LISA-style: LLaVA VLM + SAM encoder/decoder with LoRA, 13B) to segment instance and part masks, projects them to 3D and reduces them to elements; Constraint Monitor has GPT-4o generate NumPy code over element positions, tracked with CoTracker; a violation halts execution and returns a reason for re-planning.
inputs: Multi-view RGB-D observations, task instruction, previous subgoal and failure feedback.
outputs: Boolean failure flag plus textual reason, per timestep; next subgoal and constraints.
params: ConSeg-13B (segmentation module); GPT-4o for code generation.
trainingData: ConSeg fine-tuned on a multi-granularity dataset built from BridgeData V2: 10,181 trajectories, 219,356 images, auto-labeled with GPT-4o, Grounded SAM and Semantic SAM, plus 100 trajectories per simulator.

headlineResults.benchmark: CLIPort, Omnigibson, RLBench + real world, severe disturbances
Real-world reasoning pick & place (grasp animals by distance to fruit)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces per-frame VLM VQA with one-time VLM-written constraint code over tracked geometric elements, adding proactive detection.
notes: P14 lists it under model-written rules (§3.1.3) and as a trained-model verifier for failure/uncertainty. Wraps an open-loop policy into a closed-loop system.

name: Robometer
resolvedTitle: Robometer: Scaling General-Purpose Robotic Reward Models via Trajectory Comparisons
org: USC; UT Dallas; MIT; University of Washington; Ai2; NVIDIA
problem: General-purpose robot reward models are trained only on frame-level progress labels from expert demos, which scales poorly because failed and suboptimal trajectories have ambiguous absolute progress and get thrown away.
keyIdea: Train with a dual objective: frame-level progress regression that anchors reward magnitude on expert data, plus trajectory-level pairwise preference loss that imposes global ordering and can use unlabeled failed trajectories; also predict per-frame success.
architecture: VLM-based reward model with progress, preference and success heads; preference pairs built from real failures and augmentations (video rewinding, cross-task comparisons).
inputs: Video frames of a trajectory and a language task description (pairs of trajectories for the preference objective).
outputs: Frame-level progress (reward), per-frame success probability, trajectory preference.
params: 4B (as 'Robometer-4B' in TOPReward's comparison; not confirmed from the Robometer pages read)
trainingData: RBM-1M: over one million trajectories across 21 robot embodiments (single-arm, bimanual, mobile, plus human demos), including many suboptimal and failed trajectories.

headlineResults.benchmark: Reward benchmarks + 6 OOD scenes at 3 institutions
Downstream online RL, offline RL, IL data filtering, failure detection

whatChangedVsParent: Adds inter-trajectory preference supervision on top of progress regression so large failure-heavy datasets become usable for reward learning.
notes: Model weights, RBM-1M and training code released at robometer.github.io. P14 places it under 'human preference / trained model'. Exact VLM backbone not confirmed from pages read (paper cites Qwen3-VL).

name: VLAC
resolvedTitle: A Vision-Language-Action-Critic Model for Robotic Real-World Reinforcement Learning
org: Shanghai AI Lab
problem: Real-world RL for VLAs is bottlenecked by sparse, hand-crafted, task-specific rewards and inefficient exploration.
keyIdea: A single InternVL-based model that, given two observations and a language goal, outputs a signed progress delta and a done signal (critic), and under a different prompt outputs action tokens (policy); used inside an asynchronous real-world RL loop with graded human-in-the-loop help.
architecture: InternVL backbone, autoregressive; pairwise progress head c(o_i, o_i+dt; task) labeled as dt/(T-i); auxiliary task-description and done objectives; negative and mismatched samples to learn regression/stagnation and reject irrelevant prompts; PPO with tokenized delta-EEF actions for RL.
inputs: Pair of image observations plus task text (critic); observation plus task (policy).
outputs: Signed progress delta, done flag; action tokens.
actionRepr: Autoregressive tokenized delta end-effector actions.
trainingData: Over 3000 hours of human data, 1200 hours of public robot manipulation data (e.g. Bridge, DROID, RoboSet, FMB, AgiBot World), over 15 hours of self-collected data, plus VQA/perception datasets (paper also states more than 4,000 hours of language-annotated manipulation data).

headlineResults.value: further 50% improvement, up to 100% final success

headlineResults.metric: episodes per robot to reach 80% success

whatChangedVsParent: Unifies critic and policy in one VLM and makes progress pairwise and start-point agnostic.
limitations: Human-in-the-loop timing and reset choice are heuristic; the PPO + tokenized-action recipe does not transfer directly to diffusion/flow policies; multi-task online RL still shows reward-scale drift and forgetting.
notes: Code and model released (InternRobotics/VLAC). P14 lists VLAC as a trained-model progress verifier.

name: Robo-Dopamine
resolvedTitle: Robo-Dopamine: General Process Reward Modeling for High-Precision Robotic Manipulation
org: Peking University; BAAI; University of Sydney; CASIA
problem: Learned process reward models lack step-awareness, rely on single-view perception (missing occluded fine-grained progress), and are used with reward shaping that can change the optimal policy (a 'semantic trap').
keyIdea: Train a General Reward Model (GRM) that predicts hop-normalized relative progress between multi-view BEFORE/AFTER states conditioned on initial and goal states, fuse incremental, forward-anchored and backward-anchored estimates, and use it in RL through policy-invariant potential-based reward shaping.
architecture: GRM built on RoboBrain 2.0 (Qwen2.5-VL-style) at 3B and 8B; inputs are task prompt plus multi-view images of init, goal, before and after; outputs a discrete relative progress token in [-1, 1]. Step-wise discretization from human keyframes; hop labels normalized by remaining or covered distance. Dopamine-RL: one-shot GRM adaptation from a single demo plus policy-invariant shaping, compatible with PPO, ReinFlow, Cal-QL etc.
inputs: Task text; multi-view images of initial, goal, BEFORE and AFTER states.
outputs: Relative progress hop (e.g. '+15%' or '-4%'); fused dense reward.
trainingData: 35M samples from about 3,400 hours of video, over 100K trajectories and over 350 tasks (real robots, simulation, egocentric human video; e.g. AgiBot World, DROID, RoboCasa, LIBERO, EgoDex). Trained on 128 H100s: about 8 days (3B), 14 days (8B).

headlineResults.metric: success after about 150 online rollouts (about 1 hour)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds step-aware hop normalization, multi-view fusion and policy-invariant shaping on top of VLAC/GVL-style progress rewards.
notes: P14 lists it as a trained progress and execution-quality verifier. TOPReward notes Robo-Dopamine needs extra task-specific demonstrations for each new task.

name: VLM-RM
resolvedTitle: Vision-Language Models are Zero-Shot Reward Models for Reinforcement Learning
org: FAR AI; Vertebra; ETH Zurich; Anthropic
problem: RL needs either a hand-specified reward or expensive human feedback; prior VLM-reward work needed heavy fine-tuning or ad-hoc procedures.
keyIdea: Use CLIP zero-shot: reward = cosine similarity between the image embedding of the current state and the text embedding of a one-sentence task prompt, optionally with goal-baseline regularization that projects out directions irrelevant to goal vs a neutral baseline prompt.
architecture: Frozen CLIP (RN50 up to OpenCLIP ViT-bigG-14) as reward; goal-baseline regularization with strength alpha; SAC or DQN (stable-baselines3) as the RL learner.
inputs: Rendered image of the environment state; task and baseline text prompts.
outputs: Scalar reward per state.
trainingData: No reward training. Environments: CartPole, MountainCar (original and textured), MuJoCo Humanoid-v4 with modified textures and camera.

headlineResults.value: 5 of 8 at 100% success (kneeling, lotus, standing, arms raised, splits)

headlineResults.metric: success with original vs modified textures and camera

whatChangedVsParent: Shows a large enough off-the-shelf CLIP works as a reward without fine-tuning, and adds goal-baseline projection.
limitations: Relies on the text prompt capturing the intent; fails on fine pose distinctions (hands on hips, arms crossed) and on non-photorealistic renderings; risk of misspecification grows with task complexity.
notes: Code released (AlignmentResearch/vlmrm). Not manipulation; humanoid pose tasks in simulation.

name: RoboCLIP
resolvedTitle: RoboCLIP: One Demonstration is Enough to Learn Robot Policies
org: USC; UC Berkeley; Stanford; Google Research
problem: Reward design is hard and imitation learning needs many in-domain expert demonstrations.
keyIdea: Use a pretrained video-language model (S3D trained on HowTo100M) without fine-tuning: the episode-end reward is the dot product between the embedding of the agent's rollout video and the embedding of a single task specifier (text or one video demo, even of a human).
architecture: Frozen S3D video and text encoders; sparse reward at episode end (rollout downsampled to 32 frames, center-cropped); PPO policy on state; optional fine-tuning with one demo.
inputs: Rollout video; task text or one demonstration video.
outputs: Sparse episode-level similarity reward.
trainingData: No reward training. Metaworld (Drawer-Close, Door-Close, Button-Press, etc.) and Franka Kitchen (Kettle, Slide, Hinge).

headlineResults.comparedTo: GAIL, AIRL (given true state and one demo)

headlineResults.benchmark: Harder tasks after pretraining + one-demo fine-tuning

whatChangedVsParent: Uses a video (not image) VLM so the reward captures motion, and allows out-of-domain human video or text as the task spec.
limitations: Works best where the environment aligns visually with the VLM's training data; biases of large VLMs can carry into agents; multiple demos blended by dot product helped less than one.
notes: Static-image CLIP ablation gave no useful pretraining signal.

name: TOPReward
resolvedTitle: TOPReward: Token Probabilities as Hidden Zero-Shot Rewards for Robotics
org: University of Washington; Allen Institute for AI; Amazon; UNC Chapel Hill
problem: Training-free VLM progress estimators like GVL work only with proprietary models because open-source VLMs are bad at producing calibrated numbers in text, and trained reward models need large curated datasets.
keyIdea: Skip numeric generation: feed a video prefix plus the instruction and ask whether the video completes the task, then use the log-probability of the token 'True' as a progress reward, evaluated over K prefixes and min-max normalized within the episode.
architecture: Frozen video VLM (Qwen3-VL-8B/32B, Molmo2-8B, Gemini-2.5-Pro); direct prompt scoring without chat template; success score combines prefix margin and full-video Yes/No log-odds; reward-weighted BC via clipped exp(beta * reward increment).
inputs: Video prefix and language instruction.
outputs: Per-prefix completion log-probability (progress), success score, BC weights.
trainingData: None for the reward. Evaluated on ManiRewardBench (130 real tasks, 4 platforms: Franka, SO-100/101, single and bimanual YAM) and 33 filtered Open X-Embodiment datasets.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real SO-100 reward-weighted BC, 'place doll in box'

whatChangedVsParent: Reads the VLM's internal token probability instead of asking it to generate progress numbers, making open-source VLMs usable as zero-shot progress rewards.
limitations: Inherits VLM perception limits for fine spatial or small-object states; per-episode normalization is non-causal; sensitive to chat template and answer-token choice; weaker with Gemini because the API forces a chat template.
notes: Training-free, so there are no weights of its own; backbones are open (Qwen3-VL, Molmo2). P14 lists it as a training-free progress verifier.

name: SuccessVQA
resolvedTitle: Vision-Language Models as Success Detectors
org: DeepMind; UC Berkeley
problem: Bespoke learned success detectors and reward models work only for narrow task and visual conditions and need new annotations for every variation.
keyIdea: Frame success detection as video question answering ('Did the robot successfully {task}?' -> yes/no) and fine-tune a pretrained Flamingo on human success annotations, giving one architecture across domains.
architecture: Flamingo 3B; vision encoder, Perceiver Resampler and cross-attention layers fine-tuned, language model frozen; 8-frame clips (211 frames downsampled from 30 to 1 FPS); episode verdict from first/last clip (robotics) or any-clip (playroom).
inputs: Short video clip plus success question.
outputs: Yes/no answer (binary success).
trainingData: IA Playroom: 546,887 trajectories (1,421,111 clips); real robot gear manipulation: 101,789 demonstrations over 6 tasks with human reward annotations; Ego4D FHO clips.
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces per-domain bespoke success classifiers with one fine-tuned generative VLM using a unified VQA format.
limitations: Still gaps vs bespoke models on some robot tasks (e.g. gear removal); large-VLM inference is slow for online use; needs enough in-domain fine-tuning data, since zero/few-shot is insufficient.
notes: P14 lists SuccessVQA as a trained-model task-success verifier, consistent with the paper (Flamingo fine-tuned on in-domain human labels). Zero-shot Flamingo was at chance (50%) on Ego4D, so fine-tuning is essential.

name: REFLECT
resolvedTitle: REFLECT: Summarizing Robot Experiences for Failure Explanation and Correction
org: Columbia University
problem: Robots need to detect and explain failures in long-horizon tasks, but LLMs reason over text while robot logs are unstructured multisensory streams, and prior failure-explanation work covered only narrow failure types.
keyIdea: Convert multisensory robot data (RGB-D, audio, proprioception) into a hierarchical text summary (sensory scene graphs -> key-event captions -> subgoal-end states) and query an LLM progressively: verify each subgoal, explain execution failures from the event summary, else analyze the plan; the explanation then drives a correction planner.
architecture: Perception: MDETR object detection, CLIP object-state classification, AudioCLIP sound labels, heuristic spatial relations on aggregated semantic point clouds to build task-informed scene graphs. Reasoning and correction planning: GPT-4, with LLM actions mapped to executable ones via sentence embeddings.
inputs: Post-execution RGB-D video, audio, robot states; task, plan and goal.
outputs: Failure localization (timestep), natural-language explanation, correction plan.
trainingData: No training. RoboFail dataset: 100 AI2THOR failure scenarios (10 tasks x 10) and 30 real UR5e failure demos over 11 tasks.
whatChangedVsParent: Adds a multisensory hierarchical summary and progressive subgoal-first failure querying instead of open-ended LLM Q&A over raw captions.
limitations: Scene-graph heuristics may not hold in complex scenes; object-state detection needs a candidate state list; assumes the rest of the environment is static; less effective for low-level control failures.
notes: Post-hoc (not real-time) failure explanation. Audio was important: removing it cut real-world execution-failure explanation accuracy by about 20 points. RoboFail was later reused as an eval set by AHA and RoboFAC.

name: AHA
resolvedTitle: AHA: A Vision-Language-Model for Detecting and Reasoning Over Failures in Robotic Manipulation
org: NVIDIA; University of Washington; UCSP; MIT; NTU; Allen Institute for AI
problem: VLM/LLM-based robot systems treat failure detection as binary success classification and give no explanation of why a sub-task failed; there was no large failure dataset to train on.
keyIdea: Instruction-tune an open VLM to answer 'did this sub-task succeed? if not, why?' in free-form language, using FailGen, which procedurally perturbs successful simulated demos to create labeled failures in 7 modes (no grasp, slip, translation, rotation, missing rotation, wrong action order, wrong object).
architecture: LLaVA-v1.5 recipe: frozen image encoder and tokenizer, fine-tuned 2-layer projector and LLaMA-2-13B LLM; input image is a grid of keyframes (columns = time up to current sub-task, rows = camera views) plus a sub-task prompt.
inputs: Multi-view keyframe grid of the trajectory so far; sub-task description.
outputs: Yes/No success plus a natural-language failure reason.
trainingData: AHA dataset from FailGen over 79 RLBench tasks: about 49K failure image-question pairs, co-trained with 665K VQA conversations and 100K LVIS instances.

headlineResults.metric: average gain over six compared VLMs
headlineResults.comparedTo: LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT-34B, Qwen-VL, Gemini-1.5 Flash, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-ICL

headlineResults.benchmark: Downstream: Eureka reward reflection, PRoC3S TAMP, Manipulate-Anything verification

whatChangedVsParent: Turns failure detection into free-form failure reasoning and supplies a scalable procedural failure-data generator.
limitations: Explanations stay close to the 7 failure modes in the fine-tuning taxonomy; failure data come from perturbed simulation, not large pretrained policies' natural failures.
notes: Described as open-source by the authors. P14 lists AHA as a trained verifier for failure/uncertainty and for evaluating behavior.

name: RoboFAC
resolvedTitle: RoboFAC: A Comprehensive Framework for Robotic Failure Analysis and Correction
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)
problem: VLAs trained only on successful demos cannot diagnose or recover from failures, general MLLMs lack fine-grained manipulation-failure knowledge and are slow via API, and existing failure datasets are simple and give no multi-level corrections.
keyIdea: Build a large video QA dataset of manipulation failures with a 6-type hierarchical taxonomy (task planning, motion planning, execution control) and fine-tune a small Qwen2.5-VL to do task understanding, failure analysis and high-/low-level correction, used as an external critic for a running VLA.
architecture: Qwen2.5-VL (3B and 7B): frozen vision encoder, fully fine-tuned MLP merger and LLM for one epoch. Deployed alongside GR00T N1 to give high-level (sub-task sequence) and low-level (end-effector direction) corrections.
inputs: Robot manipulation video plus question.
outputs: Task identification/plan, success judgement, failure type, failing substage, explanation, high- and low-level corrections.
trainingData: 9,440 erroneous trajectories and 78,623 QA pairs across 53 scenes (14 simulated ManiSkill tasks, 6 real tasks); trained on 60K simulated QA pairs, tested on 10K sim + 8K real QA pairs (real data never used in training).
whatChangedVsParent: Uses video (not keyframe images), long-horizon and dynamic tasks, multi-dimensional QA, and low-level correction, and runs as a small local model.
limitations: Integration of corrections into the robot loop is not yet seamless; applied only to end-to-end VLAs, not hierarchical planner/controller stacks.
notes: Model and dataset released at github.com/MINT-SJTU/RoboFAC. In real-world perception-heavy dimensions (failure detection, task identification) GPT-4o still scored higher.

name: RoVer
resolvedTitle: RoVer: Robot Reward Model as Test-Time Verifier for Vision-Language-Action Model
org: SIAT (CAS); Peng Cheng Laboratory; Sun Yat-sen University; NTU; Shanghai AI Lab
problem: Improving VLAs usually means scaling data and model size, which is costly for robotics; VLA success also fluctuates run to run.
keyIdea: Test-time scaling for a frozen VLA: a small process reward model scores candidate actions and also predicts an action-space direction toward a better action; candidates are expanded along that direction and the top-scoring action is executed, with shared perception features cached across candidates.
architecture: GPT-2-style transformer initialized from GR-1 (MAE vision encoder, CLIP text encoder, Perceiver Resampler), action amplifier MLP, reward head and direction head. Trained with Bradley-Terry preference loss on anchor-centered better/worse action pairs (closer to expert = better) plus cosine direction loss.
inputs: Current third-person and wrist RGB, robot state, language, candidate 7-D action.
outputs: Scalar process reward and normalized refinement direction (6-D pose on CALVIN).
actionRepr: Selects among 7-DoF end-effector delta actions (6-D pose + gripper) from the base policy.
trainingData: CALVIN ABC split (only 20% of training set sampled), 100 epochs.
whatChangedVsParent: Compared with RoboMonkey's 7B verifier, uses a 0.2B verifier that also predicts a refinement direction to guide candidate expansion.
limitations: For chunked policies like MoDE, only the first action of each chunk is scored, so gains are less stable (chunk-step mismatch).
notes: ICLR 2026. Also tested on a real robot with Diffusion Policy as base.

name: AHEAD
resolvedTitle: Intercepting the Future: Latent-Space Predictive World Model for Dynamic VLA Manipulation
org: Carnegie Mellon University
problem: VLAs assume the scene is static between observation and execution, so they fail on moving objects (conveyors, rolling balls, projectiles) where latency exceeds the time available to grasp.
keyIdea: A predict-then-act wrapper: a small motion-aware latent world model forecasts future VLA patch tokens for task-relevant moving patches, rolls forward until sample variance (uncertainty) crosses a threshold, and feeds the predicted tokens to the frozen VLA action decoder.
architecture: Frozen OpenVLA 7B (vision encoder, Llama 2 backbone, action head). Added: RAFT optical flow for per-patch velocity/acceleration; language-and-motion saliency mask selecting 30-60 of 196 patches; 4-layer transformer encoder to a compact latent; conditional flow-matching dynamics with analytical kinematic conditioning V_k = V_0 + A k dt; S=5 samples for uncertainty-based adaptive halting (K_max = 10); MLP decoder splicing tokens back.
inputs: Three consecutive RGB frames, language instruction.
outputs: Predicted future patch tokens, which the frozen OpenVLA turns into an action.
actionRepr: OpenVLA's discrete tokenized 7-DoF actions (unchanged).
params: 4.9M trainable on top of frozen 7B OpenVLA
trainingData: Pretraining on manipulation video features, then fine-tuning on about 200 in-domain xArm 7 trajectories.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real xArm 7, conveyor and rolling-ball tasks

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike LaDi-WM, uses flow matching with explicit optical-flow kinematics and adaptive spatial/temporal rollout instead of full-scene fixed-horizon latent diffusion.
limitations: Assumes roughly constant-acceleration object motion over the horizon; highly stochastic post-collision dynamics break this and performance degrades.
notes: P14 groups AHEAD under 'predictive lookahead with world models' as a trained inference-time verifier; its uncertainty from 5 sampled rollouts governs how far to predict rather than selecting among actions.

name: FOREWARN
resolvedTitle: From Foresight to Forethought: VLM-In-the-Loop Policy Steering via Latent Alignment
org: Carnegie Mellon University; UC Berkeley
problem: Generative imitation policies often contain the right behavior mode but pick a wrong or context-inappropriate one at runtime, and off-the-shelf VLMs cannot judge the consequences of low-level action plans.
keyIdea: Split steering into foresight and forethought: a latent world model predicts the outcome of each candidate action plan, and a VLM aligned to those latent states narrates each predicted outcome in text and then picks the plan that best fits the task description.
architecture: DreamerV3 RSSM world model (frozen after pretraining) predicts T=64 latent states per plan (downsampled to T/4); latents are linearly projected into Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct's token space and the projector + LLM are LoRA fine-tuned to produce behavior narrations. At runtime: 100 Diffusion Policy samples grouped into K=6 modes via NMS, narrated, then the VLM selects one.
inputs: Current observation (wrist + third-person images, proprioception), candidate action plans, task description.
outputs: Behavior narration per plan and the selected plan index.
actionRepr: Selects among 64-step action plans sampled from a Diffusion Policy.
trainingData: Per task: 100 teleoperated demos for the base policy and 250 real rollouts (successes and failures) plus demos for the world model (300 train, 50 test); manually annotated narrations for VLM fine-tuning.

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Cup / Bag / Fork, novel task descriptions

whatChangedVsParent: Lets a VLM verify candidate plans by reasoning over world-model latents translated to text rather than over raw actions or decoded images.
limitations: Assumes the base policy already contains a good mode; errors come mainly from imprecise world-model imagination with limited data; inference overhead of large models; Llama-3.2 visual reasoning is weaker than its language reasoning.
notes: RSS 2025. An initial title search resolved to an unrelated paper (SAPS, 2606.15568); corrected via arXiv id. P14 lists FOREWARN as a pretrained-verifier inference-time method.

name: Foresight
resolvedTitle: Foresight: Failure Detection for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation with Action-Conditioned World Model Latents
org: University of Michigan; Princeton University; University of Virginia
problem: Failure detection for long-horizon manipulation is underexplored: failure onset is ambiguous, dense temporal labels are unavailable, and existing detectors use policy-specific internals or short-horizon visual anomalies.
keyIdea: Feed action-conditioned predicted latents from a world model (what the scene should look like after the policy's next action chunk) into a causal sequence detector trained only on trajectory-level success/failure labels, with time-varying thresholds from functional conformal prediction.
architecture: V-JEPA 2-AC: frozen ViT-Giant encoder plus a 24-layer action-conditioned predictor trained from scratch per dataset; latents mean-pooled to 1408-d; detector = 2-layer causal Transformer (dim 256, 4 heads) with sinusoidal positions, sigmoid failure score; FCP calibration on held-out successful rollouts.
inputs: 8-frame observation window and the policy's predicted action chunk (7-D to 23-D depending on robot).
outputs: Per-timestep failure score and alarm when it exceeds the calibrated threshold.
trainingData: Rollouts from OpenVLA, pi0-FAST, pi0.5 (sim) on LIBERO-Long, ManiSkill-Long (4 tasks with 8+ subgoals) and BEHAVIOR-1K (avg 8,557 steps); real ReactorX-200 (ACT, pi0.5, SmolVLA) and Franka (GR00T N1.5) rollouts.
whatChangedVsParent: Uses action-conditioned world-model latents instead of policy-internal features, so the same detector design works across policies.
limitations: Large world models add compute and latency, limiting use for fast reactive tasks; conformal guarantees require calibration data matching deployment; cross-policy transfer can be asymmetric.
notes: P14: Foresight monitors the single committed action block rather than comparing candidates, and uses conformal calibration with trajectory-level labels, matching the paper.

name: GRAPE
resolvedTitle: GRAPE: Generalizing Robot Policy via Preference Alignment
org: UNC-Chapel Hill; University of Washington; University of Chicago
problem: VLAs trained by supervised fine-tuning only imitate successful rollouts, generalize poorly to unseen tasks, and cannot be aligned to objectives like safety or efficiency; on-policy RL with explicit rewards is too costly.
keyIdea: Trajectory-wise preference optimization (TPO, a DPO-style loss over whole trajectories) on the VLA's own online rollouts, with preferences ranked by a guided-cost reward: VLM-decomposed stages, keypoint-based stage costs written by GPT-4o, the policy's own likelihood, and task success.
architecture: OpenVLA 7B backbone with LoRA. GCPG reward = 0.01 * self log-likelihood + 0.01 * prod_stage exp(-cost) + 2 * success; stage decomposition by Hamster VLM, keypoints via Grounded-SAM / SAM + DINOv2; top vs bottom trajectories per task paired; iterated for several rounds.
inputs: Image observation and language instruction (OpenVLA).
outputs: Discrete tokenized 7-DoF actions (OpenVLA).
actionRepr: OpenVLA autoregressive discretized 7-DoF end-effector actions.
trainingData: Real Franka SFT set of 220 pick-and-place, 50 button-press, 50 knock-down demos; TPO sampled 5 trajectories per task over 15 tasks; simulation in Simpler-Env and LIBERO.

headlineResults.metric: success rate gain, in-domain / unseen tasks

whatChangedVsParent: Moves preference optimization from step-level DPO to trajectory level and automates preference labels with VLM-generated stage costs.
notes: P14 lists GRAPE as model-intrinsic (self-reward) verifier for safety and execution quality, and under direct reward optimization for policy learning.

name: Demo-SCORE
resolvedTitle: Curating Demonstrations using Online Experience
org: Stanford University
problem: Demonstration datasets mix strategies of varying reliability; some are hard for a robot policy to reproduce, and such unreliable demos are hard even for humans to spot.
keyIdea: Train a policy on all demos, roll it out at several checkpoints, train a small classifier to separate successful from failed rollout states (cross-validated across checkpoints to avoid overfitting), then drop demos whose average predicted success is below a threshold and retrain.
architecture: Step classifier: small MLP (2 hidden layers, 8 units) on proprioceptive state with dropout 0.3 and weight decay 0.1; C=4 (sim) or 5 (real) checkpoints; threshold = mean predicted success over the chosen classifier's training rollouts. Base policies: Diffusion Policy (Robosuite) and ACT (ALOHA).
inputs: Proprioceptive states of rollouts (with success labels) and of demonstrations.
outputs: Filtered demonstration set (episode or chunk level).
trainingData: Simulated Robosuite square peg and ALOHA peg insertion with mixed-strategy demos (e.g. 200 Human + 400 scripted); real ALOHA tasks (Strawberry, Chocolate, Jellybean, Sharpie, Spoon); as few as 10 rollouts per checkpoint.

headlineResults.benchmark: Square peg with only 10 rollouts per checkpoint

whatChangedVsParent: Uses the policy's own rollout outcomes to label which demonstrated strategies are reliable, instead of hand curation or loss-based weighting.
notes: Name in P14 is Demo-SCORE (Chen et al.); the arXiv title is 'Curating Demonstrations using Online Experience'. Cross-validation across checkpoints was crucial: without it average success dropped from 94.4% to 88.5%.

name: SCIZOR
resolvedTitle: SCIZOR: A Self-Supervised Approach to Data Curation for Large-Scale Imitation Learning
org: UT Austin; NVIDIA Research
problem: Large imitation-learning datasets mix in suboptimal and redundant transitions; existing robot curation needs manual labels and works only at dataset or trajectory granularity, ignoring the quality of individual state-action pairs.
keyIdea: Self-supervised, transition-level curation: a task-progress predictor (trained with temporal-distance classification) removes chunks that make less progress than elapsed time, and a joint state-action deduplication module removes redundant chunks.
architecture: Two modules: (1) a lightweight progress estimator on the first/last frames of each chunk, scoring suboptimality V = T - T_p with temporal discounting and a transition/trajectory score mixture; (2) a video encoder on frames+actions, K-means clustering, and removal of chunks whose intra-cluster cosine similarity exceeds a threshold (SemDeDup-style).
inputs: Demonstration trajectories (video frames + actions)
outputs: Curated dataset (deletion masks over state-action chunks) used to train any IL policy
trainingData: Open X-Embodiment (>1M trajectories; Octo trained with Magic Soup and RT-X mixtures), RoboMimic Multi-Human (Can, Square), Sirius-Fleet (1,500 real rollouts with human interventions, 8 tasks)
whatChangedVsParent: Moves curation from dataset-level (Re-Mix) or trajectory-level (DemInf, Demo-SCORE) to individual state-action transitions, without annotations or online rollouts.
limitations: Deduplication simply concatenates state and action features; assumes most data within a trajectory is good; assumes roughly linear task progress, so it can misflag deliberate pauses or repetitive behaviors (e.g., stirring, waiting).
notes: Published at ICRA 2026 per the P14 survey reference. On RoboMimic it underperforms trajectory-level DemInf because that dataset is explicitly split by operator quality. Manual analysis shows removed segments are mostly manipulation failures, lagging motion and stalls.

name: Tri-Info
resolvedTitle: Tri-Info: Generalizable, Interpretable Failure Prediction for VLA Models via Information Theory
org: InfoBodied AI Lab, The University of Hong Kong
problem: Existing VLA failure detectors are either embedding-based (strong in-domain but tied to one architecture's latent geometry, no transfer) or single-score (e.g., STAC) with little diagnostic value; none is both generalizable and interpretable.
keyIdea: Treat VLA control as a closed-loop information pipeline; successful and failed rollouts show different entropy/mutual-information signatures. Three signals, H(A_t), I(A_t;A_t+1) and I(S_t,S_t+1;A_t), capture action diversity, temporal consistency and action-state coupling, and they transfer across models because they do not depend on embedding coordinates.
architecture: Eight entropy/MI metrics computed over sliding windows of state embeddings (visual encoder) and action embeddings (pre-decoder layer, or final-step velocity field for flow models), reduced to three by correlation analysis; one GRU per signal, fused, with a functional conformal-prediction time-varying threshold.
inputs: Per-step state and action embeddings from any VLA
outputs: Per-timestep failure probability plus an alarm when it crosses a conformal threshold; per-signal diagnostics (freeze, drift, phantom grasp)
trainingData: 3,290 rollouts (2,495 success / 795 fail) from 6 VLAs (pi0, pi0.5, FLOWER, UniVLA, GR-1, ACT) on LIBERO-10, CALVIN, ALOHA sim, plus real ALOHA (120 cup-on-plate, 60 block-in-cup)

headlineResults.benchmark: Sim-to-real + morphology shift (pi0.5 LIBERO -> ACT ALOHA-real)

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces architecture-specific embedding classifiers (SAFE) and single consistency scores (STAC) with a small set of information-theoretic signals that transfer across models, environments and sim-to-real without retraining.
limitations: Its diagnostics are alarms, not recovery actions; it matches but does not beat the best baselines in-domain, where temporal modelling of any single signal already saturates accuracy.
notes: The alpha threshold trades earlier alarms for accuracy, and the trade-off is not strictly monotonic.

name: HideAndSeek
resolvedTitle: Hide-and-Seek in Trajectories: Discovering Failure Signals for VLA Runtime Monitoring
org: University of Wisconsin-Madison; Georgia Institute of Technology
problem: Step-level failure labels are expensive; SAFE-style detectors copy the trajectory label to every timestep, which mislabels the normal actions before failure onset, and resampling or VLM-judge monitors are too slow for real time.
keyIdea: Treat failure detection as coarsely supervised (MIL-like) learning. An inter-trajectory contrastive loss makes the most failure-like step of a failed rollout score above the most failure-like step of a successful one. An intra-trajectory loss pushes post-onset scores above pre-onset scores around a proxy onset, the sharpest score increase.
architecture: LSTM detector over window-pooled VLA action embeddings (action token or action head; hidden state before the velocity head at the final denoising step for flow models); one-sided functional conformal prediction gives time-varying thresholds.
inputs: Per-step internal action embeddings of a VLA (OpenVLA, pi0, pi0.5)
outputs: Per-step failure score and a runtime alarm
trainingData: Rollouts with trajectory-level success labels from LIBERO-10, VLABench and a real UFactory xArm 6 (CUBE and KITCHEN suites), with seen/unseen task splits
whatChangedVsParent: Instead of assigning the trajectory label uniformly to every step as SAFE does, it localizes the failure-indicative steps with contrastive MIL-style losses (+19.4 bACC over uniform labelling on OpenVLA).
limitations: Averages over degree-of-freedom dimensions of embeddings (may lose joint-specific kinematic cues); purely perceptual failures may not show up in action embeddings alone.
notes: NeurIPS 2026. Code and videos are released via a project page. Failure onsets for timeliness analysis were annotated with GPT-5.2 and checked against human annotations.

name: MG-Select
resolvedTitle: Verifier-free Test-Time Sampling for Vision Language Action Models
org: KAIST; Seoul National University; RLWRLD
problem: Greedy single-inference VLAs lack precision; test-time scaling with external verifiers (V-GPS, RoboMonkey) needs extra RL/reward training and generalizes poorly to unseen conditions.
keyIdea: Masking Distribution Guided Selection: sample N action candidates and pick the one whose token distribution has the highest KL divergence from a reference distribution produced by the same VLA with the state and/or language inputs masked. The optional MG-Select* adds joint training with condition dropout.
architecture: Autoregressive VLA (pi0-FAST; also OpenVLA). Parallel temperature sampling of N candidates, token-wise KL(Q||P) against a condition-masked reference (temperature-regularized, tau=4), aggregated over the first 5 FAST tokens; a single shared prefill cuts latency.
inputs: Images, proprioceptive state, language instruction
outputs: Selected action chunk (Best-of-N)
actionRepr: FAST-tokenized action chunks decoded autoregressively; Best-of-N selection among N=4 candidates
trainingData: Fine-tuning on RoboCasa (30/100/300 demos per task), BridgeData V2 (for SIMPLER-WidowX), LIBERO; real Franka: pi0-FAST-DROID fine-tuned on 60 demos per task
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces an external trained verifier (value function or VLM reward model) with an intrinsic confidence score, KL to a condition-masked reference distribution from the same model.
limitations: Applies to autoregressive (token-distribution) VLAs; the best masking variant differs by environment (state masking works best on SIMPLER, text masking on RoboCasa); parallel sampling adds latency without the single-prefill optimization.
notes: The survey name 'MG-Select' is the method name; the paper title is 'Verifier-free Test-Time Sampling'. P14 cites it as ICLR 2026. On LIBERO with OpenVLA it lowers Spatial and Goal slightly while raising the average (69.2 to 70.8).

name: TACO
resolvedTitle: Steering Vision-Language-Action Models as Anti-Exploration: A Test-Time Scaling Approach
org: Institute of AI, China Telecom; USTC; Tsinghua University; HKUST
problem: After SFT, flow- or diffusion-based VLAs still carry redundant action modes from pretraining and multimodal demos, so success depends heavily on the sampled noise (0% to 80% on the same task for two fixed noises).
keyIdea: Test-time Anti-exploration via pseudo-COunts: train a Coin-Flipping Network (CFN) on the VLA's internal representations of SFT data, then sample several action chunks and execute the one with the highest pseudo-count, keeping actions within the support of the dataset as anti-exploration offline RL does, with no gradient updates to the VLA.
architecture: Frozen VLA (pi0, pi0.5, RDT, OpenVLA) plus a lightweight MLP CFN (residual MLP blocks, output dim 20) on internal representations from a single denoising step of noised actions; a shared observation KV cache reduces multi-sample latency.
inputs: Observation, instruction and candidate action chunks (via VLA internal features)
outputs: Selected action chunk with the maximum pseudo-count
actionRepr: Selects among N sampled action chunks (chunk size 50 in the RoboTwin setup) from the base VLA
trainingData: Task SFT datasets: RoboTwin 1.0/2.0, LIBERO, SimplerEnv (BridgeV2), plus a real dual-arm platform

headlineResults.comparedTo: OpenVLA reproduced 54.0%; RoboMonkey +6.7 (56.5% on its 49.8% base)

whatChangedVsParent: Turns the offline-RL anti-exploration penalty into a gradient-free test-time selector, using a pseudo-count estimator on VLA internal features instead of RL fine-tuning or a large learned verifier.
limitations: It cannot evaluate newly synthesized actions produced purely by perturbation, and it relies on the representational quality of the underlying VLA. It also assumes that SFT-data density correlates with success, so it only reinforces modes already present in the data.
notes: Code: github.com/breez3young/TACO. A shared observation KV cache cuts inference time by 73.2% at M=32 candidates (RTX 4090). On LIBERO-Long with pi0.5 it adds only +1.8 (94.8% to 96.6%).

name: VIPER
resolvedTitle: Video Prediction Models as Rewards for Reinforcement Learning
org: UC Berkeley
problem: Hand-designing rewards is laborious; video-based rewards that condition only on the current observation miss temporal structure, and adversarial ones (AMP/GAIfO) suffer mode collapse.
keyIdea: Train an autoregressive video prediction model on expert videos and use its conditional log-likelihood ln p(x_t+1 | x_{t-k:t}) of the agent's next frame as the reward, plus an exploration bonus derived from a KL/trajectory-distribution-matching objective.
architecture: VQ-GAN frame tokenizer (64x64 images to 8x8 or 16x16 codes) plus a VideoGPT-style autoregressive transformer with task conditioning; the reward is used with any RL algorithm (DrQ + RND, DreamerV3 + Plan2Explore).
inputs: Agent pixel observations (frame history)
outputs: Dense scalar reward per transition
trainingData: Expert videos: top-50 (DMC) / top-100 (Atari) of 1000 oracle rollouts per task; 100 motion-planner demos per RLBench task
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces discriminator-based (AMP) or single-frame rewards with likelihoods from a pretrained video prediction model, which capture temporal consistency and train stably.
limitations: Needs in-domain expert videos; on stochastic or noisy data the agent may seek states that minimize model uncertainty; results are sensitive to the VQ code size and context length (short context gives myopic behavior).
notes: Source code and datasets are released (escontrela.me/viper). Shows cross-embodiment generalization for tabletop manipulation. Diffusion Reward (Huang et al.) later argues that VIPER's log-likelihood reward drops for unseen expert videos.

name: Diffusion Reward
resolvedTitle: Diffusion Reward: Learning Rewards via Conditional Video Diffusion
org: Shanghai Qi Zhi Institute; CUHK; Sichuan University; Tsinghua IIIS; Shanghai AI Lab
problem: Video-likelihood rewards (VIPER) struggle to model complex expert video distributions and give poor rewards on out-of-distribution expert videos; adversarial rewards are brittle.
keyIdea: A video diffusion model conditioned on expert-like history generates less diverse futures, so the negative conditional entropy of the history-conditioned diffusion model serves as a reward, combined with an RND novelty bonus and the sparse task reward.
architecture: VQ-GAN latent codes plus a VQ-Diffusion transformer conditioned on the preceding frames; entropy is estimated via the variational bound from M (=1) denoised samples; the policy is trained with DrQv2.
inputs: Historical frames of the agent's visual observations (64x64 RGB)
outputs: Dense reward (negative conditional entropy + RND + sparse task reward)
trainingData: Action-free expert videos: 20 per MetaWorld task (5,039 frames) and 50 per Adroit task (3,346 frames); real robot: 20 videos (Allegro hand) and 50 expert videos (button press)

headlineResults.benchmark: Real Button Press offline RL (expert data)

whatChangedVsParent: Swaps VIPER's autoregressive VideoGPT log-likelihood reward for the conditional entropy of a video diffusion model, which generalizes better to unseen tasks.
limitations: Reward inference is slower than baselines (9.7 h wall time vs 8.3 to 8.8 h on the Door task); generalization to unseen tasks is weaker than on seen tasks, and the paper suggests larger models or text conditioning to improve it.
notes: ECCV 2024. Code is at diffusion-reward.github.io. Zero-shot rewards work on 8 unseen MetaWorld tasks.

name: MOPO
resolvedTitle: MOPO: Model-based Offline Policy Optimization
org: Stanford University; UC Berkeley
problem: Model-free offline RL constrains the policy to the data support and cannot generalize beyond it, while online model-based RL has no mechanism against exploiting model errors under offline distribution shift.
keyIdea: Optimize the policy in an uncertainty-penalized MDP whose reward is r - lambda*u(s,a), where u is an estimate of dynamics-model error. The paper proves this maximizes a lower bound on the true return and trades off gain against the risk of leaving the data support.
architecture: MBPO backbone: an ensemble of N probabilistic Gaussian dynamics models (next state + reward); penalty u(s,a) = max over the ensemble of the Frobenius norm of the predicted std; short model rollouts from dataset states; policy trained with SAC on real + model data.
inputs: Static offline dataset of (s, a, r, s') transitions
outputs: Policy
actionRepr: Continuous actions from a SAC Gaussian policy
trainingData: D4RL MuJoCo (halfcheetah, hopper, walker2d; random, medium, mixed, medium-expert), plus OOD tasks halfcheetah-jump and ant-angle
whatChangedVsParent: Adds an uncertainty-based soft reward penalty to MBPO so model-based policy optimization becomes safe offline; MOReL instead uses a hard HALT threshold.
limitations: The ensemble-variance error estimator has no theoretical guarantee; performance on narrow datasets (e.g., D4RL medium) could improve with policy regularization; it fails when the new task needs states entirely outside the data support (ant at 60 or 90 degrees).
notes: NeurIPS 2020; code at github.com/tianheyu927/mopo. The D4RL table values were not in the retrieved pages. For the verifier surveys, MOPO's ensemble-uncertainty penalty is the canonical example of a model-intrinsic verifier (P14 ref 41).

name: MOReL
resolvedTitle: MOReL: Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning
org: Cornell University; University of Washington; Google Brain; Microsoft Research India
problem: Offline RL had been almost entirely model-free; naive model-based planning on a learned model exploits model errors in regions not covered by the data.
keyIdea: Learn a pessimistic MDP: an unknown state-action detector (USAD) flags pairs where the model cannot be trusted, and these transition to an absorbing HALT state with a large negative reward. Policy value in this P-MDP approximately lower-bounds true value, and the resulting method is minimax optimal up to log factors.
architecture: Ensemble of 4 two-layer ReLU MLP dynamics models; practical USAD thresholds the maximum pairwise ensemble discrepancy; policy is a 2-layer tanh MLP trained with model-based NPG, optionally initialized from behavior cloning.
inputs: Static offline dataset of transitions
outputs: Policy
actionRepr: Continuous actions from an MLP Gaussian policy
trainingData: Gym MuJoCo (Hopper, HalfCheetah, Ant, Walker2d) with 5 logging-policy datasets each (about 1M steps per dataset), plus D4RL

headlineResults.comparedTo: best prior (BRAC) SOTA in 5 of 20; BCQ, BEAR

whatChangedVsParent: Applies E3/R-MAX-style known/unknown partitioning to the offline setting as pessimism (HALT state), rather than as optimism for exploration.
limitations: USAD relies on a heuristic ensemble-discrepancy threshold (a tunable hyperparameter) instead of the idealized TV-distance guarantee; how well it works depends on data coverage and representation quality.
notes: NeurIPS 2020 (the arXiv v3 adds D4RL results). Unlike MOPO's soft penalty, MOReL uses a hard termination threshold. In the verifier taxonomy it is a model-intrinsic, uncertainty-based verifier.

name: Ward et al. (world-model uncertainty)
resolvedTitle: Foundational World Models Accurately Detect Bimanual Manipulator Failures
org: Stanford University; Watney Robotics
problem: Failure modes of bimanual visuomotor robots cannot be written down by hand in their huge image and proprioceptive state spaces, and multi-camera high-rate data makes real-time anomaly detection hard.
keyIdea: Train a probabilistic, history-conditioned world model on nominal data only, in the latent space of NVIDIA's pretrained Cosmos Tokenizer. Its predictive uncertainty (the mean predicted std) is used as a non-conformity score, with conformal prediction calibrating the failure threshold.
architecture: Cosmos Tokenizer latents of gripper-camera views, fused with learned projections of proprioceptive state and actions, fed to a transformer that predicts a Gaussian tensor over future latents (VAE-style); curriculum up to a 32-step autoregressive horizon; about 569.7k trainable parameters.
inputs: History window of multi-view images, proprioceptive states (52-D) and actions (41-D)
outputs: Next-state prediction with uncertainty; failure alarm via a conformal threshold
trainingData: Push-T (1,028 nominal training rollouts; 2,048 failure rollouts over 4 modes for evaluation); new Bimanual Cable Manipulation dataset from WR1 data-center robots (83 nominal train/val, 7 calibration, 7 nominal + 9 failure test)
whatChangedVsParent: Uses a world model's own predictive uncertainty, computed in a frozen foundation-model latent space, as the failure score instead of density or reconstruction-based OOD scores.
limitations: Conformal exchangeability assumptions are violated; benign distribution shifts (e.g., background color) can raise false alarms; it inherits unknown biases from the pretrained tokenizer; the real dataset is small.
notes: Resolved as the Ward et al. paper cited by P14 (ICRA 2026). The authors state the gain over the next-best learned method as +3.8% failure-detection rate. The data-center robot was teleoperated remotely, so the failures come from a manual policy, not an autonomous one.

name: Latent reachability (Nakamura)
resolvedTitle: Generalizing Safety Beyond Collision-Avoidance via Latent-Space Reachability Analysis
org: Carnegie Mellon University; TU Delft
problem: Hamilton-Jacobi reachability has been limited to hand-engineered collision constraints on low-dimensional states with first-principles dynamics, so it cannot guard against failures that are hard to write down but visible in images (spills, toppling).
keyIdea: Latent Safety Filters run HJ reachability inside the latent space of a generative world model. The failure set is specified as a classifier on latents, and a discounted safety Bellman equation is solved by RL in the world model's imagination, giving both a safety monitor V and a safety policy that overrides the base policy when V is near zero.
architecture: World model (RSSM in simulation; DINO-WM with a DINOv2 encoder on hardware) + latent failure classifier l(z) trained with a margin loss on safe/unsafe observations + an RL-approximated safety value function (DDQN-style) + a least-restrictive switching filter (threshold epsilon = 0.4).
inputs: RGB observations (3rd-person + wrist cameras) and proprioception; the base policy's proposed action
outputs: Safety value (monitor) and a filtered action (task action or safety-policy action)
actionRepr: Filter over the base policy's actions (switches to a learned safety policy)
trainingData: Diverse robot observation-action data of mixed quality (successes, random exploration, unsafe demos) for world-model learning, plus binary safe/failure labels on observations; tasks: Dubins car, simulated block manipulation in clutter, real Franka Research 3 lifting an open Skittles bag
whatChangedVsParent: Moves HJ reachability from a hand-specified low-dimensional state space into a learned world-model latent space, with failures specified by a learned classifier instead of signed distance functions.
limitations: Can only protect against outcomes the world model can predict, so some unsafe data is needed; the least-restrictive filter acts at the last moment; it must be recomputed for new constraints; errors in the world model, classifier and value function mean there are no formal guarantees; it failed on OOD M&M bags whose dynamics differ.
notes: RSS 2025. Follow-ups in the survey: AnySafe (constraint-parameterized latent filters), uncertainty-aware latent safety filters (Seo et al.), and latent CBFs.

name: PNCBF
resolvedTitle: How to Train Your Neural Control Barrier Function: Learning Safety Filters for Complex Input-Constrained Systems
org: MIT; MIT Lincoln Laboratory
