problem: Valid control barrier functions are hard to construct for high-relative-degree systems with input limits; neural CBFs need a known safe set and scale poorly, while grid-based HJ reachability is impractical above about 5 state dimensions.
keyIdea: The maximum-over-time constraint-violation value function of any nominal policy is itself a valid CBF, so a neural CBF can be learned by policy evaluation. Iterating (CBF-QP controller becomes the new nominal policy) acts as policy iteration and grows the safe set.
architecture: MLP value network (3x256, tanh) trained with a discounted max-over-time policy-evaluation loss on rollouts of the nominal policy; used online in a CBF quadratic program that minimally modifies any nominal control; up to 3 policy-iteration rounds.
inputs: System state (known control-affine dynamics) and nominal control
outputs: CBF value; safety-filtered control via CBF-QP
actionRepr: Continuous control filtered by a QP under box input constraints
trainingData: Rollouts of a nominal policy in simulation: double integrator, Segway, F-16 ground-collision avoidance (16-D state, 3-D control), two-agent quadcopter (12-D state, 4-D control); hardware: two quadrotors avoiding a Boston Dynamics Spot
whatChangedVsParent: Learns the CBF by policy evaluation of a max-over-time cost instead of minimizing CBF-condition violation losses, so it needs no hand-picked safe set and handles input constraints.
limitations: Requires an accurate dynamics model (model errors can make the filter unsafe on real systems); without separate verification of the descent condition, the learned PNCBF carries no formal safety guarantee.
notes: ICRA 2024 (P14 ref 28). This is a control-theory safety filter rather than a manipulation method; the verifier survey lists it under rule-based/formal physical-constraint verification.

name: RoboReward
resolvedTitle: RoboReward: General-Purpose Vision-Language Reward Models for Robotics
org: Stanford University; UC Berkeley
problem: Real-robot RL is bottlenecked by rewards that need human labels or brittle hand-crafting; VLM reward models are poorly evaluated on real robots, and robot datasets (OXE) are success-heavy with few failures to learn from.
keyIdea: Build a reward dataset by 'inverse-HER' negative augmentation: counterfactually relabel successful episodes with wrong or near-miss instructions, and temporally clip them into partial-progress outcomes. Then fine-tune VLMs to predict a 1 to 5 end-of-episode progress score.
architecture: Fine-tuned Qwen3-VL Instruct (4B and 8B) video-language models that take the task text and rollout video and output a discrete progress label in {1..5}.
inputs: Task instruction + full rollout video
outputs: Episodic progress score 1 to 5 (used as a sparse RL reward)
trainingData: ~45,000 scored episodes from OXE (subsampled up to 1,200 per dataset) and RoboArena (DROID); 54,135 augmented examples in total; RoboRewardBench test set has 2,831 human-verified episodes over 14 embodiments

headlineResults.metric: correlation of reward accuracy with RL performance

whatChangedVsParent: Unlike OpenGVL (value order on successful expert videos, 6 tasks), it trains and benchmarks VLMs for episodic reward over successes and failures across many embodiments, using synthetic negatives.
limitations: Limited to short-horizon, end-of-episode rewards; still well short of human rewards in RL; generalization across embodiments is uneven (e.g., weak on UTokyo xArm Bimanual with error 1.394).
notes: Dataset, 4B/8B checkpoints and the evaluation suite are released (HELM leaderboard). Ablation: removing negative augmentation raises overall MAE from 0.845 to 1.450. The RL algorithm used was DSRL on a BridgeData V2 diffusion policy.

name: OpenGVL
resolvedTitle: OpenGVL - Benchmarking Visual Temporal Progress for Data Curation
org: Lute; IDEAS Research Institute; Simple Automation; Poznan University of Technology; University of Warsaw
problem: Public robot data is growing fast (more than 2.6M episodes on Hugging Face as of Aug 2025) but is poorly curated. GVL showed that VLMs can predict task progress, but only closed models had been evaluated and there was no open benchmark or tool.
keyIdea: Replicate and extend Generative Value Learning (in-context VLM progress prediction on shuffled frames, scored by Value-Order Correlation) as an open benchmark for open-source VLMs, and use VOC to flag bad episodes and datasets for curation.
architecture: Benchmark and tooling, not a new model: VLM prompted with 0 or 2 context episodes and 15 shuffled frames, outputs per-frame completion %, scored by VOC (rank correlation with true frame order); hidden human and bimanual electronic-assembly tasks prevent contamination; Hugging Face Space leaderboard.
inputs: Task instruction + shuffled video frames (plus optional in-context example episodes)
outputs: Per-frame task-completion percentages; VOC score per episode/dataset
trainingData: Evaluation only: 50 episodes each from nyu_door, berkeley_mvp, cmu_stretch, nyu_franka (OXE/LeRobot) plus 2 hidden tasks; curation case studies on LeRobot Hub datasets
parents: GVL (Vision Language Models are In-Context Value Learners)
whatChangedVsParent: Open-source replication and extension of GVL with a public benchmark, hidden tasks, open-model comparison, and a data-curation workflow.
limitations: All models were tested at temperature 1.0 with a single prompt template; trajectories were sampled uniformly from expert demonstrations; a high VOC is necessary but not sufficient evidence of data quality.
notes: CoRL 2025. Benchmark and code are public (Hugging Face Space). RoboReward later contrasts itself with OpenGVL: OpenGVL measures value order on successful demos only, with few tasks.

name: DP-Attacker
resolvedTitle: Diffusion Policy Attacker: Crafting Adversarial Attacks for Diffusion-based Policies
org: Georgia Institute of Technology
problem: Diffusion policies had not been studied under adversarial attack, and standard gradient attacks on end-to-end networks do not work well on their chained, stochastic denoising.
keyIdea: A white-box attack suite that perturbs the conditioning image by attacking the one-step noise-prediction loss instead of the full denoising chain. It covers online vs offline, global digital perturbations vs physical patches, and targeted vs untargeted attacks, all optimized with PGD.
architecture: PGD on the image (L-inf budget sigma, e.g. 0.03) maximizing (untargeted) or minimizing toward a target action (targeted) the DDPM noise-prediction error of the DP denoiser; patches trained with random affine transforms and rendered as textured boxes in simulation.
inputs: Visual observations of a pretrained (white-box) Diffusion Policy
outputs: Adversarial image perturbation or physical adversarial patch
trainingData: Attacks on Chi et al.'s released Diffusion Policy checkpoints (CNN and Transformer) on PushT and Robomimic Can, Lift, Square, Transport, Tool Hang (PH/MH)

headlineResults.benchmark: Robomimic Square PH (Transformer DP), targeted online

parents: adversarial attacks on latent diffusion models
whatChangedVsParent: Adapts diffusion-model adversarial losses (noise-prediction loss) to attack the observation conditioning of diffusion policies, instead of an end-to-end action loss or the diffused variable.
limitations: Simulation only (no real-world tests); no defense proposed; assumes white-box access.
notes: Analysis suggests the visual encoder is what gets attacked (large shifts in encoded features). A perturbation under 3% of pixel range can drop success from 100% to 0%.

name: UADA / UPA / TMA
resolvedTitle: Exploring the Adversarial Vulnerabilities of Vision-Language-Action Models in Robotics
org: Rochester Institute of Technology; U.S. Naval Research Laboratory; Lamar University; Meta AI; UMKC; University of Rochester; Rutgers University
problem: The adversarial robustness of VLAs had barely been studied, and standard classifier attacks do not target what matters for robots: fine-grained discretized actions (adjacent bins differ by about 0.007) and spatial trajectories.
keyIdea: Three robot-specific objectives optimize a small adversarial image patch: UADA (Untargeted Action Discrepancy Attack) maximizes normalized action deviation via probability-weighted bins; UPA (Untargeted Position-aware Attack) distorts end-effector direction and magnitude; TMA (Targeted Manipulation Attack) uses cross-entropy to push chosen DoFs toward a target.
architecture: Patch optimization (5% of a 224x224 image) with AdamW, inner loops and random affine/rotation transforms (EoT-style) against OpenVLA's tokenized 256-bin action head; white-box, with transfer across OpenVLA-LIBERO variants.
inputs: Camera image of a white-box OpenVLA (patch pasted into view)
outputs: Adversarial patch (digital or printed physical)
trainingData: Patches generated with openvla-7b-libero-long (simulation) and openvla-7b on BridgeData V2 (physical); evaluated on LIBERO Spatial/Object/Goal/Long and a real UR10e + Robotiq gripper
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces generic misclassification objectives with action-space and geometry-aware objectives tailored to discretized VLA robot actions.
limitations: Physical-world attacks are much weaker than digital ones (>43% vs 85.9%); patches are model-specific; evaluated mainly on OpenVLA variants; common defenses (JPEG, noise, median blur, bit depth) mostly fail to stop it, and no defense is proposed beyond suggestions.
notes: Survey (P13) name 'UADA / UPA / TMA' refers to this one paper's three attack objectives. Code is linked via an anonymous repository. The generated patches visually resemble robot-arm joints, which the authors read as a training-view bias.

name: Tex3D
resolvedTitle: Tex3D: Objects as Attack Surfaces via Adversarial 3D Textures for Vision-Language-Action Models
org: East China Normal University; Zhongguancun Academy; CFAR A*STAR; Tsinghua University; Harbin Institute of Technology
problem: Existing VLA attacks use language perturbations or 2D patches, which are view-specific, conspicuous and hard to deploy physically. Adversarial 3D object textures are more realistic, but simulators like MuJoCo give no gradient path back to object appearance.
keyIdea: End-to-end optimization of adversarial 3D textures on manipulated objects. Foreground-Background Decoupling renders the target object in differentiable Nvdiffrast, aligned with MuJoCo, and composites it into the scene. Trajectory-Aware Adversarial Optimization weights behaviorally critical frames and parameterizes the texture as per-vertex colors.
architecture: Dual renderer (MuJoCo background + Nvdiffrast foreground with MVP and lighting alignment); frame weights from latent velocity/acceleration of a pretrained visual encoder via temperature softmax; vertex-color texture parameterization; untargeted and targeted action-loss objectives; EoT for physical transfer.
inputs: White-box VLA, task instruction, target object mesh
outputs: Adversarial texture map for the object
trainingData: LIBERO (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long) with OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, pi0, pi0.5; plus real-robot tests
whatChangedVsParent: Moves VLA attacks from 2D image patches to object-bound 3D textures optimized through a differentiable rendering path inside the simulator, and adds trajectory-aware frame weighting.
limitations: Naturalness-constrained (L0) perturbations are somewhat less effective than unconstrained ones (a stealth vs strength trade-off); it needs white-box gradients and object meshes; per-step optimization costs about 7.2 s.
notes: ACM MM 2026. Project page: vla-attack.github.io/tex3d. Removing foreground/background decoupling raises per-step time from about 7.2 s to about 24.8 s.

name: VLA-Fool
resolvedTitle: When Alignment Fails: Multimodal Adversarial Attacks on Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Westlake University; Penn State; Sony Research; Xidian University
problem: Prior VLA attacks look at one modality at a time, mostly assume white-box access, and ignore cross-modal misalignment between perception and instruction.
keyIdea: One suite of textual, visual and cross-modal attacks under white-box and black-box threat models. Text: Semantically guided GCG (SGCG) with four linguistic modes, plus suffix/prefix prompt injection. Vision: object- or arm-mounted patches and noise. Cross-modal: maximize the change in patch-token cosine alignment.
architecture: Attack suite against OpenVLA-7B fine-tuned on LIBERO: SGCG (GCG with POS-constrained semantic candidate sets for referential ambiguity, attribute substitution, scope blurring, negation), black-box prompt injection, gradient-ascent patches (L2 action deviation), black-box noise families, and a cross-modal misalignment loss on vision/text embeddings.
inputs: Instruction text and/or camera image of the victim VLA
outputs: Adversarial instruction, patch/noise, or joint perturbation
trainingData: LIBERO (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long), 5 trials per task, fine-tuned OpenVLA-7B
whatChangedVsParent: Brings text, visual and cross-modal misalignment attacks together, including black-box variants, and adds semantically guided GCG focused on VLA-relevant linguistic cues.
limitations: Simulation only, on a single victim model (fine-tuned OpenVLA); real-robot evaluation and defenses are left as future work.
notes: The survey (P13) name 'VLA-Fool' is the framework name; the paper title is 'When Alignment Fails'. There is a text-inconsistency in the paper: the suffix-2 average is reported as 82.26% in the table but 83.33% in the text; the table value is used here.

name: JailWAM
resolvedTitle: JailWAM: Jailbreaking World Action Models in Robot Control
org: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Nanjing University; Defense Innovation Institute, Chinese Academy of Military Science
problem: World Action Models follow instructions and act directly, so jailbreak instructions can cause physical harm. LLM/VLM/video jailbreak evaluations judge digital outputs and do not transfer to heterogeneous low-level action outputs, and exhaustive closed-loop simulation of candidates is expensive.
keyIdea: A jailbreak evaluation framework for WAMs. LLM-generated jailbreak instructions from templates are screened by Visual-Trajectory Mapping, which renders actions as multi-view trajectory charts, and a fine-tuned VLM Risk Discriminator with three safety levels. A Dual-Path Verification Strategy confirms only flagged candidates in closed-loop simulation with human review.
architecture: LLM prompt generator (e.g., Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.5, GPT-5.2) + VTM (accumulated action displacements drawn as trajectory charts) + a Qwen3-VL Risk Discriminator fine-tuned on Gemini pre-annotations corrected by humans (Level 0 Safety Compliance, 1 Motion Failure, 2 Catastrophic Risk) + RoboTwin closed-loop verification.
inputs: Target WAM, initial observation/state, candidate jailbreak instructions
outputs: Jailbreak instructions verified to induce unsafe behavior; risk level per candidate
trainingData: RoboTwin simulation (LingBot-VA, Light-WAM, X-WAM, Image-WAM, Motus, X-VLA); zero-shot transfer to LIBERO (Cosmos-Policy, pi0.5)
whatChangedVsParent: Moves jailbreak evaluation from digital outputs to consequences of physical actions, with a cross-architecture visual trajectory representation and a learned risk screen.
limitations: Open-loop screening misses unsafe behaviors that only emerge in closed-loop execution (it caught 17 of 23 cases); many prompts depend on scene initialization (cross-seed reliability falls with more seeds); attacks transfer weakly to pi0.5 (5.0% ASR) and were weaker on X-WAM (23.0%).
notes: Formatted for AAAI 2027. Evaluation is simulation only. Transferred LIBERO attacks produced only Level-1 motion failures (no catastrophic cases).

name: RedVLA
resolvedTitle: RedVLA: Physical Red Teaming for Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Institute for AI, Peking University; State Key Laboratory of General AI
problem: There is no proactive way to find a VLA's physical safety risks before deployment. LLM/VLM red teaming targets semantic intent, and VLA attacks perturb pixels or prompts rather than the physical scene.
keyIdea: Physical red teaming: keep the instruction fixed and inject a single risk object into a task-feasible scene. Critical interaction regions come from benign end-effector trajectories. Gradient-free, trajectory-feature-driven optimization then refines the object's pose until a target unsafe predicate fires (state-level, cumulative or conditional safety costs).
architecture: Two stages: (I) Risk Scenario Synthesis (interaction identification from benign rollouts, a taxonomy of risk predicates, risk-object instantiation); (II) Risk Amplification (black-box iterative horizontal-plane pose updates guided by trajectory spatial features, at most 10 iterations). Defense: SimpleVLA-Guard, a lightweight monitor on internal VLA representations trained from RedVLA data.
inputs: Black-box VLA rollouts, benign scene, risk-object library, safety predicates
outputs: Risk scene configurations that elicit unsafe behaviors; guard model for online intervention
trainingData: LIBERO with 10 risk scenario suites (3 safety cost types x 4 hazard categories); victims: OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, VLA-Adapter, VLA-Adapter-Pro, pi0, pi0.5

headlineResults.benchmark: LIBERO risk suites, 5 models excl. OpenVLA

whatChangedVsParent: Shifts VLA red teaming from pixel/prompt perturbations toward black-box physical risk-object injection that preserves task feasibility and instruction semantics, and targets unsafe behavior rather than task failure.
limitations: Needs benchmarks where the victim VLA already performs well (hard to apply to weak models or new embodiments); relies on a hand-defined set of predicates, risk objects and violations, which limits risk diversity.
notes: Code and assets are at redvla.github.io under CC BY-NC 4.0. Stronger models (higher benign SR) showed higher ASR, which the paper frames as a performance-safety trade-off.

name: DropVLA
resolvedTitle: DropVLA: An Action-Level Backdoor Attack on Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Institute of Trustworthy Embodied AI, Fudan University; City University of Hong Kong
problem: Existing VLA backdoors are untargeted (BadVLA) or hijack whole tasks or trajectories (GoBA, AttackVLA); fine-grained control over individual safety-critical action primitives had not been explored.
keyIdea: An action-level backdoor that forces a reusable primitive (here open-gripper, i.e. dropping the object) within 0.05 s of trigger onset at attacker-chosen decision points. It works in a pipeline-black-box setting with a tiny data-poisoning budget, and uses window-consistent relabeling so overlapping chunked training windows get consistent supervision.
architecture: Data poisoning only: insert a visual trigger (a red patch, or a small blue cube physically), optionally a text trigger, into a few episodes from the onset step; relabel a contiguous block of gripper actions (+1 to -1); standard OFT/LoRA fine-tuning of OpenVLA-7B; decision point defined by an object-height threshold.
inputs: Fine-tuning demonstration data (poisoned subset)
outputs: Backdoored VLA that drops the object on trigger
trainingData: LIBERO-Spatial (10 tasks, 432 episodes, 52,970 frames) for OpenVLA-7B; real Franka 7-DoF with pi0-FAST (3 tasks, 4% poisoning)
controlRateHz: 500 (simulation control frequency used for the reaction window)
whatChangedVsParent: Targets a single reusable low-level action with tight timing, rather than untargeted failure or goal/trajectory hijacking, and uses window-consistent relabeling for chunked fine-tuning.
limitations: Single target action; evaluated within LIBERO with OpenVLA-7B; moving the trigger to image locations outside the poisoning coverage sharply reduces ASR; text-only triggers are unstable at low poisoning budgets; real-world success is much lower (20%).
notes: Code at github.com/megaknight114/DropVLA. Suggested defenses: runtime gating of safety-critical actions with force/state consistency checks, trigger-surface stress tests, and data provenance hygiene.

name: GoBA
resolvedTitle: Goal-oriented Backdoor Attack against Vision-Language-Action Models via Physical Objects
org: The University of Auckland; KAUST
problem: Existing VLA backdoors (TrojanRobot, BadVLA) require white-box model access and only cause untargeted task failure, not specific attacker-chosen behavior.
keyIdea: Goal-oriented backdoor through data poisoning alone. A small fraction of human-collected demos contain a physical object trigger (e.g., a toxic-labelled box or a cookie) and a backdoor goal (pick up the trigger object and place it in a fixed region), with the instruction left unchanged. At test time the VLA behaves normally without the trigger and pursues the attacker's goal when the trigger is present.
architecture: No model access: inject BadLIBERO backdoor demonstrations (12 per task) into LIBERO at an injection rate of about 10%, then fine-tune the victim VLA with its standard recipe; three-level evaluation (nothing to do / try to do / success to do).
inputs: Poisoned demonstration data
outputs: Backdoored VLA (OpenVLA, pi0) with trigger-conditioned goal behavior
trainingData: BadLIBERO: LIBERO (Long, Goal, Object, Spatial) plus backdoor demos, IR 10% (ablations 2%, 1%)
whatChangedVsParent: Needs no access to the model (only the data) and enforces a specific goal with a physical-object trigger, instead of white-box, untargeted failure.
limitations: Much weaker on autoregressive OpenVLA than flow-matching pi0 (58.4% vs 97.0%); success drops at 1% injection (22.9% level-3); hard-to-grasp trigger objects shift outcomes from success to 'try to do'; simulation only.
notes: BadLIBERO is released on Hugging Face (ZZR42/BadLIBERO), with code at goba-attack.github.io. Trigger color matters (a pure-white package reached 77.3% level-3); trigger size has little effect.

name: BEAT
resolvedTitle: BEAT: Visual Backdoor Attacks on VLM-based Embodied Agents via Contrastive Trigger Learning
org: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
problem: VLM-based embodied agents that plan from egocentric images open a new attack surface: object triggers in the scene. Object triggers vary widely with viewpoint and lighting, and naive SFT backdoors either misfire (up to 80% false activations) or fail to activate.
keyIdea: Implant a multi-step malicious policy that activates when a trigger object appears. Training data combines benign, backdoor and contrastive trajectories, and a two-stage recipe runs SFT and then Contrastive Trigger Learning (CTL), a DPO-style preference step on paired trigger-present vs trigger-free inputs that sharpens the trigger decision boundary.
architecture: Fine-tune VLM agents (Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct, InternVL3-8B with LoRA; GPT-4o SFT only via API) that output high-level discrete actions; benign data from multiple VLM agents, backdoor trajectories from a rule-based agent, and contrastive pairs for CTL.
inputs: User instruction, interaction history, current egocentric frame
outputs: High-level action; backdoored model switches to an attacker plan (e.g., put knife on sofa, drop vase) on trigger
actionRepr: Discrete high-level action primitives (e.g., move, grasp, put_on_top)
trainingData: VAB-OmniGibson (trigger: knife) and EB-ALFRED (trigger: vase); 100 benign + 100 backdoor test scenarios per benchmark
whatChangedVsParent: Extends agent backdoors from static text triggers and single-step outputs to variable visual object triggers with multi-step malicious policies, and adds preference-based contrastive trigger learning for precise activation.
limitations: CTL was evaluated only on open-source VLMs (GPT-4o API lacks image DPO); VAB-OmniGibson relies on bounding-box annotations for triggers; simulation only; continual benign SFT can erase the backdoor.
notes: ICLR 2026. Targets high-level VLM planning agents, not low-level VLA motor policies. Backdoor plans average 9.0 steps after activation.

name: PolicyCleanse
resolvedTitle: PolicyCleanse: Backdoor Detection and Mitigation for Reinforcement Learning
org: University of Maryland; Simular Research; Northwestern University; UC Riverside
problem: In competitive multi-agent RL, a Trojan agent can be backdoored (BackdooRL) to fail as soon as an opponent performs a trigger action sequence. No method existed to detect such agents, and triggers are action sequences of unknown length in continuous space, which defeats classifier-style trigger reverse engineering.
keyIdea: An activated Trojan agent's accumulated reward degrades noticeably after a few steps, even against a still or random opponent. PolicyCleanse trains a separate opponent policy (PPO) with the target's negated reward to reverse-engineer pseudo trigger actions, using a performing phase and an observing phase over parallel randomized environments. An agent is flagged via a MAD outlier test, and the backdoor is mitigated by unlearning: fine-tuning on episodes mixing pseudo triggers and benign actions.
architecture: Detector policy: 2-layer MLP (64 units) trained with PPO (stable-baselines) against the frozen target; anomaly threshold via median absolute deviation (index 4); mitigation by continued training of the Trojan (LSTM) agent on pseudo-trigger plus benign trajectories.
inputs: Black-box access to the target agent in its environment (observations, transitions, rewards)
outputs: Trojan/benign verdict, pseudo trigger actions, and a mitigated (purified) policy
trainingData: MuJoCo competitive games (OpenAI multi-agent competition): Run-To-Goal (Ants, Humans), You-Shall-Not-Pass, Sumo (Humans); Trojan agents built with BackdooRL
whatChangedVsParent: Brings trigger reverse engineering from image classifiers to multi-agent RL by optimizing an opponent policy on reversed reward, and adds unlearning-based mitigation.
limitations: Sensitive to adaptive attacks (the authors argue these make the backdoor less effective or stealthy); pseudo triggers differ from true triggers; evaluated only against BackdooRL-style attacks in competitive MuJoCo games.
notes: ICCV 2023 per arXiv v5. This is not a robot-manipulation method: P13 cites it as an RL backdoor defense. Detection accuracy rises with a longer observing phase and is best at 50 steps.

name: RoboSafe
resolvedTitle: RoboSafe: Safeguarding Embodied Agents via Executable Safety Logic
org: Beihang University; 360 AI Security Lab; Univ. of Sydney; NTU; Peking University; BAAI
problem: Runtime guardrails for VLM-driven embodied agents rely on static rules or prompt-level control and miss implicit risks: contextual risk (a benign action made hazardous by scene state) and temporal risk (hazards emerging from action sequences, e.g. leaving a stove on).
keyIdea: A hybrid-reasoning runtime guardrail that generates executable, predicate-based safety logic (Python) over a Hybrid Long-Short Safety Memory: Backward Reflective Reasoning over recent trajectory infers temporal predicates and triggers replanning; Forward Predictive Reasoning uses retrieved long-term safety knowledge plus observations to block contextually risky actions.
architecture: Black-box guardrail around an existing embodied agent. Guardrail VLM (Gemini-2.5-flash by default) + long-term knowledge memory (seeded from 8 SafeAgentBench examples, retrieved with text-embedding-3-small) + short-term working memory of the trajectory; a Python interpreter executes the generated safety logic and returns PASS / BLOCK / REPLAN.
inputs: Global instruction, current multimodal observation, agent's proposed action, recent trajectory
outputs: Safety action in {block, replan} or pass
trainingData: No training; safety knowledge generated from 8 simulated SafeAgentBench examples (train split); evaluated on SafeAgentBench-derived detailed-unsafe, long-horizon-unsafe and safe instruction sets in AI2-THOR

headlineResults.comparedTo: outperforms other defenses by +45.75% on average

whatChangedVsParent: Replaces static rules/prompted checks (AgentSpec, Poex, ThinkSafe) with VLM-generated executable predicate logic that reasons both backward over time and forward over context.
limitations: Authors list generalisation to more diverse robot platforms and scalability to more complex long-horizon tasks and unforeseen adversarial attacks as future work; real-robot test is two case-study tasks on a 6-DoF myCobot 280-Pi arm.
notes: Code 'will be released upon acceptance' (not released at time of preprint). Not a policy: a runtime guardrail for LLM/VLM task planners (high-level actions), not low-level control.

name: SafePlan
resolvedTitle: SafePlan: Leveraging Formal Logic and Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Enhanced Safety in LLM-based Robotic Task Planning
org: Purdue University (SMART Lab, Byung-Cheol Min)
problem: LLM-based robot task planning/allocation pipelines inherit QA-oriented safety mechanisms that fail to reject physically unsafe prompts and do not verify generated plans/code against preconditions and invariants.
keyIdea: Multi-component CoT framework built on formal logic: a Prompt Sanity COT Reasoner (societal, organizational, individual layers with deontic Forbidden/Permissible labels) screens prompts; an Invariant COT Reasoner (LTL-style invariants, preconditions, postconditions) guides code generation and then verifies the generated task-allocation code.
architecture: Three LLM calls: (1) sanity/invariant reasoner produces invariants, pre- and postconditions; (2) code-generation LLM uses them as few-shot guidance; (3) invariant reasoner verifies the code (up to 3 times) before execution. Tested with GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro.
inputs: Natural-language task prompt + scene description; object list and robot skills
outputs: Accept/reject decision; verified multi-robot task-allocation Python code
trainingData: No training; new benchmark of 621 expert-curated prompt/scene pairs (127 safe, 494 unsafe) across assistive, navigation and manipulation domains; 18 error-prone AI2-THOR tasks (from SMART-LLM/ProgPrompt)

headlineResults.comparedTo: same LLMs with natural-language system prompt

whatChangedVsParent: Adds formal-logic CoT prompt screening and invariant/pre/postcondition verification on top of LLM task-allocation pipelines like SMART-LLM.
limitations: Paper notes future work on dynamic and complex scenarios; accepting safe tasks drops (e.g. 70.9% for Gemini 1.5 Pro), and simulation evaluation covers only 18 tasks.
notes: Operates on LLM task planners/multi-robot task allocation, not low-level control.

name: TRAP
resolvedTitle: TRAP: Tail-aware Ranking Attack for World-Model Planning
org: Soochow University
problem: Existing backdoor/adversarial attacks target one-step predictions, latents or policy outputs, which world-model planners wash out through multi-step dynamics and trajectory ranking.
keyIdea: A deployment-time, trigger-conditioned (visual patch) attack that targets the relative ranking of imagined trajectories: a tail-aware ranking loss suppresses the few high-score decision-critical trajectories, with sign and magnitude gating losses to stabilise optimisation while preserving clean behaviour.
architecture: White-box optimisation of an l_inf-bounded visual patch (delta = eps*tanh(rho)) on proxy trajectories; loss = L_tail + L_sign + L_mag + TV + L2 regularisers; attacks DreamerV3 (latent imagination) and TD-MPC2 (latent MPC).
inputs: Agent observation with patch trigger
outputs: Perturbed planning outcome (attack)
trainingData: Small set of proxy trajectories collected by running the pretrained agent; no training-data poisoning or parameter tampering
whatChangedVsParent: Moves the attack objective from per-step predictions/returns to the ranking of the high-value tail of imagined trajectories.
limitations: White-box access to world model and planner assumed; evaluated on control benchmarks (DreamerV3, TD-MPC2) rather than real robots.
notes: DISAMBIGUATION: not TRAP 'Targeted Redirecting of Agentic Preferences' (Kang, Yeon, Singh, NeurIPS 2025), which attacks web/computer-use agents. P13 ref [78] describes the tail-aware ranking attack on world-model planners, which matches this paper. The paper calls itself an inference-time 'backdoor' (trigger) attack, though it is closer to a universal adversarial patch. Quantitative numbers were not extracted in this pass (headlineResults left empty).

name: PhysCond-WMA
resolvedTitle: When World Models Dream Wrong: Physical-Conditioned Adversarial Attacks against World Models
org: Nanyang Technological University; University of Szeged
problem: Generative driving world models rely on physical-condition inputs (HDMaps, 3D boxes) that expose an unstudied attack surface; naive condition perturbation breaks visual quality or fails to change semantics.
keyIdea: First white-box attack that perturbs physical-condition channels (HDMap embeddings, 3D-box features) with a two-stage scheme: quality-preserving guidance keeps reverse-diffusion loss under a threshold, then momentum-guided (EMA) denoising accumulates target-aligned gradients for temporally coherent semantic shifts.
architecture: Attack on conditional video-diffusion world models (DriveDreamer, DriveDreamer2); SSCD used as semantic alignment model; tau=0.15, 25 diffusion steps; targets created by SDXL inpainting.
inputs: Physical conditions (HDMap, 3D boxes) + image condition
outputs: Attacked multi-view driving video
trainingData: nuScenes (850 videos; 700 train / 150 val)

headlineResults.benchmark: Downstream 3D detection (FCOS3D) trained on attacked data

whatChangedVsParent: Moves diffusion adversarial attacks from pixel/text inputs to the physical-condition channels of driving world models.
limitations: Only verified with image targets as input condition (video/text targets unexplored); ASR evaluation criteria (GPT-5 and human raters) are not a complete standard.
notes: Autonomous-driving world models, not manipulation. P13 lists it under world-model rule-violation attacks.

name: CtrlAttack
resolvedTitle: CtrlAttack: A Unified Attack on World-Model Control in Diffusion Models
org: Wuhan University; Nanyang Technological University; Beijing Institute of Technology
problem: Diffusion image-to-video models increasingly act like world models, but robustness of their learned state transitions under trajectory-control conditions is unstudied, and white-box vs black-box settings are hard to model uniformly.
keyIdea: Perturb the trajectory-control condition as a low-dimensional (DCT-basis) velocity field integrated over time into a smooth displacement field, systematically shifting generated motion; instantiated as gradient-based attack in latent space (white-box) and query-based natural-evolution-strategy attack on trajectory conditions (black-box).
architecture: Attack framework over trajectory-conditioned I2V diffusion models: MOFT, DragAnything, SG-I2V, AnyI2V.
inputs: Input image + trajectory control signal
outputs: Perturbed video trajectory (attack)
trainingData: VIPSeg validation set, 100 sampled videos; DragAnything control regions/trajectories
whatChangedVsParent: Attacks the temporal trajectory-control channel (state transitions) instead of pixels or text prompts, with one parameterisation shared across white- and black-box settings.
limitations: Focuses on a single controlled trajectory; multi-object / multi-trajectory interactions left for future work.
notes: Victims are general video generators, not robot world models; P13 frames it as a world-model control attack.

name: HomeGuard
resolvedTitle: HomeGuard: VLM-based Embodied Safeguard for Identifying Contextual Risk in Household Task
org: Shanghai AI Laboratory; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Beihang University; HUST
problem: VLM embodied agents miss contextual risks (benign commands made hazardous by scene state); rule-based safeguards do not scale in cluttered scenes and prompt-based VLM safeguards suffer unfocused perception, missing risks or hallucinating them.
keyIdea: Context-Guided Chain-of-Thought (CG-CoT): active perception first grounds bounding boxes for interaction targets and constraint objects, then semantic risk judgment conditions on these visual anchors; trained with SFT then RFT (GRPO) using process rewards on intermediate grounding.
architecture: Qwen3-VL-4B/8B-Thinking base, LoRA SFT on curated HomeSafe grounding dataset + general instruction data, then GRPO reinforcement fine-tuning with process rewards; 4-step structured reasoning (intent screening, target inspection, constraint analysis, integrated assessment).
inputs: Household scene image + instruction
outputs: Safe/unsafe label, hazard explanation, violated safety principle, target/constraint bounding boxes
trainingData: HomeSafe dataset (built via counterfactual editing pipeline) plus general instruction-following data
whatChangedVsParent: Adds explicit visual-anchor grounding before safety judgment and process-reward RFT, versus holistic prompted VLM safety checks.
limitations: Operates on 2D images (3D/depth left for future), handles static rather than dynamic hazards, and has not yet been deployed on physical robots for closed-loop long-horizon manipulation.
notes: Bounding boxes also used as spatial waypoints/constraints for downstream planners (demo with RoboBrain2.5-8B trajectories).

name: STRONG-VLA
resolvedTitle: STRONG-VLA: Decoupled Robustness Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models under Multimodal Perturbations
org: Westlake University; Zhejiang University; Xidian University
problem: VLAs are fragile under joint visual and linguistic perturbations, and joint training on clean+perturbed data creates conflicting gradients between robustness and task fidelity.
keyIdea: Decouple robustness from task alignment: Stage I fine-tunes on a severity-ordered curriculum of multimodal perturbations; Stage II re-aligns on clean data (same loss, different input distribution).
architecture: Fine-tuning recipe applied to OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT and pi0; benchmark of 28 perturbation types (12 textual, 16 visual), some held out as unseen.
inputs: Camera images + language instruction (perturbed)
outputs: Robot actions (backbone's native action head)
actionRepr: Inherited from backbone (OpenVLA tokens, OFT chunks, pi0 flow matching)
trainingData: LIBERO demonstrations with synthetic perturbations; real-world AIRBOT Play tests
whatChangedVsParent: Replaces all-at-once perturbation augmentation (e.g. RobustVLA) with a two-stage curriculum-then-clean-refinement schedule.
limitations: Robustness to unseen visual perturbations remains limited (can fall below raw model); perturbation taxonomy and difficulty metrics are hand-designed; real-world validation is small (2 tasks, 10 trials each).
notes: Venue: ACM MM 2026. Real robot: AIRBOT Play with OpenVLA-OFT.

name: AgentPoison
resolvedTitle: AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases
org: University of Chicago; UIUC; UW-Madison; UC Berkeley
problem: RAG/memory-based LLM agents retrieve from unverified knowledge bases; existing jailbreak and in-context backdoor attacks fail to reliably get malicious demonstrations retrieved.
keyIdea: Backdoor via memory/knowledge-base poisoning: optimise a trigger (constrained, gradient-guided discrete optimisation) so triggered queries map to a unique, compact region of the retriever embedding space, guaranteeing retrieval of injected malicious demonstrations while benign queries behave normally; no model training needed.
architecture: Attack on RAG agents; losses for uniqueness, compactness, target action and coherence; white-box retriever access, transfers to other embedders incl. OpenAI-ADA.
inputs: User query with optimised trigger
outputs: Target adversarial agent action (e.g. sudden stop)
trainingData: Agent-Driver memory (23k experiences), StrategyQA knowledge base (10k Wikipedia passages), EHRAgent memory augmented to 700 experiences
whatChangedVsParent: Optimises the trigger for retrieval in embedding space (uniqueness + compactness) rather than using suboptimal fixed triggers (BadChain) or degrading all retrievals (CPA).
limitations: Requires white-box access to the RAG embedder for trigger optimisation (mitigated empirically by transfer).
notes: Code/data released at github.com/BillChan226/AgentPoison. Published at NeurIPS 2024. The only 'embodied' target is an LLM autonomous-driving agent (Agent-Driver); not a manipulation policy attack.

name: ERT
resolvedTitle: Embodied Red Teaming for Auditing Robotic Foundation Models
org: MIT (Improbable AI Lab); Amazon
problem: Benchmarks for language-conditioned robot policies use small, human-curated instruction sets and only measure task success, missing failures from alternative phrasings and unsafe behaviour.
keyIdea: Automated red teaming with a VLM (GPT-4o): given an environment image and under-specified task name, generate feasible instructions, iteratively refine with failure examples via in-context learning, and pick the most diverse set (best-of-M on CLIP embedding diversity).
architecture: Red-team VLM (GPT-4o) + robot policy evaluation loop; diversity via CLIP embeddings; M=5 samples per refinement.
inputs: Environment image + task description
outputs: Set of diverse instructions that cause policy failure
trainingData: No training; CALVIN (27 tasks, ~400 instructions), RLBench (18 tasks), SimplerEnv (OpenVLA)
whatChangedVsParent: Brings LLM red-teaming to embodied policies by grounding instruction generation in images and using execution feedback.
limitations: VLM-generated instructions may not discover every failure mode; study limited to manipulation tasks.
notes: Code/videos on project page (s-karnik.github.io/embodied-red-team-project-page). Also shows policies following unsafe instructions (qualitative).

name: CBA
resolvedTitle: Compromising Embodied Agents with Contextual Backdoor Attacks
org: Beihang University; NUS; Zhongguancun Lab; NTU; USTC; A*STAR
problem: LLM code-generation pipelines for embodied agents rely on few-shot contextual demonstrations, which an attacker can poison to make a black-box LLM emit programs with hidden, context-dependent defects.
keyIdea: Contextual Backdoor Attack: optimise poisoned in-context demonstrations through an LLM-judge vs LLM-modifier adversarial game with CoT; dual-modality activation where a textual trigger word set makes the LLM emit defective code and a visual trigger object in the environment activates the defect; five defect modes (malicious behaviour, availability, shutdown control, biased content, privacy extraction).
architecture: Target LLM GPT-3.5-turbo (also Davinci-002, Gemini); judge Davinci-002; modifiers GPT-3.5-turbo; 20 optimisation iterations, 8 ICL samples, poisoning ratio 0.5.
inputs: User instruction (with textual trigger) + environment (with visual trigger)
outputs: Backdoored program for the agent
trainingData: Hand-built pool of 100 in-context samples; ProgPrompt (VirtualHome), VoxPoser (RLBench, 13 tasks), VisProg (NLVR, GQA, image editing, knowledge tagging), real autonomous vehicle
whatChangedVsParent: Poisons the source LLM's contextual demonstrations so defects propagate through generated code into downstream agents, with dual textual/visual activation.
limitations: Assumes attacker can supply poisoned demonstrations/functional modules to the LLM context and place physical triggers in the environment.
notes: Journal version appears to be IEEE TIFS 2025 ('Compromising LLM Driven Embodied Agents with Contextual Backdoor Attacks', cited so by RoboSafe). Code promised upon publication.

name: Surprise Recognition
resolvedTitle: World Model Robustness via Surprise Recognition
org: Georgia Institute of Technology
problem: World-model RL agents face out-of-distribution sensor noise and failures that cannot all be anticipated by robust training, leading to unstable or unsafe behaviour.
keyIdea: Use the world model's own Bayesian surprise (KL between posterior and prior latent) to detect corrupted inputs: multi-representation rejection sampling masks the most surprising sensors (O(n log n) selection) and single-representation rejection sampling rejects/denoises surprising frames; trained with random multi-representation dropout.
architecture: Inference-time filter on DreamerV3 (RSSM) agents plus a pixel-space variant for the Cosmos-Predict 2.5 diffusion world model.
inputs: Multi-sensor observations (camera, LiDAR, BEV variants) or single video stream
outputs: Filtered latent state for the policy / filtered conditioning frames
trainingData: CARLA (Stop Sign, Right Turn, Four-Lane tasks) and Safety Gymnasium; Cosmos robot pouring task for the video-model study
whatChangedVsParent: Turns the world model's intrinsic surprise signal into a sensor-selection / frame-rejection mechanism rather than relying on robust training or fixed dropout.
limitations: Assumes at least one sensor stays uncorrupted in the multi-sensor setting; evaluated in driving simulators and Safety Gymnasium, not real robots.
notes: Code released (github.com/Bluefin-Tuna/WISER). CARLA/Safety-Gym gains are reported as plots (performance surfaces), no single headline number extracted.

name: AFM
resolvedTitle: Adversarial Flow Matching for Imperceptible Attacks on End-to-End Autonomous Driving
org: UESTC (Shenzhen Institute for Advanced Study); Nanyang Technological University
problem: Attacks on end-to-end driving agents (VLA and modular) are either white-box (unrealistic), query-based (too slow) or transfer-based (weak), and pixel-additive perturbations are visually conspicuous.
keyIdea: Gray-box generative attack that exploits only Transformer-backbone gradients: invert a clean frame into a flow-matching latent, then jointly perturb the latent initialisation and the neural average velocity field so one-step (1-NFE) generation yields an imperceptible adversarial image that distorts Transformer features.
architecture: Frozen VAE encoder/decoder + flow-matching sampler with mean-velocity field; losses weighted by spatial mask and attention maps; latent-std consistency constraint.
inputs: Clean camera frame (+ gradients of victim's Transformer backbone)
outputs: Adversarial frame
trainingData: Victims: TransFuser (modular) and SimLingo (VLA); CARLA open-loop scenarios and closed-loop Bench2Drive (10 routes)
whatChangedVsParent: Uses one-step flow matching with dual latent + velocity-field perturbations instead of multi-step diffusion or pixel-additive attacks.
limitations: 6.7 s per frame precludes real-time per-frame attacks at 30 Hz (authors propose intermittent injection or offline physical patches); requires gradients of the Transformer backbone.
notes: CONFLICT: P13 Table 12 classifies AFM as 'White-box' attack on E2E AD models; the paper itself frames it as a gray-box attack (only Transformer-backbone gradients, not full model). Driving, not manipulation.

name: Robo-Troj
resolvedTitle: MuTRAP: Multi-trigger Trojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems (earlier versions titled 'Robo-Troj: Attacking LLM-based Task Planners')
org: Binghamton University (SUNY)
problem: LLM-based robot task planners are typically a frozen server LLM adapted per robot with soft-prompt tuning; this adaptation stage is an unexamined backdoor attack surface, and single-trigger backdoors are easy to detect.
keyIdea: Implant a multi-trigger backdoor in the soft-prompt parameters: first optimise a categorical trigger-token distribution (Gumbel-softmax) to maximise malicious-plan generation, then sample several triggers to poison training data for soft-prompt tuning, so each trigger elicits a feasible malicious plan while clean inputs stay benign.
architecture: Frozen backbone LLM (GPT2-large, GPT-J-6B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1 distills) + 2-hidden-layer MLP soft-prompt encoder producing 64 soft-prompt tokens; trigger length K=2, typically p=2 triggers, 0.1 poison ratio.
inputs: Task description (+ optional trigger word)
outputs: Task plan (action sequence)
trainingData: 5000 VirtualHome-Env instances (converted to NL) for training; original VirtualHome programs for testing; plans executed in VirtualHome simulator
whatChangedVsParent: Moves the backdoor into per-robot soft-prompt parameters with optimised multiple triggers, instead of prompt-level ICL poisoning (CBA) or full LLM fine-tuning (BALD).
limitations: Threat model assumes attacker supplies the domain dataset or controls soft-prompt tuning; evaluation is mostly VirtualHome plan generation.
notes: NAME CHANGE: v3 of arXiv 2504.17070 (June 2026) is retitled MuTRAP and accepted at IROS 2026; P13 cites it as 'Robo-troj: Attacking LLM-based task planners'. Project page mutrap.github.io/MuTRAP. P13 describes it as 'poisonous fine-tuning of soft-prompts ... when trigger words appear', consistent.

name: J-DAPT
resolvedTitle: Preventing Robotic Jailbreaking via Multimodal Domain Adaptation
org: University of Padova; Stanford University; CMU; University of Pennsylvania; NVIDIA Research
problem: Jailbreak classifiers trained on general-purpose datasets fail to transfer to robotics, where robot-specific jailbreak data is scarce and what counts as unsafe differs; LLM-as-detector is accurate but too slow.
keyIdea: J-DAPT (Jailbreak Domain adAPTation): fuse text and image embeddings via cross-attention, then align general jailbreak datasets to the robot domain with a domain classifier (importance weights) plus CORAL covariance alignment, and train a lightweight classifier without any robotic jailbreak examples.
architecture: Frozen embedding models (CLIP, DinoTXT, etc.) + cross-attention fusion with residual + CORAL adaptation + importance-weighted feed-forward classifier.
inputs: Text query + scene image(s)
outputs: Safe / unsafe (jailbreak) label
trainingData: General: DAQUAR (benign) and JailBreakV JB28K (28,000 adversarial); domain benign data: LingoQA, nuScenes, ABOships-PLUS, LaRS, 84 quadruped videos; test jailbreaks generated with RoboPAIR

headlineResults.comparedTo: 9.9x faster than fastest comparably accurate LLM detector

whatChangedVsParent: Adds multimodal attention fusion and unsupervised domain adaptation to data-driven jailbreak classifiers so they transfer to robotics without robot jailbreak data.
limitations: Some embedding models (BLIP, SigLIP) show inverted/poor outputs after adaptation; authors see it as one layer in a multi-layer defence pipeline.
notes: Project page j-dapt.github.io. Targets VLM/LLM high-level planners (driving, maritime, quadruped navigation), not manipulation VLAs.

name: LIBERO-X
resolvedTitle: LIBERO-X: Robustness Litmus for Vision-Language-Action Models
org: Meituan; Beihang University
problem: LIBERO-style benchmarks saturate (~90%) because test scenes mirror training, perturbations are applied one dimension at a time with no difficulty progression, and training data is homogeneous (one scene, one task, template trajectories).
keyIdea: A five-level cumulative evaluation hierarchy (L1 local spatial jitter, L2 extended spatial, L3 scene-topology changes, L4 unseen/confounding objects and attributes, L5 semantic-equivalent instruction rewrites) with multi-label task annotations, plus a high-diversity teleoperated training set where each scene supports many tasks.
architecture: Benchmark on MuJoCo/LIBERO with PDDL scene/task definitions; time limit 1.1x average human completion time.
trainingData: 2,520 teleoperated demonstrations, 600 tasks, 100 scenes

headlineResults.metric: success rate (pi0.5 / GR00T-N1.5 / pi0 / OpenVLA-OFT / X-VLA)
success rate (pi0.5 / GR00T-N1.5 / pi0 / OpenVLA-OFT / X-VLA)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds compounded, progressively harder perturbations and a new diverse teleoperated training set rather than reusing LIBERO's original trajectories.
limitations: Simulation only; findings show models near zero on tasks with three or more subtasks.
notes: Project page zackhxn.github.io/LIBERO-X. Cited in P13 as a VLA robustness benchmark and in X1 as a benchmark.

name: VIMA-Bench
resolvedTitle: VIMA: General Robot Manipulation with Multimodal Prompts
org: Stanford; NVIDIA; Caltech; UT Austin; Tsinghua; Macalester
problem: Robot task specification comes in many incompatible forms (language, goal images, one-shot demos, novel concepts, constraints), each handled by specialised models, and no benchmark tested multimodal-prompted manipulation with systematic generalisation.
keyIdea: Express diverse tabletop tasks as multimodal prompts interleaving text and images; VIMA-Bench (on the Ravens simulator) provides 17 procedurally generated task templates, 600K+ expert trajectories and a four-level generalisation protocol (placement, combinatorial, novel task, novel concept/task); VIMA agent uses object tokens and cross-attention.
architecture: VIMA: pre-trained T5 prompt encoder (T5-Base, 111M) + transformer decoder conditioned via cross-attention on object-centric tokens from Mask R-CNN; 7 sizes from 2M to 200M parameters (excluding encoder).
inputs: Multimodal prompt (text + images/video frames) + observations
outputs: Motor actions (autoregressive)
actionRepr: Autoregressively decoded high-level motor primitives (pick-and-place / push poses) per step
trainingData: 600K+ expert trajectories in VIMA-Bench (Ravens/PyBullet)

headlineResults.comparedTo: best alternative design (VIMA-Gato/Flamingo/GPT) with same data

whatChangedVsParent: Unifies task specification into multimodal prompts with object-centric tokens and cross-attention conditioning, and provides a benchmark with a four-level generalisation protocol.
limitations: Simulation tabletop with high-level action primitives; object tokens rely on a detector fine-tuned in-domain.
notes: Simulator, dataset, code and checkpoints open-sourced (vimalabs.github.io). ICML 2023. Card treats VIMA-Bench as the benchmark and VIMA as its reference agent.

name: COLOSSEUM
resolvedTitle: THE COLOSSEUM: A Benchmark for Evaluating Generalization for Robotic Manipulation
org: University of Washington; USC; Universidad Catolica San Pablo; Allen Institute for AI; NVIDIA
problem: Most robot policies are evaluated in environments nearly identical to training, so robustness to environmental changes (colour, texture, lighting, distractors, camera, physics) is not measured systematically.
keyIdea: Extend RLBench with 20 tasks and 14 perturbation factors (object/receiver colour, texture, size; light colour; table colour/texture; distractors; background texture; camera pose; object friction and mass), yielding 20,371 unique perturbed task instances, plus a 3D-printable real-world counterpart.
architecture: Benchmark built on RLBench / PyRep / CoppeliaSim; training on 100 unperturbed demos per task, evaluation 25 episodes per test set (235 test sets).
trainingData: 100 demonstrations per task (unperturbed) for training; real-world: Franka Panda, 4 tasks, 5 demos each

headlineResults.benchmark: COLOSSEUM, 5 SotA policies (incl. PerAct, RVT, R3M-MLP, MVP-MLP, VoxPoser)

whatChangedVsParent: More perturbation axes (14) over more tasks (20) than FactorWorld/KitchenShift, adds physical-property perturbations and a real-world replica.
limitations: Real-world study limited to 4 tasks with two alternate variations per factor and imperfect replication of poses; one training seed per baseline.
notes: Code and 3D-print assets open-sourced (robot-colosseum.github.io). Found distractors, target colour and lighting most harmful; object size least.

name: VLABench
resolvedTitle: VLABench: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Language-Conditioned Robotics Manipulation with Long-Horizon Reasoning Tasks
org: Fudan University
problem: Existing manipulation benchmarks (RLBench, CALVIN, LIBERO) use template instructions and short skills, and do not test world knowledge, implicit user intent, long-horizon reasoning, or cross-category generalisation that VLAs claim.
keyIdea: 100 task categories (60 primitive, 40 composite) spanning mesh/texture, spatial, common-sense/world-knowledge, semantic, physical-law and long-horizon reasoning dimensions, with unseen-category object splits, a graduated Progress Score, and an automated skill-library data-generation pipeline; evaluates VLAs, VLM workflows and VLMs (via DSL).
architecture: MuJoCo / dm_control simulator; 163 object categories, 2,164 assets; default Franka Panda; RRT-based scripted trajectory generation with SLERP and Bezier smoothing; GPT-4 instruction augmentation.
trainingData: Automatically generated demonstrations per task (standardised dataset for fine-tuning)
whatChangedVsParent: Adds knowledge, semantic and reasoning-heavy tasks with category-level unseen splits and partial-credit scoring on top of skill-centric benchmarks.
limitations: Paper reports current VLAs and VLMs (incl. GPT-4o) struggle; simulation only.
notes: Open-source benchmark (vlabench.github.io). Specific per-model success numbers were not extracted in this pass.

name: GemBench
resolvedTitle: Towards Generalizable Vision-Language Robotic Manipulation: A Benchmark and LLM-guided 3D Policy
org: Inria; Ecole normale superieure; CNRS; PSL
problem: Simulation benchmarks mostly test language-conditioned policies on the tasks they were trained on (or only on environment perturbations), not on generalisation to new objects, articulations and long-horizon compositions.
keyIdea: GemBench on RLBench: 16 training tasks (31 variations, 7 action primitives) and 44 test tasks (92 variations) in four levels: L1 novel placements, L2 novel rigid objects, L3 novel articulated objects, L4 novel long-horizon tasks. Also proposes 3D-LOTUS (language-conditioned point-cloud transformer) and 3D-LOTUS++ (LLM task planning + VLM grounding + 3D-LOTUS motion control).
architecture: 3D-LOTUS: point cloud transformer with cross-attention language conditioning and classification-style (binned) position/rotation keypose prediction; 3D-LOTUS++ adds an LLM planner (LLaMA3-8B) and VLM grounding (OWLv2 + SAM).
inputs: Multi-view RGB-D (point cloud) + language instruction + proprioception
outputs: Next end-effector keypose and gripper state
actionRepr: Keyframe end-effector pose (discretised position bins per point, discretised rotation) + gripper open/close
trainingData: RLBench scripted demonstrations for 16 tasks / 31 variations; real robot: UR5, 20 teleop demos per variation
whatChangedVsParent: Adds a four-level test protocol for new tasks/objects (vs. COLOSSEUM's environment perturbations) and a modular LLM+VLM+3D-policy method.
limitations: Object grounding is the main bottleneck on L1-L2; the 3D motion policy struggles on long-horizon tasks with initial states far from training; LLM planner lacks visual input.
notes: Benchmark, code and trained models released (di.ens.fr/willow/research/gembench). ICRA 2025.

name: AGNOSTOS
resolvedTitle: Exploring the Limits of Vision-Language-Action Manipulation in Cross-task Generalization
org: HKUST (Guangzhou); University of Hong Kong; Sun Yat-sen University; HKUST
problem: Existing benchmarks (COLOSSEUM, GemBench, etc.) mostly test within-task visual variations; zero-shot generalisation of VLAs to entirely unseen tasks is largely unmeasured.
keyIdea: AGNOSTOS on RLBench: train on the standard 18 tasks (200 demos each, 3,600 total), test zero-shot on 23 unseen tasks in two levels (13 Level-1 sharing objects or motions, 10 Level-2 with neither); plus X-ICM, which prompts an LLM with in-context demonstrations from seen tasks chosen by a dynamics-diffusion similarity model.
architecture: X-ICM: off-the-shelf Qwen2.5-Instruct (7B / 72B) prompted with K=18 textualised demos (object 3D positions on a 100^3 grid, 7-D key actions with 5-degree rotation bins); dynamics-guided sample selection via a diffusion model predicting final from initial observation.
inputs: Language instruction + object positions (textualised)
outputs: Sequence of 7-D key actions (position, roll-pitch-yaw, gripper)
actionRepr: Key-action sequence of discretised 7-D end-effector poses output as text
trainingData: 3,600 RLBench demonstrations over 18 seen tasks
whatChangedVsParent: Targets cross-task (unseen task) generalisation with two semantic difficulty levels and benchmarks foundation, human-video-pretrained and in-domain VLAs together.
limitations: X-ICM remains weak on tasks with both novel objects and motions; visual information only enters as textualised object positions; simulation uses ground-truth object positions for zero-shot baselines.
notes: Code: github.com/jiaming-zhou/X-ICM; NeurIPS 2025. Task-difficulty categorisation done by GPT-4o and verified by three experts.

name: GenManip
resolvedTitle: GenManip: LLM-driven Simulation for Generalizable Instruction-Following Manipulation
org: Shanghai AI Laboratory; Xi'an Jiaotong University; Zhejiang University; Nanjing University
problem: Tabletop simulation platforms lack realistic, diverse, controllable scenarios and a standardised benchmark to compare modular foundation-model systems and end-to-end policies on instruction-following generalisation.
keyIdea: Isaac Sim platform with an LLM-driven task-oriented scene graph (ToSG) that generates tasks, constrains layouts and evaluates goal satisfaction; 10K annotated 3D assets; GenManip-Bench of 200 human-refined scenarios across spatial, appearance, common-sense and long-horizon reasoning.
architecture: Isaac Sim; GPT-4 synthesises ToSGs; automatic demonstration generation with motion planning and grasping (AnyGrasp) using privileged information; evaluation up to 9000 physics steps with SR and SPL.
trainingData: 10K object assets with VL annotations; automated behaviour-cloning data (100-1K episodes in scaling study)

headlineResults.metric: success on unseen instructions / unseen objects

whatChangedVsParent: Uses a structured task-oriented scene graph for controllable LLM task/layout generation and logical success checking, with a human-curated evaluation set.
limitations: Full-scale evaluation of end-to-end methods across all 200 scenarios left for future work due to compute; modular systems struggle with spatial perception.
notes: Code promised at project page. CVPR 2025.

name: BEHAVIOR-1K
resolvedTitle: BEHAVIOR-1K: A Human-Centered, Embodied AI Benchmark with 1,000 Everyday Activities and Realistic Simulation
org: Stanford University; UT Austin; UIUC; USC; Salesforce Research
problem: Embodied AI benchmarks use researcher-chosen tasks and face a diversity-realism trade-off; none are grounded in what people actually want robots to do.
keyIdea: Survey 1,461 people over 2,090 activities to pick the 1,000 most wanted (909 top-ranked plus 91 from BEHAVIOR-100), define them in the predicate-logic BDDL with a knowledge base of objects/states/transition rules, and simulate them in OmniGibson (Omniverse/PhysX 5) with rigid, deformable, cloth, fluid and thermal effects.
architecture: OmniGibson simulator on NVIDIA Omniverse + PhysX 5; 50 scenes (houses, gardens, restaurants, offices, stores), 9,000+ object models over 1,900+ categories; extended states (temperature, soaked, toggled, dirtiness).
trainingData: Benchmark/knowledge base; baselines trained with RL (visuomotor and action-primitive variants)
whatChangedVsParent: Scales BEHAVIOR-100 by 10x to 1,000 survey-grounded activities across 50 scene types, and moves to OmniGibson for fluids, deformables and thermal effects.
limitations: Ray-traced rendering ~60 fps for a 60-object house (slower than iGibson 2.0's ~100 fps); excludes activities involving humans; no perception/actuation noise models yet for sim-to-real.
notes: Preliminary version at CoRL 2022; this card uses the 2024 arXiv version. Baselines 'can only solve single activities with significant injection of domain knowledge'. Project: behavior.stanford.edu.

name: HomeRobot
resolvedTitle: HomeRobot: Open-Vocabulary Mobile Manipulation
org: Georgia Tech; FAIR (Meta AI); Carnegie Mellon; Simon Fraser University
problem: Mobile manipulation research simplifies settings (discrete actions, small object sets, single rooms) and results are not reproducible across labs with different robots and environments.
keyIdea: Define Open-Vocabulary Mobile Manipulation (find an object on a start receptacle, pick it, find the goal receptacle, place it) with a simulation benchmark in Habitat on HSSD scenes and a matched real-world benchmark on the low-cost Hello Robot Stretch, plus the open HomeRobot software stack with identical sim/real APIs.
architecture: Modular OVMMAgent state machine (FindObj, Gaze, Pick, FindRec, Place); heuristic (Fast-Marching planner + semantic map) and RL (DDPPO) skill baselines; DETIC for open-vocabulary segmentation.
inputs: RGB-D, proprioception, object/receptacle names
outputs: Navigation and manipulation actions (continuous)
trainingData: 60 HSSD scenes (38/12/10 train/val/test), 2,535 objects in 129 categories, 21 receptacle categories; real: 3-room apartment, 8 object categories
whatChangedVsParent: Joins open-vocabulary navigation and pick-and-place in multi-room homes with a reproducible real-world counterpart on a standard affordable robot.
limitations: Pick is a high-level action in sim (gripper interaction not simulated); FMM planner treats the robot as a cylinder; DETIC misclassification dominates failures.
notes: Open-source library github.com/facebookresearch/home-robot; basis of the NeurIPS 2023 HomeRobot OVMM challenge. CoRL 2023. Stretch cost stated as about $25,000 USD.

name: Franka Kitchen
resolvedTitle: Relay Policy Learning: Solving Long-Horizon Tasks via Imitation and Reinforcement Learning
org: UC Berkeley (BAIR); Google (Robotics at Google)
problem: Long-horizon multi-stage manipulation is hard for hierarchical RL (exploration, segmentation, rewards) and hierarchical imitation methods are not amenable to RL fine-tuning.
keyIdea: Introduces the MuJoCo Franka kitchen environment (9-DoF Franka with microwave, four burners, light switch, kettle, hinged and sliding cabinets) and Relay Policy Learning: goal-conditioned two-level policies learned from unstructured play demos via relay relabelling, then fine-tuned with RL.
architecture: High-level goal-setter picks a subgoal every H=30 steps; low-level goal-conditioned policy acts each step; both 2-layer 256-unit MLPs; fine-tuning with natural policy gradient/TRPO variants, then distillation into one multi-goal policy.
inputs: 30-D state (arm + object positions) + goal state
outputs: 9-D joint-velocity actions (7 arm + 2 gripper)
actionRepr: Joint velocities, 9-DoF
trainingData: 400 unstructured human VR (PUPPET MuJoCo) play demonstrations, each manipulating four scene elements
whatChangedVsParent: Fixed-length goal-relabelled hierarchical imitation that is designed to be RL-fine-tunable, rather than segmenting demos into skills.
limitations: Authors list generalisation to longer sequences, extrapolation beyond demonstration data, off-policy RL and real-robot learning as future work.
notes: Franka Kitchen as a standard benchmark is usually used via the D4RL offline-RL packaging (kitchen-complete / partial / mixed) and later Gymnasium-Robotics; the environment originates in this CoRL 2019 paper. RL fine-tuning results are reported in plots (not extracted).

name: RoboVerse
resolvedTitle: RoboVerse: Towards a Unified Platform, Dataset and Benchmark for Scalable and Generalizable Robot Learning
org: UC Berkeley, PKU, USC, UMich, UIUC, Stanford, CMU, UCLA, BIGAI
problem: Simulated datasets and benchmarks are fragmented across simulators with incompatible interfaces, making data/task reuse and reproducible cross-benchmark evaluation laborious.
keyIdea: MetaSim abstracts diverse simulators behind a simulator-agnostic config (MetaConfig) and a unified Handler API, enabling cross-simulator task/trajectory migration, hybrid simulation (one simulator's physics + another's renderer) and cross-embodiment retargeting; on top of it, a large unified synthetic dataset and IL/RL benchmarks with generalization levels.
architecture: Three-layer MetaSim: universal configuration system (agents, objects, task, sensors, physics), aligned simulator backends via a Handler class (launch/get_states/set_states/step), and a Gym-style env wrapper. Backends include Isaac Lab/Isaac Sim, Isaac Gym, MuJoCo, SAPIEN, Genesis, PyBullet, CoppeliaSim.
inputs: Tasks, assets and trajectories migrated from existing benchmarks, teleoperation, LLM-assisted task generation, real-to-sim reconstruction
outputs: Unified synthetic dataset + standardized IL/RL benchmarks
trainingData: ~500k unique trajectories, 276 task categories, ~5.5k assets; >50M state transitions (intro). Migrated sources include ManiSkill, RLBench, CALVIN, Meta-World, robosuite, MimicGen, GAPartNet, Open6DOR, ARNOLD, LIBERO, SIMPLER, GraspNet, GarmentLab, UniDoorManip, plus VLN-CE R2R/RxR, HumanoidBench, Humanoid-X.
whatChangedVsParent: Rather than another single-simulator benchmark, unifies existing benchmarks and simulators under one simulator-agnostic interface and dataset format.
limitations: Paper has a Limitations section (not retrieved); appendix shows tested simulators violate basic conservation laws (momentum, angular momentum, kinetic energy), cautioning against direct sim-to-real of complex behaviours.
notes: Code and dataset released (roboverseorg.github.io). Paper reports experiments on IL, RL, world-model learning, sim-to-real and sim-to-sim-to-real, but specific numeric results were not in retrieved pages. Scale figures differ inside the paper: Fig. 1 caption says '>1,000 tasks and >10 million transitions' while intro says ~500k trajectories/276 task categories/>50M transitions — cite with care.

name: TacSL
resolvedTitle: TacSL: A Library for Visuotactile Sensor Simulation and Learning
org: NVIDIA, University of Washington
problem: Visuotactile sensors (e.g., GelSight) are expensive to simulate (contact, deformation, illumination, imaging), so simulation could not be used for large-scale tactile policy learning or sim-to-real.
keyIdea: GPU-parallel visuotactile simulation inside Isaac Gym/Sim producing tactile RGB images and normal/shear force fields >200x faster than prior SOTA, plus a learning toolkit and a new RL algorithm, Asymmetric Actor-Critic Distillation (AACD), that reuses a pretrained privileged low-dim critic to train a tactile-image actor.
architecture: Tactile image: compliant-contact model + depth rendering + depth-to-RGB mapping; force field: penalty-based model using SDF queries of contacting object at tactile points, computed in parallel on GPU. Toolkit: two GelSight sensor models, three randomized assembly environments (e.g., peg insertion, nut-bolt), offline (BC) and online (DAgger) distillation, asymmetric actor-critic PPO, and AACD.
inputs: Tactile RGB images and/or tactile force fields, wrist camera images, proprioception (student); privileged state incl. object poses, contact forces (teacher/critic)
outputs: Robot actions for contact-rich assembly (peg insertion, nut-and-bolt)
actionRepr: Per-step RL/distilled policy actions (PPO-based); exact action parameterization not retrieved
trainingData: Simulated experience in Isaac Gym with domain randomization (soft-contact parameters) and tactile image augmentation

headlineResults.value: 1631 FPS with 512 parallel envs on RTX 3090
headlineResults.comparedTo: Taxim 7.28 FPS on one CPU core (>200x speedup)

whatChangedVsParent: Moves visuotactile image and force-field simulation onto the GPU inside a general-purpose simulator, handles arbitrary meshes (not just primitives), and adds AACD for high-dimensional tactile RL.
limitations: Rigid-body/penalty approximations of elastomer deformation rather than FEM; limitations section not retrieved.
notes: Paper states 'we plan to open-source' the module. Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real peg insertion on a Franka with GelSight; exact sim-to-real success numbers not retrieved. It is a simulator/toolkit rather than a benchmark in the strict sense.

name: ManiFeel
resolvedTitle: ManiFeel: Benchmarking and Understanding Visuotactile Manipulation Policy Learning
org: Purdue University
problem: Visuotactile imitation learning lacks a reproducible, large-scale simulation benchmark comparable to visual IL benchmarks, so most tactile results are one-off real-world studies without systematic comparison.
keyIdea: A simulation benchmark (IsaacGym, TacSL-style tactile sim) with contact-rich and visually degraded tasks and a modular pipeline varying sensing modality (vision, +TacRGB, +TacFF), tactile representation, and policy head, validated against real-world trends.
architecture: Multimodal observation encoder: per-modality encoders (ResNet18 for vision/tactile; equivariant ResNet18 for EquiDiff) over current+previous frames, concatenated with 7-D proprioception, feeding a policy head (Diffusion Policy, Equivariant Diffusion Policy, Flow Matching).
inputs: RGB camera(s), tactile RGB image (TacRGB) or tactile force field with normal + 2D shear (TacFF), EEF pose proprioception
outputs: Robot actions
actionRepr: Action sequences from diffusion / flow-matching policy heads (DP, EquiDiff, FM)
trainingData: Teleoperated human demonstrations; 13 task setups: 9 simulation (peg/USB/power-plug insertion, gear assembly, nut-bolt, bulb installation, occluded peg reorientation, occluded object search, dim-light ball sorting) + 4 real-world
whatChangedVsParent: Turns visuotactile IL from ad-hoc real-world demos into a controlled sim benchmark with systematic modality/representation/policy ablations.
limitations: Evaluates only pairwise vision+single-tactile-modality combos and no advanced fusion; representative subsets used for some studies; sim-real gap in absolute success due to limited tactile fidelity and unmodeled contact.
notes: Success rates averaged over 3 seeds x 50 inits x last 10 epochs (~1500 evals). Key finding: force fields help contact-rich insertion/screwing, tactile images help exploration/perception tasks. Codebase, datasets, checkpoints stated as open-sourced.

name: WorldArena
resolvedTitle: WorldArena: A Unified Benchmark for Evaluating Perception and Functional Utility of Embodied World Models
org: Tsinghua University (lead); HKU, Princeton, CAS, USTC, PKU, NUS
problem: Embodied world model evaluation focuses on perceptual video quality and ignores functional utility for downstream decision-making, and covers few robot-specialized models.
keyIdea: Evaluate embodied world models on (1) 16 video-quality metrics over 6 sub-dimensions, (2) three embodied functions — data engine, policy evaluator, action planner — and (3) human evaluation, and fold video metrics into a single EWMScore.
architecture: Benchmark on RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual data (50 scenarios). Data engine: fine-tuned WM + VPP-style IDM generates video-action pairs to train pi0.5; policy evaluator: pi0.5 policies roll out in action-conditioned WM, VLM judges success, correlated vs RoboTwin sim; action planner: WM+IDM actions executed in RoboTwin.
inputs: Initial frame + instruction (or actions) to world model
outputs: Scores: EWMScore, task-utility metrics, human ratings
trainingData: RoboTwin 2.0 dataset; 70 annotators rated 3500 videos

headlineResults.comparedTo: r=0.600 vs data-engine performance; r=0.360 vs action-planner performance

whatChangedVsParent: Adds functional embodied-task evaluation (data engine, policy evaluator, action planner) alongside perceptual metrics, over 14 models including robot-specific WMs.
limitations: Single scenario family (bimanual RoboTwin); authors note current WMs still far from reliable closed-loop control; future work to add more models.
notes: Public leaderboard at worldarena.ai. 14 models evaluated incl. Veo 3.1, Wan 2.2/2.6, Cosmos-Predict 2.5, CtrlWorld, WoW, GigaWorld-0, Vidar, TesserAct, IRASim, RoboMaster, Genie Envisioner, CogVideoX. Key message: perception-functionality gap. Human eval: CtrlWorld best physical adherence among embodied WMs; CtrlWorld correlates strongly with sim in policy evaluation, Cosmos-Predict 2.5 weakly.

name: WoW-World-Eval
resolvedTitle: Wow, wo, val! A Comprehensive Embodied World Model Evaluation Turing Test
org: Peking University; Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics; HKUST
problem: Video-generation benchmarks target general settings or isolated dimensions; standard video-quality scores correlate poorly with human judgment in embodied settings and ignore planning and executability.
keyIdea: An image+text-to-video benchmark over 609 curated robot manipulation samples scoring five abilities (perception, planning, prediction, generalization, execution) with 22 metrics, plus two Turing tests: a human real-vs-generated 2AFC test and an Inverse Dynamics Model (GC-IDM) test that executes generated videos on a real robot.
architecture: Metrics grouped into Video Quality, Instruction Understanding, Planning Reasoning, Physical Law, Execution Accuracy; GPT + human data cleaning; GC-IDM (from WoW) converts generated video to gripper-centric actions for real-robot replay on 9 tasks.
inputs: Initial image + text instruction
outputs: Generated video scored by metrics; IDM-derived real-robot success
trainingData: 609 robot manipulation samples (public + in-house), human-annotated

headlineResults.metric: Pearson r (overall score vs human eval)

whatChangedVsParent: Adds planning and real-robot execution (IDM Turing Test) dimensions that prior WM benchmarks lacked.
limitations: Human Turing test used 13 participants; IDM test restricted to 9 in-house tasks; authors from the WoW team, whose models score best (potential bias).
notes: Same group as the WoW world model — note possible home-advantage. Deceive-human ratio correlates with overall score r=0.679.

name: RoboWM-Bench
resolvedTitle: RoboWM-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating World Models in Robotic Manipulation
org: Peking University; Tsinghua University; Lightwheel
problem: Existing world-model benchmarks measure visual quality and physical plausibility but not whether predicted behaviours can be turned into executable actions that complete manipulation tasks; real-robot validation is costly and unscalable.
keyIdea: Convert generated human-hand videos (HaMeR pose tracking + retargeting, Phantom-style) and robot videos (inverse dynamics model) into actions and execute them in real-to-sim reconstructed scenes (LeHome engine, 4D Gaussian backgrounds), scoring step-level checkpoints and task success.
architecture: Real-to-sim pipeline (Gaussian background, SAM-3D object reconstruction, pose estimation, camera calibration); IDM taking two consecutive frames -> joint-space action chunk, pretrained on masked sim Franka data then fine-tuned on real trajectories.
inputs: Initial image + task description to video world model
outputs: Step-level and task-level execution success
actionRepr: Extracted EEF poses + gripper opening (human retargeting) or joint-space action chunks (IDM)
trainingData: IDM: large-scale sim Franka trajectories + 50 real trajectories per task

headlineResults.value: Wan 2.6 strongest overall (e.g., 83% Pick Object, 40% Fold Towel)
100% success and failure consistency (10+10 trajectories per task, 7 tasks)

whatChangedVsParent: Execution-grounded evaluation in reproducible real-to-sim simulation rather than real robots or perceptual scores; covers both human-hand and robot videos.
limitations: Execution success depends on video-to-action extraction; depth not available for generated frames; contact-sensitive/boundary grasps remain failure modes; deformable and long-horizon tasks near-zero for most models.
notes: Near-saturated PAI-Bench domain scores vs discriminative RoboWM-Bench scores — perceptual plausibility ≠ executability. Released code includes evaluation scripts.

name: Dream.exe
resolvedTitle: Dream.exe: Can Video Generation Models Dream Executable Robot Manipulation?
org: Show Lab, National University of Singapore; University of Oxford; Tencent
